kontext:
11.2 Definitions

As regulations and safety specific literature are written in English language originally, exact translations into the particular country’s official language is at times difficult. Hence, it is likely to be confusing, how a specific “happening” or “identified safety related situation” has to be handled. Therefore, before the detailed instructions, it is important to explain the terminology used.
Accident An occurrence associated with the operation of an airplane which takes place between the time any person boards the airplane with the intention of flight until such time as all such persons have disembarked, in which:
1. A person is fatally or seriously injured (see term below) as a result of: being in contact with the airplane, or

direct contact with any part of the airplane, including parts which have become detached from the airplane, or

direct exposure to jet blast;

Except when the injuries are from natural causes, self-inflicted or inflicted by other persons or when the injuries are to stowaways hiding outside the areas normally available to the passengers and crew; or

2. The airplane sustains damage or structural failure which: adversely affects the structural strength, performance or flight characteristics of the airplane, and

would normally require major repair or replacement of the

affected component, except for engine failure or damage,

when the damage is limited to the engine, its cowlings or

accessories; or for damage limited to propellers, wingtips, antennas, tires, brakes, fairings, small dents or holes in the

airplane skin; or

3. The airplane is missing or is completely inaccessible

Serious An incident involving circumstances indicating that an accident nearly Incident occurred. The following items are typical examples of incidents that are likely to be serious incidents: near collisions requiring an avoidance maneuver to avoid a collision or an unsafe situation or when an avoidance action would have been appropriate

controlled flight into terrain only marginally avoided

aborted take-off on a closed or engaged runway

take-off from a closed or engaged runway with marginal separation from obstacles

landings or attempted landings on a closed or engaged runway

gross failures to achieve predicted performance during take-off or initial climb

fires and smoke in the passenger compartment, in cargo compartments or engine fires, even though such fires were extinguished by the use of

extinguishing agents

events requiring the emergency use of oxygen by the flight crew

aircraft structural failures or engine disintegration not classified as an accident

multiple malfunctions of one or more airplane systems seriously

affecting the operation of the airplane

flight crew incapacitation in flight

fuel quantity requiring the declaration of an emergency by the flight crew

take-off or landing incidents. Incidents such as undershooting,

overrunning or running off the side of runways

system failures, weather phenomena, operations outside the approved flight envelope or other occurrences, which could have

caused difficulties controlling the aircraft

failures of more than one system in a redundancy system

mandatory for flight guidance and navigation Note: The difference between an accident and a serious incident lies only in the result.

Incident An occurrence, other than an accident, associated with the operation of an aircraft, which affects or could affect the safety of operation.

Serious An injury which is sustained by a person in an accident and which:
Injury
requires hospitalization for more than 48 hours, commencing within seven days from the date the injury was received, or

results in a fracture of any bone (except simple fractures of fingers, toes or nose), or

involves lacerations which cause severe hemorrhage, nerve, muscle or tendon damage, or

involves injury to any internal organ, or

involves second or third degree burns or any burns affecting more than 5% of the body surface, or

involves verified exposure to infections substances or injurious radiation.

An Injury is classified as fatal if death results from the injury within thirty (30) days from the date of the accident.

CERM Handling of severe irregularities/ accidents has been covered in the helvetic document “Crisis and Emergency Response Manual”
(CERM).

The CERM is a guideline for the approach the Crisis and

Emergency Response Team (CERT) takes when addressing an emergency or catastrophic situation present in helvetic.

Occurrence Any safety-related event which endangers or which, if not

corrected or addressed, could endanger an aircraft, its occupants or any other person and includes in particular an accident or

serious incident.

Just ‘just culture’ according Regulation (EU) No 376/2014 means a Culture culture in which front-line operators or other persons are not

punished for actions, omissions or decisions taken by them that are commensurate with their experience and training, but in which

gross negligence, willful violations and destructive acts are not tolerated.

Hazard Condition or object with the potential to cause injury to personnel

damage to equipment or structures

loss of material

reduction of ability to perform a prescribed function.

kontext:
11.5.1 Just Culture Principle

In order to encourage employees to report, safety-relevant reports are treated according to the ‘just culture’ principles. Just culture means that employees and contracted personnel who report or are mentioned in any occurrence report will not be subject to any prejudice or disciplinary action by helvetic or by the organization for which the services are provided on the basis of the information supplied by the reporter.

The protection does not apply to any of the following situations or operational behaviors:

1. in cases of willful misconduct;

2. where there has been a manifest, severe and serious disregard of an obvious risk and profound failure of professional responsibility to take such care as is evidently required in the circumstances, causing foreseeable damage to a person or property, or which seriously compromises the level of aviation safety.

For further reading, refer also to OMM 7.1 Just Culture
fragen.frage_en: In which case does Just Culture protection not apply to reporting employees?
antworten_en: If the report is made later than 24 hours
In case of willful misconduct
If the error leads to a mandatory occurrence report
If the report is made anonymously
fragen.erklaerung_en: Excluded are willful misconduct and manifest, serious disregard of an obvious risk.

kontext:
11.9.4.1 Flight and Cockpit Voice Recorder Systems

Flight recorders on the helvetic Embraer fleet are digital recording units (DVDR) combining three different functionalities. Recording of: audio information from cockpit area microphones and primary crew microphones [cockpit voice recorder (CVR)]. datalink messages [data link recorder (DLR)] all available flight data [flight data recorder (FDR)] CVRs have at least 2 hours of voice recording capacity and must only be de- activated to protect records in due time.
FDRs have a flight time recording capacity which allows read out or de-activation in due time after an occurrence. De-activation during flight or on ground by the flight crew is not allowed.
Note: If a flight is conducted with a deactivated CVR check with MCC for MEL Regulation(s).

The DVDR automatically starts recording audio information as soon as the

aircraft is powered up. Flight data recording begins when the first engine is started.
After power down the DVDRcontinue recording audio information for 10 minutes.

In the event the airplane becomes involved in an accident or serious incident, the

Commander must ensure the protection of all related flight records, and if

necessary, the associated DVDR to the extent possible. This can include the

retention of the DVDR in safe custody until its disposition.

The removal of the flight recorder systems from the aircraft will be determined by

the investigating authority in the state conducting the investigation with due regard to the seriousness of the occurrence.
fragen.frage_en: What applies to the flight recorders (DVDR) of the helvetic Embraer fleet?
antworten_en: The CVR has a recording capacity of at least 2 hours; after power down the DVDR still records 10 minutes of audio

Flight data recording begins at aircraft power up
The flight crew may deactivate the FDR on the ground after each flight
fragen.erklaerung_en: CVRs have a capacity of at least 2 h; FDR recording starts with the first engine, audio continues for 10 min after power down.

kontext:
1.4.1 Authority, Duties and Responsibilities of the Commander (CMD)

The Commander (CMD) exercises the final authority over the safe operation of the helvetic aircraft he is assigned to fly.
He is responsible, as soon as he arrives on board until he leaves the airplane at the end of the flight, for: the safety of all crew members, passengers and cargo

He is responsible to adapt the operationally applicable elements of the SSCC defined in OMM 1.1 to the given situation and implement them in a mission- focussed manner.
He is responsible, from the moment the airplane is first ready to move for the purpose of taxiing prior to take-off until the moment it finally comes to rest at the end of the flight and the engines used as primary propulsion units are shut down, for: the operation and safety of the airplane

All persons on board the aircraft shall obey all lawful directions given by the Commander (CMD). The Commander (CMD) exercises command over all crew members:

from check-in until check-out for a flight or series of flights The Commander (CMD) has the final responsibility regarding

flight initiation according to 8.1.10 - Operational Flight Plan

continuation, termination or diversion of a flight according to 8.3.2.24 -

Meteorological Information.

OM-A Responsibilities

He exercises full command over all other persons on board of a helvetic aircraft: from the time the doors are closed for the initiation of a flight until the doors are opened after the completion of a flight

While exercising his authority the Commander (CMD) has the right to: give all commands he deems necessary for the purpose of ensuring the safety of the aircraft and of persons or property carried therein

to disembark any person or any part of the cargo, which, in his opinion, may represent a potential hazard to the safety of the aircraft or its occupants

From the moment he comes on board until he leaves the aircraft at the end of the flight

kontext:
1.4.2.2 Duties and Responsibilities of Senior Cabin Attendants (SEN)

The Senior Cabin Attendant (SEN) is directly responsible to the Commander (CMD) of the flight for the cabin safety.

The authorities of a Senior Cabin Attendant (SEN) are: to issue legal and mandatory instructions towards the Cabin Attendants (CAB)

to request access to the Aircraft Cabin Log (ACL)
to reject an aircraft regarding unsatisfactory technical cabin issues

to request a debriefing within the whole crew or with an individual crew member of the operational crew

to request a staff appraisal

The responsibilities are: to direct, coordinate and organize the functions and tasks of the cabin crew and, at the prescribed times, report “cabin and galley secure” or “cabin and galley not secure”

to be responsible to the Commander (CMD) for the conduct and

coordination of cabin safety procedures and for their observance by the cabin crew and by all passengers information of the flight crew about all irregularities and malfunctions observed by cabin crew members or passengers

to contact the flight crew for instructions when deemed necessary

to ensure that he applies all operational procedures and checklists in accordance with the Operations Manual (OM) and the Cabin Safety

Procedures Manual (CSPM)

completion of all cabin related documents

to function as the communication link between flight and cabin crew and,

when necessary, the passengers

checking of the catering and the relevant equipment

to direct – when necessary – cabin emergency procedures and an

emergency evacuation

OM-A Responsibilities

discontinue non-safety related duties during turbulence in absence of any instruction from the flight crew, advise the flight crew of the level of turbulence and the need for the fasten seat belt signs to be switched on.
This should be followed by the cabin crew securing the passenger cabin and other applicable areas

check the distribution tool at least once a week or before flight duty after a longer period away; read and acknowledge the relevant contents

not to operate as crew member on an airplane unless he is qualified for duty in accordance with 5.3 - Cabin Crew.

check e-mail at least once a week and before flight or training duties, whichever results in more current information

to conduct familiarisation flights for Senior Cabin Attendants (SEN) and Cabin Attendants (CAB), if training according to OM-D 2.5.2 is completed

in case of suspension or revocation of the personal cabin crew attestation by the competent authority, that the cabin crew attestation must be returned to the respective superior and the HCC has to be informed without delay

He is responsible to adapt the operationally applicable elements of the SSCC defined in OMM 1.1 to the given situation and implement them in a mission- focussed manner.

Notwithstanding the overriding authority of the Commander (CMD) it is of utmost importance that the Senior Cabin Attendant (SEN), at any time, draws the attention of the Commander (CMD) to facts, circumstances or unfavourable variables which may impair cabin safety and which may not yet have been

noticed by the Commander (CMD).

4.2.1 Flights with Two Pilots Qualified as Commander

If more than one flight crew member of the same crew holds the qualification for Commander (CMD) only one pilot is designated as Commander (CMD) of the flight.
The command of the flight is assigned on the flight assignment.
During any flight, other than:

training flights, or line flying under supervision, or

check flights and non-revenue flights

the CMD of the aircraft occupies the left hand seat on the flight deck.

OM-A 4 Crew Composition

This means that
the CMD holding the qualification to operate in either pilot’s seat will act as Copilot (COP) on the right hand seat despite of the fact that he might be more experienced

than the pilot on the left hand seat.

During: training flights

check flights

line flying under supervision

where the responsible instructor has access to the controls, the Type Rating Instructor (TRI) or the Line Training Commander (LTC) is always designated as the Commander (CMD) of the flight. He then may have to occupy the right hand seat in the flight deck.

During: line flying under supervision

Line Orientated Evaluation of Competence (LOE)

where the Type Rating Instructor (TRI) or the Line Training Commander (LTC) occupies the flight deck jump seat, he can not act as Commander (CMD) of the flight, since he has no access to the flight controls.

When more than one flight crew member of the same crew holds the qualification for Commander (CMD) it is of the utmost importance to properly and clearly brief all other crew members about the actual chain of command. Any change in command during a flight shall be announced to all crew members in a clear

manner.

OM-A 4 Crew Composition

The more experienced of the two pilots, who is then also CMD
The pilot qualified for both seats, as he may not fly as COP on the right
Seat allocation is free and agreed in the briefing

4.1.3.1 Crewing of inexperienced Crew Members

A crew member is considered inexperienced immediately following the completion of its type rating, command or conversion course and the associated line flying under supervision.

The Operations Control (OCC) receives this list from crew planning and is responsible for correct pairing.

If the introduction of a new aircraft type necessitates a lesser number of sectors or hours the intended schedule must be agreed upon with the Swiss FOCA.
The responsibility lies with the Accountable Manager (ACM).
In this case special attention shall be given to the minimum amount of sectors or hours for Line Training Commanders (LTC) on new aircraft type.

kontext:
4.1.11 Supernumeraries

A person in addition to the crew that is not a crew member, but is on board during commercial or non-commercial operations and is not classified as a passenger by the operator or the authority.

Such person is typically any of the following: an inspector, auditor or observer authorized by helvetic and the State to be on board the aircraft in the performance of his or her duties (e.g. CAA flight operations inspector, IOSA auditor, IOSA observer)

assigned to a passenger flight by helvetic to conduct certain customer service activities (e.g. serving beverages, conducting customer relations, selling tickets) in the cabin; not designated to perform any safety duties

any other individual that has a relationship with helvetic, is not classified as a passenger by the authority and authorised by helvetic and the State to be on board the aircraft (e.g. courier, contract coordinator, individual with operator required knowledge and abilities travelling to/from a duty assignment, company employee or dependent)
Non-operating crew members, company employees and employee dependents occupying passenger seats on passenger flights are considered as passengers.

Supernumeraries are not part of the minimum crew complement as stated under

4.1.9 - Minimum Crew Complement. They shall not wear a uniform which may identify them to passengers as a qualified crew member, shall not occupy required cabin crew assigned stations and do not impede the cabin crew members in their duties.

A supernumerary shall be assigned a designated seat, which may be either a

jump seat or a passenger seat.

OM-A 4 Crew Composition

kontext:
5.2.2 Recent Experience for Commanders

A pilot must not operate an aircraft as Commander (CMD) unless he has carried out, within the preceding 90 days, at least three take-offs and three landings as Pilot Flying (PF) in an aircraft or an approved flight simulator of the type to be used. The flight simulator must be acceptable to the National Aviation Authority (NAA) and qualified to level CG, C or D.
The period of 90 days may be extended up to a maximum of 120 days by line flying under the supervision of a Type Rating Instructor (TRI).
When the above-mentioned period is expired,
a flight training including at least three take-offs and landings as Pilot Flying (PF) of an aircraft not carrying passengers or cargo or an equivalent simulator training must be accomplished.

The aircraft or flight simulator must be of the relevant type.
The responsibility for compliance with these requirements lies with the respective pilot. He must log the relevant data in a pilot’s logbook. For back-up, dispatch maintains an overview of each flight crew member’s recency.
In addition to the recent experience mentioned above, the following rules shall be applied:
If a Commander (CMD) is absent for more than 4 months, but still within the validity of the checks required according to OM-D 2.1.6, a Requalification Training (RQT) is required.
For the Requalification training refer to OM-D 2.1.9

kontext:
5.4.1.2 Line Training Commander (LTC)

Within helvetic, the term “Line Training Commander (LTC)” has the same meaning as “Line Evaluator” within the EBT framework.

LIFUS and Line Orientated Evaluations of competence (LOE) are performed during conversion training and Command Training requiring Line Training Commanders (LTC). Line Evaluators are required during recurrent training or checking within the EBT framework.

Thus, helvetic uses the single term “LTC” for both roles.

In order to qualify for initial Line Training Commander (LTC) training the applicant must meet the following minimum requirements: valid type rating as commander on the type of aircraft used for instruction or evaluation

valid line evaluation
line experience within helvetic of at least 12 months and 500 hours on type

in multi-pilot operations and according to 4.1.3.1.1 - Flight Crew Members

enrolled in helvetic’s EBT program as a flight crew member while being graded as “competent” during at least: two recurrent simulator training

one LOE evidence of excellent knowledge of helvetic’s operating procedures (e.g. operational and training documentation, use of checklists, level of technical knowledge as per OM-B)

human factors (evidence of necessary soft skills)

Previous experience with instructional duties within or beyond aviation is

desirable, e.g. as: ground instructor

flight instructor (e.g. CRI, IRI, FI, TRI)

managerial training staff with experience in a feedback process for the monitoring of line operations (e.g. EBT LOE, LOSA)

fragen.zitat: No alcoholic beverages shall be consumed for a period of at least 24 hours after vaccination.
kontext:
6.1.2 Immunization

In accordance with the World Health Organization’s (WHO) International Health Regulations many countries prescribe vaccination of crew members and passengers against defined diseases, often specifying that such immunization is only required upon entry “after leaving or transiting infected areas”.
Each crew member scheduled for flight duty abroad must satisfy any requirement for vaccination, to have himself vaccinated in time, and to be able to produce – during his tour of duty – the appropriate WHO-approved “Certificate of Vaccination or Revaccination”.
Vaccination and Revaccination shall take place not less than 24 hours before commencement of flight duty, unless otherwise stated. In case of strong reaction medical advice shall be obtained in view of a possible impairment of fitness for flight duty.
No alcoholic beverages shall be consumed for a period of at least 24 hours after vaccination.

Vaccinations which may be obligatory and their validity:
Yellow fever (from 10 days after, for lifetime)

Vaccinations which are recommended and their validity:
Cholera (from 7 days until 6 months after vaccination)

Typhoid (from 7 days until 3 years after vaccination)

Poliomyelitis (after 3 vaccinations up to 10 years) Tetanus (after 3 vaccinations up to 10 years)

COVID-19(1) (from 1 to 2 weeks after the vaccination)

Note 1: Crew members must not be engaged in any safety relevant duty (e.g. flight duty) for a period of 48 hours after each dose of COVID-

19 vaccine. In case side effects persist for more than 48 hours following the vaccination, crew members shall consult their AME.

The waiting period shall be extended until the time when the side

effects completely disappear.

OM-A 6 Health Precautions

Malaria prophylaxis, though not immunization in the strict sense of the word, should be mentioned here; crew members scheduled for flight duty to malaria infected countries shall obtain, on the advice of their flight medical doctor, the appropriate medication and apply it as prescribed.
Note: Crew members shall be aware of the fact that there are many extremely dangerous diseases against which vaccination is not possible.

Only general rules may be given here for health-conscious behavior in foreign countries: observe strict hygiene in eating drinking (amoebic dysentery, brucellosis),

do not bathe in stagnant water (bilharziasis),

in infested (e.g., bush/jungle) areas, wear long sleeved shirts and long trousers to prevent or minimize bites by disease-carrying insects (filariasis, malaria, encephalitis, sleeping sickness) or by outright poisonous insects or animals (spiders, scorpions, snakes); use insect-repellant.

OM-A 6 Health Precautions

kontext:
6.2.3 Alcohol and Intoxicating Liquids

A crew member and operations personnel other than crew members shall not: consume alcohol less than 8 hours prior to the specified reporting time for any duty within operations (e.g. flight duty, training or the commencement of standby duty)

commence any duty within operations (e.g. flight duty period) with a blood alcohol level in excess of (the lowest is applicable): 0.2 %o or 0,1 mg alcohol per litre respiratory air or the national statutory limits (zero alcohol)

consume alcohol during any duty within operations (e.g. flight duty, training or the commencement of standby duty)

Since the metabolism of alcohol in the blood is very slow, it is highly recommended that crew members refrain from the consumption of alcohol 16 hours before the expected commencement of flight duty, training or reserve duty (standby).
As a matter of helvetic company policy, employees in uniform (e.g. crew members after termination of flight duty, deadheading crew members) shall not consume any alcoholic beverages.

The misuse of any intoxicating liquids is strictly prohibited for crew members and

operations personnel other than crew members.

The rule applies only in public at the airport

6.2.2 Prevention of Misuse of Psychoactive Substances

Indications of psychoactive substance abuse can be very wide-ranging.

increased energy and confidence

kontext:
7.1.7 Maximum Daily Flight Duty Period (FDP)

Any duty, including training and office duties, performed prior to a flight or prior to a series of flights (except standby – refer to 7.1.10 - Standby, Reserve and Duties at the Airport) shall count as Flight Duty Period (FDP). helvetic plans all crew members to report 60 minutes before scheduled time of departure of the first flight. For line introduction and Line Orientated Evaluation of Competence (LOE) for flight crew and familiarization flights or line check for cabin crew, a reporting time of 75 minutes shall be planned.
Travel longer than 3 hours shall count fully as Flight Duty Period (FDP) if followed by a subsequent flight duty period.

For the maximum flight duty period for flight training refer to OM-D 3.4.8.

OM-A 7 Flight Time Limitations

kontext:
7.2.4 Delayed Reporting or Short-notice Flight Cancellation

In the event of unforeseen circumstances a delayed reporting procedure may be applied if the time until the scheduled reporting time is more than one hour at home base or more than 30 minutes away from home base and the crew member can remain at his suitable accommodation.
In such a case, if the crew member is informed by phone (or by SMS in case of possible interference with sleeping patterns) about the delayed reporting time, the maximum Flight Duty Period (FDP) is calculated as follows:
One notification of a delay leads to the calculation of the maximum FDP according to
when the delay is less than 4 hours, the maximum FDP is calculated based on the original reporting time and the FDP starts counting at the delayed reporting time

when the delay is 4 hours or more, the maximum FDP is calculated based on the more limiting of the original or the delayed reporting time and the FDP starts counting at the delayed reporting time

If the reporting time is further amended, the FDP starts counting 1 hour after the second notification or at the original delayed reporting time if this is earlier As an exception, when the operator informs the crew member of a delay of 10 hours or more in reporting time and the crew member is not further disturbed by the operator, such delay of 10 hours or more counts as a rest

period.
Any delay which is communicated to the crew member 10 hours or more before the delayed reporting time does not count as delayed reporting and no additional regulations apply.

In the event when the first flight segment(s) has to be removed (but the following ones remain) or changed to another flight segment(s), and this change is done

less than one hour ahead of original reporting time, a ground duty is added in the

duration of 5min starting at the original reporting time.

If due to an unforeseen circumstance flight must be cancelled after the reporting time for duty, ground duty is added which starts at the original reporting time, and

finishes either at the time when decision for cancellation was made (if crew was

not yet at the aircraft) or 30min after the decision was made (if crew performed any flight duty prior to the affected one).

antworten_en: Based on the delayed reporting time; the FDP starts at the original reporting time
Based on the more restrictive of the two reporting times
The delay counts as rest period, the FDP is recalculated
Based on the original reporting time; the FDP starts at the delayed reporting time
fragen.erklaerung_en: For a delay of less than 4 hours, the original reporting time applies for the max. FDP, while counting starts from the delayed one.

This applies only if the crew member does not rest at his residence, or temporary accommodation.

fragen.frage: Der CMD hat eine FTL-Limite per Commander's Discretion um mehr als eine Stunde überschritten. Bis wann muss helvetic der Behörde eine Kopie des Reports senden?

kontext:
7.2.1 Modification of the Limits on Flight Duty, Duty or Rest Periods

During actual flight operation, which starts after the whole crew has reported for any duty, the Commander (CMD) shall have the possibility to modify the limits on flight duty, duty and rest periods in the event of conditions described as unforeseen circumstances.
The exercise of commander’s discretion shall be considered exceptional and shall be avoided at home base when standby or reserve crew members are available.
The conditions shall comply with the following: the maximum daily FDP which results after applying 7.1.7 - Maximum Daily Flight Duty Periode (FDP) or 7.1.9 - Split Duty may not be increased by more than 2 hours.

the maximum basic daily FDP that results after applying 7.1.7.1 - Maximum Daily FDP for Acclimatised Crew Members shall be used to calculate the limits of commander’s discretion, if commander’s discretion is applied to an FDP which has been extended under the provisions of 7.1.7.3 - Maximum Daily FDP for Acclimatised Crew Members with the Use of Extensions without In-flight Rest

if on the final sector within a FDP the allowed increase is exceeded because of unforeseen circumstances after take-off, the flight may continue to the planned destination or alternate aerodrome the rest period following the FDP may be reduced but can never be less

than 10 hours

The commander shall consult all crew members on their alertness levels before deciding the modifications.
Additionally, he shall take due consideration of additional factors that might decrease a crew member’s alertness levels, such as:
WOCL encroachment

weather conditions

complexity of the operation and/or airport environment

airplane malfunctions or specifications

flight with training or supervisory duties

increased number of sectors

circadian disruption

individual conditions of affected crew members (time since awake, sleep- related factor, workload, etc.)

7.2.2 Duties in case of Modification of the Limits on Flight Duty, Duty or Rest Periods

helvetic will assess on a regular basis the series of pairings where commander’s

discretion has been exercised in order to be aware of possible inconsistencies in their rostering. The FRMS meeting monitors the amount of FTL modifications and other FTL exceedances via the BI tool according to 2.4.5.1.8 - FRMS Meeting.

The Commander (CMD) shall submit an IT report to helvetic flight operations

management whenever a limit on flight duty, duty or rest period has been

modified by his discretion or whenever a limitation as stated within this chapter has been violated in excess of one hour. This report shall be handled according

to OMM 7 Reporting Scheme.

Whenever the above-mentioned modification or a reported violation is beyond one hour, helvetic shall send a copy of the report to the competent authority not
later than 28 days after the event.
The RPO will monitor FTL exceedances and request reports from the commander, whenever a report is missing.

fragen.erklaerung_en: OM-A 7.2.2: If the modification exceeds one hour, helvetic sends a copy to the authority at the latest 28 days after the event.

kontext:
9.4.6.1 Portable Electronic Devices (PED) Containing Batteries

These Portable Electronic Devices (PED), which may include medical devices such as Portable Oxygen Concentrators (POC) and consumer electronics such as cameras, mobile phones, laptops and tablets containing batteries when carried by passengers or crew for personal use, should be carried in carry-on baggage.
These provisions apply to dry batteries, nickel-metal hydride batteries, lithium batteries and wet non-spillable batteries.
If devices are carried in checked baggage passenger must pack it so to protect the device from damage and to prevent unintentional activation, and device must be fully switched off (not in sleep or hibernation mode).
Spare batteries must be individually protected to prevent short circuits by placement in the original retails packaging or by otherwise insulating terminals, e.g. by taping over exposed terminals or placing each battery in a separate plastic bag or protective pouch and carried in carry-on baggage only.
Each person is limited to a maximum of 20 spare batteries, unless helvetic GOP would approve individual requests for carriage of more spare batteries.

Lithium batteries are subject to following conditions: each installed or spare battery must not exceed: for lithium metal or lithium alloy batteries, a lithium content of not more than 2 g or for lithium ion batteries, a watt-hour rating of not more that 100 Wh

batteries must be of type that meets the requirements of the UN Manual of Tests and Criteria, Part III, subsection 38.3

each person is limited to a maximum of 15 PED, unless helvetic GOP would

approve individual requests for carriage of more than 15 PED

articles containing lithium metal or lithium ion cells or batteries, the primary

purpose of which is to provide power to another device, e.g. power banks,

are permitted in carry-on baggage only, and must be individually protected to prevent short circuits by placement in the original retails packaging or by

otherwise insulating terminals, e.g. by taping over exposed terminals or placing each battery in a separate plastic bag or protective pouch

electronic cigarettes, e-cigars and other personal vaporizers containing

lithium batteries are permitted in carry-on baggage only, recharging of these devices or batteries on board the aircraft is not permitted, and measures

must be taken to prevent accidental activation

electronic cigarette lighters powered by lithium batteries must meet following

conditions: only lighters with a safety cap or means of protection against unintentional activation are permitted on one’s person recharging of these devices or batteries on board is not permitted, and measures must be taken to prevent accidental activation

baggage equipped with a lithium battery, other than lithium button cells: if the baggage is to be checked in, the lithium battery must be removed from the baggage and carried in the cabin or the baggage must be carried in the cabin baggage where the lithium battery is designed to charge other devices and cannot be removed is forbidden for carriage

Additional requirements for non-spillable wet batteries: each person is limited to a maximum of 2 spare batteries in carry-on baggage only, subject to following conditions: batteries must meet the requirements of Special Provision A67 (see IATA DGR 4) and must not contain any free or unabsorbed liquid the strength of each battery must not exceed 12 V or 100 Wh each spare battery must be protected from short circuit by insulation of battery terminals
fragen.frage_en: How many spare batteries for PED may a person carry at most without special GOP approval?
fragen.erklaerung_en: OM-A 9.4.6.1: maximum 20 spare batteries and 15 PED per person, unless GOP approves otherwise.

9.4.6 Dangerous Goods in Checked and Carry-on Baggage

medical oxygen gaseous oxygen or air cylinders required for medical use. Each cylinder must not exceed 5kg gross weight. Cylinders, valves and regulators, where fitted, must be protected from damage that could cause inadvertent release of contents. This applies alos for medically trained persons.

carbon dioxide, solid (dry ice) in quantities not exceeding 2.5 kg per person when used to pack perishables not subject to the Dangerous Goods Regulations, provided the package permits the release of carbon dioxide gas. Each item of checked baggage must be marked "dry ice" or "carbon dioxide, solid" and with the net weight of dry ice or an indication that there is 2.5 kg or less dry ice

avalanche rescue backpack one per passenger, containing a cartridge of compressed gas in division 2.2, may be equipped with a pyrotechnic trigger mechanism containing not more than 200 mg net of Division 1.4S. The backpack must be packed in such a manner that it cannot be accidentally activated. The airbags within the backpack must be fitted with pressure relief valves

small non-flammable gas cartridges fitted into a self-inflating safety device such as life jacket or vest:
(a) no more than two personal safety devices per person
(b) device must be packed in such a manner that it cannot be accidentally

activated

(c) limited to carbon dioxide or other suitable gas in Division 2.2 without a

subsidiary risk

(d) cartridge(s) must be for inflation purposes

(e) the device must be fitted with no more than two small cartridges

(f) not more than two spare cartridges

Not more than four small cylinders of carbon dioxide or other suitable gas in

Division 2.2 without a subsidiary risk, per person for other devices.
The water capacity of each cylinder must not exceed 50mL.

chemical agent monitoring equipment instruments containing radioactive material not exceeding the activity limits specified in Table 10.3D (IATA DGR), e.g. Chemical Agent Monitor (CAM) or Rapid Alarm and Identification Device Monitor (RAID-M), securely packed and without lithium batteries, when carried by staff members of the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW) on official travel

lithium battery-powered electronic devices
(a) portable medical electronic devices (PMED), such as Automated External Defibrillators (AED), Nebulizer, Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP) containing lithium metal or lithium ion cells or batteries may be carried by passengers for medical use providing lithium content does not exceed 8g for lithium metal batteries, or watt-hour rating does not exceed 160 Wh for lithium metal batteries

(b) portable electronic devices, such as power tools, video cameras and laptops containing lithium batteries may be carried providing watt-hour rating does not exceed 160 Wh

In both cases batteries must be of type that meets the requirements of the UN Manual of Test and Criteria, Part III, subsection 38.3.
Devices in checked baggage must be completely switched off and must be protected from damage. baggage with installed lithium batteries

non removable batteries: batteries must not contain more than 0.3 g lithium metal or for lithium ion must not exceed 2.7 Wh removable batteries: batteries must be removed if baggage is to be

checked in, removable batteries must be carried in the cabin

fragen.frage: Ein PED in der Kabine brennt. Was gilt gemäss Checklist für Dangerous Goods Incidents in the Passenger Cabin?

kontext:
9.6.3 Checklist for Dangerous Goods Incidents in the Passenger Cabin

During Flight

notify the Commander (CMD)

identify the item – if not possible to identify the item right away (source of fire), apply the next step first and then attempt to identify it

in case of fire: use standard procedures/check use of water

in case of fire or smoke involving a portable electronic device (PED): use standard procedure obtain and use appropriate fire extinguisher

retrieve and use protective equipment, as applicable to the situation

remove external electrical power from device (if applicable)
– attenention do not attempt to remove the battery from the device
douse device with water (or other non-flammable liquid) to cool cells and prevent ignition of adjacent cells

do not move device and monitor for any reigniting

when the device has cooled, place it in a suitable container filled with enough water (or non-flammable liquid) to submerge the device, and stow the container to prevent spillage

in case of overheated battery electrical smell involving PED: instruct the passenger to turn off the device immediately

remove external electrical power from device, turn off in seat power (if applicable)
– attention, do not attempt to remove the battery from the device

instruct the passenger to keep the device visible and monitor closely

consider as a precautionary measure to put the PED into a LIPO bag and to stow the closed bag into a non-flammable container (e.g. waste bin- or galley-container)

remove power to remaining electrical outlets until the aircraft’s system can be determined to be free of faults, if the device was previously plugged in

in case of spillage or leakage: collect emergency response kit or other useful items

put on rubber gloves and smoke hood or smoke mask – portable oxygen

move passengers away from area and distribute wet towels or cloths

place DG item in polyethylene bags

stow polyethylene bags treat affected seat cushions or covers in the same manner as DG item

cover spillage on carpet and floor

regularly inspect items stowed away and contaminated furnishings

kontext:
9.7.2 Reporting

The Dangerous Goods (DG) occurrence report shall be submitted in case of:
Dangerous Goods (DG) accidents

Dangerous Goods (DG) incidents

as well as any occasion: when undeclared or wrongly declared Dangerous Goods (DG) are discovered in cargo, mail or unaccompanied baggage or

when accompanied baggage contains Dangerous Goods (DG) which passengers or crew are not permitted to take on aircraft

when DG are discovered to have been carried when not loaded, segregated, separated or secured in accordance with DGR provisions, or

when DG are discovered to have been carried as cargo without NOTOC having been provided or has been incorrectly completed.
An initial report, which may be made by any means, shall be dispatched by the Safety Manager (SM) or his deputy within 72 hours of the occurrence,

to the National Aviation Authority (NAA) of the state: in which the aircraft is registered (i.e. Swiss FOCA), and

in which the incident occurred If exceptional circumstances prevent the in time reporting, above mentioned authorities shall be informed as soon as possible.

The Dangerous Goods (DG) occurrence shall be reported through helvetic’s

main SMS reporting tool as the primary source. In case access is not available or

not granted, DG occurrence report form shall be used. The Dangerous Goods

(DG) occurrence report form can be found in the APM 4 Ground Operations.

Report shall be duly completed and sent as soon as possible, even if all the information is not available. Copies of all relevant documents and any

photographs should be attached to this report.

Providing it is safe to do so, all dangerous goods, packages, documents, etc, relating to the occurrence shall be retained until after the initial report has been

sent to the authorities, and they have indicated whether these should continue to be retained.

Whenever DG accident or incident constitutes an aircraft accident, serious incident or incident, it is required to submit separate reports for both

occurrences.

Note: Occurrences related to flights operated on behalf of Swiss International Air Lines shall be reported to NAA by helvetic.

kontext:
11.5.4 Time Line for Reporting

The chart below illustrates the general flow of information, main deadlines and stages of the reporting into ECCAIRS2 This reporting flow starts from the moment the occurrence is detected (T0). From this moment, the individual employee shall report it to helvetic via the SMS Tool as soon as possible, but latest within 72 hours.

kontext:
11.5.5.2 Anonymous Report

An anonymous report is a report without identifying the reporter himself. It is a feature in the SMS Tool when employees wish to remain unknown. kontext: 11.6.1 Accident and Serious Incident Reporting
The Flight Crew shall notify without delay the helvetic OCC and Piquet Officer whenever he or any other crew member learns of the occurrence of an accident or serious incident.

kontext:
11.9.4.1 Flight and Cockpit Voice Recorder Systems

Flight recorders on the helvetic Embraer fleet are digital recording units (DVDR) combining three different functionalities. Recording of: audio information from cockpit area microphones and primary crew microphones [cockpit voice recorder (CVR)]. datalink messages [data link recorder (DLR)] all available flight data [flight data recorder (FDR)] CVRs have at least 2 hours of voice recording capacity and must only be de- activated to protect records in due time.
FDRs have a flight time recording capacity which allows read out or de-activation in due time after an occurrence. De-activation during flight or on ground by the flight crew is not allowed.
Note: If a flight is conducted with a deactivated CVR check with MCC for MEL Regulation(s).

The DVDR automatically starts recording audio information as soon as the

aircraft is powered up.
Flight data recording begins when the first engine is

started. After power down the DVDRcontinue recording audio information for 10 minutes.
In the event the airplane becomes involved in an accident or serious incident, the

Commander must ensure the protection of all related flight records, and if

necessary, the associated DVDR to the extent possible. This can include the

retention of the DVDR in safe custody until its disposition.

The removal of the flight recorder systems from the aircraft will be determined by

the investigating authority in the state conducting the investigation with due regard to the seriousness of the occurrence.

fragen.erklaerung_en: OM-A 11.9.4.1: Audio is recorded from power-up, flight data from the start of the first engine.

kontext:
11.10 Guideline for dealing with serious Incidents or Accidents

The following steps shall aid the cockpit crew as a guide in the event of a serious incident or accident and does not make claims of being complete. finish all required checklists and corresponding duties

inform ATC (if necessary inform local authorities)

do not make any statements! Just provide the most necessary facts pertaining to satisfy the reporting requirements

initiate/take care of PAX and crew (first aid, doctor, medical assistance, etc.)

if possible, power down the aircraft as early as possible (e.g. after evacuation) to preserve recorded data by DVDR

inform helvetic OCC and Piquet Officer; leave contact address to ensure that you can be contacted by helvetic

gather as many pieces of evidence as possible flight documents, passenger list (PIL), cargo documents (NOTOC) pictures or screenshots, witnesses, sketches, etc.

if documents have to be handed over to authorities, try to document this (by whom, why, where, when etc.). If possible requested documentation shall be

handed over exclusively to the national accident investigation authorities or the helvetic safety department try not to hand over ID-Cards, Passport or licenses

ensure that you can be contacted by the local authorities

do not sign any document or statement!

in case of actual or suspected tail-strike or if there is any justifiable doubt

about weight and balance,
order ground crew to have the belly load reweighed and documented before any offloading starts

keep entire crew together (request special meeting room for get-together) separate the crew as far as possible from the media and passengers

(special hotel, hospital, etc.) perform a crew debriefing with all relevant facts. All crew members shall

make notes about observations during the incident accident. make a list of all cellphone numbers of the involved crew members and share it among the entire crew.

keep helvetic informed about location of the crew

keep your family informed and instruct them to keep all information purely inside the family

avoid posting any information via social media

OM-A 12 Rules of the Air

12 Rules of the Air 12.0-1

kontext:
11.6 Reporting of Occurrence

Any cockpit or cabin crew member shall report to the commander any fault, failure, malfunction or defect which she/he believes may affect the airworthiness or safe operation of the aircraft, including emergency systems, and any incident that endangered or could have endangered the safety of operation. The tables in chapter 11.6.2 - Mandatory Occurrence Reporting list the expected reporter (flight crew, cabin crew, maintenance staff and ground handling) to each mandatory occurrence.
However, during flight operation the crew may define one crew member who writes the report. The final responsibility lies with the CMD.

If a crew member other than the CMD writes the report, the safety management will ensure the CMD of the affected flight will be informed as well.
Any occurrences shall be reported as fast as reasonably possible, but no later than 72 hours.

Guideline for checking if operational occurrence or other legal reporting requirement is present:

1. First check with: a. 11.6.2 - Mandatory Occurrence Reporting b. 11.7 - List of Other Legal Reporting Requirements Note: Table of Contents for faster access is presented on next page.

2. Depending on the severity of the occurrence decide between: a. Accident or Serious Incident Reporting (Definition in 11.2 - Definitions)

b. Otherwise Occurence Reporting

c. Check if Occurrence requires immediate ATC Notification as specified

in 11.6.2.4 - ATC Reporting

Note: As a general rule: Whenever you are in doubt, file an “Occurence Report” via the helvetic SMS Tool.

OM-A Reporting Occurences

Table of Contents for faster Access

kontext:
1.13 Piquet Officer (PQO)

The Piquet Officer (PQO) duty is assigned to a group of nominated persons being part of the helvetic organisation. The nomination to the Piquet Officer (PQO) group is done by the Accountable Manager (ACM).
The goal of this function is to grant a single point of contact for Flight Operations Officer (FOO) on duty particularly outside of usual office hours.
The Piquet Officer (PQO) fulfills his duty in a weekly cycle starting and ending on Wednesdays at 12:00 (noon).

The Piquet Officer must be reachable via his mobile phone outside usual office hours (usual office hours: Monday to Friday 07:00LT till 18:00LT). Non-availabilities shall be avoided whenever possible.
If unavoidable, non-availabilities shall be covered by delegation or sharing of the assigned duty with another Piquet Officer group member. helvetic Operations Control Center (OCC) shall be informed about any non-availability and the respective replacement of such a duty as early as possible (telephone or e-mail).
During normal office hours, the Piquet Officer (PQO) duty and responsibility shall automatically be assigned to a helvetic management member available in the office by decision of the Flight Operations Officers (FOO) on duty.
The published Piquet Officer (PQO) duty plan can be found in a semi-permanent Admin Note named Ops Management Piquet.
This note is updated by the Administration Personnel (ADM) in a half-yearly cycle.

OM-A Responsibilities

The Piquet Officer (PQO) is responsible for: supporting and maintaining the helvetic operation of airplanes in irregular situations in respect of safety, security and economy

providing communication and cooperation between the Operations Control Center (OCC) and members of the helvetic Operations Management (refer to 2.4.2 - helvetic Operations Management)

the promotion of commercially sound decisions in cooperation with the Flight Operations Officer (FOO) with other members of the helvetic Operations Management. Decisions shall be based on regulations laid down in the Operations Manuals (OM) and additional helvetic publications defined in 0.1
- Introduction

the integration of the customer relations management either by the Flight Operations Officer (FOO) on duty or by himself if deemed advisable (e.g. delays 2 hours, re-bookings, flight cancellations)

re-direction of requests to other members of the helvetic Operations Management (subject matter experts) unless he is competent to take appropriate actions or decisions on his own

informing the corporate management (refer to 1.1.1 - Corporate Management sequence COO – CFO – CEO) about the irregularity and corrective actions in case of major issues (e.g. cancellation of flights with major consequences such as nightstop, airplane damage)

the activation of the Emergency Response Team (ERT) in coordination with the Accountable Manager (ACM) or his deputy according to the Crisis and Emergency Response Manual (CERM)

arranging testing for psychoactive substances in case of a serious incident

or accident or if misuse is suspected and removing investigated crew member from duty until clarified. Refer to:

helvetic HR Manual

OM-A Responsibilities

kontext:
7.3.6 Implemented Fatigue Risk Mitigation

Based on the necessity of having qualified personnel available to the required extent, an effective crew planning plays a major role in achieving any FRMS aims.
Crew Planning (CRP) shall: consider fatigue risk additionally to legal flight time limitations

plan night flights with minimal waiting time

consider rest time before night flights and use common sense when planning deadheading or positioning
According to the SAFTE model helvetic defines the critical level of effectiveness at 77% of the maximum human performance.

The goal is to reduce the time exposure with actual duty time performed below this criterion.
If there are duty plans in the future with FRMS efficiency level below 85% and it is not possible to correct it due to the rotation planning (e.g. night duties), preventive measures shall be taken in order that the actual planning will not be below 77% efficiency level (e.g. no reserves before and after)

8 Operating Procedures 8.-1-1

fragen.frage: Welche Rolle spielt Flight Data Monitoring (FDM) im helvetic FRMS?
antworten: FDM ist die primäre prädiktive Methode des FRMS
FDM ist kein funktionales Element des FRMS, kann aber als Quelle für fatigue-bezogene Analysen genutzt werden

fragen.erklaerung: OM-A 7.3.3.1: Da ein eindeutiger Fatigue-Nachweis aus FDM fehlt, ist FDM kein funktionales FRMS-Element, aber eine mögliche Datenquelle.

kontext:
7.3.3.1 Hazard Identification

For hazard identification process refer to OMM Chapter 4.3 Hazard Identification.
The following methodologies shall be used to identify fatigue related hazards:
Predictive:
Sleep, Activities, Fatigue and Task Effectiveness Model (SAFTE) The SAFTE-model is:

based on 15 years of fatigue modelling experience

validated against laboratory and simulator measures of fatigue

validated and calibrated to predict accident risk by the US Department of Transportation

accepted by the US Department of Defence (Air Force, Army, Navy, Marines) as the common war fighter fatigue model

Fatigue Avoidance Scheduling Tool (FAST) FAST uses the SAFTE-model as described above considers time zone changes and is valid for any city pair

mimics typical sleep patterns

considers total duty period, commuting, flight time and number of route sectors counts on naps prior to anticipated late starts

considers split sleep (split sleeping periods) when appropriate

automatically inserts in-flight sleep for augmented crews

(currently not applied by helvetic)

Proactive:

reporting of fatigue risks

analysis of planned versus actual time worked

FTL use of commander’s discretion

FAST analysis of actual flown schedules

Reactive: fatigue and confidential reports

audit reports

incidents

Flight Data Monitoring (FDM) events whereas outcomes of fatigue could show undesirable effects in Flight Data Monitoring (FDM) without any doubt, specific evidence of root causes clearly and solely addressing fatigue has not yet been proven based on scientific research.
Therefore, for the time being helvetic does not define FDM as a functional element of FRMS.
However, FDM can be used as a source to analyse fatigue-related events which were either reported by crew members or if analysis results point towards a relation between fatigue and FDM-events.
fragen.frage_en: What role does flight data monitoring (FDM) play in the helvetic FRMS?
antworten_en: FDM is the primary predictive method of the FRMS
FDM is not a functional element of the FRMS, but can be used as a source for fatigue-related analyses
FDM events automatically trigger a fatigue report
FDM replaces the SAFTE/FAST model for planning
fragen.erklaerung_en: OM-A 7.3.3.1: As clear evidence of fatigue from FDM is lacking, FDM is not a functional FRMS element, but a possible data source.

fragen.frage: (E1) Wer trägt gemäss OM-B die Entscheidung und Verantwortung für einen Rejected Takeoff (RTO)?
antworten: Der Pilot, der die Störung zuerst erkennt
Der Pilot Flying
Der Captain

fragen.erklaerung: Wer die Störung zuerst erkennt, muss sie ansagen; Entscheid und Verantwortung für den RTO liegen aber beim Captain.
fragen.quelle: OM-B E1 3.3.1 Rejected Takeoff - RTO, S. 3.3-1
fragen.zitat: but the decision and responsibility to perform an RTO remain to the captain.
kontext:
3.3.1 Rejected Takeoff - RTO

During the takeoff phase, an RTO procedure is initiated before V1 if any adverse

or abnormal event occurs that could affect the safety of flight. Many faults can cause a decision to reject, like engine fire, engine failure and some other system

faults or events. If an adequate decision to reject is taken, do not delay the RTO.
Delaying the decision increases the risk of a runway overrun, because it takes a

few seconds for the engines to spool down to idle thrust.

A successful RTO depends on:
Accurate alert and monitoring during all takeoff phase,

Captains timely decision,

All callouts made on a loud, clear, and precise communication way,

Adequate briefing, procedures, and coordination.

Responsibility Whoever first identifies the undesirable event or malfunction must announce it,
but the decision and responsibility to perform an RTO remain to the captain.

Once the decision is made, initiate the RTO immediately.

Actions Actions are taken considering that, during all takeoff procedures, the LSP keeps his hand on the thrust levers until V1 is reached,

Once the RTO decision has been made, the following actions are: set thrust

levers to idle, disconnect the autothrottle, verify autobrake actuation or

manually apply maximum brakes, and apply reverse thrust as required,

The autobrake RTO mode provides the maximum deceleration rate, which is

equivalent to the maximum manual braking. To decrease workload in this scenario it is recommended to use autobrake in RTO mode, although the

pilot can manually override the autobrake as required.

Note: if an RTO is performed below 60 KIAS (before HOLD is announced) and AT is not disconnected, Autothrottle moves the thrust levers back to TO/GA detent if both throttles are reduced to a position not below 40 degrees TLA. If throttles are moved below 40 degrees TLA or reverse thrust is applied during an RTO, the AT disconnects,

directional control is kept by applying rudder pedal steering,

monitor airplane deceleration, cancel any aural warnings upon malfunction identification, verify reverse thrust status, and advise

ATC,

the engine should be commanded from MAX REV to MIN REV at or above 60 KIAS, and it is recommended to close the thrust reversers at 30 KIAS

if necessary, thrust reverse can be used until airplane comes to a complete stop, considering airplane speed, runway length available, slippery surfaces with ice, snow and so forth,

the airplane should remain on the runway until it is clear that an emergency evacuation is not necessary and the whole scenario is analyzed. If necessary, request external aids to vacate the runway to a safe position according to ATC instructions,

if RTO decision was taken due to fire, consider positioning the airplane so that fire is on the downwind of fuselage, if an RTO is performed, the FMS takeoff and landing data may

reset after two minutes. If a new takeoff is intended, the FMS takeoff and landing data must be re-entered and confirmed before

the takeoff.

Low and High Energy Speeds The sooner an RTO decision is taken, the greater is the chance to safely stop within runway limits. RTO above V1 may lead to a runway overrun and is the main cause of overrun accidents,

Low energy speed is considered up to, approximately, 80 KIAS,

During takeoff, the 80 KIAS callout has three main proposes: pilot

incapacitation check, airspeed crosscheck and the transition from Low to High Energy speed,

For High energy speeds only reject the takeoff if there is a malfunction that severely affects the flight safety, such as but not limited to:

Engine failures resulting in loss of thrust, Fire or fire warning, Severe damages.

For High energy speeds, it is recommended to continue the takeoff if a tire burst occurs,

kontext:
3.3.1 Rejected Takeoff - RTO

During the takeoff phase, an RTO procedure is initiated before V1 if any adverse

or abnormal event occurs that could affect the safety of flight. Many faults can cause a decision to reject, like engine fire, engine failure and some other system

faults or events. If an adequate decision to reject is taken, do not delay the RTO.
Delaying the decision increases the risk of a runway overrun, because it takes a

few seconds for the engines to spool down to idle thrust.

A successful RTO depends on:
Accurate alert and monitoring during all takeoff phase,

Captains timely decision,

All callouts made on a loud, clear, and precise communication way,

Adequate briefing, procedures, and coordination.

Responsibility Whoever first identifies the undesirable event or malfunction must announce it, but the decision and responsibility to perform an RTO remain to the captain.
Once the decision is made, initiate the RTO immediately.

Actions Actions are taken considering that, during all takeoff procedures, the LSP keeps his hand on the thrust levers until V1 is reached,

Once the RTO decision has been made, the following actions are: set thrust

levers to idle, disconnect the autothrottle, verify autobrake actuation or

manually apply maximum brakes, and apply reverse thrust as required,

The autobrake RTO mode provides the maximum deceleration rate, which is

equivalent to the maximum manual braking. To decrease workload in this scenario it is recommended to use autobrake in RTO mode, although the

pilot can manually override the autobrake as required.

Note: if an RTO is performed below 60 KIAS (before HOLD is announced) and AT is not disconnected, Autothrottle moves the thrust levers back to TO/GA detent if both throttles are reduced to a position not below 40 degrees TLA. If throttles are moved below 40 degrees TLA or reverse thrust is applied during an RTO, the AT disconnects,

directional control is kept by applying rudder pedal steering,

monitor airplane deceleration, cancel any aural warnings upon malfunction identification, verify reverse thrust status, and advise

ATC,

the engine should be commanded from MAX REV to MIN REV at or above 60 KIAS, and it is recommended to close the thrust reversers at 30 KIAS

if necessary, thrust reverse can be used until airplane comes to a complete stop, considering airplane speed, runway length available, slippery surfaces with ice, snow and so forth,

the airplane should remain on the runway until it is clear that an emergency evacuation is not necessary and the whole scenario is analyzed. If necessary, request external aids to vacate the runway to a safe position according to ATC instructions,

if RTO decision was taken due to fire, consider positioning the airplane so that fire is on the downwind of fuselage, if an RTO is performed, the FMS takeoff and landing data may

reset after two minutes. If a new takeoff is intended, the FMS takeoff and landing data must be re-entered and confirmed before

the takeoff.

Low and High Energy Speeds The sooner an RTO decision is taken, the greater is the chance to safely stop within runway limits. RTO above V1 may lead to a runway overrun and is the main cause of overrun accidents,
Low energy speed is considered up to, approximately, 80 KIAS,

During takeoff, the 80 KIAS callout has three main proposes: pilot

incapacitation check, airspeed crosscheck and the transition from Low to High Energy speed,

For High energy speeds only reject the takeoff if there is a malfunction that severely affects the flight safety, such as but not limited to:

Engine failures resulting in loss of thrust, Fire or fire warning, Severe damages.

For High energy speeds, it is recommended to continue the takeoff if a tire burst occurs,

Upon reaching V1, if no decision has been taken, continue the takeoff.
After V1, there is no assurance that the airplane is capable to stop within the remaining runway length.

fragen.frage: (E1) Engine Failure nach V1: Der Ausfall tritt zwischen V2 und V2 + 10 KIAS auf. Auf welche Speed wird gepitcht?
antworten: V2
VFS
V2 + 10 KIAS
Aktuelle Speed
fragen.erklaerung: Unter V2 wird auf V2, zwischen V2 und V2+10 auf die aktuelle Speed und über V2+10 auf V2+10 KIAS gepitcht.
fragen.quelle: OM-B E1 3.6.3 Engine Failure above V1, S. 3.6-2
fragen.zitat: engine failure between V2 and V2 + 10 KIAS: pitch for the present speed
kontext:
3.6.3 Engine Failure above V1

If an engine failure occurs above V1, control airplane direction, aiming to keep airplane on runway centerline by smoothly applying rudder.
As soon as an Engine Failure or FIRE is recognized (not always followed by loss of thrust) and affected engine identified, check maximum thrust on EICAS.

After rotation, set aileron in neutral and use rudder and yaw trim to keep wings level. High aileron input raises the spoilers and increases drag.

As reference, the slip/skid indicator is approximately to off center and

between 0° to 5° of bank after engine failure. It depends on speed, gross weight,

and altitude. Generally the control wheel in the neutral position is a good indication of the lowest drag for single engine.
Crew must keep close attention at first positive rate of climb to retract landing gear, monitoring airplane profile.
The TO mode first guidance is based on takeoff weight and flap setting, limited to a minimum pitch of 7° and maximum of 18°.
Crew must follow the flight director guidance to maintain V2 to V2 10 KIAS up to acceleration altitude, according to the following three different conditions: engine failure below V2: pitch for V2
engine failure between V2 and V2 10 KIAS: pitch for the present speed

engine failure above V2 10 KIAS: pitch for V2 10 KIAS Takeoff thrust is limited to 5 (optionally 10) minutes after takeoff. It is recommended that emergency procedures to be accomplished as soon as safe

altitude has been reached (at least 400 ft AGL or according to local minimums).

When engine failure occurs after takeoff, noise abatement procedures no longer apply.

Following an Engine Failure, ATTCS adjusts operating engine thrust to its

respective RSV mode. If the maximum thrust is not reached for any reason, advance the thrust levers to maximum thrust.

On departure procedures with acceleration altitudes above 1000 ft, emphasize

during takeoff briefing that, in the event of an Engine Failure, Engine Fire (with loss of thrust), or any other malfunction requiring a memory item, actions can be

commanded at an altitude lower than the acceleration altitude, but not lower than 400 ft. Airplane must be stabilized and on the profile.

For One Engine Inoperative, limit the bank angle to:

15° at V2

20° at V2 5 KIAS

25° at V2 10 KIAS

antworten: VFS

fragen.zitat: The driftdown speed is represented by the Green Dot and provides the lower descent gradient.
kontext:
3.6.7 Engine Failure In Flight Driftdown

Following an engine failure or inflight engine shutdown, an airplane may not be able to maintain its cruise altitude. The driftdown profile assures the airplane altitude is kept as high as possible throughout the descent.
The driftdown speed is represented by the Green Dot and provides the lower descent gradient.

During a driftdown, the available thrust increases as the airplane descends.

Eventually, at a certain altitude the available thrust becomes equal to the airplane drag, and the airplane levels off. This altitude is called the gross level off altitude.

The gross level off altitude, when corrected for gradient margins by 1.1% (2 engines), 1.4% (3 engines), or 1.6% (4 engines), is called the net level

off altitude. It depends on the atmospheric temperature and the airplane weight.
Regulations (FAR 121.191/CAT.POL.A.215/CAR 705.58) require that the airplane clears all terrain by a given margin when an engine fails.
Two means of compliance for enroute obstacle clearance are allowed: the net level-off altitude must clear all enroute obstacles by at least 1000ft or the net flight path must clear all enroute obstacles between the point where the engine is assumed to fail and an airport where a landing can be made by at least 2000ft

(Drift Down Profile)

fragen.frage: (E1) Welche Aussage zum Wiederanlassen im Flug (Auto Relight oder manuell) ist gemäss OM-B korrekt?
antworten: Der FADEC schützt vor Hot Start, aber nicht vor Hung Start
Der FADEC bricht einen Hot Start im Flug automatisch ab
Der FADEC bietet keinen Schutz vor Hot Start, Hung Start oder Failure to light off
Nur beim Auto Relight besteht voller FADEC-Schutz
fragen.erklaerung: Bei Starts im Flug hat der FADEC keinen Schutz für Hot Starts, Hung Starts oder Failure to light off; die Crew muss selbst reagieren.
fragen.quelle: OM-B E1 3.6.8 Engine In-Flight Start, S. 3.6-21
fragen.zitat: During in-flight engine starts, using auto relight or manual starts, the FADEC has no protection for hot starts, hung starts or failure to light off.
kontext:
3.6.8 Engine In-Flight Start

In the event of engine flameout, the FADEC automatically turns on both igniters and schedules fuel flow to initiate the relight process. A WML icon is displayed next to the affected engine N2 and represents that an auto relight is being attempted.

Engine may accelerate to idle slowly during the start, especially at high altitudes.
The auto relight is successful if positive steady N2 acceleration is obtained

without ITT overtemperature nor any other engine parameter fluctuation. If those conditions are satisfied, the start is progressing normally.

If ITT overtemperature happens, or engine parameters fluctuate the auto relight

should be considered unsuccessful and aborted. Crew manually aborts auto relight by moving the START/STOP Selector to STOP.
If engine restart is considered, follow the ENGINE AIRSTART procedure.
Engine restart should be considered based on the flight crew's assessment of each situation. In general, engine restart should be avoided in the following situations:

If the engine failed after it has exceeded any engine limitation

If the engine was intentionally shut down after it was not able

to operate at idle without exceeding limitations, or

If engine damage is suspected

Engine damage may be associated with fire, loud noise, engine exceedance,

lack of rotation, abnormal oil pressure, or abnormal oil temperature. Engine

vibrations accompanied by other engine abnormal indications may also indicate

possible engine damage.
During in-flight engine starts, using auto relight or manual starts, the FADEC has no protection for hot starts, hung starts or failure to light off.

Crew must take

appropriate action in case of an abnormal start.
fragen.frage_en: (E1) Which statement on in-flight relight (auto relight or manual) is correct according to OM-B?
antworten_en: The FADEC protects against hot start, but not against hung start
The FADEC automatically aborts a hot start in flight
The FADEC provides no protection against hot start, hung start or failure to light off
Only with auto relight is there full FADEC protection
fragen.erklaerung_en: For in-flight starts, the FADEC has no protection for hot starts, hung starts or failure to light off; the crew must react themselves.

kontext:
3.6.9 One Engine Inoperative 3D-Approach

The same procedure as described in chapter 3D-Approaches should be used, with the following amendments: use Slat/Flap 5 for landing

during approach, when stabilised on final:

set the rudder trim to neutral set fuel crossfeed to OFF (if applicable)

Approach Preparation plan to be stabilised on final in landing configuration at about 8 NM

pilot should maintain the directional control using the rudder pedals

Go Around During the approach, if an engine failure occurs prior to engage the AUTOLAND mode, the approach can be performed with the AUTOLAND engaged.
If an engine failure occurs after the AUTOLAND engagement, a go-around must be performed.

During a go-around, be prepared to overcome the directional control.
The parallel rudder disengages when the Flight Director GO-AROUND mode is

changed to any other vertical mode.

refer to 2.5.3 - 3D IFR Approach

fragen.zitat: The actions identified with ● are recall items. They must be performed expeditiously and from memory.
kontext:
ANAC APPROVED 4-00

REVISION 22 code 01 Page 3 AFM-1913
INTRODUCTION

This Section provides the emergency and abnormal procedures to be performed in case of a system malfunction or failure, in order to maintain the airworthiness of the airplane.
The actions identified with are recall items. They must be performed expeditiously and from memory.

The other actions should be performed as soon as the condition permits.
Some procedures require to LAND AT THE NEAREST SUITABLE AIRPORT. This statement may be presented below the associated emergency/abnormal characterization or at the beginning of a task that requires so. When the crew determines that significant threat to safety is present, they should always accomplish the earliest possible descent and land at the nearest suitable airport regardless of having this statement present in the procedure.
Procedures which are considered to be “basic airmanship” or related to malfunctions or failures on the ground are not presented.
Malfunctions or failures not cleared before takeoff must be treated as dispatch deviation.
The procedures contained herein assume that:
Airplane systems are operating normally before the failure, All emergency/abnormal checklists are performed in the order they are presented in the procedure, Normal procedures have been properly accomplished, System controls are in normal condition before the initiation of the associated procedure, Aural warnings are silenced as applicable. kontext:
3.9.1 Traffic Alert and Collision Avoidance System (TCAS)

The pilot must not initiate evasive manoeuvres using Traffic Advisory information (TA) only, without visually sighting conflicting traffic.

The traffic display and advisories are intended for assistance to visually locate

the indicated conflicting traffic.

Manoeuvres that are in the opposite direction of the Resolution Advisory (RA) are extremely hazardous, especially RAs involving altitude crossing, and thus

are prohibited unless it is visually determined to be the only means to assure

safe separation.
WARNING: It is possible in some cases to have insufficient airplane performance to follow the TCAS command without flying into stall warning or buffet.
Conditions where this may occur include:
Bank angle in excess of 15 degrees.

Operations at airports above 5300ft MSL or temperatures greater than ISA 28°C (50°F).

Engine inoperative.

Failure to configure the airplane to go around, following a climb

RA in landing configuration.
Failure to advance thrust to max continuous thrust, following a climb RA at reduced thrust.

Speeds less than normal operating speed.

Abnormal configurations which reduce performance

(e.g. gear down).

TCAS command reversal to a "CLIMB-CLIMB NOW".

Buffet margin less than 0.3 G.

If stall warning occurs during an RA manoeuvre, immediately

abandon the RA and execute stall recovery procedures. TCAS II continues to provide RA`s during stall warning and recovery

procedure. If high speed buffet is encountered when initially responding to an RA, relax pitch force as necessary to reduce

buffet, but still continue to manoeuvre.

Note: The consequences of not following an RA may result in additional RAs in which aural alert and visual annunciations may not agree with each other. A non-compliance by one airplane can result in reduced vertical separation with the need to achieve safe horizontal separation by visual means.

Using every available means, clear the airspace into which you are

going to manoeuvre. If needed, promptly and smoothly adjust the airplane’s pitch to fly into the green rectangle (if displayed), and fly

out of the red trapezoidal shaped avoidance zone(s). This should require no more than 0.75 g to 1.25 g manoeuvre 0.25 g).

Exaggerated responses to TCAS RAs are not desirable or appropriate, because of the other potential traffic conflicts and ATC consequences. From level flight, proper response to a TCAS RA typically results in an overall altitude deviation of 300 to 500 ft to resolve a traffic conflict.

If a CLIMB RA is issued with the airplane in the landing configuration, a normal go-around should be initiated including the appropriate thrust increase and configurationchange.

Compliance with TCAS RA is required, unless the pilotconsiders unsafe to do so.

The pilot should promptly return to the previous ATCclearance after

the TCAS voice message "Clear of Conflict" is announced.
An immediate smooth response to an RA is required to obtain maximum

separations. TCAS II algorithms arebased on the pilot

starting the initial manoeuvre within 5 seconds of the RA

and within 2 1/2 seconds for additionalcorrective RAs (increases or reversals).

Any delay in responding to RAs will reduce the separations provided.

TCAS II may lose the track or altitude information about the threat

airplane during an RA. If so, the RA will terminatewithout a “Clear of Conflict” annunciation.
