kontext:
3.10.1 Windshear Policy

The most important policy is to avoid a windshear. Although windshear detection and annunciation system is installed, pilots may not perceive that an area of a potential windshear could be encountered ahead. Therefore some aids must be used by flight crews to develop an awareness of windshear causes and perceive danger signals to successfully avoid it. The following information can be used:

Presence of thunderstorms, microburst, convective clouds, squall line

Visual observation of strong winds near the ground Onboard weather radar

Pilots or Air Traffic Services reports

Windshear escape guidance is provided by the FGCS Flight Director function, and is annunciated as WSHR in green in the vertical flight mode annunciator field when active. ROLL becomes the active lateral mode and the autopilot disconnects when windshear escape guidance is activated.
Windshear detection is enabled between 10 ft and 1500 ft AGL,

and escape guidance may be initiated when the following conditions are met:
Manually when a windshear Caution or Warning is detected and the pilot presses the TO/GA Button When a windshear Warning is detected and Thrust Levers are set to TO/GA position or beyond Automatically when the AFCS flight director mode is in Takeoff or Go- Around mode and a windshear Warning is detected

The windshear escape guidance mode does not automatically revert to any other flight guidance mode. The pilot must manually select another mode in order to exit windshear escape guidance, and the ability to successfully transition to another vertical guidance mode requires that the activation criteria described

above be false.

3.10.1.2 Approach

The most important way to cope with windshear is to avoid areas of known or potential windshear occurrence such as thunderstorms.
Severe windshear may be defined as a rapid change in wind direction or velocity.
The result is airspeed changes greater than 15 kt or vertical speed changes greater than 500 ft/min.

Whenever a windshear is suspected during approach and landing, the following precautions are taken:

use Flaps 5 for landing

establish a stabilized approach by no lower than 1000 ft AFE

use the most suitable runway that avoids the areas of suspected windshear and is compatible with the crosswind or tailwind limitations

avoid large thrust reductions or trim changes in response to sudden airspeed increases as these may be followed by airspeed decreases

develop an awareness of normal airspeed, attitude, and vertical speed. The crew should closely monitor the vertical flight path instruments, such as, vertical speed and altimeters, and callout any deviations.

Flight crew should consider performing the windshear escape maneuver whenever windshear clues are present without EGPWS announcement.

whenever a windshear caution is annunciated during approach through the

fragen.zitat: The PF must disengage the autothrottle and simultaneously reduce the AOA.
kontext:
3.12.3 Stall Recovery Maneuver

Upon recognizing a stall condition, stick shaker activation or feeling the stall buffeting, the crew must initiate the stall recovery procedure immediately.

Note: Stick shaker activation causes the automatic disengagement of the

autopilot. Beware that, in icing, the autopilot may mask heavy or

asymmetric control forces due to airframe icing. The autopilot may even

disconnect earlier because of excessive roll rates, roll angles, or excessive pitch.
The PF must disengage the autothrottle and simultaneously reduce the AOA.

Push the control column to apply nose down, level the wings and adjust the thrust as required. The PM must confirm autopilot and autothrottle are disengaged, and monitor altitude and speed of the airplane.

Note: Due to the different control laws in direct mode, larger control column deflections may be necessary to achieve the desired pitch attitude when

compared to normal mode operation.

Note: In direct mode, no fly-by-wire functionality is available. More control column input may be required to get the same pitch change.

The PF must retract the speed brake and maintain the nose down command until the airplane is effectively out of the stall condition. With the airplane out of stall the stall warnings are deactivated.

Due to the nose down attitude, during the recovery the airplane accelerates. The PM should monitor the speed to avoid the airplane flying above the VMO/MMO or

other applicable speed limit. The PM should also monitor and inform any other airplane limitation exceedance. At high altitudes, normally smooth and small

control inputs are required to keep speed and rate of climb within reasonable

values.
Once out of stall, return the airplane to the normal flight path. Apply commands gradually to avoid secondary stalls. It may take less force to generate the same load factor as altitude increases.
A common template to deal with stall recoveries to all types of airplanes is desirable. The EJETS automatism, provided by the fly-by-wire system in the Normal mode, helps reducing the workload in certain scenarios.
With the airplane flying in the normal mode, the fly-by-wire functionalities automatically neutralize any pitch up tendency caused by engine thrust. In this case applying MAX thrust during the stall recovery procedure should not result in any pitch up tendency. If any tendency appears, maintain the nose down command and reduce engine thrust.

Additionally, when in the normal mode, setting the thrust levers to MAX position automatically disengages the autothrottle and retracts the speed brakes, reducing the workload during the recover maneuver.

OM-B E1 Procedures

fragen.frage_en: (E1) What must the PF do simultaneously during stall recovery?

fragen.frage: (E1) In grosser Höhe spürt der Pilot Stall Buffeting, bevor der Stick Shaker auslöst. Was ist gemäss OM-B zu tun?
antworten: Den Autopilot trennen
Nichts, solange kein Stick Shaker aktiv ist
Nur die Speedbrake einfahren
Auf FLCH wechseln
fragen.erklaerung: In grosser Höhe kann Buffeting vor dem Stick Shaker auftreten; dann muss der Pilot den Autopilot trennen (Stall Recovery).
fragen.quelle: OM-B E1 3.12.3 Stall Recovery Maneuver, S. 3.12-5
fragen.zitat: At high altitudes pilot may feel the stall buffeting before the stick shaker. In this case pilot shall disengage the autopilot.
kontext:
3.12.3 Stall Recovery Maneuver

Upon recognizing a stall condition, stick shaker activation or feeling the stall buffeting, the crew must initiate the stall recovery procedure immediately.

Note: Stick shaker activation causes the automatic disengagement of the

autopilot. Beware that, in icing, the autopilot may mask heavy or

asymmetric control forces due to airframe icing. The autopilot may even

disconnect earlier because of excessive roll rates, roll angles, or excessive pitch.

The PF must disengage the autothrottle and simultaneously reduce the AOA.

Push the control column to apply nose down, level the wings and adjust the thrust as required. The PM must confirm autopilot and autothrottle are disengaged, and monitor altitude and speed of the airplane.

Note: Due to the different control laws in direct mode, larger control column deflections may be necessary to achieve the desired pitch attitude when

compared to normal mode operation.

Note: In direct mode, no fly-by-wire functionality is available. More control column input may be required to get the same pitch change.

The PF must retract the speed brake and maintain the nose down command until the airplane is effectively out of the stall condition. With the airplane out of stall the stall warnings are deactivated.

Due to the nose down attitude, during the recovery the airplane accelerates. The PM should monitor the speed to avoid the airplane flying above the VMO/MMO or

other applicable speed limit. The PM should also monitor and inform any other airplane limitation exceedance. At high altitudes, normally smooth and small

control inputs are required to keep speed and rate of climb within reasonable

values.
Once out of stall, return the airplane to the normal flight path. Apply commands gradually to avoid secondary stalls. It may take less force to generate the same load factor as altitude increases.
A common template to deal with stall recoveries to all types of airplanes is desirable. The EJETS automatism, provided by the fly-by-wire system in the Normal mode, helps reducing the workload in certain scenarios.
With the airplane flying in the normal mode, the fly-by-wire functionalities automatically neutralize any pitch up tendency caused by engine thrust. In this case applying MAX thrust during the stall recovery procedure should not result in any pitch up tendency. If any tendency appears, maintain the nose down command and reduce engine thrust.

Additionally, when in the normal mode, setting the thrust levers to MAX position automatically disengages the autothrottle and retracts the speed brakes, reducing the workload during the recover maneuver.

Applies nose down and levels the wings until out Monitors altitude and

of stall. speed. Performs any

Upon Stick Shaker necessary callout. activation or Applies thrust as required. feeling the stall buffeting. Accelerates the airplane to a safe speed.
Reconfigures the Retracts speed brakes. airplane as necessary.

After recovery, return to the normal flight path.

Note 1:
At high altitudes pilot may feel the stall buffeting before the stick shaker. In this case pilot shall disengage the autopilot.
After recovery, if the airplane is in landing or takeoff configuration, retract landing gear and flaps as in a normal go-around procedure.
fragen.frage_en: (E1) At high altitude the pilot feels stall buffeting before the stick shaker activates. What is to be done according to OM-B?
antworten_en: Disconnect the autopilot
Nothing, as long as no stick shaker is active
Only retract the speedbrake
Switch to FLCH
fragen.erklaerung_en: At high altitude, buffeting may occur before the stick shaker; the pilot must then disconnect the autopilot (stall recovery).

fragen.frage: (E1) Nose High Upset: Nose-down Input und Thrust-Reduktion erzeugen keine Nose-down Pitch Rate. Welche Massnahme sieht das OM-B vor?
antworten: Das Flugzeug 45° bis 60° rollen
Volles Seitenruder in eine Richtung
Gear ausfahren
Stabilizer Trim voll nose-down
fragen.erklaerung: Pitch kann dann durch Rollen auf 45° bis 60° (oder Beibehalten der Bank in einer Kurve) kontrolliert werden; übermässiger Trim/Rudder ist zu vermeiden.
fragen.quelle: OM-B E1 3.11.4 Nose High Recovery Maneuver, S. 3.11-3
fragen.zitat: pitch may be controlled by rolling the airplane 45° to 60°
kontext:
3.11.4 Nose High Recovery Maneuver

A large out-of-trim condition could be encountered if the autopilot is disengaged.
If the autopilot and autothrottle are responding correctly to stop the divergence, keep them engaged.

If required, the PF should disengage the autopilot and autothrottle and the PM should confirm that they are disengaged. The PM should monitor attitude and

speed of the airplane throughout the recovery and announce any continued divergence.

The PF should apply as much nose-down pitch control and incremental trim input(s) as required to obtain a nose-down pitch rate. Excessive use of pitch down trim can make the recovery phase of the upset more difficult.
If necessary, the PF should reduce thrust to help achieving a nose-down pitch rate. Thrust should only be reduced to the point where control of the pitch is achieved.

If nose-down/thrust inputs are not successful in achieving a nose-down pitch rate,
pitch may be controlled by rolling the airplane 45° to 60°,

or maintain the bank angle if in a turn, until pitch angle is reduced.

Recover to level flight may require use of pitch trim to manage control forces during large airspeed changes. Pilots should monitor pitch command to avoid entering a stall due to premature recovery at low speed or excessive load factor

at high speed.
WARNING: Excessive use of pitch trim or rudder may increase the upset divergence or may result in high structural loads.

fragen.frage_en: (E1) Nose high upset: Nose-down input and thrust reduction do not produce a nose-down pitch rate. Which measure does the OM-B provide?
antworten_en: Roll the aircraft 45° to 60°
Full rudder in one direction
Extend the gear
Stabilizer trim full nose-down
fragen.erklaerung_en: Pitch can then be controlled by rolling to 45° to 60° (or maintaining the bank in a turn); excessive trim/rudder is to be avoided.

fragen.frage: (E1) Unreliable Airspeed: Welche Systeme müssen getrennt werden?
antworten: Nur der Autopilot
Autothrottle und Autopilot
Flight Director und Yaw Damper
Nur der Autothrottle
fragen.erklaerung: AT und AP nutzen die Speed-Anzeige für ihre Regelung und müssen getrennt werden; auch der FD kann unzuverlässig sein.
fragen.zitat: When this scenario occurs the Autothrottle and Autopilot must be disengaged,
kontext:
3.7.4 Unreliable airspeed

Unreliable airspeed indications are usually associated with partial loss of the pitot static system. It may happen when there is blocking, damage, or freeze as well as deterioration of system parts.
The flight crew can recognize an unusual indication by monitoring airspeed indications and crosschecking PFD 1, 2 and IESS. IAS and ALT miscompare monitor annunciations can also be used to aid pilots to identify this condition.
When this scenario occurs the Autothrottle and Autopilot must be disengaged,

since these systems use the airspeed indications to adjust their gains. The Flight Director may be also unreliable and should not be followed.
With the Autothrottle and Autopilot disengaged, the crew must maintain proper

control of the airplane using pitch attitude and power settings.

QRH - Emergency and Abnormal Procedures sections present Unreliable Airspeed tables to be used on each flight phase.

The use of Speedbrake should be avoided since the capacity of the flight crew to

monitor the speed change might be compromised.

Under an Unreliable Airspeed scenario, the Flight Path Angle (FPA) on PFD, Flight Path Vector (FPV) on HGS, Altitude, and Vertical Speed indications may

also be unreliable.
Ground Speed indication available on PFD and GPS altitude may also be used

as reference if PFD indication is unreliable.

At pilot’s discretion, when the airplane is stabilized under correct pitch attitude and power setting, instruments should be crosschecked to help identify any

possible reliable instrument. In case a reliable source is identified, ADS reversion

may be attempted.
fragen.frage_en: (E1) Unreliable airspeed: Which systems must be disconnected?
antworten_en: Only the autopilot
Autothrottle and autopilot
Flight director and yaw damper
Only the autothrottle
fragen.erklaerung_en: AT and AP use the speed indication for their control and must be disconnected; the FD may also be unreliable.

fragen.frage: (E1) Warum soll bei Unreliable Airspeed die Speedbrake vermieden werden?
antworten: Weil die Fähigkeit der Crew, die Speed-Änderung zu überwachen, beeinträchtigt sein kann
Weil sie den Stall Warning Margin verschiebt
Weil sie im Direct Mode nicht funktioniert
Weil sie die Pitot-Sonden stört
fragen.erklaerung: Die Speedbrake ist zu vermeiden, da die Crew die resultierende Speed-Änderung nicht zuverlässig überwachen kann.
fragen.zitat: The use of Speedbrake should be avoided since the capacity of the flight crew to monitor the speed change might be compromised.

fragen.frage_en: (E1) Why should the speedbrake be avoided in case of unreliable airspeed?
antworten_en: Because the crew's ability to monitor the speed change may be impaired
Because it shifts the stall warning margin
Because it does not work in direct mode
Because it disturbs the pitot probes
fragen.erklaerung_en: The speedbrake is to be avoided because the crew cannot reliably monitor the resulting speed change.

fragen.frage: (E1) Die Overspeed Aural Warning hat im Flug ausgelöst. Wer entscheidet über die Freigabe des Flugzeugs ohne Maintenance Action?
antworten: Der Commander nach eigener Prüfung
Der Flight Operations Duty Officer
MCC, das in jedem Fall kontaktiert werden muss
Die lokale Line Maintenance ohne MCC
fragen.erklaerung: Der finale Entscheid liegt bei MCC; MCC muss in jedem Fall kontaktiert werden (max. KIAS, Flaps-Stellung, Dauer).
fragen.quelle: OM-B E1 3.13.1 Over Speed Aural Warning Triggered, S. 3.13-2
fragen.zitat: The final decision to release the aircraft back to service without maintenance action will be made by MCC. Therefore, MCC must be contacted in any case.
kontext:
3.13.1 Over Speed Aural Warning Triggered

This procedure gives guidance to the crew when the over speed aural warning has been triggered during the flight. The aircraft can be released back to service without any maintenance action if certain conditions are met.

The final decision to release the aircraft back to service without maintenance action will be made

by MCC. Therefore, MCC must be contacted in any case.
fragen.frage_en: (E1) The overspeed aural warning activated in flight. Who decides on release of the aircraft without maintenance action?
antworten_en: The Commander after his own assessment
The Flight Operations Duty Officer
MCC, which must be contacted in every case
Local line maintenance without MCC
fragen.erklaerung_en: The final decision rests with MCC; MCC must be contacted in every case (max. KIAS, flap setting, duration).

fragen.frage: (E1) Was ist bei Aktivierung der Low Speed Aural Warning zu tun?
antworten: Thrust erhöhen und, falls nötig und möglich, Pitch reduzieren
Sofort die Stall Recovery einleiten
Flaps um eine Stufe ausfahren
Speedbrake einfahren und AP trennen
fragen.erklaerung: Low Speed Aural Warning: Thrust zur Speed-Zunahme setzen, ggf. Pitch reduzieren; erst bei Stick Shaker die Stall Recovery einleiten.
fragen.quelle: OM-B E1 3.12.4 Low Speed Aural Warning, S. 3.12-5
fragen.zitat: Upon low speed aural warning activation, the flight crew shall apply thrust to increase airspeed and, if required and conditions permit, reduce pitch angle.
kontext:
3.12.4 Low Speed Aural Warning

The Low Speed Aural Warning indicates a low energy condition.

Upon low speed aural warning activation, the flight crew shall apply thrust to

increase airspeed and, if required and conditions permit, reduce pitch angle.

The low speed aural alert is inhibited when a high thrust setting is selected.

If stick shaker is activated, the stall recovery maneuver shall be initiated.
fragen.frage_en: (E1) What is to be done when the low speed aural warning activates?
antworten_en: Increase thrust and, if necessary and possible, reduce pitch
Immediately initiate stall recovery
Extend flaps by one step
Retract speedbrake and disconnect AP
fragen.erklaerung_en: Low speed aural warning: set thrust to increase speed, reduce pitch if applicable; initiate stall recovery only at stick shaker.

fragen.frage: (E1) Eine Störung, die eine Crew-Aktion erfordert, tritt unter IMC unterhalb von 1000 ft AFE im Approach auf. Was sieht das OM-B vor?
antworten: Approach fortsetzen und nach dem Landing QRH abarbeiten
Approach auf CAT I downgraden
Nur bei Warnings einen Go-around
Go-around
fragen.erklaerung: Jede Störung mit erforderlicher Crew-Aktion unter 1000 ft AFE in IMC soll zu einem Go-around führen.
fragen.quelle: OM-B E1 3.0.3 Malfunctions during Approach, S. 3.0-4
fragen.zitat: Any airplane malfunction requiring crew action below 1000 ft AFE under IMC should lead to a go-around.
kontext: 2.5.3.5.5 Malfunctions

Any airplane malfunction requiring crew action below 1000 ft AFE under IMC

should lead to a go-around.

Malfunctions above 1000 ft AFE must be evaluated by the crew. It should lead to a go-around if necessary procedures cannot be completed before reaching 1000 ft.

Note: In case of any failure that affects the flight director approach mode or the ability to continue the same approach category, the decision to continue on a downgraded approach category must be made if approach minimums have been set at or above 500 ft AFE.

In case of go-around, follow the normal go-around procedure. A new approach may only be performed when the appropriate action is

accomplished and malfunction consequences properly evaluated.
Following an Autothrottle failure below 500 ft, the approach may be continued if the airspeed is under control and stabilized.
fragen.frage_en: (E1) A malfunction requiring crew action occurs in IMC below 1000 ft AFE on approach. What does the OM-B provide?
antworten_en: Continue the approach and work through the QRH after landing
Downgrade the approach to CAT I
Go-around only for warnings
Go-around
fragen.erklaerung_en: Any malfunction requiring crew action below 1000 ft AFE in IMC should result in a go-around.

fragen.frage: (E1) Ein im Flug zurückgesetzter Circuit Breaker springt erneut heraus. Was gilt?
antworten: Ein zweiter Reset ist nach 2 Minuten Abkühlzeit erlaubt
Reset nur mit MCC-Freigabe
Kein weiterer Reset-Versuch
Reset erlaubt, wenn die QRH das System als essentiell einstuft
fragen.erklaerung: CBs werden im Flug nur zurückgesetzt, wenn für den sicheren Abschluss des Fluges zwingend oder von der Checkliste verlangt; springt er erneut, kein weiterer Versuch.
fragen.quelle: OM-B E1 3.1 Circuit Breaker Reset, S. 3.1-1
fragen.zitat: Should the circuit breaker trip again, no further attempt should be made to reset that circuit breaker.
kontext:
3.1 Circuit Breaker Reset

A tripped circuit breaker is usually a result of an abnormality in the electrical load or in associated wiring. Circuit breakers must not be reset in-flight, unless it is imperative to reset the circuit breaker for the safe completion of the flight.

Should the circuit breaker trip again, no further attempt should be made to reset that

circuit breaker.
The reset of a circuit breaker is also permitted were the checklist specifically directs to do so.
fragen.frage_en: (E1) A circuit breaker reset in flight trips again. What applies?
antworten_en: A second reset is permitted after 2 minutes of cooling time
Reset only with MCC approval
No further reset attempt
Reset permitted if the QRH classifies the system as essential
fragen.erklaerung_en: CBs are reset in flight only if essential for safe completion of the flight or required by the checklist; if it trips again, no further attempt.

fragen.frage: (E1) Ohne Performance Tool wird die VAP für einen Abnormal-Approach bestimmt. Welches Maximum gilt auf trockener Runway?
antworten: VREF NEW + 10 kt
VREF NEW + 5 kt
VREF NEW + 15 kt
VREF NEW + 20 kt
fragen.erklaerung: VAP = VREF NEW + 1/2 Headwind + Gust, limitiert auf +10 kt (dry) bzw. +20 kt (nicht trocken oder Autoland).
fragen.quelle: OM-B E1 3.0.4 Approach and Landing Speeds for Abnormal Conditions, S. 3.0-5
fragen.zitat: VAP = V REF NEW + 10 kt on dry runways
kontext:
3.0.4 Approach and Landing Speeds for Abnormal Conditions

For approach and landing speeds determination, the performance tool (ePerf) shall be used as the primary calculation method.
If the performance tool is unavailable, the VREF, VAC, and VFS speeds are presented in the QRH.

VREF Setting for Abnormal Conditions

If the performance tool is unavailable, a new VREF must be defined with information derived from the QRH:

VREF NEW VREF FLAPS FULL abnormal speed correction

VAP Setting for Abnormal Conditions The recommended method for approach speed calculation is to add one half of the steady headwind component plus the gust increment above the steady wind to the reference speed:

VAP VREF NEW 1/2 steady headwind component gust increment

The VAP is limited to: minimum: VAP VREF NEW 0 kt

maximum:
VAP V REF NEW 10 kt on dry runways

or

VAP V REF NEW 20 kt on other than dry runways

or VAP V REF NEW 20 kt when performing Autoland on wet or dry runways

VAC Setting for Abnormal Conditions

If the performance tool is unavailable, for landing in abnormal conditions, VAC

shall be set to the highest of:
fragen.frage_en: (E1) Without a performance tool, the VAP for an abnormal approach is determined. What maximum applies on a dry runway?
antworten_en: VREF NEW + 10 kt
VREF NEW + 5 kt
VREF NEW + 15 kt
VREF NEW + 20 kt
fragen.erklaerung_en: VAP = VREF NEW + 1/2 headwind + gust, limited to +10 kt (dry) or +20 kt (not dry or autoland).

fragen.frage: (E1) Bis zu welchem Fuel Imbalance ohne EICAS-Meldung darf die Korrektur gemäss OM-B als Normal Procedure (ohne QRH) betrachtet werden?
fragen.erklaerung: Ein Imbalance ohne EICAS-Meldung bis 360 kg (800 lb) gilt als Normal Procedure; vor Crossfeed ist ein Fuel Leak auszuschliessen.
fragen.zitat: exceeded 360 kg (800 lb) may be considered a normal procedure.
kontext:
2.4.1.7 Fuel Imbalance

Fuel efficiency can be affected as primary control surfaces are deflected to compensate for the imbalance condition.
A fuel imbalance for which no EICAS message is displayed and has not yet
exceeded 360 kg (800 lb) may be considered a normal procedure.

It does not

require the use of the QRH. However, it is recommended to assure no fuel leak is in place.

This can be done by comparing both fuel quantity indications on EICAS with fuel remaining information indication on FMS before attempting a fuel crossfeed.

Note: If the FUEL IMBALANCE caution message is not displayed on the EICAS and a crossfeed is performed, the advisory message FUEL EQUAL - CROSSFEED OPEN is displayed regardless of the imbalance value.
It may lead to an extra imbalance condition.
fragen.frage_en: (E1) Up to what fuel imbalance without EICAS message may correction be considered a normal procedure (without QRH) according to OM-B?
fragen.erklaerung_en: An imbalance without EICAS message up to 360 kg (800 lb) is considered a normal procedure; a fuel leak must be ruled out before crossfeed.

fragen.frage: (E1) Welche maximale Querneigung gilt beim Manövrieren zum Landing mit Abnormal Slat/Flap Configuration?
fragen.erklaerung: Abnormal Slat/Flap: Bank max. 20°, langes Final mind. 8 NM, AP empfohlen, Gewicht reduzieren.
fragen.quelle: OM-B E1 3.7.2 Abnormal Slat / Flap Configuration, S. 3.7-2
fragen.zitat: limit bank angle to 20° maximum when maneuvering for landing
kontext:
3.7.2 Abnormal Slat Flap Configuration

If flap or slat fails at a specific position, select the desired flap or slat position and use data according to QRH configuration tables. The best performance combination of Slat/Flap is the one that results in the lowest speed.

The following items are valid for all abnormal Slat/Flap configuration approaches and landings:

use of autopilot is recommended

if possible reduce gross weight to lowest practicable (burn off fuel) to

reduce VREF

check landing distance (select the longest runway available)
limit bank angle to 20° maximum when maneuvering for landing

establish a long final approach, at least 8 NM at recommended speed

attitude and speed are higher than normal

establish landing configuration early, flight large patterns and long final

plan touchdown at 1000 ft touchdown zone, a go-around should be

made if landing occurs beyond touchdown zone flare enough just to reduce the rate of descent, do not float and touchdown at the normal touchdown zone

over threshold set thrust levers to IDLE

after touchdown, apply forward control column, reverse thrust and

brakes without delay
fragen.frage_en: (E1) What maximum bank angle applies when manoeuvring for landing with abnormal slat/flap configuration?
fragen.erklaerung_en: Abnormal slat/flap: bank max. 20°, long final at least 8 NM, AP recommended, reduce weight.

fragen.frage: (E1) Wo befindet sich die Least Risk Bomb Location (LRBL)?
antworten: Vorne links bei der Door 1L
Hinten rechts beim letzten Fenster
Hinten, möglichst nahe der Mitte des zweitletzten Fensters auf der linken Seite
Im Bereich der Overwing Exits rechts
fragen.erklaerung: Die LRBL liegt hinten, möglichst nahe der Mitte des zweitletzten Fensters auf der linken Flugzeugseite.
fragen.quelle: OM-B E1 3.16 Least Risk Bomb Location (LRBL), S. 3.16-1
fragen.zitat: as close as possible to the center of the second-last window on the airplane left side.
kontext:
3.16 Least Risk Bomb Location (LRBL)

The location inside the airplane’s cabin where structural or system damage are least likely to jeopardize flight safety. The Least Risk Location (LRBL) is sited aft,
as close as possible to the center of the second-last window on the airplane left side.
fragen.frage_en: (E1) Where is the Least Risk Bomb Location (LRBL)?
antworten_en: Forward left at door 1L
Aft right at the last window
Aft, as close as possible to the centre of the second-to-last window on the left side
In the area of the overwing exits on the right
fragen.erklaerung_en: The LRBL is located aft, as close as possible to the centre of the second-to-last window on the left side of the aircraft.

fragen.frage: (E1) Am Boden zeigt sich Rauch/Feuer im Cargo Compartment bei geschlossener Cargo Door. Was gilt gemäss OM-B?
antworten: Cargo Door nicht öffnen; Passagiere disembarken (oder evakuieren) und Ground Crew informieren
Cargo Door öffnen, um die Quelle zu lokalisieren
Sofort beide Cargo Extinguisher auslösen und Door öffnen
Nur die Cargo Door entriegeln, damit die Feuerwehr Zugang hat
fragen.erklaerung: Bei geschlossener Tür darf sie nicht geöffnet werden; alle Passagiere müssen aussteigen bzw. evakuiert werden und die Ground Crew ist zu informieren.
fragen.quelle: OM-B E1 3.5.1 On Ground Cargo Compartment Smoke or Fire, S. 3.5-1
fragen.zitat: cargo door is closed, the cargo compartment door must not be opened.
kontext:
3.5.1 On Ground Cargo Compartment Smoke or Fire

In case of cargo compartment smoke or fire conditions are presented and the
cargo door is closed, the cargo compartment door must not be opened.

All passengers are required to be disembarked (or evacuated) and the ground crew must be communicated to evaluate the condition and take the appropriate actions.
Additionally, in case the cargo compartment doors are opened on ground and fire

conditions are presented, the crew is recommended not to actuate the fire extinguishers before coordinating with ground crew to investigate and eliminate the fire source, according to company policy and local authorities rules.
fragen.frage_en: (E1) On the ground, smoke/fire appears in the cargo compartment with the cargo door closed. What applies according to OM-B?
antworten_en: Do not open the cargo door; disembark passengers (or evacuate) and inform ground crew
Open the cargo door to locate the source
Immediately discharge both cargo extinguishers and open the door
Only unlock the cargo door so that the fire brigade has access
fragen.erklaerung_en: With the door closed it must not be opened; all passengers must disembark or be evacuated and the ground crew must be informed.

fragen.frage: (E1) Welcher Vertical Mode wird für den Emergency Descent mit Autopilot empfohlen?
antworten: VNAV
FLCH
V/S
FPA
fragen.erklaerung: FLCH ist wegen Airspeed- und Altitude-Protection und geringer Arbeitslast der empfohlene Mode.
fragen.zitat: FLCH mode is recommended vertical mode due to airspeed and altitude protection, as well as low crew workload.
kontext:
DESCENDING WITH AUTOPILOT ENGAGED

Use of automated resources is recommended.
FLCH mode is recommended vertical mode due to airspeed and altitude protection, as well as low crew workload.

If crew performs an emergency descent, alert the maneuver via PA. Select

10000 ft ASL or MEA, whichever is higher, and select FLCH. If VNAV is engaged, press VNAV button on the guidance panel, and then press FLCH.

Set or verify thrust levers IDLE and extend speedbrake. Select SPEED Knob to MANUAL and target speed to maximum appropriate. If structural integrity is in

doubt, especially after an explosive depressurization, use flight controls with

care, and maintain current speed.
Crew must descend straight ahead or initiate turn with maximum 30° bank. HDG mode can be used to turn the airplane off the airway, it is recommended to start a turn before commencing the Emergency Descent.

kontext:
LOSS OF ALTITUDE

If descending due to cabin depressurization, the crew members should don masks and establish communication immediately.
Opening the mask stowage box automatically initiates the oxygen flow. Pressing the harness inflation control valve inflates the harness, enabling its quick donning. Releasing the button deflates the harness firmly fitting it to the head.
The mask is designed to be donned within 5 seconds.
When the oxygen mask stowage box is opened the mask microphone is

automatically activated and the headset boom microphone is deactivated.
The speakers are also automatically activated and the communication reception is possible through the speakers or the headsets.

Oxygen masks are operated at three selectable modes: The NORMAL provides supplemental oxygen, diluted with cabin air. It is capable to maintain a safe

physiologic level until a preset altitude, where the user inhales 100% oxygen.
The 100% mode is mandatory during an emergency descent,

as it is not diluted

with cabin air, regardless cabin altitude. The EMER mode is useful to remove

smoke and fumes, as it is no diluted oxygen regardless of cabin altitude with a slightly positive pressure. When the mask is on emergency mode, the air pressure and flow make communication more difficult. To avoid communication

disruption, it is recommended not to use the EMER setting continuously. Select

the mode back to 100% or Normal after the mask is clear of smoke, fumes, or condensation.

Once mask usage is not necessary, pilots must close the oxygen mask stowage box and press reset button, enabling hand/headset microphone booms.

kontext:
“BRACE, BRACE”.

Plan to land with maximum flap available and burn off fuel to a minimum onboard to increase buoyancy. Leave the gear UP.

Consider landing parallel to waves taking in account wind direction and sea

condition.
If at all possible, land parallel to the swell, not across it.

The best location is along the crest of the swell which minimizes the chance of a

wingtip digging into the water. Second best is in the trough or bottom of the swell.

Maintain airspeed at VREF and 200 - 300 ft/min rate of descent or as low as possible. Rotate smoothly the attitude (approx 10° to 12° nose up) during flare and keep flying the airplane at all times until touchdown. After touchdown, reduce thrust to idle. If engine is not running, maintain minimum speed of 130 KIAS.
After the airplane has come to rest, proceed to assigned ditching stations and evacuate as soon as possible, assuring that all passengers are out of the

airplane. Note that entry into water is always considered "catastrophic" and the cabin crew can initiate evacuation without further instructions from the flight

deck.

fragen.zitat: E195-E1: 1.5 units nose up re-trimming
kontext:
2.3.3.3.1 General

Before the takeoff sequence, the flight crew shall have the Before Takeoff Checklist completed thoroughly.

In order not to interfere with takeoff preparations, perform the departure and takeoff briefing before starting the engines.

Different techniques are used in the takeoff phase. The definitions of the types

used in the day by day operation are described in the next chapters.

2.3.3.3.1.1 Stabilizer Trim Setting for Takeoff

The E1 variants show a nose down tendency after lift-off. This tendency is more distinctive on the E195-E1.
Reasonable re-trim values:
E190-E1 0.5 units nose up re-trimming
E195-E1: 1.5 units nose up re-trimming

Background information:
The certified take-off stabiliser trim setting is a compromise of different factors:

AEO initial climb

OEI initial climb

nose wheel controllability during engine failure below V1

Therefore, a requirement for a certain amount of retrimming to maintain V2+10 during take-off is a normal and expected behaviour.

The nose down tendency position of the stabiliser helps to improve the grip of

the nose wheels and thus the controllability in an engine out condition during take-off roll.

Due to the different aircraft geometries, the behavior among the variants is

different.

kontext:
2.3.3.3.7 Flex Takeoff

This method is also known as assumed temperature takeoff thrust.
A Takeoff with less thrust than the maximum takeoff thrust is used.
When operating with flex takeoff thrust, thrust setting parameters used to establish thrust for takeoff are not considered as operating limits.

If REF ATTCS (on takeoff data setting) is set to ON and one of the following events occurs, flex takeoff is canceled and ATTCS automatically commands RSV

thrust:

Difference between both engine N1 values is greater than 15%

OEI (One Engine Inoperative)

Thrust levers are moved to MAX detent

Windshear is detected

When used with derated takeoff thrust, this method provides larger thrust reductions and may increase engine life. Less severe operation means lower:
Fuel flow degradation rate, reducing fuel burn over the on-wing life of engine

Inter Turbine Temperature (ITT) degradation rate (Increases time-on-wing)

Maintenance costs, reducing shop visit rate and cost per shop visit Note:
The use of this method is prohibited on contaminated runways.

kontext:
2.5.1.2.3 Instrument Approaches

Approximately 50 NM before descent, pilots should perform the approach briefing.
It is recommended to set instruments before the briefing.

For items to be covered by the briefing, refer to OM-A 8.3.2.26 Approach Briefing.

Pilots must keep close attention to the altitude and speed restrictions according

to the charts. Some airports are provided with contingency and special

procedures.

Based on the information available, like NOTAMs, weather reports, forecast, ATC reports, PIREPs, the crew should calculate the landing distance for the current conditions. Compare the calculated distance with the runway distance available.
If conditions change during descent and approach, the crew should consider recalculating the required landing distance. At pilot’s discretion, reassess the conditions and evaluate if a maximum performance landing should be considered.
Speeds are set according to the weight and flap selection, considering weather status (CAT II, ice conditions and so on).
On the FPL page, the waypoint altitude constraint during descent must be assigned as DES. The Constraint type is displayed directly above altitude constraints. The FMS automatically assigns constraints in the first half of the flight plan as climb (CLB). Those in the last half are assigned as descent (DES).

If necessary, the pilots can change the constraint type. For climb constraints, C and CLB are accepted pilot entries. For descent constraints, D or DES are accepted pilot entries.
Select the Autobrake according to runway conditions and type of operation. The

use of Thrust Reversers must be briefed to decide which taxiway is supposed to

be used to vacate the runway. Pilots must evaluate special runway conditions,

like slippery and contaminated. In case the crew plans to use additional speed

for the approach due to wind gusts on surface, the landing distance is increased.
It is necessary to discuss the outcome on the landing distance during the

approach briefing.

Airplane status and operational restrictions must be discussed during the briefing. If any failure that affects the required landing distance occurs in the final

approach, consider a missed approach. Evaluate the situation and the runway length available. Failures that affect the landing distance are commonly

associated to brakes, ground spoilers, and thrust reversers.

Perform an instrument crosscheck as soon as cleared by ATC to intercept the final approach course. Crosscheck radios and minimums for that specific approach. For far ILS captures, verify if intercepted course is in accordance with

the MARKERS indications and the PFD MAP display. If any discrepancy is

found, disengage the AP and take the appropriate corrective action.

2.5.8.3 Go-Around

No approach should be initiated unless the prevailing conditions have been understood and the crew found that landing is acceptable without undue risk.
Philosophically all approaches should be treated as approaches followed by missed approaches, and landing should be treated as the alternate procedure.
This mindset depends on a good approach briefing, on the knowledge of the

missed approach procedure and on proper programming of the FMS.

Enough visual cues must exist to continue the approach below DA(DH) or MDA.
If visual cues are lost due to shallow fog, snow flurries, or heavy precipitation,

immediately initiate a go-around and fly the published missed approach procedure.

Although the PF is initially the responsible for the go-around callout, the PM may also make this callout. The PF immediate response to this callout by the PM is execution of a missed approach.
Go around, when properly executed, involve little loss of altitude below the altitude at which the go-around is “started”.
Conducting a missed approach when not stabilized on a final approach course should be as follows: if a go-around is required at any time while maneuvering in the traffic pattern and visual conditions cannot be maintained, perform a climbing turn toward the runway of intended landing

when over the airport and climbing, turn (in the shortest direction) to the

missed approach fix and proceed with published procedure to initiate the go-around press TO/GA Button, ensure go-around thrust is set (TO/GA position) or manually apply go-around thrust. Verify FMA

annunciations (GA, TRACK, and GA). The TRACK mode is activated

when TO/GA Button is pressed and disengaged when another lateral mode becomes active. The selection of another vertical mode deactivates

the GA mode. An automatic go-around cannot be initiated after touch

down

the GA pitch mode initially commands a go-around attitude and then

transitions to speed as the rate of climb increases. The GA roll mode maintains existing ground track

rotate the airplane to the initial pitch of 8° nose up if flying manually or

follow the FD guidance and monitor the AP

select the flap according to the following table:

Landing Slat/Flap Go Around Slat/Flap

Maintain “Mode Awareness” by monitoring the FMA to determine the engaged pitch and roll modes. This check ensures that the correct mode is selected and is being reflected by the airplane behavior.

If MISSED APPR is activated, the missed approach procedure from the database is inserted into the FMS flight plan whenever the GA mode is active and the

kontext:
2.6.1.11 Rejected Landing

Rejected landing initiated prior to touchdown Press the TO/GA button, advance the thrust levers to TO/GA position and perform a go-around procedure. The go-around may result in a touchdown.
Rejected landing initiated after touchdown

Press the TO/GA button, advance the thrust levers to TO/GA position, disconnect Autopilot and Autothrottle, and perform a manual go-around procedure.
Ground spoilers retract and autobrake disarms as thrust levers are advanced for

a rejected landing initiated after touchdown.

If after touchdown thrust reverser is applied, a full stop landing must be

accomplished.

The thrust levers require time to transition from reverse to forward

thrust, and there is the possibility that it does not remain stowed in the forward thrust position.

Attention must be given to the intended flight path as the published missed

approach procedure may not be valid after passing the published missed approach point. Reengage the automation as required.

OM-B E1 2 Normal Procedures

fragen.frage: (E1) Was ist nach einem schweren Bounce beim Landing zu tun?
antworten: Landing-Attitude halten und mit Thrust weich aufsetzen

kontext:
2.6.1.12 Bounced Landing

The bouncing occurs more often during landings by one or a combination of the following factors:
Windshear

Low-level turbulence

High flare initiation

Excessive rate of descent

Late flare initiation

Incorrect flare technique

Excessive airspeed

Power on touchdown

The key factor for a successful landing is a stabilized approach and proper thrust/ flare coordination. Do not extend the flare at idle thrust as it significantly increases landing distance. Reducing to idle before the flare also requires an increase in pitch. Flaring high and quickly reducing thrust to idle can cause the airplane to settle abruptly.

Do not apply stabilizer trim during the flare.
Recovery from Light Bounce

When a light bounce occurs, maintain or re-establish a normal landing attitude.

Increasing pitch can lead to a tail strike. Beware of the increased landing distance and use power as required to soften the second touchdown.

It is difficult to evaluate landing distance remaining and the airplane energy.

Recovery from a Severe Bounce
When a more severe bounce occurs, initiate a go-around and do not attempt to land.

Press the TO/GA button and advance thrust levers to TO/GA.

Hold the flare attitude until the engines spool up and reset stabilizer trim, then follow normal go-around procedures.

If the airspeed drops below VREF, initiate a go-around procedure and retract the

flaps only when the airspeed becomes greater than VREF.

fragen.erklaerung_en: In case of a heavy bounce: initiate go-around (TO/GA), hold flare attitude until the engines spool up; no landing attempt.

kontext:
2.6.1.4.2 Emergency Parking Brake

Some Emergency and Abnormal procedures require the pilot to use the Emergency Parking Brake to stop the airplane during landing.
When this event happens, the following protections are not available:
Locked Wheel Protection,

Antiskid Protection, and

Touchdown Protection.

At high speeds, apply the Emergency Parking Brake handle to stop the airplane monitoring the Emergency Parking Brake light and maintain steady pressure.
The brake system provides enough pressure to start braking.
As speed decreases the required handle deflection increases to maintain continuous braking.
If a tire burst occurs applying the Emergency Parking Brake, do not release the Emergency Parking Brake handle until the airplane stops.
CAUTION: Avoid landing on runways with RWYCC 4 through 1.

For Emergency and Abnormal procedures that require the use of the Emergency/Parking Brake to stop the airplane, landing on contaminated runways (RWYCC 4 through 1) should be avoided, as the airplane may skid during landing roll. Such procedures only present landing performance data for RWYCC

6 (DRY) and 5 (GOOD).

kontext:
2.2.3.2.5 Abnormal Engine Start Indications

On ground, the FADEC provides automatic protection against starting failures and will automatically command an auto-restart in the event of an impending hot start, hung start or a failure to light. If the auto-restart attempt fails, the engine start will be automatically aborted by the FADEC.
Even with the protections provided by the FADEC, the engine start must be manually aborted when an Abnormal Engine Start indication is observed.

The Abnormal Engine Start indications are:
no positive oil pressure indication within 10 seconds after N2 speed starts to increase

there is no positive N1 speed indication after N2 reaches 45%

ITT exceeds start limit (Hot Start)

oil pressure stabilizes below the engine limits

an intermittent electrical, pneumatic, or starter malfunction occurs before the starter disengagement

Note: in case an automatic abort occurs or engine start is manually aborted due to abnormal engine indications, its cause must be investigated and corrected before further attempts to start the engines.

in case the engine start is manually aborted due to a hot start, an engine dry motoring is recommended.

one additional engine start is allowed if the FADEC commands an

automatic abort in case the N2 speed does not increase after the

START/STOP Selector is placed to the run position or the N2

speed begins to decrease before commanded fuel flow, provided “ENG 1(2) NO DISPATCH” or “ENG 1(2) SHORT DISPATCH”

EICAS messages are not displayed, nor are other abnormal parameters observed.

kontext:
2.3.1.6 Rudder Steering use and Turning Radius

For straight ahead taxiing or for small changes of direction, the use of rudder pedal steering mode may be used.
The maximum steering angle of rudder pedal is 7°.

Exercise care on the operation of the steering handle at speeds above 10 kt, as it’s very responsive.
Handwheel steering mode should be used for wider turn angles. To operate in this mode the handle must be kept pressed otherwise the system reverts to rudder pedals. Whenever the handle is pressed, the system reverts back to the handwheel steering.

The wheel deflection as function of handle deflection is not linear. For detailed information refer to AOM section 14-13.
Let the airplane move a little forward before starting a turn and avoid stopping the airplane in a turn as excessive thrust is required to start taxiing again. After

completing a turn and before stopping, center the nosewheel and allow the

airplane to roll straight ahead for a short distance.

Nosewheel skidding may occur with:

Excessive steering angle;

High taxi speed during turns;

On wet surfaces during turn.

When taxiing, make turns with the largest feasible turn radius possible. The minimum turn radius should still allow the tire closer to the center of the turn to continue rolling. When making a tight turn, the tires are subject to high lateral

loads and can experience damage. Asymmetric thrust may be used in tight turns to minimize side loads on gear and tires.

Minimize using thrust from outboard engine in 180° turn, particularly if outboard engine overhangs dusty areas next to the taxiway.
The tail tip or the wingtip, depending on each airplane model, have the largest arc while turning and determines the minimum obstruction clearance path.

2.3.1.7 180-Degree Turn

During the maneuver, maintain a ground speed around 5 kt. Exercise additional care on wet or contaminated runways, as tires may skid. Start aligned over the centerline and use the handwheel steering to turn the airplane left 30° in the direction of the runway edge. When LSP is over the runway edge apply progressively full right steering command. If necessary, use asymmetric thrust and/or differential braking. Once completed 180-degree turn, return the handwheel steering to the neutral position re-aligning the airplane with the centerline.
fragen.frage_en: (E2) What maximum nosewheel steering angle does rudder pedal steering allow?

60 KIAS

kontext:
2.3.3.3.7 Flex Takeoff

This method is also known as assumed temperature takeoff thrust.
A Takeoff with less thrust than the maximum takeoff thrust is used.
When operating with flex takeoff thrust, thrust setting parameters used to establish thrust for takeoff are not considered as operating limits.
If REF ATTCS (on takeoff data setting) is set to ON and one of the following events occurs, flex takeoff is canceled and ATTCS automatically commands RSV thrust:

difference between both engine N1 values is greater than 15%,

OEI (One Engine Inoperative),

thrust levers are moved to MAX detent,

windshear is detected.

When used with derated takeoff thrust, this method provides larger thrust reductions and may increase engine life. Less severe operation means lower: fuel flow degradation rate, reducing fuel burn over the on-wing life of engine,

Inter Turbine Temperature (ITT) degradation rate (Increases time-on-wing),

maintenance costs, reducing shop visit rate and cost per shop visit.
Note: The use of this method is prohibited on contaminated runways.

kontext:
TAIL STRIKE AVOIDANCE (TSA)

Tail Strike Avoidance (TSA) function is a fly-by-wire feature to avoid tail strikes.
During Takeoff TSA function controls airplane pitch angle by reducing control column authority in the nose up direction.

TSA function is not capable to protect the airplane from tail strikes in over abused rotation.
TSA function is enabled up to 30 ft during takeoff operation.

kontext:
2.3.3.3.6 Slat Flap Retraction

Flap retraction is accomplished after the specified acceleration altitude is reached. The minimum acceleration altitude for Slat/Flap retraction is 1000 ft.

The flaps should be retracted using the flap retraction speed “F-BUG” and pitch

angle adjusted to maintain a slight rate of climb. After Slat/Flap retraction is complete, accelerate to enroute climb speed.

During flap retraction, the next flap setting should be selected when the F-Bug is

reached.

The F-Bug calculation algorithm is designed so as to meet minimum safe margins to VFE and Shaker speed. A minimum margin of 20% above the stall

speed is set for the next flap.

In case of “F-BUG” disappears before total accomplishment of Slat/Flap

retraction, retract Slat/Flap following Green Dot +10 kt.

fragen.frage: (E2) Welches Noise Abatement Profil wird für den Takeoff verwendet, wenn kein anderes publiziert ist?

NADP 1
ICAO A

fragen.zitat: For take-off, noise abatement profile NADP 2 should be used unless a different profile is published.
kontext:
2.3.3.3.14 Noise Abatement Procedures

Noise abatement procedures minimize the overall exposure to noise on the ground and at the same time maintain the required levels of flight safety. There are several methods, including preferential runways and routes, as well as noise abatement procedures for takeoff and approach. The appropriateness of any of the procedures depends on the physical layout of the airport and its surroundings. In all cases give priority to safety considerations.
Pilots are required to adhere to the noise abatement procedures published specifically for each airport. There are different procedures for noise abatement, and the items listed here are just a guide to help pilots to perform a takeoff with noise reduction:
Set speed required for the procedure on SPEED Knob or on FMS DEPARTURE page. If using FMS SPEED, set 3000 ft as the vertical limit.
Use MCDU DEPARTURE LIMIT page to set the speed limit and VNAV engagement height. The DEPARTURE LIMIT page has the following fields:
Speed Limit: The crew should adjust this value to speed limit of the applicable noise abatement procedure,

AFE Limit: This field is used to enter the vertical limit of the departure area,

VNAV CAP AFE: This field is used to set the VNAV capture height.

Note: The FMS departure speed limit functionality commands the speed restriction during takeoff only when the airplane is flying below the vertical limit.

If an engine failure occurs, terminate the noise abatement procedure.

In this case, an engine failure procedure and profile should be performed.

Note: Some charts make reference to ICAO A or ICAO B procedures which are

similar to NADP 1 and NADP 2 respectively.

The characteristic difference between ICAO A and ICAO B, resides on the

location of the noise relief area. The difference is maintained for NADP 1 and NADP 2. ICAO A and NADP 1 are procedures to protect areas located close to

the airport. ICAO B and NADP 2 are procedures to protect areas located distant from the airport.

For take-off, noise abatement profile NADP 2 should be used unless a different

profile is published.

Information regarding noise abatement profiles can be found

in the Jeppesen route manual. The acceleration altitude shall be minimum 1000 ft AFE. The altitude and speed constraints on the departure route must be respected.
Refer to OM-A 8.3.2.17 - Flight Profiles Take-off

2.3.3.3.14.1 NADP 1 ICAO A Procedure

Climb at V2 +10 KIAS until 800 ft (NADP 1) or 1500 ft (ICAO A) AFE.

Verify VNAV engagement at the height set on MCDU: at or above 800 ft (NADP 1) or 1500 ft (ICAO A) AFE. Verify that climb thrust is set and continue climbing at V2 10 to 20 KIAS.

At 3000 ft AFE, the airplane is released from the speed limit. Accelerate and retract SLAT/FLAP on schedule or following the F-BUG.

2.3.3.3.14.2 NADP 2 ICAO B Procedure

Climb at V2 +10 KIAS until 800 ft (NADP 2) or 1000 ft (ICAO B) AFE.

Verify VNAV engagement at the height set on MCDU: at or above 800 ft (NADP 2) or 1000 ft (ICAO B) AFE.
Verify that climb thrust is set and maintain VFS 10 KIAS until 3000 ft

At 3000 ft AFE, accelerate to the enroute climb speed.

antworten_en: NADP 2
NADP 1
ICAO A
No profile, acceleration at discretion
fragen.erklaerung_en: The OM-B E2 prescribes NADP 2 as standard unless another profile is published; the acceleration altitude is at least 1000 ft AFE.

fragen.frage: (E2) Welcher Climb Thrust Mode wird standardmässig verwendet?
antworten: CLB-1, ausser bei Flex Takeoff
CON bis FL100, danach CLB-1
CLB-1 auf allen Strecken
CLB-2, ausser CLB-1 ist aus Performance-Gründen nötig
fragen.erklaerung: CLB-2 ist der Standard; CLB-1 nur, wenn es aus Performance-Gründen erforderlich ist.
fragen.zitat: CLB-2 shall be used for all routes unless CLB-1 is required for performance reasons.
kontext:
2.3.5.4.4 Climb Thrust Selection

The PW1900G Engines have two modes of climb thrust: CLB-1 and CLB-2.
CLB-2 shall be used for all routes unless CLB-1 is required for performance reasons.

The takeoff thrust is automatically changed to climb thrust when a vertical mode, like VNAV or FLCH, is engaged. Throughout the flight, the FADEC automatically maintains the correct thrust setting.

Note: For takeoffs with autothrottle OFF, after the engagement of the first vertical mode, during the initial CLIMB, the EICAS indicates CLB-1 or CLB-2, while the takeoff thrust remains at TO/GA. In order to change the thrust from TO/GA to CLIMB, reduce thrust levers from TO/GA until matching the climb thrust N1 target shown on EICAS. Then, keep following the N1 target shown on EICAS during the remainder of the climb.

When the takeoff thrust is lower than climb thrust, if one thrust lever is reduced to outside of the takeoff flat region while the other is not, one engine remains at TO thrust and the other accelerates to CLB thrust, resulting in a N1 asymmetry. The flight crew can correct the asymmetry by reducing the affected engine thrust lever until matching the climb thrust N1 target shown on EICAS. Once asymmetry is corrected, use

thrust levers and autothrottle as required.

E190-E2 models (1)

CLB-1 and CLB-2 thrust ratings change with altitude

after takeoff, CLB-1 provides higher climb thrust than CLB-2

at high altitudes, CLB-2 provides higher climb thrust than CLB-1

Note 1: During flight, changing the climb mode is not recommended, as it

will reduce engine lifetime and increase maintenance costs.

E195-E2 models CLB-1: maximum climb rate

CLB-2: climb thrust derated from CLB-1
fragen.frage_en: (E2) Which climb thrust mode is used by default?
antworten_en: CLB-1, except for flex takeoff
CON up to FL100, then CLB-1
CLB-1 on all routes
CLB-2, unless CLB-1 is required for performance reasons
fragen.erklaerung_en: CLB-2 is the standard; CLB-1 only if required for performance reasons.

fragen.frage: (E2) Wie ist VAP für Normal Operations begrenzt?
antworten: Minimum VREF, maximum VREF + 10 kt
Minimum VREF + 5 kt, maximum VREF + 20 kt
Minimum VREF + 5 kt, maximum VREF + 15 kt
Minimum VREF + 10 kt, maximum VREF + 25 kt
fragen.erklaerung: VAP = VREF + halber Steady Headwind + Gust-Inkrement, begrenzt auf VREF + 5 kt bis VREF + 20 kt.
fragen.zitat: minimum of VREF + 5 kt maximum of VREF + 20 kt.
kontext:
2.5.1.3 Approach and Landing Speeds

For approach and landing speeds determination, ePerf shall be used as the primary calculation method.
If ePerf is unavailable the VREF, VAC and VFS speeds are presented in the QRH Approach and Landing Speed tables.
VAP is determined based on VREF, considering the wind corrections.

Note: Performance values calculated by the CAFM consider the threshold

is passed at the screen height with VREF.

For Normal Operations VAP is used until 50 ft.
The speed increment to VREF depends on the corrections described in the paragraph VAP Setting for Normal Operations and shall be considered for landing performance calculations.

Anytime the EICAS message STALL PROT ICE SPEED remains displayed during approach on normal or abnormal conditions, the speeds must be adjusted for ice accretion.

VAP Setting for Normal Operation The recommended method for approach speed calculation is to add one half of the steady headwind component plus the gust increment above the steady wind

to the reference speed:
VAP VREF 1/2 steady headwind component gust increment

The VAP is limited to:

(1)

minimum of VREF 5 kt

maximum of VREF 20 kt.

Note 1: A maximum performance landing acc. to 2.6.1.6 - Maximum Performance Landing may be considered, if the landing distance

is limiting.

The following table shows examples of VAP calculation:
Winds Wind Correction Approach Speed (VAP) 8 kt Headwind 4 kt VREF 5 kt 20 kt Headwind 35 kt Gust 10 kt 15 kt VREF 20 kt 10 kt Crosswind 25 kt 0 kt 15 kt VREF 15 kt Gust 10 kt Tailwind 0 kt VREF 5 kt

Note: The VAP does not consider wind corrections for tailwind. The tailwind component and any additive to the VREF must be considered in the landing distance calculations.

In case of limiting runway length consider Maximum Performance Landing Technique, as described in 2.6.1.6 - Maximum Performance Landing.

For abnormal conditions refer to 3.0.4 - Approach and Landing Speeds for Abnormal Conditions.

VAC Setting

For landings in abnormal conditions, set VAC equal to the higher between new VREF and VAC from the approach and landing speeds table.

antworten_en: Minimum VREF, maximum VREF + 10 kt

Minimum VREF + 10 kt, maximum VREF + 25 kt

fragen.frage: (E2) Welche Flaps-Stellung muss verwendet werden, wenn zwischen Flaps 3 und Landing Flaps FULL eine Zwischenstellung nötig ist?

Flaps 3 beibehalten

fragen.zitat: the intermediate flap setting must be flaps 4.
kontext:
FLAPS MANEUVERING SPEEDS

Note: the Flaps Maneuvering Speeds provide at least 1.3 g margin over stick shaker speed, which is equivalent to a shaker-free bank angle of 40°. These speeds ensure such margin for all weights up to the Maximum Landing Weight, with or without ice accretion.

if using FMS speeds, waypoint speed constraints take priority over approach speeds, and the FMS can command speeds below the Green Dot and Flap Maneuvering Speeds.

To avoid reaching speeds above VFE, the following recommendations also apply: use F-Bug for flap retraction

use Green Dot as the reference for flaps extension.
When not possible to decelerate to Green Dot, Green Dot 20 kt can be used. It guarantees enough margin to the VFE of next flap position

avoid retracting or extending flaps when closer to VFE (i.e. greater than Vfe -10 kts)

initiate the descent before or at the calculated Top of Descent (TOD) to allow room for deceleration

2.5.1.2.2.3 Flaps Choice The use of flaps 5 provides lower fuel consumption and reduced approach noise levels. In a comparison, a final approach segment with flaps 5 burns 10 kg less

than a flaps FULL landing.

Consider using flaps FULL when the field length requires its use. Additional

runway limitations, such as known slippery conditions may require its use.

Also consider flaps FULL when the STALL PROT ICE SPEED is present in the

EICAS (even without actual icing conditions).
If an intermediate flap setting between flaps 3 and landing flaps FULL is required,
the intermediate flap setting must be flaps 4.

Moreover, the use flap 5 as an intermediate flap is not recommended since this setting triggers the landing logic which automatically sets the approach speed for

flaps FULL if the FMS speed control is in use. This scenario could lead to an undesired aircraft state.

Note: At flight crews discretion the moment of flap and gear extension may be

delayed as long as the stabilised approach criteria are met. For

reference refer to the flight patterns of the 3D- and 2D-Approaches.

Flaps 2
Flaps 4

fragen.frage: (E2) Bis wann muss das Flugzeug bei einem ILS CAT I mit Gear down und Landing Flaps konfiguriert sein (auch bei Far ILS Captures)?
antworten: Vor 1000 ft AFE
Vor 500 ft AFE

fragen.zitat: the airplane must be configured with gear down and landing flaps before 1000 ft AFE.
kontext:
2.5.3.3 ILS CAT I

When performing an ILS CAT I, use the autopilot and autothrottle to minimize crew workload.
Following technique is recommended:
When starting the deceleration segment, approaching the airport while either being radar vectored or using own navigation, slow the airplane to 210 KIAS. At base leg, select flap 1 reducing to flap 1 maneuvering speed. When maneuvering to intercept the localizer, select flap 2 reducing to flap 2

maneuvering speed.
When cleared for the approach and with the airplane established on an intercept heading of less than 90° of the inbound track, select the APPR mode on the guidance panel. It arms the LOC and GS. Set the required vertical speed using VNAV/FPA/FLCH or VS to capture the glideslope.
Once captured, the glideslope becomes active. Set the go-around altitude on the Guidance Panel. When on final inbound, extend landing gear, select flap 3 reducing to flap 3 maneuvering speed.
Before 1000 ft AFE, select landing flaps, reducing to the VAP. For far ILS captures, the gear extension and landing flaps can be delayed. However,
the airplane must be configured with gear down and landing flaps before 1000 ft AFE.
If the airplane cannot meet the stabilized approach criteria, execute a missed approach.
fragen.frage_en: (E2) By when must the aircraft be configured with gear down and landing flaps on an ILS CAT I (also for far ILS captures)?

Before the FAF
Before 1500 ft AFE
fragen.erklaerung_en: Gear and landing flaps may be delayed, but must be set before 1000 ft AFE.

kontext:
2.5.6 Steep Approach

The Steep Approach procedure is applicable to approaches where the angle of descent on final path for landing is greater than or equal 4.5°.
The maximum tailwind for steep approach is 10 kt.

It must be flown following the standards applicable for the type of approach (i.e. 3D- or 2D-Approach).
The use of AP and AT is recommended, but no restrictions apply for Steep

Approaches with autopilot and (or) autothrottle disengaged.
For Steep Approach operations with glideslope inoperative, the preferred vertical mode is V/S instead of FPA. Also, for airplanes equipped with SVS, it is recommended the use of SVS OFF for PFD configuration.

fragen.frage: (E2) Bei welcher Speed muss der Thrust nach dem Landing spätestens von MAX REV auf MIN REV reduziert sein?
antworten: Bei 80 KIAS
Bei 30 KIAS
Bei oder über 60 KIAS
Bei 100 KIAS
fragen.erklaerung: MAX REV wird bei oder über 60 KIAS auf MIN REV reduziert, das Schliessen der Reverser wird bei 30 KIAS empfohlen.
fragen.zitat: Smoothly reduce the engine thrust from MAX REV to MIN REV at or above 60 KIAS, and it is recommended to close the thrust reversers when reaching 30 KIAS.
kontext:
2.6.1.2 Landing Procedure

For a normal landing procedure, establish the landing configuration, gear down and flaps, early on the final approach or at the outer marker on an ILS or FAF on a non-precision approach. Airspeed, power and descent rate also should be stabilized early. Changes in airspeed require changes in thrust and attitude. If the airspeed is 10 KIAS above target approach speed, an airspeed deviation is considered significant. Indicated airspeed may not be less than the VREF or VAP.
If the stabilized approach parameters are not met before reaching the stabilized approach height, initiate a go-around.

Make sure that the airplane is properly trimmed during the approach. It maximizes elevator authority for the flare or in the event of a missed approach.
Target approach speed is VAP, which is VREF plus wind correction. As the airplane approaches the touch down point, initiate the flare approximately at 20 ft to 10 ft.
Reduce the rate of descent and slowly reduce thrust levers to idle. Plan the flare so that thrust levers are at idle when the airplane touches down. Normally a 2° to 3° pitch change is enough for the flare.
Plan to touchdown at the runway touchdown zone, which is typically located 1000 ft ahead from the runway threshold. Monitor the final approach path using all reference available. Do not allow the airplane to float in ground effect, which unnecessarily increases the landing distance and risk of a tail strike.
After main wheel touches down, use autobrake or apply manual braking as required for the runway condition and length available while easing the nosewheel onto the runway. Pull the thrust reverser triggers and take the thrust

levers to reverse. Verify spoilers actuation. The autobrake disarms by gradually pressing brake pedals.
Use reverse thrust consistent with runway conditions and modulate as required.
Apply thrust reversers cautiously and observe how the airplane responds before

full reverse is used.

Use MAX REV thrust when landing over wet, slippery, and contaminated runways. Maintain MAX REV thrust until the airspeed is approximately 80 KIAS.

Smoothly reduce the engine thrust from MAX REV to MIN REV at or above 60

KIAS, and it is recommended to close the thrust reversers when reaching 30 KIAS.

Thrust reverser is more effective at high speeds. The use of reverse below

60 KIAS increases the chances of foreign object ingestion by the engine.

During Emergency/Abnormal landings, the thrust reversers can be used until the airplane comes to a complete stop.

Rudder control is effective to approximately 60 kt. Rudder pedal steering is enough for maintaining directional control during the rollout. Do not use the

nosewheel steering tiller until reaching taxi speed.
As soon as the airplane leaves the runway, turn off the strobe and landing lights.

However, the nose taxi light must remain on throughout the taxi regardless of the

time of the day.
Note: Performance values calculated by the performance tool consider the threshold is crossed at the screen height and at VREF. Any increment to VREF must be considered.
fragen.frage_en: (E2) At what speed must thrust be reduced from MAX REV to MIN REV after landing at the latest?
antworten_en: At 80 KIAS
At 30 KIAS
At or above 60 KIAS
At 100 KIAS
fragen.erklaerung_en: MAX REV is reduced to MIN REV at or above 60 KIAS; closing the reversers is recommended at 30 KIAS.

fragen.frage: (E2) Um wie viel nimmt die Landing Distance ungefähr zu, wenn die Schwelle 10 kt über VREF überflogen wird?
fragen.erklaerung: 10 kt über VREF ergeben ca. +20%; 100 ft Schwellenhöhe ca. +35%, 3 s längere Flare ca. +25%.
fragen.zitat: If the airplane crosses the threshold with 10 kt above the VREF, the landing distance increases by approximately 20%.
kontext:
If the airplane crosses the threshold with 10 kt above the VREF, the landing

distance increases by approximately 20%.

Crossing the threshold at 100 ft instead of the normal screen height increases the landing distance by

approximately 35%.

Extending the flare during landing increases the landing distance. The airplane touches down the runway at a point ahead of the runway touchdown zone, which is located at 1000 ft from the runway threshold. Extending the flare by 3 seconds increases the landing distance by approximately 25%.
Considering an unstabilized approach, with the airplane crossing the threshold at 100 ft, above VREF and with 3 seconds of extended flare, the landing distance increases by approximately 80%. In this situation, the distance necessary to stop the airplane exceeds the operational margins provided by the dispatch required landing distance.

The preceding information, and the graphic that follows, assumes an airplane landing at maximum landing weight, on dry runway.

kontext:
2.6.1.11 Rejected Landing

For Normal and Autoland approaches, the REJECTED LANDING procedure is similar to the GO-AROUND PROCEDURE.

Rejected Landing Initiated Prior to Touchdown Press the TO/GA button, advance the thrust levers to TO/GA position and perform a go-around procedure. The go-around may result in a touchdown.

Rejected Landing Initiated After Touchdown

Press the TO/GA button, advance the thrust levers to TO/GA position, disconnect

Autopilot and Autothrottle, and perform a manual go-around procedure.

Ground spoilers retract and autobrake disarms as thrust levers are advanced

for rejected landing initiated after touchdown.
If after touchdown reverse thrust is applied, a full stop landing must be made.

The thrust levers require time to transition from reverse to forward thrust, and

there is the possibility that it does not remain stowed in the forward thrust position.

Attention must be given to the intended flight path as the published missed approach procedure may not be valid after passing the published missed

approach point. Reengage the automation as required.

kontext: 2.5.3.5.5 Malfunctions
Any airplane malfunction requiring crew action below 1000 ft AFE under IMC should lead to a go-around.

Malfunctions above 1000 ft AFE must be evaluated by the crew. It should lead to a go-around if necessary procedures cannot be completed before reaching 1000 ft.

kontext:
3.3.1 Rejected Takeoff - RTO

During the takeoff phase, an RTO procedure is initiated before V1 if any adverse or abnormal event occurs that could affect the safety of flight. Many faults can cause a decision to reject, like engine fire, engine failure and some other system faults or events. If an adequate decision to reject is taken, do not delay the RTO.
Delaying the decision increases the risk of a runway overrun, because it takes a few seconds for the engines to spool down to idle thrust.
A successful RTO depends on:
Accurate alert and monitoring during all takeoff phase,

Captains timely decision,

All callouts made on a loud, clear, and precise communication way,

Adequate briefing, procedures, and coordination.

Responsibility Whoever first identifies the undesirable event or malfunction must announce it,
but the decision and responsibility to perform an RTO remain to the captain.

Once the decision is made, initiate the RTO immediately.
Actions

Actions are taken considering that, during all takeoff procedures, the LSP keeps his hand on the thrust levers until V1 is reached, Once the RTO decision has been made, the following actions are: set thrust

levers to idle, disconnect the autothrottle, verify autobrake actuation or

manually apply maximum brakes, and apply reverse thrust as required,

The autobrake RTO mode provides the maximum deceleration rate, which is equivalent to the maximum manual braking. To decrease workload in this

scenario it is recommended to use autobrake in RTO mode, although the pilot can manually override the autobrake as required.

Note: if an RTO is performed below 60 KIAS (before HOLD is announced) and AT is not disconnected, Autothrottle moves the thrust levers back to TO/GA detent if both throttles are reduced to a position not below 40 degrees TLA. If throttles are moved below 40 degrees TLA or reverse thrust is applied during an RTO, the AT disconnects,

directional control is kept by applying rudder pedal steering,

monitor airplane deceleration, cancel any aural warnings upon malfunction identification, verify reverse thrust status, and advise ATC,

the engine should be commanded from MAX REV to MIN REV at or above 60 KIAS, and it is recommended to close the thrust reversers at 30 KIAS

if necessary, thrust reverse can be used until airplane comes to a complete stop, considering airplane speed, runway length available, slippery surfaces with ice, snow and so forth,

the airplane should remain on the runway until it is clear that an emergency evacuation is not necessary and the whole scenario is analyzed. If necessary, request external aids to vacate the runway to a safe position according to ATC instructions,

if RTO decision was taken due to fire, consider positioning the airplane so that fire is on the downwind of fuselage, if an RTO is performed, the FMS takeoff and landing data may

reset after two minutes. If a new takeoff is intended, the FMS takeoff and landing data must be re-entered and confirmed before

the takeoff.

Low and High Energy Speeds The sooner an RTO decision is taken, the greater is the chance to safely stop within runway limits. RTO above V1 may lead to a runway overrun and is the main cause of overrun accidents,

Low energy speed is considered up to, approximately, 80 KIAS,

During takeoff, the 80 KIAS callout has three main proposes: pilot incapacitation check, airspeed crosscheck and the transition from Low to High Energy speed,

For High energy speeds only reject the takeoff if there is a malfunction that severely affects the flight safety, such as but not limited to:

Engine failures resulting in loss of thrust, Fire or fire warning, Severe damages.

For High energy speeds, it is recommended to continue the takeoff if a tire burst occurs,

Upon reaching V1, if no decision has been taken, continue the takeoff.
After V1, there is no assurance that the airplane is capable to stop within the remaining runway length.

OM-B E2 Procedures

REJECTED TAKEOFF - ACTIONS and CALLOUTS

kontext:
3.6.3 Engine Failure above V1

If an engine failure occurs above V1, control airplane direction, aiming to keep airplane on runway centerline by smoothly applying rudder.
As soon as an Engine Failure or FIRE is recognized (not always followed by loss of thrust) and affected engine identified, check maximum thrust on EICAS.
After rotation, use rudder and yaw trim to avoid large wheel inputs while maintaining wings leveled. Large wheel inputs raise the spoilers and increase drag.
Crew must keep close attention at first positive rate of climb to retract landing gear, monitoring airplane profile.
After landing gear retraction, the Best Beta function activates (slip/skid indicator becomes cyan). Use rudder and yaw trim to center the slip/skid indicator. Wheel deflection and a small bank angle may be required to keep heading.
The TO mode first guidance is based on takeoff weight and flap setting, limited to a minimum pitch of 8° and maximum of 18°.
Crew must follow the flight director guidance to maintain V2 to V2 +10 kt up to acceleration altitude, according to following three different conditions: engine failure below V2: pitch for V2
engine failure between V2 and V2 +10 kt: pitch for the present speed

engine failure above V2 +10 kt: pitch for V2 +10 kt Takeoff thrust is limited to 5 (optionally 10) minutes after takeoff. It is recommended that emergency procedures to be accomplished as soon as safe

altitude has been reached (at least 400 ft AGL or according to local minimums).

When engine failure occurs after takeoff, noise abatement procedures no longer

apply.

Following an Engine Failure, ATTCS adjusts operating engine thrust to its

respective RSV mode. In event the maximum thrust is not reached for any reason, advance the thrust levers to maximum thrust.

On departure procedures with acceleration altitudes above 1000 ft, emphasize

during takeoff briefing that, in the event of an Engine Failure, Engine Fire (with loss of thrust), or any other malfunction requiring a memory item, actions can be

commanded at an altitude lower than the acceleration altitude, but not lower than 400 ft. Airplane must be stabilized and on the profile.

For One Engine Inoperative, limit the bank angle to: 15° at V2

20° at V2 +5 kt

25° at V2 +10 kt
