fragen.zitat: An Injury is classified as fatal if death results from the injury within thirty (30) days from the date of the accident.
kontext:
11.2 Definitions

As regulations and safety specific literature are written in English language originally, exact translations into the particular country’s official language is at times difficult. Hence, it is likely to be confusing, how a specific “happening” or “identified safety related situation” has to be handled. Therefore, before the detailed instructions, it is important to explain the terminology used.
Accident An occurrence associated with the operation of an airplane which takes place between the time any person boards the airplane with the intention of flight until such time as all such persons have disembarked, in which:
1. A person is fatally or seriously injured (see term below) as a result of: being in contact with the airplane, or

direct contact with any part of the airplane, including parts which have become detached from the airplane, or

direct exposure to jet blast;

Except when the injuries are from natural causes, self-inflicted or inflicted by other persons or when the injuries are to stowaways hiding outside the areas normally available to the passengers and crew; or

2. The airplane sustains damage or structural failure which: adversely affects the structural strength, performance or flight characteristics of the airplane, and

would normally require major repair or replacement of the

affected component, except for engine failure or damage,

when the damage is limited to the engine, its cowlings or

accessories; or for damage limited to propellers, wingtips, antennas, tires, brakes, fairings, small dents or holes in the

airplane skin; or

3. The airplane is missing or is completely inaccessible

Serious An incident involving circumstances indicating that an accident nearly Incident occurred. The following items are typical examples of incidents that are likely to be serious incidents: near collisions requiring an avoidance maneuver to avoid a collision or an unsafe situation or when an avoidance action would have been appropriate

controlled flight into terrain only marginally avoided

aborted take-off on a closed or engaged runway

take-off from a closed or engaged runway with marginal separation from obstacles

landings or attempted landings on a closed or engaged runway

gross failures to achieve predicted performance during take-off or initial climb

fires and smoke in the passenger compartment, in cargo compartments or engine fires, even though such fires were extinguished by the use of

extinguishing agents

events requiring the emergency use of oxygen by the flight crew

aircraft structural failures or engine disintegration not classified as an accident

multiple malfunctions of one or more airplane systems seriously

affecting the operation of the airplane

flight crew incapacitation in flight

fuel quantity requiring the declaration of an emergency by the flight crew

take-off or landing incidents. Incidents such as undershooting,

overrunning or running off the side of runways

system failures, weather phenomena, operations outside the approved flight envelope or other occurrences, which could have

caused difficulties controlling the aircraft

failures of more than one system in a redundancy system

mandatory for flight guidance and navigation Note: The difference between an accident and a serious incident lies only in the result.

Incident An occurrence, other than an accident, associated with the operation of an aircraft, which affects or could affect the safety of operation.

Serious An injury which is sustained by a person in an accident and which:
Injury requires hospitalization for more than 48 hours, commencing within seven days from the date the injury was received, or

results in a fracture of any bone (except simple fractures of fingers, toes or nose), or

involves lacerations which cause severe hemorrhage, nerve, muscle or tendon damage, or

involves injury to any internal organ, or

involves second or third degree burns or any burns affecting more than 5% of the body surface, or

involves verified exposure to infections substances or injurious radiation.
An Injury is classified as fatal if death results from the injury within thirty (30) days from the date of the accident.

CERM Handling of severe irregularities/ accidents has been covered in the helvetic document “Crisis and Emergency Response Manual”
(CERM).

The CERM is a guideline for the approach the Crisis and

Emergency Response Team (CERT) takes when addressing an emergency or catastrophic situation present in helvetic.

Occurrence Any safety-related event which endangers or which, if not

corrected or addressed, could endanger an aircraft, its occupants or any other person and includes in particular an accident or

serious incident.

Just ‘just culture’ according Regulation (EU) No 376/2014 means a Culture culture in which front-line operators or other persons are not

punished for actions, omissions or decisions taken by them that are commensurate with their experience and training, but in which

gross negligence, willful violations and destructive acts are not tolerated.

Hazard Condition or object with the potential to cause injury to personnel

damage to equipment or structures

loss of material

reduction of ability to perform a prescribed function.
fragen.frage_en: When is an injury considered fatal according to the definitions in OM-A 11.2?
antworten_en: If death occurs within 7 days from the date of the accident
If death occurs within 30 days from the date of the accident
If death occurs within 48 hours after hospital admission
If death occurs within 90 days from the date of the accident
fragen.erklaerung_en: An injury is considered fatal if death occurs within thirty (30) days from the date of the accident.

kontext:
11.5.4 Time Line for Reporting

The chart below illustrates the general flow of information, main deadlines and stages of the reporting into ECCAIRS2 This reporting flow starts from the moment the occurrence is detected (T0). From this moment, the individual employee shall report it to helvetic via the SMS Tool as soon as possible, but latest within 72 hours. Once the occurrence report is filed, the safety department will validate this report within an additional 72 hours. If it becomes evident that the report describes a mandatory occurrence, the report will be forwarded to the authority ECCAIRS2).

A follow up of a mandatory occurrence will be sent from the SMS Tool as default

not later than 27 days.

Purely internal reports (not sent to the authority) should be closed 6 months after

creation.
In order to track ongoing corrective actions of the final report, the PIL Tool may be used.

kontext:
11.9.5.3 Suspension of Crew Members

After any accident, the crew members concerned may be automatically

suspended from flying duties without any contractual changes.
They should not be allowed to fly until completion of the inquiry, unless explicit permission is given by the Accountable Manager (ACM).
fragen.frage_en: What applies according to OM-A 11.9.5.3 to the Crew Members concerned after an Accident?

kontext:
1.8.2 Duties and Responsibilities

The EFB Administrator (EFB) is responsible for: the overall control and administration of the EFB-System

ensuring of hard- and software conformity to the applicable standards

the maintenance of hardware components including spare battery

the proper implementation of the EFB-System into the Safety Management System (SMS)

procedure establishment, ensuring that these are strictly adhered to, and that no unauthorized changes take place

timely and correct updates of data contained on EFB (e.g. obstacle database)

checking potential security issues associated with the applications installed

He is responsible for the link between the EFB provider and the company.
The EFB Administrator (EFB) duty to conduct audits random checks is delegated to the Compliance Monitoring Manager (CMM).

The overall control of the EFB-System consists as a minimum of the following:

permanent monitoring of EFB-related system behaviour out of pilot reports and feedbacks reporting system anomalies to Nominated Person Flight Operation (FOP)

monthly verification of validity and expiration of EFB Application software

and database

permanent monitoring of services and standards of the hard- and software

suppliers in regard to system integrity

providing information to the Nominated Person Training (TNG) for the

implementation of related procedures in the respective training modules, whenever amendments to the systems are made

providing information in written form to the Nominated Person Flight

Operations (FOP) for the establishments of standard operating procedures (SOP) in relation to the EFB-System, whenever amendments are

implemented

specifying comprehensive provisions in written form for implementation standards, system requirements, operational practices, policies and procedures, whenever the situation arises

OM-A Responsibilities

kontext: 1.13 Piquet Officer (PQO)

The Piquet Officer (PQO) duty is assigned to a group of nominated persons being part of the helvetic organisation. The nomination to the Piquet Officer (PQO) group is done by the Accountable Manager (ACM).

The goal of this function is to grant a single point of contact for Flight Operations Officer (FOO) on duty particularly outside of usual office hours.
The Piquet Officer (PQO) fulfills his duty in a weekly cycle starting and ending on Wednesdays at 12:00 (noon). The Piquet Officer must be reachable via his mobile phone outside usual office hours (usual office hours: Monday to Friday 07:00LT till 18:00LT). Non-availabilities shall be avoided whenever possible.
If unavoidable, non-availabilities shall be covered by delegation or sharing of the assigned duty with another Piquet Officer group member. helvetic Operations Control Center (OCC) shall be informed about any non-availability and the respective replacement of such a duty as early as possible (telephone or e-mail).
During normal office hours, the Piquet Officer (PQO) duty and responsibility shall automatically be assigned to a helvetic management member available in the office by decision of the Flight Operations Officers (FOO) on duty.
The published Piquet Officer (PQO) duty plan can be found in a semi-permanent Admin Note named Ops Management Piquet.
This note is updated by the Administration Personnel (ADM) in a half-yearly cycle.

OM-A Responsibilities

The Piquet Officer (PQO) is responsible for: supporting and maintaining the helvetic operation of airplanes in irregular situations in respect of safety, security and economy

providing communication and cooperation between the Operations Control Center (OCC) and members of the helvetic Operations Management (refer to 2.4.2 - helvetic Operations Management)

the promotion of commercially sound decisions in cooperation with the Flight Operations Officer (FOO) with other members of the helvetic Operations Management. Decisions shall be based on regulations laid down in the Operations Manuals (OM) and additional helvetic publications defined in 0.1
- Introduction

the integration of the customer relations management either by the Flight Operations Officer (FOO) on duty or by himself if deemed advisable (e.g. delays 2 hours, re-bookings, flight cancellations)

re-direction of requests to other members of the helvetic Operations Management (subject matter experts) unless he is competent to take appropriate actions or decisions on his own

informing the corporate management (refer to 1.1.1 - Corporate Management sequence COO – CFO – CEO) about the irregularity and corrective actions in case of major issues (e.g. cancellation of flights with major consequences such as nightstop, airplane damage)

the activation of the Emergency Response Team (ERT) in coordination with the Accountable Manager (ACM) or his deputy according to the Crisis and Emergency Response Manual (CERM)

arranging testing for psychoactive substances in case of a serious incident

or accident or if misuse is suspected and removing investigated crew member from duty until clarified. Refer to:

helvetic HR Manual

OM-A Responsibilities

Any typing mistakes or writing errors must only be corrected in the following manner: mistakes (e.g. GEN 1 U/S instead of GEN 2 U/S): the wrong entry (i.e. digit 1) shall be crossed out in a manner that remains legible, a new entry (i.e., digit 2) shall be added, and the amendment shall be verified by adding the assigned 3LC and signature adjacent to it.

21 Stunden

fragen.zitat: Continuous Hours of Reaction Speed or Blood Alcohol Wakefulness Effectiveness Concentration (BAC in ‰) (% Baseline) 18.5 *77 0.5 21 70 0.8
kontext:
7.3.1.1 Blood Alcohol Concentration (BAC) Scale

When working with fatigue models, the effect of fatigue may be compared to the

effect of blood alcohol concentration to calibrate the severity of fatigue.
However, fatigue and the effects of alcohol are not identical.

The FAST SAFTE model applies *77% of the maximum reaction speed or

effectiveness as criterion for impaired performance.

Wakefulness Effectiveness Concentration

(BAC in Baseline)

fragen.frage_en: After how many hours of continuous wakefulness does performance correspond to a blood alcohol concentration of 0.5 ‰ (77 % effectiveness) according to the BAC scale in OM-A 7.3.1.1?

18.5 hours
21 hours
24 hours
fragen.erklaerung_en: According to the BAC scale, 18.5 hours of continuous wakefulness correspond to 77 % reaction speed or 0.5 ‰ BAC (21 hours: 70 %, 0.8 ‰).

fragen.frage: Künftige Duty Plans weisen ein FRMS-Effizienzniveau unter 85 % auf und lassen sich wegen der Rotationsplanung nicht korrigieren. Was ist gemäss OM-A zu tun?
antworten: Präventive Massnahmen, damit die Planung nicht unter 77 % fällt
Die Rotation muss durch Commander's Discretion abgesichert werden
Die Duty Plans sind der FOCA zur Genehmigung vorzulegen
Keine Massnahme, solange 77 % nicht unterschritten werden
fragen.erklaerung: Bei Duty Plans unter 85 % FRMS-Effizienz, die nicht korrigierbar sind, sind präventive Massnahmen zu treffen (z.B. keine Reserven davor und danach), damit die Planung nicht unter 77 % fällt.
fragen.zitat: with FRMS efficiency level below 85% and it is not possible to correct it due to the rotation planning (e.g. night duties), preventive measures shall be taken
kontext:
7.3.6 Implemented Fatigue Risk Mitigation

Based on the necessity of having qualified personnel available to the required extent, an effective crew planning plays a major role in achieving any FRMS aims.
Crew Planning (CRP) shall: consider fatigue risk additionally to legal flight time limitations

plan night flights with minimal waiting time

consider rest time before night flights and use common sense when planning deadheading or positioning

According to the SAFTE model helvetic defines the critical level of effectiveness at 77% of the maximum human performance. The goal is to reduce the time exposure with actual duty time performed below this criterion.
If there are duty plans in the future
with FRMS efficiency level below 85% and it is not possible to correct it due to the rotation planning (e.g. night duties), preventive measures shall be taken

in order that the actual planning will not be below 77% efficiency level (e.g. no reserves before and after)

8 Operating Procedures 8.-1-1
fragen.frage_en: Future Duty Plans show an FRMS efficiency level below 85 % and cannot be corrected because of rotation planning. What must be done according to OM-A?
antworten_en: Preventive measures so that the planning does not fall below 77 %
The rotation must be secured by Commander's Discretion
The Duty Plans must be submitted to FOCA for approval
No measure, as long as 77 % is not undercut
fragen.erklaerung_en: For Duty Plans below 85 % FRMS efficiency that cannot be corrected, preventive measures must be taken (e.g. no reserves before and after) so that the planning does not fall below 77 %.

fragen.frage: Auf wie vielen Jahren Fatigue-Modellierungserfahrung basiert das von helvetic verwendete SAFTE-Modell gemäss OM-A?
antworten: 10 Jahre
20 Jahre

fragen.erklaerung: Das SAFTE-Modell basiert auf 15 Jahren Erfahrung in der Fatigue-Modellierung und ist gegen Labor- und Simulatormessungen validiert.
fragen.zitat: The SAFTE-model is: based on 15 years of fatigue modelling experience validated against laboratory and simulator measures of fatigue
kontext:
7.3.3.1 Hazard Identification

For hazard identification process refer to OMM Chapter 4.3 Hazard Identification.
The following methodologies shall be used to identify fatigue related hazards:
Predictive:
Sleep, Activities, Fatigue and Task Effectiveness Model (SAFTE)

The SAFTE-model is:

based on 15 years of fatigue modelling experience

validated against laboratory and simulator measures of fatigue

validated and calibrated to predict accident risk by the US Department of Transportation

accepted by the US Department of Defence (Air Force, Army, Navy, Marines) as the common war fighter fatigue model

Fatigue Avoidance Scheduling Tool (FAST) FAST uses the SAFTE-model as described above considers time zone changes and is valid for any city pair

mimics typical sleep patterns

considers total duty period, commuting, flight time and number of route sectors counts on naps prior to anticipated late starts

considers split sleep (split sleeping periods) when appropriate

automatically inserts in-flight sleep for augmented crews

(currently not applied by helvetic)

Proactive:

reporting of fatigue risks

analysis of planned versus actual time worked

FTL use of commander’s discretion

FAST analysis of actual flown schedules

Reactive: fatigue and confidential reports

audit reports

incidents

Flight Data Monitoring (FDM) events whereas outcomes of fatigue could show undesirable effects in Flight Data Monitoring (FDM) without any doubt, specific evidence of root causes clearly and solely addressing fatigue has not yet been proven based on scientific research. Therefore, for the time being helvetic does not define FDM as a functional element of FRMS. However, FDM can be used as a source to analyse fatigue-related events which were either reported by crew members or if analysis results point towards a relation between fatigue and FDM-events.
fragen.frage_en: On how many years of fatigue modeling experience is the SAFTE model used by helvetic based according to OM-A?
antworten_en: 10 years
20 years
25 years
15 years
fragen.erklaerung_en: The SAFTE model is based on 15 years of experience in fatigue modeling and is validated against laboratory and simulator measurements.

kontext:
7.3.4 FRMS Safety Assurance Processes

In order to validate the effectiveness of the fatigue safety risk controls and continuously monitor FRMS performance, all available data shall be collected and analysed.
The sources of data may include, but are not limited to: fatigue report summary and investigations

analysis of actual flown schedules (FRMS and FTL)

regular inspections of facilities, tools, documentation and procedures

audit and survey

reviews and fatigue studies

Additionally FRMS shall be part of the change management process defined in OMM Chapter 4.7 Management of Change.
All data shall be prepared before and analysed during the Safety Review Board (SRB).
If the analysis shows that the targets are not being met, the Accountable Manager (ACM) shall initiate the Fatigue Risk Assessment described under 7.3.3 - Fatigue Risk Management (FRM) Process.

kontext:
EMBRAER 195 AR 52450 52290 45800 42600

To comply with the performance and operating limitations of the regulations, the maximum allowable takeoff and landing operational weights may be equal to, but not greater than design limits.
The takeoff weight (weight at brake release or at start of takeoff run) is the lowest between MTOW and the following weights:
Maximum takeoff weight as calculated using the approved software, and as limited by field length, climb and brake energy.

Maximum takeoff weight, as limited by enroute, and landing operating requirements.
The landing weight is the lowest among MLW and the following weights calculated using the approved software:
Maximum landing weight as limited by runway.
Maximum approach and landing weight as limited by altitude, temperature and climb gradient.
LOADING

fragen.frage: Welche Einflüsse berücksichtigen die Constraints, mit denen die operationellen CG-Limits (curtailed envelope) aus den zertifizierten Limits abgeleitet werden?
antworten: Gear/Flap Retraction, Fuel Density, Passenger Seating
Pitch Trim Setting, OAT und Pressure Altitude
Runway Slope, Wind und Runway Condition Code
Engine Thrust Rating, Flap Setting und V-Speeds
fragen.erklaerung: Die Curtailments berücksichtigen Änderungen der Balance u.a. durch Gear and Flap Retraction, Fuel Density Variation, Passenger Seating und Cargo Location Variation.
fragen.zitat: These constraints account for changes in the airplane balance condition due to the following: gear and flap retraction fuel density variation passenger seating variation cargo location variation
kontext:
6.4.1 Curtailed Center of Gravity Envelope

Regulations require to further limit the manufacturer center of gravity envelope of the aircraft. Operational center of gravity limits are derived by applying appropriate constraints to the certified limits.

These constraints account for changes in the airplane balance condition due to the following: gear and flap retraction

fuel density variation

passenger seating variation

cargo location variation

in-flight passenger and crew movement

fuel loading and usage

Adherence to the curtailed mass and balance limitations assures: that the certified weight and center of gravity limits are not exceeded

enables proper selection of horizontal stabilizer trim for takeoff facilitates loading flexibility within the certified loading limits

helvetic uses an appropriate loading document (e.g manual loading instruction or

DCS) for fuel and payload distribution. The use of an appropriate loadsheet

serves for these balance checks of the aircraft. The curtailments are in

accordance with the approved manufacturer document BC-123.

For further information regarding curtailed envelopes refer to

6.1.15 - Different Loadsheet Envelopes.

For the manual loadsheet envelope refer to:

6.7.3.2.1.5 - Index and MAC Diagram for Manual Loadsheet E190-E2

6.7.3.2.2.5 - Index and MAC Diagram for Manual Loadsheet E195-E2

OM-B E2 6 Mass and Balance

kontext:
0.9 Rectification Intervals

Repair of inoperative systems or components, deferred in accordance with the MEL, must be effected at or prior to the rectification intervals established by the following designators: «A» Category No standard interval is specified. However, items in this category shall be rectified in accordance with the conditions stated in the MEL. i. Where a time period is specified in calendar days or flight days, the interval excludes the day of discovery. ii. Where a time period is specified other than in calendar days or flight days, it shall start at the point when the defect is deferred in accordance with the MEL. «B» Category Items in this category shall be repaired within three (3) consecutive calendar days (72 hours), excluding the day the malfunction was recorded in the Aircraft Technical Log (ATL) «C» Category Items in this category shall be repaired within ten (10) consecutive calendar days (240 hours), excluding the day the malfunction was recorded in the Aircraft Technical Log (ATL)

«D» Category Items in this category shall be repaired within one hundred and twenty (120) consecutive calendar days (2880 hours), excluding the day the malfunction was recorded in the Aircraft Technical Log (ATL)

Note: In EASA-MMEL/MEL the term «rectification interval» is used instead of «repair time», however, the meaning is exactly the same.
The designators are inserted on the right side of the item column 1.
Minimum Equipment List Embraer E1

kontext:
0.1 Introduction

This Minimum Equipment List [MEL] is based on the Embraer170/175/190/195 series EASA Master Minimum Equipment List [MMEL] This MEL takes into consideration Helvetic Airways AG particular aircraft equipment, configuration and operational conditions, the area of operation, EUOPS requirements and FOCA requirements.
This MEL will not deviate from any applicable Airworthiness Directive or any other Requirement and will be no less restrictive than the MMEL.
The operational and maintenance procedures referenced in the MEL are based on the operational and maintenance procedures referenced in the MMEL.
Modified procedures by helvetic provide at least the same level of safety, as required by the MMEL.
Operational and maintenance notes present advisory information and are not procedures required to be followed per MEL.
The MEL is intended to permit operations with inoperative items of equipment for a specified period of time until rectification has to be accomplished.
Rectifications are to be accomplished at the earliest opportunity, but within the time-frame specified in the MEL.
MEL Conditions and Limitations do not relieve the Commander from determining that the aircraft is in a fit condition for safe operation with specified unserviceable items or systems allowed by the MEL.
The provisions of the MEL are applicable until the aircraft commences the flight, i.e. the point when an aeroplane begins to move under its own power for the purpose of preparing for take-off.
Any decision to continue a flight following a failure or unserviceability which becomes apparent after the commencement of a flight must be the subject of pilot judgement and good airmanship. If a failure or unserviceability is subject to a MEL restriction and will result in an AOG condition due to a lack of maintenance personnel or equipment at the destination, depending on the moment of occurrence, a return to point of departure shall be considered. The Commander may continue to make reference to and use of the MEL as appropriate.
By approval of the MEL the Authority permits dispatch of the aircraft for revenue, ferry or training flights with certain items or components inoperative provided an acceptable level of safety is maintained by use of appropriate operational or maintenance procedures, by transfer of the function to another operating component, or by reference to other instruments or components providing the required information.

For dispatch with airframe or engine parts missing, refer to the
CONFIGURATION DEVIATION LIST [CDL].

kontext:

The operation procedure will refer to helvetic Maintenance Control Center (MCC) which will supply the relevant documents which are required to accomplish the Crew Applied MEL procedure.
MCC will provide the respective AMM task and support the Commander during the execution of the Crew Applied MEL procedure.

Two NG FMS

One MCDU

Three Displays Units

kontext:
ENG 1(2) NO DISPATCH

During engine start procedure, if the FADEC selects a failed ignition channel A, the EICAS message ENG 1(2) NO DISPATCH is displayed. With this condition, maintenance action is required before dispatch. Swapping the connectors at the exciter boxes moves the inoperative ignition channel from A to B. During the subsequent engine start, the FADEC selects ignition channel B. Since ignition channel B is failed after the swap, a missed light-off is detected and the EICAS message ENG 1 (2) SHORT DISPATCH is displayed.
Maintenance Note:
If ENG 1(2) NO DISPATCH message is displayed, swap the connectors at the exciter boxes and move the inoperative ignition channel from A to B. Since channel A of the exciter box is powered through essential bus, it must always be operative.

fragen.zitat: This is the speed at which rotation to a normal take-off attitude must begin in order to reach V2 by 35ft (dry) or 15ft (wet).VR must not be less than V1 and must be at least 1.05 times Vmca.
kontext:
4.0.1.3 Speed

General The airplane is assumed to accelerate with all engines operating from a standing start point to the point where the critical engine fails (Vef). The airplane continues to accelerate, with one engine inoperative to the point where the engine failure is recognised (V1). If the take-off is continued, using only aerodynamic control and average pilot skills, the airplane accelerates with one engine inoperative, to the point at which V2 is achieved at 35ft above the end of the runway.
If take-off is to be rejected, maximum braking is applied at V1, throttles retarded,

spoilers extended. No credit is taken for the use of reverse thrust during the certification process (dry runway).
V1

At and below V1 the take-off can be rejected and the aircraft will stop within the

accelerate stop distance available. At and above V1 the take-off can be

continued in case of an engine failure. V1 must not be less than Vmcg and must

not be greater than Vmbe.

This is the speed at which rotation to a normal take-off attitude must begin in order to reach V2 by 35ft (dry) or 15ft (wet).VR must not be less than V1 and

must be at least 1.05 times Vmca.

V2

V2, take-off safety speed, which must be reached by 35ft (dry) or (15ft wet) with

one engine inoperative. V2 must not be less than 1.1 Vmca or 1.2Vs.

OM-B E1 4 Performance

VMCG

This is the minimum control speed on the ground, from which directional control of the airplane can be maintained on the ground after an engine failure without the use of brakes or nose-wheel steering. In other words, it is the minimum speed at which the control surfaces are effective on the ground.

VMCA

VMCA is the lowest speed, at which control of the airplane can be maintained in the air after an engine failure. Banking slightly into the good engine usually

enhances engine out capability. VMCA is determined for the airplane with a

5° maximum bank angle during certification process.

VMBE

This is the maximum speed at which the brakes can absorb all the energy required to stop the airplane at a given mass. V1 must always be less than VMBE.

VR ≥ VMBE and at least 1.2 × VS
VR ≥ V1 and at least 1.13 × VSR
fragen.erklaerung_en: VR must not be less than V1 and must be at least 1.05 × VMCA.

fragen.zitat: Third Segment (Level Off Height) This is the acceleration height, which must be at least 400ft AAE (critical engine inoperative). The program uses 1500ft AAE as the minimum first level off segment for take-off performance calculations.
kontext:
4.0.1.5 Climb Segments

First Segment

Is the segment from lift-off up to the point at which the gear is fully retracted. The climb gradient is positive which allows the airplane to reach V2 (35ft for a dry or 15ft for a wet runway) not later than at the end of the take-off distance (TOD).

Second Segment Is the segment from gear retraction to the point where the flaps and slats are retracted. The minimum climb gradient that is required during this segment is 2.4% (in case of engine failure after V1) for a twin engine aircraft.

Third Segment (Level Off Height) This is the acceleration height, which must be at least 400ft AAE (critical engine inoperative). The program uses 1500ft AAE as the minimum first level off

segment for take-off performance calculations.

This segment is used for acceleration to retract the flaps and slats and to accelerate to the optimum climb speed. This segment is assumed to be in level flight, so that excessive thrust can be used for acceleration. The minimum climb gradient is 1.2% and must remain positive.

The segment ends when maximum time allowed for use of take off thrust is reached, which depends on the regulation being used.

OM-B E1 4 Performance

Final Take Off Segment Is the segment from the end of the third segment until the aircraft reaches 1500ft above the take-off surface or more if required for obstacle clearance. This segment will only exist if thrust must be reduced to MCT before the aircraft reaches 1500ft according to regulations.

kontext:
4.0.1.2 Declared Distances

Take Off Run Available (TORA)

The length of a runway, which is declared available by the appropriate authority

and suitable for the ground run of an aircraft taking-off.

Accelerate Stop Distance Available (ASDA)

The length of a runway, which is declared available by the appropriate authority

and suitable for the ground run of an aircraft taking-off plus the length of stopway, if such stopway is declared available by the appropriate authority and is capable

of bearing the mass of the aircraft under the prevailing operating conditions.

Take-Off Distance Available (TODA)

The length of a runway available, plus the length of clearway available (if provided).

Landing Distance Available (LDA) The length of a runway, which is declared available by the appropriate authority and suitable for the ground roll of an aircraft.

OM-B E1 4 Performance

Stopway An area at the end of the runway in the direction of take-off, not less wide than the runway and centred upon its existing centreline. It is able to support the aircraft during an aborted take-off,

without causing structural damage to the aircraft.

Clearway

An area at the end of the runway in the direction of take-off, not less than 500ft wide, centred on the extended centreline, and under the control of the airport

authorities. It must not exceed an upslope of 1.25%, above which no object or terrain can protrude. Threshold lights may protrude but have height restrictions. A

clearway may not exceed half the runway length.
fragen.frage_en: How is a stopway defined according to OM-B?

The part of the TORA not usable for landing
fragen.erklaerung_en: A stopway is an area at the end of the runway in the direction of takeoff, no narrower than the runway, capable of supporting the aircraft during a rejected takeoff without structural damage.

– The Maximum Assumed Temperature (MaxAT) is limited to the minimum flex takeoff thrust (60% maximum rated TO-1 RSV thrust).

The operator shall at regular intervals check the maximum thrust in order to detect any possible engine deterioration, unless the operators has an adequate engine performance monitoring program.

Flex takeoff thrust should be used whenever possible in order to save engine life.

kontext:
STATIC TAKEOFF TECHNIQUE

The Takeoff performance data presented by the manuals or calculated by the software when the Static Takeoff Mode is selected are based on the following takeoff technique:
– Thrust levers set to TO/GA position with the airplane stopped and brakes applied,
–

Green ATTCS indication presented on the EICAS if it is set to ON on the MCDU,
– Brakes released after the N1 from both engines are stabilized and equal to the N1 target,

– When VR is attained the airplane is rotated to the flight director pitch angle until 35 ft or until reaching either V2 for OEI or V2 10 KIAS for AEO. If the flight director is inoperative, the airplane is rotated according to the takeoff pitch angle displayed on the TAKEOFF page from the MCDU,
– Landing gear retracted when a positive rate of climb is achieved.
The following steps consider that one engine failed at VEF:
– The best beta (slip/skid indicator) is kept aligned,
– Pitch angle adjusted as required to maintain not less than V2 up to the level off height,
– Slat/Flaps retracted to 0 position at level off height according to the reference indication (F) for flap retraction speed,
– The airplane is accelerated to VFS simultaneously with slat/flap retraction,
– At VFS the engine thrust rate is set to maximum continuous, and
– The airplane resumes climb maintaining VFS.

NOTE: The takeoff field length performance considers the greater of the horizontal distance OEI, or 115% of the horizontal distance AEO.

5-01

kontext:
8.3.2.25.1 General

The flight crew should choose the runway with the best performance margin under the prevailing weather conditions.
Due regard shall be given to other meteorological and operational factors (e.g. ATC requirements, preferential runway system, runway condition, noise abatement procedures, wind condition during all phases of flight, thunderstorms in the vicinity of the airport).
Special attention shall be paid to the condition of the runway regarding type of contaminant and associated wind limitations.
The Runway Condition Assessment Matrix (RCAM) provides guidelines to determine the runway condition to be used for performance calculation.
The available runway length shall be equal or exceed the required distance obtained by the respective aircraft type performance tool or other approved data.
The performance calculation should be based on the latest available weather report and runway conditon report (RCR) or equivalent information based on the RCR.
The best source of information provides the Automatic Terminal Information Service (ATIS).
For the runway intended to use, the following consideration shall be done: the existing weather conditions at the time of departure arrival

the takeoff- approach- configuration used under these condition the actual runway condition

the information on wind contained in METAR/SPECI/ATIS reports (average

of a 10-minute period) should be the basis for the performance calculations, while instant wind information reported by the tower shall be monitored to

ensure that the wind speed during takeoff/approach does not exceed the

assumptions made for performance calculations.

The result of the performance calculation shall be verified amongst the flight

crew during the briefing and shall be recorded on the Operational Flight Plan (OFP) or in the EFB system in a traceable manner (real conditions, result of

calculation, explanatory remarks).

8.3.2.25.1.1 Takeoff Performance

The determination of takeoff performance data for wet and contaminated runways should be based on the reported runway surface condition in terms of contaminant and depth.
In the case of a contaminated runway, the flight crew shall consider the option to wait until the runway is cleared. If this is impracticable, applicable performance adjustments must be applied by using the type specific performance tool or approved data (e.g. AFM).
The take-off must be started either from the runway beginning, or from an authorized take-off point according to OM-C which must be considered in the takeoff performance calculation.
The weather report should not be older than 30 minutes before commencing takeoff.

8.3.2.25.1.2 Landing Performance

The crew shall be satisfied that, according to the information available, the condition of the runway intended to be used, will not prevent a safe approach, landing or missed approach, having regard to the performance information.
The initial in-flight landing distance assessment should be carried out when the weather report and the RCR are obtained, usually around TOD. If the planned duration of the flight does not allow the flight crew to carry out the assessment in non-critical phases of the flight, the assessment should be carried out before

departure.
When meteorological condition may lead to a degradation of the runway surface condition, the assessment shall include considerations of how much deterioration in runway surface friction characteristics may be tolerated, so that a quick

decision can be made prior to landing.

The flight crew shall monitor the evolution of the actual conditions during the

approach, to ensure that they do not degrade below the condition that was

determined to be the minimum acceptable during the initial in-flight landing distance assessment.

For calculating the in-flight landing performance, use the type specific

performance software tool or refer to:

AOM E1 5-35 Operational Landing Distance

AOM E2 5-35 Operational Landing Distance

Note: The performance software tool automatically adds a 15% safety margin to the calculated operational landing distance.

If calculations are performed manually via AOM this margin has to be added by the crew.

8.3.2.25.2 Runway Condition Report (RCR)

The assessment of the Landing Distance at Time of Arrival LDTA begins with the acuisition of the latest available weather information and the RCR.
The RCR is divided in two sections:

1. the aircraft performance section which contains information that is directly relevant in a performance computation. This section includes a Runway Condition Code (RWYCC), the contaminant type, depth and coverage for each third of the runway.

Step Climbs are employed as means for maintaining cruise flight levels closer to optimum altitudes for as long as possible throughout the flight.

The step climb function is permitted. The SECONDARY FLIGHT PLAN is available for performance optimization and replaced the WHAT-IF page.
Step climbs use the cruise speed command when using the FMS speeds and the altitude change is 5000 ft or less. Climbs greater than 5000 ft use the climb

speed commands.

kontext:
WIND ALTITUDE TRADE

In order to maintain the same ground specific range at another altitude than the one planned initially, the Airplane Operation Manual (AOM) has tables that allow

the determination of the break-even wind.

The optimum altitude is normally calculated for zero wind, but wind is a factor

that may justify operations considerably above or below the optimum altitude.

If the optimum altitude headwind is stronger than lower altitude headwind, for

example, it might be advantageous to fly at a lower altitude (and weaker headwind). This action saves more fuel and is called wind-altitude trade.

fragen.erklaerung_en: If the headwind at the optimum altitude is stronger than lower down, it may be advantageous to fly lower with a weaker headwind; this saves fuel (wind-altitude trade).

kontext:
6.1.15 Different Loadsheet Envelopes

AFM Envelope This is the center of gravity envelope designed by the aircraft manufacturer during flight testing. The margins are close to the physical/aerodynamical limits of the aircraft and therefore not usable during daily flight operations. This envelope can be found in the AFM.
DCS Loadsheet Envelope The envelope for DCS loadsheets is tailored to daily operations. Uncertainties of actual vs. calculated mass and balance values in daily operations require more restrictive envelope limits (e.g. use of standard passenger masses, inflight movement of passengers, seat row trim). This envelope can be found in the Aircraft Handling Manual (AHM) and is forwarded to contracted handling agencies and is usually not visible to the flight crews.
Manual Loadsheet Envelope The envelope for a manual (IFS or paper) loadsheets is even more restrictive.
Using section trim (e.g. section A, B, C) leads to more uncertainties within the calculation process and requires a more restrictive envelope.
This envelope includes a designated section reserved for ferry flights. The ferry flight section is applicable if calculating a manual loadsheet for flights with no passengers on board.
Note: Any pantry code acc. to OM-0 9 Pantry Codes may be used for calculating ferry flight loadsheets.

fragen.frage: (E1) Ab welcher Dry-Ice-Menge im Frachtraum ist die Flight Crew gemäss AOM zu informieren?

fragen.zitat: Notify the flight crew whenever the amount of dry ice stowed in the cargo compartment exceeds 440 lb (200 kg), as recommended by the IATA Dangerous Goods Regulations.
kontext:
LOADING AIRPLANE

Avoid storing dry ice on airplanes for extended periods of time. Dry ice should be the last cargo to be loaded and first cargo to be unloaded.
Notify the flight crew whenever the amount of dry ice stowed in the cargo compartment exceeds 440 lb (200 kg), as recommended by the IATA Dangerous Goods Regulations.

Flight crew should be aware of the effects of high concentrations of CO2. FAA AC 91-76 may be used as a reference.

In case the flight crew suspects a high concentration of CO2 in the cockpit or cabin, it is recommended to use emergency oxygen supply and land at the nearest suitable airport.

In case of an event of depressurization, flight crew must follow the appropriate QRH procedure. At FL100, the emergency ram air provides sufficient airflow to dilute CO2 concentration.

In case of failure of one bleed or one pack, the QRH procedure remains unchanged. The maximum dry ice loading considers airflow provided by one engine bleed and one air conditioning pack.

The maximum recommended load of dry ice considers that only one bleed and one pack are operative. Therefore, flight diversion is not necessary solely due to an eventual failure of one bleed or one pack.

kontext: GENERAL RECOMMENDATIONS

It is not recommended to transport dry ice in the cabin and in the galleys. If small quantities are present in the galley, it is required to compute this dry ice mass in the calculation of the total dry ice.

Airplanes equipped with FWD cargo compartment ventilation system

Prior to enter into the forward cargo compartment, in which a large amount of dry ice has been loaded, ensure that adequate ventilation is provided checking that the cargo ventilation system is running properly.

Live animals must not be transported on a forward cargo compartment loaded with dry ice.

In case of failure of the cargo ventilation system during flight, the CO2 sublimated in the cargo compartment is trapped. The airplane can continue the flight normally, but after landing it is required to ventilate the compartment in which CO2 buildup is suspected.

NOTE: If the cargo compartment used for dry ice transportation is not equipped with a ventilation system, make sure CO2 levels are within acceptable limits before entering the cargo compartment. When cargo door is opened, the area immediately outside the door may also experience a high CO2 concentration. It is recommended to wear oxygen mask and portable oxygen cylinder inside these areas if adequate ventilation is not provided.

At least one air conditioning pack (or equivalent ground cart ventilation) shall be operating while persons are on board of an airplane transporting dry ice.

fragen.zitat: Eventually, at a certain altitude the available thrust becomes equal to the airplane drag, and the airplane levels off. This altitude is called the gross level off altitude.
kontext:
3.6.7 Engine Failure In Flight Driftdown

Following an engine failure or inflight engine shutdown, an airplane may not be able to maintain its cruise altitude. The driftdown profile assures the airplane altitude is kept as high as possible throughout the descent. The driftdown speed is represented by the Green Dot and provides the lower descent gradient.

During a driftdown, the available thrust increases as the airplane descends.
Eventually, at a certain altitude the available thrust becomes equal to the airplane drag, and the airplane levels off. This altitude is called the gross level off altitude.

The gross level off altitude, when corrected for gradient margins by 1.1% (2 engines), 1.4% (3 engines), or 1.6% (4 engines), is called the net level

off altitude. It depends on the atmospheric temperature and the airplane weight.
Regulations (FAR 121.191/CAT.POL.A.215/CAR 705.58) require that the airplane clears all terrain by a given margin when an engine fails.
Two means of compliance for enroute obstacle clearance are allowed: the net level-off altitude must clear all enroute obstacles by at least 1000ft or the net flight path must clear all enroute obstacles between the point where the engine is assumed to fail and an airport where a landing can be made by at least 2000ft

(Drift Down Profile)

kontext:
DRIFTDOWN PROCEDURE

After an engine failure or inflight engine shutdown during cruise, the driftdown procedure may be required.
Pilot should select AT OFF and place thrust lever of operational engine in TO/GA and set thrust rating to “CON”.

Adjust ALT SEL Controller to appropriate altitude in accordance with route analysis and set driftdown speed. When reaching driftdown speed, select FLCH and perform

applicable checklist. Notify ATC and monitor descent.

Note: Follow the Green Dot displayed on the speed tape for driftdown.

It is not required to disengage the AT in case of annunciated engine failure.

Once the pilot confirms the engine out condition on MCDU prompt, the FMS engages the EO AUTO driftdown mode. The FMS automatically commands (through AT) thrust lever to TO/GA, thrust rating to CON, and cruise altitude as the EO MAX ALT. The FMS also targets the green dot speed if FMS speed is used. When this speed is reached, the vertical mode transitions to FLCH if Altitude Selector has been dialed down.

10 minutes at 1500 ft in ISA conditions
fragen.erklaerung_en: After descent and continuation to an adequate airport, ADDE must cover holding of 15 minutes at 1500 ft (ISA) as well as approach and landing.

fragen.frage: Wann beginnt gemäss OM-A das In-flight Fuel Management?
antworten: Mit dem Start der APU vor dem Boarding der Passagiere
Mit dem Line-up auf der Runway nach der Take-off Clearance
Mit laufenden Engines und der ersten Bewegung des Flugzeugs aus eigener Kraft mit Flugabsicht
Mit dem Takeoff bzw. dem Einfahren des Landing Gears nach dem Takeoff
fragen.erklaerung: Das In-flight Fuel Management beginnt mit laufenden Engines und der ersten Bewegung aus eigener Kraft mit der Absicht zu fliegen.
fragen.zitat: The in-flight fuel management begins with the engines running and the first movement of the aircraft under own power with the intention to fly.
kontext: 8.3.7.1 Policy
The in-flight fuel management begins with the engines running and the first movement of the aircraft under own power with the intention to fly.

The flight crew must continuously monitor the fuel situation and observe any change in the operational environment (e.g. status of the destination and alternate aerodrome, deviation from the flight plan, operational status of the aircraft, meteorological conditions).
The use of fuel after flight commencement for objectives other than the ones originally intended during pre-flight planning require reanalysis and, if applicable, adjustment of the planned operation.
The flight shall be conducted to ensure that the usable fuel expected to remain upon landing at the destination aerodrome is not less than: the final reserve fuel plus alternate fuel, or the final reserve plus additional fuel where no alternate aerodrome is required

If an in-flight fuel check indicates that the expected fuel remaining on arrival at the destination will be close to or even less than above mentioned amount, refer to 8.3.7.3 - Fuel Close to the Required Minimum.

In any case the crew must ensure to proceed to an aerodrome with not less than the planned final reserve fuel remaining upon landing.
fragen.frage_en: When does in-flight fuel management begin according to OM-A?
antworten_en: With APU start before passenger boarding
With line-up on the runway after the takeoff clearance
With engines running and the first aircraft movement under its own power with the intention to fly
With liftoff or gear retraction after takeoff
fragen.erklaerung_en: In-flight fuel management begins with engines running and the first movement under own power with the intention to fly.

fragen.frage: Was muss die Crew beim Fuel Check vor dem Takeoff verifizieren?
antworten: Dass die Extra Fuel noch vollständig vorhanden ist, sonst ist ein neuer OFP anzufordern
Dass die Contingency Fuel noch mindestens 5 % der Trip Fuel beträgt, sonst ist zu tanken
Dass die Tankverteilung links/rechts um höchstens 100 kg abweicht, sonst ist auszugleichen
Dass nicht mehr als die geplante Taxi Fuel verbraucht wurde, sonst ist die Fuel-Situation neu zu beurteilen
fragen.erklaerung: Vor dem Takeoff ist zu prüfen, dass nicht mehr als die geplante Taxi Fuel verbraucht wurde; andernfalls ist die Fuel-Situation neu zu beurteilen.
fragen.zitat: (the crew must verify that not more than the planned taxi fuel was used otherwise a re-assessment of the fuel situation shall be done)
kontext:
8.3.7.2 Fuel Monitoring and Fuel Checks

The flight crew must continuously monitor the fuel situation and distribution to identify any trend in comparison with time elapsed.
Fuel checks must be performed: before leaving the parking position

before take-off
(the crew must verify that not more than the planned taxi fuel was used otherwise a re-assessment of the fuel situation shall be done)

after reaching initial cruising altitude overhead or abeam a waypoint listed on the OFP

in cruise at hourly intervals, overhead or abeam a waypoint listed on the OFP until leaving cruising altitude

Airborne, each fuel check must be recorded on the Operational Flight Plan (OFP) including the: actual fuel on board

actual fuel used

The actual fuel on board/used shall be evaluated to:

compare the actual fuel used with the planned fuel used compare the actual fuel on board with fuel required for the remainder of the flight

determine the usable fuel that is expected to remain upon landing at the

destination aerodrome
fragen.frage_en: What must the crew verify during the fuel check before takeoff?
antworten_en: That the extra fuel is still fully available, otherwise a new OFP must be requested
That contingency fuel is still at least 5% of trip fuel, otherwise refuel
That left/right tank imbalance does not exceed 100 kg, otherwise balance
That no more than the planned taxi fuel has been used, otherwise reassess the fuel situation
fragen.erklaerung_en: Before takeoff, verify that no more than the planned taxi fuel has been used; otherwise the fuel situation must be reassessed.

fragen.frage: In-flight Re-planning zu einer Destination, für die KEIN Destination Alternate erforderlich ist: Welches Element gehört NICHT zur geforderten Mindestmenge an Bord?
antworten: Destination Alternate Fuel
Contingency Fuel
Final Reserve Fuel
Extra Fuel
fragen.erklaerung: Ohne erforderliches Destination Alternate besteht die Summe aus Remaining Trip, Contingency, Final Reserve, Additional und Extra Fuel; Destination Alternate Fuel entfällt.
fragen.zitat: is not less than the sum of: remaining trip fuel contingency fuel final reserve fuel additional fuel extra fuel
kontext:
8.3.7.4 In-flight Re-planning Procedure

When in-flight re-planning is performed the Operational Flight Plan (OFP) must be amended accordingly.
When re-planning to a destination for which a destination alternate is required, the flight crew must ensure that the usable fuel on board at the point from which the revised operational flight plan applies is not less than the sum of: remaining trip fuel

contingency fuel

destination alternate fuel

final reserve fuel

additional fuel if required

extra fuel

When re-planning to a destination for which a destination alternate is not required, the flight crew must ensure that the usable fuel on board at the point from which the revised operational flight plan applies

is not less than the sum of: remaining trip fuel

contingency fuel

final reserve fuel additional fuel

extra fuel

In the event of in-flight replanning, at the point from which the revised operational flight plan applies, the expected landing mass shall not be greater than

the maximum landing mass and performance requirements shall meet the expected limitations. These include but are not limited to:

landing performance

approach climb performance
fragen.frage_en: In-flight re-planning to a destination for which NO destination alternate is required: which element is NOT part of the required minimum on board?
antworten_en: Destination alternate fuel
Contingency fuel
Final reserve fuel
Extra fuel
fragen.erklaerung_en: Without a required destination alternate, the total consists of remaining trip, contingency, final reserve, additional and extra fuel; destination alternate fuel does not apply.

fragen.frage: Wann ist gemäss OM-A bei ATC eine Delay Information anzufordern?
antworten: Wenn die erwartete Holding-Zeit an der Destination 10 Minuten überschreitet
Wenn unvorhergesehene Umstände zu einem Landing mit weniger als Final Reserve plus allfälliger Alternate Fuel führen könnten
Sobald die geplante Extra Fuel vollständig aufgebraucht ist
Wenn das berechnete Landing mit weniger als Final Reserve Fuel erfolgen wird
fragen.erklaerung: Delay Information ist anzufordern, wenn unvorhergesehene Umstände zu einem Landing mit weniger als Final Reserve Fuel plus allenfalls nötiger Fuel zum Alternate führen könnten; ein Landing unter FRF erfordert dagegen MAYDAY FUEL.
fragen.zitat: Delay information shall be requested from ATC when unanticipated circumstances may result in landing at the destination aerodrome with less than final reserve fuel plus any fuel required to proceed to an alternate aerodrome if required.
kontext: 8.3.7.5.1 Delay Information Request

Delay information shall be requested from ATC when unanticipated circumstances may result in landing at the destination aerodrome with less than final reserve fuel plus any fuel required to proceed to an alternate aerodrome if required.

There is no specific phraseology defined. The flight crew should use the information obtained from this request to determine the best course of action (e.g. to determine when it would be necessary to divert to an alternate aerodrome or to make additional declarations related to the fuel state).
fragen.frage_en: When must delay information be requested from ATC according to OM-A?
antworten_en: When the expected holding time at the destination exceeds 10 minutes
When unforeseen circumstances could lead to a landing with less than final reserve plus any alternate fuel
As soon as the planned extra fuel is completely used
When the calculated landing will be with less than final reserve fuel
fragen.erklaerung_en: Delay information must be requested if unforeseen circumstances could lead to a landing with less than final reserve fuel plus any fuel required for the alternate; a landing below FRF, in contrast, requires MAYDAY FUEL.

fragen.frage: Wer hat die Autorität für den endgültigen Entscheid über die auf einem Flug mitgeführte Fuel-Menge?
antworten: Operations Control (OCC) über den OFP
Der Flight Operations Officer (FOO)
Der Commander (CMD)
Der Pilot Flying des jeweiligen Sektors
fragen.erklaerung: Gemäss OM-A 8.1.7.1 hat der Commander die Autorität für den finalen Entscheid über die mitgeführte Fuel-Menge.
fragen.zitat: The Commander (CMD) holds the authority for the final decision regarding the amount of fuel to be carried on each flight.
kontext:
8.1.7.1 Fuel Planning

For helvetic operations the basic fuel scheme with variations is used.
Based on the appropriate consumption figures for each stage of flight as contained in the Operations Manual OM-B 5 for the specific aircraft type, the fuel on board at the start of each flight must be sufficient to cover the elements listed in: 8.1.7.4 - Basic Procedure or 8.1.7.5 - Procedure without Alternate or 8.1.7.6 - Procedure with Closed Destination or 8.1.7.7 - Procedure with Fuel En-route Alternate (Fuel-ERA) or 8.1.7.8 - Procedure with Reduced Contingency Fuel (RCF)

Operations Control prepares an Operational Flight Plan (OFP) containing the fuel calculation for the associated conditions.
For company fuel policies, refer to 8.1.10.1 - Operational Flight Plan – Format and Contents

The Commander (CMD) holds the authority for the final decision regarding the

amount of fuel to be carried on each flight.
fragen.frage_en: Who has the authority for the final decision on the amount of fuel carried on a flight?
antworten_en: Operations Control (OCC) via the OFP
The Flight Operations Officer (FOO)
The Commander (CMD)
The pilot flying of the respective sector
fragen.erklaerung_en: According to OM-A 8.1.7.1, the commander has the authority for the final decision on the amount of fuel carried.

fragen.frage: Wann muss für einen IFR-Departure ein Take-off Alternate im OFP angegeben werden?
antworten: Nur wenn das Wetter am Departure Aerodrome unter den Take-off-Minima liegt
Bei jedem Flug mit einer geplanten Flugzeit von mehr als 3 Stunden
Wenn die Destination nur GNSS-basierte Approach-Verfahren anbietet
Wenn das Wetter am Departure Aerodrome unter den OEI-Landing-Minima liegt oder eine Rückkehr ausgeschlossen ist (z.B. Night Ban)
fragen.erklaerung: Ein Take-off Alternate ist nötig, wenn das Wetter am Departure Aerodrome unter den Minima für ein Landing unter OEI-Bedingungen liegt oder andere Umstände eine Rückkehr verhindern.
fragen.zitat: weather conditions at the departure airport are less than the applicable minima for landing under One Engine Inoperative (OEI) conditions, or other operational conditions exist that would preclude a return to the departure airport
kontext:
8.1.5.3.2 Departure Aerodrome

OEI Minima or better

For an IFR flight initiation, a take-off alternate shall be available and specified in the Operational Flight Plan (OFP), if:

weather conditions at the departure airport are less than the applicable minima for landing under One Engine Inoperative (OEI) conditions, or other operational conditions exist that would preclude a return to the departure airport
(e.g. night ban, planned closure for state flight)
fragen.frage_en: When must a takeoff alternate be stated in the OFP for an IFR departure?
antworten_en: Only if the weather at the departure aerodrome is below takeoff minima
On every flight with a planned flight time of more than 3 hours
If the destination offers only GNSS-based approach procedures
If the weather at the departure aerodrome is below OEI landing minima or a return is excluded (e.g. night ban)
fragen.erklaerung_en: A takeoff alternate is required if the weather at the departure aerodrome is below the minima for a landing under OEI conditions or other circumstances prevent a return.

fragen.frage: Wo liegt das Zentrum des Kreises, innerhalb dessen ein Fuel En-route Alternate (Fuel-ERA) liegen muss?
antworten: Auf der Route, von der Destination entfernt um 25 % der Gesamtdistanz oder 20 % plus 50 NM, je nachdem was grösser ist
Auf der Route, genau in der Mitte zwischen Departure Aerodrome und Destination
Auf der Route, von der Destination entfernt um 20 % der Gesamtdistanz plus 100 NM
Am Decision Point, der möglichst nahe an der Destination liegen soll
fragen.erklaerung: Das Kreiszentrum liegt auf der geplanten Route in einer Distanz von der Destination von 25 % der Flight-Plan-Distanz oder mindestens 20 % plus 50 NM, je nachdem was grösser ist.
fragen.zitat: the centre of this circle lies on the planned route at a distance from the destination aerodrome, whichever is greater: equal to 25% of the total flight plan distance or at least 20% of the total flight plan distance plus 50 NM
kontext:
8.1.5.5.4 Planning based on Fuel En-route Alternate (Fuel-ERA)

A flight may be planned with a contingency fuel of 3%, provided that a Fuel En- route Alternate (Fuel-ERA) has been selected.
For the Fuel-ERA the following applies: the Fuel-ERA shall be located within a circle with a radius equal to 20% of the total flight plan distance

the centre of this circle lies on the planned route at a distance from the destination aerodrome, whichever is greater: equal to 25% of the total flight plan distance or at least 20% of the total flight plan distance plus 50 NM

all distances shall be calculated in still-air conditions

the Fuel-ERA shall be nominated in the operational flight plan
fragen.frage_en: Where is the center of the circle within which a fuel en-route alternate (Fuel-ERA) must be located?
antworten_en: On the route, at a distance from the destination of 25% of total distance or 20% plus 50 NM, whichever is greater
On the route, exactly midway between departure aerodrome and destination
On the route, at a distance from the destination of 20% of total distance plus 100 NM
At the decision point, which should be as close as possible to the destination
fragen.erklaerung_en: The circle center is on the planned route at a distance from the destination of 25% of the flight plan distance or at least 20% plus 50 NM, whichever is greater.

fragen.frage: Welche maximale Flugdauer gilt für eine Planung ohne Destination Alternate?
antworten: Höchstens 4 Stunden (bei In-flight Re-planning höchstens 2 Stunden Restflugzeit)
Höchstens 6 Stunden (bei In-flight Re-planning höchstens 4 Stunden Restflugzeit)
Höchstens 6 Stunden (bei In-flight Re-planning höchstens 3 Stunden Restflugzeit)
Höchstens 8 Stunden (bei In-flight Re-planning höchstens 6 Stunden Restflugzeit)
fragen.erklaerung: Die geplante Flugdauer darf 6 Stunden nicht überschreiten, bei In-flight Re-planning die verbleibende Flugzeit 4 Stunden.
fragen.zitat: the duration of the planned flight from take-off to landing does not exceed 6 hours, or in the event of in-flight re-planning, the remaining flight time to destination does not exceed 4 hours
kontext:
8.1.5.5.2 Planning without Destination Alternate

A flight may be planned without destination alternate, provided:
the duration of the planned flight from take-off to landing does not exceed 6 hours, or in the event of in-flight re-planning, the remaining flight time to destination does not exceed 4 hours

two separate runways are usable at the destination

the appropriate meteorological reports and/or forecasts indicate that for the period from 1 hour before to 1 hour after the expected time of arrival, the ceiling is at least 2 000 ft (600 m) or the circling height plus 500 ft (150 m), whichever is greater, and ground visibility is at least 5 km

no adverse weather forecast (e.g. thunderstorm, sandstorm, fog-patches irrespective of PROB or TEMPO in the forecast)

the wind is within AFM/OM-B limits for the planned approach, no gusts, no wind shears expected or forecast braking action at least medium

Refer to 8.1.7.3.6 - Additional Fuel for ADDNAR fuel considerations.

Note: Runways on the same airport are considered to be separate runways when they are separate landing surfaces, each having an approach

procedure based upon a separate navigation aid, which may overlay or cross such that, if one of the runways is blocked, it will not prevent the

planned operation on the other runway.
fragen.frage_en: Which maximum flight duration applies for planning without a destination alternate?
antworten_en: Max. 4 hours (for in-flight re-planning max. 2 hours remaining flight time)
Max. 6 hours (for in-flight re-planning max. 4 hours remaining flight time)
Max. 6 hours (for in-flight re-planning max. 3 hours remaining flight time)
Max. 8 hours (for in-flight re-planning max. 6 hours remaining flight time)
fragen.erklaerung_en: The planned flight duration must not exceed 6 hours, and for in-flight re-planning the remaining flight time must not exceed 4 hours.

fragen.frage: Welche Alternate Fuel wird bei einer Planung mit Closed Destination für die Fuel-Berechnung berücksichtigt?
antworten: Die Summe der Alternate Fuel beider Alternates
Die Alternate Fuel zum näher gelegenen Alternate
Die grössere der beiden Alternate-Fuel-Mengen
Die Alternate Fuel zum Alternate mit dem besseren Wetter
fragen.erklaerung: Bei Closed Destination muss für die Fuel-Berechnung die höhere Menge an Alternate Fuel berücksichtigt werden.
fragen.zitat: the weather forecast for both alternates is at or above the planning minima required For fuel calculation the higher quantity of alternate fuel must be considered.
kontext:
8.1.5.5.3 Planning with Closed Destination

A flight may be planned as a closed destination when the destination forecast is below landing minima or when no meteorological information for the destination aerodrome is available (METAR TAF) or the destination aerodrome is temporary closed for any other reason (e.g. snow removal, power failure, etc.)

provided that: at least two weather-permissible alternates are available

the weather forecast for both alternates is at or above the planning minima required

For fuel calculation the higher quantity of alternate fuel must be considered.
fragen.frage_en: Which alternate fuel is taken into account in the fuel calculation when planning with a closed destination?
antworten_en: The sum of the alternate fuel of both alternates
The alternate fuel to the nearer alternate
The greater of the two alternate fuel quantities
The alternate fuel to the alternate with the better weather
fragen.erklaerung_en: With a closed destination, the higher quantity of alternate fuel must be taken into account for the fuel calculation.

fragen.frage: Wo soll bei einer Planung mit Reduced Contingency Fuel (RCF) der Decision Point liegen?
antworten: Genau auf halber Strecke zwischen Departure Aerodrome und Destination
Am Top of Descent vor der Destination 2 (Refuelling Stop)
So nahe wie praktikabel am Departure Aerodrome, um eine Rückkehr zu ermöglichen
So nahe wie praktikabel an der Destination, um die benötigte Contingency Fuel zu minimieren
fragen.erklaerung: Der Decision Point kann an jeder geeigneten Position liegen, soll aber so nahe wie praktikabel an der Destination sein, um die erforderliche Contingency Fuel zu minimieren.
fragen.zitat: The Decision Point may be placed at any suitable position along the intended route and should be located as close as practicable to the destination in order to minimise required contingency fuel.
kontext:
8.1.5.5.5 Planning with Reduced Contingency Fuel (RCF)

Planning with Reduced Contingency Fuel (RCF) may only be applied if basic planning cannot be achieved due to the following operational limitations: load or range or take-off performance or fuel unavailability

The planned route will include a Decision Point at which the flight crew decides whether to continue to the destination aerodrome or divert to the nominated Destination 2 aerodrome (optional refuelling stop), based on the actual fuel state.
The Decision Point may be placed at any suitable position along the intended route and should be located as close as practicable to the destination in order to minimise required contingency fuel.
fragen.frage_en: Where should the decision point be located when planning with reduced contingency fuel (RCF)?
antworten_en: Exactly halfway between departure aerodrome and destination
At the top of descent before destination 2 (refuelling stop)
As close as practicable to the departure aerodrome to allow a return
As close as practicable to the destination to minimize the required contingency fuel
fragen.erklaerung_en: The decision point may be at any suitable position, but should be as close as practicable to the destination to minimize the required contingency fuel.

fragen.frage: Was gilt bei helvetic für die Planung zu einer Isolated Destination?
antworten: helvetic führt keine Isolated-Destination-Operationen durch
Erlaubt mit zusätzlich 2 Stunden Holding Fuel
Erlaubt, sofern an der Destination zwei separate Runways verfügbar sind
Erlaubt mit FOP-Genehmigung und 30 Minuten Extra Fuel
fragen.erklaerung: OM-A 8.1.5.5.6 hält fest, dass helvetic keine Operationen zu Isolated Destinations durchführt.
fragen.zitat: Planning to Isolated Destination helvetic does not conduct isolated destination operations.
kontext:
Planning to Isolated Destination

helvetic does not conduct isolated destination operations.
fragen.frage_en: What applies at helvetic for planning to an isolated destination?
antworten_en: helvetic does not conduct isolated destination operations
Permitted with an additional 2 hours of holding fuel
Permitted provided two separate runways are available at the destination
Permitted with FOP approval and 30 minutes of extra fuel
fragen.erklaerung_en: OM-A 8.1.5.5.6 states that helvetic does not conduct operations to isolated destinations.

The following conditions apply to the use of converted meteorological visibility (CMV) instead of RVR:

for flight planning purposes, a conversion factor of 1.0 shall be used

for purposes other than flight planning the following conversion table shall be used

RVR CMV reported VIS multiplied by:
Light elements in operation Day Night high intensity approach and 1.5 2 runway lights any type of light installation 1.0 1.5 other than above no lights 1.0 n/a

The table may be used except: for take-off minima calculations

if the RVR is available(1)

Note 1:
If no specific RVR is reported (e.g. “RVR more than 1500 m”) and the required minimum RVR for the approach is higher than that

antworten_en: 1.0 to 2.0 depending on lighting, per table
fragen.erklaerung_en: A conversion factor of 1.0 is to be used for flight planning purposes; the table applies only for other purposes.

fragen.frage: Mit welchem Faktor wird VS1G multipliziert, um die für die Approach Category massgebende VAT zu bestimmen?
fragen.erklaerung: VAT entspricht VSO x 1.3 oder VS1G x 1.23; bei Verfügbarkeit beider gilt der höhere resultierende Wert.

kontext:
8.1.3.1 Airplane Approach Category

The criterion taken into consideration for the classification of airplanes by categories is the Indicated Airspeed (IAS) at threshold (VAT).
It is equal to:

the stall speed VSO multiplied by 1.3; or

the 1-g-stall-speed VS1G multiplied by 1.23

The values for the stall speeds are taken for the landing configuration at the maximum certified landing mass. If both, stall speeds VSO and VS1G are available,

the higher resulting value for VAT shall be applied.

Airplane Approach Category VAT in KIAS 91

91 120

121 140

141 165 166 210

E-Jet
fragen.frage_en: By which factor is VS1G multiplied to determine the VAT relevant for the approach category?
fragen.erklaerung_en: VAT equals VSO x 1.3 or VS1G x 1.23; if both are available, the higher resulting value applies.

fragen.frage: Welche Lichter müssen bei Nachtoperationen für alle Anflugarten in Betrieb sein?
antworten: Runway Edge Lights, Threshold Lights und Runway End Lights
Approach Lights, Touchdown Zone Lights und Runway Edge Lights
Runway Centre Line Lights, Threshold Lights und PAPI
Runway Edge Lights, Runway Centre Line Lights und Taxiway Lights
fragen.erklaerung: In der Nacht müssen für alle Anflugarten Runway Edge Lights, Threshold Lights und Runway End Lights operationell sein.

kontext:
8.1.3.5 Effect of Temporarily Failed or Downgraded Ground Equipment on

Landing Minima

These procedures and instructions apply to both dispatch and in-flight situations.
Flight crews are not expected to consult these instructions after passing 1000 ft AAE. If ground equipment, other than the primary approach aid in use, fails at this late stage, the approach may continue at the flight crew’s discretion.
If failures are known before this stage, the effect on the approach shall be considered using:
OM-C 1 Route Manual Pubs (applicable region) General Airway Manual Aerodrome Operating Minimums – EASA Air Operations, pt 15 “Failed or Downgraded Equipment”.

Only the facilities mentioned in the applicable table under pt 15 shall be used to

determine the effect of temporarily failed or downgraded equipment.

threshold lights

runway end lights
fragen.frage_en: Which lights must be operational for all approach types during night operations?
antworten_en: Runway edge lights, threshold lights and runway end lights
Approach lights, touchdown zone lights and runway edge lights
Runway centre line lights, threshold lights and PAPI
Runway edge lights, runway centre line lights and taxiway lights
fragen.erklaerung_en: At night, runway edge lights, threshold lights and runway end lights must be operational for all approach types.

fragen.frage: Ab welchem Punkt wird von der Crew nicht mehr erwartet, die Anweisungen zu ausgefallenen oder herabgestuften Bodenanlagen zu konsultieren?
antworten: Nach dem Passieren des FAF
Nach dem Passieren von 1000 ft AAE
Nach dem Passieren von 500 ft AAE
Nach dem Erreichen der DA/MDA
fragen.erklaerung: Nach 1000 ft AAE müssen die Anweisungen nicht mehr konsultiert werden; ein später Ausfall (ausser der primären Approach Aid) erlaubt die Fortsetzung nach Ermessen der Crew.
fragen.zitat: Flight crews are not expected to consult these instructions after passing 1000 ft AAE.
kontext:
8.1.3.5 Effect of Temporarily Failed or Downgraded Ground Equipment on

Landing Minima

These procedures and instructions apply to both dispatch and in-flight situations.
Flight crews are not expected to consult these instructions after passing 1000 ft AAE.

If failures are known before this stage, the effect on the approach shall be considered using:
OM-C 1 Route Manual Pubs (applicable region) General Airway Manual Aerodrome Operating Minimums – EASA Air Operations, pt 15 “Failed or Downgraded Equipment”.

Only the facilities mentioned in the applicable table under pt 15 shall be used to

determine the effect of temporarily failed or downgraded equipment.
During night operations, the following lights have to be operational for all types of approaches: runway edge lights

threshold lights

runway end lights

kontext:
8.1.3.3 Take-off Minima

The take-off minima shall be selected to ensure sufficient guidance to control the aircraft in the event of both a rejected take-off in adverse circumstances and a continued take-off after failure of the critical engine.
Where there is a specific need to see and avoid obstacles on departure and/or for a forced landing, additional conditions (e.g. ceiling), shall be specified in the OM-C.
The minima of the required meteorological RVRor VIS for take-off are listed in the following table:

Minimum RVR or VIS (1) Facilities 500 m (day) Nil (2) Centre line markings or 400 m (day) Runway edge lights or Runway centre line lights

Runway end lights (3) 400 m (night) and Runway edge lights or runway centreline lights

Note 1:

The required RVR VIS must be available for a take-off runway part of

at least the length of the Accelerate Stop Distance (ASD).

The reported RVR or VIS value representative of the initial part of the take-off run can be replaced by pilot assessment.
Note 2: The pilot is able to continuously identify the take-off surface and

maintain directional control.

Note 3: Runway end lights may be substituted by colour-coded runway edge

lights or colour-coded runway centre line lights.

When the reported visibility is below that required for take-off and RVR is not

reported

or when neither reported visibility, nor RVR is available

a take-off may only be commenced if the flight crew can determine that the

visibility along the take-off runway is equal to, or better than the required minimum. This may require a runway visit to assess the actual visibility.

For Take-offs under VFR operations refer to 8.3.1.1 - Flights Taking-off from

VFR Airports expecting an IFR Clearance for the En-route Portion of the Flight.
For Take-offs with less than 400m RVR refer to 8.4.4.1 - Low Visibility Take-off with RVR of less than 400 m.
fragen.frage_en: Takeoff minima per OM-A 8.1.3.3: For which runway section must the required RVR/VIS be available at minimum?

At least over the length of the accelerate stop distance (ASD)
Only in the touchdown zone (TDZ)

An approach which is flown in a controlled and appropriate manner in terms of configuration, energy and control of the flight path
