fragen.frage: Wie schnell kann ein Type I Fluid nach Überschreiten der Holdover Time vom flüssigen in den festen Zustand übergehen (Flash Freeze)?
antworten: In etwa 5 Minuten
In nur etwa 30 Sekunden
In etwa 2 Minuten
In etwa 15 Minuten
fragen.erklaerung: Ein Type I Fluid kann nach Überschreiten der HOT in nur 30 Sekunden zu Eis werden (Flash Freeze).
fragen.zitat: since a Type I fluid may then change its condition from fluid to solid state (ice) in as little as 30 seconds. This effect is known as a flash freeze.
kontext:
8.2.4.3.1 Type I Fluid (un-thickened type)

This group is the widely known manufactured to the military specifications MIL-A-3243 or MIL-D-8243. The fluid must consist of at least 80 ethylene or propylene glycol, or 80 of a mixture of both. If diluted with water the fluid must have a freezing point of at least 10 degrees below the ambient temperature.
The mix of fluid and water must be heated to 60 degrees Celsius (140 degrees F) minimum at the nozzle.
Type I fluids provide protection mainly against re-freezing in conditions where precipitation is not expected. Special care must be taken not to exceed the Holdover Time (HOT),
since a Type I fluid may then change its condition from fluid to solid state (ice) in as little as 30 seconds. This effect is known as a flash freeze.
fragen.frage_en: How quickly can a Type I fluid change from liquid to solid state (flash freeze) after the holdover time has been exceeded?
antworten_en: In about 5 minutes
In only about 30 seconds
In about 2 minutes
In about 15 minutes
fragen.erklaerung_en: A Type I fluid can turn to ice in only 30 seconds after the HOT has been exceeded (flash freeze).

fragen.frage: Ab welcher Speed bricht die Viskosität eines Type II Fluids zusammen, sodass es von den Flächen abfliesst?
antworten: Ab etwa 60 Knoten
Erst bei Erreichen von VR
Ab etwa 30 Knoten
Ab etwa 100 Knoten
fragen.erklaerung: Sobald die Speed 30 Knoten oder mehr erreicht, bricht die Viskosität zusammen und das Fluid fliesst ab.
fragen.zitat: As soon as the speed exceeds 30 knots or more, the viscosity breaks down, causing the fluid to flow off the aerodynamic surfaces.
kontext:
8.2.4.3.2 Type II Fluids (thickened type)

These fluids have a thickener added in the form of high molecular polymers to a base material consisting of a minimum of 50 glycol. These provide the fluid with special viscosity properties, which are a function of the temperature and wind shear forces. When the aircraft is at rest or traveling at low speeds (ground operation), the fluid forms a uniform film over wing and tail plane.
As soon as the speed exceeds 30 knots or more, the viscosity breaks down, causing the fluid to flow off the aerodynamic surfaces.

This leaves the aircraft clean.
The rapid flow-off of Type II fluids is guaranteed even under arctic conditions (i.e. at temperatures of -25°C).

With Type II fluids AEA specifies a minimum freezing point of -32° C in undiluted form and -10° C when diluted with 50 water. A minimum of four hours protection against ice formation at -5° C under conditions of high humidity (surface temperature of -5° C and air temperature of 0°C) is specified.

A 30 minutes protection period against freezing rain under conditions of surface

and air temperatures of -5°C is also specified.

Type II fluids provide also protection against refreezing in conditions of

precipitation.

Fluids based on alcohol are prohibited because they can cause window crazing.
The higher viscosity of Type II fluids has the advantage of a longer holdover time,

but may cause problems to aircraft types with a low lift-off speed due to the

viscous property. The low lift-off speed might not be sufficient to allow the fluid to run back and disappear from the air foil. As a consequence the center of

pressure will change, resulting in a delayed rotation and lift-off. It is therefore imperative to check the instructions in the Operations Manual OM-B.
fragen.frage_en: From which speed does the viscosity of a Type II fluid break down so that it flows off the surfaces?
antworten_en: From about 60 knots
Only when reaching VR
From about 30 knots
From about 100 knots
fragen.erklaerung_en: As soon as the speed reaches 30 knots or more, the viscosity breaks down and the fluid flows off.

fragen.frage: Welche Visibility entspricht gemäss OM-A-Richtlinie zur HOT-Bestimmung einer moderaten Niederschlagsintensität?
fragen.erklaerung: Die Tabelle ordnet Moderate einer Visibility von ≤ 1000 m und > 500 m zu (Light > 1000 m, Heavy ≤ 500 m).
fragen.zitat: The following table is a guideline to estimate the precipitation intensity by visibility to determine the correct HOT: Intensity Visibility Light > 1000m Moderate ≤ 1000m and > 500m Heavy ≤ 500m
kontext:
8.2.4.9 Holdover Times for Type I, II and IV Fluids

Holdover Time (HOT) is the estimated time anti-icing fluid prevents ice, snow or frost from forming or accumulating on the treated surfaces of an aircraft.
The protection time is dependent upon the weather conditions and fluid mixture selected and cannot be precisely predetermined for each application.
The table on the following page is only a SAMPLE table and shall not be used for operational purposes. For actual hold over time tables refer to OM-0 9 Hold Over Time (HOT) Table.
Note: The lower limit of the published time span is used to indicate the estimated time of protection during moderate precipitation and the upper limit indicates the estimated time of protection during light precipitation.
High moisture content, high wind velocity or jet blast may reduce Holdover Time (HOT) below the lowest time stated in the range.
Holdover Time (HOT) may also be reduced when the aircraft skin temperature is lower than the Outside Air Temperature (OAT).
Therefore, the indicated times should be used only in conjunction with a pre-take-off check.

The Holdover Time (HOT) starts at the beginning of the application (for a one- step-procedure) respectively at the beginning of the second step (for a two-step- procedure).
The SAMPLE table on the next page gives an indication as to the time frame of protection that could reasonably be expected under conditions of precipitation.

However, due to the many variables that can influence Holdover Time (HOT), these times should not be considered as minimums or maximums as the actual time of protection may be extended or reduced, depending upon the particular conditions existing at the time.

Type II and IV fluids contain a pseudo-plastic thickening agent, which enables

the fluid to form a thicker liquid wetting film on external aircraft surfaces. This film

provides a longer holdover time especially in conditions of freezing precipitation.

With this type of fluid additional holdover time will be provided by increasing the concentration of the fluid in the fluid/water mix, with maximum holdover time

available from undiluted fluid.

The following table is a guideline to estimate the precipitation intensity by

visibility to determine the correct HOT:

Intensity Visibility Light 1000m

Moderate 1000m and 500m

Heavy 500m

Note: A degraded type II or IV fluid shall be used with the holdover time

guideline for type I fluids. A type II or IV fluid is considered to be

degraded if the viscosity is below the minimum limit as provided by the fluid manufacturer.

Aircraft surfaces treated with anti-icing fluids should appear glossy, smooth and

wet. An indication that protection is deteriorating is the loss of gloss or dulling of the surfaces as the fluid gradually turns to slush.

The Operations Manual OM-B may require a very specific pre-flight wing ice

check (e.g. as physical touch). A thorough review of these procedures is essential.
fragen.frage_en: Which visibility corresponds to a moderate precipitation intensity according to the OM-A guideline for HOT determination?
fragen.erklaerung_en: The table assigns moderate to a visibility of ≤ 1000 m and > 500 m (light > 1000 m, heavy ≤ 500 m).

fragen.frage: Was muss der Commander tun, wenn er vor dem Takeoff eine Bestätigung des eisfreien Zustands des Flugzeugs benötigt?
antworten: Beim De-icing-Personal den Anti-icing Code erneut anfordern
Die Holdover Time um 50 % reduzieren und dann starten
Den Tower um einen Runway Inspection Check bitten
Eine Sichtkontrolle durchführen oder anordnen oder zur Rampe zurückkehren
fragen.erklaerung: Der CMD muss eine Sichtkontrolle selbst durchführen, eine anordnen oder zur Rampe zurückkehren.
fragen.zitat: If, at any time prior to take-off, the Commander (CMD) requires conformation of the ice free status of the aircraft, he must: carry out a visual inspection, or order a visual inspection, or return to the ramp
kontext:
8.2.4.10 Responsibilities

The aircraft Commander (CMD) is responsible for effective de-icing and anti-icing in accordance with the provisions of the Operations Manual OM-B.
His request for the de-icing treatment and for the fluid mixtures used will always take precedence over locally recommended procedures.
The Commander (CMD) has the authority to obtain de/ anti-icing whenever he determines that it is necessary.
For large aircraft, the Commander (CMD) may not be able to personally check for the correct treatment. In this case, the person releasing the aircraft after the de-icing process is responsible for its performance and verification of the results.
He will communicate the ISO, AEA or SAE de-icing code to the flight crew to confirm the correct de-icing. The general transfer of operational responsibilities takes place at the moment the aircraft starts movement under its own power.

If, at any time prior to take-off, the Commander (CMD) requires conformation of the ice free status of the aircraft, he must: carry out a visual inspection, or order a visual inspection, or return to the ramp
fragen.frage_en: What must the commander do if he needs confirmation that the aircraft is free of ice before takeoff?
antworten_en: Request the anti-icing code again from the de-icing personnel
Reduce the holdover time by 50% and then take off
Ask the tower for a runway inspection check
Perform or order a visual check, or return to the ramp
fragen.erklaerung_en: The CMD must perform a visual check himself, order one, or return to the ramp.

kontext:
8.4.1.3 Category II Approaches

CAT II weather minima have been established to provide sufficient visual references at Decision Height (DH) to permit: a manual landing (which must not necessarily to be made manually) or a manually flown missed approach

If the approach is flown using autopilot, for a manual landing the autopilot shall remain engaged until after the pilot has achieved visual reference.
For type specific limitations regarding use of autopilot for CAT II approaches refer to type specific OM-B.
The DH shall be determined by the use of a radio altimeter and be not lower than the highest of: the minimum DH specified in the type specific AFM or

the applicable obstacle clearance height (OCH) for the category of aircraft or

the DH to which the flight crew is qualified to operate or 100 ft above threshold

The minimum Runway Visual Range (RVR) is a function of the Decision Height

(DH) and Aircraft Category:

DH (ft) (1) minimum RVR according to Aircraft Category

A, B, C 100 – 120 300 300 350 (2)

121 – 140 400 400

141 – 199 450 450

Note 1: 100 ft DH above threshold. Radio Altimeter (RA) indication may be

less or higher depending on the terrain profile during approach.

Note 2: An RVR of 300 m may be used for a Category D airplane

conducting an autoland or using HUDLS to touchdown.

fragen.erklaerung_en: The CAT II DH must not be lower than the highest of AFM minimum, OCH, crew qualification or 100 ft above threshold.

fragen.frage: Was gilt bei einem Ausfall im Fail-operational Landing System, der unterhalb der Alert Height (AH) auftritt?
antworten: Es ist zwingend ein Go-around einzuleiten
Der Ausfall wird üblicherweise ignoriert und der Approach fortgesetzt
Der Approach ist bis zur DH fortzusetzen und dann abzubrechen
Das Landing darf nur bei einer RVR über 300 m fortgesetzt werden
fragen.erklaerung: Es ist allgemeine Praxis, einen Ausfall unterhalb der AH zu ignorieren und den Approach fortzusetzen.
fragen.zitat: It is general practice to ignore a failure when it occurs below the Alert Height (AH), and to continue the approach.
kontext:
8.4.1.7 Alert Height (AH)

An Alert Height (AH) is a height above the runway, based on the characteristics of the aircraft and its fail-operational automatic landing system, above which a Category III approach would be discontinued and a missed approach initiated if a failure occurred in one of the redundant parts of the automatic landing system, or in the relevant ground equipment.
It is general practice to ignore a failure when it occurs below the Alert Height (AH), and to continue the approach.
fragen.frage_en: What applies to a failure in the fail-operational landing system that occurs below the alert height (AH)?
antworten_en: A go-around must be initiated
The failure is usually ignored and the approach continued
The approach must be continued to DH and then discontinued
The landing may be continued only at an RVR above 300 m
fragen.erklaerung_en: It is general practice to ignore a failure below AH and continue the approach.

kontext:
8.4.1.4 Category III Approaches

A category III (CAT III) approach is a precision approach with lower than CAT II minima.
Where the Decision Height (DH) and Runway Visual Range (RVR) do not fall within the same category, the RVR will determine in which category the operation is to be considered.

In contrast to other operations, some category III weather minima do not provide sufficient visual references to allow a manual landing. The minima only permit the pilots to decide if the aircraft will land in the touchdown zone and to ensure safety during roll-out. Therefore an automatic landing system is mandatory to perform category III operations. Its reliability must be sufficient to control the aircraft to touchdown and if applicable during roll-out phase until reaching a safe taxi speed.

kontext:
8.3.8.2 Thunderstorms

Thunderstorms are classified as:

frontal thunderstorms

air mass thunderstorms

Frontal thunderstorms may exist as:

warm front thunderstorms

cold front thunderstorms

occluded front thunderstorms

Air mass thunderstorms are divided into:

convective thunderstorms

orographic thunderstorms

Frontal thunderstorms form in squall lines and generate heavy rain and possibly hail and produce strong gusty winds and possibly tornadoes.
Large horizontal wind changes in speed and direction at different altitudes are characteristic for a frontal thunderstorm. Resulting airflows in the storm accelerate to much higher vertical speeds, which ultimately results in higher horizontal wind speeds at the surface.
Air mass thunderstorms are caused either by thermal convection or by moist air moving uphill on the windward side of a mountain.
Air mass thunderstorms appear to be randomly distributed in unstable air and develop from local heating of the earth’s surface. As the heated air rises it cools and subsequently forms cumulus clouds. As the cumulus stage continues to develop, precipitation forms in the higher portion of the cloud and falls out.
Precipitation signals the beginning of the mature stage and pressure of a downdraft.
In the later stages of development, the heated updraft creating the thunderstorm is cut off by rainfall, and the thunderstorm begins to dissipate. Many thunderstorms produce an associated cold air gust front as a result of the down flow and out rushing rain-cooled air. These gust fronts are usually very turbulent and are a serious threat during take-off and landing.
The vertical extension of thunderstorms is up to 25 000 ft during winter time and up to the troposphere during summer, the horizontal range is 10 to 20 km.
Besides the dangerous situations already mentioned, there may be additional dangers from sudden heavy precipitation with poor visibility below the clouds, possibly hail showers, heavy icing formation, and severe turbulence.

Lightning is not a direct danger for the crew and passengers of an aircraft in flight, as the electrical load will remain at the surface of the aircraft (Faraday Cage). Lightning strikes may, however, disturb or damage the navigation system.

If the aircraft is not equipped with radar or if the radar is inoperative, any cloud that appears, through visual inspection: tall,

The radar equipment shall be intermittently operated on long ranges in order to

The local activity of thunderstorms can often be of relatively short nature, (i.e. 20 to 30 minutes). 8.3.8.2.1 Possibility of lightning strikes in wintertime

There is a strong relationship between temperatures around 0°C and lightning strikes to airplanes. Most lightning strikes to airplanes occur close to freezing temperatures. Conditions that cause precipitation may also cause electrical

with precipitation and cloud creation.

kontext:
8.3.8.3.1 Types of Ice

The usual cloud sized small droplets tend to follow the aerodynamic flow around the wing. They are swept away, while larger, heavier droplets tend to impinge aft of the leading edge. The larger (and hence heavier) the droplet (drizzle or rain sized), the further aft it will impinge. Furthermore, large droplets are relatively warm and as a result they tend to run back and spread out in liquid state before freezing. This effect is known as flow back. Its effect depends directly upon size, temperature and velocity of water droplets and wing surface temperature.
Impingement and flow back result in ice collecting not only on the leading edge, but also on the upper and lower surfaces of a wing, where there may be no ice protection.
Rime Ice Rime ice is associated with stratiform clouds and forms when droplets are small and the temperature is relatively cold (-15°C or below). Not all of the droplets follow the airflow. Some impact upon the wing and tail plane leading edges with little or no flow back, freezing quickly into rime ice. Therefore, leading edge anti-

and deicing equipment is relatively effective against this type of ice.
Clear Ice Clear ice is associated with cumuliform clouds and forms when the temperature

is relatively warm (-10°C or above). Droplet sizes are relatively large (drizzle or

rain sized), and they tend to impinge further aft and flow back before freezing to

form sheet ice on the upper and lower surfaces of the wing. These areas may not be protected by anti- and deicing equipment. Any deposit greater than light can

significantly degrade performance, causing problems in roll and pitch control

with, in the extreme case, uncontrollable pitch up and stall.
Clear ice can form on airfoil surfaces with few visual cues to the flight crew. The

absence of the usual indications, such as ice formation on the windshield posts

and wipers, does not mean that clear ice is not forming. The terms freezing drizzle or freezing rain in a terminal forecast or weather report indicate a strong

probability of conditions for clear ice.
Mixed Ice

Mixed ice is a combination of clear and rime ice with all the hazards of both. It forms when droplets vary in size (e.g. drizzle in stratiform clouds) and the

temperature is in the range of -10°C to -15°C. The proportional makeup varies

with the weather system.

kontext:
8.3.8.3.4 Control Anomalies in Icing Conditions

The formation of ice on the aircraft structure could create a situation from which the flight crew might have difficulties recovering and, in some instances, may not be able to recover at all. For this reason, the following information describes two particular types of control upsets likely to be encountered during flight in severe icing conditions.
Roll Upset Roll upset is an un-commanded and un-controlled roll phenomenon, which may occur as a consequence of, or prior to, a wing stall, due to: anomalous forces, that cause the ailerons to deflect, or loss of effectiveness of the ailerons

Deflections of ailerons or loss of aileron effectiveness may be caused by ice accumulation in a sensitive area of the wing aft of the de-icing area. It occurs under unusual circumstances associated with super cooled large droplets and rarely under normal cloud droplets in a very narrow temperature range near freezing level. Roll upset can result from severe icing conditions even without the usual symptoms of ice accumulation or a perceived aerodynamic stall.
Pilots can minimize the chance of a roll upset by being sensitive to cues that identify severe icing conditions and by promptly exiting the severe icing conditions before control or handling characteristics of the aircraft are degraded to a hazardous level.

It is important to review the Operations Manual OM-B for aircraft type specific information. Additionally, pilots should check any available bulletins related to icing by the aircraft manufacturer.

Tail Plane Stall

Tail plane (empennage) stall is another significant hazard of airframe icing. Sharp

edged surfaces are more susceptible to collecting ice than large and blunt ones.

For this reason, the tail plane may begin accumulating ice before the wings and can accumulate it faster. There have been reports of ice on the tail plane without

any visible ice on the wing. This can also occur, if the tail plane has not been or cannot be deiced.

A tail plane stall occurs when, as with the wing, the critical angle of attack is

exceeded. Since the horizontal stabilizer counters the natural nose down tendency caused by the center of lift of the main wing being located aft of the

center of gravity, the aircraft will react by pitching nose down, sometimes uncontrollably, when the tail plane is stalled. Application of flaps can aggravate or

initiate the stall. Use caution when applying flaps during approach, if there is the possibility of icing on the tail plane.
Perhaps the most important characteristic of a tail plane stall is the relatively high airspeed at the onset and, if it occurs, the suddenness and magnitude of the nose down pitch.

A stall is more likely to occur when the flaps are approaching the fully extended position, after nose down pitch and airspeed changes following flap extension, or during flight through wind gusts.
Once a tail plane stall is encountered, the stall condition tends to worsen with increased airspeed and possibly may worsen with increased power settings at the same flap setting. Airspeed, at any flap setting, in excess of the aircraft manufacturer’s recommendations for the flight and environmental conditions, accompanied by un-cleared ice contamination on the tail plane, may result in a tail plane stall and uncommanded pitch down from which a recovery may not be possible. A tail plane stall may occur at speeds less than the flap extension speed.

kontext:
8.3.8.4 Turbulence

Turbulence is defined as a disturbed, irregular flow of air with embedded irregular whirls or eddies and waves. An aircraft in turbulent flow is subjected to irregular and random motions while, more or less, maintaining its intended flight path.
The intensity specifications for turbulence reporting have been defined as follows: light: slight discomfort

moderate: moderate changes in aircraft attitude or altitude accompanied by small variations in airspeed; walking is difficult, loose objects move around

severe: abrupt changes in aircraft attitude or altitude; the aircraft may be out of control for short periods accompanied by large variations in airspeed; occupants are forced violently against seatbelts; loose objects are tossed around Turbulence may be one of the following types: convective turbulence

orographic turbulence

Clear Air Turbulence (CAT)

wake turbulence

Convective turbulence is caused by thermal instability and is met in connection with the development and activity of thunderstorms.
It can cause extreme air motion with vertical speeds up to 6 000 ft/min.

Mostly it is encountered with severe turbulence in connection with thunderstorm activity.

Mountain waves at the lee side of a mountain may cause severe turbulence,

called orographic turbulence. Typical signs are lenticular, rotor clouds and clouds

with waterfall appearance. The strongest turbulence may be found in rotor

clouds.

Clear Air Turbulence (CAT) is of special significance, since its presence cannot be detected before it is encountered. It is caused by large wind shears with rapid

changes of wind direction horizontally or vertically.

Abrupt changes of the wind direction in a sharp trough line may cause considerable turbulence and a change of flight level will normally alleviate the

problem. Clear Air Turbulence (CAT) may also be expected on the upper side of a sloping tropopause.

Further large horizontal and vertical shears of wind speed in the transition zone between cold and warm air masses as well as at the tropopause associated with

jet streams may cause severe Clear Air Turbulence (CAT). These areas of

turbulence are normally shallow, narrow and extended patches, which move with the wind.

kontext:
8.2.1.4 Safety Precautions

Weather If thunderstorms are in the vicinity, fuelling and de-fuelling operations must be suspended.
Operation of Electrical Systems
During pressure refuelling, electrical and electronic systems except for weather radar and HF transmitters, may be operated to the extent required for pre-flight preparation.

In the event of an emergency (e.g. APU fire, smoke of unknown origin), the operation must be stopped and an immediate disembarkation, eventually even an evacuation must be initiated.
Fuel Spillage If during refuelling a fuel spill is noticed by the crew, handling agent or fuel service provider, the following actions shall be initiated without delay.
Below listed actions shall be applied whenever fuel spill is noticed, no matter if crew or passengers are on board or not. fuelling process shall be stopped immediately

appropriate ground handling personnel shall be informed

airport fire brigade shall be alerted for immediate actions

qualified person on board shall be informed immediately

(e.g. flight crew, maintenance) Operation of Engines and APU

engine start during fuelling is not allowed

refuelling with an engine running is not allowed

APU start during fuelling is not allowed

fuelling with APU running is allowed without restrictions

Precautions for Fuelling with Wide-Cut Fuel Wide-cut fuel (designated JET B, JP-4 or AVTAG) is an aviation turbine fuel that falls between gasoline and kerosene in the distillation range and consequently, compared to kerosene (e.g. JET A, JET A1), it has the properties of higher volatility (vapour pressure), lower flash point and lower freezing point Wherever possible, the use of wide-cut fuel types should be avoided.
If a situation arises such that only wide-cut fuels are available for refuelling/defuelling, flight crews shall be aware that mixtures of wide-cut fuels and kerosene turbine fuels can result in the air/fuel mixture in the tank being in the combustible range at ambient temperatures.
The extra precautions set out below are advisable to avoid arcing in the tank due to electrostatic discharge. The risk of this type of arcing can be minimised by the use of a static dissipation additive in the fuel. When this additive is present in the proportions stated in the fuel specification, the normal fuelling precautions set out below are considered adequate.

wide-cut fuel is considered to be involved when it is being supplied or when it is already present in aircraft fuel tanks

when wide-cut fuel has been used, this shall be recorded in the technical log. The next two uplifts of fuel should be treated as though they too involved the use of wide-cut fuel

when refuelling defuelling with turbine fuels not containing a static dissipator, and where wide- cut fuels are involved, a substantial reduction on fuelling flow rate is advisable. Reduced flow rate, as recommended by fuel suppliers has the following benefits: it allows more time for any static charge build-up in the fuelling

equipment to dissipate before the fuel enters the tank

it reduces any charge which may build up due to splashing

until the fuel inlet point is immersed, it reduces misting in the tank and

consequently the extension of the flammable range of the fuel

the flow rate reduction necessary is dependent upon the fuelling equipment in use and the type of filtration employed on the airplane fuelling distribution

system. It is difficult, therefore, to quote precise flow rates. Reduction in flow

rate is advisable whether pressure fuelling or over-wing fuelling is employed

with over-wing fuelling, splashing should be avoided by making sure that the delivery nozzle extends as far as practicable into the tank. Caution should

be exercised to avoid damaging bag tanks with the nozzle

antworten_en: VHF radio and transponder

fragen.erklaerung_en: During pressure refuelling, electrical and electronic systems may be operated as needed, except weather radar and HF transmitters.

kontext:
8.2.1.5 Fuelling with Passengers on Board

During normal operations it may be necessary to fuel or de-fuel an aircraft with passengers on board. Passengers may embark, disembark or remain on board during fuelling and de-fuelling operation provided that the following precautions are observed: local procedures must be verified and adhered to

a member of the flight crew must remain on the flight deck

a two way communication between the flight crew member in the cockpit and a cabin crew member in the cabin must be established

a two way communication between ground crew supervising the refuelling and the qualified personnel on board the airplane is assured (via intercommunication system, direct person-to-person contact or any other method of communication)

fuelling personnel shall be informed that passengers will be on board during fuelling and immediate communication to a flight crew member being on the flight deck shall be established either via inter-communication system or direct person-to-person contact

all cabin crew members shall be informed by the Commander (CMD).
For callouts refer to 8.3 App. 1 - Communication Wording CSPM 2 Appendix 1 Communication Wording

all cabin crew members shall be able to communicate among cabin crew members and passengers (e.g. via PA, hand signals (body language) or megaphone)

cont.

the fuelling may start only after positive confirmation of the Senior cabin crew member (SEN) towards the Commander CMD has taken place verifying that the following precautionary measures are taken (for callouts refer to 8.3 App. 1 - Communication Wording CSPM 2 Appendix 1 Communication Wording): the fasten seat belt signs must be off, the no smoking signs must be on, together with interior lighting to enable emergency exits to be identified

passengers are to be briefed not to smoke at any time on the ground and to remain seated until the fuelling has been completed, refer to OM- 0 4 CCM
in principle, for all aircraft types, at least a minimum of two passenger cabin doors shall be opened and passenger stairs jetways must be positioned at these doors

if only one passenger stair jetway is available, the requirement for the second passenger cabin door may be met by positioning a cabin crew member, who will remain at a second door throughout the refuelling process. The door should not be automatic armed, unless required in an emergency

in the cabin, a cabin crew member shall be positioned next to the boarding door and be prepared for an immediate emergency evacuation, the rest of the cabin crew members shall be positioned in the vicinity of their assigned doors/exits (refer to CSPM 5 Standard

Operation Position/Area “Fuelling with Passengers on Board”) on all exits the outside-area shall remain clear during fuelling operations

routes to the emergency exits shall be unobstructed

if the presence of fuel vapour is detected inside the aircraft, or any other

hazard arises fuelling or de-fuelling shall be stopped immediately

if deemed necessary by the crew, a de-boarding shall be performed via the stairs or an evacuation via the escape slides, if deemed necessary limited to

the non-spilled side

fuelling and de-fuelling with wide cut fuel (e.g. Jet B or equivalent) is prohibited with passengers on board

after completion of fuelling the Commander (CMD) will notify the Senior

cabin attendant (SEN) which means that normal duties may be resumed.
For callouts refer to 8.3 App. 1 - Communication Wording

CSPM 2 Appendix 1 Communication Wording

Commander (CMD) is responsible for evaluating the situation on the particular airport at the given time, and determining a person responsible for the fueling operation and communication to the flight crew during fueling with passengers on board. That can be one of the following positions: ground staff (ideally flight supervisor)

fueling personnel, should there be means of communication with the flight crew in place

one of the flight crew members

If none of the above positions can assure proper supervision, fueling with passengers on board shall not be performed.

The minimum number of cabin crew required in these circumstances

shall be

one per pair of floor-level emergency exits on each passenger deck, or one for

every 50, or fraction of 50, passengers present on board, whichever is greater.

kontext:
8.2.2.1 Embarkation and Disembarkation

Before the embarkation of the passengers, the ground staff must brief them on all relevant safety aspects (e.g. no smoking regulations) effective during boarding the aircraft. When jet ways are in use, ground staff must be positioned at appropriate locations to provide supervision and assistance.
When passengers are required to walk on the ramp, they shall be escorted by ground staff to the aircraft or their approved transport; passenger routes shall be clear of oil, ice, snow and other hazards and shall be selected in a way that prevents from damages and accidents (e.g. no passing below wings or engines).
Whenever passengers are embarking, on board or disembarking at least one flight crew member shall be on board.
Boarding shall not commence until the Commander (CMD) or his representative (i.e. Senior Cabin Attendant – SEN) has given the clearance.
Disembarkation shall not commence until the crew has received confirmation from the ground staff that passenger steps or jet ways are safely in position and that ground equipment will not be a hazard.
For embarkation and disembarkation when fuelling is in progress, refer to 8.2.1.5 - Fuelling with Passengers on Board.
Only in exceptional cases and with the consent of the Commander (CMD), the embarkation or disembarkation of passengers is permissible with one engine of the aircraft operating.

Under no circumstances
Always, provided the engine on the far side is running
Only with the handling agent's approval
fragen.erklaerung_en: Boarding or disembarking with an engine running is permitted only in exceptional cases and with the CMD's approval.

Wenn die Behebung voraussichtlich mehr als 60 Minuten dauert

kontext:
8.2.2.1.2 Boarding of Passengers During Technical Malfunction Handling

Stopping the boarding process could cause massive additional delays. History shows the most technical malfunction rectification can be completed within a reasonable time frame. In order to keep delays at the minimum, the following guideline shall be observed in regard to boarding of passengers during technical malfunction handling.

Parked at the jet way: passengers should be ready for boarding at any time

passengers boarding the jet way up to the passenger door should be considered

Parked at open stand (bus transport):
boarding should not be stopped unless it is obvious the malfunction rectification takes a longer period (e.g. more than 30 minutes)

passengers waiting time in the bus before the aircraft should be considered

Note: Passengers shall be properly informed about boarding delays.
fragen.frage_en: Technical problem, aircraft at a remote stand (bus transport): when should boarding be stopped?
antworten_en: Always immediately, until the problem is fully resolved
Only if the rectification is obviously going to take longer (e.g. more than 30 minutes)
If the rectification is expected to take more than 10 minutes
If the rectification is expected to take more than 60 minutes
fragen.erklaerung_en: At a remote stand, boarding should not be stopped unless the rectification obviously takes longer, e.g. more than 30 minutes.

kontext:
8.2.2.2 Allocation of Seats

The allocation of seats to passengers by ground staff depends upon the aircraft type, its seating version, aspects of mass and center of gravity and the class of transportation (if any) held by the individual passenger.
Aircraft type-specific instructions for crew concerning seating restrictions for passengers are listed in the Cabin Safety and Procedures Manual CSPM 2.1.2.5 Seating Restrictions Passengers who should be seated where they will not obstruct access to safety equipment or exits or otherwise impede the crew in carrying out their duties are: persons, who are physically or mentally handicapped to the extent that they would have difficulty in moving quickly if asked to do so

persons, whose sight or hearing is impaired to the extent that they might not readily become aware of instructions given to begin evacuating the aircraft

children and infants, whether or not they are accompanied by an adult

persons in custody and those who are being deported

persons whose physical size would prevent them from being able to move quickly

persons with guide dogs or pet animals

Reseating groups of passengers without Commander (CMD) approval is not permitted.
However, the cabin crew members are authorised to reseat able-bodied

passengers and persons with reduced mobility (PRM).

Refer to 8.2.2.3.3 - Able Bodied Person (ABP)

CSPM 2.1.2.7.3 Able Bodied Person (ABP)

If there are blocked seats on the Passenger Information List (PIL) because of

trim and balance, it is not allowed to reseat passengers into those seats without the Commander’s approval. If passengers reseat themselves without crew approval, cabin crew shall move them back to their original seats.
fragen.frage_en: Who must approve the reseating of a group of passengers?
antworten_en: Any cabin crew member, without consultation
Ground staff exclusively
The commander (CMD)
The senior cabin attendant (SEN)
fragen.erklaerung_en: Reseating groups of passengers without CMD approval is not permitted; cabin crew may only reseat ABP and PRM.

equipment

kontext:
8.2.2.5 Permissible Size and Mass of Carry-on Baggage

The necessity for secure stowage of carry-on luggage limits the permissible size and weight of carry-on luggage. helvetic briefs passengers when booking (online confirmation) and at check-in upon the maximum size and mass of carry-on luggage.
When boarding is in progress ground staff and, at the aircraft, crew members shall visually scan the carry-on luggage held by passengers. Where carry – on luggage exceeds the allowances in size or weight the hand luggage shall be carried in the baggage compartment as checked-in baggage.
Due to security regulations a “delivery at aircraft” procedure for such baggage is not possible. This implies, that the respective baggage is returned to the passenger at the final destination

in the arrival sector of the airport with any other checked-in baggage.
For loading instructions refer to 8.2.2.7 - Securing of Load in the Cabin.
The following shall be applied to oversized carry-on luggage:
Station Baggage Tags Available: ask the passenger if he has his travel documents or medicine with himself as the luggage will be returned to the passenger on the baggage belt at the final destination arrival hall

ask the passenger if he has any kind of spare lithium batteries or e-cigarettes in the luggage and ask him to take it out of the checked-in

luggage

separate the respective piece of baggage

ask passenger for boarding card

The white limited release tag has to be completed with the following information: flight number and destination (for multi leg journey, the final destination has to be stated on top followed by the transit destinations)

write down passenger name and seat number on tag

attach tag to luggage

stuck one bar-code sticker onto luggage

sticker two: write down passenger name and seat number on the second bar-code sticker and hand it over to ground personnel prior to door closing

the handling staff will tag the luggage and add the luggage to the corresponding passenger check-in record

the handling agent shall thereafter carry the oversized luggage to the baggage compartment and organize loading

Station Baggage Tags NOT Available: ask the passenger if he has his travel documents and/or medicine with himself as the luggage will be delivered on the baggage belt

ask the passenger if he has any kind of spare lithium batteries in the luggage and ask him to take it out of the checked-in luggage

ask the passenger if he as a mercury barometer or thermometer in the luggage and ask him to take it out of the checked-in luggage

separate the respective piece of baggage

ask passenger for boarding card

fill out helvetic Airways baggage tag

label the hand luggage

inform the ground staff about the luggage and hand over the boarding card

together with the copy of the baggage label to check-in the luggage into the check-in system

the handling staff will add the luggage to the corresponding passenger

check-in record

antworten_en: As delivery at aircraft on disembarking directly at the aircraft door
With the other checked baggage at the final destination; delivery at aircraft is not possible
After the flight from the senior cabin attendant in the forward galley
With the next flight, as it is left behind

fragen.frage: Wie sind kranke und behinderte Passagiere sowie PRM normalerweise zu boarden und auszuladen?
antworten: Zusammen mit den übrigen Passagieren nach Sitzreihen
Als letzte einsteigen und als erste aussteigen

Separat, nach allen anderen einsteigen und vor allen anderen aussteigen

fragen.zitat: Sick and disabled passengers and PRM should be boarded separately (normally prior to all other passengers) as well as disembarked separately (normally after all other passengers have left the cabin).
kontext:
8.2.2.3.2 Handling and Boarding

Before accepting sick, disabled and handicapped passengers for transportation, helvetic shall have ascertained the availability, from departure to arrival, of staff trained and qualified to meet their needs and of the appropriate medical equipment.
The number of PRM`s shall not exceed the number of able bodied persons.
They shall be briefed separately by the crew. Consider that in an emergency, the cabin crew can only assist them, once the cabin has been evacuated.
Passengers with disabilities as circumscribed under WCHR, WCHS and WCHC above, shall be allocated seat rows between passenger cabin doors and over- wing but not at the over wing exits. (for airplane specific limitations refer to CSPM 2) They shall be seated next to the window. In this way, when the aircraft is being evacuated, they can – without impeding others – be assisted to reach the end of the line forming at the emergency exits and to leave the aircraft.
Sick and disabled passengers and PRM should be boarded separately (normally prior to all other passengers) as well as disembarked separately (normally after all other passengers have left the cabin).

Note: It is the care company’s duty to escort the PRM to and from their seat (not only to and from the aircraft door) and to assist with cabin baggage storage.

The Commander (CMD) shall be notified by the Senior Cabin Attendant (SEN) if Persons with Reduced Mobility (PRM) are listed on the Passenger Information

List (PIL).
For the carriage of gas cylinders, drugs, medicines, other medical material, wet cell or lithium battery powered wheel chairs refer to the 9.4.4 - Carriage of Wheelchairs and Other Mobility Aids and 10 - Security.

No transportation, under any circumstances, shall be provided to a person who:

has a contagious or infectious disease (e.g. open tuberculosis, infectious

hepatitis; scarlet fever, diphtheria, chickenpox)

has suffered a heart attack or stroke within the last eight weeks

requires medical treatment by pneumatically or electrically operated

apparatus, which, for specific reasons, is not allowed to be operated on board (for limitations refer to the Operations Manual OM-A 10)
fragen.frage_en: How are sick and disabled passengers as well as PRM normally to be boarded and disembarked?
antworten_en: Together with the other passengers by seat row
Board last and disembark first
Separately, board before all others and disembark after all others
Separately, board after all others and disembark before all others
fragen.erklaerung_en: PRM and sick passengers should board separately (normally before all others) and disembark separately (normally after all others).

8.3.10.4 Use of Headset

Each flight crew member required to be on flight deck shall wear the headset and use the boom microphone as the primary device for communication.

On Ground: when receiving the ATC departure clearance via voice communication

when engines are running

Note: The reception of the departure clearance (e.g SID) is of special importance. Therefore, it has to be assured, that both flight crew members listen to the given clearance.

In Flight: when flying below transition altitude level or climb and descent below 10.000 feet above the aerodrome of departure after take-off and the aerodrome of destination before landing, except for cruise flight, whichever is higher

whenever deemed necessary by the Commander (CMD)

inflight according to 8.3.10.2 - Flight Crew Members Leaving their Station

8.3.11.3 Passengers

The cabin crew shall have the passengers instructed and briefed and be assured that each passenger on board occupies a seat or berth with his safety

belt, restraining belt or, where provided, harness properly secured:

during taxiing

before and during take-off and landing

whenever deemed necessary by the commander in the interest of safety

(e.g. turbulences, emergency situations)

In addition, it shall be recommended to passengers to keep, when occupying

their seats, their safety belts secured during the entire flight. (refer to OM-0 4 Cabin Communication Manual (CCM))
The Senior Cabin Attendant is entitled to order the need for the fasten seat belt signs to be switched on during turbulence.

Handling staff, cabin crew and the Commander (CMD) shall ensure that multiple

occupancy of aircraft seats may only be allowed on specified seats and does not occur other than by one adult and one infant who is properly secured by a supplementary loop belt or other restraint device.

8.3.15.2 Crew Briefing

A cabin crew briefing shall be conducted by the Commander (CMD) prior to each flight or series of flights (if operated at the same day and by the same flight deck and cabin crew). He will inform his crew of particulars and events pertinent to the operation of the flight.
The crew briefing should not be longer than three minutes and must include at least:

confirmation that the planned crew is present, fit to fly and that the assigned crew members are qualified for the duty assigned to

expected flight times

expected meteorological conditions at departure, destination and en-route

open questions Note: In case a flight is accompanied by Swiss In-flight Security Officers (Tiger) refer to 10.10.7 - Swiss in-flight Security Officers (Tiger) Procedures.

Kein Crewwechsel und ein entsprechender Eintrag im ATL

kontext:
8.3.15.3.1 Procedure to omit cabin emergency equipment check

If a crew personally takes over the airplane from another crew, a further emergency equipment check may be omitted if the following is true: equipment is complete, or any discrepancies or malfunctions are recorded

in the ATL or ACL

a verbal briefing regarding the equipment status is received by the previous SEN in plain language

The cabin emergency equipment check may also be omitted when the airplane has been left unattended for any period of time if following has been applied:

all passengers and service doors are sealed (either in- or outside)

the seal numbers are correct and the seals are untempered when returning

to the aircraft

no crew change takes place

For callouts refer to 8.3 Appendix 1, Prior to Boarding CSPM 2 Appendix 1 Communication Wording.

Before each flight, a cabin check shall be performed before the boarding process takes place and following items must be checked: the function of the shoulder harness at each jump seat

verify that the seat belts are available on each jump seat

verify that all passenger seats are equipped with seat belts

check each passenger seat gets access to the safety on board card in the seat pocket

check each seat pocked is equipped with a safety on board card

check each seat pocked in an emergency exit row is equipped with an emergency door exit briefing card

check that a life vest is located under each passenger seat

lavatory check, according to the lavatory check procedure

In the interest of hygiene, passenger comfort and wellbeing the cabin crew shall check that the cabin (inclusive of lavatories and galleys) has been cleaned and tidied up appropriately. The cabin crew members shall keep in mind that the appearance of the cabin interior at boarding shapes the helvetic public image.
Safety and courtesy render it necessary to ensure that no un-stowed catering,

galley or other equipment inconveniences boarding passengers nor impedes the orderly flow of boarding.

No crew change and a corresponding entry in the ATL
fragen.erklaerung_en: The check may be omitted if all doors were sealed, the seal numbers are correct and the seals intact, and no crew change takes place.

fragen.frage: Welche kurzzeitige Abweichung ist bei RNAV/RNP während und unmittelbar nach Kurven maximal zulässig (Beispiel RNP 5)?
antworten: Bis zur halben Navigationsgenauigkeit, d.h. 2.5 NM
Bis zur einfachen Navigationsgenauigkeit, d.h. 5 NM
Bis zur doppelten Navigationsgenauigkeit, d.h. 10 NM
Keine; auch in Kurven gilt höchstens 1 NM
fragen.erklaerung: Kurzzeitige Abweichungen in und nach Kurven sind bis maximal zur einfachen Navigationsgenauigkeit erlaubt, bei RNP 5 also 5 NM.
fragen.zitat: Brief deviations from this standard (e.g. overshoots or undershoots) during and immediately after turns, up to a maximum of one times the navigation accuracy (i.e. for RNP 5 = 5 NM), are allowed.
kontext:
8.3.2.8.1 Policy

Flight Crews are expected to maintain route center lines, as depicted by on- board lateral deviation indicators or flight guidance, during all RNP operations unless authorized to deviate by ATC or under emergency conditions.
For normal operations, cross-track error or deviation (the difference between the RNAV or RNP system computed path and the aircraft position relative to the path) shall be limited to ±1/2 the navigation accuracy associated with the route (i.e. for RNP 5 2.5 NM).

8.3.2.8.1.4 Precision Area Navigation (PRNAV) Operation

Precision Area Navigation (PRNAV) supports the gradual decommissioning of ground-based navigation infrastructure and enables more efficient routing within terminal areas.
The onboard PRNAV system must achieve an accuracy of ±1 NM for at least 95% of the flight time.

For PRNAV operation only hard coded waypoints may be used. The manual creation of new waypoints is not permitted. Flight progress must be monitored using primary flight displays and verified through cross-checks with conventional navigation aids, supported by the MCDU.

Before reaching the Initial Approach Waypoint (IAWP), a navigation reasonableness check is required as follows:

For multi-sensor systems (i.e. GPS and IRS): the flight crew must confirm before commencing the approach that the GNSS sensor is the active source for position computation

the flight crew must verify that the displayed RNP value is suitable for the intended PBN operation

If no GPS equipment is available:

navigation must rely on conventional aids (e.g. display the bearing and range to a VOR/DME using the RNAV system and compare it with the RMI indication tuned to the same VOR/DME) The difference in bearing and range shall not be greater than 5° 1 NM.

The flight crew must be prepared to be able to revert to a conventional arrival

procedure in case of loss of PRNAV capability and inform ATC:

“UNABLE RNP 1 DUE TO (state reason)”.

kontext:
8.3.2.8.4 Lateral Navigation Error

The inability to achieve the required lateral navigation accuracy may be due to navigation errors related to aircraft tracking and positioning.
The Total System Error (TSE) consists of three main errors:
Path Definition Error (PDE)

Flight Technical Error (FTE)

Navigation System Error (NSE)

Note:
The E-Jet FMS monitors and presents to the pilot the Estimated Position Uncertainty (EPU), which reflects mainly the NSE and partially the FTE only.

Path Definition Error (PDE) Occurs when the path defined in the RNAV system does not correspond to the

desired path, i.e. the path expected to be flown over the ground (e.g. fly by or fly

over at various speeds). One method to define a specific path during turns are,

for instance Radius to Fix (RF) legs.

Flight Technical Error (FTE) FTE relates to the flight crew or autopilot’s ability to follow the defined path or

track, including any display error (e.g. CDI centering error). FTE can be

monitored by the autopilot or flight crew procedures. The extent to which these procedures need to be supported by other means depends, for example, on the

phase of flight and the type of operations. Such monitoring support could be provided by a map display.

Navigation System Error (NSE)

NSE refers to the difference between the aircraft’s estimated position and actual position.

OM-A 8 Operating Procedures

kontext:
8.3.21.7.2 Ground based Emergency Services not Available

If landed in an uninhabited area the crew shall take the following action: apply first aid if necessary

check that the ELT is functioning Note: on no account attempt to use the speech facility until a Search and Rescue (SAR) aircraft is either heard or seen in the area, since it causes heavy drain on the battery capacity.

check the aircraft radios and ascertain whether radio communication is possible by this means

prepare all available signaling equipment and light a smoke fire

prepare a temporary shelter

conserve food and water supplies as much as possible; it should be remembered, however, that sufficient food and water to support life can normally be found in the environment

remain in the vicinity of the aircraft, as this will give the best indication of the position of the survivors; there are some situations in which the possibility of moving to seek assistance may have to be considered but normally, unless there is obvious local habitation, or other forms of assistance close at hand, no move should be considered at least before the ELT batteries have

expired;
even if the ELT should be damaged, survivors should remain with the aircraft for at least 48 hours

if special circumstances indicate that a move should be made, a trail should

trail.

kontext:
12.2.6.1 Normal Practices and Procedures after entering RVSM Airspace

Flight crews shall comply to any aircraft operating restrictions, if required for the specific aircraft group: limits on indicated Mach number (basic flight envelope upper Mach boundary), given in the RVSM airworthiness approval
Note: all helvetic aircraft with RVSM approval shall be compliant to full RVSM flight envelope

Emphasis shall be placed on promptly setting the sub-scale on all primary and standby altimeters to 1013.2 hPa when passing the transition altitude, and rechecking for proper altimeter setting when reaching the initial cleared flight level.
In level cruise it is essential that the aircraft is flown at the cleared flight level.
This requires that particular care is taken to ensure that ATC clearances are fully understood and followed. The aircraft shall not intentionally depart from a cleared flight level without a positive clearance from ATC, unless the crew is conducting contingency or emergency manoeuvres.
When changing levels, the aircraft shall not be allowed to overshoot or undershoot the cleared flight level by more than 45m (150 ft). If installed, the level off should be accomplished using the altitude capture feature of the automatic altitude-control system.

An automatic altitude-control system shall be operative and engaged during level cruise, except when circumstances, such as the need to re-trim the aircraft or turbulence, require disengagement. In any event adherence to the assigned cruise level should be done by reference to one of the two primary altimeters.
Following loss of the automatic height keeping function, any consequential

restrictions will need to be observed.

Therefore:

ensure that the altitude-alerting system is operative

cross-check at intervals of approximately one hour the primary altimeters; a minimum of two shall agree within ±200 ft (±60 m); failure to meet this

condition will require that the altimetry system is reported as defective and

notified to ATC; the usual scan of flight deck instruments shall suffice for altimeter cross-checking on most flights

in normal operations, the altimetry system being used to control the aircraft

shall be selected for the input to the altitude reporting transponder, transmitting information to ATC

OM-A 12 Rules of the Air

If the pilot is notified by ATC of an assigned altitude deviation of 300 ft (90 m) or more then the flight crew shall take appropriate action to return to the cleared flight level as quickly as possible.
If the pilot is advised in real time that the aircraft has been identified by a height- monitoring system that the Total Vertical Error (TVE) is greater than ±300 ft (±90m) and or if an Altimetry System Error (ASE) greater than ±245 ft (±75 m) is experienced, the flight crew should follow established regional procedures to protect the safe operation of the aircraft. This assumes that the monitoring system will identify the TVE or ASE within the set limits for accuracy.
Caution should be exercised due to problems of visual perceptions of other aircraft during darkness at 1000 ft separation, and when encountering local phenomena such as northern lights. This applies to aircraft in the opposite and same flight direction, and during turns. Use of the TCAS will verify what actual separation exists from nearby aircraft.

8.1.1.5 Inoperative Engines – Performance Requirements

In addition to the minimum flight altitude requirements stated above, aircraft operated according to performance class A must meet the following performance requirements for One Engine Inoperative (OEI) en-route flight path.
In the event of the loss of one engine at the most critical point along the route and in the meteorological conditions expected for the flight, the net flight path must: have a positive gradient at 1 500 ft above the airport of intended landing, and must either have a positive gradient at least 1 000 ft above all terrain and obstructions within 5 NM to either side of the intended track, or permit the aircraft to continue the flight from the cruising altitude to an airport at which a landing can be made while clearing vertically, by at least 2 000 ft, all obstacles within 5 NM to either side of the intended track (e.g. drift down procedure).

kontext:
8.3.4.2.1 Altitude Awareness

To stay actively alert flight crews shall: crosscheck that the assigned altitude is above the minimum safe altitude confirm assigned altitudes or flight levels towards ATC and to each other

monitor the Flight Guidance System (FGS) and automatic altitude alerting

system during dynamic phases very closely (e.g. altitude capturing, change

of vertical speed) and refrain from or interrupt other duties during this period of time (e.g. briefings, recordings on OFP, other communication)

altitude the Pilot Monitoring (PM) must reconfirm it with ATC.

8.3.1 VFR IFR Policy

Except for non revenue flights described in the Operations Manual 8.7 - Non- Revenue Flights, no helvetic flight shall be operated without the full use of air traffic control or advisory services.

Exemptions from this general policy are permitted only according to 8.0.1.5 - Flight Rules.
These flights will be identified on the ATC-flight plan as follows: “Y” – when the flight is started under IFR and later changed to VFR

“Z”

– when the flight is started under VFR and later changed to IFR

kontext:
8.3.1.6 IFR in Uncontrolled Airspace

In general, flights into uncontrolled airspace (classes F and G) shall be avoided.
However, Instrument Flight Rules (IFR) operations in uncontrolled airspace are applied in some countries.
While flying IFR in uncontrolled airspace the following procedures and restrictions shall be applied: airspace classes F and G: for air traffic advisory service and Flight Information Service (FIS) refer to OM-C 1 Route Manual, Rules, ICAO Rules of the air

usually, only one IFR traffic at the time given may fly IFR in the assigned airspace F

cruising levels: shall be selected appropriate to the magnetic track, refer to OM-C/ Rules and Regulations

communication: maintain a listening watch and establish two-way communication with Air Traffic Services (ATS). Standard position reports (e.g. blind transmissions) shall be given
take-off and departure: the IFR departure clearance must be obtained prior to departure by any means (e.g. radio communication, phone call to ATC).

Separation between IFR traffic can be granted by timed clearance expiries

approach and landing: the IFR approach clearance must be obtained prior to start the approach from the Initial Approach Fix (IAF). Thereafter, ATC will usually give instruction to monitor the local aerodrome frequency (e.g. AFIS).
Standard position reports shall be transmitted enabling as well VFR traffic to gain an overview concerning the traffic situation. In VMC conditions with

local VFR traffic special attention must be given to the behavior of such

aeroplanes (e.g. basic flying instruction, solo-flights) which might dictate a

smooth integration into the local VFR traffic patterns

special attention must be given to an active and systematic look-out when

flying in mixed IFR/VFR airspace (airspace classes E and F)

Traffic Alert and Collision Avoidance System (TCAS) shall be operative

CAT II, CAT II/III operation is not allowed

kontext:
12.3.1.7 Time

Aviation communication uses Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) for all operations.

The word "local" or the time zone equivalent shall be used to denote local when local time is given during radio and telephone communications.
The term "Zulu" may be used to denote UTC.

Example: 0920 UTC “zero niner two zero”

Time may be stated in minutes only (two figures) in radiotelephone communications when no misunderstanding is likely to occur.

When stating an estimate generally the time at the event must be stated rather than the duration until the event.
Example:

“helvetic 121, what is your estimate over EKRIT?”

“helvetic 121, estimate EKRIT at 1915”

kontext:
8.3.21.2 RAAR PPAA FORD NITS

Whenever for technical or operational reasons during a flight abnormal or emergency procedures must be applied all company policies remain intact.
Abnormal and emergency procedures consist of four major phases:
R ecognition

A nalysis

A ction

R eassessment

During the application of abnormal and emergency procedures the Crew Resource Management (CRM) becomes, compared with normal operations, an even more crucial component. Therefore, the Commander (CMD) must concentrate with the highest priority on the assessment and distribution of its human and technical resources and to constantly reevaluate and optimize his decisions. The crew must prevent itself from any form of actionist behavior and uncoordinated or unfocused dealing with the problem at hand.
Whenever confronted with an emergency or abnormal situation, the first priority lies in the proper flying and monitoring of the aircraft.
Crew duties must be distributed clearly, basically the following sequence applies:
P ower the PF takes the initiative. Check thrust and order appropriate

setting for the engine(s) operating normally P erformance check configuration and minimum maximum speed

A nalysis both pilots shall assess the situation, where the lead of the

analyze lies with the Pilot Monitoring (PM)

A ction action shall be taken according to emergency abnormal

checklist, OM-B abnormal operation, flight procedures and knowledge

Use company channels and co-operate as soon as possible with the cabin crew.
Create favorable conditions for approach and landing by e.g:

requesting ATC assistance (Priority, Emergency)

careful selection of landing airport with suitable weather conditions, approach aids, runway as applicable

For the abnormal operation helvetic uses abnormal and emergency checklists.
All checklists are named.
When the situation changes to the worse the aim for the safety of the aircraft, its passengers, crew and cargo become the only operational goal.
If this goal can no longer be achieved by the use of the helvetic Standard Operating Procedures (SOP), diversion from these published procedures will be accepted. Any diversion from published procedures for the safety of the aircraft, its passengers, crew and cargo must be exercised only after due consideration by the crew (i.e. no matter how inconvenient such a decision might be for either or both helvetic and passengers).
If the helvetic Standard Operating Procedures (SOP) seem no longer adequate to deal with the situation at hand, an emergency must be declared.

As a general guideline, a declaration of an emergency or urgency can be evaluated and communicated to ATC as follows:
EICAS WARNING land at the nearest suitable airport:

kontext:
8.3.8.1 Air Traffic Control In-flight Weather Avoidance Assistance

To the extent possible, ATC controllers will issue pertinent information on weather or chaff areas and assist flight crews in avoiding these areas when requested.
Flight crews should respond to a weather advisory by acknowledging it and, if considered necessary, requesting an alternative course of action as follows: request to deviate off course by stating the number of miles and the direction of the requested deviation; when the requested deviation is approved, the flight crew is expected to provide its own navigation, maintain the altitude as assigned by Air Traffic Control (ATC) and to remain within the specified range (mileage) of his original course

request a new route to avoid the affected area

request a change of altitude

request radar vectors around the affected areas.

For obvious reasons of safety, the flight crew operating under IFR with traffic separation provided by Air Traffic Control (ATC)) shall not deviate from the course or altitude respectively flight level without a proper clearance. When weather conditions encountered are so severe that an immediate deviation is necessary and time will not permit approval from Air Traffic Control (ATC) the flight crew’s emergency authority may be exercised.

When a flight crew requests clearance for a deviation or for an Air Traffic Control (ATC) radar vector, the controller shall evaluate the air traffic situation within the affected area and coordinate with other controllers before replying to the request.
Therefore, it should be remembered by flight crew members that the controller’s primary function is to provide safe separation between aircraft. Any additional

service, (e.g. weather avoidance assistance), can only be provided to the extent

that it is not detrimental to the primary function. The separation workload is

generally greater than normal when weather disrupts the usual flow of traffic.

It is very important that the request for deviation or radar vectors is forwarded to

Air Traffic Control (ATC) as far in advance as possible.

The following information should be furnished to Air Traffic Control (ATC) when requesting clearance to detour around weather activity: the flight number

a general statement about the intention

the reason for the request

proposed point where detour will commence

proposed route and extent of detour (direction and distance)

point where original route will be resumed

flight conditions (VMC or IMC)

time limitations when necessary

The assistance that might be rendered by Air Traffic Control (ATC) will depend upon the weather information available to controllers. Due to the extremely transitory nature of severe weather situations, the controller’s weather information may be of limited value if based on weather observed on radar only.
Frequent updates by pilots giving specific information can be of considerable value. Therefore, a Pilot Report (PIREP) shall be offered by flight crews who encounter severe weather conditions.
fragen.frage_en: Which item is among the information to be transmitted to ATC when requesting to deviate around weather?
antworten_en: The number of passengers on board
The remaining endurance in minutes
The point at which the original route is resumed
The radar tilt setting
fragen.erklaerung_en: To be transmitted are, among others, start, route and extent of the deviation, the point of resuming the original route and the flight conditions (VMC/IMC).

12.3.2.3 Clarification and Acceptance of Clearances

Several factors such as use of non-standard wordings, high workload of ATC- controllers or flight crews, ambiguous wordings, formally correct but substantially questionable contents, non-standard routings, call sign confusion, or requests may lead to critical situations. For this reason, at least two flight crew members must monitor and confirm clearances issued by ATC.

kontext:
8.3.6.4 Reaction to TCAS TA and TCAS RA

Traffic Advisories (TA)
A Traffic Advisory (TA) is intended to alert the flight crew that a Resolution Advisory (RA), requiring a change in flight path, may follow.

For detailed actions and callouts refer to type specific OM-B.

Resolution Advisories (RA) A Resolution Advisory (RA) is intended to advise pilots of the vertical manoeuvre they should carry out in order to achieve or maintain adequate separation from an established threat.
The manoeuvres shall follow the indication of the advisory and never be made in a direction opposite to that given by the system.
If an instruction to manoeuvre is received simultaneously from a Resolution Advisory (RA) and from ATC, and both instructions are in conflict, the advice given by the Traffic Collision Avoidance System (TCAS) must be followed.
Note: Visually acquired traffic may not be the same traffic causing an RA.
The visual perception of an encounter may be misleading, particularly at night.

Whenever a Resolution Advisory (RA) requires a climb while the aircraft is in landing configuration, a go-around shall be initiated.

It is emphasized that the Traffic Collision Avoidance System Mark II (TCAS II) relies upon information received from the transponders of the surrounding

aircraft. Resolution Advisories (RA) will only be generated if both the receiving

aircraft and the potential intruder are transmitting transponder signals in mode C or higher. The equipment is not capable of resolving with complete accuracy the

bearing, heading or vertical rates of intruding aircraft. Pilots should therefore not

attempt to manoeuvre on the basis of the system display.

For detailed actions and callouts refer to type specific OM-B.

kontext:
8.3.6.3 Avoidance of Aircraft Collision

The see-and-avoid strategy with a careful look out is a basic element for the avoidance of collisions, regardless of advanced aircraft operations and more sophisticated ground and in-flight devices. Thus, whenever weather conditions permit, it is the duty of the flight crew to keep a sharp look out.
The flight crew shall organize the flight deck work in a way that at least one crew member may fulfill this requirement. The ACAS II (TCAS) indication must be used for assistance. It must, however, be understood that the ACAS II indication is limited to aircraft with an operating transponder. That may exclude the indication of other traffic (e.g. balloons, gliders).
Flight crew members must keep “head down work” to a minimum: in the vicinity of an aerodrome

during descent to an aerodrome

during climb out from an aerodrome

in areas where the traffic is dense
An early engagement of the autopilot is required in order to facilitate the look out.

Irrespective of the type of clearance received from ATC a look out for conflicting traffic in VMC is an absolute necessity.
Traffic information given by ATC is of great value. It must, however, always be

kept in mind that ATC information includes known traffic only and therefore may be incomplete.
In order to protect the eyes from the sun, only the use of sunglasses and sun visors is permitted. The use of objects restricting the look out is prohibited during

flight.

kontext:
8.3.6.1 General

The Traffic Collision Avoidance System (TCAS) is a technology which found its way into aviation during the late nineties of the past century. The motivation for its introduction has been the desire for an improvement of flight safety in an increasing traffic density, especially around major hubs. Traffic Collision Avoidance System (TCAS) addresses the problem through recognition and avoidance of potential hazard of in-flight collisions.
It does neither replace traffic separation by Air Traffic Control (ATC) nor the sharp look-out of the flight crew whenever visibility permits.

It does, however, support the flight crew in situations when the visual recognition of conflicting traffic is impaired (e.g. IMC conditions, night, traffic from dead-angle positions). It also assists in decision-making about the necessary correcting actions when a traffic conflict starts to develop.
Flight crews shall therefore use the Traffic Collision Avoidance System (TCAS) at all times. Nevertheless, they should bear in mind that several problems and limitations of the system have been identified during the first years of implementation. Future improvements in hardware and software are to be expected.
Necessary prerequisite to the function of any Traffic Collision Avoidance System (TCAS) equipment is the operation of the transponder in Mode C or Mode S.
In other words: The Traffic Collision Avoidance System (TCAS) can only detect aircraft which transmit a correct transponder code.
It should be noted that Traffic Collision Avoidance System Mark II (TCAS II) is not

capable of accurately resolving the bearing and heading of conflicting traffic.
Traffic Advisory (TA) information for conflicting traffic is limited to vertical avoidance manoeuvres.

fragen.erklaerung_en: TCAS replaces neither ATC separation nor the crew's sharp look-out whenever visibility permits.

thermal tropopause altitude: Wake vortex decays more slowly below the tropopause where there is therefore an increased risk of encountering

kontext:
8.3.9.1.4 Precautionary Measurements and Reactions

The variability in the generator airplane rate of climb or descent makes it quite difficult to estimate exactly where the vortex is. Consequently, during the en- route phase of flight, pilots should expect possible wake encounters when other traffics in proximity appear to be on similar tracks ahead, crossing above your level, climbing or descending ahead through your flight path, while wind direction is likely to move the wake towards your trajectory.
As precautionary measures, operators and pilots should be aware that: when possible, condensation trails should be used to visualise wakes and estimate if their flight path brings them across

more attention should be given when flying below the tropopause altitude, as the likelihood of wake encounter increases. The tropopause altitude varies (between days, between locations) and can be found on meteorological charts

upwind lateral offset should be used if the risk of a wake encounter is suspected, when allowed by airspace regulations or via specific ATC approval. Also, a change of FL to cross “HEAVY” or “SUPER” traffics from above can be used when feasible and authorised by ATC

In case of a wake encounter, pilots should: be aware that experience has demonstrated that

if the pilot reacts at the first

roll motion, when in the core of the vortex, the roll motion could be potentially amplified by this initial piloting action

be aware that some in-flight incidents have demonstrated that pilot inputs may exacerbate the unusual attitude condition with rapid roll control

reversals carried out in an “out of phase” manner

be aware that if the autopilot is engaged, intentional disconnection can

complicate the scenario, and the autopilot will, in most cases, facilitate the recovery

try to avoid large rudder deflections that can create important lateral

accelerations, which could then generate very large forces on the vertical

stabiliser that may exceed the structural resistance. Although some recent aircraft types are protected by fly-by-wire systems, typically, the use of the

rudder does not reduce the severity of the encounter nor does it improve the ease of recovery

make use of specific guidance in the OM-B where available
