fragen.zitat: In this condition, this accumulator provides hydraulic power to the associated flight controls from the beginning of RAT deployment until the ACMP 3A is restarted.
kontext:
HYDRAULIC SYSTEM 3 ACCUMULATOR

The Hydraulic System 3 accumulator is similar to the Hydraulic System 1 and 2 accumulators, except for its operation during an electrical emergency.
In this condition, this accumulator provides hydraulic power to the associated flight controls from the beginning of RAT deployment until the ACMP 3A is restarted.
fragen.frage_en: What is the task of the Hydraulic System 3 accumulator in an Electrical Emergency?
antworten_en: It supplies the Emergency/Parking Brake for six brake applications
It supplies the associated Flight Controls from RAT deployment until ACMP 3A restarts
It maintains pressure for Landing Gear extension
It drives the PTU until the RAT is deployed
fragen.erklaerung_en: In an Electrical Emergency, the System 3 accumulator supplies the associated Flight Controls from the start of RAT deployment until ACMP 3A restarts.

fragen.frage: Was kommandiert der FADEC bei einem Engine Flameout bezüglich der Hydraulik?
antworten: Schliessen des Hydraulic SOV und Start der PTU
Automatischen Start der ACMP 3B
Unload der zugehörigen EDP, um das Drehmoment zu reduzieren und einen Windmill Restart zu erleichtern
Erhöhung des EDP-Drucks, um die Flight Controls zu sichern
fragen.erklaerung: Bei einem Flameout kommandiert der FADEC automatisch das Unload der zugehörigen EDP; die Druckreduktion senkt die Last am Engine und erleichtert den Windmill Restart.
fragen.zitat: in the event of engine flameout, the FADEC automatically commands the unload of the respective EDP, which reduces the hydraulic system pressure.
kontext:
ABNORMAL OPERATION

The Hydraulic Systems 1 and 2 are equipped with an overheating protection system. Normal temperature display is green, high temperature is amber reverse video, and overheat is red reverse video.
High and overheat temperatures generate a CAS message. In the event of hydraulic system overheat, the HYD 1(2) OVERHEAT EICAS warning message is displayed. In this case, the flight crew can manually command the SOV through a guarded pushbutton on the hydraulic system control panel.

Also,
in the event of engine flameout, the FADEC automatically commands the unload of the respective EDP, which reduces the hydraulic system pressure.
This depressurization reduces the torque loads on the engine and facilitates a windmill restart.
fragen.frage_en: What does the FADEC command with regard to hydraulics in case of an Engine Flameout?
antworten_en: Closing the Hydraulic SOV and starting the PTU
Automatic start of ACMP 3B
Unloading of the associated EDP to reduce torque and facilitate a Windmill Restart
Increasing EDP pressure to secure the Flight Controls
fragen.erklaerung_en: In case of a Flameout, the FADEC automatically commands unloading of the associated EDP; the pressure reduction lowers the load on the engine and facilitates the Windmill Restart.

kontext:
HYDRAULIC SYSTEMS 1 AND 2............................ 14-11-10.... 1

HYDRAULIC

14-11-TOC

Page 2/2 Table of Contents REVISION 15

The airplane has three independent hydraulic systems to provide power for:
– landing gear including the main landing gear doors
– nose wheel steering
– brakes
– flight controls (ailerons, elevator, rudder, ground, and multifunction spoilers), and
– thrust reversers.
Normal operation of the hydraulic system is automatic.

The hydraulic systems do not have any fluid communication point.
Therefore, it is not possible to transfer hydraulic fluid from one system to another.

All three systems use fire resistant hydraulic fluid and operate at a nominal pressure of 3000 psig.

The parameters and indications of the hydraulic system are displayed on both MFD synoptic pages.

System messages are displayed on the EICAS display.

14-11-01

ORIGINAL Page 1/2

fragen.erklaerung_en: The three hydraulic systems have no Fluid Communication Point, so no transfer of hydraulic fluid is possible.

kontext:
ELECTRIC HYDRAULIC PUMPS

Both Electric Hydraulic Pumps are alternating current motor pumps (ACMP). Electric Hydraulic Pump 3A (ACMP 3A) is the primary power source for Hydraulic System 3. The AC ESS BUS powers the ACMP 3A.

A two-position selector knob on the hydraulic panel enables the flight crew to select OFF or ON positions. There is no automation associated with this pump. So in normal operation, the flight crew turns the pump ON and OFF during engine start and shutdown, respectively.
Electric Hydraulic Pump 3B (ACMP 3B) is the backup for the Electric Hydraulic Pump 3A. The AC BUS 2 power the ACMP 3B.
The flight crew selects manual or automatic operation through the three-position selector knob on the hydraulic control panel. Normal operation is automatic.
fragen.frage_en: What is the role of ACMP 3B and which bus supplies it?
antworten_en: Primary pump of System 3, supplied by the AC ESS BUS
Backup of ACMP 3A, supplied by AC BUS 2
Backup of EDP 2, supplied by AC BUS 1
Backup of ACMP 3A, supplied by DC ESS BUS 3
fragen.erklaerung_en: ACMP 3B is the backup of ACMP 3A and is supplied by AC BUS 2; normal operation is AUTO.

fragen.zitat: Whenever the airplane is in a leveled flight and spends more than 2 min in a condition that there is possibility of undetected ice formation (undetected ice envelope), wing and engine ice protection systems activate automatically.
kontext:
UNDETECTED ICE PROTECTION

Regardless of the ice detectors actuation, the AMS Controllers monitor non-icing parameters such as TAT, TAS, and Altitude, in order to preclude any possibility of undetected ice accumulation on wings and engines.

The Advisory EICAS messages ICE CONDITION and STALL PROT ICE SPEED are also displayed.

These conditions are the following:
– Airplane in flight.
– Altitude below 30000 ft.
– Combination of air temperature, altitude and speed indicators.
– Airspeed between 95 KIAS and 365 KIAS.

14-12-10

Page 10/14 Ice Protection System REVISION 15

– Vertical speed between -200 ft/min and +200 ft/min.

Whenever the airplane is in a leveled flight and spends more than 2 min in a condition that there is possibility of undetected ice formation (undetected ice envelope), wing and engine ice protection systems activate automatically.
The ice protection systems will stay activated for 3 min after one or more of these conditions become false.

fragen.erklaerung_en: If the aircraft spends more than 2 min in level flight in the Undetected Ice Envelope, Wing and Engine Ice Protection are activated automatically.

fragen.frage: Unter welchen Bedingungen ist ein ICE SPEED RESET der Stall Protection möglich?

Nach mehr als 10 min ohne Eisdetektion, unabhängig von der SAT
Ice Detectors detektieren kein Eis und SAT ist mindestens 5°C
fragen.erklaerung: Der Reset der Referenz-Speeds ist möglich, wenn die Ice Detectors kein Eis detektieren und die SAT bei oder über 5°C liegt.
fragen.zitat: The reset of reference speed is possible when: – Ice detectors are not detecting icing conditions – SAT is at or above 5°C.
kontext:
RESET OF STALL PROTECTION ICE SPEED

After airplane encounters icing conditions, the system automatically increases the reference speeds for activation of stall protections. Stall protections are triggered at higher speeds, and longer landing distances are required to land the airplane. The EICAS message STALL PROT ICE SPEED is displayed to indicate that ice speeds are the reference for stall protection (Refer to 14-03-30 EICAS
MESSAGES).

If airplane surfaces are free of ice during approach and landing, the reference speeds for stall protection can be reset to normal stall speeds. The reset of reference speeds is accomplished switching the Ice Protection MODE Selector to ICE SPEED RESET position.

The reset of reference speed is possible when:
– Ice detectors are not detecting icing conditions
– SAT is at or above 5°C.
Flight crew must assure that the airplane is free of ice before resetting ice speeds.
fragen.frage_en: Under which conditions is an ICE SPEED RESET of the Stall Protection possible?
antworten_en: Ice Detectors detect no ice and SAT is at least 0°C
Only on the ground with engines at idle
After more than 10 min without ice detection, regardless of SAT
Ice Detectors detect no ice and SAT is at least 5°C
fragen.erklaerung_en: The reset of the reference speeds is possible when the Ice Detectors detect no ice and SAT is at or above 5°C.

fragen.frage: Wann führt das Wing Anti-Ice System seinen automatischen Selbsttest im Flug durch?
antworten: Bei Erreichen von 10000 ft AGL und frühestens 2 min nach Lift-off, nicht im Single Engine Betrieb

Bei jedem Lift-off sofort nach dem Gear Up
Bei Erreichen der Cruise Altitude, auch im Single Engine Betrieb

fragen.zitat: The wing anti-ice system tests itself inflight when 10000 ft AGL is reached and at least 2 min after liftoff. Test does not occur if in single engine operation.
kontext: ICE PROTECTION SYSTEM TEST
The wing anti-ice system tests itself inflight when 10000 ft AGL is reached and at least 2 min after liftoff. Test does not occur if in single engine operation.

The wing Anti-Ice Valves open during test and the A- Ice Synoptic page indicates that valves have opened.

14-12-10

Page 6/14 Ice Protection System REVISION 15

Pre-Mod. SB 190E2-21-0023 (AMS Black Label 5.0)

The automatic test of the wing anti-ice system occurs every flight cycle.

Post-Mod. SB 190E2-21-0023 (AMS Black Label 5.0)

The automatic test of the wing anti-ice system occurs every 25 flight cycles. Whenever the wing anti-ice is activated, the cycle counter resets to zero.

The test duration is up to 35 s.

If a failure occurs during IBIT, the message A-I WING FAIL is displayed.

The Test selector knob on the Ice Protection Panel provides a manual test for the wing and engine anti-ice systems for maintenance use.
fragen.frage_en: When does the Wing Anti-Ice System perform its automatic self-test in flight?
antworten_en: On reaching 10000 ft AGL and no earlier than 2 min after lift-off, not in single-engine operation
At 1700 ft AGL or 2 min after lift-off
At every lift-off immediately after Gear Up
On reaching Cruise Altitude, also in single-engine operation
fragen.erklaerung_en: The Wing Anti-Ice self-test takes place at 10000 ft AGL and at least 2 min after lift-off; in single-engine operation it does not take place.

LANDING GEAR RETRACTION

Positioning the LG lever to UP position releases the nose and main landing gear locks and pressurizes the actuators to retract the LG.
When retraction is completed, the landing gear is held in place by the uplocks.
The braking system automatically brakes the MLG wheels during retraction. The NLG wheels rotation stops using a rubber spinbrake by contact with the tires.

NOTE: – If for any reason the gear lever locks in the DOWN position after takeoff, the retraction could damage the LG bay. In case of an emergency that requires obstacle clearance, press the down lock release button to release the lever and move it to the UP position. The LG retracts, improving performance.
– If the hydraulic pump driven by the engine 2 fails to provide pressure, the PTU automatically pressurizes the LG system to allow retraction.

AIR GROUND POSITIONING SYSTEM

The air/ground positioning system senses whether the airplane is on the ground or in flight. This information is used in other airplane systems logic. The sensors are installed on each landing gear and are independent from each other.

On ground, the LG NO DISPATCH caution message is displayed on the EICAS when the airplane detects a failure in the air/ground positioning system.
In flight, the LG WOW SYS FAIL caution message is displayed on the EICAS when the airplane detects a loss of reliable sensors indication.

The DC ESS BUS 1 powers the outboard brake controller, while the DC ESS BUS 2 powers the inboard brake controller.

The NLG has steer-by-wire control powered by hydraulic system 2 and electronically controlled by the Nose Wheel Steering Control Module.

The steering system is segregated from the landing gear to improve availability.

– External steering disengage switch in the engaged position.
– Press the handwheel. When released, rudder pedal steering is automatically engaged.

kontext:
2.3.1.6 Rudder Steering use and Turning Radius

For straight ahead taxiing or for small changes of direction, the use of rudder pedal steering mode may be used. The maximum steering angle of rudder pedal is 7°.
Exercise care on the operation of the steering handle at speeds above 10 kt, as it’s very responsive.
Handwheel steering mode should be used for wider turn angles. To operate in this mode the handle must be kept pressed otherwise the system reverts to rudder pedals. Whenever the handle is pressed, the system reverts back to the handwheel steering.

The wheel deflection as function of handle deflection is not linear. For detailed information refer to AOM section 14-13.
Let the airplane move a little forward before starting a turn and avoid stopping the airplane in a turn as excessive thrust is required to start taxiing again. After

completing a turn and before stopping, center the nosewheel and allow the

airplane to roll straight ahead for a short distance.

Nosewheel skidding may occur with:

Excessive steering angle;

High taxi speed during turns;

On wet surfaces during turn.

When taxiing, make turns with the largest feasible turn radius possible. The minimum turn radius should still allow the tire closer to the center of the turn to continue rolling. When making a tight turn, the tires are subject to high lateral

loads and can experience damage. Asymmetric thrust may be used in tight turns to minimize side loads on gear and tires.

Minimize using thrust from outboard engine in 180° turn, particularly if outboard engine overhangs dusty areas next to the taxiway.
The tail tip or the wingtip, depending on each airplane model, have the largest arc while turning and determines the minimum obstruction clearance path.

2.3.1.7 180-Degree Turn
During the maneuver, maintain a ground speed around 5 kt. Exercise additional care on wet or contaminated runways, as tires may skid.

Start aligned over the centerline and use the handwheel steering to turn the airplane left 30° in the direction of the runway edge. When LSP is over the runway edge apply progressively full right steering command. If necessary, use asymmetric thrust and/or differential braking. Once completed 180-degree turn, return the handwheel steering to the neutral position re-aligning the airplane with the centerline.

kontext:
2.3.1.6 Rudder Steering use and Turning Radius

For straight ahead taxiing or for small changes of direction, the use of rudder pedal steering mode may be used. The maximum steering angle of rudder pedal is 7°.
Exercise care on the operation of the steering handle at speeds above 10 kt, as it’s very responsive.

Handwheel steering mode should be used for wider turn angles. To operate in this mode the handle must be kept pressed otherwise the system reverts to rudder pedals. Whenever the handle is pressed, the system reverts back to the handwheel steering.

The wheel deflection as function of handle deflection is not linear. For detailed information refer to AOM section 14-13.
Let the airplane move a little forward before starting a turn and avoid stopping the airplane in a turn as excessive thrust is required to start taxiing again. After

completing a turn and before stopping, center the nosewheel and allow the

airplane to roll straight ahead for a short distance.

Nosewheel skidding may occur with:

Excessive steering angle;

High taxi speed during turns;

On wet surfaces during turn.

When taxiing, make turns with the largest feasible turn radius possible. The minimum turn radius should still allow the tire closer to the center of the turn to continue rolling. When making a tight turn, the tires are subject to high lateral

loads and can experience damage. Asymmetric thrust may be used in tight turns to minimize side loads on gear and tires.

Minimize using thrust from outboard engine in 180° turn, particularly if outboard engine overhangs dusty areas next to the taxiway.
The tail tip or the wingtip, depending on each airplane model, have the largest arc while turning and determines the minimum obstruction clearance path.

2.3.1.7 180-Degree Turn

During the maneuver, maintain a ground speed around 5 kt. Exercise additional care on wet or contaminated runways, as tires may skid. Start aligned over the centerline and use the handwheel steering to turn the airplane left 30° in the direction of the runway edge. When LSP is over the runway edge apply progressively full right steering command. If necessary, use asymmetric thrust and/or differential braking. Once completed 180-degree turn, return the handwheel steering to the neutral position re-aligning the airplane with the centerline.

fragen.frage: Warum wird gemäss OM-B die Bugradsteuerung (Handwheel) während des Takeoff Runs nicht empfohlen?
antworten: Weil sie über 30 kt automatisch abgeschaltet wird
Weil sie die Rudder Pedals blockiert

Weil sie den Takeoff Configuration Warning auslöst

kontext:
2.3.3.3.8 Takeoff Run and Thrust Settings

Align the airplane using as reference the runway centerline. During takeoff run, pedals are used to steer the airplane.
The use of nose wheel steering is not recommended during takeoff run because of its high efficiency, which might lead to airplane overreaction.

As the groundspeed increases, the authority of nose wheel steering reduces and the rudder becomes more effective.
The takeoff (TO) mode is represented by crossbars on the PFD and commands the airplane to maintain a pitch attitude reference.

When the airplane lines up and is ready for takeoff, arm the AT.
Advance the thrust levers to 40% N1.
The engines should stabilize momentarily and power settings verified before both throttles are advanced beyond 50° TLA.
Advance thrust levers to TO/GA detent and verify that N1 reaches takeoff thrust (N1 target), engine parameters are normal and ATTCS set as required.
If ATTCS is ON, with thrust levers to TO/GA, ATTCS indication on EICAS changes from white to green (armed). If ATTCS indication remains white on EICAS, confirm thrust levers are set to TO/GA position.
The AT takes over above 50° TLA when advancing the thrust levers to the TO/GA detent. If any AT malfunction occurs, disconnect the AT and set the desired thrust manually. If thrust is set manually, advance thrust levers to TO/GA detent. ROLL indication changes to TRACK when the airplane is above 100 KIAS during

takeoff run.
The ENG TLA NOT TOGA EICAS message is displayed during the takeoff if the thrust levers are out of the TO/GA position. It happens even if the N1 has already reached the takeoff thrust (N1 target).

Make sure that the thrust levers are set to TO/GA position before 60 kt, when AT HOLD mode is activated, to prevent this message from occurring.
If ENG TLA NOT TOGA EICAS message appears during takeoff run, PF should advance thrust levers to TO/GA position and continue the takeoff.

Note: After takeoff thrust is set, LSP takes control over the thrust levers until V1 is announced. The LSP is always responsible for aborting the takeoff. All abnormalities during the takeoff run are called out in a loud and clear voice.

FUEL 1 (2) LO LEVEL message may appear spuriously (EICAS quantity indication green) when flying with high pitch or bank angles.
It happens especially during takeoff and climb out with fuel quantity just above the expected to trigger FUEL 1 (2) LO LEVEL EICAS message.
fragen.frage_en: Why is nose wheel steering (handwheel) not recommended during the takeoff run according to OM-B?
antworten_en: Because it is automatically switched off above 30 kt
Because it blocks the rudder pedals
Because of its high effectiveness, which can lead to an overreaction of the aircraft
Because it triggers the Takeoff Configuration Warning
fragen.erklaerung_en: During the takeoff run, steering is done with the pedals; nose wheel steering is not recommended because of its high effectiveness and possible overreaction.

The CAS list message comparison annunciation is shown on both PFDs to indicate that the CAS lists from the two monitor warning systems do not match. The annunciation consists of the letters CAS MSG displayed inside a cutout box.

kontext:
AURAL WARNING PRIORITY LEVELS

There are four aural warning priority levels, from the highest to the lowest:
– Emergency (level 3).
– Abnormal (level 2).
– Advisory (level 1).
– Information (level 0).
Emergency: corresponds to a situation that requires the immediate action of the pilot.
The master warning annunciator is repeated with three-second intervals between alerts until the master warning reset switch is pressed.

Abnormal: corresponds to an abnormal situation such as system malfunction or failures that have no immediate impact on safety.
Whenever an abnormal fault occurs, a master caution tone is presented every five seconds until the master caution reset switch is pressed.

Advisory: corresponds to the recognition of a situation such as system malfunction or failures leading to loss of redundancy or degradation of a system.

Information: corresponds to an information situation.

kontext:
TAKEOFF CONFIGURATION WARNING

A dedicated aural warning indicates that airplane configuration is not in suitable takeoff condition. The aural warning is activated whenever the airplane is on the ground, thrust is applied, and at least one of the following conditions is met:
– Flaps are not in takeoff position ("NO TAKEOFF FLAPS").
–
Flaps position is not in agreement with the Flaps position selected in the FMS Takeoff page 2/2. ("NO TAKEOFF FLAPS").

– The Emergency/Parking Brake is applied ("NO TAKEOFF
BRAKES").

– Pitch trim is out of green range ("NO TAKEOFF TRIM").
– Any spoiler panel is deployed ("NO TAKEOFF SPOILER").
More than one warning may be generated if more than one condition is met.

A test button is provided to allow checking the takeoff configuration by simulating power levers in the advanced position. If the airplane is in takeoff configuration, the voice message "TAKEOFF OK" is generated.
If the airplane is not set to takeoff configuration, the aural warning referred to the associated takeoff configuration deviation is generated.

kontext:
MONITOR WARNING FUNCTION (MWF)

The MWF (Monitor Warning Function) continuously monitors the condition of airplanes systems and avionics, generates visual alerts (EICAS messages), and also correlates these CAS messages with aural alerts.

There are two monitor warning function computers in separated modular avionics units (MAUs) continually monitor the status of airplanes and avionics systems.

One MWF has priority and alerts the flight crew by generating alert messages in the CAS display window. Some warnings also have sounds (voice or tone).
The other MWF is a backup. If the priority MWF fails, the display computer automatically selects and uses the data from the backup MWF.
Alert messages are prioritized and color-coded for display. The MWF also controls message timing, flight crew acknowledgement, and the scrolling of the CAS messages in the CAS display window.

kontext:
GROUND PROXIMITY WARNING SYSTEM

The EGPWS calculates these seven basic functions by comparing the airplane position to an internal terrain database to output alerts and displays that show the airplane situation.

Mode 1 - Excessive descent rates with SINK RATE and PULL UP aural warnings.

NOTE: Steep Approach operation implies to the airplane a vertical speed higher than the normal. For this reason the Steep Approach mode once activated, adds fixed positive biases to both the SINK RATE curve, and the PULL UP curve permitting steeper than normal instrument approaches without unwanted alerts.

Mode 6 - Advisory callouts with BANK ANGLE, APPROACHING MINIMUMS, MINIMUMS, and selected callout altitude aural warnings.

TRAFFIC DATA

The traffic data appears either above or below the intruder airplane symbol on the MFD. The data is presented as follows:

kontext:
TCAS STATUS ANNUNCIATIONS

The TCAS information is displayed on the MFD and PFD. There are six types of TCAS mode annunciations:
– TCAS FAIL – This annunciation is displayed when TCAS data indicates a TCAS failure. TCAS FAIL is also displayed when TCAS data is invalid or when TCAS data was not correctly received for 10 s.
– TCAS TEST – This annunciation is displayed when the TCAS computer indicates that functional test is active.
– TCAS OFF – This annunciation is displayed when TCAS provides a valid indication that the computer is in stand by mode.
– TA ONLY – This annunciation indicates that the TCAS is not selected to provide resolution advisories or is inhibited. The TA mode provides only surveillance of the surrounding airspace. In this mode, TCAS tracks proximate airplane and generates traffic advisories. No resolution advisories are issued in this mode.
– TA/RA – This annunciation is displayed when TCAS provides a valid indication that the computer is in TA/RA mode. This annunciation is only displayed on both TCAS MFD displays. TA/RA mode is the normal operation mode providing full TCAS coverage.
In this mode, TCAS tracks airplane in the surrounding airspace and generates traffic advisories or resolution advisories, as the situation requires.
– TCAS RA FAIL – This annunciation indicates that TCAS is not able to provide resolution advisories.
The annunciation is displayed if the resolution advisory data is invalid or not received for 5 s or if information required to display the TCAS RA data on the PFD is missing or failed

(for example, if attitude, or groundspeed is failed or missing). This annunciation is only displayed on the PFD.

Windshear detection mode operates automatically below 1800 ft Above Ground Level (AGL), with alerts available at 1200 ft AGL and below.

Page 68/72 Navigation REVISION 14

If more than one flight crew member of the same crew holds the qualification for Commander (CMD) only one pilot is designated as Commander (CMD) of the flight.
The command of the flight is assigned on the flight assignment.
During any flight, other than:

training flights, or line flying under supervision, or

check flights and non-revenue flights

the CMD of the aircraft occupies the left hand seat on the flight deck.

kontext:
1.4.2.3 Duties and Responsibilities of Cabin Attendants (CAB)

A cabin crew member on flight duty performs in the interests of safety of passengers, duties assigned by helvetic operations or by the commander of the airplane.
Cabin Attendants (CAB) ensure, under the overall authority and responsibility of the Commander (CMD) and the Senior Cabin Attendant (SEN), cabin safety (i.e., the safety of the passengers and the safety of cabin load and galleys). They form the link between the passengers and the flight crew.
Cabin crew members must report to the Commander (CMD) – usually through the Senior Cabin Attendant (SEN) – all circumstances that endanger or may endanger cabin safety.

The authorities of a Cabin Attendant (CAB) are: to request access to the Aircraft Cabin Log (ACL)

to request a debriefing within the whole crew or just with an individual crew member of the operation crew (e.g. CMD, SEN, etc.)

to request a staff appraisal

The responsibilities of a Cabin Attendant (CAB) are: participation in the crew briefing

to ensure that he applies all operational procedures and checklists in

accordance with the Operations Manual (OM) and the Cabin Safety Procedures Manual (CSPM) acquisition of the relevant information and particulars pertinent to the

individual flight

checking the safety and other cabin equipment and immediately reporting

deficiencies to the Senior Cabin Attendant (SEN) for further action

boarding of passengers at their prescribed positions

providing an optimum level of comfort and service for the passengers

ensuring proper cleaning of the aircraft cabin

ensuring re-catering for the upcoming flight

occupation of their emergency stations in the event of an emergency

directing – when necessary – cabin emergency procedures and an

emergency evacuation

OM-A Responsibilities

check the distribution tool at least once a week or before flight duty after a longer period away; read and acknowledge the relevant contents

not to operate as crew member on an airplane unless he is qualified for duty in accordance with 5.3 - Cabin Crew

check e-mail at least once a week and before flight or training duties, whichever results in more current information

in case of suspension or revocation of the personal cabin crew attestation by the competent authority, the cabin crew attestation must be returned to the respective superior and the HCC has to be informed without delay

He is responsible to adapt the operationally applicable elements of the SSCC defined in OMM 1.1 to the given situation and implement them in a mission- focussed manner.
Notwithstanding the overriding authority of the Commander (CMD), it is of utmost importance that the Cabin Attendant (CAB), at any time, draws the attention of the Commander (CMD) to facts, circumstances or unfavourable variables which may impair cabin safety and which may not yet have been noticed by the Commander (CMD).
fragen.frage_en: To whom must Cabin Attendants (CAB) report circumstances that endanger (or may endanger) Cabin Safety according to OM-A, and via whom as a rule?
antworten_en: The Safety Manager, as a rule via a report in the SMS Tool
The First Officer (COP), as a rule directly via the Cabin Interphone
The Commander (CMD), as a rule via the Senior Cabin Attendant (SEN)
The Head of Cabin Crew (HCC), as a rule after the flight
fragen.erklaerung_en: Cabin Crew Members must report to the CMD, usually via the SEN, all circumstances that endanger or may endanger Cabin Safety.

kontext: 4.1.3.1 Crewing of inexperienced Crew Members
A crew member is considered inexperienced immediately following the completion of its type rating, command or conversion course and the associated line flying under supervision.

The crew planning creates, with the crew master plan, a list of any inexperienced flight crew members and plans the crew schedule accordingly.
The Operations Control (OCC) receives this list from crew planning and is responsible for correct pairing.
If the introduction of a new aircraft type necessitates a lesser number of sectors or hours the intended schedule must be agreed upon with the Swiss FOCA.
The responsibility lies with the Accountable Manager (ACM).
In this case special attention shall be given to the minimum amount of sectors or hours for Line Training Commanders (LTC) on new aircraft type.

fragen.frage: Welchen Qualifikationslevel muss ein Flight Simulator gemäss OM-A 5.2.2 haben, damit Take-offs und Landings für die Recent Experience des CMD zählen?

kontext:
5.2.2 Recent Experience for Commanders

A pilot must not operate an aircraft as Commander (CMD) unless he has carried out, within the preceding 90 days, at least three take-offs and three landings as Pilot Flying (PF) in an aircraft or an approved flight simulator of the type to be used.
The flight simulator must be acceptable to the National Aviation Authority (NAA) and qualified to level CG, C or D.

The period of 90 days may be extended up to a maximum of 120 days by line flying under the supervision of a Type Rating Instructor (TRI).
When the above-mentioned period is expired, a flight training including at least three take-offs and landings as Pilot Flying (PF) of an aircraft not carrying passengers or cargo or an equivalent simulator training must be accomplished.
The aircraft or flight simulator must be of the relevant type.
The responsibility for compliance with these requirements lies with the respective pilot. He must log the relevant data in a pilot’s logbook. For back-up, dispatch maintains an overview of each flight crew member’s recency.
In addition to the recent experience mentioned above, the following rules shall be applied:
If a Commander (CMD) is absent for more than 4 months, but still within the validity of the checks required according to OM-D 2.1.6, a Requalification Training (RQT) is required.
For the Requalification training refer to OM-D 2.1.9

Level A, B or C (acceptable to the NAA)
Exclusively Level D
fragen.erklaerung_en: The flight simulator must be acceptable to the NAA and qualified at Level CG, C or D.

fragen.frage: Ab wann und wie lange ist die (empfohlene) Cholera-Impfung gemäss OM-A 6.1.2 gültig?

fragen.zitat: Vaccinations which are recommended and their validity: Cholera (from 7 days until 6 months after vaccination)
kontext:
6.1.2 Immunization

In accordance with the World Health Organization’s (WHO) International Health Regulations many countries prescribe vaccination of crew members and passengers against defined diseases, often specifying that such immunization is only required upon entry “after leaving or transiting infected areas”.
Each crew member scheduled for flight duty abroad must satisfy any requirement for vaccination, to have himself vaccinated in time, and to be able to produce – during his tour of duty – the appropriate WHO-approved “Certificate of Vaccination or Revaccination”.
Vaccination and Revaccination shall take place not less than 24 hours before commencement of flight duty, unless otherwise stated. In case of strong reaction medical advice shall be obtained in view of a possible impairment of fitness for flight duty. No alcoholic beverages shall be consumed for a period of at least 24 hours after vaccination.

Vaccinations which may be obligatory and their validity:
Yellow fever (from 10 days after, for lifetime)

Vaccinations which are recommended and their validity:
Cholera (from 7 days until 6 months after vaccination)

Typhoid (from 7 days until 3 years after vaccination)

Poliomyelitis (after 3 vaccinations up to 10 years) Tetanus (after 3 vaccinations up to 10 years)

COVID-19(1) (from 1 to 2 weeks after the vaccination)

Note 1: Crew members must not be engaged in any safety relevant duty (e.g. flight duty) for a period of 48 hours after each dose of COVID-

19 vaccine. In case side effects persist for more than 48 hours following the vaccination, crew members shall consult their AME.

The waiting period shall be extended until the time when the side

effects completely disappear.

OM-A 6 Health Precautions

Malaria prophylaxis, though not immunization in the strict sense of the word, should be mentioned here; crew members scheduled for flight duty to malaria infected countries shall obtain, on the advice of their flight medical doctor, the appropriate medication and apply it as prescribed.
Note: Crew members shall be aware of the fact that there are many extremely dangerous diseases against which vaccination is not possible.

Only general rules may be given here for health-conscious behavior in foreign countries: observe strict hygiene in eating drinking (amoebic dysentery, brucellosis),

do not bathe in stagnant water (bilharziasis),

in infested (e.g., bush/jungle) areas, wear long sleeved shirts and long trousers to prevent or minimize bites by disease-carrying insects (filariasis, malaria, encephalitis, sleeping sickness) or by outright poisonous insects or animals (spiders, scorpions, snakes); use insect-repellant.

OM-A 6 Health Precautions

antworten_en: From 10 days after vaccination, lifelong
From 1 day to 12 months after vaccination

From 7 days to 6 months after vaccination
fragen.erklaerung_en: According to OM-A, the cholera vaccination is valid from 7 days to 6 months after vaccination.

fragen.frage: Welche Substanzen sind gemäss OM-A 6.2.1 von der Definition der Psychoactive Substances ausgenommen?

kontext:
6.2.1 Definition of Psychoactive Substances

A psychoactive substance is a drug or other substance that affects how the brain works and causes changes in mood, awareness, thoughts, feelings, or behavior.
Examples of psychoactive substances include alcohol, opioids, cannabinoids, sedatives and hypnotics, cocaine, other psycho stimulants, hallucinogens, and volatile solvents, and certain pain medicines.

Also, many illegal drugs, such as heroin, LSD, cocaine, amphetamines and certain pain medicines.
Caffeine and tobacco are excluded.

fragen.erklaerung_en: OM-A 6.2.1 counts, among others, alcohol, opioids, cannabinoids and sedatives as psychoactive substances; caffeine and tobacco are excluded.

7.1.1 General

All information about flight and duty time limitations and rest requirements, as well as the rules about exceedances of flight duty time limitations and/or reductions of rest periods, are established for all flight and cabin crew members of helvetic and are in compliance with EASA AIR OPS PART ORO - Subpart FTL, relevant Certification Specification (CS.FTL) and the complementary national provisions of Switzerland.
All flights are planned as to be completed within the allowable flight duty period, taking into account the time necessary for all pre-flight duties, all subsequent flights, turn-arounds and all post flight duties.
helvetic will publish weekly duty rosters for its crew members four weeks in advance. The duty roster will be published latest every Sunday evening.

kontext:
7.1.5 Definitions

acclimatised: a state in which a crew member’s circadian biological clock is synchronised to the time zone where the crew member is. A crew member is considered to be acclimatised to a 2-hour wide time zone surrounding the local time at the point of departure. When the local time at the place where a duty commences differs by more than 2 hours from the local time at the place where the next duty starts, the crew member, for the calculation of the maximum daily flight duty period, is considered to be acclimatised in accordance with the values in the Table below.

Time difference (h) Time elapsed since reporting at reference time between reference time and local time where the crew member starts the next duty 48 48 – 71:59 72 – 95:59 96-119:59 ≥120 <4 ≤6

≤9 ≤12

‘B’ means acclimatised to the local time of the departure time zone,

‘D’ means acclimatised to the local time where the crew member starts his her next duty, and

‘X’ means that a crew member is in an unknown state of acclimatisation.

accommodation: for the purpose of standby and split duty, a quiet and comfortable place not open to the public with the ability to control light and temperature, equipped with adequate furniture that provides a crew member with the possibility to sleep, with enough capacity to accommodate all crew members present at the same time and with access to food and drink

suitable accommodation: for the purpose of standby, split duty and rest, a separate room for each crew member located in a quiet environment and equipped with a bed, which is sufficiently ventilated, has a device for regulating temperature and light intensity, and access to food and drink
adequate furniture: a seat that reclines at least 45° back angle to the vertical, has a seat width of at least 20 inches (50cm) and provides leg and foot support

augmented flight crew: a flight crew which comprises more than the minimum number required to operate the aircraft, allowing each flight crew member to leave the assigned post, for the purpose of in-flight rest, and to be replaced by another appropriately qualified flight crew member

block off: the time when an aircraft is moving from its parking position for the purpose of taking off block on: the time after flight, when an aircraft comes to a stop

at the parking position and all engines are shut down

block time: the time between an aircraft first moving from its

parking place for the purpose of taking off until it comes to rest on the designated parking position and

all engines or propellers are shut down.

break: period of time within an flight duty period, shorter

than a rest period, counting as duty and during which a crew member is free of all tasks

delayed reporting: the postponement of a scheduled FDP by helvetic

before a crew member has left the place of rest

disruptive schedules: a crew member’s roster which disrupts the sleep opportunity during the optimal sleep time window by comprising an FDP or a combination of FDPs which encroach, start or finish during any portion of the day or of the night where a crew member is acclimatised.
A schedule may be disruptive due to early starts, late finishes or night duties

fragen.frage: Was muss der Commander gemäss OM-A 7.2.1 tun, bevor er die Limiten mittels Commander's Discretion modifiziert?
antworten: Alle Crew Members zu ihrem Alertness Level konsultieren
Die Behörde vorgängig per E-Mail über die Modifikation informieren
Die schriftliche Zustimmung des Piquet Officer (PQO) einholen
Eine FRMS-Berechnung im SAFTE-Modell durchführen lassen

fragen.zitat: The commander shall consult all crew members on their alertness levels before deciding the modifications.
kontext:
7.2.1 Modification of the Limits on Flight Duty, Duty or Rest Periods

During actual flight operation, which starts after the whole crew has reported for any duty, the Commander (CMD) shall have the possibility to modify the limits on flight duty, duty and rest periods in the event of conditions described as unforeseen circumstances.
The exercise of commander’s discretion shall be considered exceptional and shall be avoided at home base when standby or reserve crew members are available.
The conditions shall comply with the following: the maximum daily FDP which results after applying 7.1.7 - Maximum Daily Flight Duty Periode (FDP) or 7.1.9 - Split Duty may not be increased by more than 2 hours.

the maximum basic daily FDP that results after applying 7.1.7.1 - Maximum Daily FDP for Acclimatised Crew Members shall be used to calculate the limits of commander’s discretion, if commander’s discretion is applied to an FDP which has been extended under the provisions of 7.1.7.3 - Maximum Daily FDP for Acclimatised Crew Members with the Use of Extensions without In-flight Rest

if on the final sector within a FDP the allowed increase is exceeded because of unforeseen circumstances after take-off, the flight may continue to the planned destination or alternate aerodrome the rest period following the FDP may be reduced but can never be less

than 10 hours
The commander shall consult all crew members on their alertness levels before deciding the modifications.

Additionally, he shall take due consideration of additional factors that might decrease a crew member’s alertness levels, such as:
WOCL encroachment

weather conditions

complexity of the operation and/or airport environment

airplane malfunctions or specifications

flight with training or supervisory duties

increased number of sectors

circadian disruption

individual conditions of affected crew members (time since awake, sleep- related factor, workload, etc.)

7.2.2 Duties in case of Modification of the Limits on Flight Duty, Duty or Rest Periods

helvetic will assess on a regular basis the series of pairings where commander’s

discretion has been exercised in order to be aware of possible inconsistencies in their rostering. The FRMS meeting monitors the amount of FTL modifications and other FTL exceedances via the BI tool according to 2.4.5.1.8 - FRMS Meeting.

The Commander (CMD) shall submit an IT report to helvetic flight operations

management whenever a limit on flight duty, duty or rest period has been

modified by his discretion or whenever a limitation as stated within this chapter has been violated in excess of one hour. This report shall be handled according

to OMM 7 Reporting Scheme.

Whenever the above-mentioned modification or a reported violation is beyond one hour, helvetic shall send a copy of the report to the competent authority not

later than 28 days after the event.

The RPO will monitor FTL exceedances and request reports from the commander, whenever a report is missing.
fragen.frage_en: What must the Commander do according to OM-A 7.2.1 before modifying the limits by means of Commander's Discretion?
antworten_en: Consult all crew members on their alertness level
Inform the authority by e-mail in advance of the modification
Obtain the written consent of the Piquet Officer (PQO)
Have an FRMS calculation performed in the SAFTE model
fragen.erklaerung_en: Before deciding on the modification, the Commander must consult all crew members on their alertness level and take other factors such as WOCL or weather into account.

fragen.frage: helvetic informiert ein Crew Member über eine Verspätung der Reporting Time von 10 Stunden oder mehr und stört es danach nicht weiter. Wie zählt diese Zeit gemäss OM-A 7.2.4?
antworten: Sie zählt vollständig als FDP

fragen.zitat: As an exception, when the operator informs the crew member of a delay of 10 hours or more in reporting time and the crew member is not further disturbed by the operator, such delay of 10 hours or more counts as a rest
kontext:
7.2.4 Delayed Reporting or Short-notice Flight Cancellation

In the event of unforeseen circumstances a delayed reporting procedure may be applied if the time until the scheduled reporting time is more than one hour at home base or more than 30 minutes away from home base and the crew member can remain at his suitable accommodation.
In such a case, if the crew member is informed by phone (or by SMS in case of possible interference with sleeping patterns) about the delayed reporting time, the maximum Flight Duty Period (FDP) is calculated as follows:
One notification of a delay leads to the calculation of the maximum FDP according to when the delay is less than 4 hours, the maximum FDP is calculated based on the original reporting time and the FDP starts counting at the delayed reporting time

when the delay is 4 hours or more, the maximum FDP is calculated based on the more limiting of the original or the delayed reporting time and the FDP starts counting at the delayed reporting time

If the reporting time is further amended, the FDP starts counting 1 hour after the second notification or at the original delayed reporting time if this is earlier

As an exception, when the operator informs the crew member of a delay of 10 hours or more in reporting time and the crew member is not further disturbed by the operator, such delay of 10 hours or more counts as a rest

period.
Any delay which is communicated to the crew member 10 hours or more before the delayed reporting time does not count as delayed reporting and no additional regulations apply.

In the event when the first flight segment(s) has to be removed (but the following ones remain) or changed to another flight segment(s), and this change is done

less than one hour ahead of original reporting time, a ground duty is added in the

duration of 5min starting at the original reporting time.

If due to an unforeseen circumstance flight must be cancelled after the reporting time for duty, ground duty is added which starts at the original reporting time, and

finishes either at the time when decision for cancellation was made (if crew was

not yet at the aircraft) or 30min after the decision was made (if crew performed any flight duty prior to the affected one).
fragen.frage_en: helvetic informs a crew member of a delay of the Reporting Time of 10 hours or more and does not disturb him further afterwards. How does this time count according to OM-A 7.2.4?
antworten_en: It counts fully as FDP
It counts as Rest Period
It counts 50% as duty
It counts as Standby other than Airport Standby
fragen.erklaerung_en: As an exception, a delay of 10 hours or more counts as Rest Period if the crew member is not disturbed further afterwards.

kontext:
9.1.1 General Policy

Basic requirement for transportation of dangerous goods is the permanent approval by the authority which will be reflected on the Air Operator’s Certificate. helvetic holds the permission for transportation of Dangerous Goods (DG) as cargo.

The transport of dangerous goods is performed according to the IATA Dangerous

Goods Regulations (DGR) and the ICAO Technical Instructions (TI) for the Safe Transport of Dangerous Goods by Air.

For purpose of access to references in this chapter, valid edition of IATA DGR is

located in helvetic headquarters, and it is the responsibility of the handling agents to provide same access to their employees involved in handling of DG.
Operational point of contact for anything related to dangerous goods is Nominated Person Ground Operations (GOP).
All reasonable measures are to be taken by helvetic to prevent the transport of dangerous goods (DG) without the necessary approvals, or which are not allowed to be transported by air.

kontext:
11.5.4 Time Line for Reporting

The chart below illustrates the general flow of information, main deadlines and stages of the reporting into ECCAIRS2 This reporting flow starts from the moment the occurrence is detected (T0). From this moment, the individual employee shall report it to helvetic via the SMS Tool as soon as possible, but latest within 72 hours. Once the occurrence report is filed, the safety department will validate this report within an additional 72 hours. If it becomes evident that the report describes a mandatory occurrence, the report will be forwarded to the authority ECCAIRS2).

A follow up of a mandatory occurrence will be sent from the SMS Tool as default

not later than 27 days.

Purely internal reports (not sent to the authority) should be closed 6 months after

creation.

In order to track ongoing corrective actions of the final report, the PIL Tool may be used.

11.5.5.1 Confidential Report

Any occurrence report can be filed as “Confidential Report”. The safety department guarantees the confidentiality of such Confidential Report by ensuring that the identities of any persons mentioned and flight information is kept anonym.
The Confidential Report is exclusively processed and evaluated by the safety department.

A confidential report can be filed via SMS Tool by selecting “Confidential Report to Safety Department” in the drop-down menu of the “Area of Occurrence”:

Note: Based on the information provided by the source and depending on a constellation of circumstances, others may be able to infer, deduce or assume the identity of the source of the information provided. The safety department will prevent this as far as possible.

11.5.5.3 Potential for Improvement Report

According to the company's strategy OMM 1.2.6 Strategy

all non-safety issues,

which might improve the company should be reported via the “Potential for Improvement” report.

occurrence report as a separate report.

improvement in the helvetic documentation structure

improvement in any documentation enhancing the understanding or reducing miss-interpretation of the written text

improvement in the company`s communication

improvement in any system used by helvetic

minimize any costs

optimize usage of tools

Retain the originals until the Safety Manager arrives
Make copies (photos) of all documents he hands over
Obtain an acknowledgement of receipt from the FOCA

fragen.frage: Wer bestimmt gemäss OM-A 11.9.4.1 über den Ausbau der Flight Recorder Systems nach einer Occurrence?
antworten: Der Safety Manager von helvetic nach Rücksprache mit dem ACM
Die CAMO in Absprache mit dem Hersteller des DVDR
Der Commander in Absprache mit dem Maintenance Control Center
Die Untersuchungsbehörde des Staats, der die Untersuchung durchführt
fragen.erklaerung: Der Ausbau der Flight Recorder Systems wird von der Untersuchungsbehörde des untersuchenden Staats unter Berücksichtigung der Schwere der Occurrence bestimmt.
fragen.zitat: The removal of the flight recorder systems from the aircraft will be determined by the investigating authority in the state conducting the investigation with due regard to the seriousness of the occurrence.
kontext:
11.9.4.1 Flight and Cockpit Voice Recorder Systems

Flight recorders on the helvetic Embraer fleet are digital recording units (DVDR) combining three different functionalities. Recording of: audio information from cockpit area microphones and primary crew microphones [cockpit voice recorder (CVR)]. datalink messages [data link recorder (DLR)] all available flight data [flight data recorder (FDR)] CVRs have at least 2 hours of voice recording capacity and must only be de- activated to protect records in due time.
FDRs have a flight time recording capacity which allows read out or de-activation in due time after an occurrence. De-activation during flight or on ground by the flight crew is not allowed.
Note: If a flight is conducted with a deactivated CVR check with MCC for MEL Regulation(s).

The DVDR automatically starts recording audio information as soon as the

aircraft is powered up. Flight data recording begins when the first engine is started. After power down the DVDRcontinue recording audio information for 10 minutes.
In the event the airplane becomes involved in an accident or serious incident, the

Commander must ensure the protection of all related flight records, and if

necessary, the associated DVDR to the extent possible. This can include the

retention of the DVDR in safe custody until its disposition.

The removal of the flight recorder systems from the aircraft will be determined by

the investigating authority in the state conducting the investigation with due regard to the seriousness of the occurrence.
fragen.frage_en: Who decides on the removal of the Flight Recorder Systems after an occurrence according to OM-A 11.9.4.1?
antworten_en: The helvetic Safety Manager after consultation with the ACM
The CAMO in consultation with the DVDR manufacturer
The Commander in consultation with the Maintenance Control Center
The investigation authority of the state conducting the investigation
fragen.erklaerung_en: The removal of the Flight Recorder Systems is determined by the investigation authority of the investigating state, taking the severity of the occurrence into account.

fragen.frage: Was soll gemäss OM-A 11.9.5.2 (Insurance) nach einem Ditching ein Crew Member tun, sofern dies ohne Gefährdung der eigenen Sicherheit möglich ist?
antworten: Das Flugzeug sofort an Land schleppen lassen
An Bord bleiben, um Salvage Claims zu verhindern
Das Wrack zur Beweissicherung fotografieren und verlassen
Die Flight Recorder ausbauen und an Land in Sicherheit bringen
fragen.erklaerung: Bei einem Ditching soll ein Crew Member an Bord bleiben, wenn dies ohne Gefährdung der eigenen Sicherheit möglich ist, um Salvage Claims zu verhindern.
fragen.zitat: in the event of aircraft ditching a crew member should remain aboard if it is possible to do so without prejudicing his own safety on order to prevent salvage claims;
kontext:
11.9.5.2 Insurance

As soon as sufficient information has been received by the company, instructions will be given whether it is necessary to leave the aircraft at the accident site pending insurance investigation.
Until such instructions are received, the aircraft may not be moved, even if permitted by local authorities, except in the following circumstances: when it is necessary to move the aircraft in order to release trapped or

injured persons ditching;
in the event of aircraft ditching a crew member should remain aboard if it is possible to do so without prejudicing his own safety on order to prevent salvage claims;

arrangements should be made to recover the aircraft to the nearest place of

safety as early as possible

when the aircraft is likely to suffer further damage if left in its present location

when removal is requested by local authorities (e.g. because a runway is obstructed

when from the helvetic perspective the risk of media interest (attraction) is unacceptable.
fragen.frage_en: What should a crew member do after a ditching according to OM-A 11.9.5.2 (Insurance), provided this is possible without endangering his own safety?
antworten_en: Have the aircraft towed ashore immediately
Stay on board to prevent salvage claims
Photograph the wreck for evidence and leave it
Remove the flight recorders and take them ashore for safekeeping
fragen.erklaerung_en: In a ditching, a crew member should stay on board if this is possible without endangering his own safety, in order to prevent salvage claims.

fragen.frage: In welcher zusätzlichen Funktion agiert der Fleet Manager (FM) gemäss OM-A 1.7.1?
antworten: Als Technical Check Pilot in der Funktion eines Vorgesetzten für Technical Check Flights
Als Performance Specialist für alle Aircraft Performance Issues inklusive Driftdown
Als EFB Administrator in der Funktion eines Verantwortlichen für Random Checks
Als Piquet Officer in der Funktion eines Stellvertreters des Accountable Managers

fragen.zitat: The Fleet Manager acts also as Technical Check Pilot in the function of a superior regarding all activities related to 8.7.4.7 - Technical Check Flights
kontext:
1.7.1 Job Description

The Fleet Manager (FM) serves as a link between the flight operations department and the flight crew members of the appropriate fleet regarding operational matters (i.e. procedures and technical documentation).
He also acts as a link between the flight operations department and the Continuous Airworthiness Management Organization (CAMO). He is responsible for maintaining the fleet-respective Minimum Equipment List (MEL) and the OM-B.
The Fleet Manager acts also as Technical Check Pilot in the function of a superior regarding all activities related to 8.7.4.7 - Technical Check Flights
fragen.frage_en: In what additional function does the Fleet Manager (FM) act according to OM-A 1.7.1?
antworten_en: As Technical Check Pilot in the function of a supervisor for Technical Check Flights
As Performance Specialist for all aircraft performance issues including driftdown
As EFB Administrator in the function of a person responsible for Random Checks
As Piquet Officer in the function of a deputy of the Accountable Manager
fragen.erklaerung_en: The Fleet Manager also acts as Technical Check Pilot in the function of a supervisor for all activities related to Technical Check Flights (8.7.4.7).

kontext:
1.13 Piquet Officer (PQO)

The Piquet Officer (PQO) duty is assigned to a group of nominated persons being part of the helvetic organisation. The nomination to the Piquet Officer (PQO) group is done by the Accountable Manager (ACM).
The goal of this function is to grant a single point of contact for Flight Operations Officer (FOO) on duty particularly outside of usual office hours.
The Piquet Officer (PQO) fulfills his duty in a weekly cycle starting and ending on Wednesdays at 12:00 (noon). The Piquet Officer must be reachable via his mobile phone outside usual office hours (usual office hours: Monday to Friday 07:00LT till 18:00LT). Non-availabilities shall be avoided whenever possible.
If unavoidable, non-availabilities shall be covered by delegation or sharing of the assigned duty with another Piquet Officer group member. helvetic Operations Control Center (OCC) shall be informed about any non-availability and the respective replacement of such a duty as early as possible (telephone or e-mail).

During normal office hours, the Piquet Officer (PQO) duty and responsibility shall automatically be assigned to a helvetic management member available in the office by decision of the Flight Operations Officers (FOO) on duty.

The published Piquet Officer (PQO) duty plan can be found in a semi-permanent Admin Note named Ops Management Piquet.
This note is updated by the Administration Personnel (ADM) in a half-yearly cycle.

OM-A Responsibilities

The Piquet Officer (PQO) is responsible for: supporting and maintaining the helvetic operation of airplanes in irregular situations in respect of safety, security and economy

providing communication and cooperation between the Operations Control Center (OCC) and members of the helvetic Operations Management (refer to 2.4.2 - helvetic Operations Management)

the promotion of commercially sound decisions in cooperation with the Flight Operations Officer (FOO) with other members of the helvetic Operations Management. Decisions shall be based on regulations laid down in the Operations Manuals (OM) and additional helvetic publications defined in 0.1
- Introduction

the integration of the customer relations management either by the Flight Operations Officer (FOO) on duty or by himself if deemed advisable (e.g. delays 2 hours, re-bookings, flight cancellations)

re-direction of requests to other members of the helvetic Operations Management (subject matter experts) unless he is competent to take appropriate actions or decisions on his own

informing the corporate management (refer to 1.1.1 - Corporate Management sequence COO – CFO – CEO) about the irregularity and corrective actions in case of major issues (e.g. cancellation of flights with major consequences such as nightstop, airplane damage)

the activation of the Emergency Response Team (ERT) in coordination with the Accountable Manager (ACM) or his deputy according to the Crisis and Emergency Response Manual (CERM)

arranging testing for psychoactive substances in case of a serious incident

or accident or if misuse is suspected and removing investigated crew member from duty until clarified. Refer to:

helvetic HR Manual

OM-A Responsibilities
fragen.frage_en: Who takes over the duties of the Piquet Officer (PQO) during normal office hours according to OM-A 1.13?
antworten_en: The Senior FOO on duty, until the rostered PQO can be reached

The Piquet Officer rostered according to the PQO Duty Plan, regardless of his presence
The Manager Operations Control (MOC), at the decision of the Accountable Manager
fragen.erklaerung_en: During normal office hours, the PQO duty is automatically assigned to a helvetic management member available in the office, at the decision of the FOO on duty.

The following documents, or copies thereof, shall be carried on board of all helvetic aircraft and shall, within a reasonable time of being requested to do so by a person authorized by a National Aviation Authority (NAA), be produced by the Commander (CMD) of the aircraft to that person:

kontext:
7.3.3.1 Hazard Identification

For hazard identification process refer to OMM Chapter 4.3 Hazard Identification.
The following methodologies shall be used to identify fatigue related hazards:
Predictive:
Sleep, Activities, Fatigue and Task Effectiveness Model (SAFTE) The SAFTE-model is:

based on 15 years of fatigue modelling experience

validated against laboratory and simulator measures of fatigue

validated and calibrated to predict accident risk by the US Department of Transportation

accepted by the US Department of Defence (Air Force, Army, Navy, Marines) as the common war fighter fatigue model

Fatigue Avoidance Scheduling Tool (FAST) FAST uses the SAFTE-model as described above considers time zone changes and is valid for any city pair

mimics typical sleep patterns

considers total duty period, commuting, flight time and number of route sectors counts on naps prior to anticipated late starts

considers split sleep (split sleeping periods) when appropriate

automatically inserts in-flight sleep for augmented crews

(currently not applied by helvetic)

Proactive:

reporting of fatigue risks

analysis of planned versus actual time worked

FTL use of commander’s discretion

FAST analysis of actual flown schedules

Reactive: fatigue and confidential reports

audit reports

incidents

Flight Data Monitoring (FDM) events whereas outcomes of fatigue could show undesirable effects in Flight Data Monitoring (FDM) without any doubt, specific evidence of root causes clearly and solely addressing fatigue has not yet been proven based on scientific research. Therefore, for the time being helvetic does not define FDM as a functional element of FRMS. However, FDM can be used as a source to analyse fatigue-related events which were either reported by crew members or if analysis results point towards a relation between fatigue and FDM-events.
fragen.frage_en: Which function of the Fatigue Avoidance Scheduling Tool (FAST) is currently not applied by helvetic according to OM-A 7.3.3.1?
antworten_en: Taking time zone changes into account for any city pairs
Automatic insertion of in-flight sleep for Augmented Crews
Taking naps before expected late takeoffs into account
Taking split sleep into account, where appropriate
fragen.erklaerung_en: FAST automatically inserts in-flight sleep for Augmented Crews; this is currently not applied by helvetic.

kontext:
7.3.6 Implemented Fatigue Risk Mitigation

Based on the necessity of having qualified personnel available to the required extent, an effective crew planning plays a major role in achieving any FRMS aims.

Crew Planning (CRP) shall: consider fatigue risk additionally to legal flight time limitations

plan night flights with minimal waiting time

consider rest time before night flights and use common sense when planning deadheading or positioning

According to the SAFTE model helvetic defines the critical level of effectiveness at 77% of the maximum human performance. The goal is to reduce the time exposure with actual duty time performed below this criterion.
If there are duty plans in the future with FRMS efficiency level below 85% and it is not possible to correct it due to the rotation planning (e.g. night duties), preventive measures shall be taken in order that the actual planning will not be below 77% efficiency level (e.g. no reserves before and after)

1.4.4.7 Reduced and Derated Takeoff Thrust

Approved methods:
Assumed Temperature

Derated Takeoff Thrust Modes other than T/O-1

For both methods:

Operations are allowed if the airplane meets all applicable performance

requirements at the planned takeoff weight

Operators must establish means to ensure that the engines are capable of producing full takeoff thrust without exceeding any engine operating limits.
The system check can be periodically performed by conducting a T/O-1 mode takeoff without using Assumed Temperature. The Engine Performance Trend Monitoring program may be used to extend the time intervals between takeoff demonstrations.

Application of reduced takeoff thrust is always at the pilot's discretion

For Assumed Temperature method only:
Operation is not allowed on runways contaminated with standing water, slush, snow, or ice, and is not allowed on wet runways unless suitable performance accountability is made for the increased stopping distance on

the wet surface.
The total thrust reduction is limited to 25% of each takeoff thrust mode

The pilot may cancel the Assumed Temperature at any time during the

takeoff operation by setting the thrust lever to the MAX position

1.4.10.9 General Limitations

The FMS does not correct the speed targets, including approach and go around speeds, for ice conditions or non-normal conditions. It is the pilot responsibility to ensure that the speeds are within the limits in these conditions.

The use of GPS is limited to airspace where GPS is approved by the appropriate governing authority.

The use of FMS Speed requires the respective FD vertical guidance mode to be active.

The pilot must ensure that displayed guidance data from non-usable stations is not used for navigation purposes by the flight crew. The NOTAM function in the FMS does not always inhibit tuning of a NOTAM selected station by the FMS when in AUTO tune mode. Note that the FMS will not use NOTAM selected

station data for FMS position determination.

Airplane operating outside SBAS coverage area are required to have an

alternate airport flight planning with other operational approved navigation

equipment available to the operation.

OM-B E2 1 Limitations

The pilots must compare any procedures/route retrieved from the FMS database with those published on the procedure charts. Differences between the charts and the FMS information up to 3 degrees are acceptable. Otherwise, the coded procedure must not be used.

Operation above 72°30.0' north latitude and below 59°30.0' south latitude is prohibited due to unreliable magnetic heading, unless at least one Inertial Reference System (IRS) is verified operational as a sensor to the FMS. In this case, the system will automatically switch to TRUE heading.

FMS performance management calculations have not been certified by Certification Authorities. FMS performance management information is advisory information only, and may not be used as a basis for fuel load planning or airplane range predictions.

If GPS RAIM is annunciated as not available during any phase of flight and airplane is operating outside SBAS coverage area, the pilot must monitor FMS guidance data and crosscheck with raw data from an alternate source (i.e. VOR, DME, or IRS).
LP minima is not supported and cannot be performed. On such procedure, if a LNAV minimum exists, VGP may be used down to the LNAV minima only.
The pilot must rely on the altimeters as the primary vertical reference.

kontext:
0.9 Rectification Intervals

Repair of inoperative systems or components, deferred in accordance with the MEL, must be effected at or prior to the rectification intervals established by the following designators: «A» Category No standard interval is specified. However, items in this category shall be rectified in accordance with the conditions stated in the MEL.

ii. Where a time period is specified other than in calendar days or flight days, it shall start at the point when the defect is deferred in accordance with the MEL. «B» Category Items in this category shall be repaired within three (3) consecutive calendar days (72 hours), excluding the day the malfunction was recorded in the Aircraft Technical Log (ATL) «C» Category Items in this category shall be repaired within ten (10) consecutive calendar days (240 hours), excluding the day the malfunction was recorded in the Aircraft Technical Log (ATL) «D» Category Items in this category shall be repaired within one hundred and twenty (120) consecutive calendar days (2880 hours), excluding the day the malfunction was recorded in the Aircraft Technical Log (ATL) Note: In EASA-MMEL/MEL the term «rectification interval» is used instead of «repair time», however, the meaning is exactly the same.

kontext:
0.6 Criteria For Dispatch

The decision of the Commander of the flight to have allowable inoperative items corrected prior to flight will take precedence over the provisions contained in the MEL. The MEL cannot take into account multiple unserviceabilities. Therefore, before dispatching an aircraft with multiple MEL items inoperative,
it must be ensured that any interface or inter-relationship between inoperative items will not result in degradation of the level of safety and or an undue increase in crew workload.

It is particularly in this area of multiple discrepancies and especially discrepancies in related systems that good judgement based on the circumstances of the situation must be applied including considerations in regard to actual meteorological en-route conditions.

kontext:
0.7 Maintenance Action

Every effort shall be made by Maintenance to correct all technical defects as early as practicable possible and that the aircraft can be released from a maintenance station in fully operational condition. The Commander must be informed by a certified Maintenance Organisation as soon as practicable, should it be impossible to rectify the inoperative item prior to departure.
Whenever an aircraft is released by Maintenance for dispatch with items inoperative, the following is required: the technical log book aboard the aircraft must contain a detailed description of the inoperative items(s), special advice to the flight crew, if necessary, and information about corrective action taken. if the flight crew has direct access to control(s), switches and/or indicator(s) related to inoperative unit(s) or component(s), the status must be clearly placarded. (e.g. Placard Associated IDG Selector - IDG 1 (2) INOP) Note To a practicable extent, placards should be located adjacent to the control or indicator affected by the deficiency.
If inadvertent operation could result in a hazardous condition, such equipment must be rendered inoperative (physically) as given in the appropriate Maintenance Procedure.

kontext:
0.8 Definitions and Symbols

For the purpose of this MEL the following definitions shall apply: a. «Visual Meteorological Conditions (VMC) means the atmospheric environment is such that would allow a flight to proceed under the Visual Flight Rules applicable to the flight. This does not preclude operating under Instrument Flight Rules. b. «Day» operation is any flight conducted from the point of take-off to landing between 30 minutes before sunrise and 30 minutes after sunset. c. (dash) in columns 3 or 4 indicates a variable quantity. Additionally, a dash is used when the exact item count is not operationally significant, for example: when the component cannot be individually quantified or when the quantity is inherently large and non-limiting for dispatch a. «Icing Condition the atmospheric environment is such that ice can form on the aircraft or in the engine(s) b. «Commencement of flight the point when an aircraft begins to move under its own power for the purpose of preparing for take off. c. «Inoperative means the equipment does not accomplish its intended purpose or is not consistently functioning within its design operating limits or tolerances. d. Some systems have been designed to be fault tolerant and are monitored by digital computers which transmit fault messages to a centralised computer for the purpose of maintenance. The presence of this category of message does not mean that the system is inoperative. e. «Combustible Material» material which is capable of catching fire and burning. In particular: if a MEL item prohibits loading of combustible (or flammable or inflammable) material, no material may be loaded except the following:
1. Cargo handling equipment (unloaded, empty or with ballast);
2. Fly away kits (excluding e.g. cans of hydraulic fluid, cleaning solvents, batteries, capacitors, chemical generators, etc.); NOTE: If serviceable tyres are included, they should only be inflated to a minimum pressure that preserves their serviceability;
3. Inflight service material (return catering only closed catering trolleys/boxes, no newspapers, no alcohol or duty free goods). f. Print in different typeface (e.g. italics): items which according to MEL are subject to national regulations (e.g. «as required by EASA») text or numbers that are different from the original MMEL entry.
Minimum Equipment List Embraer E1

MEL E1 0 Preamble
j. «(M)» symbol indicates a requirement for a specific maintenance procedure which must be accomplished prior to operation with the listed item inoperative.

Normally these procedures are accomplished by maintenance personnel; any other personnel qualified and authorized to perform certain functions must be defined in the MME and MEL. Appropriate (M)-procedures are required to be published as part of the operator`s manual or MEL. k. «(O)» symbol indicates a requirement for a specific operations procedure which must be accomplished in planning for and/or operating with the listed item inoperative. Normally these procedures are accomplished by the flight crew; any other personnel qualified and authorized to perform certain functions must be defined in the MME and in the MEL. Appropriate (O)- procedures are required to be published as part of the operator`s manual or l. «(P)» symbol requires inoperative equipment, component, system or function to be placarded in the flightdeck to inform and remind the crewmembers of the equipment condition. m. «Deleted» in the remarks column after a sequence item indicates that the item was previously listed but is now required to be operative if installed. n. «Out of sight» remark means that inoperative equipment shall be be stowed in a place which prevents it to be used or mistaken as operational equipment. o. «Extended Overwater» means operations over water at a distance away from land suitable for making an emergency landing, greater than that corresponding to 120 minutes at cruising speed or 400 NM, whichever is the lesser.

kontext:
0.8 Definitions and Symbols

For the purpose of this MEL the following definitions shall apply: a. «Visual Meteorological Conditions (VMC) means the atmospheric environment is such that would allow a flight to proceed under the Visual Flight Rules applicable to the flight. This does not preclude operating under Instrument Flight Rules. b. «Day» operation is any flight conducted from the point of take-off to landing between 30 minutes before sunrise and 30 minutes after sunset. c. (dash) in columns 3 or 4 indicates a variable quantity. Additionally, a dash is used when the exact item count is not operationally significant, for example: when the component cannot be individually quantified or when the quantity is inherently large and non-limiting for dispatch a. «Icing Condition the atmospheric environment is such that ice can form on the aircraft or in the engine(s) b. «Commencement of flight the point when an aircraft begins to move under its own power for the purpose of preparing for take off. c. «Inoperative means the equipment does not accomplish its intended purpose or is not consistently functioning within its design operating limits or tolerances. d. Some systems have been designed to be fault tolerant and are monitored by digital computers which transmit fault messages to a centralised computer for the purpose of maintenance. The presence of this category of message does not mean that the system is inoperative. e. «Combustible Material» material which is capable of catching fire and burning. In particular: if a MEL item prohibits loading of combustible (or flammable or inflammable) material, no material may be loaded except the following:
1. Cargo handling equipment (unloaded, empty or with ballast);
2. Fly away kits (excluding e.g. cans of hydraulic fluid, cleaning solvents, batteries, capacitors, chemical generators, etc.); NOTE: If serviceable tyres are included, they should only be inflated to a minimum pressure that preserves their serviceability;
3. Inflight service material (return catering only closed catering trolleys/boxes, no newspapers, no alcohol or duty free goods). f. Print in different typeface (e.g. italics): items which according to MEL are subject to national regulations (e.g. «as required by EASA») text or numbers that are different from the original MMEL entry.

Appropriate (M)-procedures are required to be published as part of the operator`s manual or MEL. k. «(O)» symbol indicates a requirement for a specific operations procedure which must be accomplished in planning for and/or operating with the listed item inoperative. Normally these procedures are accomplished by the flight crew; any other personnel qualified and authorized to perform certain functions must be defined in the MME and in the MEL. fragen.frage: Ein Thrust Reverser der E2 ist deaktiviert und in Forward Thrust Position verriegelt. Wann kommandiert der FADEC der operativen Seite Reverse Thrust?
antworten: Wenn die Groundspeed nach dem Touchdown über 60 kt liegt
Wenn der Thrust Lever der operativen Seite Reverse anfordert und der Thrust Lever der betroffenen Seite auf Idle steht
Wenn beide Thrust Levers gleichzeitig in die Reverse Position gezogen werden
Wenn der Thrust Lever der operativen Seite Reverse anfordert, unabhängig von der betroffenen Seite
fragen.erklaerung: Der FADEC der operativen Seite kommandiert Reverse Thrust nur, wenn deren Thrust Lever Reverse anfordert und der Thrust Lever der betroffenen Seite auf Idle steht.
