fragen.frage: Welche SID und welche STAR berücksichtigt der OFP bei der Berechnung der Trip Fuel?

kontext:
8.1.7.3.2 Trip Fuel

Trip fuel includes fuel for take-off and climb from the aerodrome elevation to the initial cruising

level/altitude, taking into account the expected departure routing

from top of climb (TOC) to top of descent (TOD), including any step climb or

step descent

from TOD to the point where the approach procedure is initiated, taking into account the expected arrival routing

for making an approach and landing at the destination aerodrome

Note:

On the OFP, the shortest SID and the longest STAR are taken into account. Therefore, SWIFAT corrections may be required by the flight

crew.

Refer to 8.1.10.2 - Operational Flight Plan Format and Decoding

(Overview).
fragen.frage_en: Which SID and which STAR does the OFP consider when calculating Trip Fuel?
antworten_en: The shortest SID and the longest STAR
The longest SID and longest STAR in each case
The longest SID and the shortest STAR
The SID and STAR filed in the ATC Flight Plan
fragen.erklaerung_en: Per OM-A, the OFP considers the shortest SID and the longest STAR; therefore SWIFAT corrections by the Crew may be necessary.

is required

The values are provided for informational purposes only and are not intended as

fragen.frage: In-flight Re-planning: Welchen Wert darf das erwartete Landing Weight ab dem Punkt, ab dem der revidierte OFP gilt, nicht überschreiten?
antworten: Das ursprünglich im OFP geplante Landing Weight
Die Maximum Landing Mass

Die Maximum Zero Fuel Mass

fragen.zitat: the expected landing mass shall not be greater than the maximum landing mass and performance requirements shall meet the expected limitations.
kontext:
8.3.7.4 In-flight Re-planning Procedure

When in-flight re-planning is performed the Operational Flight Plan (OFP) must be amended accordingly.
When re-planning to a destination for which a destination alternate is required, the flight crew must ensure that the usable fuel on board at the point from which the revised operational flight plan applies is not less than the sum of: remaining trip fuel

contingency fuel

destination alternate fuel

final reserve fuel

additional fuel if required

extra fuel

When re-planning to a destination for which a destination alternate is not required, the flight crew must ensure that the usable fuel on board at the point from which the revised operational flight plan applies is not less than the sum of: remaining trip fuel

contingency fuel

final reserve fuel additional fuel

extra fuel

In the event of in-flight replanning, at the point from which the revised operational flight plan applies,

the expected landing mass shall not be greater than

the maximum landing mass and performance requirements shall meet the expected limitations.

These include but are not limited to:

landing performance

approach climb performance
fragen.frage_en: In-flight re-planning: Which value must the expected landing weight not exceed from the point at which the revised OFP applies?
antworten_en: The landing weight originally planned on the OFP
The Maximum Landing Mass
The Maximum Take-off Mass minus Trip Fuel
The Maximum Zero Fuel Mass
fragen.erklaerung_en: In in-flight re-planning, the expected landing weight must not exceed the Maximum Landing Mass, and the performance requirements must be met.

fragen.frage: Was muss die Flight Crew gemäss OM-A zwischen zwei Flügen bezüglich Engine-Öl sicherstellen?
antworten: Dass nach jedem Flug Öl nachgefüllt wurde

Dass kein übermässiger Ölverbrauch stattgefunden hat
Dass eine Ölprobe zur Analyse entnommen wurde
fragen.erklaerung: Zwischen den Flügen genügt es sicherzustellen, dass kein übermässiger Ölverbrauch stattgefunden hat; vor dem Flug muss das Öl gemäss OM-B aufgefüllt sein.
fragen.zitat: before flight, that the engine oil contents have been topped up in accordance with the regulations of the Operations Manual OM-B between flights, that no excess oil consumption has taken place
kontext:
8.1.7.9 Oil

The engine oil contents must obviously be sufficient to cover the same elements as those for the fuel.
It will be sufficient for the flight crew to ensure the following:

before flight, that the engine oil contents have been topped up in accordance with the regulations of the Operations Manual OM-B

between flights, that no excess oil consumption has taken place
fragen.frage_en: What must the Flight Crew ensure between two flights regarding engine oil, per OM-A?
antworten_en: That oil was topped up after each flight
That the oil temperature has dropped below 50 °C
That there has been no excessive oil consumption
That an oil sample was taken for analysis
fragen.erklaerung_en: Between flights it is sufficient to ensure there has been no excessive oil consumption; before the flight the oil must be replenished per OM-B.

fragen.frage: Planung ohne Destination Alternate: Wann gelten zwei Runways am selben Flugplatz als separate Runways?
antworten: Wenn sie unterschiedliche Runway-Richtungen haben, unabhängig von der Approach Procedure
Wenn beide Runways über ein ILS CAT II/III verfügen
Wenn es getrennte Landeflächen mit je eigener, auf separater Navigationshilfe basierender Approach Procedure sind
Wenn sie parallel und mindestens 1000 m voneinander entfernt sind
fragen.erklaerung: Separate Runways sind getrennte Landeflächen mit je einer Approach Procedure auf separater Navigationshilfe, sodass eine Blockierung der einen die andere nicht betrifft.
fragen.zitat: Runways on the same airport are considered to be separate runways when they are separate landing surfaces, each having an approach procedure based upon a separate navigation aid
kontext:
8.1.5.5.2 Planning without Destination Alternate

A flight may be planned without destination alternate, provided: the duration of the planned flight from take-off to landing does not exceed 6 hours, or in the event of in-flight re-planning, the remaining flight time to destination does not exceed 4 hours

two separate runways are usable at the destination

the appropriate meteorological reports and/or forecasts indicate that for the period from 1 hour before to 1 hour after the expected time of arrival, the ceiling is at least 2 000 ft (600 m) or the circling height plus 500 ft (150 m), whichever is greater, and ground visibility is at least 5 km

no adverse weather forecast (e.g. thunderstorm, sandstorm, fog-patches irrespective of PROB or TEMPO in the forecast)

the wind is within AFM/OM-B limits for the planned approach, no gusts, no wind shears expected or forecast braking action at least medium

Refer to 8.1.7.3.6 - Additional Fuel for ADDNAR fuel considerations.

Note:

Runways on the same airport are considered to be separate runways when they are separate landing surfaces, each having an approach

procedure based upon a separate navigation aid,

which may overlay or cross such that, if one of the runways is blocked, it will not prevent the

planned operation on the other runway.
fragen.frage_en: Planning without Destination Alternate: When are two runways at the same aerodrome considered separate runways?
antworten_en: When they have different runway directions, regardless of the approach procedure
When both runways have an ILS CAT II/III
When they are separate landing surfaces, each with its own approach procedure based on a separate navigation aid
When they are parallel and at least 1000 m apart
fragen.erklaerung_en: Separate runways are separate landing surfaces, each with an approach procedure based on a separate navigation aid, so that blockage of one does not affect the other.

fragen.frage: In welchem Fall darf ein Flug unter anderem als Closed Destination geplant werden?
antworten: Wenn an der Destination nur eine Runway verfügbar ist
Wenn die geplante Flugzeit 6 Stunden übersteigt
Wenn die Destination ein Isolated Aerodrome ist
Wenn für die Destination keine meteorologischen Informationen (METAR/TAF) verfügbar sind
fragen.erklaerung: Eine Planung als Closed Destination ist u.a. möglich, wenn keine METAR/TAF für die Destination vorliegen, sofern zwei weather-permissible Alternates verfügbar sind.
fragen.zitat: when no meteorological information for the destination aerodrome is available (METAR / TAF)
kontext:
8.1.5.5.3 Planning with Closed Destination

A flight may be planned as a closed destination when the destination forecast is below landing minima or
when no meteorological information for the destination aerodrome is available (METAR TAF)

or the destination aerodrome is temporary closed for any other reason (e.g. snow removal, power failure, etc.)

provided that: at least two weather-permissible alternates are available

the weather forecast for both alternates is at or above the planning minima required

For fuel calculation the higher quantity of alternate fuel must be considered.
fragen.frage_en: In which case may a flight be planned, among others, as Closed Destination?
antworten_en: When only one runway is available at the destination
When the planned flight time exceeds 6 hours
When the destination is an Isolated Aerodrome
When no meteorological information (METAR/TAF) is available for the destination
fragen.erklaerung_en: Planning as Closed Destination is possible, among other cases, when no METAR/TAF is available for the destination, provided two weather-permissible Alternates are available.

fragen.frage: Unter welcher Voraussetzung darf mit Reduced Contingency Fuel (RCF) geplant werden?
antworten: Nur wenn die Basic Planning wegen operationeller Limitierungen wie Load oder Range nicht möglich ist
Nur wenn ein Fuel-ERA im OFP nominiert ist
Immer wenn für die Destination kein Alternate nötig ist
Auf allen Flügen über 3 Stunden zur Fuel-Ersparnis
fragen.erklaerung: RCF darf nur angewendet werden, wenn die Basic Planning wegen Load, Range, Take-off Performance oder Fuel-Verfügbarkeit nicht erreicht werden kann.
fragen.zitat: Planning with Reduced Contingency Fuel (RCF) may only be applied if basic planning cannot be achieved due to the following operational limitations: load or range
kontext: 8.1.5.5.5 Planning with Reduced Contingency Fuel (RCF)
Planning with Reduced Contingency Fuel (RCF) may only be applied if basic planning cannot be achieved due to the following operational limitations: load or range

or take-off performance or fuel unavailability

The planned route will include a Decision Point at which the flight crew decides whether to continue to the destination aerodrome or divert to the nominated Destination 2 aerodrome (optional refuelling stop), based on the actual fuel state.
The Decision Point may be placed at any suitable position along the intended route and should be located as close as practicable to the destination in order to minimise required contingency fuel.
fragen.frage_en: Under which condition may planning with Reduced Contingency Fuel (RCF) be used?
antworten_en: Only if Basic Planning is not possible due to operational limitations such as load or range
Only if a Fuel-ERA is nominated on the OFP
Always when no Alternate is required for the destination
On all flights over 3 hours to save fuel
fragen.erklaerung_en: RCF may only be applied if Basic Planning cannot be achieved due to load, range, takeoff performance or fuel availability.

Runway end lights (3) 400 m (night) and Runway edge lights or runway centreline lights

at least the length of the Accelerate Stop Distance (ASD).
The reported RVR or VIS value representative of the initial part of the take-off run can be replaced by pilot assessment.
Note 2: The pilot is able to continuously identify the take-off surface and

maintain directional control.

Note 3: Runway end lights may be substituted by colour-coded runway edge

When the reported visibility is below that required for take-off and RVR is not

or when neither reported visibility, nor RVR is available

a take-off may only be commenced if the flight crew can determine that the

fragen.frage: Für die Bestimmung der Approach Category sind sowohl VSO als auch VS1G verfügbar. Welcher VAT-Wert ist anzuwenden?
antworten: Der höhere der beiden resultierenden VAT-Werte

Der tiefere der beiden resultierenden VAT-Werte
Der Mittelwert beider resultierender Werte
fragen.erklaerung: Sind VSO und VS1G verfügbar, ist der höhere resultierende VAT-Wert (VSO x 1.3 bzw. VS1G x 1.23) anzuwenden.
fragen.zitat: If both, stall speeds VSO and VS1G are available, the higher resulting value for VAT shall be applied.
kontext:
8.1.3.1 Airplane Approach Category

The criterion taken into consideration for the classification of airplanes by categories is the Indicated Airspeed (IAS) at threshold (VAT).
It is equal to: the stall speed VSO multiplied by 1.3; or

If both, stall speeds VSO and VS1G are available,

kontext:
8.1.3 Methods for Determination of Aerodrome Operating Minima

Aerodrome operating minima means the limits of usability of an aerodrome for: take-off, expressed in terms of runway visual range (RVR) and/or visibility and, if necessary, ceiling

landing in 2D instrument approach operations, expressed in terms of visibility and/or RVR, minimum descent altitude/height (MDA/H) and, if necessary, ceiling

landing in 3D instrument approach operations, expressed in terms of visibility and/or RVR and decision altitude/height (DA/H) as appropriate to the type and/or category of the operation
Applied minima by crews shall take into consideration both, rules laid down in this chapter and local regulations by the applicable states, whichever is higher.

fragen.frage: Welchen Mindestanteil Glykol enthält das Basismaterial eines Type II Fluids?

fragen.zitat: These fluids have a thickener added in the form of high molecular polymers to a base material consisting of a minimum of 50 % glycol.
kontext: 8.2.4.3.2 Type II Fluids (thickened type)
These fluids have a thickener added in the form of high molecular polymers to a base material consisting of a minimum of 50 glycol.

These provide the fluid with special viscosity properties, which are a function of the temperature and wind shear forces. When the aircraft is at rest or traveling at low speeds (ground operation), the fluid forms a uniform film over wing and tail plane. As soon as the speed exceeds 30 knots or more, the viscosity breaks down, causing the fluid to flow off the aerodynamic surfaces. This leaves the aircraft clean.
The rapid flow-off of Type II fluids is guaranteed even under arctic conditions (i.e. at temperatures of -25°C).

With Type II fluids AEA specifies a minimum freezing point of -32° C in undiluted form and -10° C when diluted with 50 water. A minimum of four hours protection against ice formation at -5° C under conditions of high humidity (surface temperature of -5° C and air temperature of 0°C) is specified.

A 30 minutes protection period against freezing rain under conditions of surface

and air temperatures of -5°C is also specified.

Type II fluids provide also protection against refreezing in conditions of

precipitation.

Fluids based on alcohol are prohibited because they can cause window crazing.
The higher viscosity of Type II fluids has the advantage of a longer holdover time,

but may cause problems to aircraft types with a low lift-off speed due to the

viscous property. The low lift-off speed might not be sufficient to allow the fluid to run back and disappear from the air foil. As a consequence the center of

pressure will change, resulting in a delayed rotation and lift-off. It is therefore imperative to check the instructions in the Operations Manual OM-B.
fragen.frage_en: What is the minimum glycol content of the base material of a Type II Fluid?
fragen.erklaerung_en: Type II Fluids consist of a base material with at least 50 % glycol, to which a thickener (polymers) is added.

fragen.frage: Um wie viel kann die Oberflächentemperatur eines Flugzeugs durch Radiational Cooling in einer klaren, ruhigen Nacht unter der Umgebungsluft liegen?

Um höchstens 1 °C

fragen.zitat: Under these conditions the aircraft surface temperatures may be up to 4°C or more below that of the surrounding air.
kontext:
8.2.4.2.15 Radiational Cooling

A process by which temperature decreases, due to an excess of emitted radiation over absorbed radiation. On a typical calm clear night aircraft surfaces emit longwave radiation, however, there is no solar radiation (shortwave) coming in at night and this longwave emission will represent a constant net energy loss.
Under these conditions the aircraft surface temperatures may be up to 4°C or more below that of the surrounding air.
fragen.frage_en: By how much can an aircraft's surface temperature be below the ambient air temperature due to Radiational Cooling on a clear, calm night?
antworten_en: Up to 4 °C or more
At most 1 °C
At most 2 °C
Exactly 10 °C
fragen.erklaerung_en: Due to Radiational Cooling, surface temperatures can be up to 4 °C or more below the ambient air temperature.

fragen.frage: Bis zu welcher Umgebungstemperatur wurde gemäss OM-A bereits Clear Ice auf der Flügeloberseite im Bereich der Fuel-Tanks beobachtet?

Bis 4 °C
Bis 25 °C
fragen.erklaerung: Clear Ice durch kaltes Fuel (Cold Soaked Fuel) wurde bei Umgebungstemperaturen von bis zu 14 °C beobachtet.
fragen.zitat: remained in tanks after a long flight at high altitude. This has occurred with ambient temperatures as high as 14°C.
kontext:
8.2.4.2.2 Clear Ice

Clear ice is a layer of ice, which is transparent (and thus difficult to detect) formed during precipitation of relatively large rain drops. They partly freeze on impact upon a cold surface, releasing latent heat, which enables the remainder of the water to spread evenly. Since no air is trapped the result is a clear or glazed appearance.
Crews must be especially aware of the difficulty to detect clear ice and, in some situation, its presence may only be detected by touch. It can form on aircraft surfaces below a layer of snow and rime ice.
Significant deposits can form on upper wing surfaces in the vicinity of fuel tanks after fuelling with low temperature fuel, or when sufficient super cooled fuel
remained in tanks after a long flight at high altitude. This has occurred with ambient temperatures as high as 14°C.
Conversely, fuelling with relatively warm fuel can cause dry falling snow to melt with the danger of refreezing on the upper surface of the wing.
fragen.frage_en: Up to what ambient temperature has Clear Ice been observed on the upper wing surface in the area of the fuel tanks, per OM-A?
antworten_en: Up to 0 °C
Up to 14 °C
Up to 4 °C
Up to 25 °C
fragen.erklaerung_en: Clear Ice caused by cold fuel (Cold Soaked Fuel) has been observed at ambient temperatures of up to 14 °C.

fragen.frage: Wie ist ein Verlust der Richtungskontrolle bei einem Rejected Takeoff unter Icing Conditions zu bekämpfen?
antworten: Mit maximalem Reverse und Differenzialbremsen
Durch sofortiges Setzen der Parking Brake
Mit asymmetrischem Reverse Thrust auf der Gegenseite
Mit Idle Reverse oder vorübergehend Forward Idle Thrust
fragen.erklaerung: Asymmetrischer Reverse Thrust ist verboten; Richtungsverlust wird mit Idle Reverse oder vorübergehend Forward Idle Thrust bekämpft, das Seitenruder ist primäre Steuerhilfe.
fragen.zitat: Under no circumstances asymmetric reverse thrust shall be used for directional control. In contrary, loss of directional control must be counteracted by setting of idle reverse or temporary selection of forward idle thrust.
kontext:
8.2.4.24 Rejected Take-off in Icing Conditions

Directional control problems may be aggravated during a rejected take-off due to excessive anti-skid cycling and individual wheel skidding.
The rudder must be used as the primary steering aid.

Under no circumstances asymmetric reverse thrust shall be used for directional control. In contrary, loss of directional control must be counteracted by setting of idle reverse or temporary selection of forward idle thrust.

Note: If rejected take off occurs with a de-iced aircraft before next departure de-icing should be taken into consideration.

OM-A 8 Operating Procedures
fragen.frage_en: How is a loss of directional control to be countered during a rejected takeoff in icing conditions?
antworten_en: With maximum reverse and differential braking
By immediately setting the Parking Brake
With asymmetric Reverse Thrust on the opposite side
With Idle Reverse or temporarily Forward Idle Thrust
fragen.erklaerung_en: Asymmetric Reverse Thrust is prohibited; loss of directional control is countered with Idle Reverse or temporarily Forward Idle Thrust, and the rudder is the primary steering aid.

fragen.frage: Bei welchen Temperaturen kann sich bei langen Ground Holds mit Engines im Leerlauf und hoher Luftfeuchtigkeit Eis in den Engine-Einläufen bilden?
antworten: Auch bei Temperaturen über 10 °C
Nur bei Temperaturen unter -10 °C
Nur bei Temperaturen unter 0 °C
Nur unter 5 °C bei sichtbarer Feuchtigkeit
fragen.erklaerung: Gemäss OM-A kann sich Eis in den Engine-Einläufen bei hoher Luftfeuchtigkeit auch bei Temperaturen über 10 °C bilden.
fragen.zitat: Ice can form in engine inlets at temperatures above 10°C with high humidity present during extensive ground holds with the engines at idle.
kontext:
8.2.4.20 Ramp and Taxi Precautions

Icy conditions on the ramp and in the gate area means that the push back vehicle may not be able to develop sufficient traction to push the aircraft with its engines running. Therefore, it is recommended to have the aircraft pushed back, to a position from which it can taxi forward, before starting engines. Standing on an icy patch even idle thrust may be sufficient to move the aircraft forward, although the parking brake is set.
Abnormal engine indications may occur during engine start especially caused by the low oil temperature (and therefore high viscosity), with oil pressure exceeding normal limits until the oil temperature rises. This is acceptable provided the engine is operated at not more than idle thrust until the indications are back to normal.
There is a possibility for engine inlet ice to build-up during taxi and ground holding operation.
Ice can form in engine inlets at temperatures above 10°C with high humidity present during extensive ground holds with the engines at idle.

If visible moisture is present with a temperature below that specified in the Operations Manual OM-B, engine nacelle anti-ice systems shall be switched on after completion of the engine start procedure.
Probe and sensor heating systems shall be switched on before taxiing, according

to the checklist procedures.

Taxi shall take place with great care and significantly lower speeds than normal.

Neither aircraft, nor ground vehicles are capable of stopping quickly on icy or

contaminated surfaces. When guide lamp installations are available, use of them shall be made to align the aircraft in the gate area. Snow may cover the normal

taxi markings. Braking and steering capabilities shall be tested frequently.

Maintaining a greater distance than normal from other traffic helps to avoid jet- blast, which could adversely affect anti-ice treatment and prevents from blow of

contaminants into the aircraft.

Engine thrust may need to be higher than normal to overcome the drag caused by slush or snow. Changes should be made slowly and carefully to avoid blowing

equipment or contaminants into other aircraft. At intervals during prolonged taxi and immediately before take-off, engines shall be run up to higher settings as specified in the Operations Manual OM-B.

Flaps should be kept up when taxiing through slush or standing water, with pre-take-off checks held until the flaps can be lowered again.
Holding shall be done well clear of an active runway as a landing aircraft is more likely to deviate from the centreline when braking conditions are marginal.
Slush thrown up by landing aircraft can be ingested by engines, cause airframe damage and degrade the anti-ice treatment.
fragen.frage_en: At what temperatures can ice form in the engine inlets during long Ground Holds with engines at idle and high humidity?
antworten_en: Even at temperatures above 10 °C
Only at temperatures below -10 °C
Only at temperatures below 0 °C
Only below 5 °C with visible moisture
fragen.erklaerung_en: Per OM-A, ice can form in the engine inlets in high humidity even at temperatures above 10 °C.

kontext:
8.2.4.15 Information to the Commander

After de-icing the successful completion of either the visual check or the clear ice check (if required) shall be transmitted to the Commander (CMD Under normal circumstances a qualified ground handling agent is responsible for the correct and comprehensive de-icing of the aircraft and for the visual check upon completion, paying particular attention to the upper surfaces of the wings and stabilizer. The visual check may be performed by a flight crew member.
After completion of a deicing only procedure, where no anti-icing holdover time is applicable the Post Deicing Report shall be transmitted to the flight crew with following elements: fluid type statement that anti-icing holdover time do not apply date (optional) the statement “post-deicing check completed”

After completion of anti-icing procedure anti-icing code has to be transmitted by qualified staff to the flight crew to confirm satisfactory de-icing/anit-icing. The Commander (CMD will decide whether the Holdover Time (HOT) is adequate for taxiing and take-off.
The anti-icing code states the treatment (de-icing or anti-icing) applied to the aircraft.
It includes the:

fluid type and name

concentration

local time at start of anti-icing

date (optional)

statement: “post de-icing/anti-icing check completed”

The protection period is measured from the time of treatment start (start

of second step during two-step procedure).

Example 1:
Type 1, 25/75, 0630H, 01.11.01, post de-icing anti-icing check completed

Example 2:
Type 4, Killfrost ABC-S Plus,100/0, 0600H, 01.02.02, post de-icing anti-

icing check completed The mixing ratio is stated by volume with the de-icing fluid quoted first. A 25/75

mixture contains 25% de-icing fluid and 75% of water.

When the mixture used

differs from those tabulated, the next lower concentration code shall be used.

The next lower Concentration Code

The next higher Concentration Code
fragen.erklaerung_en: If the mixture deviates from the tabulated values, the next lower Concentration Code must be used.

fragen.frage: Wie viele Autolands (actual oder simuliert) werden zur Erhaltung der Recency im Linienbetrieb empfohlen?

Mindestens sechs innerhalb von zwölf Monaten
Mindestens zwei innerhalb von drei Monaten
Mindestens einer pro Monat
fragen.erklaerung: Empfohlen sind mindestens drei Autolands innerhalb von sechs Monaten; sonst sind sie im Simulator durchzuführen.
fragen.zitat: it is recommended to perform at least three autolands (actual or simulated) during regular line operation within six months.
kontext:
8.4.6.6.1 General

The simulated CAT II/III approach with autoland serves to train low visibility procedures and demonstrate the reliability of the aircraft’s equipment towards the National Aviation Authority (NAA). In order to maintain pilots’s recency,
it is recommended to perform at least three autolands (actual or simulated) during regular line operation within six months.
However, if this could not be fulfilled, the autolands shall be performed in the simulator. The simulated CAT II/III approach with autoland legally remains a CAT I approach.
fragen.frage_en: How many autolands (actual or simulated) are recommended to maintain recency in line operations?
antworten_en: At least three within six months
At least six within twelve months
At least two within three months
At least one per month
fragen.erklaerung_en: At least three autolands within six months are recommended; otherwise they must be performed in the simulator.

fragen.frage: Ab wann werden die ATC Low Visibility Procedures (LVP) wirksam?
antworten: Wenn die MID-RVR unter 800 m fällt oder das Ceiling unter 300 ft liegt
Wenn die TDZ-RVR auf 600 m oder weniger fällt oder das Ceiling 200 ft oder weniger beträgt
Wenn die TDZ-RVR unter 400 m fällt oder das Ceiling unter 100 ft liegt
Wenn die TDZ-RVR unter 550 m fällt oder das Ceiling unter 200 ft liegt
fragen.erklaerung: LVP werden wirksam, wenn die TDZ-RVR 600 m oder weniger beträgt oder das Ceiling 200 ft oder tiefer liegt.
fragen.zitat: ATC Low Visibility Procedures (LVP) become effective when the touch down zone (TDZ) Runway Visual Range (RVR) falls to 600 m or below or the ceiling is 200 ft or below.
kontext:
8.4.8.3 ATC Low Visibility Procedures

The ATC Low Visibility Procedures (LVP) are ground procedures at the airport, designed to prevent the entry of ground vehicles and taxiing aircraft into areas protected for take-off and landing. In addition they protect the sensitive areas of the ILS transmission and regulate the flow of air traffic on the approach.
ATC Low Visibility Procedures (LVP) become effective when the touch down zone (TDZ) Runway Visual Range (RVR) falls to 600 m or below or the ceiling is 200 ft or below.

ATC will always report the touch down zone (TDZ) Runway Visual Range (RVR).
Midfield point (MID) RVR values and roll-out RVR values will only be reported if: they are less than the TDZ RVR and below 800 m

when less than 400 m

when requested by the pilot
fragen.frage_en: When do the ATC Low Visibility Procedures (LVP) become effective?
antworten_en: When the MID RVR falls below 800 m or the ceiling is below 300 ft
When the TDZ RVR falls to 600 m or less or the ceiling is 200 ft or less
When the TDZ RVR falls below 400 m or the ceiling is below 100 ft
When the TDZ RVR falls below 550 m or the ceiling is below 200 ft
fragen.erklaerung_en: LVP become effective when the TDZ RVR is 600 m or less or the ceiling is 200 ft or lower.

fragen.frage: Was gilt grundsätzlich, wenn bei einem CAT II/III-Approach unterhalb 1000 ft AGL ein Ausfall auftritt?
antworten: Fortsetzung, sofern bereits Sichtreferenzen bestehen
Fortsetzung auf CAT I-Minima ohne neues Briefing
Go-around und Neubeurteilung der Systemfähigkeiten
Fortsetzung des Approach mit einer höheren DH
fragen.erklaerung: Unter 1000 ft AGL bedeutet jeder Ausfall einen Go-around mit Neubeurteilung; Ausnahme ist ein Einzelausfall unter AH bei fail-operational CAT III.
fragen.zitat: Below 1000 ft AGL the occurrence of any failure implies a go-around and a reassessment of the system capabilities.
kontext:
8.4.7 Failures and Associated Actions

In general there are three possible responses to the failure of any system, instrument or other element during the approach. continuation of the approach to the planned minima

reversion to higher minima

go-around and reassessment of the capabilities

The nature of the failure and the point of its occurrence will determine which response is appropriate.
As a general rule, if a failure occurs above 1000ft AGL, the approach may be continued reverting to a higher Decision Height (DH), providing the appropriate conditions are met (refer to 8.4.1.3 - Category II Approaches and 8.4.1.4 - Category III Approaches for the respective minima).
Below 1000 ft AGL the occurrence of any failure implies a go-around and a reassessment of the system capabilities.

Another approach may then be initiated to the appropriate minima for the given aircraft status.
For exceptions consult the aircraft type specific Operations Manual OM-B E1 2.5.3.5.5 - Malfunctions

OM-B E2 2.5.3.5.5 - Malfunctions

This rule has been adopted under the consideration that below 1000 ft AGL there is not sufficient time left for the crew to perform the necessary switching, to check system configuration and limitations and to brief for new minima. In a category III dual (fail operational) situation, however, a single failure below the Alert Height

(AH) does not necessitate a go-around.
fragen.frage_en: What generally applies if a failure occurs below 1000 ft AGL during a CAT II/III approach?
antworten_en: Continue if visual references are already established
Continue to CAT I minima without a new briefing

kontext:
8.4.6.1 Visual References for CAT II III Approaches

Operations with Decision Height (DH) – category II and III approaches.
It should be stressed that the Decision Height (DH) is the lower limit of the decision zone during which, in limiting conditions, the PF will be assessing the visual references. He should approach this zone prepared for a go-around, but with no pre-established judgement. The PF should make the decision according

to the quality of the approach and the way the visual references develop as the Decision Height (DH) is approached.
During category II III operations the conditions required at the Decision Height

(DH) in order to continue the approach are:

that the visual references should be adequate to monitor the continued

approach and landing

that the flight path should be acceptable

If either or both of these conditions are not satisfied, it is mandatory to initiate a

missed approach.

During these last few seconds of a stressed time and visibility situation, it is of the utmost importance for the PF to be completely familiar with all CAT III lighting

and the runway environment. When visual acquisition is attained, the PF’s first concern is to determine the aircraft’s lateral position. He will see no more than

several centerline and touchdown zone lights.

8.4.6.1.1 Changes in Visual Segment due to different Brightness of Lights

Since the farthest object in the visual segment is generally a light, variations in the brightness of adjacent parts of the lighting pattern can produce changes in visual segment. This is particularly noticeable where high intensity approach lighting is followed by less bright runway lighting.
Also after touchdown there may be an apparent reduction of segment after passing the TDZ lights. Although the centreline lights are just as bright as the TDZ lights, they are only in a single line and this decrease in the number of lights visible can appear to the pilot as a reduction in segment.
Pilots should be aware of the intensity at which approach/runway lights are operating. Dimming must not be requested, as this reduces the visual segment considerably.

8.3.8.7 Jet Stream

Near the tropopause there can be narrow bands of wind with extremely high speeds of up to 300 knots, called jet stream. The extent in length is up to several thousand miles, the width can be several miles. The main direction of the jet stream across Europe is south-west to north.
In mid latitudes there is a common area for Clear Air Turbulence (CAT) around the jet stream, above and below the jet core and to the polar side. Taking a cross section of a jet stream looking downwind, the turbulent region would be to the left of the jet core in Northern hemisphere and to the right in Southern hemisphere.
To avoid or to leave the areas of Clear Air Turbulence (CAT) the following procedures should be applied: reducing airspeed, to reduce the acceleration due to wind shears

when flying parallel with the jet stream, changing altitudes by 1000 ft
when flying perpendicular to the jet stream, changing altitude by 1000 ft: from the warm to the cold side downwards, from the cold to the warm side upwards

if the temperature remains constant the course should be altered in order to

kontext:
8.3.8.8 Volcanic Ash Clouds

Flying through an ash cloud should be avoided by all means because of extreme hazard for the engines and the aircraft. Volcanic ash may extend for several hundred miles, and eruptions may send ash plumes up to 40 000 ft.
The weather radar can detect neither ash clouds nor volcanic dust.

If the aircraft enters an ash cloud the flight crew can expect: smoke, dust or acrid odors similar to electric sparks in the cockpit

at night heavy static discharges around the windshield

at night, St. Elmo fire or other static discharges accompanied by a bright orange glow in the engine inlets

engine surge or overheat

engine failure

unreliable airspeed indication

pressurization and electrical systems may be affected

When encountering ash cloud the following procedures are recommended: turn on continuous ignition

declare an emergency do not climb in order to over fly the ash cloud

reduce power to idle to provide additional engine stall margin and lower

turbine temperature

try to escape the ash cloud by descending and flying a 180° turn (if terrain clearance permits)

monitor attitude versus airspeed

keep as many engines running as possible

restart any engine, which was shut down due to EGT exceeding the limits; if an engine fails to restart repeated attempts should be made immediately to

avoid solidification of molten ash on the turbine blades,

turn on all accessory air bleeds including all air conditioning packs, nacelles,

and wing anti-ice; this will provide an additional engine stall margin by

reducing engine pressure

For additional procedures refer to the type specific OM-B.

Following an encounter with an ash cloud a landing at the next suitable airport is mandatory. If the visibility through the windshield is impaired a runway with auto land capability should be considered.
Flight crews are requested to make special air reports: when a volcanic eruption is observed, or when volcanic ash cloud is observed or encountered

Information on volcanic activities, including pre-eruption activity, volcanic eruption and volcanic ash clouds are transmitted to aircraft operating on routes that could be affected.
This information is also published by NOTAM and SIGMET up to a 12 hours validity period and, if necessary, recommendations on re-routings will be included.

kontext:
8.3.8.5 Wind Shear

In order to avoid dangerous wind shear phenomena it is important to know what wind shear is and in which meteorological and geographical environment it can be expected.
The following definition seems to be the most suitable for aviation:

wind shear is any rapid change in wind direction or speed along the flight path of an aircraft

Wind shear, with or without turbulence, alters the lift force acting on an aircraft, resulting in a significant sinking or rising motion.

Therefore, wind shear may be categorized as:

increasing performance shear caused by increasing headwind or decreasing

tailwind component or vertical updrafts

decreasing performance shear caused by decreasing headwind or

increasing tailwind component or vertical downdrafts

Conditions for potentially hazardous wind shears are: convective conditions (e.g. thunderstorms, rain or snow showers)

frontal systems

jet streams

strong or gusty surface winds

other cases (temperature inversion, mountain waves, sea breeze circulations)

Wind shear events are typically one to two miles in diameter and mostly occur near the ground (typically below 500 ft AGL) during take-off and landing. Both situations would see the aircraft in a low energy condition. Therefore, there is only limited time for wind shear recognition and counteraction, typically 5 to 15 seconds.
Several factors can impede wind shear recognition: marginal weather conditions

high crew work load conditions

illusion of normality; during the initial part of the wind shear encounter, everything may appear normal; even severe wind shear onset may not

provide dramatic early indications to the flight crew

Standard response of the flight crew should be: control of flight path through pitch attitude; resistance to a downward change

in pitch attitude as normal response to low airspeed

immediate increase of thrust, maximum thrust shall be applied

an approach shall be aborted

unusual stick forces may be required to maintain pitch attitude during

airspeed variations away from normal target airspeed

low airspeed must be accepted, flying at airspeeds below normal reference

speeds may be required in order to utilize the full performance capability of the aircraft (speed increments under expected wind shear threat are stated

in Operations Manual OM-B)

The term downburst describes a severe downward rush of air and its outburst of

damaging winds near the ground. It has been classified into macroburst and microburst. They are different in their size with radial outflow at the earth’s surface lasting from 3 to 20 minutes.

Downbursts can occur wherever convective weather conditions exist.
Approximately 5% of all thunderstorms produce microburst.

Downdrafts associated with microburst are typically only a few hundred to thousand meters across. When the downburst hits the ground, it spreads out horizontally and may form one or more horizontal vortex rings around the downdraft up to 2 000 ft AGL.
In downbursts with vortices very powerful updrafts and roll forces in conjunction with wind speed changes up to 45 knots can be expected.
The time period over which wind speeds exceed half the peak value may last from 1 to 8 minutes. Depending on the movement and the height of the base of parent cloud, microburst may occur as: stationary or moving

surface or midair

wet or dry

Microburst has occurred in relatively dry conditions of light rain or precipitation that evaporates before reaching the earth’s surface.
Frontal wind shear is present in both cold and warm fronts, but exists in a different relative location in each type of front. Because the cold front boundary slopes back behind the frontal surface, the wind shear line also slopes back. The frontal boundary of the warm front slopes upward ahead of the surface front and

so does the wind shear. Significant wind shears can be expected if there is a large difference in surface temperature 6°C) across the front and if the front is moving rapidly at more than 30 knots.
Large wind speeds changes near the ground can be found in many

meteorological situations, including the frontal conditions. Terrain irregularities or

buildings, which interrupt the wind flow, can produce significant wind shears close to the ground.

antworten_en: Approximately 5 %
Approximately 1 %
Approximately 25 %
Approximately 50 %
fragen.erklaerung_en: Around 5 % of all thunderstorms produce a microburst.

kontext:
8.3.8.2 Thunderstorms

Thunderstorms are classified as:

frontal thunderstorms

air mass thunderstorms

Frontal thunderstorms may exist as:

warm front thunderstorms

cold front thunderstorms

occluded front thunderstorms

Air mass thunderstorms are divided into:

convective thunderstorms

orographic thunderstorms

Frontal thunderstorms form in squall lines and generate heavy rain and possibly hail and produce strong gusty winds and possibly tornadoes.
Large horizontal wind changes in speed and direction at different altitudes are characteristic for a frontal thunderstorm. Resulting airflows in the storm accelerate to much higher vertical speeds, which ultimately results in higher horizontal wind speeds at the surface.
Air mass thunderstorms are caused either by thermal convection or by moist air moving uphill on the windward side of a mountain.
Air mass thunderstorms appear to be randomly distributed in unstable air and develop from local heating of the earth’s surface. As the heated air rises it cools and subsequently forms cumulus clouds. As the cumulus stage continues to develop, precipitation forms in the higher portion of the cloud and falls out.
Precipitation signals the beginning of the mature stage and pressure of a downdraft.
In the later stages of development, the heated updraft creating the thunderstorm is cut off by rainfall, and the thunderstorm begins to dissipate. Many thunderstorms produce an associated cold air gust front as a result of the down flow and out rushing rain-cooled air. These gust fronts are usually very turbulent and are a serious threat during take-off and landing.
The vertical extension of thunderstorms is up to 25 000 ft during winter time and up to the troposphere during summer, the horizontal range is 10 to 20 km.

Besides the dangerous situations already mentioned, there may be additional dangers from sudden heavy precipitation with poor visibility below the clouds, possibly hail showers, heavy icing formation, and severe turbulence.

Lightning is not a direct danger for the crew and passengers of an aircraft in flight, as the electrical load will remain at the surface of the aircraft (Faraday Cage). Lightning strikes may, however, disturb or damage the navigation system.

If storm clouds have to be over flown, vertical separation from cloud tops of at least 5 000 ft must always be maintained. It is difficult to estimate this separation, but Air Traffic Control (ATC) or meteorological charts may provide information about the altitude of the cloud.
If the aircraft is not equipped with radar or if the radar is inoperative, any cloud that appears, through visual inspection: tall,

or growing rapidly, or with an anvil top

shall be laterally avoided by at least 10 NM.

The radar equipment shall be intermittently operated on long ranges in order to

avoid the development of situations where no alternative remains but the penetration of hazardous areas.

Flying under a cumulonimbus overhang shall be avoided, too. If it is unavoidable, antenna tilt shall occasionally be selected to full up to determine, if possible, whether precipitation (which may be hail) exists in or is falling from the overhang.
Flight crews are strongly advised to continue monitoring the weather radar in order to select the safest track for penetration under all circumstances.
The local activity of thunderstorms can often be of relatively short nature, (i.e. 20 to 30 minutes). Therefore, if a take-off or landing is planned during times of thunderstorm activity, consideration of the development of the storm shall determine whether avoidance of the worst effects can be accomplished with a delay.
Rule of thumb to estimate buildup of thunderstorms (ts):
Calculate difference in temperature between FL180 (500 hPa) and FL50 (850 hPa).
If difference is: 25° or less: no ts or very unlikely

26° - 27°: ts possible

28° - 31°: ts likely

32° or more: severe ts likely

kontext:
8.3.8.3.1 Types of Ice

The usual cloud sized small droplets tend to follow the aerodynamic flow around the wing. They are swept away, while larger, heavier droplets tend to impinge aft of the leading edge. The larger (and hence heavier) the droplet (drizzle or rain sized), the further aft it will impinge. Furthermore, large droplets are relatively warm and as a result they tend to run back and spread out in liquid state before freezing. This effect is known as flow back. Its effect depends directly upon size, temperature and velocity of water droplets and wing surface temperature.
Impingement and flow back result in ice collecting not only on the leading edge, but also on the upper and lower surfaces of a wing, where there may be no ice protection.
Rime Ice Rime ice is associated with stratiform clouds and forms when droplets are small and the temperature is relatively cold (-15°C or below). Not all of the droplets follow the airflow. Some impact upon the wing and tail plane leading edges with little or no flow back, freezing quickly into rime ice. Therefore, leading edge anti-

and deicing equipment is relatively effective against this type of ice.
Clear Ice Clear ice is associated with cumuliform clouds and forms when the temperature

is relatively warm (-10°C or above). Droplet sizes are relatively large (drizzle or

rain sized), and they tend to impinge further aft and flow back before freezing to

form sheet ice on the upper and lower surfaces of the wing. These areas may not be protected by anti- and deicing equipment. Any deposit greater than light can

significantly degrade performance, causing problems in roll and pitch control

with, in the extreme case, uncontrollable pitch up and stall.
Clear ice can form on airfoil surfaces with few visual cues to the flight crew. The

absence of the usual indications, such as ice formation on the windshield posts

and wipers, does not mean that clear ice is not forming. The terms freezing drizzle or freezing rain in a terminal forecast or weather report indicate a strong

probability of conditions for clear ice.
Mixed Ice

Mixed ice is a combination of clear and rime ice with all the hazards of both. It forms when droplets vary in size (e.g. drizzle in stratiform clouds) and the

temperature is in the range of -10°C to -15°C.

The proportional makeup varies

with the weather system.

kontext:
8.3.8.4 Turbulence

Turbulence is defined as a disturbed, irregular flow of air with embedded irregular whirls or eddies and waves. An aircraft in turbulent flow is subjected to irregular and random motions while, more or less, maintaining its intended flight path.
The intensity specifications for turbulence reporting have been defined as follows: light: slight discomfort
moderate: moderate changes in aircraft attitude or altitude accompanied by small variations in airspeed; walking is difficult, loose objects move around

severe: abrupt changes in aircraft attitude or altitude; the aircraft may be out of control for short periods accompanied by large variations in airspeed; occupants are forced violently against seatbelts; loose objects are tossed around Turbulence may be one of the following types: convective turbulence

orographic turbulence

Clear Air Turbulence (CAT)

wake turbulence

Convective turbulence is caused by thermal instability and is met in connection with the development and activity of thunderstorms. It can cause extreme air motion with vertical speeds up to 6 000 ft/min. Mostly it is encountered with severe turbulence in connection with thunderstorm activity.

Mountain waves at the lee side of a mountain may cause severe turbulence,

called orographic turbulence. Typical signs are lenticular, rotor clouds and clouds

with waterfall appearance. The strongest turbulence may be found in rotor

clouds.

Clear Air Turbulence (CAT) is of special significance, since its presence cannot be detected before it is encountered. It is caused by large wind shears with rapid

changes of wind direction horizontally or vertically.

Abrupt changes of the wind direction in a sharp trough line may cause considerable turbulence and a change of flight level will normally alleviate the

problem. Clear Air Turbulence (CAT) may also be expected on the upper side of a sloping tropopause.

Further large horizontal and vertical shears of wind speed in the transition zone between cold and warm air masses as well as at the tropopause associated with

jet streams may cause severe Clear Air Turbulence (CAT). These areas of

turbulence are normally shallow, narrow and extended patches, which move with the wind.

Abrupt changes in attitude and altitude; aircraft momentarily out of control
Only slight passenger discomfort
fragen.erklaerung_en: Moderate turbulence: moderate changes in attitude or altitude with small airspeed variations, walking is difficult, loose objects move.

Cabin doors (passenger and service doors) shall be operated by crew members only.

the aircraft parking brakes have been set, or the chocks are in position

8.2.1.5 Fuelling with Passengers on Board

During normal operations it may be necessary to fuel or de-fuel an aircraft with passengers on board. Passengers may embark, disembark or remain on board during fuelling and de-fuelling operation provided that the following precautions are observed: local procedures must be verified and adhered to

a member of the flight crew must remain on the flight deck

a two way communication between the flight crew member in the cockpit and a cabin crew member in the cabin must be established

a two way communication between ground crew supervising the refuelling and the qualified personnel on board the airplane is assured (via intercommunication system, direct person-to-person contact or any other method of communication)

fuelling personnel shall be informed that passengers will be on board during fuelling and immediate communication to a flight crew member being on the flight deck shall be established either via inter-communication system or direct person-to-person contact

all cabin crew members shall be informed by the Commander (CMD).
For callouts refer to 8.3 App. 1 - Communication Wording CSPM 2 Appendix 1 Communication Wording

all cabin crew members shall be able to communicate among cabin crew members and passengers (e.g. via PA, hand signals (body language) or megaphone)

cont.

the fuelling may start only after positive confirmation of the Senior cabin crew member (SEN) towards the Commander CMD has taken place verifying that the following precautionary measures are taken (for callouts refer to 8.3 App. 1 - Communication Wording CSPM 2 Appendix 1 Communication Wording): the fasten seat belt signs must be off, the no smoking signs must be on, together with interior lighting to enable emergency exits to be identified

passengers are to be briefed not to smoke at any time on the ground and to remain seated until the fuelling has been completed, refer to OM- 0 4 CCM

in principle, for all aircraft types, at least a minimum of two passenger cabin doors shall be opened and passenger stairs jetways must be positioned at these doors

if only one passenger stair jetway is available, the requirement for the second passenger cabin door may be met by positioning a cabin crew member, who will remain at a second door throughout the refuelling process. The door should not be automatic armed, unless required in an emergency

in the cabin, a cabin crew member shall be positioned next to the boarding door and be prepared for an immediate emergency evacuation, the rest of the cabin crew members shall be positioned in the vicinity of their assigned doors/exits (refer to CSPM 5 Standard

Operation Position/Area “Fuelling with Passengers on Board”) on all exits the outside-area shall remain clear during fuelling operations

routes to the emergency exits shall be unobstructed

if the presence of fuel vapour is detected inside the aircraft, or any other

hazard arises fuelling or de-fuelling shall be stopped immediately

if deemed necessary by the crew, a de-boarding shall be performed via the stairs or an evacuation via the escape slides, if deemed necessary limited to

the non-spilled side

fuelling and de-fuelling with wide cut fuel (e.g. Jet B or equivalent) is prohibited with passengers on board

after completion of fuelling the Commander (CMD) will notify the Senior

cabin attendant (SEN) which means that normal duties may be resumed.
For callouts refer to 8.3 App. 1 - Communication Wording

Commander (CMD) is responsible for evaluating the situation on the particular airport at the given time, and determining a person responsible for the fueling operation and communication to the flight crew during fueling with passengers on board. one of the flight crew members

Der CMD übernimmt grundsätzlich die Aufgaben beider Rollen
fragen.erklaerung: Um Missverständnisse zu minimieren, führen PF und PM keine Aufgaben der anderen Rolle aus, ausser der andere bittet darum.
fragen.zitat: to minimise misunderstandings, both PF and PM refrain from performing duties of the other role unless asked to do so by their peer
kontext:
8.3.0.8 Fleet Configuration

Modern airplanes used in airline operations usually carry standardised equipment and vary amongst each other only rarely within the same fleet.
Should a specific airplane within the fleet carry different equipment which could result in operational issues, training according to OM-D 2.1.2 Differences and Familiarisation Training shall be performed by each crew member before operating this specific tail number.

8.3.0.9 8.3.0.9 MCC Principles

This chapter intends to create a mental link between higher level policies and lower level SOPs, aiming to distinguish between CRM- and MCC-principles. „Playground“ we are aware that Knowledge, Skills and Attitudes (KSA) are to be seen as fundamentals

helvetic management creates a working environment enabling flight crews intrinsically motivating themselves

we are willing to accept that striving for self-discipline and a high level of performance is fundamental

we accept that safety is paramount and not negotiable, remaining aware at the same time that safety must be embedded in a commercially effective and efficient environment

we are willing to accept that operational daily life often offers „grey zones“ requiring all parties involved to apply a holistic problem-solving process potentially leading to various suitable solutions

we take full responsibility for decisions taken when faced with situations where no procedures or guidance exists

we do not “hide” behind regulations or superiors

„Operational conclusions“ we are aware that defined requirements and SOPs shall contribute to

reduce tiring discussions about minor, non-safety relevant items

we are aware of a general increase in complexity and counteract associated

risks by remaining vigilant about the „big picture“ while reducing workload and distraction by refraining from non safety-relevant micro-management

we refrain from exaggerated individual interpretations and implementation at

purely theoretical levels without enhancing safety at a practical level

when rating risks we aim to base our judgement at a realistic level based on

the current environment meaning that we refrain from drawing conclusions based on exaggerated assumptions

we are aware of the difference between „experience” and „expertise“, remaining mentally open for technological and procedural developments

based on „what“ rather than „who“ is right

we refrain from inventing or applying derived SOPs based on oral transmission by whoever, we challenge peers distributing rumours to apply SOPs as published while aiming to capture the “spirit behind”

„Operational behaviour“ we respect the roles and associated duties as PF and PM

we actively adhere to our own and accept the peer’s role as PF and PM

we are aware that the PF‘s workload is normally higher than the PM‘s purely based on his role, meaning the PM should refrain from inputs a split second before the PF is expected to act
to minimise misunderstandings, both PF and PM refrain from performing duties of the other role unless asked to do so by their peer

the PM accepts decisions and proceedings taken by the PF as long as he remains within the defined framework

both flight crew members shall refrain from forcing peers to adjust non safety-relevant minor items to their individual preferences going beyond SOPs

we welcome sharing of experience by contributing individual thoughts as long as they are clearly declared as such and not communicated as „best industry practice“ in any form of operational recommendations or orders

we communicate in a positive-minded, straightforward and direct manner by using clear and unhidden statements, irrespective of each role or function
fragen.frage_en: What applies under the MCC Principles regarding performing tasks of the other role (PF/PM)?
antworten_en: Both refrain from doing so unless asked by the other pilot
The PF performs all PM tasks themselves below FL 100
The PM may take over PF tasks at any time if more efficient
The CMD generally takes over the tasks of both roles
fragen.erklaerung_en: To minimize misunderstandings, PF and PM do not perform tasks of the other role unless the other asks.

fragen.frage: Seat Blocking zur Trimmkorrektur auf der E1-Flotte: Wie viele aufeinanderfolgende Sitzreihen dürfen maximal blockiert werden?
antworten: Drei Reihen, auch einzelne Sitze möglich
Vier Reihen, nur ganze Reihen im hinteren Kabinenteil
Sechs Reihen, nur im vorderen Kabinenteil
Zwei Reihen, beliebig in der Kabine
fragen.erklaerung: Es dürfen nur ganze Reihen, maximal vier aufeinanderfolgende und nur im hinteren Teil der Kabine blockiert werden.
fragen.zitat: only entire rows must be blocked (e.g. 28A/C/D/F) a maximum of four consecutive rows may be blocked blocking is only permitted in the rear section of the aircraft
kontext:
8.2.2.2.1 Seat Blocking – E190 E195 Fleet

To address trim issues on the E1 fleet, blocking of last seat rows is introduced in accordance with the following guidelines. This procedure is applicable for flights under the Swiss International Air Lines (LX) flight number.

8.2.2.2.1.1 Communication

The number and location of seat rows to be blocked will be communicated to the crew through:

1. Passenger Information List (PIL)

2. ACARS Message to Flight Deck (sent automatically)

3. final loadsheet

8.2.2.2.1.2 Blocking Guidelines

only entire rows must be blocked (e.g. 28A/C/D/F)

a maximum of four consecutive rows may be blocked

blocking is only permitted in the rear section of the aircraft

8.2.2.2.1.3 Equipment for Seat Blocking

each aircraft is equipped with 9 seat block belts labeled: “Section closed – please do not occupy these seat rows.”

belts are stored in the last overhead bin on the left-hand side of the cabin in a red bag labeled with “helvetic”)

(last overhead bin on the left-hand side of the cabin including red bag labeled with “helvetic”)

8.2.2.2.1.4 Installation Process

Time required: Approximately 2 minutes Steps for installation:

1. retrieve the required number of belts from the designated overhead bin

2. attach the belts securely across the designated rows to block access

3. verify that all blocked rows comply with the communicated instructions

(blocked seat row)

8.2.2.2.1.5 Process in case of missing Blocking Belts

conduct normal boarding process

after boarding is completed, CAB 2L ensures that no blocked seat rows are occupied by passengers

perform an ACL entry if less than 9 blocked seat belts available
fragen.frage_en: Seat blocking for trim correction on the E1 fleet: What is the maximum number of consecutive seat rows that may be blocked?
antworten_en: Three rows, individual seats also possible
Four rows, whole rows only in the rear cabin section
Six rows, front cabin section only
Two rows, anywhere in the cabin
fragen.erklaerung_en: Only whole rows may be blocked, a maximum of four consecutive ones and only in the rear part of the cabin.

fragen.frage: Was gilt für fremde Crew Members, die in Uniform an Bord reisen?
antworten: Sie dürfen nicht als ABP eingesetzt werden
Sie sind nur bei einer Evakuierung zu informieren, ein Briefing ist nicht nötig
Sie sind als ABP einzusetzen und bei freien Sitzen an oder nahe den Over-wing Exits zu platzieren
Sie sind im Cockpit Jump Seat zu platzieren
fragen.erklaerung: Fremde Crew Members in Uniform sind als ABP einzusetzen; bei freien Sitzen an den Over-wing Exits sind sie dorthin umzusetzen und zu briefen.
fragen.zitat: Whenever foreign crew members are on board in uniform they shall be used as ABP. If seats at the over-wing exits are empty ABPs should be reseated and be placed at the over-wing exits or close by.
kontext:
8.2.2.3.4 Able Bodied Person (ABP)

Suitable, Able Bodied Persons (ABP) are: crew on dead heading or pleasure travel.
Whenever foreign crew members are on board in uniform they shall be used as ABP. If seats at the over-wing exits are empty ABPs should be reseated and be placed at the over-wing exits or close by.

They shall be briefed about the exits and asked if they would help in case of an emergency.

policemen

firemen

military persons in uniform

medical personnel (doctors, nurses)

others who seem physically and mentally fit to perform the task

Choose, command, reseat, brief suitable passengers for the following duties: to open emergency exits upon your order, if required

to assist children and passengers with reduced mobility, or injured passengers

to assist crew in taking care of an UMNR in case of an emergency (e.g. evacuation) to assist in removing and operating ditching, survival and emergency

equipment

to guard unsafe door and exits or damaged escape slides

to assist passengers sliding down the slides

to assist passengers on the ground

to assist crew in handling of a security threat

(e.g. unruly passengers, hijack situations)

Note: An Able Bodied Person (ABP) should not take his own decision.
He is to follow the specific orders given by the cabin crew members.

A clear and precise briefing is of utmost importance.

Note: Cabin Crew shall be aware that a child under the age of 12 years,

separated from the accompanying adult, who is traveling in another cabin class, shall be considered as an UMNR therefore a ABP is required in case of emergency.

8.2.2.4 Transportation of Inadmissible Passengers, Deportees and Persons in Custody

Refer to: Ground Operations Manual (GOM) 4.1.5 - Special Category Passengers
fragen.frage_en: What applies to foreign crew members travelling on board in uniform?
antworten_en: They must not be used as ABP
They are to be informed only in case of an evacuation; a briefing is not necessary
They are to be used as ABP and, if seats are free, placed at or near the over-wing exits
They are to be placed on the cockpit jump seat
fragen.erklaerung_en: Foreign crew members in uniform are to be used as ABP; if seats are free at the over-wing exits, they are to be moved there and briefed.

fragen.frage: Für welches Gewicht ist das Child Safety Device CARES bei helvetic zugelassen?
antworten: Für Infants bis 10 kg
Für Kinder von 15 bis 30 kg
Für Kinder von 5 bis 15 kg
Für Infants/Kinder von 10 bis 20 kg

fragen.zitat: helvetic allows the use of the child safety device CARES for infants / children of 10 to 20 kg.
kontext: 8.2.2.9.9 Child Safety Device CARES
helvetic allows the use of the child safety device CARES for infants children of 10 to 20 kg.

The following type of child safety device CARES are considered to be acceptable: the device is approved in the USA in accordance with 14 CFR 21.305 (d) and is furnished with the following label: “FAA approved in accordance with 14 CFR 21.305 (d) approved for aircraft use only“

The following installation procedure shall strictly be observed: place the additional belt (part of the CARES equipment) around the backrest of the passenger seat and pull it tight

place the infant/children on the aircraft passenger seat

thread in the standard seat belt (lap belt) of the passenger seat into the lower loops of the shoulder belts

fasten the passenger seat belt (lap belt) and pull it tight (the seat belt (lap belt) must be pulled tight sufficiently in order to secure the infant child properly otherwise the installation of the child safety device CARES is not allowed)

fasten the chest clip

pull the shoulder belts tight

Note: Whenever the fasten seat belt sign is on, at least during take-off and landing, the infant child must be secured either by a Child Safety Device CARES as described above, or in a car type infant seat (refer to Car Type Infant Seat) or by an infant belt (refer to CSPM 3).

The following installation restrictions apply for child safety device CARES: seat must be vacant, otherwise the infant/children must be secured with a loop belt (refer to CSPM 3.13.2 Infant Belt)

the seat belt (lap belt) must be pulled tight sufficiently in order to secure the infant child properly otherwise the installation of the child safety device CARES is not allowed

the installation shall be done on a passenger seat next to the window

in general seating restriction for infants shall be observed (refer to CSPM 2.1.2.6 Seating Restrictions)

Note: the installation of the child harness device must not hinder the other passengers in moving quickly to the nearest exits.
fragen.frage_en: For which weight is the Child Safety Device CARES approved at helvetic?
antworten_en: For infants up to 10 kg
For children from 15 to 30 kg
For children from 5 to 15 kg
For infants/children from 10 to 20 kg
fragen.erklaerung_en: helvetic permits CARES for infants or children from 10 to 20 kg.

Bis 12 Monate
Bis 2 Jahre

fragen.frage: Wie wird die Cabin Crew nach einer ausserplanmässigen Aufforderung, sich zu setzen und anzuschnallen, wieder freigegeben?
antworten: Über eine PA-Durchsage des Commanders
Durch den SEN nach eigenem Ermessen
Über das Cabin Interphone System
Durch Ausschalten der Fasten Seat Belt Signs
fragen.erklaerung: Die Aufforderung erfolgt via PA durch den CMD, die Freigabe wird über das Cabin Interphone System übermittelt.
fragen.zitat: A release from this command will be distributed through the cabin interphone system.
kontext:
8.3.11.2 Cabin Crew Members

During take-off and landing, and whenever deemed necessary by the Commander (CMD) in the interest of safety, each cabin crew member shall be properly secured by all safety belts and harnesses provided.
In case of an unscheduled request to the cabin crew members to take their seats and to secure their seat belts (i.e. except for take-off and landing) the Commander (CMD) will announce through the Public Announcement (PA) system. (refer to 8.3 App. 1 - Communication Wording and CSPM 2 Appendix 1 Communication Wording)
A release from this command will be distributed through the cabin interphone system.
fragen.frage_en: How is the Cabin Crew released again after an unscheduled instruction to sit down and fasten seat belts?
antworten_en: Via a PA announcement by the Commander
By the SEN at their own discretion
Via the Cabin Interphone System
By switching off the Fasten Seat Belt Signs
fragen.erklaerung_en: The instruction is given via PA by the CMD; the release is communicated via the Cabin Interphone System.

fragen.frage: Was ist vor dem Öffnen der Flight Deck Door zu tun, wenn kein Vorhang installiert ist?
antworten: Die Kabinenbeleuchtung ausschalten
Die Fasten Seat Belt Signs einschalten
Die Passagiere der ersten Reihe bitten, sitzen zu bleiben
Mit einem Trolley den Weg zur vorderen Galley blockieren
fragen.erklaerung: Ist kein Vorhang installiert, ist ein Trolley zu verwenden, um den Weg zur vorderen Galley zu blockieren.
fragen.zitat: if a curtain is installed, it shall be closed before the flight deck door is opened to prevent view to the flight deck area. If no curtain is installed, a trolley shall be used to block the way to the forward galley
kontext:
8.3.12.1 Closing and Locking of Flight Deck Door

Three different terms are used in connection with the flight deck door:

1. open

2. closed (but not locked)

3. locked (closed and secured with a lock)

with passengers on board the flight deck door shall be closed and locked from the time all external doors are closed following embarkation until any such door is opened for disembarkation, except when necessary to permit access and egress by authorized persons. A situation in which the doors are closed but not locked during flight is not permitted.

for communication and identification between the flight deck and cabin the interphone shall be used

if a curtain is installed, it shall be closed before the flight deck door is opened to prevent view to the flight deck area. If no curtain is installed, a trolley shall be used to block the way to the forward galley

before opening the flight deck door check that the area behind the flight deck door, the forward entrance area, and the galley area are clear of any passengers or other unauthorised persons by using the cabin surveillance

system or alternative means Possible special requirements by foreign authorities will be communicated via

OM-C 3 Route Competence.

OM-A 8 Operating Procedures
fragen.frage_en: What must be done before opening the Flight Deck Door if no curtain is installed?
antworten_en: Switch off the cabin lighting
Switch on the Fasten Seat Belt Signs
Ask the passengers in the first row to remain seated
Block the way to the forward galley with a trolley
fragen.erklaerung_en: If no curtain is installed, a trolley must be used to block the way to the forward galley.

fragen.frage: Ein Pilot will das Cockpit verlassen, aber die drei Kamerawinkel des CSS sind nicht alle verfügbar. Wie wird identifiziert?
antworten: Über Interphone und Türspion (Peephole) als alternative Identifikationsmittel
Durch Klopfzeichen ohne weitere Prüfung
Gar nicht; das Cockpit darf dann nicht verlassen werden
Durch kurzes Öffnen der Tür zur Sichtkontrolle
fragen.erklaerung: Fehlen die drei CSS-Winkel, gilt das Verfahren Admission to flight deck - CAB entering flight deck mit Interphone und Peephole als alternative Identifikation.
fragen.zitat: Note: In case that all 3 angles of CSS are not available – procedure “Admission to flight deck – CAB entering flight deck” shall be used. Interphone and peephole shall be used as an alternative means of identification.
kontext:
8.3.12.1.1 Leaving the Flight Deck

Pilot states the intention to leave the flight deck transfers the controls/ATC to the second pilot Both pilots check 3 angles of the CSS Situation is OK, no person in Pax are in lavatory/galley area or galley/lavatory area curtain is situation unclear and/or curtain not closed closed Pilot leaves the flight deck, closes the Call SEN via interphone to clarify the doors and blocks the FD doors with situation (e.g. close the curtain/place his body until the doors are closed the trolley/check the lavatory) Pilot remaining on Fflight deck: Follow procedure: Admission to FD - lock the door CAB entering FD

Note: In case that all 3 angles of CSS are not available – procedure “Admission to flight deck – CAB entering flight deck” shall be used.
Interphone and peephole shall be used as an alternative means of identification.
fragen.frage_en: A pilot wants to leave the cockpit, but not all three CSS camera angles are available. How is identification done?
antworten_en: Via interphone and peephole as alternative means of identification
By knocking signal without further checks
Not at all; the cockpit must then not be left
By briefly opening the door for visual check
fragen.erklaerung_en: If the three CSS angles are missing, the procedure Admission to flight deck - CAB entering flight deck applies, with interphone and peephole as alternative identification.

fragen.frage: Was ist für eine Person, die einen freien Crew Seat benutzt, in jedem Fall erforderlich?
antworten: Eine Bewilligung des FOCA
Ein gültiges Passagierticket für den betreffenden Flug
Eine abgeschlossene Cabin-Crew-Ausbildung
Ein Cockpit Permit des Accountable Managers
fragen.erklaerung: Für die Benutzung eines freien Crew Seats ist in jedem Fall ein gültiges Passagierticket erforderlich.
fragen.zitat: In any case a valid passenger ticket is required for that flight.
kontext:
8.3.13 Use of Vacant Crew Seats

The final decision as to the disposition of other vacant crew seats, rests with the Commander (CMD).
The person using a vacant Crew Seat: is an employee or member of the Board of Directors of helvetic

is listed on an updated name register in OM-0 Chapter 9, or is a representative of the Swiss FOCA with an appropriate identification and is required for the performance of his official duties, or the passenger is personally known to a crew member, or is staff of another airline, or a company related to airline industry
In any case a valid passenger ticket is required for that flight.

The Senior Cabin Attendant (SEN) shall brief a person who has been granted permission to occupy a vacant cabin crew seat on all safety relevant aspects connected with that seat and, if it is at an emergency exit, on how to operate the door in an emergency (stressing, however, that the door shall be opened only after the appropriate command has been given).
Vacant crew seats located at emergency exits must not be occupied by persons lacking of sufficient strength or dexterity to operate the emergency exit, to exit

expeditiously and to assist others in getting off an escape slide.
fragen.frage_en: What is required in every case for a person using a free Crew Seat?
antworten_en: A permit from the FOCA
A valid passenger ticket for the flight concerned
Completed Cabin Crew training
A Cockpit Permit from the Accountable Manager
fragen.erklaerung_en: A valid passenger ticket is required in every case for using a free Crew Seat.

fragen.frage: Unter welcher Bedingung kann einem Passagier mit Zürcher Flughafenausweis (AIC) ein Cockpit Permit erteilt werden?
antworten: Nur wenn der Ausweis alle Flughafenzonen enthält
Nur bei einem roten Ausweis
Wenn der Ausweis mindestens eine ZRH-Flughafenzone enthält, unabhängig von der Ausweisfarbe
Nie; Flughafenausweise berechtigen nicht zu einem Cockpit Permit
fragen.erklaerung: Ein Cockpit Permit ist möglich, wenn der AIC mindestens eine ZRH-Zone (fette Grossbuchstaben) enthält, unabhängig von der Farbe des Ausweises.
fragen.zitat: the passenger holds an airport ID from Zurich Airport (AIC) containing at least one of the ZRH airport zones (i.e. bold capital letters), irrespective of the colour of the airport identification cards
kontext:
8.3.12 Admission to Flight Deck

No person, other than flight crew members assigned to a flight, shall be admitted to, or carried on, the flight deck unless the Commander (CMD) himself or his designated deputy is present on the flight deck, and unless this person: is a member of the operating crew or is an auditor listed on the flight assignment (e.g IOSA, CARA) or is a representative of the Swiss FOCA with an appropriate identification and is required for the performance of his official duties

Alternatively other persons may be accepted if the following conditions are fulfilled: admission to flight deck (Cockpit permit) is granted by the Commander (CMD)

a valid passenger or observer ticket has been issued for the flight or a series of flights for flight deck observers not employed by helvetic, the process for the issuance of tickets is described in OM-0 9

A cockpit permit may be granted provided:

the passenger is personally known to a crew member or is staff of an airline within the Lufthansa group (identification through crew member-certificate or company ID)

or

the passenger holds an airport ID from Zurich Airport (AIC) containing at

least one of the ZRH airport zones (i.e. bold capital letters), irrespective of

the colour of the airport identification cards

or

the passenger has successfully completed the process described in OM-0 9 Observer Flights for non-2L Observers

Note: Any passenger occupying the Cockpit Jump-Seat shall be at least 12 Years of age

The Commander (CMD) is responsible that a person who has been granted a permission to enter the flight deck: has received a briefing on all safety relevant aspects including the sterile flight deck policy and escape path to be used in case of emergency prior to departure and as necessary for the reminder of the flight

does not cause distraction or interference with the operation of the flight

refrains from use of any audio or video recording devices (e.g. tape recorder, cameras of any kind, mobile phone). Exceptions in written form may be granted by the Accountable Manager (ACM) or Nominated Person Flight Operations (FOP)

Note: Special regulations may apply for certain countries (e.g. UK, Israel).
Refer to OM-C Route Competence for further information.

No cockpit permit is required for: persons according to the List of helvetic Employees in the OM-0 9

In all cases, the final acceptance of the person admitted to flight deck remains with the Commander (CMD).

As stated in OCM 3.18, Operations Control (OCC) is in charge to coordinate the

exchange of information between all relevant parties.
The granted admission to the flight deck shall be noted in the Flight Briefing Documentation Tool or on the relevant flight assignment.

Refer to 8.1.13 - Flight Assignment Folder.
fragen.frage_en: Under which condition can a Cockpit Permit be issued to a passenger with a Zurich airport pass (AIC)?
antworten_en: Only if the pass contains all airport zones
Only with a red pass
If the pass contains at least one ZRH airport zone, regardless of pass colour
