8.3.2.4.1 FMS Navigation (as primary means)

Modification of Navigation Database the flight crew shall neither insert nor modify waypoints by manual entry into a procedure (departure, arrival or approach) that has been retrieved from the database

user-defined data may be entered and used for waypoint altitude or speed constraints on a procedure where not included in the navigation database coding

Departure Safe terrain clearance during take-off and climb is also dependent on navigation accuracy. If the departure procedures are stored in the navigation database of the Flight Management Systems (FMS): the onboard navigation system must be in the update mode

the system computed positions shall be checked against displayed navigation aids (e.g. cross-checks with VOR/DME on RMI) whenever the Actual Navigation Performance (ANP) is less than the Required Navigation Performance (RNP)

If these conditions cannot be met, take-off and climb must be performed according to conventional radio navigation.

Approach

If the arrival procedures for descent and approach are stored in the navigation

database of the Flight Management Systems (FMS):

the onboard navigation system must be in the update mode.

Its use is restricted down to the Minimum Safe Sector Altitude (MSA) or

intermediate approach altitude if being radar vectored, unless the system is certified for use in the approach according to the Operations Manual OM-B.

the system computed positions must be checked against displayed

navigation aids (e.g. cross-checks with VOR/DME on RMI) for accuracy whenever the Actual Navigation Performance (ANP) is less

fragen.frage: Welche Abdeckung bietet der ILS Glide Path normalerweise?

kontext:
8.3.2.5 Navigation Aids

Navigation aids shall be selected for coverage (i.e. signal strength) and geometry. They must allow for adequate cross checking. Distance information for cross checks shall be used only if a DME is co-located with a VOR that coincides with a waypoint. DME co-located to ILS or approach localizers normally indicate zero DME at touch down and, therefore, unless otherwise specified, are not suitable for navigational purposes other than the final approach. If, however, used for the approach, the DME reading must be confirmed with the approach charts.
En-route facilities may be expected to provide reliable information along the published routes. VHF facilities (i.e. VOR) require a line of sight position of the receiver. NDB reception is available over distances beyond the horizon, but may be affected by atmospheric electromagnetic activity, shore lines and others.
Locators in terminal areas normally provide reliable guidance within 25 NM distance only.
The ILS localizer beam width is normally 3° to either side of the centerline while the range available for guidance is 25 NM. Within 30° to either side of this sector, coverage is provided normally to the extent that a full scale deflection to the correct side is available.
The ILS glide path azimuth coverage sector width is normally 8° to either side of the centerline. The range extends normally to at least 10 NM.

The elevation available for guidance ranges normally from at least 2° above to 1,5° below the nominal glide path, below which full scale fly-up deflection is available.

Aberrations affecting reception, ranging from multi path interference to fluctuations due to reflections from taxiing aircraft and antennas may still occur within the ILS coverage sector. Under Low Visibility Procedures (LVP) these disturbances are addressed and minimized through ATC and airport procedures.

If not otherwise specified for certain procedures, manually tuned navigation aids

must be positively identified at the time of selection.

Whenever elements of information relative to the position of the aircraft seem to

be contradictory, the reliability of all relevant navigation aids should be verified by additional independent means.

Navigation and approach aids must not be used whenever:

positive identification is not possible, or

reports or other information (e.g. NOTAM) indicate that a system might be unreliable or inadequate for en-route navigation or approach

Published minima apply only with the unrestricted availability of approach aids.
fragen.frage_en: What coverage does the ILS Glide Path normally provide?
antworten_en: 3° either side of the centerline and 25 NM
8° either side of the centerline and a range of at least 10 NM
10° either side of the centerline and 8 NM
35° either side of the centerline and 18 NM
fragen.erklaerung_en: The ILS Glide Path normally covers 8° either side of the centerline, with a range of at least 10 NM.

kontext:
8.3.2.4.2 Conventional Navigation non-RNAV Navigation

Different options of loaded aerodrome FMS-databases exist: full data": Aerodrome Reference Point (ARP), runways, STAR's, approaches, SID's.

"reduced data": Aerodrome Reference Point (ARP), sometimes runways and approaches

"no data": no data at all

If the flight crew does not receive any information in advance the full data of the destination is stored in the FMS. Otherwise the flight crew will previously be informed about the loaded Aerodrome FMS-database status: "reduced" or "no" FMS-data. If so the SID clearance shall be requested early and pre-coordination to obtain the most suitable conventional SID shall be done. The assigned SID shall either be programed by given lead radials and distances from navigation- aids or coordinates. For arrival the expected STAR, approach and missed approach shall be preprogrammed either by given lead radials and distances from navigation-aids or coordinates.
The position must be checked continuously against displayed navigation aids (e.g. cross-checks with VOR/DME on RMI).
The communication towards ATC shall be in an open and pro-active manner.

RNAV-operations are allowed with hard-coded waypoints and therefore with "full

data" only.

ILS facilities of all categories are known to produce false beams outside their coverage sectors due to radiation aberrations. These side beams may be captured by the airborne systems without producing a warning flag. In order to

ensure proper localizer beam capture, the ILS mode shall not be armed until the

vicinity of the beam has been ascertained and crosschecked against

independent navigation aids. The capture process shall be monitored by the

same means.

A DME distance check at glide slope intercept shall be performed whenever possible. An altitude check must be performed at the FAF/FAP.

kontext:
8.3.2.8.1 Policy

Flight Crews are expected to maintain route center lines, as depicted by on- board lateral deviation indicators or flight guidance, during all RNP operations unless authorized to deviate by ATC or under emergency conditions.
For normal operations, cross-track error or deviation (the difference between the RNAV or RNP system computed path and the aircraft position relative to the path) shall be limited to ±1/2 the navigation accuracy associated with the route (i.e. for RNP 5 2.5 NM). Brief deviations from this standard (e.g. overshoots or undershoots) during and immediately after turns, up to a maximum of one times the navigation accuracy (i.e. for RNP 5 5 NM), are allowed.

Note: Some aircraft do not display or compute a path during turns. Pilots of these aircraft may not be able to adhere to the ±1/2 accuracy standard during route turns, but are still expected to satisfy the standard during intercepts following turns and on straight segments.
The numerical figure succeeding the term RNAV or RNP refers to the lateral navigation accuracy (Total System Error (TSE)) in NM, which has to be achieved at least 95% of the flight time

(e.g. RNP 5 refers to a to required accuracy of 5NM). For RNP APCH and A-RNP, the lateral navigation accuracy depends on each segment.

requirement for performance monitoring and alerting, designated by the prefix RNAV (e.g. RNAV 5, RNAV 1, RNAV APCH).

A navigation specification based on area navigation that includes the requirement

for performance monitoring and alerting, designated by the prefix RNP (e.g. RNP

fragen.frage: Unter welcher Bedingung darf am Boden ein ausgelöster Circuit Breaker zurückgesetzt werden?

kontext:
8.3.24 Circuit Breaker Reset

Tripped circuit breakers usually indicate a system malfunction and a reset should be carefully evaluated, as the risk of an electrical fire should never be underestimated. No cabin crew member shall reset a circuit breaker without prior consultation with the Commander (CMD).
In flight, only one reset attempt shall be performed and only according to the appropriate check list

in an emergency situation, if the safety of the flight is definitely improved by doing so

No reset is allowed after a second trip of any circuit breaker.
On ground a reset shall only be performed after maintenance has ascertained the reason for the circuit breaker trip and has established that there is no airworthiness concern.

No flight shall be commenced with a tripped circuit breaker which is not secured by a safety ring. (e.g. If a system has been deactivated and deferred according to CAMP, due to a tripped circuit breaker, a circuit breaker ring shall be installed)

Note: Maintenance may pull some circuit breakers as part of there normal procedures. In case of doubt a crosscheck with maintenance shall be performed.

Refer also to:
E1: OM-B 3.1 Circuit Breaker Reset

E2: OM-B 3.1 Circuit Breaker Reset
fragen.frage_en: Under which condition may a tripped circuit breaker be reset on the ground?

At any time, once, by the Flight Crew
After consultation with the SEN
After a waiting time of two minutes
fragen.erklaerung_en: On the ground, a CB may only be reset if Maintenance has determined the reason and established that there are no airworthiness concerns.

kontext:
8.3.26 The Misuse of Laser

Misuse of lasers is becoming more and more of a problem in aviation. Pilots can be severely blinded by such laser attacks. As a result safety of the operation can be jeopardized.
Following some hints how to deal with a laser attack: look away from the laser beam if possible. Do not try to find the light source by staring at the laser. If possible, note location of laser source

shield eyes and consider feasibility of lowering/raising ‘sun blinds’ to reduce the effect of the laser

avoid rubbing the eyes to reduce the potential risk for corneal abrasion

consider feasibility of turning up the cockpit lights to minimize any further illumination effects

consider, as Pilot Flying (PF), handing over the flight controls to the Pilot Monitoring (PM), as far as he has not been blinded by the light

consider engaging autopilot if flying manually

consider the option of a go around

report all illuminations to Air Traffic Control (ATC) and provide coordinates, if

available

file a report via the IT Rep Sys
fragen.frage_en: Which action does the OM-A recommend in the event of a laser attack?
antworten_en: Rub the eyes to restore vision quickly
Turn up the cockpit lighting to minimize further dazzle effects
Switch off the autopilot immediately and fly manually
Look into the laser beam to locate the source precisely
fragen.erklaerung_en: The OM-A recommends, among other things, not rubbing the eyes and increasing the cockpit lighting to minimize further dazzle effects.

kontext:
8.3.22.2 Definition of Decompression

A decompression is the convergence of the cabin pressure to the air pressure outside of the aircraft at flying altitude. The time needed for this convergence depends on the size of the hole, the size of the cabin and the difference of the air pressure inside and outside the cabin.
The following definitions of decompression relate to the time required for the cabin pressure to decrease to ambient pressure: type time of convergence consequence
slow one minute or more incident rapid one second to one minute accident
explosive less than one second accident
fragen.frage_en: How is a Slow Decompression defined and classified per OM-A?

Pressure equalization in one second to one minute; consequence: Incident

8.3.22.4 Post Decompression Duties

After the level off at a safe altitude the Commander (CMD) will order the Senior Cabin Attendant (SEN) to report to the Commander (CMD), according to 8.3 Appendix 1, Post Decompression. The information to the cabin crew is then relayed via the Senior Cabin Attendant (SEN).
At the same time this indicates that movement through the cabin is safe and the cabin crew can start their post decompression duties attend crew members and passengers needing additional oxygen

implement first aid measures

Inform the Commander (CMD) via the Senior Cabin Attendant (SEN) about the well being of crew and passengers and possible damage to the aircraft (i.e. noise, cracks, vibrations)

stow and secure drop out mask near emergency exits (i.e. pull cut the dropout masks away in these specific rows)

stow away used oxygen bottles before landing

Depending on the situation further emergency procedures may be called upon by the Commander (CMD) (e.g. an evacuation after landing).
Refer to 8.3.21.3 - Crowd Control CSPM 4.2.2 - Crowd Control

fragen.zitat: If no action from the flight deck occurs (e.g. airplane movement, public announcement) the cabin crew shall notify the flight crew by an emergency call about the deployment of the oxygen masks
kontext:
8.3.22.3.2 Rapid or Explosive Decompression

Since the difference between a rapid and an explosive decompression is not obvious to a cabin crew member on duty, the applicable procedures are the same. The oxygen mask will automatically drop from the compartments above the passenger seats, galleys and lavatories.
The flight crew will put on their oxygen masks and establish communication.
Information to the cabin crew follows as soon as practical and will take place only via the PA announcement system, with the wording according to 8.3 Appendix 1, Rapid Explosive Decompression CSPM 2 Appendix 1 Communication Wording

An emergency descent will be initiated immediately.
If no action from the flight deck occurs (e.g. airplane movement, public announcement) the cabin crew shall notify the flight crew by an emergency call about the deployment of the oxygen masks

and confirm that the flight crew have donned their oxygen masks as well.
As soon as the cabin crew members recognize a rapid or explosive decompression: reach for the nearest mask

secure yourself at the present position (i.e. sit down and fasten the seat belts, if necessary on the lap of a passenger) inform passengers to take their mask, use body language and if possible

shout the orders according to 8.3 Appendix 1, Rapid Explosive Decompression CSPM 2 Appendix 1 Communication Wording Note: Mask must be kept on all the time.

secure trolleys in the cabin, if possible

When released by the flight crew via PA announcement system:

proceed to their emergency stations

Senior Cabin Attendant (SEN) check on the flight crew and be prepared to assist in the case of pilot incapacitation.

wait for further information from the flight deck and Senior Cabin Attendant (SEN).
fragen.frage_en: Rapid Decompression: The masks have dropped, but there is no reaction from the cockpit (aircraft movement, PA). What does the Cabin Crew do?

It independently initiates evacuation preparation
It waits for further information without making contact
It opens the Flight Deck Door with the Emergency Code
fragen.erklaerung_en: If there is no reaction from the cockpit, the Cabin Crew reports the mask deployment by Emergency Call and has it confirmed that the pilots are wearing masks.

kontext:
8.3.22.1 General

Our ambient air is a gaseous mixture of approximately 78% Nitrogen

approximately 21% Oxygen

approximately 1% other gases

The density of the air decreases with the increase of flight altitude. On a certain altitude the density is so low, that the partial Oxygen pressure is too low for survival.
To enable people to travel in comfort at high altitudes, modern passenger aircraft are equipped with a pressurized cabin.
The relative cabin altitude will usually not exceed an equivalent of 2400 m above sea-level.

For people in good health there is no risk at this altitude, while for people with cardiovascular diseases or other health problems some additional oxygen may be required at these altitudes.

first aid oxygen

available.

Requirements and Definitions

kontext:
12.2.6.1 Normal Practices and Procedures after entering RVSM Airspace

Flight crews shall comply to any aircraft operating restrictions, if required for the specific aircraft group: limits on indicated Mach number (basic flight envelope upper Mach boundary), given in the RVSM airworthiness approval Note: all helvetic aircraft with RVSM approval shall be compliant to full RVSM flight envelope

Emphasis shall be placed on promptly setting the sub-scale on all primary and standby altimeters to 1013.2 hPa when passing the transition altitude, and rechecking for proper altimeter setting when reaching the initial cleared flight level.
In level cruise it is essential that the aircraft is flown at the cleared flight level.
This requires that particular care is taken to ensure that ATC clearances are fully understood and followed. The aircraft shall not intentionally depart from a cleared flight level without a positive clearance from ATC, unless the crew is conducting contingency or emergency manoeuvres.
When changing levels, the aircraft shall not be allowed to overshoot or undershoot the cleared flight level by more than 45m (150 ft).
If installed, the level off should be accomplished using the altitude capture feature of the automatic altitude-control system.

An automatic altitude-control system shall be operative and engaged during level cruise, except when circumstances, such as the need to re-trim the aircraft or turbulence, require disengagement. In any event adherence to the assigned cruise level should be done by reference to one of the two primary altimeters.
Following loss of the automatic height keeping function, any consequential

restrictions will need to be observed.

Therefore:

ensure that the altitude-alerting system is operative

cross-check at intervals of approximately one hour the primary altimeters; a minimum of two shall agree within ±200 ft (±60 m); failure to meet this

condition will require that the altimetry system is reported as defective and

notified to ATC; the usual scan of flight deck instruments shall suffice for altimeter cross-checking on most flights

in normal operations, the altimetry system being used to control the aircraft

shall be selected for the input to the altitude reporting transponder, transmitting information to ATC

OM-A 12 Rules of the Air

If the pilot is notified by ATC of an assigned altitude deviation of 300 ft (90 m) or more then the flight crew shall take appropriate action to return to the cleared flight level as quickly as possible.
If the pilot is advised in real time that the aircraft has been identified by a height- monitoring system that the Total Vertical Error (TVE) is greater than ±300 ft (±90m) and or if an Altimetry System Error (ASE) greater than ±245 ft (±75 m) is experienced, the flight crew should follow established regional procedures to protect the safe operation of the aircraft. This assumes that the monitoring system will identify the TVE or ASE within the set limits for accuracy.
Caution should be exercised due to problems of visual perceptions of other aircraft during darkness at 1000 ft separation, and when encountering local phenomena such as northern lights. During flights above the transition altitude an aircraft is flown with the altimeters set to standard reading Flight Levels (FL).

If OAT (warmer) -15 °C at aerodrome: increase height by 4% for every 10 °C below ISA (simplified method) or use the correction table below (accurate method)

kontext: 8.3.3.3 Change of Altimeter Settings

Immediately after any change of the altimeter settings, the set values shall be

cross-checked and both crew members confirm the values to be within tolerance

according to the Operations Manual OM-B. This procedure shall include metric altimeters if installed and when being used (e.g. in CIS States).

If an altimeter indication is not within the specified tolerance the abnormal procedures according to the Operations Manual OM-B shall be applied.

In addition to the tolerances defined in Operations Manual OM-B, the following altimeter tolerances shall be respected:

for RNP APCH operations using Baro-VNAV: two altimeters must not differ more than 100 ft at or before the final approach fix (FAF)

in RVSM airspace: according to 12.2.6.1 - Normal Practices and Procedures after entering RVSM Airspace

For the practical application of the above basic requirements the Minimum En- route Altitude (MEA) is defined as the lowest published altitude between radio fixes that meets obstacle clearance requirements between those fixes and in most areas assures acceptable navigational and radio signal coverage.
The published Minimum En-route Altitude (MEA) provides a terrain clearance of at least 1000 ft over the highest obstacle within the normal airway width (5 NM each side of the airway centerline)
and over high terrain, where the highest reference point is 5001 ft MSL or higher, of 2000 ft.

fragen.frage: OEI en-route: Welche Anforderung an den Net Flight Path kann alternativ zum Drift-down-Verfahren erfüllt werden?

fragen.zitat: must either have a positive gradient at least 1 000 ft above all terrain and obstructions within 5 NM to either side of the intended track
kontext:
8.1.1.5 Inoperative Engines – Performance Requirements

In addition to the minimum flight altitude requirements stated above, aircraft operated according to performance class A must meet the following performance requirements for One Engine Inoperative (OEI) en-route flight path.
In the event of the loss of one engine at the most critical point along the route and in the meteorological conditions expected for the flight, the net flight path must: have a positive gradient at 1 500 ft above the airport of intended landing, and
must either have a positive gradient at least 1 000 ft above all terrain and obstructions within 5 NM to either side of the intended track,

or permit the aircraft to continue the flight from the cruising altitude to an airport at which a landing can be made while clearing vertically, by at least 2 000 ft, all obstacles within 5 NM to either side of the intended track (e.g. drift down procedure). As in the particular event of a drift down procedure the 95% containment of the navigational accuracy cannot be guaranteed at any time, helvetic extends the width margin to 10 NM either side of track.

The above calculations must consider the influence of wind, in reference to: 2.4.7.1 - New Operation Process

8.1.2 Criteria and Responsibilities for the Authorization of the Use of Aerodromes
fragen.frage_en: OEI en-route: Which Net Flight Path requirement can be met as an alternative to the drift-down procedure?

Positive gradient at least 500 ft above all terrain within 2 NM
Positive gradient at least 1000 ft above all terrain within 5 NM either side of track
fragen.erklaerung_en: The Net Flight Path must either have a positive gradient at least 1000 ft above all terrain within 5 NM either side, or allow a drift-down with 2000 ft clearance.

8.3.4.2.1 Altitude Awareness

To stay actively alert flight crews shall: crosscheck that the assigned altitude is above the minimum safe altitude confirm assigned altitudes or flight levels towards ATC and to each other

smooth integration into the local VFR traffic patterns

special attention must be given to an active and systematic look-out when

Traffic Alert and Collision Avoidance System (TCAS) shall be operative

CAT II, CAT II/III operation is not allowed

8.3.1 VFR IFR Policy

Except for non revenue flights described in the Operations Manual 8.7 - Non- Revenue Flights, no helvetic flight shall be operated without the full use of air traffic control or advisory services.

Exemptions from this general policy are permitted only according to 8.0.1.5 - Flight Rules.

“Z”

fragen.frage: Welche Phrase wird verwendet, wenn eine ganze Meldung wiederholt werden soll?

"SAY AGAIN"

"SAY AGAIN ALL AFTER"

kontext:
12.3.1.11 Corrections and Repetitions

When an error has been made in transmission, the word “CORRECTION” shall

be spoken, the last correct group or phrase repeated, and then the correct

version transmitted.

If a correction can best be made by repeating the entire message, the phrase

“CORRECTION, I SAY AGAIN” shall be used before the message is transmitted a second time.

If the receiving station is in doubt as to the correctness of the message received,

a repetition either in full or in part shall be requested.

If repetition of an entire message is required, the words “SAY AGAIN” shall be

spoken.

If repetition of a portion of a message is required, the phrase “SAY AGAIN ALL BEFORE… (first word satisfactorily received)” shall be used or “SAY AGAIN…

(word before missing portion) TO…(word after missing portion)” or “SAY AGAIN ALL AFTER… (last word satisfactorily received)”.

OM-A 12 Rules of the Air

kontext:
12.3.1.7 Time

Aviation communication uses Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) for all operations. The word "local" or the time zone equivalent shall be used to denote local

when local time is given during radio and telephone communications.
The term "Zulu" may be used to denote UTC.

kontext:
12.3.2.3 Clarification and Acceptance of Clearances

Several factors such as use of non-standard wordings, high workload of ATC- controllers or flight crews, ambiguous wordings, formally correct but substantially questionable contents, non-standard routings, call sign confusion, or requests may lead to critical situations. For this reason, at least two flight crew members must monitor and confirm clearances issued by ATC. If any flight crew member is in doubt if a clearance has been understood correctly or if one flight crew member has missed a clearance, confirmation from ATC must be requested, by use of different simple and clear words.
High alertness of crews is required in relation to vertical navigation, especially in mountainous or hilly terrain during radar vectoring.

Example:
ATC: “helvetic 385, descend to 4000 feet,

flight crew: ”To confirm – our position is 20 miles west of minimum radar vectoring altitude is 6000 feet, confirm descent to 4000 feet at present position

usually, ATC will realize the error and revise their instruction

if the flight crew is still in doubt, they shall inform ATC concerning their non- compliance and advise them about their intentions: unable to comply, we descend to 6000 feet until overhead due terrain clearance, helvetic 385.”
fragen.frage_en: In which situation does the OM-A require particularly high attention to clearances regarding vertical navigation?

kontext:
8.3.6.3 Avoidance of Aircraft Collision

The see-and-avoid strategy with a careful look out is a basic element for the avoidance of collisions, regardless of advanced aircraft operations and more sophisticated ground and in-flight devices. Thus, whenever weather conditions permit, it is the duty of the flight crew to keep a sharp look out.
The flight crew shall organize the flight deck work in a way that at least one crew member may fulfill this requirement. The ACAS II (TCAS) indication must be used for assistance.
It must, however, be understood that the ACAS II indication is limited to aircraft with an operating transponder. That may exclude the indication of other traffic (e.g. balloons, gliders).

Flight crew members must keep “head down work” to a minimum: in the vicinity of an aerodrome

during descent to an aerodrome

during climb out from an aerodrome

in areas where the traffic is dense

An early engagement of the autopilot is required in order to facilitate the look out.
Irrespective of the type of clearance received from ATC a look out for conflicting traffic in VMC is an absolute necessity.
Traffic information given by ATC is of great value. It must, however, always be

kept in mind that ATC information includes known traffic only and therefore may be incomplete.
In order to protect the eyes from the sun, only the use of sunglasses and sun visors is permitted. The use of objects restricting the look out is prohibited during

flight.

fragen.zitat: It does, however, support the flight crew in situations when the visual recognition of conflicting traffic is impaired (e.g. IMC conditions, night, traffic from dead-angle positions).
kontext:
8.3.6.1 General

The Traffic Collision Avoidance System (TCAS) is a technology which found its way into aviation during the late nineties of the past century. The motivation for its introduction has been the desire for an improvement of flight safety in an increasing traffic density, especially around major hubs. Traffic Collision Avoidance System (TCAS) addresses the problem through recognition and avoidance of potential hazard of in-flight collisions. It does neither replace traffic separation by Air Traffic Control (ATC) nor the sharp look-out of the flight crew whenever visibility permits.
It does, however, support the flight crew in situations when the visual recognition of conflicting traffic is impaired (e.g. IMC conditions, night, traffic from dead-angle positions).

It also assists in decision-making about the necessary correcting actions when a traffic conflict starts to develop.
Flight crews shall therefore use the Traffic Collision Avoidance System (TCAS) at all times. Nevertheless, they should bear in mind that several problems and limitations of the system have been identified during the first years of implementation. Future improvements in hardware and software are to be expected.
Necessary prerequisite to the function of any Traffic Collision Avoidance System (TCAS) equipment is the operation of the transponder in Mode C or Mode S.
In other words: The Traffic Collision Avoidance System (TCAS) can only detect aircraft which transmit a correct transponder code.
It should be noted that Traffic Collision Avoidance System Mark II (TCAS II) is not

capable of accurately resolving the bearing and heading of conflicting traffic.
Traffic Advisory (TA) information for conflicting traffic is limited to vertical avoidance manoeuvres.
fragen.frage_en: In which situations does TCAS particularly support the Crew per OM-A?
antworten_en: When there is a risk of collision with obstacles and terrain
In lateral separation in the radar area
When visual detection is impaired, e.g. IMC, night or traffic in blind spots
Exclusively on the ground during taxi
fragen.erklaerung_en: TCAS assists when visibility of conflicting traffic is impaired (IMC, night, blind spots); it replaces neither ATC separation nor look-out.

kontext:
8.3.2.21.2 TCAS

The rate of climb or descent shall be selected based on operational conditions.
Given the widespread use of collision avoidance systems (ACAS II), the rate of climb or descent must be closely monitored to ensure it does not exceed: 1500 FPM when within 2000 feet of the cleared altitude

1000 FPM in the presence of potentially conflicting traffic when within 1000

feet of the cleared altitude When passing 2000 feet before the cleared altitude or flight level and the rate exceeds 1500 FPM:

the PM shall call out "APPROACHING ALTITUDE FLIGHT LEVEL."

the PF will then take corrective action and respond with "CHECKED."

Note: The directive to make a call at 2000 feet

is based on European Airspace recommendations. These guidelines advise reducing the vertical speed

to a maximum of 1500 feet per minute (FPM) to prevent unnecessary

Traffic Collision Avoidance System (TCAS) alerts caused by high closure rates.

These rate restrictions do not apply during departure when climbing to the initial

cleared altitude or flight level, as defined in the SID or departure clearance.

kontext:
8.3.9 Wake Turbulence

Wake turbulence is generated by air exchange due to the pressure differential between the lower and upper surface of the wing. This exchange causes counter rotating vortices trailing from the outer wing tips. The larger the aircraft the larger are the vortices. The wake of a large aircraft may require large control inputs on an aircraft flying in the area behind it. These control inputs may exceed the roll control capability of the following aircraft. The flight crew must be aware of the location of the vortex flow generated by a preceding aircraft and adjust his flight path accordingly.
Tests with large and heavy aircraft have shown that the vortex flow field – in a plane cutting through the wake at any point downstream – covers an area about twice the wing span in width and one wing span in depth. The vortices from the two tips remain spaced and will drift with the wind. The vortices will sink with a rate of descent of 400 – 500 fpm. There is a tendency that the vortices will level off at about 800 – 1 000 ft below the flight path. Vortex strength diminishes with time and distance behind the aircraft.
Vortex generation will begin on rotation when the nose wheel lifts off the ground and ends, when the nose wheel touches down on landing. In conditions with very weak or calm winds, the remaining vortices from a landing aircraft may persist up to 5 minutes or even longer.
All this has prompted National Aviation Authorities (NAA) and ICAO to establish minimum separation criteria.

OM-A 8 Operating Procedures

ICAO Definitions The International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) classifies aircraft into wake turbulence categories based on their maximum certificated take-off mass (MTOM) and the strength of the wake vortices they generate.
Category MTOM Examples Light (L) 7.000 kg Cessna 172 Medium (M) 7.000 kg - 136.000 kg Embraer E-Jets Heavy (H) (1) 136.000 kg Boeing 747 Super (J) exceptionally strong wake turbulence Airbus A380

Note 1: Some types like the Boeing 757, despite having an MTOM below 136.000 kg, are treated as Heavy due to their strong wake turbulence.
Note: In the United Kingdom the aircraft series Boeing 707, DC-8, VC-10 and IL-62 are considered medium (M) and shall be announced as such in the initial contact with ATC.

However, this regulation does not affect the composition of flight plans which shall be completed in accordance with the ICAO wake turbulence categorisation.

Additional Information Apart from the above ICAO or RECAT standards for vortex separation, the controller or the flight crew may arrange for a larger separation to compensate for calm conditions or for other terrestrial factors, which might enforce or retain the vortex energy for a longer time. The same may apply for operations into parallel or near parallel runways, where in crosswind situations the danger may exist, that vortices are encountered from a preceding aircraft approaching or departing from the parallel runway.
On the other hand separation may be reduced in strong crosswind conditions when operating into or out of single runway environments.
A departing aircraft will not be permitted to commence take-off until the preceding departing aircraft has crossed the end of the runway-in-use or has started a turn or until all preceding landing aircraft are clear of the runway-in-use.
A landing aircraft will not be permitted to cross the beginning of the runway on its final approach until the preceding departing aircraft has crossed the end of the

runway-in-use, or has started a turn, or until all preceding landing aircraft are clear of the runway-in-use.
More information can be found in OM-C Chapter Rules and Regulation.
In case adequate separation cannot be provided or when vortices are

encountered despite adequate separation, the following should be remembered:

during approach and landing behind a vortex generating aircraft, landing

should be aimed at a touch down point at the runway past the touch down

point of the heavier aircraft – if runway length permits

when taking-off, the lift-off point of the preceding aircraft should be remembered; if possible arrangement shall be made for a lift-off point well

before the lift-off point of the preceding aircraft; if this cannot be done,

delaying the take-off for some seconds – depending upon the size of the preceding aircraft and wind conditions on ground may be considered

when approaching behind a vortex generating aircraft, it should be realized,

that flying above the flight path of the preceding aircraft means to avoid the vortex zones – at least until short before touch down.

Mental preparation to abandon the approach using proper Operations Manual OM-B technique including use of maximum thrust setting is important.

kontext:
8.3.9.1.4 Precautionary Measurements and Reactions

The variability in the generator airplane rate of climb or descent makes it quite difficult to estimate exactly where the vortex is. Consequently, during the en- route phase of flight, pilots should expect possible wake encounters when other traffics in proximity appear to be on similar tracks ahead, crossing above your level, climbing or descending ahead through your flight path, while wind direction is likely to move the wake towards your trajectory.
As precautionary measures, operators and pilots should be aware that:
when possible, condensation trails should be used to visualise wakes and estimate if their flight path brings them across

more attention should be given when flying below the tropopause altitude, as the likelihood of wake encounter increases. The tropopause altitude varies (between days, between locations) and can be found on meteorological charts

upwind lateral offset should be used if the risk of a wake encounter is suspected, when allowed by airspace regulations or via specific ATC approval. Also, a change of FL to cross “HEAVY” or “SUPER” traffics from above can be used when feasible and authorised by ATC

In case of a wake encounter, pilots should: be aware that experience has demonstrated that if the pilot reacts at the first

roll motion, when in the core of the vortex, the roll motion could be potentially amplified by this initial piloting action be aware that some in-flight incidents have demonstrated that pilot inputs may exacerbate the unusual attitude condition with rapid roll control

reversals carried out in an “out of phase” manner

be aware that if the autopilot is engaged, intentional disconnection can

complicate the scenario, and the autopilot will, in most cases, facilitate the recovery

try to avoid large rudder deflections that can create important lateral

accelerations, which could then generate very large forces on the vertical

stabiliser that may exceed the structural resistance. Although some recent aircraft types are protected by fly-by-wire systems, typically, the use of the

rudder does not reduce the severity of the encounter nor does it improve the ease of recovery

make use of specific guidance in the OM-B where available

kontext:
8.3.2.23 Holding Pattern, Procedure Turns

For holding procedures and procedure-turns refer to the Operations Manual OM-C. In holding patterns and procedure turns the rate of descent shall not exceed 1500 fpm.
Great attention shall be paid to the compliance with the holding speed limitations.
For local regulations refer to the Operations Manual OM-C.
If unable to comply (i.e. when holding in a clean configuration is not possible at the assigned speeds) and if the limitations are not in force for the purpose of obstacle clearance a higher than standard holding speed may be negotiated with ATC.
For the timing of a holding pattern refer to the Operations Manual OM-C (Route Manual).

When a clearance is received specifying the time of departure from the holding fix, the flight crew shall adjust the pattern within the limits of the established holding procedure in order to leave the fix as near to the time specified as practicable.
Corrections shall be made in both heading and timing to compensate for the effects of wind. A correction shall also be made if the entry speed was excessive due to an unexpected holding clearance.
Turning to the inbound leg of a holding pattern not utilizing the FMS, a 90o – 45o interception shall be flown.
Holdings and procedure turns should be flown with 25° bank.

After an engine failure or inflight engine shutdown during cruise, the driftdown procedure may be required. Pilot should select AT OFF(1) and place thrust lever of operational engine in TO/GA and set thrust rating to “CON”. kontext:
ENGINE FAILURE

For most normal cruise weights and altitudes, the airplane is not able to maintain its cruise altitude following an engine failure. It begins to descend (drift down) and the pilot sets thrust at the remaining engine to maximum continuous. In order to remain as high as possible, the pilot may follow the optimum driftdown profile, which is based on the optimum driftdown speed. This speed reduces the absolute descent gradient, allowing the airplane to level-off at a higher altitude.

For two-engine airplanes, regulations establish that the driftdown calculations should consider the actual airplane gradient (gross gradient) decreased by 1.1% climb gradient to obtain the net gradient.
The airplane calculated path following the net gradient is called the enroute net flight path and is used to ensure enroute obstacle clearance (FAR 25.123 CS 25.123).

During a driftdown, the available thrust increases as the airplane descends. Eventually, at a certain altitude, the available thrust becomes equal to the airplane drag, where the airplane can fly at a constant altitude. This altitude is called the gross level off altitude.

When drawing the net path, the altitude where the net gradient is equal to zero is the net level-off. Both the gross and the net level-offs depend on the airplane configuration, actual weight, and atmospheric conditions.

As the net gradient at the net level-off is zero, the actual climb gradient (gross gradient) is 1.1%.

Regulations (FAR 121.191 AIR OPS CAT.POL.A.215) require that the airplane be able to clear all terrain by a given margin when an engine fails. Two means of compliance for enroute obstacle clearance are allowed:
– The net level-off altitude must clear all enroute obstacles by at least 1000 ft; or
– The net flight path must clear all enroute obstacles between the point where the engine is assumed to fail and an airport where a landing can be made by at least 2000 ft.

REVISION 27 Emergency/Abnormal Operation Page 35/86

kontext:
FLIGHT PLANNING - FUEL TANKERING

Fuel price variations at different airports may require carrying more fuel than the minimum required on a flight leg. The procedure of loading this extra amount of fuel (or surplus fuel) in order to minimize fuel costs is known as Fuel Tankering.

Since the surplus fuel tankered results in additional fuel burnoff (due to the weight increase) it is important to analyze the costs of the extra fuel transportation operation.

The following tables are designed to determine the break-even fuel price on departure airport and it may be used whenever there is difference on fuel price comparing to destination. Tables are provided for LRC and M 0.78 cruise schedule.

Enter the trip distance on the table and read the fuel surplus ratio according to cruise altitude. The break-even fuel price is the price at departure multiplied by the fuel surplus ratio. If break-even fuel price is lower than destination price, it is economically feasible to execute fuel tankering.

The additional maintenance costs involved with increased weight operations (additional brakes and tires wearing) are not considered.
It is important to remind that whenever fuel tankering is considered, the estimated landing weight at destination should be lower than the Maximum Landing Weight.

Example Analyze the possibility to proceed with fuel tankering between two airports distant 600 NM from each other, using LRC speed schedule cruising on FL350. Consider the following fuel prices:

Departure Airport: 1.80 US$/Gal.

Destination Airport: 2.00 US$/Gal.
– Enter the LONG RANGE CRUISE table for 600 NM trip distance and FL350, the FUEL SURPLUS RATIO is 1.05.

REVISION 23 Simplified Flight Planning Page 29/34

– The BREAK-EVEN PRICE is 1.80 (price at departure) multiplied by 1.05 1.89 US$/Gal.
Since fuel price on destination airport (2.00 US$/Gal) is greater than break-even fuel price (1.89 US$/Gal), it is economically feasible the fuel tankering operation between these two airports.

The landing weight must not exceed the Quick Turn Around Weight
The landing weight must be at least 2000 kg below the MZFW
The landing weight may be up to 5 % above the MLW if the break-even price is reached
fragen.erklaerung_en: For any tankering consideration, the estimated landing weight at the destination must be below the Maximum Landing Weight; additional maintenance costs (brakes, tyres) are not taken into account.

kontext:
OBSTACLE OBSTACLE

Prior to departure, execute a detailed route analysis using terrain data inside the obstacle accountability area, which is a corridor along the route. Alternatively, use Minimum Enroute Altitude, (MEA), or Minimum Off Route Altitude (MORA).

Determine if the net level-off is, at least, 1000 ft above the highest obstacle. If not, or if the associated weight penalties are unacceptable, work on a detailed driftdown procedure, based on an engine failure at the most critical point.

The airplane must clear all obstacles during the descent net path by at least 2000 ft.
Determine the minimum cruise altitude and the Point of No Return (PNR) by the intersection of two driftdown paths. The first path is to continue to the next enroute alternate airport (ERA), and the second path is to return to the previous one.

If an engine failure occurs after the PNR, the airplane drifts down on course. If the failure occurs before PNR, the airplane has to turn back.

If take-off is to be rejected, maximum braking is applied at V1, throttles retarded,

At and below V1 the take-off can be rejected and the aircraft will stop within the

This is the minimum control speed on the ground, from which directional control of the airplane can be maintained on the ground after an engine failure without the use of brakes or nose-wheel steering. In other words, it is the minimum speed at which the control surfaces are effective on the ground.

VMCA

4.0.1.5 Climb Segments

First Segment
Is the segment from lift-off up to the point at which the gear is fully retracted. The climb gradient is positive which allows the airplane to reach V2

(35ft for a dry or 15ft for a wet runway) not later than at the end of the take-off distance (TOD).

Second Segment Is the segment from gear retraction to the point where the flaps and slats are retracted. The minimum climb gradient that is required during this segment is 2.4% (in case of engine failure after V1) for a twin engine aircraft.

Third Segment (Level Off Height) This is the acceleration height, which must be at least 400ft AAE (critical engine inoperative). The program uses 1500ft AAE as the minimum first level off

segment for take-off performance calculations. This segment is used for acceleration to retract the flaps and slats and to accelerate to the optimum climb speed. This segment is assumed to be in level flight, so that excessive thrust can be used for acceleration. The minimum climb gradient is 1.2% and must remain positive.

The segment ends when maximum time allowed for use of take off thrust is reached, which depends on the regulation being used.

OM-B E1 4 Performance

Final Take Off Segment Is the segment from the end of the third segment until the aircraft reaches 1500ft above the take-off surface or more if required for obstacle clearance. This segment will only exist if thrust must be reduced to MCT before the aircraft reaches 1500ft according to regulations.

kontext:
2.6.1.7 Landing on Wet, Slippery or Contaminated Runways

Wet or contaminated runways have much lower friction levels than a dry runway.
Friction depends on the runway surface, materials, and conditions. Runway contamination may reduce friction to low levels. A runway is contaminated whenever standing water, ice, snow, slush, frost in any form, heavy rubber, or other substances are present.

If such conditions exist at the time of arrival and

were not considered during dispatch, conduct a landing distance reassessment.
The QRH presents tables to aid this analysis.

Hydroplaning always occurs to some degree when operating on fluid-

contaminated runway. The degree of hydroplaning depends on the following factors:

absence of runway surface roughness and inadequate drainage

depth and type of contaminant

tire inflation pressure

Additional considerations, as follows, should be taken: use Maximum Performance Landing techniques

conduct a positive landing to ensure initial wheel spin-up and initiate firm ground contact upon touchdown. Such technique avoids hydroplaning on wet runways and reduces the strength of any ice bond that, during flight, might have been eventually formed on brake

and wheel assemblies. apply maximum reverse thrust. Do not use asymmetric reverse thrust on slippery and icy runways.

apply firm and symmetrical pressure on brakes pedal

if the airplane loses friction with the runway, do not apply

Emergency/Parking Brake, as it inhibits antiskid protection. Maintain

runway centerline applying rudder, and keep firm and symmetrical braking.

Note: Landing on wet runways could be performed not using thrust reversers.

Landing performance must comply with the runway distance available.

QUICK TURN AROUND WEIGHT

For normal operation, the temperature of the brakes can be monitored through the brake temperature indication in the MFD.

In accordance with the MMEL, the airplane may be dispatched when the brake temperature indication is not working properly. In this situation, if a quick subsequent takeoff is planned after landing, the Quick Turn Around Weight Tables must be used.

According to the tables, if the actual landing weight is equal to or lesser than the quick turn around weight, a subsequent takeoff can be safely performed. Otherwise, a cooling down period of 32 minutes is required after chocks on. Additionally, check that the wheel thermal plugs have not melted prior to the subsequent takeoff.

NOTE:

If the tires are not flat after 32 minutes, the wheel thermal plugs integrity is preserved.

The tables in the following pages are provided for maximum manual braking and no runway slope.

kontext:
6.1.15 Different Loadsheet Envelopes

AFM Envelope This is the center of gravity envelope designed by the aircraft manufacturer during flight testing. The margins are close to the physical/aerodynamical limits

of the aircraft and therefore not usable during daily flight operations. This envelope can be found in the AFM.

DCS Loadsheet Envelope The envelope for DCS loadsheets is tailored to daily operations. Uncertainties of

actual vs. calculated mass and balance values in daily operations require more

restrictive envelope limits (e.g. use of standard passenger masses, inflight movement of passengers, seat row trim).
This envelope can be found in the Aircraft Handling Manual (AHM) and is forwarded to contracted handling agencies and is usually not visible to the flight crews.

Manual Loadsheet Envelope The envelope for a manual (IFS or paper) loadsheets is even more restrictive.
Using section trim (e.g. section A, B, C) leads to more uncertainties within the calculation process and requires a more restrictive envelope.
This envelope includes a designated section reserved for ferry flights. The ferry flight section is applicable if calculating a manual loadsheet for flights with no passengers on board.
Note: Any pantry code acc. to OM-0 9 Pantry Codes may be used for

calculating ferry flight loadsheets.

OM-B E1 6 Mass and Balance

kontext:
GENERAL RECOMMENDATIONS

Protect the animals from stressful situations, like excessive noise, solar radiation, draft, high or low temperatures.

The containers used to this transport must be the appropriate for each type of animal, as recommended by IATA Live Animal Regulations.

To minimize the stress, handle the animals with great care. While waiting for the shipment, maintain the animals in a waiting room with controlled temperature and protected from noise and air flow. The adverse climatic conditions could cause more stress to the animals.
The ambient should be dark to make the animals calmer and comfortable while waiting for shipment. Keep apart animals of different species, specially which are natural enemies, such as cats and dogs.
On the other hand, animals of the same species would be calmer if kept together.

Load the animals just before departure and unload just after arrival.
This procedure is recommended to minimize the exposition to high or low temperatures on the ground,

where the cargo compartment ventilation is not effective. Place live animals as close as possible to the cargo ventilation inflow. Avoid obstruction between the cargo ventilation inflow and the containers.

Specially in the hot season, prefer to schedule the animal shipment for the night period, when the temperatures are lower than during the day.
For the more sensitive animals, such as little birds, which would not resist high temperatures, it is an important requirement. In addition,

fragen.frage: Crosswind Takeoff (E1): Warum soll der Control Wheel Ausschlag nicht übertrieben werden?

kontext:
2.3.3.3.10 Crosswind Takeoff

The airplane has a good control capability during takeoff with crosswind. There is no special related procedure. Maintain directional control using positive rudder and small control wheel inputs.

Runway alignment and smooth symmetrical thrust application are recommended when operating at contaminated runways.

At low speed, use the rudder pedal steering to maintain runway centerline until the rudder becomes effective. Directional deviation is corrected immediately with

smooth and positive control inputs.

During crosswind takeoffs, command control wheel into the wind to maintain wings level throughout the takeoff run.
Care should be taken to avoid using an excessive amount of control wheel to avoid causing unnecessary spoiler deployment.

During rotation, maintain control wheel in the displaced position to keep the wings level during liftoff. Smoothly recover from the sideslip by slowly neutralizing the control wheel and rudder pedals after liftoff.
fragen.frage_en: Crosswind Takeoff (E1): Why should the control wheel deflection not be exaggerated?
antworten_en: Because otherwise Tail Strike Avoidance is activated
Because otherwise the message ENG TLA NOT TOGA appears
Because otherwise Nose Wheel Steering is disconnected
Because too much control wheel unnecessarily extends spoilers
fragen.erklaerung_en: In a crosswind takeoff, the control wheel is turned into the wind; excessive deflection is to be avoided to prevent unnecessary spoiler extension.

fragen.frage: Carbon Brakes (E1): Bei welchen Brake-Temperaturen ist der Verschleiss von Carbon Brakes geringer?
antworten: Bei tiefen Temperaturen, wie bei Steel Brakes
Die Temperatur hat keinen Einfluss auf den Verschleiss
Bei hohen Temperaturen, im Gegensatz zu Steel Brakes
Nur bei Temperaturen unter 0 °C
fragen.erklaerung: Carbon Brakes verschleissen weniger bei hohen Temperaturen, Steel Brakes dagegen bei tiefen Temperaturen.
fragen.zitat: carbon brake wear is strongly affected by brake temperature. Carbon brakes wear less when operated at high temperatures while steel brakes wear less when operated at low temperatures.
kontext:
2.3.1.3 Carbon Brakes

The carbon brake assembly on the E-JETS family has a carbon brake heat sink.
This differs from traditional steel brakes since
carbon brake wear is strongly affected by brake temperature. Carbon brakes wear less when operated at high temperatures while steel brakes wear less when operated at low temperatures.

Overnight or long period parking in cold weather:
Avoid leaving the parking brake set. This decreases the chances of having brake stacks frozen together in case moisture was present before brake application.
General rules for carbon brakes:
During taxi, minimize the duration of each brake application when practical by using shorter applications with higher pressure on the pedals.

Avoid using brakes asymmetrically.
Number of brake applications:
Minimize the number of brake applications when practical. The number of

brake applications governs carbon brake wear.

Taxi when brakes are cold:

Do not intentionally use the brakes solely to heat them.

Carefully manage taxi speed. Let airplane accelerate to a maximum safe

speed. Use the brakes in one increasingly firm application to slow the airplane. Then release the brakes and allow the airplane to accelerate again.

Less frequent use of brakes with higher braking pressure improves brake

life.
Taxi when brakes are warm:

Carefully manage taxi speed. Let airplane accelerate to a maximum safe speed then use brakes in a short but firm application. This helps to keep the

brake within operating temperature range limits by allowing more cooling time and less brake friction time.
fragen.frage_en: Carbon Brakes (E1): At which brake temperatures is the wear of carbon brakes lower?
antworten_en: At low temperatures, as with steel brakes
Temperature has no influence on wear
At high temperatures, unlike steel brakes
Only at temperatures below 0 °C
fragen.erklaerung_en: Carbon brakes wear less at high temperatures, whereas steel brakes wear less at low temperatures.

fragen.frage: Wann kann am Boden die EICAS-Meldung LOAD SHED erscheinen?

Immer beim Start des zweiten Engines mit laufender APU
Wenn beide IDGs online sind und die GPU noch angeschlossen ist
Nur wenn die Batteriespannung unter 22.5 V fällt

kontext:
2.3.1.1 General

Before the taxi out sequence, the flight crew shall have the After Start Checklist completed thoroughly. This procedure is also applied for single engine taxi out.
Before taxi, both pilots have to: adjust the seats and rudder pedals; Note: Adjust the rudder pedals to allow maximum braking application with full rudder pedal deflection.

check the actual airplane parking position;

verify the airport-related charts for possible taxi routes;

if applicable write and brief the taxi clearance when received; Taxi lights shall be turned on by RSP before starting taxi. For intermediate stops

the taxi lights shall be turned off, in order to indicate to other aircraft the intention to observe their right of way.

After parking brake release LSP checks normal brakes.

During taxi:

follow the ATC taxi instructions and check the differences from the initial briefing when applicable;

use standard phraseology and read back ATC instructions.

Flight crews should minimize “heads-down” activities such as entering data into

the FMS while the airplane is moving. Briefing the taxi route reduces the cockpit workload. Contact ATC anytime there is a concern about a potential conflict.

Avoid taxiing closely behind other airplane where FOD may be blown.

LOAD SHED EICAS message may be displayed on ground if airplane is

powered by only one AC power source and indicated airspeed is at or above 50 kt.
LOAD SHED EICAS message may be also displayed in case at least one Transformer Rectifying Unit (TRU) is inoperative.
fragen.frage_en: When can the EICAS message LOAD SHED appear on the ground?
antworten_en: When the aircraft is supplied by only one AC source and IAS is 50 kt or more
Always when starting the second engine with the APU running
When both IDGs are online and the GPU is still connected
Only when the battery voltage falls below 22.5 V
fragen.erklaerung_en: LOAD SHED can appear on the ground when the aircraft is supplied by only one AC source and IAS is at least 50 kt (also with an inoperative TRU).

fragen.frage: Sinkflug mit engagiertem VPATH (E1): Eine laterale Änderung ist nötig. Wie wird vorgegangen?

Autopilot trennen und manuell im FLCH weitersinken
Auf VFLCH wechseln und die Altitude Constraints löschen

kontext:
2.4.2.2.3 VNAV Operation

The FMS calculates the TOD based on the speeds and angle entered on the PERFORMANCE INIT page. The default angle is 3°. Any change is made on the PERFORMANCE INIT page or PERF DESCENT page during the FMS initialization or in flight.

Approaching the TOD set the Altitude Selector to the cleared altitude and the FMS commands to descent upon reaching the TOD.

The FMS commands a VPATH descent unless a late descent is required or if the lateral mode is other than LNAV.

If any lateral change needs to be executed during descent with VPATH engaged,

revert the vertical mode to FPA. Execute the lateral direct to, the vertical direct to and return to VNAV.

For VFLCH descents, the altitude constraint may not be reached by the altitude constraint waypoint. VFLCH is similar to FLCH descents where the guidance is to maintain the selected speed with the engine thrust at idle.
For a late or early descent, use the Descend Now function on the FMS.
Under radar vector it is suggested to disengage VNAV and set SPEED Knob to
MANUAL.

To avoid TCAS Resolution Advisories during level offs, when pilots are aware of traffic in close vicinity at the adjacent flight level they should monitor the descent.
Reduce the vertical speed to 1500 ft/min or less at least 2000 ft before reaching the cleared flight level.
fragen.frage_en: Descent with VPATH engaged (E1): A lateral change is required. How to proceed?
antworten_en: Maintain VPATH and execute only the lateral Direct-To
Change Vertical Mode to FPA, execute lateral and vertical Direct-To, then back to VNAV
Disconnect the autopilot and continue the descent manually in FLCH
Change to VFLCH and delete the altitude constraints
fragen.erklaerung_en: Before a lateral change in a VPATH descent, change to FPA, execute the lateral and vertical Direct-To and then select VNAV again.

Auf VFLCH wechseln und FMS Speeds verwenden

fragen.frage: Wofür wird gemäss OM-B E2 die Maximum Endurance Speed verwendet?
antworten: Um die Trip Time zu minimieren
Für den Steigflug nach dem Takeoff
Für ein Holding oder um die ETA an der Destination zu verzögern
Als Driftdown Speed nach einem Engine Failure
fragen.erklaerung: Maximum Endurance ergibt maximale Flugzeit bei minimalem Fuel Flow, z. B. im Holding oder wenn die ETA verzögert werden muss.
fragen.zitat: This speed mode is used when the trip time has to be prioritized. An example is when the airplane is holding, or when the estimated time of arrival at destination needs to be delayed.
kontext:
MAXIMUM ENDURANCE

Maximum Endurance Speed provides the maximum time in-flight and the minimum fuel flow.
This speed mode is used when the trip time has to be prioritized. An example is when the airplane is holding, or when the estimated time of arrival at destination needs to be delayed.
fragen.frage_en: What is the Maximum Endurance Speed used for per OM-B E2?
antworten_en: To minimize Trip Time
For the climb after takeoff
For holding or to delay the ETA at the destination
As Driftdown Speed after an engine failure
fragen.erklaerung_en: Maximum Endurance gives maximum flight time at minimum Fuel Flow, e.g. in holding or when the ETA must be delayed.

kontext: 2.4.1.9 Turbulent Air Penetration

Flight through severe turbulence must be avoided. If not possible, reduce altitude to increase buffet margin.
AIRSPEED

Severe turbulence causes large and often rapid variations in indicated airspeed.

Do not chase the airspeed.
The maximum recommended turbulent air penetration speed is obtained from

ATTITUDE

fragen.frage: Um wie viel nimmt die Landing Distance ungefähr zu, wenn die Schwelle in 100 ft statt in der normalen Screen Height überflogen wird (E1)?
antworten: Etwa 10 %
Etwa 20 %
Etwa 50 %
Etwa 35 %
fragen.erklaerung: Das Überfliegen der Schwelle in 100 ft statt der normalen Screen Height erhöht die Landing Distance um ungefähr 35 % (10 kt über VREF: ca. 20 %).
fragen.zitat: Crossing the threshold at 100 ft instead of the normal screen height increases the landing distance by approximately 35%.
kontext:
2.6.1.9 Operational Factors Affecting Landing Distance

The required landing distance for dispatch is calculated considering that the landing is performed with:
Airplane crossing the runway threshold at the screen height of 50 ft

airplane crossing the runway threshold at VREF

use of maximum manual braking

In order to stay within the operational margins of the required landing distance,

conduct a stabilized approach and landing using the correct landing techniques.
Several environment factors, such as airport elevation, runway slope, runway conditions, and winds may affect the landing distance. However, aside those factors, if the approach and landing are performed with deviations from the standard procedures, the operational margin available reduces or may even be exceeded.
The following operational factors, among others, affect the airplane landing distance:
Unstabilized approach

Crossing runway threshold with airspeed above VREF

Crossing runway threshold above the screen height

Extended flare, touching down the runway beyond the touchdown zone

No proper application of the available deceleration devices (brakes, spoilers, and thrust reverse)

Deceleration devices not applied until a safe taxi speed is achieved

If the airplane crosses the threshold with 10 kt above the VREF, the landing distance increases by approximately 20%.

Crossing the threshold at 100 ft

instead of the normal screen height increases the landing distance by approximately 35%.

Extending the flare during landing increases the landing distance. The airplane touches down the runway at a point ahead of the runway touchdown zone, which is located at 1000 ft from the runway threshold. Extending the flare by 3 seconds increases the landing distance by approximately 25%.
Considering an unstabilized approach, with the airplane crossing the threshold at 100 ft, above VREF and with 3 seconds of extended flare, the landing distance

increases by approximately 80%. In this situation, the distance necessary to stop the airplane exceeds the operational margins provided by the dispatch required

landing distance.

The preceding information, and the graphic that follows, assumes an airplane

landing at maximum landing weight, on dry runway.
fragen.frage_en: By approximately how much does the landing distance increase if the threshold is crossed at 100 ft instead of the normal screen height (E1)?
antworten_en: About 10 %
About 20 %
About 50 %
About 35 %
fragen.erklaerung_en: Crossing the threshold at 100 ft instead of the normal screen height increases the landing distance by approximately 35 % (10 kt above VREF: approx. 20 %).

fragen.frage: Ist eine Maximum Performance Landing mit Autoland möglich (E1)?
antworten: Ja, aber nur mit Autobrake HI
Nein, eine Max. Performance Landing ist bei Autoland nicht möglich
Ja, sofern die Runway trocken ist
Nur bei CAT I Autoland, nicht bei CAT II/III
fragen.erklaerung: Gemäss OM-B ist eine Max. Performance Landing bei Autoland-Operationen nicht möglich.
fragen.zitat: Max. performance landing is not possible for autoland operations.
kontext:
2.6.1.6 Maximum Performance Landing

Maximum Performance Landing comprehends a set of techniques that leads to stopping the airplane with the least landing run.
The following recommendations apply:

review the approach procedures and speeds earlier: Keep your situation awareness over the stabilized approach and stabilized landing

is mandatory for a well-planned and executed approach

use full flap

cross the threshold at screen height of 50 ft and VREF

avoid extended flare

conduct a positive landing

apply maximum reverse thrust (if required)

immediately after the main landing gear wheels touch down, apply firm and steady maximum manual brakes. Hold pedal pressure until the airplane decelerates to a safe taxi speed within the runway

lower nose wheel immediately to the runway. It decreases lift and

increases loading on main landing gear

Note:
The same technique could be used for Flaps 5 configuration, but the landing distance increases accordingly.
Max. performance landing is not possible for autoland operations.

Guideline for use of FGP and ePerf for a Maximum Performance Landing: calculate the landing distance with 0kt speed increment (VAPP VREF)

insert VAPP VREF in the MCDU

use manual speeds for the approach until speed reduction to VREF

for the speed reduction to VREF switch to FMS speeds

the point for the final speed reduction depends on aircraft weight, wind

component, glide path angle and speed increment

assure the speed is at VREF over the threshold

Note: The maximum speed increment during final approach before reducing to VREF shall be 10 kt to comply with stabilised approach criteria.
fragen.frage_en: Is a Maximum Performance Landing with autoland possible (E1)?
antworten_en: Yes, but only with Autobrake HI
No, a Max. Performance Landing is not possible with autoland
Yes, provided the runway is dry
Only with CAT I autoland, not with CAT II/III
fragen.erklaerung_en: Per OM-B, a Max. Performance Landing is not possible during autoland operations.

fragen.frage: Welcher typische Fehler hat gemäss OM-B E2 das grösste Potenzial für einen Tail Strike beim Landing?
antworten: Den Flare zu hoch über der Runway einleiten
Ungenügende Crosswind-Korrektur im Flare
Over Rotation bei einem Touch and Go
Zu frühes Ausfahren der Thrust Reverser
fragen.erklaerung: Von den typischen Fehlern hat ein zu hoch eingeleiteter Flare das grösste Potenzial für einen Tail Strike, da die Airspeed unter VAPP sinkt.
fragen.zitat: Of these commonly made mistakes, flaring the airplane too high above the runway has the greatest potential for a tail strike and resulting damage.
kontext: Of these commonly made mistakes, flaring the airplane too high above the runway has the greatest potential for a tail strike and resulting damage.

When the flare is started too high above the runway, airspeed decreases below VAPP causing the pilot to compensate. When placed in this situation, the tendency is to continue to increase pitch to stop the excessive sink rate. The correct action to take is to immediately lower the pitch attitude and fly the airplane to the

runway before the airspeed dissipates any further. This corrective action prevents a tail strike.
Lack or poor handling could lead to a destabilized approach thus increasing the tail strike exposure.

Tail Strike Avoidance (TSA)

TSA function controls airplane pitch angle as it reduces control column authority in the nose up direction. The crew may override the TSA actuation by applying

large pitch up column inputs.
TSA function does not provide full protection against tail strikes. During landing,

the pitch angle should be maintained below 10° to ensure tail clearance.

For TSA range of operation, refer to AOM Vol. 2 - TAIL STRIKE AVOIDANCE (TSA) system description.
fragen.frage_en: Which typical error has the greatest potential for a tail strike on landing per OM-B E2?
antworten_en: Initiating the flare too high above the runway
Insufficient crosswind correction in the flare
Over rotation on a touch and go
Extending the thrust reversers too early
fragen.erklaerung_en: Of the typical errors, a flare initiated too high has the greatest potential for a tail strike, since airspeed drops below VAPP.

fragen.frage: Feuchtigkeit auf der Windschutzscheibe kann Gleitpfad-Illusionen verursachen. Wie gross kann der Fehler eine Meile vor der Runway sein?
antworten: Bis zu 50 ft
Bis zu 100 ft
Bis zu 500 ft
Bis zu 200 ft
fragen.erklaerung: Durch Lichtbrechung in der Feuchtigkeitsschicht kann der Fehler eine Meile vor der Runway bis zu 200 ft betragen, mit Risiko eines zu kurzen oder zu langen Landings.
fragen.zitat: This effect can be as much as 200 ft error at one mile from the runway which, when combine with effect mentioned above, could result in risk of landing short of runway threshold or in a long landing.
kontext:
2.6.1.10 Low Visibility Landing

When flying under conditions of haze, smoke, dust, glare, or darkness, airplane height may appear higher than it actually is. Shadows are one of the key factors of depth perception.
This effect is also encountered during night landings, or when smoke or dust appears lying low across the threshold. The effect varies with individuals and is modified by the intensity and clarity of runway lighting. Situational alert must be emphasized on 3D-Approaches, since pilots tend to reduce power and drop

below glide path as soon as the runway is in sight.
Moisture on windshield interferes with visibility and may cause any type of glide path illusion. Light rays refract (bend) as they pass through the layer of moisture of the windshield. You can appear to be above or below the glide path or left or right of centerline.
This effect can be as much as 200 ft error at one mile from the runway which, when combine with effect mentioned above, could result in risk of landing short of runway threshold or in a long landing.
Crosscheck VSI for rate of descent and fly to the touchdown aim point.
fragen.frage_en: Moisture on the windshield can cause glide path illusions. How large can the error be one mile from the runway?
antworten_en: Up to 50 ft
Up to 100 ft
Up to 500 ft
Up to 200 ft
fragen.erklaerung_en: Due to refraction in the moisture layer, the error one mile from the runway can be up to 200 ft, with the risk of landing short or long.

fragen.frage: RTO wegen eines Feuers (E1): Wie soll das Flugzeug gemäss OM-B nach Möglichkeit positioniert werden?
antworten: Mit dem Feuer auf der dem Wind abgewandten Seite (downwind) des Rumpfes
Mit dem Feuer auf der dem Wind zugewandten Seite (upwind) des Rumpfes
Immer quer zur Runway, um die Evakuierung zu erleichtern
Mit der Nase direkt in den Wind, unabhängig von der Lage des Feuers
fragen.erklaerung: Wurde der Takeoff wegen eines Feuers abgebrochen, soll das Flugzeug so positioniert werden, dass sich das Feuer downwind des Rumpfes befindet.
fragen.zitat: if RTO decision was taken due to fire, consider positioning the airplane so that fire is on the downwind of fuselage,
kontext:
3.3.1 Rejected Takeoff - RTO

During the takeoff phase, an RTO procedure is initiated before V1 if any adverse

or abnormal event occurs that could affect the safety of flight. Many faults can cause a decision to reject, like engine fire, engine failure and some other system

faults or events. If an adequate decision to reject is taken, do not delay the RTO.
Delaying the decision increases the risk of a runway overrun, because it takes a

few seconds for the engines to spool down to idle thrust.

A successful RTO depends on:
Accurate alert and monitoring during all takeoff phase,

Captains timely decision,

All callouts made on a loud, clear, and precise communication way,

Adequate briefing, procedures, and coordination.

Responsibility Whoever first identifies the undesirable event or malfunction must announce it, but the decision and responsibility to perform an RTO remain to the captain.
Once the decision is made, initiate the RTO immediately.

Actions Actions are taken considering that, during all takeoff procedures, the LSP keeps his hand on the thrust levers until V1 is reached,

Once the RTO decision has been made, the following actions are: set thrust

levers to idle, disconnect the autothrottle, verify autobrake actuation or

manually apply maximum brakes, and apply reverse thrust as required,

The autobrake RTO mode provides the maximum deceleration rate, which is

equivalent to the maximum manual braking. To decrease workload in this scenario it is recommended to use autobrake in RTO mode, although the

pilot can manually override the autobrake as required.

Note: if an RTO is performed below 60 KIAS (before HOLD is announced) and AT is not disconnected, Autothrottle moves the thrust levers back to TO/GA detent if both throttles are reduced to a position not below 40 degrees TLA. If throttles are moved below 40 degrees TLA or reverse thrust is applied during an RTO, the AT disconnects,

directional control is kept by applying rudder pedal steering,

monitor airplane deceleration, cancel any aural warnings upon malfunction identification, verify reverse thrust status, and advise

ATC,

the engine should be commanded from MAX REV to MIN REV at or above 60 KIAS, and it is recommended to close the thrust reversers at 30 KIAS

if necessary, thrust reverse can be used until airplane comes to a complete stop, considering airplane speed, runway length available, slippery surfaces with ice, snow and so forth,

the airplane should remain on the runway until it is clear that an emergency evacuation is not necessary and the whole scenario is analyzed. If necessary, request external aids to vacate the runway to a safe position according to ATC instructions,
if RTO decision was taken due to fire, consider positioning the airplane so that fire is on the downwind of fuselage,

if an RTO is performed, the FMS takeoff and landing data may

reset after two minutes. If a new takeoff is intended, the FMS takeoff and landing data must be re-entered and confirmed before

the takeoff.

Low and High Energy Speeds The sooner an RTO decision is taken, the greater is the chance to safely stop within runway limits. RTO above V1 may lead to a runway overrun and is the main cause of overrun accidents,

Low energy speed is considered up to, approximately, 80 KIAS,

During takeoff, the 80 KIAS callout has three main proposes: pilot

incapacitation check, airspeed crosscheck and the transition from Low to High Energy speed,

For High energy speeds only reject the takeoff if there is a malfunction that severely affects the flight safety, such as but not limited to:

Engine failures resulting in loss of thrust, Fire or fire warning, Severe damages.

For High energy speeds, it is recommended to continue the takeoff if a tire burst occurs,

Upon reaching V1, if no decision has been taken, continue the takeoff.
After V1, there is no assurance that the airplane is capable to stop within the remaining runway length.

OM-B E1 Procedures

REJECTED TAKEOFF - ACTIONS and CALLOUTS
fragen.frage_en: RTO due to a fire (E1): How should the aircraft be positioned per OM-B where possible?
antworten_en: With the fire on the downwind side of the fuselage
With the fire on the upwind side of the fuselage
Always across the runway to facilitate evacuation
With the nose directly into the wind, regardless of the location of the fire
fragen.erklaerung_en: If the takeoff was rejected because of a fire, the aircraft should be positioned so that the fire is downwind of the fuselage.
