kontext:
REFUELING AND DEFUELING

There is a single pressurized refueling point and a refuel/defuel control panel located under the right wing. When the access panel door is opened, an overhead panel lamp comes on for night or low light operations.

Pressurized refueling is performed with the airplane energized either by AC or battery power. A switch located on the refueling panel enables selection of either power sources.

Refueling operation modes can be either AUTO or MANUAL. When the refueling switch is in the OPEN position, the refuel control valves open enabling fuel flow. Refueling in AUTO mode the FCU (Fuel Conditioning Unit) controls the refuel shutoff valves, automatically halting refueling when the preselected value is reached. In MANUAL mode, the FCU is bypassed. Setting of the CLOSED position in the refueling control switch halts refueling.

In automatic mode, the desired wing tank fuel quantity may be selected on the fuel quantity remaining display via the INCR/DECRT switch.

In the pressurized refueling, the system will automatically close the shutoff to prevent overfilling whenever the fuel rises up to a certain level. Moreover,
the STOP L/R OVR message(s) will appear on the Refueling/Defueling control panel display when the quantity in the right, left or both wing tanks, respectively, is above its capacity.

The wing fuel tanks may be partially or completely refueled using the gravity refuel port located on top of each wing. The individual fuel quantity can be determined using the EICAS or the magnetic level indicators.

NOTE: The maximum fuel quantities indicated on the AFM are not achieved through pressurized refueling only. To achieve the maximum tank capacities, gravity refueling must be used to fill the remainder of the tank.

The airplane can be defueled by suction and/or pressure. The defuel shutoff valve is controlled by the DEFUEL switch located on the refuel/ defuel control panel.

kontext: FUEL LOW-LEVEL WARNING
Each wing tank has a dedicated Fuel Low-Level Sensor located in the collector box. The Fuel Low-Level Sensor is independent of the fuel quantity indication system.

Whenever the fuel level in the collector box is below the sensor level, it sends a fuel low-level signal to the warning system, thus triggering the FUEL LO LEVEL warning EICAS message.

NOTE: FUEL 1 (2) LO LEVEL may appear spuriously when flying with high pitch and/or bank angles.

Under normal conditions, the low-level warning message activation point is set at 400 kg of fuel in the associated wing tank.

If any scavenge pump stops transferring fuel to the Collector Box, which might be caused by an engine failure, loss of motive flow or scavenge pumps failure/blockage, the fuel contained in the Collector Box flows out so that the fuel level inside the Collector Box and the rest of the tank reaches the same level.

Under this condition, if there is up to 2800 kg (approximately) of fuel inside that tank it is possible that the level equivalent to the low-level warning activation point will be reached as the fuel level inside the collector box decreases, then FUEL 1 (2) LO LEVEL warning EICAS message displays indicating that fuel level is below the Low-Level Sensor.

Therefore, in case of loss of the transfer system to the Collector Box, the EICAS WARNING message FUEL 1 (2) LO LEVEL may display even though fuel quantity indication on the EICAS or MFD Fuel System Synoptic Page is up to 2800 kg in that tank.

NOTE: – In case of loss of the transfer system to the Collector Box followed by the EICAS warning message, fuel quantity indication monitoring during the flight is achieved through EICAS, or MFD Fuel System synoptic page.
– Engine flameout due to fuel starvation may occur if the airplane is subjected to attitudes greater than 15° nose up or down, uncoordinated maneuvers or negative g’s.

kontext:
ELECTRIC HYDRAULIC PUMPS

Both Electric Hydraulic Pumps are alternating current motor pumps (ACMP). Electric Hydraulic Pump 3A (ACMP 3A) is the primary power source for Hydraulic System 3 and it is powered by the AC ESS BUS.

A two-position selector knob located on the hydraulic panel enables the flight crew to select OFF or ON positions.
There is no automation associated with this pump. So in normal operation, the flight crew will turn the pump ON and OFF during engine start and shutdown, respectively.

Electric Hydraulic Pump 3B (ACMP 3B) is the backup for the Electric Hydraulic Pump 3A and it is powered by the AC BUS 2. The flight crew selects manual or automatic operation through the three-position selector knob on the hydraulic control panel. Normal operation is automatic.

In flight, with the selector knob in the AUTO position, the hydraulic system logic turns on the electric pump 3B whenever the electric pump 3A fails. When the selector knob is set to the ON position, the electric pump operates continuously overriding the system automation.

kontext:
ELECTRIC HYDRAULIC PUMPS

Both Electric Hydraulic Pumps are alternating current motor pumps (ACMP). Electric Hydraulic Pump 3A (ACMP 3A) is the primary power source for Hydraulic System 3 and it is powered by the AC ESS BUS.

A two-position selector knob located on the hydraulic panel enables the flight crew to select OFF or ON positions. There is no automation associated with this pump. So in normal operation, the flight crew will turn the pump ON and OFF during engine start and shutdown, respectively.
Electric Hydraulic Pump 3B (ACMP 3B) is the backup for the Electric Hydraulic Pump 3A and it is powered by the AC BUS 2.

The flight crew selects manual or automatic operation through the three-position selector knob on the hydraulic control panel. Normal operation is automatic.

In flight, with the selector knob in the AUTO position, the hydraulic system logic turns on the electric pump 3B whenever the electric pump 3A fails. When the selector knob is set to the ON position, the electric pump operates continuously overriding the system automation.

kontext:
ELECTRIC HYDRAULIC PUMP 1

The Electric Hydraulic Pump 1 (ACMP 1B) is an alternating current motor pump. It serves as a backup for the EDP 1 and it is powered by the AC BUS 2.

A three-position selector knob located on the hydraulic panel enables the flight crew to select OFF, AUTO or ON positions. In normal operation, selected position is AUTO.

14-11-10

Page 2/8 Hydraulic System Description REVISION 27

In flight, with the selector knob set to AUTO position, the Hydraulic System logic activates the electric pump in case of:
– EDP or engine fail, or
– Flaps selected to any position greater than 0°.

During landing operations, the Electric Hydraulic Pumps remain activated for 60 seconds to avoid abrupt hydraulic pressure variations in an event of engine failure.

On ground, with the selector knob set to AUTO position, the Hydraulic System logic activates the electric pump in case of:
– Flaps selected to any position greater than 0° and:
– Thrust levers set to takeoff thrust, or
– Airspeed greater than 50 kt.
Also, during takeoff when thrust levers are set to TO/GA position, the Electric Hydraulic Pumps will be activated for 60 s to avoid abrupt hydraulic pressure variations in an event of engine failure.

kontext:
REF A/I MODES OF OPERATION

The REF A/I mode of operation can be selected on ground using the OAT/visible moisture table presented in ICING CONDITIONS, COLD WEATHER AND COLD SOAK OPERATIONS supplementary procedure, in block 3-75.

The MCDU setting operates the anti-ice system and inhibits the ice detectors activation logic during takeoff until 1700 ft AGL or 2 min after liftoff, whichever occur first. The settings actuate as described below:

OFF – The anti-ice valves will be inhibited closed until the end of takeoff phase, considered in the logic as 1700 ft AGL or 2 min after liftoff. After that, the engine and wing anti-ice valves will open if ice is detected.

ENG
– Only the engine anti-ice valve will be kept open after engine start. The wing anti-ice valves remains inhibited closed.

The EICAS status message ENG TDS REF A-I ENG will be displayed to confirm the MCDU selection.

ALL – The engine anti-ice valves are commanded open after completion of engine start and the wing anti-ice valves are commanded open with wheel speed above 40 kt. The EICAS status message ENG TDS REF A-I ALL will be displayed to confirm the MCDU selection.

In ENG or ALL operation modes, the anti-ice valves will rely on ice detection above 1700 ft AGL or 2 min after liftoff.

In OFF or ENG operation modes and anti-ice mode selector knob set to ON position, the caution message “ENG REF A-I DISAG” and the advisory message “A-I MODE NOT AUTO” will be displayed on the EICAS. In this case, the pilot needs to rotate the selector knob to AUTO position.

If the REF A/I is set to ENG on the MCDU and the OAT temperature entered at the Takeoff Data Setting is below 5°C, the CAS message “ENG REF A-I DISAG” will be displayed.

AUTOBRAKE

The autobrake system provides automatic braking at maximum deceleration rates, which may vary according to runway conditions, for landings and rejected takeoffs. The system modulates hydraulic pressure to the brakes in order to provide a constant deceleration rate corresponding to the level selected. If reverse thrust is actuated, the autobrake system will modulate the brake pressure to maintain the deceleration rate constant.
The autobrake system can only be armed if the normal brake system is operational.

Antiskid, touchdown and locked wheel protections are provided during autobrake operation.

Four autobrake levels of deceleration (RTO, LO, MED, HI) are available via a selector knob on the cockpit main instrument panel.

There are two modes of autobrake control:
– Landing mode (LO, MED, HI).
– Rejected takeoff mode (RTO).
NOTE: RTO is the selected takeoff mode with the maximum deceleration rate. This deceleration is equivalent to the maximum manual braking.

kontext: NOSE WHEEL STEERING SYSTEM
The airplane nose landing gear has steer-by-wire control powered by hydraulic system 2 and electronically controlled by the Nose Wheel Steering Control Module.

OPERATION

To engage the nose wheel steering system:
– The hydraulic system 2 needs to be pressurized.
– The external steering disengage switch must be in the engaged position.
– The handwheel steering must be pressed and released for rudder pedal steering or kept pressed for handwheel steering.
NOTE: After a power up, the first steering engagement must be performed with the airplane stopped. If this condition is not met, the hardover test might not be successfully accomplished by the system and STEER FAIL message may be displayed.

The nose wheel steering has three modes of operation: the handwheel steering mode, the rudder pedal steering mode and the free wheel steering mode.

FREE WHEEL STEERING MODE

The free wheel steering mode is mostly used for towing or when the normal steering system fails.

OPERATION

The steering system can be disengaged reverting to free wheel by means of:
– The steering disengage button located on both control wheels.
– The external steering disengage switch located on the external power connection access.
In the free wheel mode, the airplane steering can be carried out by use of rudder, differential brake and/or asymmetrical thrust.

During taxi, smooth radius turns must be performed.

The free wheel mode is automatically selected when:
– Failure of the Air/Ground signal occurs.

– Nose wheel steering system failure is detected.

kontext:
FULL FACE MASK OPERATING MODES

Normal: Normal Mode provides supplemental oxygen diluted with cabin air according to the cabin pressure altitude until a preset point where the user inhales 100% oxygen. This feature is to conserve the amount of oxygen consumed from the supply source while still maintaining protective physiological levels.

100%: 100% Mode provides non-diluted oxygen to the crew regardless of cabin altitude.

Emergency: The “EMER” setting provides non-diluted oxygen regardless of cabin altitude, with a slightly positive pressure. This setting should be used to eliminate condensation or to purge smoke and toxic fumes that may get into the mask.
When the mask is on emergency mode, the air pressure and flow make communication more difficult.

To avoid communication disruption it is recommended not to use the EMER setting continuously, selecting

kontext:
AURAL WARNING PRIORITY LEVELS

There are four aural warning priority levels, from the highest to the lowest:
– Emergency (level 3).
– Abnormal (level 2).
– Advisory (level 1).
– Information (level 0).
Emergency: corresponds to a situation that requires the pilot’s immediate action.
The master warning annunciator is repeated with three-second intervals between alerts until the master warning reset switch is pressed.

Abnormal: corresponds to an abnormal situation such as system malfunction or failures that have no immediate impact on safety.
Whenever an abnormal fault occurs, a master caution tone is presented every five seconds until the master caution reset switch is pressed.

Advisory: corresponds to the recognition of a situation such as system malfunction or failures leading to loss of redundancy or degradation of a system.

Information: corresponds to a condition or status for flight crew information.

kontext:
EICAS MESSAGES PRESENTATION

The messages are grouped and presented in a chronological order accordingly to its category. The Warning category is placed at the top of the EICAS display. Below this category the system presents the Caution, Advisory and Information/Status category, in this order.

When new Warning, Caution and Advisory alert messages are displayed, they are presented flashing in inverse video for crew acknowledgment.

The warning and caution alert messages shall remain flashing in inverse video until manual crew acknowledgment via Master Warning or Caution button (respectively) is pressed. Advisory messages will automatically revert from inverse to normal video after 5 seconds they started to be displayed.

After the acknowledgment, the new message shall remain in steady normal video, at the top of its category on the EICAS display, until a new message belonging to that group appears.
The EICAS messages cannot be cancelable. They shall remain active as long as its activation condition exists.

kontext:
AURAL WARNING

The electronic display system has two aural warning drivers, which are responsible for generating and prioritizing aural warnings.
Aural warnings sound in a sequence, are never truncated, and are automatically canceled when the alerting situation no longer exists,

or when they are reset manually by the pilot. In the event of multiple alerts, the highest priority alerts sound first.

Aural warnings are used when pilots need immediate knowledge of a condition without having to look at a visual display or indicator. Aural warnings are alert tones, bells, horns, clicks, beeps and voice messages.

kontext:
APPROACHING RUNWAY (IN AIR)

The Approaching Runway (In Air) advisory is intended to enhance flight crew situational awareness on which runway the airplane is lined- up with during approach.

The aural message consists of the word “Approaching” followed by the runway identifier, for example, “Approaching Three Four Left”.

The Approaching Runway (In Air) advisory shall be enabled when all the following conditions are met:
–

height above landing field elevaiton is 750 ft or less and above 300 ft;
– airplane is within 3 NM of the runway;

– airplane heading is within approximately 20° from runway centerline;
– airplane position is within approximately 200 ft laterally of the runway centerline plus the runway width.
The absence of an Approaching Runway In-Air advisory does not necessarily imply that the airplane is approaching a surface other than a runway.
Airplanes equipped with Runway Awareness and Advisory System (RAAS), Post-Mod. LOAD 27.1

The aural message is inhibited if the approaching runway is the same as the FMS departure runway.

kontext:
TCAS STATUS ANNUNCIATIONS

The TCAS information is displayed on the MFD and PFD. There are six types of TCAS mode annunciations:
– TCAS FAIL – This annunciation is displayed when a TCAS failure is indicated by TCAS data, when TCAS data is invalid or when TCAS data was not correctly received for 10 s.
– TCAS TEST – This annunciation is displayed when the TCAS computer indicates functional test is active.
– TCAS OFF – This annunciation is displayed when TCAS provides a valid indication that the computer is in stand by mode.
– TA ONLY – This annunciation indicates that the TCAS is not selected to provide resolution advisories or is inhibited. The TA mode provides only surveillance of the surrounding airspace. In this mode, TCAS tracks proximate airplane and generates traffic advisories; no resolution advisories are issued in this mode.

14-15-40

REVISION 22 Traffic Collision Avoidance System Page 3/8

– TA/RA – This annunciation is displayed when TCAS provides a valid indication that the computer is in TA/RA mode. This annunciation is only displayed on both TCAS MFD displays. TA/RA mode is the normal operation mode providing full TCAS coverage.
In this mode, TCAS tracks airplane in the surrounding airspace and generates traffic advisories or resolution advisories, as the situation requires.
– TCAS RA FAIL – This annunciation indicates that TCAS is not able to provide resolution advisories.
The annunciation is displayed if the resolution advisory data is invalid or not received for 5 s
or if information required to display the TCAS RA data on the PFD is missing or failed (e.g., if attitude, or groundspeed is failed or missing). This annunciation is only displayed on the PFD.

When RAs are automatically inhibited below 900 ft AGL

kontext:

The TCAS system can be controlled through the MCDU and on the MFD by the CCD.

The TCAS map overlay and TCAS zoom format are available on the MFD. The map overlay format displays the TCAS information on the navigation MAP mode, on MFD.

The GAIN control varies the RTA receiver gain. There are two modes: variable and calibrated. The normal preset is calibrated mode and is used for weather avoidance.
The system will be forced into calibrated gain when RCT or TGT are selected.

The variable mode is useful for additional weather analysis and for ground mapping. In WX mode, variable gain can increase receiver sensitivity over the calibrated level to show weak targets or it can be reduced below the calibrated level to eliminate weak returns.

kontext:
INERTIAL REFERENCE SYSTEM (IRS)

The inertial system computes airplane position, ground speed, heading and attitude.

The main component of the IRS is the Inertial Reference Unit (IRU), which interfaces with the Modular Avionic Unit (MAU), Global Positioning System (GPS) and the Air Data Computer (ADC). The IRU provides output data to the PFD, weather radar, Multifunction Control Display Unit (MCDU), Flight Management System (FMS) and reversionary panel.

Primary source for the Captain`s PFD is the IRS 1 and for the First Officer`s PFD is IRS 2. In case of mode failure, power loss or loss of one IRU, the affected station can source select the other side station by means of the IRS reversionary panel button.

An automatic power up (on ground) and alignment is provided. The alignment on ground (up to 17 min) must be performed with the airplane not in movement and position manually entered primarily via MCDU or obtained automatically from the GPS.
In flight alignment is also possible to recover navigation capability using data from the GPS.

The alignment time can be checked on the IRS STATUS PAGE 1/1 on the MCDU.

REVISION 22 Navigation Page 1/36

fragen.frage: Unter welcher Bedingung akzeptiert das FMS GPS-Daten?
antworten: Nur wenn eine gültige RAIM-Zahl verfügbar ist

kontext:
RECEIVER AUTONOMOUS INTEGRITY MONITOR

(RAIM)

The GPS module executes a RAIM test to insure the integrity of the data transmitted by the satellite. RAIM is a software function that supplies an alert to the cockpit when the integrity limit exceeds a flight phase dependant threshold.

The GPS has RAIM outputs for the current position and time in the form of horizontal and vertical integrity limit (HIL and VIL) at some future place and time.

In order to compute RAIM, the GPS must have a minimum of five satellite signals.
The FMS does not accept GPS data unless a valid RAIM figure is available.

The FMS produces an alert for the flight crew on the MCDU when the GPS has lost integrity: “GPS RAIM ABOVE LIMITS”. Also an alert is generated by the FMS when the integrity will exceed the limit: “RAIM WILL EXCEED LIMIT”. A third alert will be generated by the FMS when RAIM is not available: “GPS RAIM UNAVAILABLE”.
fragen.frage_en: Under which condition does the FMS accept GPS data?
antworten_en: Only if a valid RAIM number is available
Only if both GPS units provide the same position
As soon as at least three satellites are tracked
Only if the almanac is less than 12 hours old
fragen.erklaerung_en: The FMS accepts GPS data only if a valid RAIM value is available.

kontext:
PREDICTIVE RAIM PAGE

The FMS uses the high priority GPS for predictive RAIM. The priority order for FMS 1 is GPS 1, GPS 2. The priority order for FMS 2 is GPS 2, GPS 1. If only a single GPS is available, both FMSs use it for predictive RAIM.

Should the GPS fail or the interface between the FMS and GPS not work properly, the FMS displays the message PREDICTIVE RAIM UNAVAILABLE on the PREDICTIVE RAIM page.

Predictive RAIM is calculated using GPS almanac information. The almanac within the GPS is automatically updated whenever the GPS is on and tracking satellites. The almanac within the GPS is set invalid if it is older than 3.5 days. Should this occur, the message ALMANAC

The almanac takes approximately 12–25 minutes to update once the GPS is tracking satellites.

RAIM predictions are not possible with an expired almanac.

Selecting the DEST prompt from the PREDICTIVE RAIM page displays DESTINATION RAIM page 1/2.

kontext:
PREDICTIVE RAIM (PRAIM)

The GPS also has a predictive RAIM function that provides the following types of RAIM predictions: Destination and Alternate waypoint (Pilot Select). Predictive RAIM uses an almanac function that is updated whenever the GPS is tracking satellites. Satellites can be manually deselected or enabled for destination and alternate waypoint prediction.

This function calculates whether the satellite geometry is acceptable for approach at the expected destination at the estimated time of arrival (ETA). On ground, in order for an ETA to be computed, the pilot

REVISION 22 Navigation Page 9/36
must enter an ETD (ORIGIN/ETD) in line select key 1L on the initial FLT PLAN page.

The predictive RAIM page is accessed by selecting the PRED RAIM prompt from any GPS STATUS page. When selected, the PREDICTIVE RAIM page is displayed. YES indicates RAIM is predicted to be within approach criteria. NO indicates RAIM is predicted to be unacceptable or unavailable.

kontext:
RADIO NAVIGATION SYSTEM

The radio navigation equipment is located in the Modular Radio Cabinet (MRC).

The interface with the audio is through the audio/microphone bus, and with the MCDU/PFD/MFD through the ASCB. The main components are:
– Very-high-frequency Omni-directional Range (VOR).
– Automatic Direction Finder (ADF).
– Distance Measuring Equipment (DME).
– Instrument Landing System (ILS).
– Transponder System (XPDR).
The MCDU is the primary means for radio tuning (RADIO PAGE and PROGRESS PAGE), while the CCD and PFD are the secondary means.

A tuning backup is available in MCDU 2 in case of loss of both MAUs.
If the audio bus is lost there are audio backups also.

kontext:
VERY HIGH FREQUENCY

The VHF digital radios (VDR) 1 and 2 are located in the Modular Radio Cabinets (MRC). VDR 1 and 2 interfaces with the audio system through the audio/microphone busses, and with the MCDU/PFD through the ASCB. VDR channels 1 and 2 are for voice communication only.

VDR 3 interfaces with audio system and MCDU/PFD indirectly via MRC 2 and directly to MAU 1 to data transmission. The VHF radio 3 is located on a separated radio Mini Cabinet. VDR 3 provides voice communication as well as data communications through ACARS (Aircraft Communication Addressing and Reporting System) applications.

The VHF data radio modules provide communication
in the frequency range of 118.000 MHz to 136.975 MHz with 8.33 kHz or 25 kHz.

The VHF frequency is tuned/activated through the MCDU (primary means) or CCD (PFD) and adhere to the ICAO FM immunity requirement.

A tuning backup is available in MCDU 2 in case of loss of both MAUs.
In the same way, if the audio bus is lost there are audio backups.

REVISION 27 Communication Page 9/110

SBH - Syllabic Squelch High: This is the basic squelch type and is usually best for normal voice communications. A syllabic squelch opens upon receiving a signal with voice-like characteristics while ignoring other signals.
With syllabic squelch, there is the possibility that the first syllable of a voice reception may be partially squelched. The possible adjustment levels are OFF, meaning no squelch action, minimum (MIN), medium (MED) and maximum (MAX).
SBL - Syllabic Squelch Low: This squelch is also a syllabic squelch and is intended for voice communications where the desired signal is very weak and noisy. This squelch is more prone to opening (no squelch action) on noise than the SBH squelch. The possible adjustment levels are OFF (no squelch action), minimum (MIN), medium (MED) and maximum (MAX).
SQH - (Signal/Noise Squelch High): This is a traditional signal-to- noise squelch best suited for listening to non-voice signals, or voice signals that do not respond well to one of the syllabic squelches.
Compared to the syllabic squelches, a higher signal level is generally required for this squelch to perform well. The possible adjustment levels are 0-31, where 0 is off squelch.
SQL - (Signal Level Squelch): This is a signal strength squelch which opens on any strong input signal. It opens quickly on strong signals, however also opens on strong noise or static. Use of SQL is recommended for use only with strong signals and under low noise conditions. This squelch is well suited for music broadcasts.
The possible adjustment levels are 0-31, where 0 is off squelch.
– Selection of squelch level:
If SQL/SQH squelch type is selected, the squelch level defaults to
0. The entry of an update value can be done via the scratch pad or through the tuning knob on the MCDU. If the tuning knob will be used, the squelch level value must prior be boxed, pressing the LSK 3R. In the case of numeric keys, enter the squelch level value and press the LSK 3R.
If SBL/SBH squelch type is selected, the squelch defaults to OFF.
Pressing the respective LSK varies the squelch mode. During the Power Up, the HF type defaults to SQL.
– Press LSK 5R to select EM MODE (emission mode):

Page 10/110 Communication REVISION 27

UV: conventional upper sideband. It is considered the standard for HF transmission and reception and is the most commonly used.
After the Power Up, the EM MODE defaults to the UV mode.
LV: conventional lower sideband.
AM: amplitude modulated communication. Some older stations may still use AM signals. AM is the best selection for listening to broadcast stations.
RC: reduced carrier power single sideband for frequency tracked receivers. The HF signal transmitted in some frequency is actually transmitted in a band of frequencies. When the station being contact has the ability to lock onto a transmitted frequency, it is possible to reduce power dispersion, thus reducing the transmission power requirements. When communicating with one these stations, the RC mode may be used.

kontext:
AUDIO CONTROL PANEL

There are three Audio Control Panels (ACP), located at the control pedestal and observer station. Each panel controls an independent crew station audio system and allows the flight crew to select the desired radios, navigation aids, interphones and PA systems for monitoring and transmission.

The audio panel receives inputs from all audio communication channels and aural warnings. Audio warnings for altitude alert, ground proximity warning system (GPWS), traffic collision avoidance system (TCAS), and windshear among others, are also provided through the speakers and headsets.
These warnings cannot be controlled or turned off by the flight crew.
Audio from each ACP is monitored using a headset, headphone or the related speaker, except for the observer speaker.

Only on the Observer ACP

kontext:
DIGITAL VOICE DATA RECORDER (DVDR)

SYSTEM

Airplanes equipped with Honeywell or L3 DVDR

The digital voice data recorder system (DVDR) combines a flight data recorder (FDR) and a cockpit voice recorder (CVR) in a single unit.
Two DVDR units are installed.
DVDR 1 is installed in the forward electronic bay, and the DVDR 2 in the aft electronic bay.

Each unit receives, records and preserves all required data parameters and voice recordings from the cockpit crew and area microphones.

The DVDR unit is capable of recording the last 120 min of audio information from cockpit area microphone and primary crew microphones. The FDR is capable of recording at least 25 h of flight data.

The DVDR automatically starts recording audio information as soon as power up is performed and continues until the power down. The flight data begins to be recorded when the first engine is started.

The DVDRs FDR data is available through the MCDU for maintenance purposes only.

Page 20/110 Communication REVISION 27

If the DVDR power system fails, an EICAS message is generated to indicate the failure. All DVDR EICAS messages are advisory and some of them are inhibited in critical phases of flight, such as takeoff.

Airplanes equipped with Universal DVDR

The digital voice data recorder system (DVDR) combines a flight data recorder (FDR) and a cockpit voice recorder (CVR) in a single unit.
Two DVDR units are installed. DVDR 1 is installed in the forward electronic bay, and the DVDR 2 in the aft electronic bay. Each unit receives, records and preserves all required data parameters and voice recordings from the cockpit crew and area microphones.
Additionally, the DVDR 1 is equipped with an internal RIPS (Recorder Independent Power Supply) which supplies power to the CVR whenever there is an airplane power loss.

The DVDR Universal unit is capable of recording the last 120 min of audio information from cockpit area microphone and primary crew microphones, 120 min of datalink data, and at least 25 h of flight data.
The DVDR Universal Kapture unit is capable of recording at least the last 25 h of audio information from cockpit area microphone and crew microphones (pilot, copilot, and 3rd Crew/PA), at least 25 h of datalink data, and at least 25 h of flight data.

The DVDR automatically starts recording audio information as soon as power up is performed. Flight data recording begins when the first engine is started. After power down, the DVDR continues recording audio information for 10 min. During this time, the FDR1, FDR2, and CVR2 PASS FAIL lights illuminate steady in amber on the DVDR Control Panel.

The DVDRs FDR data is available through the MCDU for maintenance purposes only.

If the DVDR power system fails, an EICAS message is generated to indicate the failure. All DVDR EICAS messages are advisory and some of them are inhibited in critical phases of flight, such as takeoff.

REVISION 27 Communication Page 21/110

kontext:
ATTENDANT CALL

The call system is used as a mean for crewmembers to gain the attention of other crewmembers and to indicate that interphone communication is desired.

Attention is gained through the use of lights and aural signals (chimes or horn).
The cockpit may be called from either flight attendant station or by the ground personnel. The ground personnel may only be called from the cockpit.

Flight attendants may be called from the cockpit through interphone buttons on the ACPs or flight attendant call button on the overhead panel, the other attendant station, or from any passenger seat (PSU) or lavatory. Call lights in the passenger cabin identify the source of incoming calls to the attendants.

Call system chime signals low, high, or high/low tones are audible in the passenger cabin through the PA system speakers. The PA speakers also provide an alerting chime signal whenever one of the following conditions occur:
– NO SMOKING, FASTEN SEAT BELT, or RETURN TO SEAT (in the lavatory) signs illuminate or extinguish
– STERILE COCKPIT light illuminates.
The attendant call lights located on the forward and aft main ceiling panel areas provide a visual indication to attendant when there is a call from the flight crew or passengers.

Page 18/110 Communication REVISION 27

COCKPIT PHILOSOPHY

The airplane flight deck is designed to:
– Provide the necessary means to accomplish the required tasks.
– Provide acceptable and reasonable workloads.
– Minimize pilot errors and its consequences.
– Facilitate training with the commonality among the E-Jets Family.
– Provide optimized ergonomics aimed at safety, ease of operation, control, and comfort requirements.

and is indicated with a detent mark between knob positions.

Knob stationary positions are marked with a white rectangle, and knob momentary positions are marked with a white triangle. To assure proper signal transmission when using the selector knobs that have momentary positions, hold the knob for at least two seconds at the positions before releasing it.

System failures are primarily monitored via EICAS messages. The synoptics are included as an aid to pilot monitoring.

Critical systems give total authority to the pilot by employing intuitive procedures for maximum airplane performance with minimum workload. Cockpit design facilitates simple tasks as much as possible, thus leading to increased control of situation and systems. Automation is used only to improve the task accomplishment, complementing but not substituting for the crew.

kontext:
VIDEO CONTROL UNIT (VCU)

VCU is the electronic device used to select the desired camera in manual or automatic mode. The VCU provides power to the cameras.

14-01-63

Page 4/4 Cabin Surveillance System REVISION 12

WATER

A central storage tank holds potable water. The potable water system supplies pressurized water to the water heaters and faucets in the lavatories, and water spigots and coffee makers in the galleys. Water is also supplied to the lavatories for the rinsing of the waste system vacuum toilets. Water is filtered for galley consumer user interfaces.

Engine and APU bleed air pressurizes the potable water system. If the engines or APU are not running on the ground, or bleed air pressure is below the optimal range during the flight, an optional air compressor pressurizes the water system.

The potable water tank has a maximum capacity of 110 (29 US Gal).
The flight attendant panels indicate the quantity and the percentage of total water quantity remaining in the tank.

The lavatory faucet has a single control button. The water supplied is mixed of hot and cold and the flow is started by pressing the button.
Adjustments for water flow and water temperature are possible to the flight attendants.

A similar optional faucet that offers touchless actuation is installed in the airplane lavatories. The faucet has a sensor screen installed below the faucet body for close proximity of hand to actuate water flow.

Water from forward lavatory washbasin and forward galley are collected to the gray water interface valve, which drains the service water to the waste tank.

Water from aft lavatory washbasins and aft galleys is automatically drained through aft drain mast on ground and in flight.

In-flight drainage is commanded by pressing the water dump pushbutton in the cockpit. Water is drained through aft and forward drain masts. The drainage may take up to 10 min. After a total drainage of water, toilet water rinsing and other systems that use water will not be available until the next refilling. Pressing the water dump pushbutton again discontinues the drainage.
If the landing gear is lowered or under any faulty drain mast heater condition, water drainage is automatically interrupted.

14-01-65

Water and Waste REVISION 1 Page 1/4

The supply line in the lavatory contains an optional water filter for removing impurities, sediment and improving the water taste and quality for passenger and crew use.

An optional ultraviolet (UV) water treatment unit may be used as a supplemental treatment device to disinfect the water as it is entering the airplane. If installed, the UV unit is positioned in the fill line downstream of the fill/drain nipple.

In case of water system leakage at either the galley or the lavatory, the respective shutoff valve may be actuated to isolate the system.

If the autodrain valve clogs, the flight attendant may manually actuate the remote actuation cable on the front of the galley. Pulling the self- drain valve handle clears the galley drain valve. Access to the lavatory valve is through the under sink cabinet door. Pulling up the ring handle clears the lavatory drain valve.

The flight attendant panel indicates a fault condition whenever:
– A fault in the respective forward or aft drain valve is detected, or
– Water level indication is not available.
In-flight drainage is not available due to a fault in the drain valve or in the drain mast heater.

WASTE

The vacuum waste system collects waste from the lavatory toilets to an aft mounted waste tank.

A vacuum generator is used to create differential pressure on the ground or at altitudes below 18000 ft. At higher altitudes, the differential between cabin pressure and ambient pressure is sufficient to transport the waste.

Pushing the flushing switch located inside the lavatory initiates toilet- flushing sequence. Water is introduced to rinse the bowl before opening of the toilet-flushing valve.

14-01-65

Water and Waste Page 2/4 REVISION 1

An optional touchless flush switch provides touchless operation. For the touchless flush switch, a sensor is incorporated in the flush switch housing to ensure that the flush switch works properly even if the passenger does not approach the center of the switch.

The touchless flush switch functions similarly to the manual switch in initiating the flush cycle of the toilet. The switch is located adjacent to the toilet so that it is visible and accessible for passenger usage. The flush switch is wall mounted and is actuated touch less or through a physical touch by the passenger after the use of the toilet.

The usable capacity of the waste tank is 121 (32 US Gal). The service tank indication illuminates on the FAP when waste tank capacity reaches 75%. When the waste tank’s full capacity is reached, the tank full indication illuminates and the vacuum toilets are disabled.

Waste tank draining is performed through the service panel on the aft right-hand side of the fuselage.

A central storage tank holds potable water. The potable water system supplies pressurized water to the water heaters and faucets in the lavatories, and water spigots and coffee makers in the galleys. Engine and APU bleed air pressurizes the potable water system. If the engines or APU are not running on the ground, or bleed air pressure is below the optimal range during the flight, an optional air compressor pressurizes the water system.

remaining in the tank.

Water from forward lavatory washbasin and forward galley are collected to the gray water interface valve, which drains the service water to the waste tank.

Water from aft lavatory washbasins and aft galleys is automatically drained through aft drain mast on ground and in flight.

After a total drainage of water, toilet water rinsing and other systems that use water will not be available until the next refilling. Pressing the water dump pushbutton again discontinues the drainage. If the landing gear is lowered or under any faulty drain mast heater condition, water drainage is automatically interrupted.

The vacuum waste system collects waste from the lavatory toilets to an aft mounted waste tank.
A vacuum generator is used to create differential pressure on the ground or at altitudes below 18000 ft.

At higher altitudes, the differential between cabin pressure and ambient pressure is sufficient to transport the waste.

The switch is located adjacent to the toilet so that it is visible and accessible for passenger usage. BLUE: a steady blue light illuminates when a passenger calls from the main cabin area.

kontext:
RAINBOW LIGHTS

Rainbow lights at the forward and aft main ceiling panel provide a visual indication to attendants when there is a call from the flight crew or passengers.

The rainbow lights consist of following colored indicator lights:
– ORANGE: a steady orange light illuminates when a passenger calls from the lavatory. Flashing orange light illuminates when smoke is detected in the lavatory.
– BLUE: a steady blue light illuminates when a passenger calls from the main cabin area.
– RED: a flashing red indicator illuminates when the flight crew makes an emergency call to the flight attendant from the cockpit.
The light stops flashing after the call is taken.
–
GREEN: a flashing green indicator illuminates when the pilot calls the flight attendant from the cockpit. The light stops flashing after the call is taken.

– AMBER: a steady amber light illuminates for a sterile light call.
An audible tone sounds by the passenger address system whenever a passenger presses any attendant call switch in a PSU or in the lavatory. The tone also sounds when the flight crew presses the attendant call switch. There is also a blue steady light on the cabin

REVISION 14 Lighting Page 7/24

ceiling, indicating from which cabin area the respective passenger call was made.

NOTE: – There is no indication on the rainbow lights when a flight attendant calls another flight attendant station. It only flashes green on both handset cradles.

FORWARD CARGO BAY VENTILATION

The ECS provides ventilation for live animals in the forward cargo bay.
This optional system contains a fan on the side of the bay which provides underfloor recirculation air into the bay. The system also

contains a shutoff valve at the outlet of the bay that closes in the event of fire and thus preventing halon from leaving the bay. In addition, in the event of fire, the forward cargo compartment fan is commanded OFF,
thus closing the check valve and preventing halon from entering the cabin.

kontext:
EMERGENCY RAM AIR VENTILATION

Emergency ram air ventilation is provided in case of pack shutdown or for smoke removal.

The flight deck pack emergency ram air ventilation valve is automatically commanded to OPEN only if both ECS cooling packs are commanded OFF or failed OFF or Dump push button on the pressurization Control Panel is pressed.

An emergency ram air ventilation check valve is provided and does not require electronic control. The emergency ram air check valve is open whenever the pressure in the ram air circuit is greater than cabin pressure.

During smoke removal, both ECS cooling packs are commanded OFF and therefore, the flight deck emergency ram air ventilation valve is commanded OPEN.

kontext:
ECS PACKS LOGIC

An ECS pack is OFF when its associated pack flow control valve (FCV) is closed. The ECS packs 1 or 2 are OFF when any of the following conditions occur:
– Bleed air source is NOT available for the pack
– The associated Pack pushbutton is OFF on the overhead panel
– Any engine is starting and there is weight-on-wheels (both packs OFF)
–
The associated engine is starting, there is no weight-on-wheels and the opposite engine is not starting

– Any engine is starting and APU is the bleed source (both packs OFF)
– Associated bleed system duct leak
– Associated packs BIT shutdown failures are present (PACK 1(2) FAIL EICAS message displayed), or
– The DUMP Button is pressed on the pressurization panel.

kontext: APU BLEED
The APU supplies bleed air on the ground or inflight. However, it is used primarily as a ground pneumatic source for the air conditioning packs (ECS) and engine starting.

The APU Bleed Check Valve prevents reverse flow to APU when operating on engine bleed.

The APU Bleed Valve (ABV) controls the APU bleed airflow to the pneumatic system.

The APU Bleed Valve may be commanded to open when the following conditions occur simultaneously:
– APU switch is set to AUTO,
– APU Bleed is available,
– no APU and left bleed duct leak, and
– anti-ice system not requested (or anti-ice system requested ON and anti-ice system is failed).

OVERHEAT DETECTION SYSTEM

The Overheat Detection System (ODS) consists of overheat sensors and electronic control. They provide rapid and reliable overheat, and leak detection for the engine bleed, APU bleed air distribution, and anti-ice supply ducting.

14-02-10

REVISION 15 Bleed Air System Page 3/6

If a single loop fails, the remaining monitors for an overheat condition (single loop operation).

kontext:
AMS CONTROLLER (AMSC)

AMS controllers 1 and 2 controls cabin pressure by commanding the outflow valve to modulate airflow through the valve from the pressurized airplane volume to the surrounding environment. AMSC 1 and 2 control both automatic and manual modes functionalities.

Each AMSC has three channels:
– Channel A performs automatic control
–
Channel B performs manual control (together with the Safety Channel) and an automatic backup mode while in electrical emergency or both Channel A are failed,

and
– Safety Channel is responsible for the following safety functions: cabin positive overpressure relief, cabin altitude limitation protection and cabin rate of change limitation.
The channels B and Safety provide a manual function as backup, enabling the crew to control cabin pressure by directly actuating the outflow valve (OFV) position.

14-02-20

Pressurization System REVISION 1 Page 1/10

The system protects the cabin against excessive positive pressure by an electronic and pneumatic protection.

The altitude limitation protection function controls the outflow valve (OFV) to a closed position if the cabin altitude exceeeds 14500 ft. The function is performed by the Safety channel.

kontext:
AP ENGAGEMENT AND DISENGAGEMENT

ENGAGEMENT

Autopilot engagement is inhibited on the ground.

In flight, the autopilot is engaged pushing the AP button on the guidance panel.

The AP engagement is verified on the FMA on both PFDs.

With the confirmation of the AP label on the FMA the autopilot is controlling the airplane pitch, roll and yaw according to the flight director selections.

After pushing the AP button on the guidance panel, the control column must be in neutral position within 2 s to guarantee the engagement of autopilot and Breakout Increase Device (BOID).

With the autopilot engaged, the BOID actuates and provides extra resistance on the control yoke. The BOID actuates to avoid inadvertent disengagement of the autopilot by the flight crew.

DISENGAGEMENT

AUTOTHROTTLE ENGAGEMENT

The AT engages on ground when all of the following conditions occur:
– no AT active failures.
– AT button pressed on the guidance panel.

The AT engages on flight when all of the following conditions occur:
– no AT active failures.
– AT button pressed on the guidance panel.
– airplane at or above 400 ft AGL.

kontext:
CLIMB THRUST RATING (CLB)

The Pratt Whitney PW1900G engines have two modes of climb thrust:
Climb 1 (CLB-1) and Climb 2 (CLB-2).

CLB-1 is the default mode after airplane power-up. The selection of CLB-1 or CLB-2 is possible on the THRUST RATING SELECT page.

14-03-20

Page 8/10 Thrust Management REVISION 14

CLB-1 and CLB-2 thrust ratings change with altitude. After takeoff, CLB-1 provides higher climb thrust than CLB-2. At high altitudes, CLB-2 provides higher climb thrust than CLB-1.

NOTE: At high altitudes, it is not recommended to change from CLB-1 to CLB-2 with the intention of increasing thrust.

– CLB-1: Maximum climb rate;
– CLB-2: Climb thrust derated from CLB-1.
If takeoff thrust rating is lower than the climb rating, the initial climb N1 target is modified to the takeoff thrust decreased by 1%.

This logic prevents the system from increasing thrust during transition from takeoff mode to climb mode. During this transition, with AT engaged, the thrust levers move from TO/GA to corresponding initial climb position. This lever movement may cause a significant rearward movement but it represents a small N1 change. After the transition, the system resumes operational logic, changing N1 target according with altitude.
N1 target

kontext: APU FUEL SUPPLY
Fuel for normal start and operation of APU is supplied by the right wing tank. If only DC power is available on ground, the DC fuel pump provides fuel to start the APU.

When the APU generator or a GPU cart provides AC power to airplane, the AC fuel pump provides fuel to APU.

After Engine 2 is running, an ejector pump in the right wing tank activates and supply fuel to provide fuel to APU. The ejector pump has priority over DC and AC fuel pumps.

It is possible to provide fuel to APU from the left wing tank via a crossfeed valve operation.

The fuel is heated in the Fuel-Oil Heat Exchanger to prevent formation of ice in the fuel supplied to APU. The Fuel-Oil Heat Exchanger also provides oil cooling.

fragen.zitat: Rotating the APU master knob to ON powers the FADEC and opens the APU fuel shutoff valve. The APU OFF indication clears on EICAS and APU speed and EGT parameters displays.
kontext: APU START
Rotating the APU master knob to ON powers the FADEC and opens the APU fuel shutoff valve. The APU OFF indication clears on EICAS and APU speed and EGT parameters displays.

The FADEC commands the air inlet door to open.

Rotating the APU master knob from ON to START (momentary position) initiates the APU automatic starting cycle.

NOTE: After the air inlet door opens, the air going into the APU windmills the turbine. If the windmilling conditon raises the APU speed above 15%, the FADEC avoids APU starting.

Electrical power from the APU generator and pneumatic bleed are available three seconds after the APU speed reaches 95%.

The FADEC automatically shuts down the APU if enough speed is not achieved during the starting cycle.

APU FUEL SUPPLY

Fuel for normal start and operation of APU is supplied by the right wing tank. If only DC power is available on ground, the DC fuel pump provides fuel to start the APU.

When the APU generator or a GPU cart provides AC power to airplane, the AC fuel pump provides fuel to APU.

kontext:
INTEGRATED DRIVE GENERATOR (IDG)

Each engine has an IDG. A dedicated generator control unit (GCU) controls and monitors each IDG. As an engine spools up, the respective IDG automatically comes on line, powering the respective AC BUS. The previous power source is disconnected from that AC BUS.

Each IDG selector knob in AUTO position sets the electrical system to automatic operation.

If a selector knob is moved to the OFF position, the respective generator line contactor opens, tripping off-line and de-exciting the related IDG.

When an IDG low oil pressure or oil overtemperature condition is detected, the CAS message IDG 1 (2) OIL displays. Additionally, an amber light illuminates next to the respective IDG selector knob on the overhead panel. The amber light indicates the IDG to be disconnected and extinguishes after the IDG disconnection.

kontext: RAM AIR TURBINE (RAT)
The Ram Air Turbine (RAT) is an emergency AC electrical device installed in the airplane nose section. In flight, there is no altitude restriction for the RAT deployment,

and the minimum deployment speed is 150 kt.

If the minimum deployment speed is respected, whenever the AC power sources are not powering the AC buses, the RAT is automatically deployed. In about 8 s, the RAT starts supplying power to the AC ESS BUS.

The RAT also powers the DC ESS BUSES through the ESS TRU. To avoid total loss of power during the RAT deployment and speeding up period, batteries are used as backup to power the DC ESS BUSES.

14-05-10

REVISION 15 AC System Page 3/6

Even if normal electrical power is re-established, once deployed, the RAT cannot be stowed back in flight. In this case, the RAT keeps providing power to the AC ESS BUS and DC ESS BUS 3.

The RAT electrical power drives the AC Motor-driven Pump (ACMP 3A) for commands on primary flight controls, including high lift system actuation. It also provides power to the essential avionics, communication, and battery recharging.

The RAT requires a minimum of 130 kt to ensure continuous power supply to AC/DC ESS BUSES. At speeds below 130 kt, the RAT is not capable of supplying power to all essential buses, so the batteries automatically connect to the DC ESS BUSES, while the RAT keeps feeding the AC ESS BUS until a certain airspeed.

In case of failure on automatic RAT deployment, a deployment handle is available to release the RAT manually.

kontext:
INTEGRATED CONTROL CENTER (ICC)

The ICC is an electrical-electronic integrated device that provides power distribution and protection for the airplane systems, SPDAs, and circuit breakers located on the cockpit sidewall panels.

There are four ICCs in the electrical system:
– Left Integrated Control Center (LICC)
– Right Integrated Control Center (RICC)
– Emergency Integrated Control Center (EICC)
– Auxiliary Integrated Control Center (AICC).
The ICCs incorporate AC/DC electrical buses, circuit breakers (CBs), contactors, fuses, Generator Control Units (GCUs), Transformer Rectifier Units (TRUs), Power Quality Monitors (PQMs), and External Power Module (EPM).
LICC and RICC are installed in the center electronics bay. EICC is installed in the forward electronics bay. AICC is installed in the aft electronics bay.
AC/DC electrical buses are the primary means of electrical power distribution. These buses are located inside the respective ICCs:

kontext:
CIRCUIT BREAKERS (CB)

Circuit Breakers are classified as either thermal or electronic CBs.

Some thermal CBs are on the cockpit sidewall panels and others are located inside the ICCs in the electronics bays.

The electronic CBs are located inside the SPDAs, in the electronics bays.

All CBs located in the electronics bays are considered remote CBs.

The flight crew can visually monitor all circuit breakers located inside the cockpit and, via MCDUs, the remote CBs in the electronics bays.

The ICCs remote thermal CBs can only be reset by maintenance personal when the airplane is on ground.

The flight crew can reset the SPDA remote electronic CBs via the

kontext:
GROUND START

During an engine start, the FADEC automatically sequences the starting system, ignition system, and fuel flow to start the engine.

The FADEC commands open the start air valve to allow the starter to accelerate the engine, and a green AES indication is displayed on EICAS. The Motor to Start (MTS) is commanded at low N2 to clear any bow in the rotor.
The ignition and fuel flow are commanded once N2 has reached enough speed (from 20% to 27% N2) to provide actuation pressure to the fuel metering valve.

The SCV closes and ignition is off when the predetermined starter cutout speed is reached, and fuel flow is scheduled to bring the engine to idle.

NOTE: FADEC 9.6.6 increases the motor to start (MTS) dwell time from 30 seconds to 45 seconds during engine start. This time may be extended by the FADEC if the engine is warmer than typical.

During a ground start, protection against starting failures is provided, including:
– Hot start
– Hung start
– Failure of N1 to rotate
– Failure to light, and
– Inability to control the igniter or fuel flow.
NOTE: – When FADEC detects a surge or an impending hot start, a fuel depulse is commanded. Fuel is cycled off for 2 seconds and back on for 12 seconds. On the ground, FADEC may attempt up to 2 fuel depulse cycles.
– When FADEC detects a fail to light or a hot or hung start, an auto-restart attempt is performed. Fuel and ignition are commanded off for at least 30 seconds. If the auto-restart attempt fails, FADEC aborts the start and commands a 30 seconds dry motoring before commanding the starter valve to close.

kontext:
INFLIGHT START

When the airplane is within the assisted start envelope (refer to ENGINE AIRSTART ENVELOPE) the FADEC commands the starter to accelerate the engine. A white AES indication is displayed when the FADEC identifies that the engine is within the assisted restart envelope. The AES indication becomes green when FADEC is commanding an assisted restart.

Outside the assisted restart envelope, the starter is not commanded, allowing the engine to windmill in the airstream to accelerate. A white WML indication is displayed when the FADEC identifies that the engine is within the windmilling restart envelope. If the N2 is lower than 8.5% within the windmilling start envelope, the FADEC commands an assisted engine start and the green AES indication is displayed. The WML indication becomes green when FADEC is commanding a windmilling start.

When the engine reaches the speed to provide actuation pressure to the fuel metering valve, the FADEC commands ignition and fuel flow.

The FADEC commands the depressurization of the Engine Driven Pump (EDP) if N2 is below 25%.

The FADEC has no protection for hot starts, hung starts, or failure to light off for in flight engine starts.

NOTE: – When FADEC detects a surge or an impending hot start, a fuel depulse is commanded.
Fuel is cycled off for 2 seconds and back on for 12 seconds. In flight, FADEC may attempt up to 10 fuel depulse cycles.

– This logic does not abort the engine start automatically.
Flight crew remains responsible for monitoring engine parameters and manually abort the start.

kontext:
STABILIZER TRIM

The manual trim is commanded through switches installed on the control columns or a backup switch on the main pedestal.

The backup trim switch and the control wheel trim switches are dual split switches. The aural warning “TRIM” triggers for 6 s when the control wheel trim or backup trim switches have failed or when only half of switch is pressed. If only one half of the switch is actuated or the failure persists for more than 6 s, that switch is automatically deactivated. In this case, the aural warning is deactivated and the applicable advisory pitch trim switch fail message is displayed on
EICAS.

In order to avoid a possible pitch trim runaway condition, manual pilot trim commands are limited to 3 s After the control wheel trim or backup trim switches have both halves pressed for more than 3 s, the timer stops the horizontal stabilizer control surface movement. If the trim switch remains pressed, the aural warning “TRIM” triggers. When the trim switch is no more pressed, the aural warning stops.

When flying in normal mode, the FCCs inhibit commands to the horizontal stabilizer via elevator offload function according to the following:
– Pitch up direction, in case of stall protection engagement.
– Pitch down direction, in case of high-speed protection engagement.
Stabilizer Trim Priority Logic

The FCCs and HSCU process the trim inputs with the following priority:
1. Backup switches.
2. Left seat switches.
3. Right seat switches.

Hydraulic System 3 supplies hydraulic power to the lower actuator.

kontext:
STEEP APPROACH MODE

The Steep Approach Mode is a fly-by-wire function which

allows the airplane to perform approaches with glide path angles up to 5.5°.

It is armed by pressing the STEEP APPROACH Button, and engages when the flap surface reaches the FULL position with the system armed.

The Steep Approach Mode automatically disarms and/or disengages when:
– The airplane is on ground,
– A Go-Around is initiated (TLA is commanded to TO/GA),
– The Stall Protection System is activated,
– The STEEP APPROACH Button is pressed, or
– The flaps are removed from the FULL position.
When the Steep Approach Mode is engaged, the multifunction spoiler pairs 4 and 6 are deployed to an offset position, and spoilers pair 5 deploys just when a increased sink rate is required. All spoiler panels deployment angle is modulated according to control laws and control column position, to work as drag devices, increasing the sink rate with no change to the airspeed. Nose up pitch commands reduce the spoilers deployment angle, and nose down pitch commands increase the spoilers deployment angle.

Additionally, the horizontal stabilizer automatically compensates the airplane pitch during Steep Approach Mode engagement and disengagement.

The stall speed, stall characteristics, the maximum lateral control and the maneuvering capabilities for full flaps are unaffected by the steep approach mode.

14-08-35

Page 4/4 Spoiler System REVISION 11

kontext:
EMERGENCY SHUTOFF FUNCTION

Electronic sensors monitor the status of Flap/Slat system. In case of fault detection, the Emergency Shutoff Protection sends a command to stop the movement of Flap/Slat panels.

The following monitors activate the emergency shutoff function:
– Flap/slat jam
– Temperature of controller units
– Overspeed of flap/slat retraction/deployment
– Torque limits
– Uncommanded movement
– Asymmetry of panels
– Panel Skew
– Disconnection detection
– Airplane configuration check.
The activation of emergency shutoff protection displays the FLAP (SLAT) FAIL message on EICAS.

If the respective surface has not reached the position selected on the Slat/Flap Lever, the SLAT-FLAP LEVER DISAG message may appear.

14-08-30

Slat/Flap System Page 2/4 ORIGINAL

When a jam occurs on any flap or slat, setting the selector lever to the previous position and again to the desired position can release it.

After the jam, the system allows the flight crew to try the release of a jammed surface for two times. When the jam monitor trips for the third time the emergency protection function deactivates the surface actuators.
The Flight Control System uses Flap and Slat position to schedule surface commands. If the FCCs lose flap (slat) position information, the FSCS system is locked with the current flap (slat) position.

kontext:
RADIO ALTIMETER SYSTEM

The radio altimeter function measures the airplane height above terrain and sends this information to be displayed on the PFD and to be used by the other airplane systems.

To determine the height, the radio altimeter transmits a signal to the ground. The time it takes to receive the signal return is converted into radio altitude.

The radio altimeter range of operation is -20 ft to 2500 ft.

When the airplane is parked at the gate or nearby,
the presence of irregular surfaces (tools, tool carts, stairs, cables) can affect the measurements of radio altimeter altitude. As a result, both PFDs may display the miscompare RAD ALT
and may trigger the EICAS message APPR 2 NOT AVAIL.
fragen.frage_en: At the gate, RAD ALT miscompare appears on both PFDs together with the message APPR 2 NOT AVAIL. According to the AOM, what is a possible cause?
antworten_en: An IESS alignment in progress
Irregular surfaces such as tools, stairs or cables under the aircraft
A BARO setting not set
A transponder switched off
fragen.erklaerung_en: Irregular surfaces (tools, tool carts, stairs, cables) at the gate can affect the RA measurement and trigger RAD ALT miscompare and APPR 2 NOT AVAIL.

fragen.frage: Was bewirkt das Drücken des CAGE Buttons am IESS?
antworten: Es setzt STD Baro
Es zeigt die ILS-Abweichungen an
Es startet die 90-s-Alignment neu und sperrt die Anzeige
Es cagt die internen Gyros, um die akkumulierte Drift zu löschen
fragen.erklaerung: Mit CAGE führt das Standby-Instrument einen Cage der internen Gyros durch, um die akkumulierte Drift zu löschen.
fragen.zitat: CAGE pushbutton: if depressed, the standby performs a CAGE in the internal gyros to cancel the accumulated drift.
kontext:
NORMAL OPERATION

During normal operation, the IESS computes and displays attitude, slip-skid indication, altitude (baro corrected), airspeed, vertical speed, Mach number and IESS.

The buttons functionalities are:
–
CAGE pushbutton: if depressed, the standby performs a CAGE in the internal gyros to cancel the accumulated drift.

– ILS button: if pressed, glideslope and localizer deviations is displayed.
– STD button: if pressed, STD baro is set. To adjust baro, rotate the knob.
– and buttons: controls display brightness.
– "Push FT-M" in the Guidance Panel: automatically displays altitude in meters.
– "MAIN PNL" in the Overhead Panel: controls IESI bezel illumination.
The IESS is powered as soon as the airplane battery 1 is selected to ON and airplane battery 2 is selected to AUTO. Then, the IESS starts its alignment phase. The initial IESS alignment takes about 90 seconds to be completed and can be identified on the screen by the "INIT 90 s" flag.

NOTE: The airplane must not be moved during the first 90 seconds after power-up, while the IESS is undergoing alignment.
Moving the airplane during this period can cause in-flight attitude indication errors that may not be noticeable on ground.
fragen.frage_en: What does pressing the CAGE button on the IESS do?
antworten_en: It sets STD baro
It displays the ILS deviations
It restarts the 90 s alignment and blanks the display
It cages the internal gyros to erase the accumulated drift
fragen.erklaerung_en: With CAGE, the standby instrument cages the internal gyros to erase the accumulated drift.

fragen.frage: Wie zeigt das IESI an, dass ein einzelner Parameter (z. B. Attitude oder Airspeed) ausgefallen ist?
antworten: Der Parameter wird durch schwarzen Hintergrund mit rotem Kreuz ersetzt
Die ganze Anzeige wechselt auf eine OUT OF ORDER Seite
Der Parameter blinkt amber
Der Parameter wird grau dargestellt
fragen.erklaerung: Im ERROR State wird der ausgefallene Parameter durch einen schwarzen Hintergrund mit rotem Kreuz ersetzt; die anderen Parameter bleiben operationell. OUT OF ORDER erscheint bei Datenverlust.
fragen.zitat: If one or several function failures are detected, the IESI enters the ERROR state. In the ERROR state, the parameter failed is replaced by a black background with a red cross
kontext:
ABNORMAL OPERATION

If there is a loss of data, an OUT OF ORDER page is displayed.
If one or several function failures are detected, the IESI enters the ERROR state. In the ERROR state, the parameter failed is replaced by a black background with a red cross,

or a warning indication is displayed.

14-09-10

REVISION 14 Flight Instruments Page 7/10

For attitude indication, slip-skid indication, airspeed indication, or air data failure the black background with a red cross replaces the failed parameters.

For ILS, the black background with a red cross replaces the corresponding pointer and scale and a warning indication is presented.

NOTE: The other parameters without the black background and the red cross remains operational.

For VMO/MMO failure, a VMO warning indication is presented.
fragen.frage_en: How does the IESI indicate that a single parameter (e.g. attitude or airspeed) has failed?
antworten_en: The parameter is replaced by a black background with a red cross
The whole display changes to an OUT OF ORDER page
The parameter flashes amber
The parameter is displayed in gray

fragen.frage: Wie wird der Angle of Attack der Air Data Smart Probes berechnet?
antworten: Über separate AoA-Vanes an jeder Seite
Aus den IRS-Daten und der Ground Speed
Über eine Verknüpfung des Static Pressure zweier Probes: ADSP 1 mit ADSP 2, ADSP 3 mit ADSP 4
Über die Verknüpfung von ADSP 1 mit ADSP 4 und ADSP 2 mit ADSP 3
fragen.erklaerung: Der AoA wird aus dem Static Pressure der Smart Probes berechnet; ADSP 1 ist mit ADSP 2, ADSP 3 mit ADSP 4 verknüpft.

kontext:
COMM/NAV/FMS OPERATIONS

– Multifunction probes, and
– Air data computer.
The ADSP/TAT senses static pressure, total pressure, angle of attack, and TAT and transmits them to the Air Data System.

The angle of attack is calculated based on an interface between the static pressure of the smart probes.
– ADSP 1 interfaces with ADSP 2.
– ADSP 3 interfaces with ADSP 4.

Each ADSP and TAT are heated to provide protection for icing build up maintaining continued sensor accuracy in icing conditions.

ADSP
fragen.frage_en: How is the angle of attack of the air data smart probes computed?
antworten_en: By separate AoA vanes on each side
From IRS data and ground speed
By linking the static pressure of two probes: ADSP 1 with ADSP 2, ADSP 3 with ADSP 4
By linking ADSP 1 with ADSP 4 and ADSP 2 with ADSP 3

fragen.zitat: In the event of a display failure, the MFD may present information by setting the reversionary panel. Certain DU internal failures result in a large red “X” covering the screen.
kontext:
PRIMARY FLIGHT DISPLAY (PFD)

Primary Flight Display provides airspeed, attitude, altitude, vertical speed, flight modes, and course deviation information. In addition to the flight instruments, flight plan, navigation, communication, terrain, traffic, and weather information are also presented on the PFD.

The Primary Flight Display is available in two different formats. The 3/4th window format: default window format for PFD. In this format, the PFD occupies 3/4th of the display area. The second is the 1/2 window

Page 4/20 Electronic Display System REVISION 14

format: displayed during a reversionary scenario, the PFD occupies half of the display area.
In the event of a display failure, the MFD may present information by setting the reversionary panel. Certain DU internal failures result in a large red “X” covering the screen.

In case of mismatched information between two PFDs, a monitor warning annunciation is displayed. If an unacceptable cross compare of any of the following parameters is detected, the correspondent annunciation is triggered.
– Pitch
– Roll
– Attitude
– Heading
– BARO altitude
– Airspeed
– Localizer
– Glideslope
– Radio altitude
– Flight path angle
– EICAS

– Crew Alerting System (CAS).
The display controller portion of the guidance panel allows the selection of PFD HSI formats, navigation sources, weather display, and bearing pointer selection.

REVISION 14 Electronic Display System Page 5/20

AVIATE

fragen.zitat: If the failed display is recovered, it is necessary to revert manually the affected display. Rotating the displays selector knob out of the AUTO deactivates the failed or reverted DU.
kontext:
DU2(3): MFD1(2).

REVISION 14 Electronic Display System Page 1/20

There are three different modes for the DU reversion control for each pilot: LEFT, RIGHT, and AUTO. All DUs are revertible, depending on which DU was lost. The PFD and EICAS are always presented.

If the selector knob is in the AUTO position, in case of display failure, an automatic logic transfers its information to the remaining units.
If the failed display is recovered, it is necessary to revert manually the affected display. Rotating the displays selector knob out of the AUTO deactivates the failed or reverted DU.

In order to both pilots have good visibility of its indications, the EICAS is always presented in the inboard of the displays. The automatic reversion logic for theDU has the following display priority, from highest to lowest:
– 1 PFD per side when airborne (the most outboard)
– 1 EICAS visible by both pilots (inboard)
– 1 MFD
– No disruption on the cross-side displays.

Nothing, the display is switched back automatically
The DU must be restarted via the MCDU
The DISPLAYS MODE knob must remain in AUTO, switching back occurs after 30 s

kontext: ABNORMAL OPERATION
In case of mode failure, power loss, or loss of one IRU, the reversion of the IRS source is performed automatically.

fragen.frage: Was ermöglicht das Alignment in Motion (AIM) des IRS?
antworten: Ein IRS-Alignment während des Taxi ohne Positionseingabe.
Die Wiederherstellung der Navigationsfähigkeit im Flug mit Daten des GPS.

Das Attitude Alignment des AHRS mit TAS-Daten im Flug.

kontext:
IRU POWER-UP AND ALIGMENT

An automatic power-up (on ground) and alignment is provided.

On ground, the system must perform the alignment with no movement of the airplane and position entered manually. Primarily via MCDU or obtained automatically from the GPS. Alignment time is up to 17 min.
With the alignment in motion (AIM) is also possible to recover navigation capability, in flight, using data from the GPS.

The crew can check the alignment time on the IRS STATUS PAGE 1/1 on the
MCDU.

REVISION 14 Navigation Page 1/72
fragen.frage_en: What does the IRS Alignment in Motion (AIM) enable?
antworten_en: An IRS alignment during taxi without position entry.
Restoring navigation capability in flight using GPS data.
An accelerated ground alignment within 5 min.
The attitude alignment of the AHRS using TAS data in flight.
fragen.erklaerung_en: With AIM, the navigation capability of the IRS can be restored in flight using GPS data.

fragen.frage: Welche MCDU-Meldung präsentiert das FMS, wenn das GPS seine Integrität verliert?
antworten: GPS RAIM UNAVAILABLE
RAIM WILL EXCEED LIMIT
PREDICTIVE RAIM UNAVAILABLE
GPS RAIM ABOVE LIMITS
fragen.erklaerung: GPS RAIM ABOVE LIMITS erscheint bei Integritätsverlust, GPS RAIM UNAVAILABLE dagegen, wenn RAIM nicht verfügbar ist.
fragen.zitat: The FMS alerts the flight crew with two messages on the MCDU: – GPS RAIM ABOVE LIMITS – GPS RAIM UNAVAILABLE The messages are respectively presented when the GPS looses integrity or when RAIM is not available:
kontext:
RECEIVER AUTONOMOUS INTEGRITY MONITOR (RAIM)

RAIM is a software function that ensures the integrity of the received GPS data.

The FMS alerts the flight crew with two messages on the MCDU:
– GPS RAIM ABOVE LIMITS

– GPS RAIM UNAVAILABLE

The messages are respectively presented when the GPS looses integrity or when RAIM is not available:

A RAIM or FOM of zero represents perfect (no error) GPS position.
Increasing values indicate a lower RAIM or FOM accuracy.
fragen.frage_en: Which MCDU message does the FMS present when the GPS loses its integrity?
antworten_en: GPS RAIM UNAVAILABLE
RAIM WILL EXCEED LIMIT
PREDICTIVE RAIM UNAVAILABLE
GPS RAIM ABOVE LIMITS
fragen.erklaerung_en: GPS RAIM ABOVE LIMITS appears on loss of integrity, whereas GPS RAIM UNAVAILABLE appears when RAIM is not available.

fragen.frage: Was bedeutet ein RAIM- oder FOM-Wert von null auf der GPS STATUS Seite?

Es werden keine Satelliten getrackt.
Die Positionsunsicherheit ist maximal.
Eine perfekte GPS-Position ohne Fehler.
fragen.erklaerung: Ein RAIM oder FOM von null steht für eine perfekte (fehlerfreie) GPS-Position; steigende Werte bedeuten geringere Genauigkeit.
fragen.zitat: A RAIM or FOM of zero represents perfect (no error) GPS position. Increasing values indicate a lower RAIM or FOM accuracy.
kontext:
– GPS RAIM UNAVAILABLE

The messages are respectively presented when the GPS looses integrity or when RAIM is not available:
