fragen.frage_en: What does a RAIM or FOM value of zero on the GPS STATUS page mean?
antworten_en: RAIM is not available.
No satellites are being tracked.
The position uncertainty is at maximum.
A perfect GPS position without error.
fragen.erklaerung_en: A RAIM or FOM of zero stands for a perfect (error-free) GPS position; increasing values mean lower accuracy.

fragen.frage: Wie wird ein Fehler im GPS-Modul im Cockpit angezeigt (neben MCDU-Anzeige)?
antworten: Caution-CAS-Meldung GPS FAIL zusammen mit Master Caution.
Rote GPS-Flagge auf dem HSI und Voice Message "GPS".
MSG-Indikator auf dem PFD und Advisory-CAS-Meldung GPS 1 FAIL bzw. GPS 2 FAIL.
Ausschliesslich auf der POS SENSORS Seite, ohne EICAS-Meldung.
fragen.erklaerung: Bei einem GPS-Fehler leuchtet der MSG-Indikator auf dem PFD und die Advisory-Meldung GPS 1 FAIL oder GPS 2 FAIL erscheint.
fragen.zitat: The Message ("MSG") indicator on the PFD illuminates, and "GPS 1 FAIL" or "GPS 2 FAIL" advisory CAS message is displayed.
kontext:
– ALTITUDE AIDING

– FAILED

REVISION 14 Navigation Page 7/72

After power is applied, the acquisition mode is used to acquire satellites. The GPS tracks four satellites to acquire its position. When fewer than four satellites are tracked, altitude aiding is the active mode, otherwise choose the appropriated navigation mode. In altitude aiding mode GPS uses altitude from the digital air data computer (ADS) to help position determination.

The GPS is also capable to receive Satelite-Based Augmentation System (SBAS) to improve signals and provide a more accurate position output.
The approach with LPV minimums is selected in the FMS and inserted on the active flight plan. Once LPV mode is engaged, the autopilot also uses the GPS deviations to control the airplane.
Any faults within the GPS module is reported on the FMS MCDU and on the EICAS.
The Message ("MSG") indicator on the PFD illuminates, and "GPS 1 FAIL" or "GPS 2 FAIL" advisory CAS message is displayed.
The GPS STATUS SENSOR page also displays the GPS failure indication.
fragen.frage_en: How is a failure of the GPS module shown in the cockpit (besides the MCDU display)?
antworten_en: Caution CAS message GPS FAIL together with master caution.
Red GPS flag on the HSI and voice message "GPS".
MSG indicator on the PFD and advisory CAS message GPS 1 FAIL or GPS 2 FAIL.
Exclusively on the POS SENSORS page, without an EICAS message.
fragen.erklaerung_en: On a GPS failure the MSG indicator on the PFD illuminates and the advisory message GPS 1 FAIL or GPS 2 FAIL appears.

fragen.frage: Was kann der Pilot auf der DESTINATION RAIM Seite tun?
antworten: Die ETA für die Destination manuell überschreiben.
GPS-Satelliten, die gemäss GPS NOTAMs ausser Betrieb sind, von der Prediction ausschliessen.
Das SBAS-Signal für einen LPV-Approach aktivieren.
Den RAIM-Grenzwert für die Approach-Phase anpassen.
fragen.erklaerung: Auf der DESTINATION RAIM Seite können Satelliten, die gemäss publizierten GPS NOTAMs ausser Betrieb sind, von der Prediction ausgeschlossen werden.
fragen.zitat: On this page, the pilot can exclude any GPS satellite scheduled to be out of service according to published GPS NOTAMs, from the DESTINATION RAIM predictions.
kontext:
PREDICTIVE RAIM (PRAIM)

The GPS predictive RAIM function is used to predict Destination and Alternate waypoint. Predictive RAIM uses an almanac function that is updated whenever the GPS is tracking satellites. Pilot can manually deselect or enable the Satellites for destination and alternate waypoint prediction.

Page 8/72 Navigation REVISION 14

When the FMS makes the automatic RAIM prediction, if RAIM will be exceeded, the RAIM WILL EXCEED LIMIT message is displayed in the MCDU scratchpad, and the MSG annunciator is displayed on the PFD.

This function calculates whether the satellite geometry is acceptable for approach at the expected destination at the estimated time of arrival (ETA). On ground, to compute an ETA, the pilot must enter an ETD (ORIGIN/ETD) on the initial FLT PLAN page.

The predictive RAIM page is accessed by selecting the PRED RAIM prompt from any GPS STATUS page. On PREDICTIVE RAIM page YES indicates that RAIM is predicted to be within approach criteria, and NO indicates that RAIM is predicted to be unacceptable or unavailable.

If GPS fails or the interface between the FMS and GPS not work properly, the FMS displays the message PREDICTIVE RAIM UNAVAILABLE on the PREDICTIVE RAIM page.

The selection of DEST prompt from the PREDICTIVE RAIM page displays DESTINATION RAIM page.
On this page, the pilot can exclude any GPS satellite scheduled to be out of service according to published GPS NOTAMs, from the DESTINATION RAIM predictions.
fragen.frage_en: What can the pilot do on the DESTINATION RAIM page?
antworten_en: Manually override the ETA for the destination.
Exclude GPS satellites that are out of service according to GPS NOTAMs from the prediction.
Activate the SBAS signal for an LPV approach.
Adjust the RAIM limit for the approach phase.
fragen.erklaerung_en: On the DESTINATION RAIM page, satellites that are out of service according to published GPS NOTAMs can be excluded from the prediction.

fragen.frage: Welcher HF Emission Mode (EM MODE) ist nach dem Power-up eingestellt?
antworten: UV (conventional upper sideband)
LV (conventional lower sideband)
AM (amplitude modulated)
RC (reduced carrier)
fragen.erklaerung: UV ist der Standard für HF und nach dem Power-up ist EM MODE auf UV voreingestellt.
fragen.zitat: UV: conventional upper sideband. It is considered the standard for HF transmission and reception and is the most commonly used. After the Power Up, the EM MODE defaults to the UV mode.
kontext:
HF PAGE 1/2:

– Press LSK 5L to cycle to the operational mode:
SMPL: transmission and reception on the same frequency.
SPLT: transmission and reception frequencies differ.
ITU: frequencies in accordance with International Telecommunication Union channel designations.
EMRG: single button access to six prestored emergency frequencies.
– Press LSK 1R to cycle the squelch type:
SBH (Syllabic Squelch High): is the basic squelch type and is usual for normal voice communications. A syllabic squelch opens upon receiving a signal with voice-like characteristics while ignoring other signals.

Page 8/52 Communication REVISION 15

With syllabic squelch, there is the possibility of the first syllable of a voice reception be partially squelched. The possible adjustment levels are OFF, meaning no squelch action, minimum (MIN), medium (MED) and maximum (MAX).
SBL (Syllabic Squelch Low): is also a syllabic squelch and is intended for voice communications where the desired signal is weak and noisy. SBL is more prone to opening (no squelch action) on noise than the SBH squelch. The possible adjustment levels are OFF (no squelch action), minimum (MIN), medium (MED) and maximum (MAX).
SQH (Signal/Noise Squelch High): is a traditional signal-to-noise squelch best suited for listening to non-voice signals, or voice signals that do not respond well to one of the syllabic squelches.
Compared to the syllabic squelches, a higher signal level is required in SQH. The possible adjustment levels are 0-31, where 0 is off squelch.
SQL (Signal Level Squelch): is a signal strength squelch which opens on any strong input signal. It opens quickly on strong signals, however also opens on strong noise or static. Use of SQL is recommended for use only with strong signals and under low noise conditions. SQL is suitable for music broadcasts. The possible adjustment levels are 0-31, where 0 is off squelch.
– Selection of squelch level:
IIf SQL or SQH squelch type is selected, the squelch level defaults to 0. The entry of an update value is done via the scratchpad or through the tuning knob on the MCDU. To use the tuning knob, place the box on the squelch level value, by pressing the LSK 3R.
In the case of numeric keys, enter the squelch level value and press the LSK 3R.
If SBL or SBH squelch type is selected, the squelch defaults to OFF. Pressing the respective LSK varies the squelch mode. During the Power Up, the HF type defaults to SQL.
– Press LSK 5R to select EM MODE (emission mode):

UV: conventional upper sideband. It is considered the standard for HF transmission and reception and is the most commonly used.
After the Power Up, the EM MODE defaults to the UV mode.

LV: conventional lower sideband.

REVISION 15 Communication Page 9/52

AM: amplitude modulated communication. Some older stations may still use AM signals. AM is the best selection for listening to broadcast stations.
RC: reduced carrier power in single sideband for frequency tracked receivers. The HF signal is, sometimes, transmitted in a band of frequencies. When the station being contact can lock onto a transmitted frequency, it is possible to reduce power dispersion.
Thus reducing the transmission power requirements. When communicating with one of these stations, it is possible to use the RC mode.
– Press NEXT button to go to HF page 2/2.

antworten_en: UV (conventional upper sideband)

AM (amplitude modulated)
RC (reduced carrier)
fragen.erklaerung_en: UV is the default for HF, and after power-up EM MODE is preset to UV.

kontext:
ON-BOARD INERT GAS GENERATION

SYSTEM

The on-board inert gas generation system (OBIGGS) generates enriched nitrogen air. The OBIGGS receives air from bleed system through Air Preparation System (APS) and flows the enriched nitrogen air to fuel tanks. The nitrogen enriched air is an inert gas and displaces fuel vapors from tanks, minimizing the fuel flammability during normal flight and ground operation.
In case of failure of APS or OBIGGS, the EICAS message FUEL INERT SYS FAIL is displayed when the airplane is on ground.

The OBIGGS activates automatically and no flight crew action is required.

kontext:
REFUELING AND DEFUELING

There is a single pressurized refueling/defueling point and a refuel/ defuel control panel located under the right wing. When the access panel door is opened with the airplane energized, the following effects occur:
– Indication of door open displays on MFD status page and on EICAS through DOOR FUELING OPEN advisory message.
– A dedicated light illuminates the refuel/defuel adapter and the refuel/defuel control panel.
Pressurized refueling is performed with the airplane energized either by AC or battery power. A switch at the refueling panel enables selection of either power sources.

Fuel transfer between tanks on ground is also available through refuel control panel.

The refuel port on top of each wing also allows the refueling of wing fuel tanks. Gravity refueling is not available for center tank. The individual fuel quantity is displayed on EICAS or MFD synoptic page.

Fuel defueling operation is possible using suction or pressure. The defueling is controlled through the refuel control panel and use the
single pressurized refueling point. The crossfeed shutoff valve must be opened to defuel the left tank.

14-10-10

Page 12/14 Fuel System Description REVISION 14

HYDRAULIC SYSTEMS 1 AND 2 RESERVOIRS

A mechanical piston pressurizes the Hydraulic Systems 1 and 2 reservoir, which supplies fluid to the pump. From the pump, fluid is then directed to the manifold, where it is filtered and routed to the user systems.

In the return line, all the fluid is filtered again. Depending on the temperature, part of the fluid either route to the heat exchanger or directed back to the reservoir.

The pump unloader valve is used to reduce the discharge pressure of ACMP 3A during its start-up. This reduction decreases the pump torque and therefore reduce the electrical power required to start the pump.

kontext: HYDRAULIC SYSTEMS 1 AND 2 ACCUMULATOR

A pressure accumulator is designed to maintain a constant pressure during periods of transient flow demands in the operation of the Hydraulic System. To avoid pump cavitation, the accumulator also keeps a residual pressure
in the hydraulic reservoir.

kontext:
ABNORMAL OPERATION

The Hydraulic System 3 is also equipped with an overheat protection system. Normal temperature display is green, high temperature is amber reverse video, and overheat is red reverse video. High and overheat temperatures generate a CAS message.

In the event of hydraulic system overheating, the HYD 3 OVERHEAT EICAS warning message is displayed. In this case, the flight crew can manually switch OFF pumps 3A and 3B on the hydraulic system control panel.

NOTE: During an Electrical Emergency condition, the Hydraulic System 3 overheating protection system is inhibited, therefore preventing the Electric Hydraulic Pumps from being turned off automatically. In this condition, the associated EICAS messages HYD 3 HI TEMP and HYD 3 OVERHEAT are also inhibited. This inhibition prevents the flight crew from switching off the only source of hydraulic power available.

14-11-10

Page 4/6 Hydraulic System Description REVISION 15

kontext:
HYDRAULIC PUMP 2

The Electric Hydraulic Pump 1 (ACMP 1B) and the Electric Hydraulic Pump 2 (ACMP 2B) are an alternating current motor pumps. They serve as a backup for the EDP 1 and 2. The AC BUS 2 powers the ACMP 1. The AC BUS 1 powers the ACMP 2.

A three-position selector knob on the hydraulic panel enables the flight crew to select OFF, AUTO (normal operation), or ON positions.
In flight, the Electric Hydraulic Pump is activated in case of EDP or engine failure.

On ground, the Electric Hydraulic Pump is automatically activated in any of the following conditions:
– During the PBIT of the respective ACMP, or
– Opposite engine is running (N2 higher than 54%) and Emergency/ Parking Brake is released.

BRAKES
The wheels of the main landing gears are equipped with multiple carbon disks to brake the airplane. The wheels of the nose landing gear have no brakes.

The right and left rudder pedals control the right and left brakes respectively, allowing the application of differential brakes to steer the airplane.

Outboard and inboard wheels of a landing gear have independent brake systems. Hydraulic system 1 provides pressure to the outboard brakes and hydraulic system 2 provides pressure to the inboard brakes. The DC ESS BUS 1 powers the outboard brake controller, while the DC ESS BUS 2 powers the inboard brake controller.

The brake system is electronically controlled and includes:
– Normal brake
– Autobrake
– Emergency/Parking Brake.

kontext:
TOUCHDOWN PROTECTION

Touchdown protection prevents the airplane from touching down with the brakes applied. It is deactivated after a spin-up occurs or some time after touchdown without spin-up.

AUTOBRAKE

The autobrake system provides automatic braking with constant deceleration at selected rates, for landings and rejected takeoffs, and according to runway conditions. The autobrake system modulates brake pressure to maintain the deceleration rate constant.
An integrated autobrake feature on BCM1 provides automatic brake application (if selected and armed) at landing or rejected takeoff, by commanding both BCMs to apply sufficient brake pressure

to achieve desired deceleration.

14-13-20

Page 2/8 Brakes REVISION 15

The autobrake system operates only when the normal brake system is operational and provides antiskid, touchdown, and locked wheel protections.

Four autobrake levels of deceleration (RTO, LO, MED, HI) are available via a selector knob on the main instrument panel in the cockpit.

There are two modes of autobrake control:
– Rejected takeoff (RTO) mode.
– Landing mode (LO, MED, HI).

kontext:
NOSE WHEEL STEERING SYSTEM

The NLG has steer-by-wire control powered by hydraulic system 2 and electronically controlled by the Nose Wheel Steering Control Module.

The steering system is segregated from the landing gear to improve availability.

OPERATION

The nose wheel steering has three modes

of operation: the handwheel steering mode, rudder pedal steering mode, and the free wheel mode.

To engage the steering system:
– Pressurize the hydraulic system 2.
– External steering disengage switch in the engaged position.
– Press the handwheel. When released, rudder pedal steering is automatically engaged.

To save weight.

So that the steering is also available in flight.
fragen.erklaerung_en: According to the AOM, the steering system is separated from the landing gear to improve availability.

The free wheel steering is active when towing or when the normal steering system fails.

OPERATION

In the free wheel mode, the airplane can steer using the rudder, differential brakes, and asymmetrical thrust.

kontext:
2.6.1.2 Landing Procedure

For a normal landing procedure, establish the landing configuration, gear down and flaps, early on the final approach or at the outer marker on an ILS or FAF on a non-precision approach. Airspeed, power and descent rate also should be stabilized early. Changes in airspeed require changes in thrust and attitude. If the airspeed is 10 KIAS above target approach speed, an airspeed deviation is considered significant. Indicated airspeed may not be less than the VREF or VAP.
If the stabilized approach parameters are not met before reaching the stabilized approach height, initiate a go-around.

Make sure that the airplane is properly trimmed during the approach. It maximizes elevator authority for the flare or in the event of a missed approach.
Target approach speed is VAP, which is VREF plus wind correction. As the airplane approaches the touch down point, initiate the flare approximately at 20 ft to 10 ft.
Reduce the rate of descent and slowly reduce thrust levers to idle. Plan the flare so that thrust levers are at idle when the airplane touches down. Normally a 2° to 3° pitch change is enough for the flare.
Plan to touchdown at the runway touchdown zone, which is typically located 1000 ft ahead from the runway threshold. Monitor the final approach path using all reference available. Do not allow the airplane to float in ground effect, which unnecessarily increases the landing distance and risk of a tail strike.
After main wheel touches down, use autobrake or apply manual braking as required for the runway condition and length available while easing the nosewheel onto the runway. Pull the thrust reverser triggers and take the thrust

levers to reverse. Verify spoilers actuation. The autobrake disarms by gradually pressing brake pedals.
Use reverse thrust consistent with runway conditions and modulate as required.
Apply thrust reversers cautiously and observe how the airplane responds before

full reverse is used.

Use MAX REV thrust when landing over wet, slippery, and contaminated runways. Maintain MAX REV thrust until the airspeed is approximately 80 KIAS.

Smoothly reduce the engine thrust from MAX REV to MIN REV at or above 60

KIAS, and it is recommended to close the thrust reversers when reaching 30 KIAS. Thrust reverser is more effective at high speeds. The use of reverse below

60 KIAS increases the chances of foreign object ingestion by the engine.

During Emergency/Abnormal landings, the thrust reversers can be used until the airplane comes to a complete stop.

Rudder control is effective to approximately 60 kt. Rudder pedal steering is enough for maintaining directional control during the rollout. Do not use the

nosewheel steering tiller until reaching taxi speed.

As soon as the airplane leaves the runway, turn off the strobe and landing lights.

However, the nose taxi light must remain on throughout the taxi regardless of the

time of the day.
Note: Performance values calculated by the performance tool consider the threshold is crossed at the screen height and at VREF. Any increment to VREF must be considered.

kontext:
2.3.1.6 Rudder Steering use and Turning Radius

For straight ahead taxiing or for small changes of direction, the use of rudder pedal steering mode may be used. The maximum steering angle of rudder pedal is 7°.
Exercise care on the operation of the steering handle at speeds above 10 kt, as it’s very responsive.
Handwheel steering mode should be used for wider turn angles. To operate in this mode the handle must be kept pressed otherwise the system reverts to rudder pedals. Whenever the handle is pressed, the system reverts back to the handwheel steering.

The wheel deflection as function of handle deflection is not linear. For detailed information refer to AOM section 14-13.
Let the airplane move a little forward before starting a turn and avoid stopping the airplane in a turn as excessive thrust is required to start taxiing again. After

completing a turn and before stopping, center the nosewheel and allow the

airplane to roll straight ahead for a short distance.

When taxiing, make turns with the largest feasible turn radius possible. The minimum turn radius should still allow the tire closer to the center of the turn to continue rolling. When making a tight turn, the tires are subject to high lateral

loads and can experience damage. Asymmetric thrust may be used in tight turns to minimize side loads on gear and tires.

Minimize using thrust from outboard engine in 180° turn, particularly if outboard engine overhangs dusty areas next to the taxiway.
The tail tip or the wingtip, depending on each airplane model, have the largest arc while turning and determines the minimum obstruction clearance path.

2.3.1.7 180-Degree Turn

During the maneuver, maintain a ground speed around 5 kt. Exercise additional care on wet or contaminated runways, as tires may skid. Start aligned over the centerline and use the handwheel steering to turn the airplane left 30° in the direction of the runway edge. When LSP is over the runway edge apply progressively full right steering command. If necessary, use asymmetric thrust and/or differential braking. Once completed 180-degree turn, return the handwheel steering to the neutral position re-aligning the airplane with the centerline.

FULL-FACE MASK OPERATING MODES

Normal: Normal Mode provides supplemental oxygen diluted with cabin air according to the cabin pressure altitude until a preset point where the user inhales 100% oxygen. This feature is to conserve the amount of oxygen consumed from the supply source while still maintaining protective physiological levels.
100%: 100% Mode provides nondiluted oxygen to the crew regardless of cabin altitude.

Emergency: The EMER setting provides nondiluted oxygen regardless of cabin altitude, with a slightly positive pressure. Flight crew should use this setting to eliminate condensation or to purge smoke and toxic fumes that may get into the mask.

Aural warnings sound in a sequence, are never truncated, and are automatically canceled when the alerting situation no longer exists, or

kontext:
TAXIWAY TAKEOFF

The advisory, Taxiway Takeoff, aware the flight crew of excessive taxi speeds or an inadvertent takeoff on a taxiway.

The aural message consists of "On Taxiway! On Taxiway!".

The Taxiway Takeoff advisory shall be enabled when all the following conditions are met:
– Airplane is on a surface other than a runway.

kontext:
TAKEOFF CONFIGURATION WARNING

A dedicated aural warning indicates that airplane configuration is not in suitable takeoff condition. The aural warning is activated whenever the airplane is on the ground, thrust is applied, and at least one of the following conditions is met:
– Flaps are not in takeoff position ("NO TAKEOFF FLAPS").
– Flaps position is not in agreement with the Flaps position selected in the FMS Takeoff page 2/2. ("NO TAKEOFF FLAPS").
– The Emergency/Parking Brake is applied ("NO TAKEOFF
BRAKES").

– Pitch trim is out of green range ("NO TAKEOFF TRIM").
– Any spoiler panel is deployed ("NO TAKEOFF SPOILER").
More than one warning may be generated if more than one condition is met.

A test button is provided to allow checking the takeoff configuration by simulating power levers in the advanced position. If the airplane is in takeoff configuration, the voice message "TAKEOFF OK" is generated.

If the airplane is not set to takeoff configuration, the aural warning referred to the associated takeoff configuration deviation is generated.

kontext:
GROUND PROXIMITY WARNING SYSTEM

The EGPWS calculates these seven basic functions by comparing the airplane position to an internal terrain database to output alerts and displays that show the airplane situation.

Mode 1 - Excessive descent rates with SINK RATE and PULL UP aural warnings.

NOTE: Steep Approach operation implies to the airplane a vertical speed higher than the normal. For this reason
the Steep Approach mode once activated, adds fixed positive biases to both the SINK RATE curve, and the PULL UP curve permitting steeper than normal instrument approaches without unwanted alerts.

Mode 2 - Excessive terrain closure rates with TERRAIN, TERRAIN and PULL UP aural warnings.

Mode 3 - Altitude loss after takeoff with a DON'T SINK, DON'T SINK aural warnings.

Mode 4 - Unsafe terrain clearance with TOO LOW TERRAIN, TOO LOW GEAR and TOO LOW FLAPS aural warnings.

Mode 5 - Excessive deviation below glideslope with a GLIDESLOPE aural warning.

Mode 6 - Advisory callouts with BANK ANGLE, APPROACHING MINIMUMS, MINIMUMS, and selected callout altitude aural warnings.
Mode 7 - Windshear alerting as WINDSHEAR, WINDSHEAR,
WINDSHEAR.

kontext:
SYSTEM (TCAS)

The TCAS detects the nearby airplanes and display symbols to represent them. The relative or absolute altitude and the vertical motion of the other airplanes are information displayed with each symbol.

The TCAS monitors a potential collision hazard and alerts the flight crew. It interrogates the mode A, mode C, and mode S operating transponders in other airplanes and calculates the flight path of the possible intruder airplane.

If the intruder airplane is also equipped with operating TCAS, the systems communicate with each other to coordinate and generate guidance for the optimal avoidance maneuver.
NOTE: Intruder airplanes that do not have operating transponders are invisible to the TCAS.

The installed TCAS system is fully compliant with the requirements of EU 1332/2011.

fragen.zitat: TCAS FAIL is also displayed when TCAS data is invalid or when TCAS data was not correctly received for 10 s.
kontext:
TCAS STATUS ANNUNCIATIONS

The TCAS information is displayed on the MFD and PFD. There are six types of TCAS mode annunciations:
– TCAS FAIL – This annunciation is displayed when TCAS data indicates a TCAS failure.
TCAS FAIL is also displayed when TCAS data is invalid or when TCAS data was not correctly received for 10 s.

– TCAS TEST – This annunciation is displayed when the TCAS computer indicates that functional test is active.
– TCAS OFF – This annunciation is displayed when TCAS provides a valid indication that the computer is in stand by mode.
– TA ONLY – This annunciation indicates that the TCAS is not selected to provide resolution advisories or is inhibited. The TA mode provides only surveillance of the surrounding airspace. In this mode, TCAS tracks proximate airplane and generates traffic advisories. No resolution advisories are issued in this mode.
– TA/RA – This annunciation is displayed when TCAS provides a valid indication that the computer is in TA/RA mode. This annunciation is only displayed on both TCAS MFD displays. TA/RA mode is the normal operation mode providing full TCAS coverage.
In this mode, TCAS tracks airplane in the surrounding airspace and generates traffic advisories or resolution advisories, as the situation requires.
– TCAS RA FAIL – This annunciation indicates that TCAS is not able to provide resolution advisories. The annunciation is displayed if the resolution advisory data is invalid or not received for 5 s or if information required to display the TCAS RA data on the PFD is missing or failed (for example, if attitude, or groundspeed is failed or missing). This annunciation is only displayed on the PFD.

14-15-55

Page 4/10 Traffic Alert and Collision Avoidance System REVISION 12
(TCAS)

kontext:
TCAS ALTITUDE RANGE MODES

The altitude range is the region, from the present position altitude, covered by TCAS system. There are four different ways to set the TCAS altitude range:
– NORMAL: shows targets that are within 2700 ft above or below current airplane altitude.
–
ABOVE: shows targets that are within 9900 ft above and 2700 ft below current airplane altitude.

– BELOW: shows targets that are within 2700 ft above to 9900 ft below current airplane altitude.
– EXPANDED: shows targets that are within 9900 ft above or below current airplane altitude.

kontext:
TCAS PRESENTATION ON MFD

The control of TCAS system is made through the MCDU and on the MFD by the CCD.

The TCAS map overlay and TCAS zoom format are available on the MFD. The map overlay format displays the TCAS information on the navigation MAP mode, on MFD.

To show TCAS on the Map Overlay, select Traffic on the MAP menu at MFD.

The zoom format is displayed in the lower portion of MFD and has a range control. Only one format is displayed at a time.
The range is selected using the CCD knob. The ranges selectable are 6, 12, 20, 40, 80 and 120 NM.

When the Map Overlay format is deselected, the Zoom display is shown.

The TCAS controls on the MFD’s of left and right side pilots are independent from each other.

NOTE: If neither map overlay nor zoom format is displayed and the full range is lower than 50 NM and a TA or RA condition is encountered, the zoom format is automatically displayed.
fragen.frage_en: Which ranges are selectable in the TCAS zoom format?

kontext:
TCAS PRESENTATION ON PFD

On RA condition, a maneuver is recommended to increase the vertical separation (corrective RA). The command bars of flight director are removed and TCAS presents:
– Two avoidance zones, represented as red trapezoids.
– A fly to zone, represented as green rectangle.
NOTE: For RA conditions where certain ranges of vertical speed are not recommended (preventive RA), only one avoidance zone is displayed.

The TCAS status annunciation is displayed in the left lower portion of the ADI.

kontext: AURAL ANNUNCIATION
For TA conditions, the aural alert "TRAFFIC–TRAFFIC" is annunciated once.

The RA aural messages associated to displayed advisories may be the following:
– "INCREASE CLIMB, INCREASE CLIMB": Increase immediately the rate of climb.
– "INCREASE DESCENT, INCREASE DESCENT": Increase immediately the rate of descent.
– "CLIMB, CLIMB NOW! CLIMB, CLIMB NOW!": The airplane is descending and stop descending and immediate climbing is necessary to provide adequate separation.
– "DESCEND, DESCEND NOW! DESCEND, DESCEND NOW!": The airplane is climbing and stop climbing and immediate descending is necessary to provide adequate separation.
– "CLIMB, CLIMB": Begin to climb immediately at the indicated rate of climb.
– "DESCEND, DESCEND": Begin to descent immediately at the indicated rate of descent.
– "LEVEL OFF, LEVEL OFF": Reduce the vertical speed to 0 ft/min.
– "CLIMB, CROSSING CLIMB, CLIMB, CROSSING CLIMB": Start a climb at indicated rate. The flight path will cross traffic’s altitude.

kontext:
GROUND MAPPING MODE (GMAP)

This mode is used to alert the flight crew about hazards caused by ground targets, especially in areas of rapidly changing terrain, such as hilly mountainous areas.

Some advantages of Ground Mapping Mode are:
–

It displays a complete picture of terrain without the need to control tilt.
– It is possible to have one pilot working the GMAP while the other is using the WXR mode.
However, it is not intended to be used or relied on ground proximity warning.

kontext:
MODE (FSBY OVRD)

The forced standby mode is a mode not selected by the flight crew and it is active when the airplane is on the ground with ground speed less than 30 kt.

The FSBY deactivates when the RAAS is active, and the airplane is aligned with the runway.

The FSBY OVRD overrides the FSBY mode and enables the operation of the radar.

– selects the FSBY OVRD checkbox on the weather tab of the MFD, and

kontext:
STANDBY MODE (STBY)

After the power-up initialization, when the crew selects the standby mode, the radar system assumes a standby condition.
In this state, the system is still energized, but it is not transmitting any RF pulses or driving the antenna.
The radar system is monitoring inputs, performing BIT, and responding to BIT requests.
fragen.frage_en: What applies to the weather radar in standby mode (STBY)?

fragen.erklaerung_en: In STBY the system is energized, but transmits no RF pulses and does not drive the antenna; BIT continues to run.

kontext:
WINDSHEAR ESCAPE GUIDANCE MODE

The Reactive Windshear Escape Guidance

Mode provides through the Flight Director a pitch command limited to sticker shaker, and commands wings level to recover from a windshear, it minimizes altitude and airspeed loss during a windshear encounter.

It is indicated by a green "WSHR" annunciation on the FMA when activated.
The other flight director modes are canceled and go-around and takeoff modes are inhibited while in a warning windshear condition. No lateral mode is inhibited while in windshear mode.

A flight path angle of 3° and track hold.

kontext:
WINDSHEAR SYSTEM TEST

All EGPWS warning functions including the windshear warning function are tested during cockpit self-test prior to takeoff. The self-test is activated using the MCDU test page.

During the test, an amber "REACTIVE WSHEAR FAIL" message is displayed on the EICAS. A red "WSHEAR" message is displayed on the PFD and a "WINDSHEAR, WINDSHEAR, WINDSHEAR" aural message is annunciated.

If the windshear warning function of the EICAS is inoperative during the test, a "WINDSHEAR INOP" aural message is annunciated.

kontext:
8.1.10 Operational Flight Plan (OFP)

An Operational Flight Plan (OFP) shall be used for all flights and will be prepared by Operations Control (OCC).
An Operational Flight Plan (OFP) must show the name of the originator. It must be signed by the Commander (CMD) before the commencement of the flight.
By signing the Operational Flight Plan (OFP) the Commander (CMD): certifies that the flight has been planned according to the regulations stipulated in OM-A, OM-B and OM-C

confirms that he has carried out a briefing or self-briefing when operating into or out of an aerodrome category B or C or special route

flight preparation according to 8.1.0 - General Policy performed

The Commander (CMD) is responsible for the correct recording of all data required according to 8.1.10.1 - OFP – Format and Content By default the flight planning system PPS is calculating all flight plans with one destination alternate and no take-off alternate. All other destination alternates (called standard alternates) are displayed at the end of the route section of the OFP. (Refer to 8.1.10.2.4 - Destination Alternates, Notes and ATC Flightplan).
If changes to the OFP are required, the following options are available:
Task Action

change destination alternate remove destination alternate via Flight Briefing Documentation Tool or (ADDNAR calculation)

contact OCC add a second destination alternate

Additionally the The Operational Flight Plan (OFP) shall be recalculated by OCC in case of:

aircraft registration changed

or on request of the Commander (CMD)

or actual ZFM differs by more than 2000kg

In exceptional cases, if the OFP needs to be adapted and cannot be delivered to

the flight crew within reasonable time, OCC shall recalculate the OFP and communicate the changes to the flight crew. In any case, the required minimum

fuel must be reconfirmed between OCC and the flight crew. The OFP shall be

available on the EFB before block-off.

antworten: Dass das Loadsheet von der Ground Operations bereits gegengezeichnet wurde

antworten_en: That the loadsheet has already been countersigned by ground operations

kontext:
8.1.9.4 CTOT Information Message

Slot information will be sent automatically to the aircraft`s mobile phone via SMS, provided by the flight planning system PPS.
This SMS will contain CTOT time and other information. The content of the SMS is compiled by the PPS system and cannot be tailored.
At a standard tower airport (non-CDM airport) a slot extension by 10 minutes can be requested once per flight.

The request for the extension must be done within 20 minutes before the COBT (Calculated Off-block time). The COBT is calculated with CTOT minus the Taxi Time (which can be found in the CTOT information message or requested with OCC). Please call OCC latest 5 minutes before COBT for a possible slot extension.
Example: CTOT 1935 TAXITIME 0010.
Slot Extension must be made with Eurocontrol earliest at 1905 and latest 1925 (1935 minus 10 minutes). Therefore call OCC by 1920 latest for a slot extension.
OCC is responsible for the correct allocation of the respective mobile phone numbers in the PPS system.

Decoding of the SMS:
TITLE

SAM, SRM or SLC: The first slot allocation is sent with a SAM (Slot Allocation Message). All changes in a slot are sent with a SRM (Slot Revision Message).
SLC (Slot Cancelled)
ARCID

ATC callsign of the affected flight.
IFPLID

Unique identifier assigned to a flight by IFPS (Eurocontrol)
ADEP

Departure aerodrome
ADES

Arrival aerodrome
EBOB

Date of the ATC FPL in format YYMMDD
EOBT

Estimated off-block time.
The departure time according to the ATC FPL (not to be mixed up with TOBT)
CTOT

Calculated take-off time
REGUL

The name of the regulation. Maybe more than one regulation may be listed. The

first regulation listed is the most restrictive one. In case the regulation starts with the ICAO code of the arrival aerodrome the capacity at the arrival aerodrome is

restricted.

fragen.frage: Wie wird die COBT (Calculated Off-Block Time) bestimmt?
antworten: CTOT minus Taxi Time
EOBT plus Taxi Time
CTOT minus 10 Minuten
TOBT plus Slot-Toleranz
fragen.erklaerung: Die COBT entspricht der CTOT minus der Taxi Time (aus der CTOT-Information oder via OCC).
fragen.zitat: The COBT is calculated with CTOT minus the Taxi Time (which can be found in the CTOT information message or requested with OCC).
fragen.frage_en: How is the COBT (Calculated Off-Block Time) determined?
antworten_en: CTOT minus taxi time
EOBT plus taxi time
CTOT minus 10 minutes
TOBT plus slot tolerance
fragen.erklaerung_en: The COBT equals the CTOT minus the taxi time (taken from the CTOT information message or obtained from OCC).

fragen.frage: Ein IFR-Flug startet unter VFR von einem Flugplatz ohne ATS Service. Was muss der Commander sicherstellen?
antworten: Dass der ATC Flight Plan vor dem Departure gecancelt und in der Luft neu aufgegeben wird
Dass die ATD erst nach der Landing zusammen mit der ATA an OCC gemeldet wird
Dass die ATD unmittelbar nach dem Departure per Telefon (Ground Representative) oder per Funk an die zuständige ATS Unit übermittelt wird
Nichts, der ATC Flight Plan wird in jedem Fall automatisch aktiviert
fragen.erklaerung: Bei einem IFR-Flug, der unter VFR von einem Flugplatz ohne ATS startet, muss der Commander sicherstellen, dass die ATD sofort per Telefon oder Funk an die zuständige ATS Unit gemeldet wird.
fragen.zitat: an Actual Time of Departure (ATD) respectively an Actual Time of Arrival (ATA) is relayed by: phone by a qualified ground representative, or radio by the flight crew to the appropriate ATS unit immediately after departure
fragen.frage_en: An IFR flight departs under VFR from an airport without ATS service. What must the Commander ensure?
antworten_en: That the ATC flight plan is cancelled before departure and refiled in the air
That the ATD is reported to OCC only after landing together with the ATA
That the ATD is relayed immediately after departure to the appropriate ATS unit by phone (ground representative) or radio
Nothing, the ATC flight plan is always activated automatically
fragen.erklaerung_en: For an IFR flight departing under VFR from an airport without ATS service, the Commander must ensure that the ATD is relayed immediately by phone or radio to the appropriate ATS unit.
kontext:
8.1.9.3 Commander’s Responsibility

During the crew briefing the Commander (CMD) must verify that a ATC flight plan has been filed with sufficient time of notice prior to departure.
Under normal circumstances the ATS unit for the departure and arrival stations transmits Actual Time of Departure (ATD) and Actual Time of Arrival (ATA) to respective ATS units. The ATC flight plan will therefore be automatically activated and deactivated.
On the rare occasion of: an IFR flight departing under VFR from an airport without ATS service

an IFR flight ending as a VFR flight at an airport without ATS service

the Commander (CMD) must ensure that

an Actual Time of Departure (ATD) respectively an Actual Time of Arrival (ATA) is relayed by: phone by a qualified ground representative, or radio by the flight crew

to the appropriate ATS unit immediately after departure
respectively after landing.

fragen.frage: In welchem Fall sind auf dem OFP ETA und ATA zu loggen statt der Überflugzeiten?
antworten: Wenn die EET länger als 2:00 Stunden ist
Wenn der OFP mehr als 20 Waypoints enthält
Wenn der Flug ohne Destination Alternate geplant ist
Wenn die EET länger als 1:20 Stunden ist
fragen.erklaerung: Geschätzte und tatsächliche Überflugzeiten sind einzutragen; ist die EET länger als 1:20 Stunden, werden ETA und ATA geloggt.
fragen.zitat: estimated and actual times overhead (exception: ETA and ATA shall be logged if EET is longer than 1:20 hours)
fragen.frage_en: In which case are ETA and ATA to be logged on the OFP instead of the times overhead?
antworten_en: If the EET is longer than 2:00 hours
If the OFP contains more than 20 waypoints
If the flight is planned without destination alternate
If the EET is longer than 1:20 hours
fragen.erklaerung_en: Estimated and actual times overhead must be recorded; if the EET is longer than 1:20 hours, ETA and ATA shall be logged.
kontext:
8.1.10.1 OFP Content

Any Operational Flight Plan (OFP), especially when filed manually, must contain the following information before the commencement of a flight:
Header aircraft registration (correct manually if changing airplane tail number)

aircraft type and variant

date of flight

flight identification (ICAO 3-letter-code and flight number plus call-sign if different)

names of flight crew members (printed on the flight assignment)

duty assignment of flight crew members (printed on the flight assignment)

place of departure

planned place of arrival

planned time of departure (off-block and take-off)

planned time of arrival (landing and on-blocks)

planned duration of flight (block time and flight time) Route section

the planned route of the flight, route segments with the respective

checkpoints, waypoints, distances, tracks, time en-route

the relevant minimum en-route altitudes for each route segment

the speed schedule for each route segment

the altitude or flight level selection for each route segment

the planned destination

the destination alternate

the take-off alternate if required

fuel calculations

During the flight operation the Operational Flight Plans (OFP) must be completed and all fields filled out. It shall be understood as a working document on the flight deck.
The following information must be recorded:
Header changes in aircraft registration (aircraft change)

actual place of arrival (if different from planned place of arrival)

actual time of departure (off-block and take-off)

actual time of arrival (landing and on-blocks)

actual duration of flight (block time and flight time)

Route section fuel calculations (fuel on board when starting engines, in-flight fuel checks)
estimated and actual times overhead (exception: ETA and ATA shall be logged if EET is longer than 1:20 hours)

changes of routing

Meteorological section ATIS at the place of departure ATIS at the place of arrival

relevant meteorological information en-route, alternates etc.

General section

in-flight re-planning calculations, if required

alternate for take-off, en-route

initial and subsequent ATC clearances

fragen.frage: Ein angepasstes OFP kann der Crew nicht rechtzeitig geliefert werden. Was muss in jedem Fall geschehen?
antworten: Die erforderliche Minimum Fuel muss zwischen OCC und Flight Crew rückbestätigt werden
Der Flug muss bis zum Eintreffen des neuen OFP verschoben werden
Die Crew rechnet den OFP selbst und unterschreibt ihn ohne Rücksprache
Es ist zusätzlich 10 % Extra Fuel zu tanken
fragen.erklaerung: OCC rechnet den OFP neu und übermittelt die Änderungen; in jedem Fall muss die erforderliche Minimum Fuel zwischen OCC und Crew rückbestätigt werden. Der OFP muss vor Block-off auf dem EFB verfügbar sein.
fragen.zitat: In any case, the required minimum fuel must be reconfirmed between OCC and the flight crew. The OFP shall be available on the EFB before block-off.
fragen.frage_en: An amended OFP cannot be delivered to the crew in time. What must happen in any case?
antworten_en: The required minimum fuel must be reconfirmed between OCC and the flight crew
The flight must be delayed until the new OFP arrives
The crew calculates the OFP itself and signs it without consultation
An additional 10 % extra fuel must be uplifted
fragen.erklaerung_en: OCC recalculates the OFP and communicates the changes; in any case the required minimum fuel must be reconfirmed between OCC and the crew. The OFP shall be available on the EFB before block-off.

kontext:
8.1.2.4 Aerodrome Categorisation for Flight Crew Competence

All aerodromes in helvetic operation are categorized according to characteristics as listed below and may, therefore, require special aerodrome competence training according to 5.2.13 - Route and Aerodrome Competence Qualification.
A list of categorised airports used by helvetic is included and maintained in Winops and available to flight crews on the distribution tool OM-C, Airport Categorisation.
Additionally, the aerodrome category will be displayed in the Flight Assignment Flight Crew Briefing. Category B airports are indicated either as (B) without aerodrome competence sheet,
or as (B ac) aerodrome competence sheet available in the OM-C. Category C airports shall always have an aerodrome competence sheet in OM-C.

kontext:
8.1.7.3.1 Taxi Fuel

Taxi fuel contains the total amount of fuel expected to be used prior to take-off, including allowances for local conditions as:
NOTAMs

meteorological conditions (e.g. winter operations, remote de-icing)

ATS procedures (e.g. LVP, collaborative decision-making (CDM))

APU operation

any anticipated delays (e.g. long taxi times)

The OFP includes a common type specific amount of taxi fuel. Any anticipated additional required amount of fuel shall be added by the flight crew.
Additional required taxi fuel may be planned in section discretionary fuel considering the fuel check before take-off

according to 8.3.7.2 - Fuel Monitoring and Fuel Checks.
Aircraft Type Taxi Fuel E-Jet 200 kg

fragen.frage: Wofür wird Contingency Fuel u.a. mitgeführt?
antworten: Für Abweichungen des einzelnen Flugzeugs von den erwarteten Verbrauchsdaten
Für das Holding am Destination Alternate
Für Economic Tankering bei Preisunterschieden
Für MEL-bedingte Mehrverbräuche gemäss Dispatch

fragen.frage_en: What is contingency fuel carried for, among other things?
antworten_en: Deviations of an individual aircraft from the expected fuel consumption data
Holding at the destination alternate
Economic tankering due to price differences
MEL-related additional consumption according to dispatch
fragen.erklaerung_en: Contingency fuel compensates for unforeseen factors such as deviations of an individual aircraft from expected consumption, weather deviations, delays and routing deviations.
kontext:
8.1.7.3.3 Contingency Fuel

At the planning stage not all factors, which could have an influence on the fuel used to the destination aerodrome, can be foreseen. Consequently,
contingency fuel is carried to compensate for items such as: deviations of an individual aircraft from the expected fuel consumption data

deviations from forecast meteorological conditions

extended unexpected delays in flight

extended unexpected taxi times

unexpected deviations from planned routings and cruising levels

Contingency fuel shall be as follows:

at holding speed at at holding speed at 3% of the planned 1500 ft above the destination airport in 1500 ft above the destination airport in trip fuel from departure to standard conditions standard conditions destination 2

kontext:
8.1.7.3.4 Alternate Fuel

Alternate fuel includes the amount of fuel required for: a missed approach from the applicable DA/H or MDA/H at the destination aerodrome to the missed-approach altitude, taking into account the complete missed-approach procedure

the climb from the missed approach altitude to the cruising level/altitude, taking into account the expected departure routing

the cruise from the Top of Climb (TOC) to the Top of Descent (TOD), taking into account the expected routing
the descent from the top of descent to the point where the approach is initiated, taking into account the longest STAR

the approach and landing at the destination alternate airport

Note: The departure aerodrome may be selected as the destination alternate aerodrome.
In case of two filed alternates according to 8.1.7.6 - Procedure with Closed Destination the greater amount of fuel shall be calculated on the OFP.

Mit der ZFM plus Contingency Fuel

Deviation of the aircraft from consumption data

kontext:
8.1.7.3.7 Extra Fuel

Extra fuel to take into account anticipated delays or specific operational constraints (e.g. maintenance work on a runway causing a delay to the normal

traffic flow of inbound traffic,

specific ATS procedure published by a NOTAM,

icing conditions during climb out, longer routing due to curfew during night-time).

kontext:
8.3.7.5.2 Minimum Fuel State Declaration

When having committed to land at a specific airport, the flight crew shall declare “MINIMUM FUEL” if any change to the existing flight plan (e.g. holding, rerouting) may result in a landing with less than planned final reserve.
This is not an emergency call, but Air Traffic Control (ATC) is informed about a possible emergency situation.

fragen.frage: Fuelling with Passengers on Board: Wann darf die Betankung beginnen?

kontext:
8.2.1.5 Fuelling with Passengers on Board

During normal operations it may be necessary to fuel or de-fuel an aircraft with passengers on board. Passengers may embark, disembark or remain on board during fuelling and de-fuelling operation provided that the following precautions are observed: local procedures must be verified and adhered to

a member of the flight crew must remain on the flight deck

a two way communication between the flight crew member in the cockpit and a cabin crew member in the cabin must be established

a two way communication between ground crew supervising the refuelling and the qualified personnel on board the airplane is assured (via intercommunication system, direct person-to-person contact or any other method of communication)

fuelling personnel shall be informed that passengers will be on board during fuelling and immediate communication to a flight crew member being on the flight deck shall be established either via inter-communication system or direct person-to-person contact

all cabin crew members shall be informed by the Commander (CMD).
For callouts refer to 8.3 App. 1 - Communication Wording CSPM 2 Appendix 1 Communication Wording

all cabin crew members shall be able to communicate among cabin crew members and passengers (e.g. via PA, hand signals (body language) or megaphone)

cont.
the fuelling may start only after positive confirmation of the Senior cabin crew member (SEN) towards the Commander CMD has taken place

verifying that the following precautionary measures are taken (for callouts refer to 8.3 App. 1 - Communication Wording CSPM 2 Appendix 1 Communication Wording): the fasten seat belt signs must be off, the no smoking signs must be on, together with interior lighting to enable emergency exits to be identified

passengers are to be briefed not to smoke at any time on the ground and to remain seated until the fuelling has been completed, refer to OM- 0 4 CCM

in principle, for all aircraft types, at least a minimum of two passenger cabin doors shall be opened and passenger stairs jetways must be positioned at these doors

if only one passenger stair jetway is available, the requirement for the second passenger cabin door may be met by positioning a cabin crew member, who will remain at a second door throughout the refuelling process. The door should not be automatic armed, unless required in an emergency

in the cabin, a cabin crew member shall be positioned next to the boarding door and be prepared for an immediate emergency evacuation, the rest of the cabin crew members shall be positioned in the vicinity of their assigned doors/exits (refer to CSPM 5 Standard

Operation Position/Area “Fuelling with Passengers on Board”) on all exits the outside-area shall remain clear during fuelling operations

routes to the emergency exits shall be unobstructed

if the presence of fuel vapour is detected inside the aircraft, or any other

hazard arises fuelling or de-fuelling shall be stopped immediately

if deemed necessary by the crew, a de-boarding shall be performed via the stairs or an evacuation via the escape slides, if deemed necessary limited to

the non-spilled side

fuelling and de-fuelling with wide cut fuel (e.g. Jet B or equivalent) is prohibited with passengers on board

after completion of fuelling the Commander (CMD) will notify the Senior

cabin attendant (SEN) which means that normal duties may be resumed.
For callouts refer to 8.3 App. 1 - Communication Wording

CSPM 2 Appendix 1 Communication Wording

Commander (CMD) is responsible for evaluating the situation on the particular airport at the given time, and determining a person responsible for the fueling operation and communication to the flight crew during fueling with passengers on board. That can be one of the following positions: ground staff (ideally flight supervisor)

fueling personnel, should there be means of communication with the flight crew in place

one of the flight crew members

If none of the above positions can assure proper supervision, fueling with passengers on board shall not be performed.

fragen.frage: Was gehört nach dem Fuelling zu den Punkten, die der Commander (oder ein von ihm nominiertes Crew Member) bestätigt?
antworten: Dass ein Gross Error Check durchgeführt wurde
Dass eine Fuel-Probe auf Wasser getestet wurde
Dass der Fuel Provider das Loadsheet unterschrieben hat
Dass die Fuel-Dichte genau 0.8 kg/l beträgt
fragen.erklaerung: Bestätigt werden u.a. Typ, Grade und Menge der Fuel, korrekter Tech Log-Eintrag und dass ein Gross Error Check durchgeführt wurde.
fragen.zitat: the detail of the fuel uplift has been correctly entered into the technical log a gross error check is carried out
fragen.frage_en: Which item is among those confirmed after fuelling by the Commander (or a crew member nominated by him)?

That a fuel sample has been tested for water
That the fuel provider has signed the loadsheet
That the fuel density is exactly 0.8 kg/l
fragen.erklaerung_en: Among others, the type, grade and quantity of fuel, the correct tech log entry and the carrying out of a gross error check are confirmed.
kontext:
8.2.1.3 Crew Checks

By deducting the fuel remaining from the previous flight, as recorded in the technical log and indicated on the aircraft fuel gauges, the flight crew calculates the amount of fuel required.
After the completion of the fuelling process the flight crew compares the actual fuel indicated with the planned ramp fuel, and the actual uplift with the planned uplift.
The Commander (CMD), or a crew member nominated by him, will confirm that: the correct type, grade and quantity of fuel has been loaded

the fuel panel and other accessories are properly secured the aircraft fuel gauges indicate that the tanks have been filled to the

required levels

the detail of the fuel uplift has been correctly entered into the technical log

a gross error check is carried out

For flight planning purposes the wind expected at 1 hour before and 1 hour after the estimated time of arrival must be within type specific OM-B limits considering the expected runway condition and type of operation (e.g. autoland).
For crosswind and tailwind components gusts shall be considered.

kontext:
8.1.5.3.3 Take-Off Alternate

Aerodrome Ceiling Type of Operation (cloud base or RVR/VIS vertical visibility) Type B instrument approach n.a. RVR operations according to OM-C Type A instrument approach ceiling at or above RVR/VIS operations DA/MDA according to OM-C Circling Approach ceiling at or above circling minima operations MDA Crosswind planning minima as per table 8.1.6.2 - Wind Limitations Wind limitations should be applied taking into account the runway condition.

For the take-off alternate aerodrome, any limitations related to OEI operations shall be taken into account
(e.g. LFSB; NOTAM states that CAT II/III operation is u/s. OEI minima is therefore CAT I minima and may be used for pre-flight planning).

Engine out service ceiling shall be taken into account.
The take-off alternate for two engine aircraft must be located within a range of 1 hour flight time at One Engine Inoperative (OEI) cruising speed according to

the AFM in still air standard conditions based on the actual take-off mass.
If a take-off alternate is required, the flight crew shall contact OCC to recalculate the Operational Flight Plan (OFP). OCC shall verify, that the distance to the take- off alternate is within the great circle distance mentioned in

8.1.2.2.4 - Distance from Adequate Aerodrome and all the requirements according to

8.0.2.25 - Weather-permissible Aerodrome (former suitable aerodrome) are

fulfilled.

kontext:
8.1.5.5.2 Planning without Destination Alternate

A flight may be planned without destination alternate, provided: the duration of the planned flight from take-off to landing does not exceed 6 hours,
or in the event of in-flight re-planning, the remaining flight time to destination does not exceed 4 hours

two separate runways are usable at the destination

the appropriate meteorological reports and/or forecasts indicate that for the period from 1 hour before to 1 hour after the expected time of arrival, the ceiling is at least 2 000 ft (600 m) or the circling height plus 500 ft (150 m), whichever is greater, and ground visibility is at least 5 km

no adverse weather forecast (e.g. thunderstorm, sandstorm, fog-patches irrespective of PROB or TEMPO in the forecast)

the wind is within AFM/OM-B limits for the planned approach, no gusts, no wind shears expected or forecast braking action at least medium

Refer to 8.1.7.3.6 - Additional Fuel for ADDNAR fuel considerations.

Note: Runways on the same airport are considered to be separate runways when they are separate landing surfaces, each having an approach

procedure based upon a separate navigation aid, which may overlay or cross such that, if one of the runways is blocked, it will not prevent the

planned operation on the other runway.

8.1.5.5.2 Planning without Destination Alternate

A flight may be planned without destination alternate, provided: the duration of the planned flight from take-off to landing does not exceed 6 hours, or in the event of in-flight re-planning, the remaining flight time to destination does not exceed 4 hours

two separate runways are usable at the destination

the appropriate meteorological reports and/or forecasts indicate that for the period from 1 hour before to 1 hour after the expected time of arrival, the ceiling is at least 2 000 ft (600 m) or the circling height plus 500 ft (150 m), whichever is greater, and ground visibility is at least 5 km

no adverse weather forecast (e.g. thunderstorm, sandstorm, fog-patches irrespective of PROB or TEMPO in the forecast)
the wind is within AFM/OM-B limits for the planned approach, no gusts, no wind shears expected or forecast braking action at least medium

Nein, Fog Patches sind unabhängig von PROB oder TEMPO ein Ausschlussgrund
Ja, wenn zusätzliche ADDNAR Fuel geladen wird
Ja, solange zwei separate Runways verfügbar sind

kontext:
8.7.4.2 Weather Conditions for Level-B Non-Revenue Flights

For level-B non-revenue flights following conditions shall be fulfilled: daytime only

the actual and forecast weather (ETD and ETA 1h) at the departure and destination at least the applicable minima for CAT I operation
no adverse weather forecast (e.g. thunderstorm, sandstorm, fog-patches irrespective of PROB or TEMPO in the forecast)

braking action at least medium

For training flights the following additional conditions should be fulfilled: the actual and forecasted wind conditions (ETD and ETA +/-1h) at the departure and destination airport shall be within the limitations for alternate airport as stipulated in 8.1.6.2 - Wind Limitations

the actual and forecasted visibility (ETD and ETA +/-1h) at the departure and destination airport shall be 5000m

the actual and forecasted ceiling (ETD and ETA +/-1h) at the departure and destination airport shall be 2000ft

If the additional conditions for training flights cannot be met, the Nominated

Person training (TNG) must be informed by the designated instructor.
After due considerations as stated in Process Manual OM-D (PMOD) 5.2 Adverse Conditions for Training Flights, the Nominated Person Training (TNG) shall explicitly approve the flight training in written form.

Deviations from the above mentioned policy for weather conditions for level-B

non-revenue flights may be granted by the Accountable Manager (ACM)

according to the actual requirements for:

delivery flights

demonstration flights

The Accountable Manager (ACM) may, however, require more restrictive weather

conditions to be met.

8.1.5.5.4 Planning based on Fuel En-route Alternate (Fuel-ERA)

A flight may be planned with a contingency fuel of 3%, provided that a Fuel En- route Alternate (Fuel-ERA) has been selected.
For the Fuel-ERA the following applies: the Fuel-ERA shall be located within a circle with a radius equal to 20% of the total flight plan distance

the centre of this circle lies on the planned route at a distance from the destination aerodrome, whichever is greater: equal to 25% of the total flight plan distance or at least 20% of the total flight plan distance plus 50 NM

the Fuel-ERA shall be nominated in the operational flight plan

kontext:
8.0.2.1 Adequate Aerodrome

An adequate aerodrome means an aerodrome on which the airplane can be operated, taking into account the following characteristics: performance requirements: runway length, slope, obstacles

runway characteristics: Pavement Classification Number (PCN), grovement

obstacle situation in the approach, missed approach and departure sectors

approach facilities (navaids, electronic and visual aids)

ancillary services: Air Traffic Services (ATS), lighting, meteorological reports, emergency services (fire fighting and rescue)

ground service facilities: fuelling, loading, deicing, general handling and the availability of immigration authorities

local conditions such as special weather situations, night flying restrictions or even political aspects which might affect operations

An adequate aerodrome must both pre-flight and in-flight be available at the expected time of use and be within range according to 8.1.2.2.4 - Distance from

Adequate Aerodrome.
However, meteorological conditions according to 8.1.3 - Methods for Determination of Aerodrome Operating Minima and 8.1.6 - Interpretation of

Meteorological Information do not have to be fulfilled neither preflight nor in-

flight for such aerodromes.

8.4.1.3 Category II Approaches

For type specific limitations regarding use of autopilot for CAT II approaches refer to type specific OM-B.
The DH shall be determined by the use of a radio altimeter and be not lower than the highest of: the minimum DH specified in the type specific AFM or the applicable obstacle clearance height (OCH) for the category of aircraft or

(DH) and Aircraft Category:

kontext:
8.4.1.4 Category III Approaches

A category III (CAT III) approach is a precision approach with lower than CAT II minima. Where the Decision Height (DH) and Runway Visual Range (RVR) do not fall within the same category, the RVR will determine in which category the operation is to be considered.
In contrast to other operations, some category III weather minima do not provide sufficient visual references to allow a manual landing. The minima only permit the pilots to decide if the aircraft will land in the touchdown zone and to ensure safety during roll-out. Therefore an automatic landing system is mandatory to perform category III operations. Its reliability must be sufficient to control the aircraft to touchdown and if applicable during roll-out phase until reaching a safe taxi speed.
The DH shall be determined by the use of a radio altimeter and be not lower than the highest of: the minimum DH specified in the type specific AFM or the DH to which the flight crew is qualified to operate

Operations with no DH should only be conducted if: operation with no DH is specified in the type specific AFM

there is no published information indicating that the approach aid or aerodrome facilities cannot support operations with no DH

the flight crew is qualified to operate with no DH The minimum RVR is a function of the Decision Height (DH):

DH (ft) Roll-out Control Guidance System RVR (m)

50 – 99 not required 175

fail-passive 125 0 – 40 or no DH fail-operational 75

8.0.2.2 Approach Ban

VIS RVR and Landing Performance Assessment If the reported visibility (VIS) or controlling RVR for the runway to be used for landing is less than the applicable minimum, or the landing performance assessment according to 8.3.2.25 - Runway Condition Assessment indicates that a safe landing cannot be assured, then an instrument approach operation shall not be continued: past a point at which the airplane is 1 000 ft above the aerodrome elevation or into the final approach segment (FAS) if the DH or MDH is higher than 1 000 ft

If the required visual reference is not established, then a missed approach shall be executed at or before the DA/H or the MDA/H.
If the required visual reference is not maintained after DA/H or MDA/H, then a balked landing shall be executed promptly.
In the case where no RVR is reported,

kontext:
8.4.8.3 ATC Low Visibility Procedures

The ATC Low Visibility Procedures (LVP) are ground procedures at the airport, designed to prevent the entry of ground vehicles and taxiing aircraft into areas protected for take-off and landing. In addition they protect the sensitive areas of the ILS transmission and regulate the flow of air traffic on the approach.
ATC Low Visibility Procedures (LVP) become effective when the touch down zone (TDZ) Runway Visual Range (RVR) falls to 600 m or below or the ceiling is 200 ft or below. ATC will always report the touch down zone (TDZ) Runway Visual Range (RVR).

Midfield point (MID) RVR values and roll-out RVR values will only be reported if: they are less than the TDZ RVR and below 800 m

when less than 400 m

when requested by the pilot

kontext:
8.4.4 Low Visibility Take-off (LVTO)

A Low Visibility Take-off (LVTO) is a take-off with the reported Runway Visual Range (RVR) of less than 550 m.
However, if at the airport of departure no Low Visibility Procedures (LVP) are established, or
if established Low Visibility Procedures are not in force, the lowest authorized RVR for take-off is 400 m.

For further details refer to 8.1.3.3 - Take-off Minima.

The maximum Runway Visual Range (RVR) at take-off is rather independent of the aircraft type and aircraft equipment, with the exception of very low Runway Visual Range (RVR) values. The take-off minima are mainly determined by the airport installations (e.g. runway lighting system, RVR measurement system).

A static take-off shall be performed if the visibility RVR is at or close to the take-

off minimum.

For the static take-off procedure refer to type specific OM-B.

If it is necessary to abandon the take-off and visibility is very limited, directional

control with reference to the runway lights will become progressively more difficult as speed is reduced, especially with brake application. As soon as the

first red white centreline lights pass under the nose of the aircraft, there are

900 m of runway left and ground speed should in no case be higher than 100 kts.
Remember that the far end of the runway may have less braking action due to

rubber deposit. If all centreline lights are red, there is less than 300 m runway available and action should be taken accordingly.

Note: The closer centreline and touchdown zone lights cannot be seen as clearly as those further away because of a relatively low light beam

angle.

OM-A 8 Operating Procedures

kontext:
8.4.2 Flight Preparation

In addition to the normal flight preparation, the following planning and preparation must be performed when Low Visibility Operation (LVO) is in force. review of the NOTAMS to ensure that the destination airport meets visual or non-visual Category II or III requirements: runway and approach lighting malfunction or degradation radio navigation aid availability RVR equipment availability ILS category changes

aircraft status: check of the aircraft Tech Log for deferred defects or other entries that affect any equipment required for Category II or III
crew qualification and recency: both Commander (CMD) and Copilot (COP) must be qualified and current for Low Visibility Operation (LVO)

weather information: the weather forecast at destination must be within airplane and crew operating minima MOTNE or SNOWTAM can give an indication of runway contamination

and braking action The alternate airport must be carefully selected, taking into consideration primarily the weather, but also the available passenger services and traffic restrictions. A take-off alternate is needed if a return to the departure airport is

not possible in case of equipment or engine failure during take-off.

Extra fuel should be considered due to increased taxiing times prior to take-off, taxiing to remote anti-ice stations or possible delays on arrival, longer separation

and possibility of go-around and second approach.

kontext: 2.5.3.5.6 Autoland

AUTOLAND 1 consists of approach, touchdown, and 5 seconds of rollout.
AUTOLAND 1 can be accomplished on CAT I, II or III approaches.

Autoland can be performed with or without autothrottle and autobrake and with one engine inoperative.

Note: If an engine fails on final approach, initiate a go-around.
If a go-around is required after a non-autoland approach, crew must be

aware that the parallel ruder engages and actuates when GO-AROUND

mode (GA) is active and the Autopilot is engaged. Once the first vertical

mode is engaged, or the ALT mode is engaged after the altitude set on

the altitude preselector is reached, the parallel rudder servo is de- energized requiring pilot input on the rudder pedals to maintain directional control.

During final approach (AEO or OEI), the system logic applies the crab technique in case of crosswind landing until 150 ft. Below 150 ft, sideslip is applied.
Loss of parallel rudder servo during Autoland disengages the autopilot causing the loss of Autoland capability.
If a go-around with autopilot engaged is required after an Autoland approach, or after a non-autoland approach, loss of parallel rudder servo disengages the autopilot.
Note: Loss of parallel rudder servo may be caused by a servo rudder system fail or by the pilots applying excessive force on the rudder pedals when

the parallel rudder servo is engaged. EICAS messages AP RUDDER NOT AVAIL and AUTOLAND 1 (2) NOT AVAIL are associated to the loss of rudder servo.

GO-AROUND

Perform the go-around procedure in the order given. If the flaps are set out of

position 5 before pressing the TO/GA button (to engage the GO-AROUND

mode), the active approach mode disengages. The flight director reverts to track

mode. The parallel rudder servo remains engaged. No pilot input to maintain directional control is required until the first vertical flight director mode is

engaged.
Once the first flight director vertical mode is engaged, or the ALT mode is

engaged after the altitude set on the altitude preselector is reached, the parallel rudder servo is de-energized, and may require pilot input.

MALFUNCTIONS

If IMC, any malfunction that pilot judges would compromise the final approach and also the flare maneuver below CAT II MINIMA should lead to an immediate

go-around.

kontext:
2.8.5.2.1 CAT II Engagement Logic

The Primus Epic integrated Avionics has a CAT II logic which is automatically activated whenever the RA/BARO Knob is set to RA position. A green APPR 2 annunciator indicates the correct setting and a white or amber APPR 1 ONLY annunciator indicates an incorrect setting. The green APPR 2 annunciator is displayed in the Autopilot Approach Status Annunciator above each FMA.

Note: Although the radio altitude setting may be adjusted down to 80 ft, if requested by an ILS CAT II Approved Chart, the Decision Height (DH) is limited to 100 ft above ground level.

2.8.5.2.1.1 CAT II Conditions of Operation

CAT II is allowed only with the green APPR 2 annunciator enabled.

To obtain a green APPR 2 annunciator the following conditions must be met:
Radio altitude below 1500 ft.

SLAT/FLAP 5.

NAV 1 on pilot's side and NAV 2 on copilot's side, both NAVs tuned to the same LOC frequency.

An active approach GS/LOC mode selected. Both courses set to same value.

Both Flight Directors operational.

Attitude and Heading valid on both PFDs.

Glide slope and Localizer deviation valid on both PFDs.

Independent IRS and ADC sources selected on both PFDs.

Valid Airspeed and Baro Altitude on both PFDs.

No comparison monitors are tripped (FPA, Altitude, Heading, Airspeed,

Baro Altitude, Localizer, Glide Slope and Radio Altitude) on both PFDs.

No back course selected.

The EICAS message APPR 2 NOT AVAIL not presented.

RA BARO Selector set to RA.

Both DISPLAY CONTROLLER Panels set to the same CAT II Decision Height.

Note: If the CAT II Instrument Approach and Landing chart do not authorize the use of RA, set RA to OFF (MINIMUMS Controller (INNER) set to 0 ft). In this case, there are no EGPWS callouts "APPROACHING MINIMUMS" and
"MINIMUMS".

When the green APPR 2 annunciator is enabled, the localizer lateral deviation scale is expanded with the external limits representing the excessive deviation points.

If one of these conditions is not met, the green APPR 2 annunciator will not appear.
If the green APPR 2 annunciation is displayed and one of the following conditions is achieved, the amber APPR 1 ONLY annunciation will flash active characters inverse video for 5 s then steady in conjunction with the RA Minimum Selected Digital Readout:

No valid Radio Altitude displayed.

Airplane no longer APPR 2 capable.

Crew selects flaps position other than 5 below 800 ft.

EICAS message SLAT-FLAP LEVER DISAG displayed.

Either Minimums Selected Readouts change from RA to BARO.

LOC frequency or inbound course mismatch.

kontext:
8.3.9 Wake Turbulence

Wake turbulence is generated by air exchange due to the pressure differential between the lower and upper surface of the wing. This exchange causes counter rotating vortices trailing from the outer wing tips. The larger the aircraft the larger are the vortices. The wake of a large aircraft may require large control inputs on an aircraft flying in the area behind it. These control inputs may exceed the roll control capability of the following aircraft. The flight crew must be aware of the location of the vortex flow generated by a preceding aircraft and adjust his flight path accordingly.
Tests with large and heavy aircraft have shown that the vortex flow field – in a plane cutting through the wake at any point downstream – covers an area about twice the wing span in width and one wing span in depth. The vortices from the two tips remain spaced and will drift with the wind. The vortices will sink with a rate of descent of 400 – 500 fpm. There is a tendency that the vortices will level off at about 800 – 1 000 ft below the flight path. Vortex strength diminishes with time and distance behind the aircraft.
Vortex generation will begin on rotation when the nose wheel lifts off the ground and ends, when the nose wheel touches down on landing. In conditions with very weak or calm winds, the remaining vortices from a landing aircraft may persist up to 5 minutes or even longer.
All this has prompted National Aviation Authorities (NAA) and ICAO to establish minimum separation criteria.

OM-A 8 Operating Procedures

ICAO Definitions The International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) classifies aircraft into wake turbulence categories based on their maximum certificated take-off mass (MTOM) and the strength of the wake vortices they generate.
Category MTOM Examples Light (L) 7.000 kg Cessna 172
Medium (M) 7.000 kg - 136.000 kg Embraer E-Jets Heavy (H) (1) 136.000 kg Boeing 747

Super (J) exceptionally strong wake turbulence Airbus A380

Note 1: Some types like the Boeing 757, despite having an MTOM below 136.000 kg, are treated as Heavy due to their strong wake turbulence.

Note: In the United Kingdom the aircraft series Boeing 707, DC-8, VC-10 and IL-62 are considered medium (M) and shall be announced as such in the initial contact with ATC. However, this regulation does not affect the composition of flight plans which shall be completed in accordance with the ICAO wake turbulence categorisation.

ICAO Wake Turbulence Separation Leading

Following Radar Non Radar Aircraft Aircraft heavy EN Separation 6 NM Separation 3 minutes super medium 7 NM 3 minutes

light 8 NM 4 minutes

heavy 4 NM 2 minutes
