Route Manual Tool – Europe Airway Manual – Air Traffic Control – Air Traffic Control Data Europe – RECAT EU Note: Embraer 190/195-E1 are classified as Lower Medium (CAT-E).
Embraer 190/195-E2 are classified as Upper Medium (CAT-D).

Additional Information Apart from the above ICAO or RECAT standards for vortex separation, the controller or the flight crew may arrange for a larger separation to compensate for calm conditions or for other terrestrial factors, which might enforce or retain the vortex energy for a longer time. The same may apply for operations into parallel or near parallel runways, where in crosswind situations the danger may exist, that vortices are encountered from a preceding aircraft approaching or departing from the parallel runway.
On the other hand separation may be reduced in strong crosswind conditions when operating into or out of single runway environments.
A departing aircraft will not be permitted to commence take-off until the preceding departing aircraft has crossed the end of the runway-in-use or has started a turn or until all preceding landing aircraft are clear of the runway-in-use.
A landing aircraft will not be permitted to cross the beginning of the runway on its final approach until the preceding departing aircraft has crossed the end of the

runway-in-use, or has started a turn, or until all preceding landing aircraft are clear of the runway-in-use.
More information can be found in OM-C Chapter Rules and Regulation.
In case adequate separation cannot be provided or when vortices are

encountered despite adequate separation, the following should be remembered:

during approach and landing behind a vortex generating aircraft, landing

should be aimed at a touch down point at the runway past the touch down

point of the heavier aircraft – if runway length permits

when taking-off, the lift-off point of the preceding aircraft should be remembered; if possible arrangement shall be made for a lift-off point well

before the lift-off point of the preceding aircraft; if this cannot be done,

delaying the take-off for some seconds – depending upon the size of the preceding aircraft and wind conditions on ground may be considered

when approaching behind a vortex generating aircraft, it should be realized,

that flying above the flight path of the preceding aircraft means to avoid the vortex zones – at least until short before touch down.

Mental preparation to abandon the approach using proper Operations Manual OM-B technique including use of maximum thrust setting is important.

fragen.frage: Warum erhöht kreuzender Verkehr, der in der Nähe steigt oder sinkt, das Risiko einer en-route Wake Turbulence?
antworten: Steigende Flugzeuge erzeugen keine Wirbel, sinkende dagegen doppelt starke
Die RVSM-Separation wird dabei auf 500 ft reduziert
Die Wirbel steigen mit 400 ft/min und treffen den Follower von unten
Die Wake kann den Flugweg des Followers mit minimaler Zeit zum Zerfall kreuzen
fragen.erklaerung: Steigt oder sinkt kreuzender Verkehr in der Nähe, kann die erzeugte Wake den Flugweg des Followers mit minimaler Zerfallszeit kreuzen, sodass stärkere Wake Turbulence auftreten kann.
fragen.zitat: crossing traffic is climbing or descending in proximity (either the generating or following airplane), the wake generated might cross the follower’s trajectory with minimum time for decay, so stronger wake turbulence might be encountered
fragen.frage_en: Why does crossing traffic climbing or descending in proximity increase the risk of en-route wake turbulence?
antworten_en: Climbing aircraft generate no vortices, descending ones twice as strong
RVSM separation is then reduced to 500 ft
The vortices rise at 400 ft/min and hit the follower from below
The wake may cross the follower's trajectory with minimum time for decay
fragen.erklaerung_en: If crossing traffic climbs or descends in proximity, the generated wake may cross the follower's trajectory with minimum time for decay, so stronger wake turbulence may be encountered.
kontext:
8.3.9.1 En-route Wake Turbulence

En-route, the vortices evolves in altitudes at which the rate of decay leads to a typical persistence of 2-3 minutes, with a typical sink rate of about 400ft/min.
Wakes will also be transported by wind.
Considering the high operating air speeds in cruise and the standard 1000 ft vertical separation in RVSM airspace, wake turbulence can be encountered up to 25 nautical miles (NM) behind the generating airplane. The most significant encounters are reported within a distance of 15 NM. However, no specific horizontal wake turbulence separation minima are detailed within PANS-ATM for en-route flight, with states utilising procedural or surveillance-based separation minima.
The encounters are mostly reported by pilots as sudden and unexpected events.
The awareness of hazardous traffic configuration and risk factors is therefore of particular importance to anticipate, avoid and manage possible wake encounters.
In the en-route phase of flight, three major factors contribute to increase the likelihood of wake turbulence: crossing traffic situation: In the case that

crossing traffic is climbing or descending in proximity (either the generating or following airplane), the wake generated might cross the follower’s trajectory with minimum time for decay, so stronger wake turbulence might be encountered

thermal tropopause altitude: Wake vortex decays more slowly below the tropopause where there is therefore an increased risk of encountering

severe wake turbulence weight of the generating airplane: Heavier airplane types generate stronger wake vortices and are likely to induce more severe wake turbulence encounters, especially for smaller airplane types

The typical hazardous trajectory crossing configurations are the following. They

are shown hereafter in a vertical plane, although the respective flight path might

also be crossing on the horizontal plane. When crossing horizontally, the lower

the crossing angle the higher the wake effect. See the following examples.

8.1.0 General Policy

EASA Air Operations uses the following expressions: planning (pre-flight (i.e. before off-block))

fuel management and in-flight re-planning (always in-flight)

During the planning stage, before commencement of each flight or series of flights, flight crews shall perform flight preparation duties to include: current maps (enroute) and charts (e.g. STAR, IAC, SID, taxi charts)

aerodrome operating hours and NOTAMs: aerodromes of departure, en- route alternates (ERA), fuel enroute alternate (Fuel-ERA), destination, destination alternate, additional ones up to the flight crew

during check-in, enroute area NOTAMs can usually not be consulted in a realistic manner as clear references to defined waypoints are usually missing. However, in case of flights into areas which dictate to do so (e.g. unfamiliar areas outside Central Europe, politically critical countries) enroute NOTAMs shall be checked.
Based on ICAO regulations, NOTAMs are limited to a period of validity up to 90 days. Should this limit be exceeded, the NOTAM must be judged as being suspect

and its validity should be verified in case of any operational relevance

meteorological conditions at departure, en-route alternates (ERA), destination and destination alternate: general weather, wind, visibility and ceiling (if required) RNP APCH operations: before selecting a destination, where the approach

depends exclusively on RNAV capability respectively on GPS-reception and

functionality, related NOTAMs shall be considered

RAIM shall be verified and granted at ETA 15 minutes: for RAIM-prediction and Fault Detection and Exclusion (FDE) refer

to 8.3.2.8.3 - RNAV and RNP Specification and Accuracy Matrix (only applicable for RNP APCH)

operational Flight Plan (OFP)

airplane performance: take-off and landing calculations, mass and balance

airplane airworthiness and status with special attention regarding the planned operation (RVSM, MNPS; etc): Aircraft Technical Log (ATL),

Minimum Equipment List (MEL) and Configuration List (CDL)

The flight will be accepted and initiated by the Commander by signing the OFP.

kontext:
8.3.8.2 Thunderstorms

Thunderstorms are classified as:

frontal thunderstorms

air mass thunderstorms

Frontal thunderstorms may exist as:

warm front thunderstorms

cold front thunderstorms

occluded front thunderstorms

Air mass thunderstorms are divided into:

convective thunderstorms

orographic thunderstorms

Frontal thunderstorms form in squall lines and generate heavy rain and possibly hail and produce strong gusty winds and possibly tornadoes.
Large horizontal wind changes in speed and direction at different altitudes are characteristic for a frontal thunderstorm. Resulting airflows in the storm accelerate to much higher vertical speeds, which ultimately results in higher horizontal wind speeds at the surface.
Air mass thunderstorms are caused either by thermal convection or by moist air moving uphill on the windward side of a mountain.
Air mass thunderstorms appear to be randomly distributed in unstable air and develop from local heating of the earth’s surface. As the heated air rises it cools and subsequently forms cumulus clouds. As the cumulus stage continues to develop, precipitation forms in the higher portion of the cloud and falls out.
Precipitation signals the beginning of the mature stage and pressure of a downdraft.
In the later stages of development, the heated updraft creating the thunderstorm is cut off by rainfall, and the thunderstorm begins to dissipate. Many thunderstorms produce an associated cold air gust front as a result of the down flow and out rushing rain-cooled air. These gust fronts are usually very turbulent and are a serious threat during take-off and landing.
The vertical extension of thunderstorms is up to 25 000 ft during winter time and up to the troposphere during summer, the horizontal range is 10 to 20 km.
Besides the dangerous situations already mentioned, there may be additional dangers from sudden heavy precipitation with poor visibility below the clouds, possibly hail showers, heavy icing formation, and severe turbulence.

Lightning is not a direct danger for the crew and passengers of an aircraft in flight, as the electrical load will remain at the surface of the aircraft (Faraday Cage). Lightning strikes may, however, disturb or damage the navigation system.

If storm clouds have to be over flown, vertical separation from cloud tops of at least 5 000 ft must always be maintained. It is difficult to estimate this separation, but Air Traffic Control (ATC) or meteorological charts may provide information about the altitude of the cloud.
If the aircraft is not equipped with radar or if the radar is inoperative, any cloud that appears, through visual inspection: tall,

or growing rapidly, or with an anvil top

shall be laterally avoided by at least 10 NM.

The radar equipment shall be intermittently operated on long ranges in order to

avoid the development of situations where no alternative remains but the penetration of hazardous areas.

Flying under a cumulonimbus overhang shall be avoided, too. If it is unavoidable, antenna tilt shall occasionally be selected to full up to determine, if possible, whether precipitation (which may be hail) exists in or is falling from the overhang.
Flight crews are strongly advised to continue monitoring the weather radar in order to select the safest track for penetration under all circumstances.
The local activity of thunderstorms can often be of relatively short nature, (i.e. 20 to 30 minutes).

Therefore, if a take-off or landing is planned during times of thunderstorm activity, consideration of the development of the storm shall determine whether avoidance of the worst effects can be accomplished with a delay.

Calculate difference in temperature between FL180 (500 hPa) and FL50 (850 hPa).
If difference is: 25° or less: no ts or very unlikely

26° - 27°: ts possible

28° - 31°: ts likely

32° or more: severe ts likely

kontext:
8.3.8.5 Wind Shear

In order to avoid dangerous wind shear phenomena it is important to know what wind shear is and in which meteorological and geographical environment it can be expected.
The following definition seems to be the most suitable for aviation:

wind shear is any rapid change in wind direction or speed along the flight path of an aircraft

Wind shear, with or without turbulence, alters the lift force acting on an aircraft, resulting in a significant sinking or rising motion.

Therefore, wind shear may be categorized as:

increasing performance shear caused by increasing headwind or decreasing

tailwind component or vertical updrafts

decreasing performance shear caused by decreasing headwind or

increasing tailwind component or vertical downdrafts

Conditions for potentially hazardous wind shears are: convective conditions (e.g. thunderstorms, rain or snow showers)

frontal systems

jet streams

strong or gusty surface winds

other cases (temperature inversion, mountain waves, sea breeze circulations)
Wind shear events are typically one to two miles in diameter and mostly occur near the ground (typically below 500 ft AGL) during take-off and landing.

Both situations would see the aircraft in a low energy condition. Therefore, there is only limited time for wind shear recognition and counteraction, typically 5 to 15 seconds.
Several factors can impede wind shear recognition: marginal weather conditions

high crew work load conditions

illusion of normality; during the initial part of the wind shear encounter, everything may appear normal; even severe wind shear onset may not

provide dramatic early indications to the flight crew

Standard response of the flight crew should be: control of flight path through pitch attitude; resistance to a downward change

in pitch attitude as normal response to low airspeed

immediate increase of thrust, maximum thrust shall be applied

an approach shall be aborted

unusual stick forces may be required to maintain pitch attitude during

airspeed variations away from normal target airspeed

low airspeed must be accepted, flying at airspeeds below normal reference

speeds may be required in order to utilize the full performance capability of the aircraft (speed increments under expected wind shear threat are stated

in Operations Manual OM-B)

The term downburst describes a severe downward rush of air and its outburst of

damaging winds near the ground. It has been classified into macroburst and microburst. They are different in their size with radial outflow at the earth’s surface lasting from 3 to 20 minutes.

Downbursts can occur wherever convective weather conditions exist.
Approximately 5% of all thunderstorms produce microburst.
Downdrafts associated with microburst are typically only a few hundred to thousand meters across. When the downburst hits the ground, it spreads out horizontally and may form one or more horizontal vortex rings around the downdraft up to 2 000 ft AGL.
In downbursts with vortices very powerful updrafts and roll forces in conjunction with wind speed changes up to 45 knots can be expected.
The time period over which wind speeds exceed half the peak value may last from 1 to 8 minutes. Depending on the movement and the height of the base of parent cloud, microburst may occur as: stationary or moving

surface or midair

wet or dry

Microburst has occurred in relatively dry conditions of light rain or precipitation that evaporates before reaching the earth’s surface.
Frontal wind shear is present in both cold and warm fronts, but exists in a different relative location in each type of front. Because the cold front boundary slopes back behind the frontal surface, the wind shear line also slopes back. The frontal boundary of the warm front slopes upward ahead of the surface front and

so does the wind shear. Significant wind shears can be expected if there is a large difference in surface temperature 6°C) across the front and if the front is moving rapidly at more than 30 knots.
Large wind speeds changes near the ground can be found in many

meteorological situations, including the frontal conditions. Terrain irregularities or

buildings, which interrupt the wind flow, can produce significant wind shears close to the ground.

kontext:
8.3.2.26 Approach Briefing

The approach briefing shall be conducted for a mental preparation and to address the procedures intended to apply for arrival, approach, missed approach, landing and after landing.

The briefing shall be completed well before the commencement of the actual approach.
However, the approach briefing should only be started after the actual meteorological information is available which gives an indication about the approach and runway in use.

It may also include procedures for non-normal situations and conditions.
The awareness briefing should be conducted before the approach briefing.
If the flight deck jump seat is occupied, the occupant shall be briefed according to 8.3.12 - Admission to Flight Deck, unless completed before (during departure briefing).

The Pilot Flying (PF) briefs the Pilot Monitoring (PM) about: chart number(s)

mental picture (1) clearance limit

lateral and vertical situation (2) constraints

runway details

ground operation

FMS verification (can be done independently at an earlier stage)

approach minimum (DA or MDA)

aircraft configuration

missed approach procedure FMS verification (can be done independently at an earlier stage)

initial aircraft manipulation

initial lateral and vertical profile including constraints

setting and use of navigation equipment use of the auto flight system (other than default values)

landing and missed approach performance calculation including FMS data

verification

For additional briefing items in connection with Low Visibility Operations (LVO),

refer to 8.4.5.4 - Category II or III Crew Briefing.

Note 1: Applicable charts shall be worked through systematically (including

verification of notes and remarks) and the FMS-loaded data shall be verified according to 8.3.2.26.1 - FMS-loaded Procedure Verification.

However, if the approach is well known by both pilots, the point “mental picture” may be shortened to FMS verification. The completion of the

verification shall be confirmed to each other during the briefing (e.g. “GIPOL28 transition and ILS 28 verified”).

Note 2: Where a rate of descent of more than 1.000 fpm will be required on

final approach (e.g. due to high ground speed or a steeper-than-normal approach path), this shall be briefed.

kontext:
8.1.9 ATC Flight Plan

The standards of ICAO Annex 2 require the submission of an ATC flight plan for all IFR flights. In the dense European region the ATC flight plan is usually the basis for the allocation of an airway slot.
Another purpose of an ATC Flight Plan is to ensure Search and Rescue (SAR) actions if a flight would become overdue at destination.

The ATC flight plan is printed at the end of the Operational Flight Plan (OFP), refer to 8.1.10 - Operational Flight Plan Refer to OM-C Route Manual

8.1.9.1 helvetic Company Procedure

The flight crew must ensure that an ATC flight plan is filed for any flight.
The OCC will provide: repetitive flight plans

individual ATC flight plans

well ahead of the intended time of operation. A copy of the flight plan must be handed to the flight crew with the flight request form.

kontext:
8.1.9.4 CTOT Information Message

Slot information will be sent automatically to the aircraft`s mobile phone via SMS, provided by the flight planning system PPS.
This SMS will contain CTOT time and other information. The content of the SMS is compiled by the PPS system and cannot be tailored.
At a standard tower airport (non-CDM airport) a slot extension by 10 minutes can be requested once per flight. The request for the extension must be done within 20 minutes before the COBT (Calculated Off-block time). The COBT is calculated with CTOT minus the Taxi Time (which can be found in the CTOT information message or requested with OCC). Please call OCC latest 5 minutes before COBT for a possible slot extension.
Example: CTOT 1935 TAXITIME 0010.
Slot Extension must be made with Eurocontrol earliest at 1905 and latest 1925 (1935 minus 10 minutes). Therefore call OCC by 1920 latest for a slot extension.
OCC is responsible for the correct allocation of the respective mobile phone numbers in the PPS system.

Decoding of the SMS:
TITLE

SAM, SRM or SLC:
The first slot allocation is sent with a SAM (Slot Allocation Message). All changes in a slot are sent with a SRM (Slot Revision Message).

SLC (Slot Cancelled)
ARCID

ATC callsign of the affected flight.
IFPLID

Unique identifier assigned to a flight by IFPS (Eurocontrol)
ADEP

Departure aerodrome
ADES

Arrival aerodrome
EBOB

Date of the ATC FPL in format YYMMDD
EOBT

Estimated off-block time.
The departure time according to the ATC FPL (not to be mixed up with TOBT)
CTOT

Calculated take-off time
REGUL

The name of the regulation. Maybe more than one regulation may be listed. The

first regulation listed is the most restrictive one. In case the regulation starts with the ICAO code of the arrival aerodrome the capacity at the arrival aerodrome is

restricted.

FUEL Policy: General:
Tankering is a practice whereby an airplane carries more fuel than required for a flight in order to reduce or avoid refueling at the destination airport.
Tankering is categorized as either operational (e.g. fuel supply shortage) or economic (due to significant fuel price difference).

The following fuel policies exist:

(e.g. due to significant fuel price difference) TANKERAGE economic tankerage shall be included in

fragen.frage: Next Flights Page: aktueller Flug A-B GAIN 500 $/T, danach B-C LOSS 150 $/T, C-D LOSS 200 $/T, D-E LOSS 200 $/T. Bis wohin ist ein Through-Tankage wirtschaftlich?
antworten: Bis D, weil die summierte LOSS (350 $/T) kleiner als der GAIN ist
Bis E, weil jeder einzelne LOSS kleiner als der GAIN ist
Nur bis B, weil auf dem nächsten Flug ein LOSS entsteht
Bis C, weil nur der direkt folgende Flug betrachtet wird
fragen.erklaerung: Through-Tankage bleibt wirtschaftlich, solange die summierte LOSS der Folgeflüge kleiner als der GAIN des aktuellen Flugs ist: bis D sind es 350 $/T, bis E wären es 550 $/T.
fragen.zitat: A through-tankage to D will be economical since the LOSS on flight 1 (B-C) and flight 2 (C-D) together (350$/T) is still less than the GAIN on the actual flight
fragen.frage_en: Next flights page: actual flight A-B GAIN 500 $/T, then B-C LOSS 150 $/T, C-D LOSS 200 $/T, D-E LOSS 200 $/T. Up to where is through-tankage economical?
antworten_en: Up to D, because the summed-up LOSS (350 $/T) is less than the GAIN
Up to E, because each single LOSS is less than the GAIN
Only up to B, because the next flight shows a LOSS
Up to C, because only the directly following flight is considered
fragen.erklaerung_en: Through-tankage remains economical as long as the summed-up LOSS of the following flights is less than the GAIN on the actual flight: 350 $/T up to D, 550 $/T up to E.
kontext:
8.1.10.2.2 Next Flights Page

Next Flights:
In case the fuel price/index for the departure and destination aerodrome is available in the flight planning system a GAIN/LOSS calculation is displayed.
This analysis is made for every flight individually and does not include any calculations from a previous or next flight. In order to see if a through-tankage is economical for more than one leg some information of the following flights on the same aircraft (in case already calculated) are shown in a table.

In case of a GAIN on the actual flight (first page of the OFP) a through-tankage may be economical as long as the LOSS on the following flights together is less

than the GAIN on the actual flight. As soon as the summed-up LOSS becomes more than the GAIN on the actual flight a through-tankage further is not economical anymore. In case of another GAIN on the following flight a through- tankage may be economical in case the GAIN on the actual flight is higher than on the following flight. Any weight/performance limitations (e.g. landing weight)

must be taken into account additionally.

Example 1:

Actual Flight (A-B): GAIN 500$/T Next Flight 1 (B-C): LOSS 150$/T

Next Flight 2 (C-D): LOSS 200$/T

Next Flight 3 (D-E): LOSS 200$/T
A through-tankage to D will be economical since the LOSS on flight 1 (B-C) and flight 2 (C-D) together (350$/T) is still less than the GAIN on the actual flight
(500$/T). A through-tankage to E is not economical since the summed-up LOSS of the following flights (550$/T) would be more than the GAIN on the actual flight

kontext:
8.2.1.6 Mixing of Fuel – Fuel Contamination

Mixing of fuel is only permitted as specified in the Operations Manual OM-B 1.
Flight and ground crews should be aware of possible fuel contamination, particularly at smaller airports.
If in a doubt or when told to do so by Operations Control Center (OCC), fuel samples shall be taken to check for contaminants.
This shall be coordinated with the fuel provider and, in case of contaminated fuel, maintenance shall be contacted.

8.0.2.25 Weather-permissible Aerodrome (former suitable aerodrome)

An adequate aerodrome where, for the anticipated time of use (i.e. ETA 1

hour), meteorological reports, or forecasts, or any combination thereof, indicate that the meteorological conditions will be at or above the required aerodrome

operating minima,
and the runway surface condition reports indicate that a safe landing will be possible.

kontext:
8.1.2.1 Approval

Before an airport is first utilised for helvetic operations it must be approved by the Nominated Person Flight Operations (FOP). He will only approve an operation to or from an adequate aerodrome which will allow for the application of normal operating procedures. These normal operating procedures must not only be applicable for take-off, approach and landing, but shall also cover all aspects of ground operation.
For the approval of an adequate aerodrome all aspects of 8.0.2.1 - Adequate Aerodrome shall be considered.
Only adequate aerodromes may be used as departure, take-off alternate, destination, destination alternate or en-route alternate.
For an emergency aerodrome refer to 8.0.2.8 - Emergency Aerodrome.

8.1.2.1.1 Categorised Airport List

The categorised airport list is designed to enhance crew awareness regarding the selection of en-route alternate and emergency aerodromes.

Im Holding über der Destination auf Wetterbesserung warten

fragen.zitat: Therefore, a diversion to an enroute alternate shall be initiated as soon as the flight crew becomes aware of such a situation, taking into account the remaining fuel on board.

kontext:
8.3.2.24 Meteorological Information

Enroute Monitoring:
During enroute phases current weather reports (e.g. ATIS, METAR via ACARS, VOLMET) shall be checked and recorded for: adequate, emergency aerodrome or Fuel Enroute Alternate (Fuel-ERA) during the time where an enroute diversion to that aerodrome would be considered in case of a sudden need

destination alternate(s) if either conditions at the destination itself or the destination alternate are likely to be critical due to any reasons (e.g. traffic situation, meteorological conditions, political unrest, strike, increased threat, technical issues)

Refer to 2.4.7.7 - Flight Monitoring for further information regarding flight continuation, diversion or termination.

Destination Monitoring:
The latest available meteorological information must be obtained and evaluated before commencing an approach. Due regard must also be given to the runway surface conditions. The best source of information during this part of a flight provides the ATIS.
Flight crews are allowed to start any approach into an aerodrome until reaching a

certain height which is defined in 8.4.5.7 - Approach Ban.
However, the situation in-flight might change in such a way that according to the latest information a landing cannot be made at both the destination and destination alternate.

Therefore, a diversion to an enroute alternate shall be initiated as soon as the

flight crew becomes aware of such a situation, taking into account the remaining

fuel on board.

kontext:
8.4.7 Failures and Associated Actions

In general there are three possible responses to the failure of any system, instrument or other element during the approach. continuation of the approach to the planned minima

reversion to higher minima

go-around and reassessment of the capabilities

The nature of the failure and the point of its occurrence will determine which response is appropriate.
As a general rule, if a failure occurs above 1000ft AGL, the approach may be continued reverting to a higher Decision Height (DH), providing the appropriate conditions are met

(refer to 8.4.1.3 - Category II Approaches and 8.4.1.4 - Category III Approaches for the respective minima).
Below 1000 ft AGL the occurrence of any failure implies a go-around and a reassessment of the system capabilities. Another approach may then be initiated to the appropriate minima for the given aircraft status.
For exceptions consult the aircraft type specific Operations Manual OM-B E1 2.5.3.5.5 - Malfunctions

OM-B E2 2.5.3.5.5 - Malfunctions

This rule has been adopted under the consideration that below 1000 ft AGL there is not sufficient time left for the crew to perform the necessary switching, to check system configuration and limitations and to brief for new minima. In a category III dual (fail operational) situation, however, a single failure below the Alert Height

(AH) does not necessitate a go-around.

2.5.3.5 ILS CAT II III

manual landing is intended for a CAT II approach, select AUTOLAND OFF on MENU MISC MENU OPR CONFIG Page 1/1.

The pilots ensure correct approach mode (APPR2 or AUTOLAND) is

annunciated on the FMA, and monitors the ILS APPR mode.
During the approach, the pilot places one hand on the throttles, guarding the TO/GA button. The other hand is kept on the control column near or next to the autopilot disconnect button.

At 80 ft above DH, when “Approaching Minimums” callout is announced, the pilot responds continuing the approach and diverts the scan to outside visual cues. When the “Minimums” automatic callout is announced, one of the following occurs:
If the proper CAT II III visual cues are not present, or if the airplane is not in a position which a descent to the runway can be made, the pilot selects TO/GA button and executes the go- around. The pilots should monitor the instruments for deviation from a normal go-around profile.

If the proper CAT II III visual cues are identifiable, and a descent to landing can be made at a normal descent rate which allows touchdown within the

touchdown zone, proceed to land (or monitor the Autoland system, if applicable). Monitor flight instruments until touchdown and any deviations from the normal descent and speed profile should be warned.

kontext:
8.3.9 Wake Turbulence

Wake turbulence is generated by air exchange due to the pressure differential between the lower and upper surface of the wing. This exchange causes counter rotating vortices trailing from the outer wing tips. The larger the aircraft the larger are the vortices. The wake of a large aircraft may require large control inputs on an aircraft flying in the area behind it. These control inputs may exceed the roll control capability of the following aircraft. The flight crew must be aware of the location of the vortex flow generated by a preceding aircraft and adjust his flight path accordingly.
Tests with large and heavy aircraft have shown that the vortex flow field – in a plane cutting through the wake at any point downstream – covers an area about twice the wing span in width and one wing span in depth. The vortices from the two tips remain spaced and will drift with the wind. The vortices will sink with a rate of descent of 400 – 500 fpm. There is a tendency that the vortices will level off at about 800 – 1 000 ft below the flight path. Vortex strength diminishes with time and distance behind the aircraft.
Vortex generation will begin on rotation when the nose wheel lifts off the ground and ends, when the nose wheel touches down on landing. In conditions with very weak or calm winds, the remaining vortices from a landing aircraft may persist up to 5 minutes or even longer.
All this has prompted National Aviation Authorities (NAA) and ICAO to establish minimum separation criteria.

OM-A 8 Operating Procedures

ICAO Definitions The International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) classifies aircraft into wake turbulence categories based on their maximum certificated take-off mass (MTOM) and the strength of the wake vortices they generate.
Category MTOM Examples Light (L) 7.000 kg Cessna 172 Medium (M) 7.000 kg - 136.000 kg Embraer E-Jets Heavy (H) (1) 136.000 kg Boeing 747 Super (J) exceptionally strong wake turbulence Airbus A380

Note 1: Some types like the Boeing 757, despite having an MTOM below 136.000 kg, are treated as Heavy due to their strong wake turbulence.

Note: In the United Kingdom the aircraft series Boeing 707, DC-8, VC-10 and IL-62 are considered medium (M) and shall be announced as such in the initial contact with ATC. However, this regulation does not affect the composition of flight plans which shall be completed in accordance with the ICAO wake turbulence categorisation.

ICAO Wake Turbulence Separation Leading

Following Radar Non Radar Aircraft Aircraft heavy EN Separation 6 NM Separation 3 minutes super medium 7 NM 3 minutes

heavy medium 5 NM 2 minutes

light 6 NM 3 minutes

heavy 3 NM 2 minutes

medium medium 3 NM 2 minutes light 4 NM 2 minutes

heavy 3 NM 2 minutes

RECAT-EU Defintions For RECAT-EU definitions refer to:
Route Manual Tool – Europe Airway Manual – Air Traffic Control – Air Traffic Control Data Europe – RECAT EU Note: Embraer 190/195-E1 are classified as Lower Medium (CAT-E).
Embraer 190/195-E2 are classified as Upper Medium (CAT-D).

Additional Information Apart from the above ICAO or RECAT standards for vortex separation, the controller or the flight crew may arrange for a larger separation to compensate for calm conditions or for other terrestrial factors, which might enforce or retain the vortex energy for a longer time. The same may apply for operations into parallel or near parallel runways, where in crosswind situations the danger may exist, that vortices are encountered from a preceding aircraft approaching or departing from the parallel runway.
On the other hand separation may be reduced in strong crosswind conditions when operating into or out of single runway environments.
A departing aircraft will not be permitted to commence take-off until the preceding departing aircraft has crossed the end of the runway-in-use or has started a turn or until all preceding landing aircraft are clear of the runway-in-use.
A landing aircraft will not be permitted to cross the beginning of the runway on its final approach until the preceding departing aircraft has crossed the end of the

runway-in-use, or has started a turn, or until all preceding landing aircraft are clear of the runway-in-use.
More information can be found in OM-C Chapter Rules and Regulation.
In case adequate separation cannot be provided or when vortices are

encountered despite adequate separation, the following should be remembered:

during approach and landing behind a vortex generating aircraft, landing

should be aimed at a touch down point at the runway past the touch down

point of the heavier aircraft – if runway length permits

when taking-off, the lift-off point of the preceding aircraft should be remembered; if possible arrangement shall be made for a lift-off point well

before the lift-off point of the preceding aircraft; if this cannot be done,

delaying the take-off for some seconds – depending upon the size of the preceding aircraft and wind conditions on ground may be considered

when approaching behind a vortex generating aircraft, it should be realized,

that flying above the flight path of the preceding aircraft means to avoid the vortex zones – at least until short before touch down.

Mental preparation to abandon the approach using proper Operations Manual OM-B technique including use of maximum thrust setting is important.

kontext:
8.3.9.1 En-route Wake Turbulence

En-route, the vortices evolves in altitudes at which the rate of decay leads to a typical persistence of 2-3 minutes, with a typical sink rate of about 400ft/min.
Wakes will also be transported by wind.
Considering the high operating air speeds in cruise and the standard 1000 ft vertical separation in RVSM airspace, wake turbulence can be encountered up to 25 nautical miles (NM) behind the generating airplane. The most significant encounters are reported within a distance of 15 NM.
However, no specific horizontal wake turbulence separation minima are detailed within PANS-ATM for en-route flight, with states utilising procedural or surveillance-based separation minima.

The encounters are mostly reported by pilots as sudden and unexpected events.
The awareness of hazardous traffic configuration and risk factors is therefore of particular importance to anticipate, avoid and manage possible wake encounters.
In the en-route phase of flight, three major factors contribute to increase the likelihood of wake turbulence: crossing traffic situation: In the case that crossing traffic is climbing or descending in proximity (either the generating or following airplane), the wake generated might cross the follower’s trajectory with minimum time for decay, so stronger wake turbulence might be encountered

thermal tropopause altitude: Wake vortex decays more slowly below the tropopause where there is therefore an increased risk of encountering

severe wake turbulence weight of the generating airplane: Heavier airplane types generate stronger wake vortices and are likely to induce more severe wake turbulence encounters, especially for smaller airplane types

The typical hazardous trajectory crossing configurations are the following. They

are shown hereafter in a vertical plane, although the respective flight path might

also be crossing on the horizontal plane. When crossing horizontally, the lower

the crossing angle the higher the wake effect. See the following examples.

kontext:
8.3.8.2 Thunderstorms

Thunderstorms are classified as:

frontal thunderstorms

air mass thunderstorms

Frontal thunderstorms may exist as:

warm front thunderstorms

cold front thunderstorms

occluded front thunderstorms

Air mass thunderstorms are divided into:

convective thunderstorms

orographic thunderstorms

Frontal thunderstorms form in squall lines and generate heavy rain and possibly hail and produce strong gusty winds and possibly tornadoes.
Large horizontal wind changes in speed and direction at different altitudes are characteristic for a frontal thunderstorm. Resulting airflows in the storm accelerate to much higher vertical speeds, which ultimately results in higher horizontal wind speeds at the surface.
Air mass thunderstorms are caused either by thermal convection or by moist air moving uphill on the windward side of a mountain.
Air mass thunderstorms appear to be randomly distributed in unstable air and develop from local heating of the earth’s surface. As the heated air rises it cools and subsequently forms cumulus clouds. As the cumulus stage continues to develop, precipitation forms in the higher portion of the cloud and falls out.
Precipitation signals the beginning of the mature stage and pressure of a downdraft.
In the later stages of development, the heated updraft creating the thunderstorm is cut off by rainfall, and the thunderstorm begins to dissipate. Many thunderstorms produce an associated cold air gust front as a result of the down flow and out rushing rain-cooled air. These gust fronts are usually very turbulent and are a serious threat during take-off and landing.
The vertical extension of thunderstorms is up to 25 000 ft during winter time and up to the troposphere during summer, the horizontal range is 10 to 20 km.
Besides the dangerous situations already mentioned, there may be additional dangers from sudden heavy precipitation with poor visibility below the clouds, possibly hail showers, heavy icing formation, and severe turbulence.

Lightning is not a direct danger for the crew and passengers of an aircraft in flight, as the electrical load will remain at the surface of the aircraft (Faraday Cage). Lightning strikes may, however, disturb or damage the navigation system.

OM-A 8 Operating Procedures

Flight Weather Radar Echo Characteristics Altitude Gradient of Rate of Shape Intensity (in 1000 ft) Intensity Change avoid by avoid by avoid by avoid by 10 NM 10 NM echoes 5 NM echoes 5 NM echoes echoes with with with showing 0 20 hooks fingers, sharp edges or strong rapid change scalloped edges strong gradients of of shape, or other intensities intensity height or protrusions intensity 20 25 avoid all echoes by 10 miles 25 30 avoid all echoes by 15 miles above 30 avoid all echoes by 20 miles

If storm clouds have to be over flown, vertical separation from cloud tops of at least 5 000 ft must always be maintained. It is difficult to estimate this separation, but Air Traffic Control (ATC) or meteorological charts may provide information about the altitude of the cloud.
If the aircraft is not equipped with radar or if the radar is inoperative, any cloud that appears, through visual inspection: tall,

or growing rapidly, or with an anvil top

shall be laterally avoided by at least 10 NM.

The radar equipment shall be intermittently operated on long ranges in order to

avoid the development of situations where no alternative remains but the penetration of hazardous areas.
Flying under a cumulonimbus overhang shall be avoided, too. If it is unavoidable, antenna tilt shall occasionally be selected to full up

to determine, if possible, whether precipitation (which may be hail) exists in or is falling from the overhang.
Flight crews are strongly advised to continue monitoring the weather radar in order to select the safest track for penetration under all circumstances.
The local activity of thunderstorms can often be of relatively short nature, (i.e. 20 to 30 minutes). Therefore, if a take-off or landing is planned during times of thunderstorm activity, consideration of the development of the storm shall determine whether avoidance of the worst effects can be accomplished with a delay.
Rule of thumb to estimate buildup of thunderstorms (ts):
Calculate difference in temperature between FL180 (500 hPa) and FL50 (850 hPa).
If difference is: 25° or less: no ts or very unlikely

26° - 27°: ts possible

28° - 31°: ts likely

32° or more: severe ts likely

kontext:
8.3.8.5 Wind Shear

In order to avoid dangerous wind shear phenomena it is important to know what wind shear is and in which meteorological and geographical environment it can be expected.
The following definition seems to be the most suitable for aviation:

wind shear is any rapid change in wind direction or speed along the flight path of an aircraft

Wind shear, with or without turbulence, alters the lift force acting on an aircraft, resulting in a significant sinking or rising motion.

Therefore, wind shear may be categorized as:

increasing performance shear caused by increasing headwind or decreasing

tailwind component or vertical updrafts

decreasing performance shear caused by decreasing headwind or

increasing tailwind component or vertical downdrafts

Conditions for potentially hazardous wind shears are: convective conditions (e.g. thunderstorms, rain or snow showers)

frontal systems

jet streams

strong or gusty surface winds

other cases (temperature inversion, mountain waves, sea breeze circulations)

Wind shear events are typically one to two miles in diameter and mostly occur near the ground (typically below 500 ft AGL) during take-off and landing. Both situations would see the aircraft in a low energy condition. Therefore, there is only limited time for wind shear recognition and counteraction, typically 5 to 15 seconds.
Several factors can impede wind shear recognition: marginal weather conditions

high crew work load conditions

illusion of normality; during the initial part of the wind shear encounter, everything may appear normal; even severe wind shear onset may not

provide dramatic early indications to the flight crew

Standard response of the flight crew should be: control of flight path through pitch attitude; resistance to a downward change

in pitch attitude as normal response to low airspeed

immediate increase of thrust, maximum thrust shall be applied

an approach shall be aborted

unusual stick forces may be required to maintain pitch attitude during

airspeed variations away from normal target airspeed

low airspeed must be accepted, flying at airspeeds below normal reference

speeds may be required in order to utilize the full performance capability of the aircraft (speed increments under expected wind shear threat are stated

in Operations Manual OM-B)

The term downburst describes a severe downward rush of air and its outburst of

damaging winds near the ground. It has been classified into macroburst and microburst. They are different in their size with radial outflow at the earth’s surface lasting from 3 to 20 minutes.

Downbursts can occur wherever convective weather conditions exist.
Approximately 5% of all thunderstorms produce microburst.
Downdrafts associated with microburst are typically only a few hundred to thousand meters across.
When the downburst hits the ground, it spreads out horizontally and may form one or more horizontal vortex rings around the downdraft up to 2 000 ft AGL.

In downbursts with vortices very powerful updrafts and roll forces in conjunction with wind speed changes up to 45 knots can be expected.
The time period over which wind speeds exceed half the peak value may last from 1 to 8 minutes. Depending on the movement and the height of the base of parent cloud, microburst may occur as: stationary or moving

surface or midair

wet or dry

Microburst has occurred in relatively dry conditions of light rain or precipitation that evaporates before reaching the earth’s surface.
Frontal wind shear is present in both cold and warm fronts, but exists in a different relative location in each type of front. Because the cold front boundary slopes back behind the frontal surface, the wind shear line also slopes back. The frontal boundary of the warm front slopes upward ahead of the surface front and

so does the wind shear. Significant wind shears can be expected if there is a large difference in surface temperature 6°C) across the front and if the front is moving rapidly at more than 30 knots.
Large wind speeds changes near the ground can be found in many

meteorological situations, including the frontal conditions. Terrain irregularities or

buildings, which interrupt the wind flow, can produce significant wind shears close to the ground.

kontext:
8.3.2.26 Approach Briefing

The approach briefing shall be conducted for a mental preparation and to address the procedures intended to apply for arrival, approach, missed approach, landing and after landing.

The briefing shall be completed well before the commencement of the actual approach. However, the approach briefing should only be started after the actual meteorological information is available which gives an indication about the approach and runway in use. It may also include procedures for non-normal situations and conditions.
The awareness briefing should be conducted before the approach briefing.
If the flight deck jump seat is occupied, the occupant shall be briefed according to 8.3.12 - Admission to Flight Deck, unless completed before (during departure briefing).

The Pilot Flying (PF) briefs the Pilot Monitoring (PM) about: chart number(s)

mental picture (1) clearance limit

lateral and vertical situation (2) constraints

runway details

ground operation

FMS verification (can be done independently at an earlier stage)

approach minimum (DA or MDA)

aircraft configuration

missed approach procedure FMS verification (can be done independently at an earlier stage)

initial aircraft manipulation

initial lateral and vertical profile including constraints

setting and use of navigation equipment use of the auto flight system (other than default values)

landing and missed approach performance calculation including FMS data

verification

For additional briefing items in connection with Low Visibility Operations (LVO),

refer to 8.4.5.4 - Category II or III Crew Briefing.

Note 1: Applicable charts shall be worked through systematically (including

verification of notes and remarks) and the FMS-loaded data shall be verified according to 8.3.2.26.1 - FMS-loaded Procedure Verification.

However, if the approach is well known by both pilots, the point “mental picture” may be shortened to FMS verification. The completion of the

verification shall be confirmed to each other during the briefing (e.g. “GIPOL28 transition and ILS 28 verified”).

Note 2: Where a rate of descent of more than 1.000 fpm will be required on

final approach (e.g. due to high ground speed or a steeper-than-normal approach path), this shall be briefed.

kontext:
8.3.2.25.1 General

The flight crew should choose the runway with the best performance margin under the prevailing weather conditions.
Due regard shall be given to other meteorological and operational factors (e.g. ATC requirements, preferential runway system, runway condition, noise abatement procedures, wind condition during all phases of flight, thunderstorms in the vicinity of the airport).
Special attention shall be paid to the condition of the runway regarding type of contaminant and associated wind limitations.
The Runway Condition Assessment Matrix (RCAM) provides guidelines to determine the runway condition to be used for performance calculation.
The available runway length shall be equal or exceed the required distance obtained by the respective aircraft type performance tool or other approved data.
The performance calculation should be based on the latest available weather report and runway conditon report (RCR) or equivalent information based on the RCR.
The best source of information provides the Automatic Terminal Information Service (ATIS).
For the runway intended to use, the following consideration shall be done: the existing weather conditions at the time of departure arrival

the takeoff- approach- configuration used under these condition the actual runway condition

the information on wind contained in METAR/SPECI/ATIS reports (average

of a 10-minute period) should be the basis for the performance calculations,

while instant wind information reported by the tower shall be monitored to

ensure that the wind speed during takeoff/approach does not exceed the

assumptions made for performance calculations.

The result of the performance calculation shall be verified amongst the flight

crew during the briefing and shall be recorded on the Operational Flight Plan (OFP) or in the EFB system in a traceable manner (real conditions, result of

calculation, explanatory remarks).

8.3.2.25.1.1 Takeoff Performance

The determination of takeoff performance data for wet and contaminated runways should be based on the reported runway surface condition in terms of contaminant and depth.
In the case of a contaminated runway, the flight crew shall consider the option to wait until the runway is cleared. If this is impracticable, applicable performance adjustments must be applied by using the type specific performance tool or approved data (e.g. AFM).
The take-off must be started either from the runway beginning, or from an authorized take-off point according to OM-C which must be considered in the takeoff performance calculation.
The weather report should not be older than 30 minutes before commencing takeoff.

8.3.2.25.1.2 Landing Performance

The crew shall be satisfied that, according to the information available, the condition of the runway intended to be used, will not prevent a safe approach, landing or missed approach, having regard to the performance information.
The initial in-flight landing distance assessment should be carried out when the weather report and the RCR are obtained, usually around TOD. If the planned duration of the flight does not allow the flight crew to carry out the assessment in non-critical phases of the flight, the assessment should be carried out before

departure.
When meteorological condition may lead to a degradation of the runway surface condition, the assessment shall include considerations of how much deterioration in runway surface friction characteristics may be tolerated, so that a quick

decision can be made prior to landing.

The flight crew shall monitor the evolution of the actual conditions during the

approach, to ensure that they do not degrade below the condition that was

determined to be the minimum acceptable during the initial in-flight landing distance assessment.

For calculating the in-flight landing performance, use the type specific

performance software tool or refer to:

AOM E1 5-35 Operational Landing Distance

AOM E2 5-35 Operational Landing Distance

Note: The performance software tool automatically adds a 15% safety margin to the calculated operational landing distance.

If calculations are performed manually via AOM this margin has to be added by the crew.

8.2.4.3.1 Type I Fluid (un-thickened type)

This group is the widely known manufactured to the military specifications MIL-A-3243 or MIL-D-8243.
The fluid must consist of at least 80 ethylene or propylene glycol, or 80 of a mixture of both.

If diluted with water the fluid must have a freezing point of at least 10 degrees below the ambient temperature.
The mix of fluid and water must be heated to 60 degrees Celsius (140 degrees F) minimum at the nozzle.
Type I fluids provide protection mainly against re-freezing in conditions where precipitation is not expected. Special care must be taken not to exceed the Holdover Time (HOT), since a Type I fluid may then change its condition from fluid to solid state (ice) in as little as 30 seconds. This effect is known as a flash freeze.

kontext:
8.2.4.2.2 Clear Ice

Clear ice is a layer of ice, which is transparent (and thus difficult to detect) formed during precipitation of relatively large rain drops. They partly freeze on impact upon a cold surface, releasing latent heat, which enables the remainder of the water to spread evenly. Since no air is trapped the result is a clear or glazed appearance.
Crews must be especially aware of the difficulty to detect clear ice and, in some situation, its presence may only be detected by touch.

It can form on aircraft surfaces below a layer of snow and rime ice.
Significant deposits can form on upper wing surfaces in the vicinity of fuel tanks after fuelling with low temperature fuel, or when sufficient super cooled fuel remained in tanks after a long flight at high altitude. This has occurred with ambient temperatures as high as 14°C. Conversely, fuelling with relatively warm fuel can cause dry falling snow to melt with the danger of refreezing on the upper surface of the wing.

kontext:
8.2.4.2.2 Clear Ice

Clear ice is a layer of ice, which is transparent (and thus difficult to detect) formed during precipitation of relatively large rain drops. They partly freeze on impact upon a cold surface, releasing latent heat, which enables the remainder of the water to spread evenly. Since no air is trapped the result is a clear or glazed appearance.
Crews must be especially aware of the difficulty to detect clear ice and, in some situation, its presence may only be detected by touch. It can form on aircraft surfaces below a layer of snow and rime ice.
Significant deposits can form on upper wing surfaces in the vicinity of fuel tanks after fuelling with low temperature fuel, or when sufficient super cooled fuel
remained in tanks after a long flight at high altitude. This has occurred with ambient temperatures as high as 14°C.
Conversely, fuelling with relatively warm fuel can cause dry falling snow to melt with the danger of refreezing on the upper surface of the wing.

kontext:
8.2.4.2.15 Radiational Cooling

A process by which temperature decreases, due to an excess of emitted radiation over absorbed radiation. On a typical calm clear night aircraft surfaces emit longwave radiation, however, there is no solar radiation (shortwave) coming in at night and this longwave emission will represent a constant net energy loss.
Under these conditions the aircraft surface temperatures may be up to 4°C or more below that of the surrounding air.

kontext:
8.2.4.11 Weather Conditions for Anti-Icing

Icing will occur when low ambient temperatures are accompanied by visible

moisture (i.e. precipitation, mist or fog). Depending upon aircraft characteristics, icing can occur at ambient temperatures considerably above the freezing point.
Aircraft specific limitations and anti-ice requirements are specified in the Operations Manual OM-B.

Anti-icing is a precautionary procedure, which uses the application of anti – icing

fluids to prevent ice deposits from forming or accumulating on the surfaces of a

clean aircraft. These fluids have a Holdover Time (HOT) which defines the period

of their effectiveness. The Holdover Time (HOT) is calculated beginning with the start of the application process. Therefore, it is essential that the application

process is continuous and performed as rapidly as possible to ensure protection through the planned take-off time.

Note: If an additional treatment should become necessary (e.g. through the

exceedance of the Holdover Time – HOT, deteriorating weather conditions),

the aircraft must first be de-iced. This will be followed by

another anti-ice procedure. Coating must not be applied before a previously applied layer has been washed down.

kontext:
8.2.4.22 Pre-Take-Off Contamination Check

If the Hold Over Time (HOT) has been exceeded or if any doubt exists regarding the continued effectiveness of the applied anti-icing treatment a check of the treated surfaces for contamination shall be performed just before the commencement of the take-off run.
Note:
Pre-Take-Off Contamination Check shall not be used when relying on allowance times instead of hold over times (applicable in cases of ice pellets or small hail).
For details on the difference between hold over times and allowance times, refer to OM-0 9 Hold Over Time Tables General section.

8.2.4.23 Take-off in Icing Conditions

Take-off is prohibited if any of the following conditions exist: snow, ice or frost deposits are adhering to the wings, tail, control surfaces, engine intakes and other critical surfaces of the aircraft.

heavy fall of wet snow with ambient temperatures around the freezing point freezing rain or freezing drizzle (i.e. FZRA, +FZRA, FZDZ, +FZDZ)

the runway braking action is reported as poor (braking coefficient 0.25 or less)

Performance limitations for take-off must be observed. Acceleration will be adversely affected by slush or standing water on the runway, which cause

significantly greater drag.

Flight crews must be alert for conditions which could affect stopping and directional control, should it become necessary to reject the take-off.

Careful line up ensures that the nose wheel is straight, as skidding of an offset nose wheel could upset directional control.

For the take off procedure, refer to type specific OM-B 2.

kontext:
8.2.4.20 Ramp and Taxi Precautions

Icy conditions on the ramp and in the gate area means that the push back vehicle may not be able to develop sufficient traction to push the aircraft with its engines running. Therefore, it is recommended to have the aircraft pushed back, to a position from which it can taxi forward, before starting engines. Standing on an icy patch even idle thrust may be sufficient to move the aircraft forward, although the parking brake is set.
Abnormal engine indications may occur during engine start especially caused by the low oil temperature (and therefore high viscosity), with oil pressure exceeding normal limits until the oil temperature rises. This is acceptable provided the engine is operated at not more than idle thrust until the indications are back to normal.
There is a possibility for engine inlet ice to build-up during taxi and ground holding operation.
Ice can form in engine inlets at temperatures above 10°C with high humidity present during extensive ground holds with the engines at idle.

If visible moisture is present with a temperature below that specified in the Operations Manual OM-B, engine nacelle anti-ice systems shall be switched on after completion of the engine start procedure.
Probe and sensor heating systems shall be switched on before taxiing, according

to the checklist procedures.

Taxi shall take place with great care and significantly lower speeds than normal.

Neither aircraft, nor ground vehicles are capable of stopping quickly on icy or

contaminated surfaces. When guide lamp installations are available, use of them shall be made to align the aircraft in the gate area. Snow may cover the normal

taxi markings. Braking and steering capabilities shall be tested frequently.

Maintaining a greater distance than normal from other traffic helps to avoid jet- blast, which could adversely affect anti-ice treatment and prevents from blow of

contaminants into the aircraft.

Engine thrust may need to be higher than normal to overcome the drag caused by slush or snow. Changes should be made slowly and carefully to avoid blowing

equipment or contaminants into other aircraft. At intervals during prolonged taxi and immediately before take-off, engines shall be run up to higher settings as specified in the Operations Manual OM-B.

Flaps should be kept up when taxiing through slush or standing water, with pre-take-off checks held until the flaps can be lowered again.
Holding shall be done well clear of an active runway as a landing aircraft is more likely to deviate from the centreline when braking conditions are marginal.
Slush thrown up by landing aircraft can be ingested by engines, cause airframe damage and degrade the anti-ice treatment.

2.8.3.3.7 Engine Run-Up Procedure

The Engine Run-Up procedure must be accomplished in any of the following conditions: in icing conditions for ground operations of more than 30 min

or in case of increased fan vibration due to fan ice accumulation

or for removal of light ice (similar to hoarfrost) or light snow in the inlet, on

the spinner, on the fan blades or on the booster area as observed during the external inspection

Note: Engine vibration may indicate maximum display value during engine run-up with no adverse effect on the engine.

or

until fan vibration indication returns to normal, whichever comes first.

monitor engine parameters and ensure normal operation.

kontext:
8.2.1.5 Fuelling with Passengers on Board

During normal operations it may be necessary to fuel or de-fuel an aircraft with passengers on board. Passengers may embark, disembark or remain on board during fuelling and de-fuelling operation provided that the following precautions are observed: local procedures must be verified and adhered to

a member of the flight crew must remain on the flight deck

a two way communication between the flight crew member in the cockpit and a cabin crew member in the cabin must be established

a two way communication between ground crew supervising the refuelling and the qualified personnel on board the airplane is assured (via intercommunication system, direct person-to-person contact or any other method of communication)

fuelling personnel shall be informed that passengers will be on board during fuelling and immediate communication to a flight crew member being on the flight deck shall be established either via inter-communication system or direct person-to-person contact

all cabin crew members shall be informed by the Commander (CMD).
For callouts refer to 8.3 App. 1 - Communication Wording CSPM 2 Appendix 1 Communication Wording

all cabin crew members shall be able to communicate among cabin crew members and passengers (e.g. via PA, hand signals (body language) or megaphone)

cont.
the fuelling may start only after positive confirmation of the Senior cabin crew member (SEN) towards the Commander CMD has taken place

verifying that the following precautionary measures are taken (for callouts refer to 8.3 App. 1 - Communication Wording CSPM 2 Appendix 1 Communication Wording): the fasten seat belt signs must be off, the no smoking signs must be on, together with interior lighting to enable emergency exits to be identified

passengers are to be briefed not to smoke at any time on the ground and to remain seated until the fuelling has been completed, refer to OM- 0 4 CCM

in principle, for all aircraft types, at least a minimum of two passenger cabin doors shall be opened and passenger stairs jetways must be positioned at these doors

if only one passenger stair jetway is available, the requirement for the second passenger cabin door may be met by positioning a cabin crew member, who will remain at a second door throughout the refuelling process. The door should not be automatic armed, unless required in an emergency

in the cabin, a cabin crew member shall be positioned next to the boarding door and be prepared for an immediate emergency evacuation, the rest of the cabin crew members shall be positioned in the vicinity of their assigned doors/exits (refer to CSPM 5 Standard

Operation Position/Area “Fuelling with Passengers on Board”) on all exits the outside-area shall remain clear during fuelling operations

routes to the emergency exits shall be unobstructed

if the presence of fuel vapour is detected inside the aircraft, or any other

hazard arises fuelling or de-fuelling shall be stopped immediately

if deemed necessary by the crew, a de-boarding shall be performed via the stairs or an evacuation via the escape slides, if deemed necessary limited to

the non-spilled side

fuelling and de-fuelling with wide cut fuel (e.g. Jet B or equivalent) is prohibited with passengers on board

after completion of fuelling the Commander (CMD) will notify the Senior

cabin attendant (SEN) which means that normal duties may be resumed.
For callouts refer to 8.3 App. 1 - Communication Wording

CSPM 2 Appendix 1 Communication Wording

Commander (CMD) is responsible for evaluating the situation on the particular airport at the given time, and determining a person responsible for the fueling operation and communication to the flight crew during fueling with passengers on board. That can be one of the following positions: ground staff (ideally flight supervisor)

fueling personnel, should there be means of communication with the flight crew in place

kontext:
8.2.1.5 Fuelling with Passengers on Board

During normal operations it may be necessary to fuel or de-fuel an aircraft with passengers on board. Passengers may embark, disembark or remain on board during fuelling and de-fuelling operation provided that the following precautions are observed: local procedures must be verified and adhered to

a member of the flight crew must remain on the flight deck

a two way communication between the flight crew member in the cockpit and a cabin crew member in the cabin must be established

a two way communication between ground crew supervising the refuelling and the qualified personnel on board the airplane is assured (via intercommunication system, direct person-to-person contact or any other method of communication)

fuelling personnel shall be informed that passengers will be on board during fuelling and immediate communication to a flight crew member being on the flight deck shall be established either via inter-communication system or direct person-to-person contact

all cabin crew members shall be informed by the Commander (CMD).
For callouts refer to 8.3 App. 1 - Communication Wording CSPM 2 Appendix 1 Communication Wording

all cabin crew members shall be able to communicate among cabin crew members and passengers (e.g. via PA, hand signals (body language) or megaphone)

cont.

the fuelling may start only after positive confirmation of the Senior cabin crew member (SEN) towards the Commander CMD has taken place verifying that the following precautionary measures are taken (for callouts refer to 8.3 App. 1 - Communication Wording CSPM 2 Appendix 1 Communication Wording): the fasten seat belt signs must be off, the no smoking signs must be on, together with interior lighting to enable emergency exits to be identified

passengers are to be briefed not to smoke at any time on the ground and to remain seated until the fuelling has been completed, refer to OM- 0 4 CCM

in principle, for all aircraft types, at least a minimum of two passenger cabin doors shall be opened and passenger stairs jetways must be positioned at these doors

if only one passenger stair jetway is available, the requirement for the second passenger cabin door may be met by positioning a cabin crew member, who will remain at a second door throughout the refuelling process.

The door should not be automatic armed, unless required in an emergency

in the cabin, a cabin crew member shall be positioned next to the boarding door and be prepared for an immediate emergency evacuation, the rest of the cabin crew members shall be positioned in the vicinity of their assigned doors/exits (refer to CSPM 5 Standard

Operation Position/Area “Fuelling with Passengers on Board”) on all exits the outside-area shall remain clear during fuelling operations

routes to the emergency exits shall be unobstructed

if the presence of fuel vapour is detected inside the aircraft, or any other

hazard arises fuelling or de-fuelling shall be stopped immediately

if deemed necessary by the crew, a de-boarding shall be performed via the stairs or an evacuation via the escape slides, if deemed necessary limited to

the non-spilled side

fuelling and de-fuelling with wide cut fuel (e.g. Jet B or equivalent) is prohibited with passengers on board

after completion of fuelling the Commander (CMD) will notify the Senior

cabin attendant (SEN) which means that normal duties may be resumed.
For callouts refer to 8.3 App. 1 - Communication Wording

CSPM 2 Appendix 1 Communication Wording

Commander (CMD) is responsible for evaluating the situation on the particular airport at the given time, and determining a person responsible for the fueling operation and communication to the flight crew during fueling with passengers on board. That can be one of the following positions: ground staff (ideally flight supervisor)

fueling personnel, should there be means of communication with the flight crew in place

one of the flight crew members

If none of the above positions can assure proper supervision, fueling with passengers on board shall not be performed.

2.2.4 Pushback

Pushback procedure is used to move the airplane from the terminal gate before flight and also to facilitate ground movement on ramps and taxiways. It is recommended to complete the Before Start Checklist before starting the manoeuvre. Assure with ground personnel that area is clear and the nose gear towing light showing green.

One towing supervisor is necessary to control the towing operation. The towing

supervisor should establish communication with towing personnel and flight crew members at all times.
The engines can be started before, during or after the pushback manoeuvre.
Power back is not allowed.

kontext:
8.1.8.5 Last Minute Changes Procedure

As explained in the definition, Last Minute Changes (LMC) to the load sheet are only permitted if the changes of the load – either plus or minus – are within the limits permitted in the Operations Manual OM-B 6.
The changes have to be entered into the Last Minute Change (LMC) sections of the load sheet. If there is no defined place for last minute changes on the loadsheet (e.g. on ACARS loadsheet), it shall be noted somewhere in open space.
As least the following content shall be stated: type of LMC (e.g. Pax., Load, Crew)

changed weight 88kg)
CMD signature and 3LC (The signature confirms the correct application of the LMC according to the limitations in OM-B 6.)

In exceptional cases – if time limitations request to do so – changes may be

relayed to the flight crew via radio, cellular telephone or the ground service interphone. The flight crew and ground staff will then amend their copies

accordingly.

The load message sent to the destination must contain the corrected figures for the actual load of passengers, cargo, baggage and mail.

OM-A 8 Operating Procedures

The standard scheduled turnaround time for all stations is allocated with 40 minutes or above.

The scheduled ground time at a station shall be reduced to the minimum declared ground time to compensate any arising flight arrival delay at a station. The minimum declared ground time is the minimum time which is

required for a full “turnaround”. This minimum declared ground time differs from aircraft type to aircraft type.

Aircraft Type declared ground time

In case of late arrival of the aircraft, not more than the above mentioned

turnaround time may be covered under irregularity code 93 and it can only be exceeded in coordination with helvetic operations control.

kontext:
8.2.2.12.3 Door Operation in Strong Winds

For the operation of aircraft doors in strong winds (i.e. maximum permissible

wind speeds, other particulars to be observed) refer to the Operations Manual OM-B. If difficulties occur when attempting to close doors in strong winds, the

aircraft shall be moved in order to position the doors concerned on the downwind side.

8.2.2.13 Safety on the Ramp, including Fire Prevention, Blast and Suction Areas

The following provisions concerning the safety of all aircraft, crews, passengers, staff and load on the ramp shall be observed: only authorized person shall have access to the ramp

the use of open fire is strictly prohibited

ramp surfaces shall be frequently checked to prevent accidents caused by slipping or skidding on oil, ice or snow; these checks shall, as far as possible, also serve to detect foreign objects on the ramp surfaces, which must be removed in order to prevent Foreign Object Damage (FOD) to the tires and other parts of the aircraft, and to preclude foreign object ingestion by an engine
ramp personnel shall wear ear protection permanently, crew members shall do so while on the ramp.

generally the yellow reflective vest must be worn on the tarmac except for crew boarding and deboarding.

Certain systems of the aircraft shall not be operated on the ramp (e.g., weather radar). For details refer to the Operations Manual OM-B.
No passenger shall enter the security zones. Access to checked baggage cannot

be granted and must be prevented by ground staff. This applies also to excess hand baggage loaded into cargo holds.

The flight crew shall verify the proper reception of the take-off clearance with a

runway

Both pilots shall report to each other the reception of the take-off clearance.
If there is an uncertainty about the clearance, verification shall be made.
A time check shall be performed or verified to determine TOGA thrust time limit (automatically performed time check by the system upon lift-off is considered acceptable).

kontext:
CONFIRM BRAKES SET

8.3.2.10.4.4 Low Visibility Taxi

A high degree of awareness is required for all low visibility taxi operations.
In order to render the aircraft visible to other traffic, display of all lights is recommended unless the own vision is thereby impaired. However, care shall be taken not to blind other traffic or ground handling staff.

8.3.2.10.4.5 Runway and Taxiway Incursion

A runway incursion is defined as any occurrence at an aerodrome involving the incorrect presence of an aircraft, vehicle or person on the protected area of a surface designated for the landing and take-off of aircraft. It may lead to a serious incident or accident with significant loss of life.
Runway incursions can be divided into several recurring scenarios.
Common scenarios are: an aircraft or vehicle crossing in front of a landing aircraft

an aircraft or vehicle crossing in front of a departing aircraft

an aircraft or vehicle crossing the runway-holding position marking

an aircraft or vehicle unsure of its position and inadvertently entering an active runway

a breakdown in communications leading to failure to follow an air traffic

control instruction In addition pilot factors that may result in a runway incursion include inadvertent non-compliance with ATC clearances. Often these cases result from a break-

down in communications or a loss of situational awareness in which pilots think

that they are at one location on the aerodrome (such as a specific taxiway or

intersection) when they are actually elsewhere, or they believe that the clearance

issued was to enter the runway, when in fact it was not.

8.3.2.10.4.6 Entering or Crossing a Runway
Crossing and line-up approval must be read back to ATC completely and both pilots must report to each other the reception thereof.

Before entering any runway the respective approach area has to be checked, also any potential conflicting traffic on the runway shall be identified.
When lining up on the departure runway both pilots shall: check heading

check runway markings (i.e. centerline lights and RWY designator)

check correct line-up (on the centerline)

perform time check

For specific callouts refer to type specific OM-B.
If lined up on the runway and held more than 90 seconds beyond anticipated departure time, contact ATC and advise that you are holding on the runway.

8.3.2.10.4.7 Taxi by Other Personnel than the Commander or the Copilot

Operator’s restriction: no other personnel than the commander or copilot shall taxi an airplane.

Following provisions would apply: if other personnel than the commander or the copilot is taxing an aeroplane it must be ensured that he has received instructions in respect of aerodrome

layout, routes, signs, markings, lights, air traffic control signals and the

operational standards of helvetic and he is competent to use radiotelephony.
