kontext:
12.2.6.1 Normal Practices and Procedures after entering RVSM Airspace

Flight crews shall comply to any aircraft operating restrictions, if required for the specific aircraft group: limits on indicated Mach number (basic flight envelope upper Mach boundary), given in the RVSM airworthiness approval Note: all helvetic aircraft with RVSM approval shall be compliant to full RVSM flight envelope

Emphasis shall be placed on promptly setting the sub-scale on all primary and standby altimeters to 1013.2 hPa when passing the transition altitude, and rechecking for proper altimeter setting when reaching the initial cleared flight level.
In level cruise it is essential that the aircraft is flown at the cleared flight level.
This requires that particular care is taken to ensure that ATC clearances are fully understood and followed. The aircraft shall not intentionally depart from a cleared flight level without a positive clearance from ATC, unless the crew is conducting contingency or emergency manoeuvres.
When changing levels, the aircraft shall not be allowed to overshoot or undershoot the cleared flight level by more than 45m (150 ft). If installed, the level off should be accomplished using the altitude capture feature of the automatic altitude-control system.

An automatic altitude-control system shall be operative and engaged during level cruise, except when circumstances, such as the need to re-trim the aircraft or turbulence, require disengagement. In any event adherence to the assigned cruise level should be done by reference to one of the two primary altimeters.
Following loss of the automatic height keeping function, any consequential

restrictions will need to be observed.

Therefore:

ensure that the altitude-alerting system is operative

cross-check at intervals of approximately one hour the primary altimeters; a minimum of two shall agree within ±200 ft (±60 m); failure to meet this

condition will require that the altimetry system is reported as defective and

notified to ATC; the usual scan of flight deck instruments shall suffice for altimeter cross-checking on most flights

in normal operations, the altimetry system being used to control the aircraft

shall be selected for the input to the altitude reporting transponder, transmitting information to ATC

OM-A 12 Rules of the Air

If the pilot is notified by ATC of an assigned altitude deviation of 300 ft (90 m) or more then the flight crew shall take appropriate action to return to the cleared flight level as quickly as possible.
If the pilot is advised in real time that the aircraft has been identified by a height- monitoring system that the Total Vertical Error (TVE) is greater than ±300 ft (±90m) and or if an Altimetry System Error (ASE) greater than ±245 ft (±75 m) is experienced, the flight crew should follow established regional procedures to protect the safe operation of the aircraft. This assumes that the monitoring system will identify the TVE or ASE within the set limits for accuracy.
Caution should be exercised due to problems of visual perceptions of other aircraft during darkness at 1000 ft separation, and when encountering local phenomena such as northern lights.
This applies to aircraft in the opposite and same flight direction, and during turns. Use of the TCAS will verify what actual separation exists from nearby aircraft.

8.3.2.21.2 TCAS

The rate of climb or descent shall be selected based on operational conditions.
Given the widespread use of collision avoidance systems (ACAS II), the rate of climb or descent must be closely monitored to ensure it does not exceed: 1500 FPM when within 2000 feet of the cleared altitude

1000 FPM in the presence of potentially conflicting traffic when within 1000

feet of the cleared altitude When passing 2000 feet before the cleared altitude or flight level and the rate exceeds 1500 FPM:

the PM shall call out "APPROACHING ALTITUDE FLIGHT LEVEL."

the PF will then take corrective action and respond with "CHECKED."

Note: The directive to make a call at 2000 feet is based on European Airspace recommendations. These guidelines advise reducing the vertical speed

to a maximum of 1500 feet per minute (FPM) to prevent unnecessary

Traffic Collision Avoidance System (TCAS) alerts caused by high closure rates.

These rate restrictions do not apply during departure when climbing to the initial

cleared altitude or flight level, as defined in the SID or departure clearance.

kontext:
8.3.2.23 Holding Pattern, Procedure Turns

For holding procedures and procedure-turns refer to the Operations Manual OM-C. In holding patterns and procedure turns the rate of descent shall not exceed 1500 fpm.
Great attention shall be paid to the compliance with the holding speed limitations.
For local regulations refer to the Operations Manual OM-C.
If unable to comply (i.e. when holding in a clean configuration is not possible at the assigned speeds) and
if the limitations are not in force for the purpose of obstacle clearance a higher than standard holding speed may be negotiated with ATC.

For the timing of a holding pattern refer to the Operations Manual OM-C (Route Manual). When a clearance is received specifying the time of departure from the holding fix, the flight crew shall adjust the pattern within the limits of the established holding procedure in order to leave the fix as near to the time specified as practicable.
Corrections shall be made in both heading and timing to compensate for the effects of wind. A correction shall also be made if the entry speed was excessive due to an unexpected holding clearance.
Turning to the inbound leg of a holding pattern not utilizing the FMS, a 90o – 45o interception shall be flown.
Holdings and procedure turns should be flown with 25° bank.

kontext:
8.3.2.10.4 Ground Movement

8.3.2.10.4.1 Policy

During any ground movement, the sterile flight deck policy applies. Actions which could distract pilots and requiring “head down” shall be avoided as far as possible. Passenger announcements or crew briefings should be completed before starting taxi. The cockpit to cabin communication and vice versa shall be limited to procedural calls.

8.3.2.10.4.2 Taxi

Following guidance has been established and shall be adhered to: during ground movement both pilots shall have access to an airport layout chart for reference and shall keep a constant vigilant look-out for conflicting traffic and obstructions of the taxi way

get used to airport charts and the special marked hot spots and take it into account during the departure briefing according to 8.3.2.14 - Departure Briefing

the pilot taxiing the aircraft shall announce in advance his intentions to the pilot monitoring with his own words (e.g. “straight ahead – second right”)

all taxi clearances shall be understood by each flight crew member. If one pilot is not listening to the ATC communication (e.g. due to communication

with cabin) he shall be briefed about the instructions received by the other pilot the pilot monitoring shall monitor the taxi progress and adherence to the

clearances and shall assist the pilot taxiing.

Whenever possible, the taxi

clearance should be typed into the scratch pad of the FMS Control unit

all taxi clearances shall be cross-checked against the aerodrome chart and aerodrome surface markings, signs, and lights

never cross illuminated red stop bars when lining up on, or crossing a

runway unless contingency procedures are in use, communicated and confirmed by the ATC that specifically allows it to do so

if there is any doubt about the clearance or the position at an aerodrome,

stop the aircraft, contact ATC immediately and follow the associated instructions

be “head-up” for a continuous watch during aerodrome surface operations

identify issues (e.g. checklist items) that shall be re-accomplished in the event of a runway change

re-briefings should be done, when possible, with parking brake set

any action which may disturb the flight crew from taxi activity shall be avoided or done with the parking brake set (e.g. announcement by PA)

Before requesting the taxi clearance, both pilots shall verify and confirm that the ground crew has given the clear signal, indicating that all ground equipment has been removed and the airplane is safe to move.
The flight crew shall carefully evaluate the situation around the aircraft, particularly the distances to other airplane and objects, select an adequate taxi speed and handle throttles accordingly. Good taxi speeds are in the range of 15 knots but may depend on the actual traffic situation.
However, taxi speed shall not exceed 30 knots unless required by ATC (e.g. backtrack). The flight crew must consider the runway condition and adapt the taxi speed whenever operating on contaminated surfaces.
It is good practice to minimize blast effects and noise, particularly during the start of the taxi roll after standstill. Braking shall be applied steady and smoothly and only in intervals. Do not “ride the brakes”.

8.3.2.10.4.3 Push Back and Towing Push back and towing movements require type specific certified equipment and the procedures are based on a close communication between flight and ground

crew members. Towbarless towing is allowed, provided the vehicle is designed to

prevent damage to the airplane.

The following specific wordings must be used to avoid misunderstandings:

Flight crew:

kontext:
4.1.6 Approach Climb Limits

The calculation of the required approach climb gradient shall be the average of the approach climb gradient over the whole missed approach trajectory.
Enter the tables at the next higher 1000 ft step for simplified and conservative calculation of the missed approach climb gradient.

E.g. Aerodrome LUX ILS 24 CAT 1 approach minima is 1413 ft, final missed approach altitude is 4000 ft.

1. Enter the Approach Climb Gradient table and read out the values at the

2000 ft table.

2. Enter the Approach Climb Gradient table and read out the values at the 4000 ft. table.

3. Calculate the average of these two readouts.

Note: The ePerf presents an OEI Missed Approach Climb Gradient. This value is a spot value at aerodrome elevation and does not take degradation of increasing altitude nor does it take the missed approach altitude in account. The ePerf calculated OEI Missed Approach Climb Gradient shall be used as a reference only. Expect a degradation of roughly 0.5 climb gradient per 1000 ft.

kontext:
4.0.1.1 Wet and Contaminated

Wet runway means a runway whose surface is covered by any visible dampness

or water up to and including 3 mm deep within the area intended to be used.

Contaminated runway is a runway where a significant portion of its surface area (whether in isolated areas or not) within the length and width being used, is covered by standing water or slush, or that has an accumulation of snow or ice.
However, in certain other situations it may be appropriate to consider the runway contaminated. For example, if the section of the runway surface that is covered with standing water or slush is located where rotation and lift-off occurs, or during the highspeed part of the takeoff roll, the retardation effect is far more significant than if it were encountered early in the takeoff while at low speed. In this situation, the runway might better be considered 'contaminated' rather than 'wet'.

Takeoff and landing performance calculation assumes a homogeneous contaminant type and depth along the entire runway length and width. If runway conditions are reported for runway thirds, performance calculation should consider the most penalizing contaminant.

However, a part of the runway may be

disregarded if the performance calculation accounts for the respective runway reduction.

kontext:
8.1.2.2.7 Landing

The Landing Distance Required (LDR) for dry runways is based on a factored landing distance, derived from the actual landing distance increased by a safety margin of 67 (multiplied by 1.67) for turbojet aircraft. That means that the aircraft must come to a full stop landing from 50 feet above threshold latest within 60% of the Landing Distance Available (LDA).
For wet or contaminated runways that landing distance required must additionally be increased by a 15% safety margin (multiplied by 1.15 or

uncorrected actual landing distance multiplied by 1.92).
For a landing of an aircraft with system failures, that require an increase of the landing distance required, the longer of the two calculated landing distances shall be applied:

actual landing distance increased by a safety margin of 67

(multiplied by 1.67), or

actual landing distance for the system failure situation as stated in the

Operations Manual OM-B 4 increased by a safety margin of 15 (multiplied by 1.15)

kontext:
8.3.2.25.1 General

The flight crew should choose the runway with the best performance margin under the prevailing weather conditions.
Due regard shall be given to other meteorological and operational factors (e.g. ATC requirements, preferential runway system, runway condition, noise abatement procedures, wind condition during all phases of flight, thunderstorms in the vicinity of the airport).
Special attention shall be paid to the condition of the runway regarding type of contaminant and associated wind limitations.
The Runway Condition Assessment Matrix (RCAM) provides guidelines to determine the runway condition to be used for performance calculation.
The available runway length shall be equal or exceed the required distance obtained by the respective aircraft type performance tool or other approved data.
The performance calculation should be based on the latest available weather report and runway conditon report (RCR) or equivalent information based on the RCR.
The best source of information provides the Automatic Terminal Information Service (ATIS).
For the runway intended to use, the following consideration shall be done: the existing weather conditions at the time of departure arrival

the takeoff- approach- configuration used under these condition the actual runway condition

the information on wind contained in METAR/SPECI/ATIS reports (average

of a 10-minute period) should be the basis for the performance calculations, while instant wind information reported by the tower shall be monitored to

ensure that the wind speed during takeoff/approach does not exceed the

assumptions made for performance calculations.

The result of the performance calculation shall be verified amongst the flight

crew during the briefing and shall be recorded on the Operational Flight Plan (OFP) or in the EFB system in a traceable manner (real conditions, result of

calculation, explanatory remarks).

8.3.2.25.1.1 Takeoff Performance

The determination of takeoff performance data for wet and contaminated runways should be based on the reported runway surface condition in terms of contaminant and depth.
In the case of a contaminated runway, the flight crew shall consider the option to wait until the runway is cleared. If this is impracticable, applicable performance adjustments must be applied by using the type specific performance tool or approved data (e.g. AFM).
The take-off must be started either from the runway beginning, or from an authorized take-off point according to OM-C which must be considered in the takeoff performance calculation.
The weather report should not be older than 30 minutes before commencing takeoff.

8.3.2.25.1.2 Landing Performance

The crew shall be satisfied that, according to the information available, the condition of the runway intended to be used, will not prevent a safe approach, landing or missed approach, having regard to the performance information.
The initial in-flight landing distance assessment should be carried out when the weather report and the RCR are obtained, usually around TOD.

If the planned duration of the flight does not allow the flight crew to carry out the assessment in non-critical phases of the flight, the assessment should be carried out before

departure.

When meteorological condition may lead to a degradation of the runway surface condition, the assessment shall include considerations of how much deterioration in runway surface friction characteristics may be tolerated, so that a quick

decision can be made prior to landing.

The flight crew shall monitor the evolution of the actual conditions during the

approach, to ensure that they do not degrade below the condition that was

determined to be the minimum acceptable during the initial in-flight landing distance assessment.

For calculating the in-flight landing performance, use the type specific

performance software tool or refer to:

AOM E1 5-35 Operational Landing Distance

AOM E2 5-35 Operational Landing Distance

Note: The performance software tool automatically adds a 15% safety margin to the calculated operational landing distance.

If calculations are performed manually via AOM this margin has to be added by the crew.

kontext:
8.3.2.25.3 The Runway Condition Assessment Matrix (RCAM)

For the overall assessment of the runway condition, the RCAM provides the flight crew with a combination of all available information: runway surface conditions: state and or contaminant

pilot report of braking action (PIREP) or Estimated Surface Friction (ESF)

The RCAM provides the maximum crosswind values for landing and takeoff performance.
It does not show the friction coefficient since there is no correlation between the coefficient measured by a vehicle and the actual aircraft braking capability.

The following Landing Performance Codes-Levels are used to assess the related

takeoff and landing performance:

6 - Dry

5 - Good

5 - Wet Grooved (if runway is grooved or Porous Friction Course (PFC))

4 - Good to Medium

3 - Medium 2 - Medium to Poor

1 - Poor

0 - Less than Poor

8.3.2.25.3.1 How to use the Runway Condition Assessment Matrix (RCAM)

The flight crew shall make a primary assessment based on runway state or runway contaminant type and depth and the OAT.
Then, the flight crew should downgrade this primary assessment if: a report (PIREP or ESF) is available and this report corresponds to a lower Runway Condition Code (RCC)

complementary information is available and is related to a possible degradation of the runway surface conditions.

If the primary means of assessment (runway state or runway contaminant type and depth) is not available, the flight crew should request it by ATC.
The flight crew shall not use a report or any other complementary information in order to upgrade a primary assessment.
A RWYCC 1 or 0 maybe upgraded by the airport operator to a maximum of RWYCC 3. This upgrade may be considered by flight crews.
Example:

Crews shall use the reported contamination level or braking action report and reference the RCAM to obtain a

corresponding RCC.
If ATC reports “Compacted Snow” and the ESF is “Good to

Medium” the equivalent RCC

can be found by referencing the

RCAM in the QRH.

PIREP’s are to be treated as informative only and may be disregarded on pilot’s

discretion. However, the lowest

Runway Condition Code (RCC) found shall be used for

performancecalculation.

For this example, the RCC is 3.

kontext:
2.6.1.4.1 Autobrake

With autobrake set to LO, MED or HI verify after touchdown the normal operation of the braking system and proper deceleration of the airplane.
At 80 kt, press the brakes pedal to disengage the autobrake and use the necessary braking force to reach a safe taxi speed.

Note: At pilot’s discretion, disengage the autobrake after touchdown at any speed by pressing the brakes pedals.

During the landing roll, if autobrake deceleration is not suitable for the stopping

distance, use manual braking as required. Apply continuous increasing pressure to the brake pedals. Use manual braking as soon as possible to achieve

maximum deceleration. Pilot must be alert for autobrake disengagement

indications during the landing roll. At pilot’s discretion, use reverse thrust with

manual braking or autobrake during landing roll until a safe speed is reached.

The autobrake works aiming a constant deceleration rate. When the braking

capability is good and the autobrake deceleration target is reached, the use of

thrust reversers is not effective.

A Takeoff with less thrust than the maximum takeoff thrust is used.

thrust:

8.1.2.2.6 Landing Climb

0.9 Rectification Intervals

Repair of inoperative systems or components, deferred in accordance with the MEL, must be effected at or prior to the rectification intervals established by the following designators: «A» Category No standard interval is specified. Where a time period is specified other than in calendar days or flight days, it shall start at the point when the defect is deferred in accordance with the MEL. «B» Category
Items in this category shall be repaired within three (3) consecutive calendar days (72 hours), excluding the day the malfunction was recorded in the Aircraft Technical Log (ATL)

ANAC APPROVED AP1-00

REVISION 1 code 01 Page 3 AFM-1913
INTRODUCTION

This Configuration Deviation List contains additional certificate limitations for operation of the airplane without certain secondary airframe and engine parts as listed herein. When the airplane is operated using the CDL, the limitations specified in the AFM must still be complied with, as amended in this Appendix. All the items that are related to the airworthiness of the airplane and not included on the list are automatically required to be installed.
The associated limitations must be listed on a placard affixed in the cockpit in clear view of the pilots and other appropriate crewmember(s). The pilot in command should be notified of each operation with a missing part(s) by listing the missing part(s) in the flight or dispatch release. The operator should list in the airplane logbook an appropriate notation covering the missing part(s) on each flight.
If an additional part is lost, the airplane may not depart the airport at which it landed following this event, until it complies with the limitation of the CDL. This, of course, does not preclude the issuance of a ferry permit to allow the airplane to be flown to a point where the necessary repairs or replacement can be made.
No more than one part for any one system may be missing, unless specific combinations of parts are included in the CDL. Unless otherwise specified, parts from different systems may be missing. The performance penalties are cumulative, unless specifically designated penalties are indicated for the combination of missing parts.
Where performance penalties are listed as negligible, no more than three negligible items may be missing without taking further penalty.
For each missing item more than three, reduce the takeoff, landing and enroute climb limits by 45 kg (100 lb).

Where performance penalties are listed as no penalty, any accumulative number of items listed as no penalty may be missing without further penalty.

APPENDIX 1

CONFIGURATION

8.1.11.2.2 Aircraft Technical Log (ATL) – Utilisation

The following sub-chapters provide instructions for the use of the ATL in normal and abnormal situations. These chapters are sorted by scenario and provide examples to increase user-friendliness.

8.1.11.2.2.1 Pre-Flight – Incomplete Tech-Log

If, prior to a flight, an aircraft has an incomplete tech-log entry, the commander shall perform the following steps: call OCC to contact previous crew for verification of the aircraft status

if OCC is unable to reach the previous crew, contact MCC to verify the aircraft status MCC shall check aircraft history of technical messages

ATL shall be closed by the operating crew verify fuel state via Flight Briefing Documentation Tool

IQSMS report shall be filed for tracking Area of Occurence: Technical Type of Occurrence: Technical Data Event Classification: Technical Documentation (ATL, MEL, Aircraft Status Report)

8.1.11.2.2.2 Pre-Flight – Aircraft Acceptance Prior to any flight, the aircraft's airworthiness and technical condition shall be assessed and confirmed by the commander by reviewing the following:

ATL to familiarise himself with any technical failure, maintenance actions

that may have occurred during previous flights and to ensure that all

recorded defect entries have been appropriately assessed and answered by helvetic maintenance and/or the contracted maintenance organisation

Acceptable Deferred Defects (ADD), briefing cards (BC) and associated MEL references as detailed in the technical information system-generated

aircraft status report

Note: If multiple MEL items are applied, the aircraft must not take off unless it

is confirmed that the interaction between inoperative components or systems will not result in an unacceptable degradation in the level of

safety and or undue increase in crew workload.

The commander confirms the aircraft acceptance by signing the appropriate ATL

field.

8.1.11.2.2.3 Pre-flight – Inspection (PFI)

During the pre-flight inspection (PFI) the availability, accessibility and serviceability of the flight deck systems and emergency equipment must be assured in accordance with:
OM-B E1 2.1.4 External Inspection OM-B E2 2.1.4 External Inspection

After the completion of the pre-flight inspection the commander is responsible that the following fields are completed in the ATL: section A, a/c registration section D, flight number section E, departure airport section F, date section P, cross in box “Crew Entry” section J, cross in box “PFI” section J, time and date of PFI section J, commander or deputy 3LC section J, commander or deputy signature

fill out fields as per 8.1.11.2.1.1 - Aircraft Technical Log Page Contents Description of COMPLAINT Side

kontext:
7.2.1 Modification of the Limits on Flight Duty, Duty or Rest Periods

During actual flight operation, which starts after the whole crew has reported for any duty, the Commander (CMD) shall have the possibility to modify the limits on flight duty, duty and rest periods in the event of conditions described as unforeseen circumstances.
The exercise of commander’s discretion shall be considered exceptional and shall be avoided at home base when standby or reserve crew members are available.
The conditions shall comply with the following: the maximum daily FDP which results after applying 7.1.7 - Maximum Daily Flight Duty Periode (FDP) or 7.1.9 - Split Duty may not be increased by more than 2 hours.

the maximum basic daily FDP that results after applying 7.1.7.1 - Maximum Daily FDP for Acclimatised Crew Members shall be used to calculate the limits of commander’s discretion, if commander’s discretion is applied to an FDP which has been extended under the provisions of 7.1.7.3 - Maximum Daily FDP for Acclimatised Crew Members with the Use of Extensions without In-flight Rest

if on the final sector within a FDP the allowed increase is exceeded because of unforeseen circumstances after take-off, the flight may continue to the planned destination or alternate aerodrome the rest period following the FDP may be reduced but can never be less

than 10 hours
The commander shall consult all crew members on their alertness levels before deciding the modifications.

Additionally, he shall take due consideration of additional factors that might decrease a crew member’s alertness levels, such as:
WOCL encroachment

weather conditions

complexity of the operation and/or airport environment

airplane malfunctions or specifications

flight with training or supervisory duties

increased number of sectors

circadian disruption

individual conditions of affected crew members (time since awake, sleep- related factor, workload, etc.)

7.2.2 Duties in case of Modification of the Limits on Flight Duty, Duty or Rest Periods

helvetic will assess on a regular basis the series of pairings where commander’s

discretion has been exercised in order to be aware of possible inconsistencies in their rostering. The FRMS meeting monitors the amount of FTL modifications and other FTL exceedances via the BI tool according to 2.4.5.1.8 - FRMS Meeting.

The Commander (CMD) shall submit an IT report to helvetic flight operations

management whenever a limit on flight duty, duty or rest period has been

modified by his discretion or whenever a limitation as stated within this chapter has been violated in excess of one hour. This report shall be handled according

to OMM 7 Reporting Scheme.

Whenever the above-mentioned modification or a reported violation is beyond one hour, helvetic shall send a copy of the report to the competent authority not

later than 28 days after the event.

The RPO will monitor FTL exceedances and request reports from the commander, whenever a report is missing.

kontext:
7.2.4 Delayed Reporting or Short-notice Flight Cancellation

In the event of unforeseen circumstances a delayed reporting procedure may be applied if the time until the scheduled reporting time is more than one hour at home base or more than 30 minutes away from home base and the crew member can remain at his suitable accommodation.
In such a case, if the crew member is informed by phone (or by SMS in case of possible interference with sleeping patterns) about the delayed reporting time, the maximum Flight Duty Period (FDP) is calculated as follows:
One notification of a delay leads to the calculation of the maximum FDP according to when the delay is less than 4 hours, the maximum FDP is calculated based on the original reporting time and the FDP starts counting at the delayed reporting time

when the delay is 4 hours or more, the maximum FDP is calculated based on the more limiting of the original or the delayed reporting time and the FDP starts counting at the delayed reporting time

If the reporting time is further amended, the FDP starts counting 1 hour after the second notification or at the original delayed reporting time if this is earlier As an exception, when the operator informs the crew member of a delay of 10 hours or more in reporting time

and the crew member is not further disturbed by the operator, such delay of 10 hours or more counts as a rest

period.

Any delay which is communicated to the crew member 10 hours or more before the delayed reporting time does not count as delayed reporting and no additional regulations apply.

In the event when the first flight segment(s) has to be removed (but the following ones remain) or changed to another flight segment(s), and this change is done

less than one hour ahead of original reporting time, a ground duty is added in the

duration of 5min starting at the original reporting time.

If due to an unforeseen circumstance flight must be cancelled after the reporting time for duty, ground duty is added which starts at the original reporting time, and

finishes either at the time when decision for cancellation was made (if crew was

not yet at the aircraft) or 30min after the decision was made (if crew performed any flight duty prior to the affected one).

kontext:
8.2.4.3.1 Type I Fluid (un-thickened type)

This group is the widely known manufactured to the military specifications MIL-A-3243 or MIL-D-8243.

The fluid must consist of at least 80 ethylene or propylene glycol, or 80 of a mixture of both. If diluted with water the fluid must have a freezing point of at least 10 degrees below the ambient temperature.

The mix of fluid and water must be heated to 60 degrees Celsius (140 degrees F) minimum at the nozzle.
Type I fluids provide protection mainly against re-freezing in conditions where precipitation is not expected. Special care must be taken not to exceed the Holdover Time (HOT), since a Type I fluid may then change its condition from fluid to solid state (ice) in as little as 30 seconds. This effect is known as a flash freeze.

kontext:
8.2.4.20 Ramp and Taxi Precautions

Icy conditions on the ramp and in the gate area means that the push back vehicle may not be able to develop sufficient traction to push the aircraft with its engines running. Therefore, it is recommended to have the aircraft pushed back, to a position from which it can taxi forward, before starting engines. Standing on an icy patch even idle thrust may be sufficient to move the aircraft forward, although the parking brake is set.
Abnormal engine indications may occur during engine start especially caused by the low oil temperature (and therefore high viscosity), with oil pressure exceeding normal limits until the oil temperature rises. This is acceptable provided the engine is operated at not more than idle thrust until the indications are back to normal.
There is a possibility for engine inlet ice to build-up during taxi and ground holding operation.
Ice can form in engine inlets at temperatures above 10°C with high humidity present during extensive ground holds with the engines at idle.

If visible moisture is present with a temperature below that specified in the Operations Manual OM-B, engine nacelle anti-ice systems shall be switched on after completion of the engine start procedure.
Probe and sensor heating systems shall be switched on before taxiing, according

to the checklist procedures.

Taxi shall take place with great care and significantly lower speeds than normal.

Neither aircraft, nor ground vehicles are capable of stopping quickly on icy or

contaminated surfaces. When guide lamp installations are available, use of them shall be made to align the aircraft in the gate area. Snow may cover the normal

taxi markings. Braking and steering capabilities shall be tested frequently.

Maintaining a greater distance than normal from other traffic helps to avoid jet- blast, which could adversely affect anti-ice treatment and prevents from blow of

contaminants into the aircraft.

Engine thrust may need to be higher than normal to overcome the drag caused by slush or snow. Changes should be made slowly and carefully to avoid blowing

equipment or contaminants into other aircraft. At intervals during prolonged taxi and immediately before take-off, engines shall be run up to higher settings as specified in the Operations Manual OM-B.

Flaps should be kept up when taxiing through slush or standing water, with pre-take-off checks held until the flaps can be lowered again.
Holding shall be done well clear of an active runway as a landing aircraft is more likely to deviate from the centreline when braking conditions are marginal.
Slush thrown up by landing aircraft can be ingested by engines, cause airframe damage and degrade the anti-ice treatment.

kontext:
8.2.4.24 Rejected Take-off in Icing Conditions

Directional control problems may be aggravated during a rejected take-off due to excessive anti-skid cycling and individual wheel skidding.

The rudder must be used as the primary steering aid.
Under no circumstances asymmetric reverse thrust shall be used for directional control.

In contrary, loss of directional control must be counteracted by setting of idle reverse or temporary selection of forward idle thrust.
Note: If rejected take off occurs with a de-iced aircraft before next departure de-icing should be taken into consideration.

kontext:
2.8.3.3.7 Engine Run-Up Procedure

The Engine Run-Up procedure must be accomplished in any of the following conditions: in icing conditions for ground operations of more than 30 min

or in case of increased fan vibration due to fan ice accumulation

or for removal of light ice (similar to hoarfrost) or light snow in the inlet, on

the spinner, on the fan blades or on the booster area as observed during the external inspection

Note: Engine vibration may indicate maximum display value during engine run-up with no adverse effect on the engine.

Make sure that the aircraft is positioned accordingly before accomplishing the following procedures. If necessary, coordinate with ATC before performing a run- up.

Brakes APPLY Apply Emergency/Parking Brake or brake pedals.

Thrust Levers ADJUST TO 54% N1

The engine thrust must be increased to a minimum of 54% N1 for 30 s

or

until fan vibration indication returns to normal, whichever comes first.

monitor engine parameters and ensure normal operation.

Thrust Levers IDLE Note: Engine Run-Up procedure can be accomplished just before, or in

conjunction with the takeoff procedure.

Do not initiate the takeoff run if airframe vibration persists.
Brakes AS REQUIRED

kontext:
2.8.3.3.7 Engine Run-Up Procedure

The engine run-up procedure shall be performed whenever 30 minutes are exceeded and all of the following conditions are fulfilled: during ground operations with engines running

when the OAT is equal to or less than 3°C

visible moisture in any form is present

Engine run-ups at intervals less than 30 minutes are recommended during freezing fog, freezing drizzle, or moderate snow conditions.
An engine run-up shall be performed as soon as practical in case of increased fan vibration due to fan ice accumulation after engine start.
Make sure that the aircraft is positioned accordingly before accomplishing the following procedures. If necessary, coordinate with ATC before performing a run- up.

Brakes APPLY Apply Emergency/Parking Brake or brake pedals.

Thrust Levers ADJUST TO 60% N1
The engine thrust level must be increased to a minimum of 60% N1 for 10 s or until fan vibration level returns to normal, whichever takes more time.

Monitor engine parameters and ensure normal operation.

Thrust Levers IDLE

Brakes AS REQUIRED

Note: According to Embraer, on the E2, a large part of the ice-shedding is

achieved from the thrust change back to idle.

2.8.3.3.16 Leaving the Airplane

Slat/Flap

Do not retract the flaps unless they are free of snow, ice or slush.

Pitch Trim SET FULL NOSE DOWN

Only applicable when Pre-De-/Anti-icing is expected during overnight parking.

Emergency/Parking Brake AS REQUIRED

For an icy ramp, it is recommended to leave Emergency Parking Brake applied. Otherwise, release Emergency Parking Brake to avoid brakes freezing.

Water and Waste System AS REQUIRED

Batteries 1 and 2 AS REQUIRED

For further details refer to AOM 13-70 Cold Soaked Preparation.

Call MCC if battery removal is required.

If air conditioning ground unit is used during parking, there is no need to remove the batteries, regardless of time and temperature.

kontext:
2.8.3.3.2 External Inspection

When operating in cold weather, the flight crew must carefully inspect the

airframe and dedicate special attention to areas where snow, ice, or frost could interfere in normal systems operation.

Wheel Chocks IN PLACE Smart Probes/TAT Sensor/Ice Detector CHECK

Verify free of ice, snow, and residual deicing/anti icing fluid.

Probes must be unblocked. Even small portions of remaining contamination may result in erroneous readings.

Air Conditioning Inlets/Outlets CLEAR OF ICE OR SNOW Protective Covers CHECK REMOVED

If required, leave engine covers installed until engine start.

Engines (including the core aft of fan blades) CLEAR OF ICE OR SNOW Heavy accumulation of ice or snow in the inlet, on the spinner, on the fan

blades or on the booster area must be removed prior to start.

Light ice similar to hoarfrost or light snow may be removed by performing

engine run-up.

A small area of thin ice at the basis of the inlet near the drain in front of the

fan blades is allowable.
Ensure that the fan is free to rotate

Landing Gear CLEAR OF ICE, UNOBSTRUCTED

Fuselage FREE OF FROST, ICE OR SNOW

Light hoarfrost on the fuselage is allowable provided that surface details

such as painting and markings are visible.

A physical inspection may be performed to ensure that there is no frost, ice

or snow accumulation.

OM-B E1 2 Normal Procedures

Wing, Tail and Control Surfaces FREE OF FROST, ICE OR SNOW

The wings upper and lower surfaces, as well as ailerons must be free of ice, snow, and frost.
A thin layer of frost up to 3 mm is acceptable on the wings lower surface.

Visual inspection of the wing upper surface may be performed from a passenger cabin window. A physical inspection may be performed to ensure

that there is no frost, ice or snow accumulation.
Cold fuel may result in frost on the wings upper surface. Expect this kind of frost when fuel remaining in each wing tank exceeds 3420 kg.

Check all control surfaces, including gaps and hinges for signs of contamination.
As the horizontal stabilizer upper surface is not visible from the ground and cockpit, the condition of the wing upper surface may be used as a reference to decide whether deicing/anti-icing is required for the horizontal stabilizer.

APU Area CLEAR OF ICE OR SNOW

kontext:
2.8.3.3.8 Taxi Out

Note:
If engine oil temperature is less than 49°C (120°F), avoid engine thrust above idle in order to prevent fuel icing.

Engine Run-Up Procedure AS REQUIRED

The tires may retain a flat shape after a prolonged parking period, a condition known as cold-set. Cold-set may induce airframe vibration during taxi-out, which extinguishes as tires recover the normal shape.
Do not initiate the takeoff run if airframe vibration persists.
If the taxiway is contaminated or treated with ice control sand, taxi in with the following considerations:
CAUTION: Taxi at reduced speed on ice-covered runways or taxiways to avoid skidding the airplane and throwing slush on wheel and brake assemblies.

Avoid single engine taxi as much as practical.

Minimize breakaway and taxi thrust. Limit taxi thrust to 40% N1.

On taxi stops, use firm brake pressure in order to warm up the brakes and to prevent ice or moisture build-ups on the brake assembly.

Antiskid protection is not available below 10 kt.
Avoid engine operation above idle during taxi stops.

Maintain a greater than normal distance behind other airplanes.

Turns should be performed at the largest turning radius, preferably at a

speed that do not required braking during the turn.

Also refer to 2.8.3.3.7 - Engine Run-Up Procedure

Slat/Flap

kontext:
8.3.2.25.3 The Runway Condition Assessment Matrix (RCAM)

For the overall assessment of the runway condition, the RCAM provides the flight crew with a combination of all available information: runway surface conditions: state and or contaminant

pilot report of braking action (PIREP) or Estimated Surface Friction (ESF)

The RCAM provides the maximum crosswind values for landing and takeoff performance. It does not show the friction coefficient since there is no correlation between the coefficient measured by a vehicle and the actual aircraft braking capability.

The following Landing Performance Codes-Levels are used to assess the related

takeoff and landing performance:

6 - Dry

5 - Good

5 - Wet Grooved (if runway is grooved or Porous Friction Course (PFC))

4 - Good to Medium

3 - Medium 2 - Medium to Poor

1 - Poor

0 - Less than Poor

8.3.2.25.3.1 How to use the Runway Condition Assessment Matrix (RCAM)

The flight crew shall make a primary assessment based on runway state or runway contaminant type and depth and the OAT.
Then, the flight crew should downgrade this primary assessment if: a report (PIREP or ESF) is available and this report corresponds to a lower Runway Condition Code (RCC)

complementary information is available and is related to a possible degradation of the runway surface conditions.

If the primary means of assessment (runway state or runway contaminant type and depth) is not available, the flight crew should request it by ATC.
The flight crew shall not use a report or any other complementary information in order to upgrade a primary assessment.

A RWYCC 1 or 0 maybe upgraded by the airport operator to a maximum of RWYCC 3. This upgrade may be considered by flight crews.
Example:

Crews shall use the reported contamination level or braking action report and reference the RCAM to obtain a

corresponding RCC.
If ATC reports “Compacted Snow” and the ESF is “Good to

Medium” the equivalent RCC

can be found by referencing the

RCAM in the QRH.

PIREP’s are to be treated as informative only and may be disregarded on pilot’s

discretion. However, the lowest

Runway Condition Code (RCC) found shall be used for

performancecalculation.

For this example, the RCC is 3.

fragen.zitat: The performance software tool automatically adds a 15% safety margin to the calculated operational landing distance. If calculations are performed manually via AOM this margin has to be added by the crew.
fragen.frage_en: Which safety margin does the performance software tool automatically add to the calculated operational landing distance?

kontext:
8.3.2.25.1 General

The flight crew should choose the runway with the best performance margin under the prevailing weather conditions.
Due regard shall be given to other meteorological and operational factors (e.g. ATC requirements, preferential runway system, runway condition, noise abatement procedures, wind condition during all phases of flight, thunderstorms in the vicinity of the airport).
Special attention shall be paid to the condition of the runway regarding type of contaminant and associated wind limitations.
The Runway Condition Assessment Matrix (RCAM) provides guidelines to determine the runway condition to be used for performance calculation.
The available runway length shall be equal or exceed the required distance obtained by the respective aircraft type performance tool or other approved data.
The performance calculation should be based on the latest available weather report and runway conditon report (RCR) or equivalent information based on the RCR.
The best source of information provides the Automatic Terminal Information Service (ATIS).
For the runway intended to use, the following consideration shall be done: the existing weather conditions at the time of departure arrival

the takeoff- approach- configuration used under these condition the actual runway condition

the information on wind contained in METAR/SPECI/ATIS reports (average

of a 10-minute period) should be the basis for the performance calculations, while instant wind information reported by the tower shall be monitored to

ensure that the wind speed during takeoff/approach does not exceed the

assumptions made for performance calculations.

The result of the performance calculation shall be verified amongst the flight

crew during the briefing and shall be recorded on the Operational Flight Plan (OFP) or in the EFB system in a traceable manner (real conditions, result of

calculation, explanatory remarks).

8.3.2.25.1.1 Takeoff Performance

The determination of takeoff performance data for wet and contaminated runways should be based on the reported runway surface condition in terms of contaminant and depth.
In the case of a contaminated runway, the flight crew shall consider the option to wait until the runway is cleared. If this is impracticable, applicable performance adjustments must be applied by using the type specific performance tool or approved data (e.g. AFM).
The take-off must be started either from the runway beginning, or from an authorized take-off point according to OM-C which must be considered in the takeoff performance calculation.
The weather report should not be older than 30 minutes before commencing takeoff.

8.3.2.25.1.2 Landing Performance

The crew shall be satisfied that, according to the information available, the condition of the runway intended to be used, will not prevent a safe approach, landing or missed approach, having regard to the performance information.
The initial in-flight landing distance assessment should be carried out when the weather report and the RCR are obtained, usually around TOD. If the planned duration of the flight does not allow the flight crew to carry out the assessment in non-critical phases of the flight, the assessment should be carried out before

departure.
When meteorological condition may lead to a degradation of the runway surface condition, the assessment shall include considerations of how much deterioration in runway surface friction characteristics may be tolerated, so that a quick

decision can be made prior to landing.

The flight crew shall monitor the evolution of the actual conditions during the

approach, to ensure that they do not degrade below the condition that was

determined to be the minimum acceptable during the initial in-flight landing distance assessment.

For calculating the in-flight landing performance, use the type specific

performance software tool or refer to:

AOM E1 5-35 Operational Landing Distance

AOM E2 5-35 Operational Landing Distance

Note:

The performance software tool automatically adds a 15% safety margin to the calculated operational landing distance.

If calculations are performed manually via AOM this margin has to be added by the crew.

fragen.frage: Welche Faustregel nennt OM-A zur Abschätzung des Beginns von Fog bei klarem Himmel?
antworten: Ab Sonnenuntergang sinkt die Temperatur um rund 2° pro Stunde; Fog bildet sich bereits 2° über dem Taupunkt
Ab einer Stunde nach dem Sonnenhöchststand sinkt die Temperatur um rund 3° pro Stunde; Fog bildet sich bei 95 % Luftfeuchtigkeit
Ab Mitternacht sinkt die Temperatur um rund 1° pro Stunde; Fog bildet sich eine Stunde nach Erreichen des Taupunkts
Ab zwei Stunden nach dem Sonnenhöchststand sinkt die Temperatur um rund 1° pro Stunde; Fog bildet sich, sobald der Taupunkt erreicht ist
fragen.erklaerung: Faustregel: Sonnenhöchststand bestimmen; zwei Stunden danach sinkt die Temperatur um rund 1° pro Stunde, und sobald sie den Taupunkt erreicht, beginnt sich Fog zu bilden.
fragen.zitat: determine the suns peak (time) two hours after the peak, the temperature drops around 1° per hour as soon as the temperature reaches the dew point, fog starts to build
fragen.frage_en: Which rule of thumb does OM-A give to estimate the beginning of fog with a clear sky?
antworten_en: From sunset the temperature drops about 2° per hour; fog builds already 2° above the dew point
From one hour after the sun's peak the temperature drops about 3° per hour; fog builds at 95 % humidity
From midnight the temperature drops about 1° per hour; fog builds one hour after reaching the dew point
From two hours after the sun's peak the temperature drops about 1° per hour; fog starts to build as soon as the dew point is reached

kontext:
8.3.8.13 Fog

Fog itself does not have to be considered as hazardous. Between autumn and spring situations may arise where fog was not forecast but appears suddenly.
This might lead to operational constraints such as in-flight delays due to enforcement of low visibility procedures or diversions.
Rule of thumb to estimate begin of fog (sky clear):

determine the suns peak (time)

two hours after the peak, the temperature drops around 1° per hour

as soon as the temperature reaches the dew point, fog starts to build

fragen.frage: Bei welcher Augenhöhe ist die Slant Visual Range (SVR) im Fog gemäss OM-A annähernd gleich der RVR?
antworten: Bei Augenhöhen unter 100 ft
Bei Augenhöhen unter 200 ft (CAT I DH)
Nur bei sehr tiefer Augenhöhe unter 30 ft
Bei Augenhöhen unter 50 ft (CAT III DH)

fragen.zitat: Only at very low eye levels (less than 30 ft) will the SVR be nearly the same as the RVR.
fragen.frage_en: According to OM-A, at which eye level is the slant visual range (SVR) in fog nearly the same as the RVR?
antworten_en: At eye levels below 100 ft
At eye levels below 200 ft (CAT I DH)
Only at very low eye levels of less than 30 ft
At eye levels below 50 ft (CAT III DH)
fragen.erklaerung_en: As fog density usually increases with height, the SVR is less than the RVR; only at very low eye levels (less than 30 ft) is the SVR nearly the same as the RVR.
kontext:
8.3.8.13.1 Description

Fog will only form and persist if particular values of temperature, humidity and wind all exist simultaneously. Small changes of any one of these parameters will result in variations in the extent, density and depth of the fog and it is this sensitivity, which is responsible for its extreme and continuous variability. Even under stable conditions, a large variation in the vertical plane of the concentration and size of water droplets is known to occur, with a tendency for the greater concentration to be at the higher levels. As it is, these factors are responsible for the visual range within the fog to increase closer to the ground.
Assuming the general case of density increasing with height, any slant visual range will be less than the RVR.
Only at very low eye levels (less than 30 ft) will the SVR be nearly the same as the RVR.

Nevertheless, in certain conditions, where fog density changes rapidly below 30 ft, poor correlation will be obtained and it is still best to make no

assumptions about visual reference from the reported RVR.

The dense and lifted fogs yield basically similar visual sequences. Where once obtained, the visual segment increases. This sequence is to be expected when

the approach is made through low cloud with or without fog underneath or into a

fog where the pilot has been unable to see the ground beforehand.

kontext:
8.4.2 Flight Preparation

In addition to the normal flight preparation, the following planning and preparation must be performed when Low Visibility Operation (LVO) is in force. review of the NOTAMS to ensure that the destination airport meets visual or non-visual Category II or III requirements: runway and approach lighting malfunction or degradation radio navigation aid availability RVR equipment availability ILS category changes

aircraft status: check of the aircraft Tech Log for deferred defects or other entries that affect any equipment required for Category II or III

crew qualification and recency: both Commander (CMD) and Copilot (COP) must be qualified and current for Low Visibility Operation (LVO)

weather information: the weather forecast at destination must be within airplane and crew operating minima MOTNE or SNOWTAM can give an indication of runway contamination

and braking action The alternate airport must be carefully selected, taking into consideration primarily the weather, but also the available passenger services and traffic restrictions. A take-off alternate is needed if a return to the departure airport is

not possible in case of equipment or engine failure during take-off.

Extra fuel should be considered due to increased taxiing times prior to take-off, taxiing to remote anti-ice stations or possible delays on arrival, longer separation

and possibility of go-around and second approach.

kontext:
2.8.3.3 Icing Conditions, Cold Weather and Cold Soak Operation

This section provides operational procedures and guidelines for cold weather operations as a supplement to the normal procedures.
For information related to ground operations, refer to 2.11.13 - Cold Weather Operation

General Icing condition is present when OAT (on ground) or TAT (in flight) is 10°C or less and any of the following conditions exist:
Visible moisture such as clouds, fog with visibility of one mile or less, rain, snow, sleet, or ice crystals.

Ice, snow, slush, or standing water on ramps, taxiways, or runways.

Note: Notwithstanding ice detector monitoring, the crew remains responsible for monitoring icing conditions and for manual activation of the ice protection system if icing conditions are present and the ice detection system is not activating the ice protection system.

Freezing Rain And Freezing Drizzle Freezing rain and freezing drizzle may cause ice formation on airplane surfaces even during short exposures and on areas not normally subjected to ice accretion. If such ice formation is noticed, the airplane may be flying under

severe icing conditions. In such situation, exit the area immediately.
Take-off is prohibited in freezing rain or freezing drizzle conditions (i.e. FZRA, +FZRA, FZDZ, +FZDZ).

Freezing Fog (Operational Engine Limitation) The following procedures apply during ground operations at OAT 3°C or below

and FZFG present.

Shortly Before Engine Start: crew shall verify current VIS (i.e. latest availabe ATIS/METAR or ATC):

if VIS above 110m: startup and taxi allowed

if VIS below 110m: delay startup until VIS >110m

During Taxi Out: single engine taxi-out is prohibitied

high engine thrust settings shall be avoided (i.e. above 40% N1)

Shortly Before Line Up and Takeoff (at Holding Point of Departure Runway): crew shall verify current VIS (i.e. latest availabe ATIS/METAR or ATC):

if VIS above 110m: takeoff allowed

if VIS below 110m: no takeoff allowed, taxi back to parking position

After Taxi-in (following a Landing or Return to Parking Position): crew shall perform a thorough visual inspection of engines as per 2.8.3.3.2 - External Inspection

Aircraft Repositioning:

engine start and taxi is allowed below 110m VIS for repositioning

after repositioning, crew shall perform a thorough visual inspection of engines as per 2.8.3.3.2 - External Inspection

OM-B E2 2 Normal Procedures

kontext:
2.6.1.7 Landing on Wet, Slippery or Contaminated Runways

Wet or contaminated runways have much lower friction levels than a dry runway.
Friction depends on the runway surface, materials, and conditions. Runway contamination may reduce friction to low levels. A runway is contaminated whenever standing water, ice, snow, slush, frost in any form, heavy rubber, or other substances are present. If such conditions exist at the time of arrival and

were not considered during dispatch, conduct a landing distance reassessment.
The QRH presents tables to aid this analysis.

Hydroplaning always occurs to some degree when operating on fluid-

contaminated runway. The degree of hydroplaning depends on the following factors:

absence of runway surface roughness and inadequate drainage

depth and type of contaminant

tire inflation pressure

Additional considerations, as follows, should be taken: use Maximum Performance Landing techniques

conduct a positive landing to ensure initial wheel spin-up and initiate firm ground contact upon touchdown. Such technique avoids hydroplaning on wet runways and reduces the strength of any ice bond that, during flight, might have been eventually formed on brake

and wheel assemblies. apply maximum reverse thrust. Do not use asymmetric reverse thrust on slippery and icy runways.

apply firm and symmetrical pressure on brakes pedal

if the airplane loses friction with the runway, do not apply

Emergency/Parking Brake, as it inhibits antiskid protection. Maintain

runway centerline applying rudder, and keep firm and symmetrical braking.

Note: Landing on wet runways could be performed not using thrust reversers.

Landing performance must comply with the runway distance available.

kontext:
2.6.1.10 Low Visibility Landing

When flying under conditions of haze, smoke, dust, glare, or darkness, airplane height may appear higher than it actually is. Shadows are one of the key factors of depth perception.
This effect is also encountered during night landings, or when smoke or dust

appears lying low across the threshold. The effect varies with individuals and is modified by the intensity and clarity of runway lighting. Situational alert must be

emphasized on precision approaches, since pilots tend to reduce power and drop below glide path as soon as the runway is in sight.

Moisture on windshield interferes with visibility and may cause any type of glide

path illusion.

Light rays refract (bend) as they pass through the layer of moisture of the windshield. You can appear to be above or below the glide path or left or right of centerline. This effect can be as much as 200 ft error at one mile from the runway

which, when combine with effect mentioned above, could result in risk of landing short of runway threshold or in a long landing.
Crosscheck VSI for rate of descent and fly to the touchdown aim point.

kontext:
8.4.3.1 Taxiing in Poor Visibility Conditions

Bear in mind that, in very low RVR values, one would expect to see bright lights at a safe distance but not unlit or poorly lit obstacles, such as aircraft tails or wing tips. From certain angles, their navigation lights do not show up well. Since aircraft movement rates will be low in these conditions, taxi as slowly as necessary for safety. Do not hesitate to request from ATC the positions of other taxiing aircraft or to ask for a “follow me” car. Take the utmost care to taxi according to the issued clearance.
Switch on taxi lights, even in daylight conditions, to make you more visible to other aircraft and vehicles.

kontext:
8.3.8.9 Heavy Precipitation

Heavy precipitation may occur as rain showers, snow showers and hail.
The greatest hazards to flight are the reduced visibility and the risk of icing in combination with low temperature.
On the ground contaminated runways may influence the performance, the crosswind limitations and provide a risk of aquaplaning. The special procedures of the Operations Manual OM-B of the respective aircraft must be followed.

Partial loss of orientation may occur after changeover from instruments to visual flying during the approach, especially in snow showers and blowing snow.

In falling or blowing snow, landing lights should be used with caution as the reflected light may actually reduce the effective visibility and even cause false

impression of drift during flare and rollout.

kontext:
8.3.3.4 Terrain Clearance – low Temperature or strong Winds

Effects of very low temperatures and strong winds must be taken into consideration whenever minimum altitudes are defined in relation to or limited by terrain. In general, the flight crew is responsible for terrain clearance. Whenever corrections are applied, ATC shall be informed.
An exception applies only while the aircraft is being radar-vectored, as the altitudes and flight levels are already compensated by ATC.

kontext:
8.1.2.2.2 Standard Instrument Departure (SID) Routes

Standard Instrument Departure (SID) routes – as published by ATC – are constructed using the procedures outlined in document 8168 PANS/OPS.
If no special altitudes are promulgated in the Standard Instrument Departure (SID), procedures are based on a: 2.5% slope plus a safety margin of 0.8%

thus requiring a climb gradient of 3.3% to be achieved in the All Engine Operative (AEO) case. The 3.3% slope starts at the end of the Take-off Distance Available (TODA) and extends to the point where the Standard Instrument Departure (SID) ends, or to the minimum safe sector altitude. The 3.3% minimum climb gradient shall be achieved also in case of engine failure (One Engine Inoperative – OEI), unless a contingency procedure (escape route) is used. If there are obstacles in the Standard Instrument Departure (SID), penetrating the 2.5% obstacle identification surface, a higher climb gradient than the 3.3% safety margin will be required.
If the aircraft mass allows for an One Engine Inoperative (OEI) climb gradient of at least 3.3% under the actual density altitude, the Standard Instrument Departure (SID) could be followed without restrictions unless it specifies minimum gradients higher than 3.3%.

If either the aircraft mass is higher than the allowable minimum or if a higher gradient than 2.5% (excluding the safety margin of 0.8%) is required, a contingency procedure (escape route) shall be developed

to allow a safe departure also in the case of an engine failure.

Note: ICAO type C charts are a reliable source for the determination of obstacles and terrain elevation. Alternatively ICAO VFR charts may be used although not all obstacles are listed. Published Minimum Sector Altitudes (MSA) are a last resort, but may occasionally be too

conservative.

OM-A 8 Operating Procedures

fragen.frage: Innerhalb welchen Anteils der LDA muss ein Turbojet auf trockener Runway aus 50 ft über der Threshold zum Stillstand kommen?
fragen.erklaerung: Die Landing Distance Required auf trockener Runway entspricht der tatsächlichen Distanz mal 1.67; das Flugzeug muss also innerhalb von 60 % der LDA zum Stillstand kommen.
fragen.zitat: That means that the aircraft must come to a full stop landing from 50 feet above threshold latest within 60% of the Landing Distance Available (LDA).
fragen.frage_en: Within which portion of the LDA must a turbojet come to a full stop on a dry runway from 50 ft above the threshold?
fragen.erklaerung_en: The landing distance required on a dry runway is the actual distance multiplied by 1.67; the aircraft must therefore come to a full stop within 60 % of the LDA.
kontext:
8.1.2.2.7 Landing

The Landing Distance Required (LDR) for dry runways is based on a factored landing distance, derived from the actual landing distance increased by a safety margin of 67 (multiplied by 1.67) for turbojet aircraft.
That means that the aircraft must come to a full stop landing from 50 feet above threshold latest within 60% of the Landing Distance Available (LDA).

For wet or contaminated runways that landing distance required must additionally be increased by a 15% safety margin (multiplied by 1.15 or

uncorrected actual landing distance multiplied by 1.92).
For a landing of an aircraft with system failures, that require an increase of the landing distance required, the longer of the two calculated landing distances shall be applied:

actual landing distance increased by a safety margin of 67

(multiplied by 1.67), or

actual landing distance for the system failure situation as stated in the

Operations Manual OM-B 4 increased by a safety margin of 15 (multiplied by 1.15)

Effect of high temperature

When executing 2D and 3D approach operations based on barometric pressure

the approach angles are steeper than charted.

kontext:
2.8.1.3 Unpressurized Flight

Limit flight level to 10000 ft if carrying passengers. For flight without passengers, flight level may be greater than 10000 ft provided crew uses oxygen (Refer to appropriate regulations).

For flights with air conditioning packs inoperative (MMEL Item 21-51-00), the following recommendations apply:

prior to flight, if a Ground Air Conditioning System is available, precondition the cabin in order to avoid high peak temperatures,

consideration should be given to passenger comfort and TAT expected to be encountered in flight.
When carrying passengers or TAT is hotter than 20°C, close passenger window shades and turn off unnecessary lights in order to minimize cabin heat.

Operating at TAT hotter than 32°C is not recommended due to the resulting high temperatures in the cabin and cockpit,

flight crew can use Total Air Temperature to predict cabin and cockpit tem- peratures during Ram Air operation, especially at longer duration flights.

kontext:
3.15.1 Overweight Landing

Overweight landing may safely be accomplished by using normal landing procedures and techniques. There are no adverse handling characteristics

associated with heavier than normal landing weights.

Select the longest available runway, when feasible. Also consider the effects of runway slope and wind effect.

Where possible avoid landing in tailwinds, on runways with negative slope or

runways with less than normal braking conditions.
Reduce the landing weight as much as possible. To save time and at pilot's discretion, it can be done using high drag configuration (landing gear and/or speed brake) and flying at a lower altitude (respect MORA and MSA).
Wind additives may be impacted by flap placard speeds.
At weights above the maximum landing weight, the maximum wind correction in the final approach may be limited by the flap maneuvering speed.
Configure the airplane earlier so there is more time to get used to the higher approach speeds. Do not carry the excess of airspeed on final.
It is recommended to land under VMC. There is more time to focus on the handling of the airplane rather than on the instruments panel.

Brake energy is not exceeded for flaps 5 or FULL landing at all gross weights.
Although, give special attention to wet or slippery runways.
The brake energy limits may be exceeded when landing at high gross weights at speeds associated with nonnormal procedures requiring flaps set at 5 or less.

Try a smooth landing. In the other hand, do not allow the airplane to float above the runway. If a long landing is likely to occur, consider a go-around.

The maximum rate of descend is 300 ft/min at touchdown.

Use maximum reverse thrust down to 60 kt.
If stop capability is in doubt use it until certain that the airplane stops within

limitations. Use brakes consistent with runway length. Autobrakes may be used.
Maintenance inspection is required after landing

(report AGW and rate of descent on the TLB).

Note: Alert ground crew if brake temperature is too high.

kontext:
8.3.8.5 Wind Shear

In order to avoid dangerous wind shear phenomena it is important to know what wind shear is and in which meteorological and geographical environment it can be expected.
The following definition seems to be the most suitable for aviation:

wind shear is any rapid change in wind direction or speed along the flight path of an aircraft

Wind shear, with or without turbulence, alters the lift force acting on an aircraft, resulting in a significant sinking or rising motion.

Therefore, wind shear may be categorized as:

increasing performance shear caused by increasing headwind or decreasing

tailwind component or vertical updrafts

decreasing performance shear caused by decreasing headwind or

increasing tailwind component or vertical downdrafts

Conditions for potentially hazardous wind shears are: convective conditions (e.g. thunderstorms, rain or snow showers)

frontal systems

jet streams

strong or gusty surface winds

other cases (temperature inversion, mountain waves, sea breeze circulations)

Wind shear events are typically one to two miles in diameter and mostly occur near the ground (typically below 500 ft AGL) during take-off and landing. Both situations would see the aircraft in a low energy condition. Therefore, there is only limited time for wind shear recognition and counteraction, typically 5 to 15 seconds.
Several factors can impede wind shear recognition: marginal weather conditions

high crew work load conditions

illusion of normality; during the initial part of the wind shear encounter, everything may appear normal; even severe wind shear onset may not

provide dramatic early indications to the flight crew

Standard response of the flight crew should be: control of flight path through pitch attitude; resistance to a downward change

in pitch attitude as normal response to low airspeed

immediate increase of thrust, maximum thrust shall be applied

an approach shall be aborted

unusual stick forces may be required to maintain pitch attitude during

airspeed variations away from normal target airspeed

low airspeed must be accepted, flying at airspeeds below normal reference

speeds may be required in order to utilize the full performance capability of the aircraft (speed increments under expected wind shear threat are stated

in Operations Manual OM-B)

The term downburst describes a severe downward rush of air and its outburst of

damaging winds near the ground. It has been classified into macroburst and microburst. They are different in their size with radial outflow at the earth’s surface lasting from 3 to 20 minutes.

Downbursts can occur wherever convective weather conditions exist.
Approximately 5% of all thunderstorms produce microburst.
Downdrafts associated with microburst are typically only a few hundred to thousand meters across. When the downburst hits the ground, it spreads out horizontally and may form one or more horizontal vortex rings around the downdraft up to 2 000 ft AGL.
In downbursts with vortices very powerful updrafts and roll forces in conjunction with wind speed changes up to 45 knots can be expected.
The time period over which wind speeds exceed half the peak value may last from 1 to 8 minutes. Depending on the movement and the height of the base of parent cloud, microburst may occur as: stationary or moving

surface or midair

wet or dry

Microburst has occurred in relatively dry conditions of light rain or precipitation that evaporates before reaching the earth’s surface.
Frontal wind shear is present in both cold and warm fronts, but exists in a different relative location in each type of front. Because the cold front boundary slopes back behind the frontal surface, the wind shear line also slopes back. The frontal boundary of the warm front slopes upward ahead of the surface front and

so does the wind shear. Significant wind shears can be expected if there is a large difference in surface temperature 6°C) across the front and if the front is moving rapidly at more than 30 knots.
Large wind speeds changes near the ground can be found in many

meteorological situations, including the frontal conditions. Terrain irregularities or

buildings, which interrupt the wind flow, can produce significant wind shears close to the ground.

A temperature increase with constant wind speed

kontext:
8.3.8.6 General Guidelines for Operation in Turbulence, Wind Shear and

Thunderstorms

The following provisions shall serve as a list of possible actions which are applicable for the operation in turbulence, wind shear and thunderstorms.
The flight crew members shall select carefully from these options according to the actual situation: procedures according to 8.3.16.10 - Preparation for an Encounter with

Turbulence

fasten shoulder harness

switch on cockpit lighting to high intensity to avoid dazzling by lightning in thunderstorm

fly the recommended turbulence speed according to the Operations Manual

OM-B

switch on engine ignition and deicing equipment according to the Operations Manual OM-B procedures

altitude: at maximum cruise altitude, the margin between low speed and high speed buffet is small and any increase of g-loads, whether caused by

manoeuvring or by turbulence, may lead to serious difficulties (coffin corner); this shall be considered when trying to top a turbulence region; therefore do

not select maximum cruise altitude; allow altitude to vary; large altitude variations are possible in severe turbulence; sacrifice altitude in order to

maintain the desired attitude and airspeed; never chase altitude; large and

persistent altitude variations may smoothly be corrected by only small elevator inputs and appropriate power corrections

airspeed and power setting: large speed fluctuations and difficulties in instrument reading are to be expected due to yawing and head on gusts, therefore: do not chase airspeed; maintain the recommended turbulence speed as target speed; set thrust as required and then do not change it unless required by large or persistent airspeed or altitude variations; the real airspeed of the aircraft will remain within reasonable limits as long as thrust is set properly, while avoiding large and rapid throttle movements, and a reasonable constant attitude can be maintained; if caught unawares by turbulence, do not slow the aircraft down hurriedly

attitude: control pitch attitude with smooth control inputs to the elevator; closely monitor the attitude and the flight director indications; all other instruments may be seriously erratic; maintain a constant attitude

use of autopilot and flight director:
since the autopilot will not be subject to false attitude interpretations or difficulties in erratic instruments, its use in the appropriate turbulence mode is mandatory;

the flight director can effectively reduce workload and is therefore mandatory for use in turbulence when manual flying is unavoidable; it will give a good reference for control about all axes and will further call for proper control inputs

recovery: should attitude control be partially lost due to severe turbulence, resulting in an upset or steep dive, the following recommendations may be helpful for a successful recovery: use appropriate means to prevent a rapid speed build-up; the pitching effect caused thereby is secondary to the need to keep the speed at a reasonable value; roll the wings level before

attempting to pitch up; if the aircraft is in a spiral dive, elevator up force will tighten the spiral; unless affected by compressibility the aircraft natural stability will result in a pitch up with increase in airspeed provided the wings are level and the trim is unaltered; elevator forces can become very heavy as speed increases, thus being a safeguard against excessive

g-loads; if stabilizer trim is used for recovery, use it with utmost caution so as

to avoid heavy loads and a possible over trim, which could result in a

renewed loss of control; if strong elevator forces are applied, the trim motors

might become ineffective (stalled); by reducing the elevator forces, the trim motors will be enabled to drive the stabilizer in the desired direction

persistent altitude variations may smoothly be corrected by only small elevator inputs and appropriate power corrections

airspeed and power setting: large speed fluctuations and difficulties in instrument reading are to be expected due to yawing and head on gusts, therefore: do not chase airspeed; maintain the recommended turbulence speed as target speed; set thrust as required and then do not change it unless required by large or persistent airspeed or altitude variations; the real airspeed of the aircraft will remain within reasonable limits as long as thrust is set properly, while avoiding large and rapid throttle movements, and a reasonable constant attitude can be maintained; if caught unawares by turbulence, do not slow the aircraft down hurriedly

attitude: control pitch attitude with smooth control inputs to the elevator; closely monitor the attitude and the flight director indications; all other instruments may be seriously erratic; maintain a constant attitude

use of autopilot and flight director: since the autopilot will not be subject to false attitude interpretations or difficulties in erratic instruments, its use in the appropriate turbulence mode is mandatory; the flight director can effectively reduce workload and is therefore mandatory for use in turbulence when manual flying is unavoidable; it will give a good reference for control about all axes and will further call for proper control inputs

recovery: should attitude control be partially lost due to severe turbulence, resulting in an upset or steep dive, the following recommendations may be helpful for a successful recovery: use appropriate means to prevent a rapid speed build-up; the pitching effect caused thereby is secondary to the need to keep the speed at a reasonable value; roll the wings level before

attempting to pitch up; if the aircraft is in a spiral dive, elevator up force will tighten the spiral; unless affected by compressibility the aircraft natural stability will result in a pitch up with increase in airspeed provided the wings are level and the trim is unaltered; elevator forces can become very heavy as speed increases, thus being a safeguard against excessive

g-loads; if stabilizer trim is used for recovery, use it with utmost caution so as

to avoid heavy loads and a possible over trim, which could result in a

renewed loss of control; if strong elevator forces are applied, the trim motors

might become ineffective (stalled); by reducing the elevator forces, the trim motors will be enabled to drive the stabilizer in the desired direction
