kontext:
8.3.8.5 Wind Shear

In order to avoid dangerous wind shear phenomena it is important to know what wind shear is and in which meteorological and geographical environment it can be expected.
The following definition seems to be the most suitable for aviation:

wind shear is any rapid change in wind direction or speed along the flight path of an aircraft

Wind shear, with or without turbulence, alters the lift force acting on an aircraft, resulting in a significant sinking or rising motion.

Therefore, wind shear may be categorized as:

increasing performance shear caused by increasing headwind or decreasing

tailwind component or vertical updrafts

decreasing performance shear caused by decreasing headwind or

increasing tailwind component or vertical downdrafts

Conditions for potentially hazardous wind shears are: convective conditions (e.g. thunderstorms, rain or snow showers)

frontal systems

jet streams

strong or gusty surface winds

other cases (temperature inversion, mountain waves, sea breeze circulations)

Wind shear events are typically one to two miles in diameter and mostly occur near the ground (typically below 500 ft AGL) during take-off and landing. Both situations would see the aircraft in a low energy condition. Therefore, there is only limited time for wind shear recognition and counteraction, typically 5 to 15 seconds.
Several factors can impede wind shear recognition: marginal weather conditions

high crew work load conditions

illusion of normality; during the initial part of the wind shear encounter, everything may appear normal; even severe wind shear onset may not

provide dramatic early indications to the flight crew

Standard response of the flight crew should be: control of flight path through pitch attitude; resistance to a downward change

in pitch attitude as normal response to low airspeed

immediate increase of thrust, maximum thrust shall be applied

an approach shall be aborted

unusual stick forces may be required to maintain pitch attitude during

airspeed variations away from normal target airspeed

low airspeed must be accepted, flying at airspeeds below normal reference

speeds may be required in order to utilize the full performance capability of the aircraft (speed increments under expected wind shear threat are stated

in Operations Manual OM-B)

The term downburst describes a severe downward rush of air and its outburst of

damaging winds near the ground. It has been classified into macroburst and microburst. They are different in their size with radial outflow at the earth’s surface lasting from 3 to 20 minutes.

Downbursts can occur wherever convective weather conditions exist.
Approximately 5% of all thunderstorms produce microburst.
Downdrafts associated with microburst are typically only a few hundred to thousand meters across.
When the downburst hits the ground, it spreads out horizontally and may form one or more horizontal vortex rings around the downdraft up to 2 000 ft AGL.

In downbursts with vortices very powerful updrafts and roll forces in conjunction with wind speed changes up to 45 knots can be expected.
The time period over which wind speeds exceed half the peak value may last from 1 to 8 minutes. Depending on the movement and the height of the base of parent cloud, microburst may occur as: stationary or moving

surface or midair

wet or dry

Microburst has occurred in relatively dry conditions of light rain or precipitation that evaporates before reaching the earth’s surface.
Frontal wind shear is present in both cold and warm fronts, but exists in a different relative location in each type of front. Because the cold front boundary slopes back behind the frontal surface, the wind shear line also slopes back. The frontal boundary of the warm front slopes upward ahead of the surface front and

so does the wind shear. Significant wind shears can be expected if there is a large difference in surface temperature 6°C) across the front and if the front is moving rapidly at more than 30 knots.
Large wind speeds changes near the ground can be found in many

meteorological situations, including the frontal conditions. Terrain irregularities or

buildings, which interrupt the wind flow, can produce significant wind shears close to the ground.

kontext:
8.3.8.12 Significant Temperature Inversions

Strong inversions in pre cold front situations may be associated with strong low altitude jet winds immediately above the ground. The main negative performance factor is caused by the decrease in engine power resulting from the temperature rise. In case of known or forecast temperature inversion corrections to the performance limits must be applied according to the Operations Manual OM-B.
At night during the spring and summer months strong jet winds can occur close to the ground. A wind shear is caused when radiation cooling reaches its maximum and a moderate to strong pressure gradient exists.
Lake and sea breeze wind shear is caused by the differential heating rate of land and water under conditions of strong solar radiation. The land heats more rapidly than the sea. When the off-shore component of the prevailing surface wind is not too large and the temperature difference is big enough, warm air is rising over the land and will be substituted by colder air from the sea.
It begins as a light breeze in the mid morning and increases through the day to 15 knots up to a height of 1200 ft and often moves up to 50 km inland.

With moist and unstable air over the land a sea breeze front with characteristics of thunderstorms may occur.
At night the sea breeze will change to a land breeze since the radiation cooling from the land surface occurs more rapidly than over the sea. The temperature differences at night are smaller than during the day and therefore the land breeze is not as strong as the sea breeze.
Normally only moderate wind shear is caused by a land or sea breeze. But, together with a microburst, when both phenomena strengthen each other, strong

wind shear may occur.
Flight crews must be aware of sea breeze wind shear especially on flights to islands in summer time where the runways are often close to the shore.

Generally airports near the coast will be more affected than those inland.

kontext:
2.8.3.4 Ice Crystal Icing

Large convective formations have the capacity to lift high concentrations of moisture to high altitudes. When this moisture reaches low ambient temperature, it freezes into ice crystals. A result of this phenomenon is that the ice crystals, although in large concentration around the deep convective storm, are small in

size.

The conditions which have shown high concentration of ice crystals are found almost exclusively in the vicinity of deep convective clouds. The most probable regions of high concentrations of ice crystals are above the red radar returns and

downwind of the storm (anvil of the cloud).

Ice crystal icing occurs with high concentration of ice crystals in them atmosphere. This phenomenon is associated to several in-flight events, from

different airplane models and manufacturers.

Most of the reported events occur in temperatures above ISA, in a range between ISA +10°C and ISA +20°C. All

the events occurred when flying near deep convective clouds.

A set of characteristics and observations from those confirmed events that may help to identify an area of high concentration of ice crystals include: flying under IMC and near (laterally or vertically) to a thunderstorm cloud

only light to moderate turbulence

absence of or light radar returns (scattered green reflections) at flight level

reports of rain at temperatures where liquid water could not exist. It was found that the rain is the result of large concentration of small ice crystals

melting in contact with the heated windshield

no significant airframe icing: When flying under ice crystal conditions, the ice crystals bounce at the airframe and do not accumulate in the cold parts of the airplane

ice crystals melt when impinging on warm surfaces of the engine.
The referred surfaces become wet and then cool to 0°C due to the impingement of additional ice crystals. As a result, ice begins to accumulate in some interior engine components and may cause loss of thrust (associated to N1 drop or N1 constant). As a result, airspeed and climb rate may be affected. In addition, engine LP vibration may increase.

The recommended action to avoid a high concentration of ice crystals is to circumnavigate the detected thundercloud or area by 25 NM or more when traffic

conditions permit.
To anticipate areas of higher ice crystal concentration, observe wind direction.
When circumnavigating a thunderstorm, use radar tilt function and also evaluate radar returns below the airplane. Areas directly above red returns might also

contain high concentration of ice crystals. Therefore, avoid flying over such

formations.

If suspected ice crystal icing affects the airplane and the engine performance

consider descending to a lower altitude, which shows to be a successful

recovering action.

CAUTION: Reducing altitude may position the airplane closer to convective

activity. After restoring airplane and engine performance, the flight crew must avoid storm conditions for the remainder of the flight.

OM-B E1 2 Normal Procedures

1.4.1 Authority, Duties and Responsibilities of the Commander (CMD)

The Commander (CMD) exercises the final authority over the safe operation of the helvetic aircraft he is assigned to fly.
He is responsible, as soon as he arrives on board until he leaves the airplane at the end of the flight, for: the safety of all crew members, passengers and cargo

He is responsible to adapt the operationally applicable elements of the SSCC defined in OMM 1.1 to the given situation and implement them in a mission- focussed manner.
He is responsible, from the moment the airplane is first ready to move for the purpose of taxiing prior to take-off until the moment it finally comes to rest at the end of the flight and the engines used as primary propulsion units are shut down, for: the operation and safety of the airplane

All persons on board the aircraft shall obey all lawful directions given by the Commander (CMD). The Commander (CMD) exercises command over all crew members:

from check-in until check-out for a flight or series of flights The Commander (CMD) has the final responsibility regarding

flight initiation according to 8.1.10 - Operational Flight Plan

continuation, termination or diversion of a flight according to 8.3.2.24 -

Meteorological Information.

OM-A Responsibilities

He exercises full command over all other persons on board of a helvetic aircraft: from the time the doors are closed for the initiation of a flight until the doors are opened after the completion of a flight

While exercising his authority the Commander (CMD) has the right to: give all commands he deems necessary for the purpose of ensuring the safety of the aircraft and of persons or property carried therein
to disembark any person or any part of the cargo, which, in his opinion, may represent a potential hazard to the safety of the aircraft or its occupants

not allow a person to be carried in the aircraft who appears to be under the influence of alcohol or drugs to the extent that the safety of the aircraft or its occupants is likely to be endangered

to refuse transportation of inadmissible passengers, deportees or persons in custody, if their carriage poses any risk to the safety of the aircraft or its occupants

OM-A Responsibilities

ensure that all operational procedures and checklists are complied with in accordance with the provisions of this Operations Manual (OM)

ensure that all crew members occupy their stations prior to take-off, final approach and landing

not permit any crew member to perform any activity during critical phases of flight except those for duties required for the safe operation of the aircraft

coordinate the work distribution within the crew to obtain a maximum of good airmanship for the conduct of the flight

ensure precise navigation and observation of minimum altitudes

comply with operating limitations and ensure the proper use and handling of the aircraft

4.2 Designation of the Commander

kontext:
1.4.2.1.1 Normal Operation

The Copilot (COP) is the second in command of a helvetic aircraft.
He is assigned to fly and therefore the deputy of the Commander (CMD).
The Copilot (COP) shall assume command of the flight when so directed by the Commander (CMD).

In case of absence of the Commander (CMD) the Copilot (COP) shall act as contact person towards other crew members or third parties and take the required actions. They shall be in accordance with actions which would have been taken by the Commander (CMD) himself.

kontext:
4.2.1 Flights with Two Pilots Qualified as Commander

If more than one flight crew member of the same crew holds the qualification for Commander (CMD) only one pilot is designated as Commander (CMD) of the flight.
The command of the flight is assigned on the flight assignment.
During any flight, other than:

training flights, or line flying under supervision, or

check flights and non-revenue flights

the CMD of the aircraft occupies the left hand seat on the flight deck.

OM-A 4 Crew Composition

This means that the CMD holding the qualification to operate in either pilot’s seat will act as Copilot (COP) on the right hand seat despite of the fact that he might be more experienced than the pilot on the left hand seat.

During: training flights

check flights

line flying under supervision

where the responsible instructor has access to the controls, the Type Rating Instructor (TRI) or the Line Training Commander (LTC) is always designated as the Commander (CMD) of the flight. He then may have to occupy the right hand seat in the flight deck.

During: line flying under supervision

Line Orientated Evaluation of Competence (LOE)

where the Type Rating Instructor (TRI) or the Line Training Commander (LTC) occupies the flight deck jump seat, he can not act as Commander (CMD) of the flight, since he has no access to the flight controls.

When more than one flight crew member of the same crew holds the qualification for Commander (CMD) it is of the utmost importance to properly and clearly brief all other crew members about the actual chain of command.

Any change in command during a flight shall be announced to all crew members in a clear

manner.

kontext:
8.3.12 Admission to Flight Deck

No person, other than flight crew members assigned to a flight, shall be admitted to, or carried on, the flight deck unless the Commander (CMD) himself or his designated deputy is present on the flight deck, and unless this person: is a member of the operating crew or is an auditor listed on the flight assignment (e.g IOSA, CARA) or is a representative of the Swiss FOCA with an appropriate identification and is required for the performance of his official duties

Alternatively other persons may be accepted if the following conditions are fulfilled: admission to flight deck (Cockpit permit) is granted by the Commander (CMD)

a valid passenger or observer ticket has been issued for the flight or a series of flights for flight deck observers not employed by helvetic, the process for the issuance of tickets is described in OM-0 9

A cockpit permit may be granted provided:

the passenger is personally known to a crew member or is staff of an airline within the Lufthansa group (identification through crew member-certificate or company ID)

or

the passenger holds an airport ID from Zurich Airport (AIC) containing at

least one of the ZRH airport zones (i.e. bold capital letters), irrespective of

the colour of the airport identification cards or

the passenger has successfully completed the process described in OM-0 9 Observer Flights for non-2L Observers

Note: Any passenger occupying the Cockpit Jump-Seat shall be at least 12 Years of age

The Commander (CMD) is responsible that a person who has been granted a permission to enter the flight deck: has received a briefing on all safety relevant aspects including the sterile flight deck policy and escape path to be used in case of emergency prior to departure and as necessary for the reminder of the flight

does not cause distraction or interference with the operation of the flight

refrains from use of any audio or video recording devices (e.g. tape recorder, cameras of any kind, mobile phone). Exceptions in written form may be granted by the Accountable Manager (ACM) or Nominated Person Flight Operations (FOP)

Note: Special regulations may apply for certain countries (e.g. UK, Israel).
Refer to OM-C Route Competence for further information.

No cockpit permit is required for: persons according to the List of helvetic Employees in the OM-0 9
In all cases, the final acceptance of the person admitted to flight deck remains with the Commander (CMD).

As stated in OCM 3.18, Operations Control (OCC) is in charge to coordinate the

exchange of information between all relevant parties.
The granted admission to the flight deck shall be noted in the Flight Briefing Documentation Tool or on the relevant flight assignment.

Refer to 8.1.13 - Flight Assignment Folder.

kontext: 8.3.28.5 Commanders Authority
The final authority to allow use of PED T-PED within the limits shown, rests with the Commander (CMD). If necessary in the interest of safety, he may restrict the use of PED T-PED.

This applies especially to situations like air turbulence (stowage of loose devices) or low visibility conditions (avoid any potential interference with the avionics systems).
At the commander’s discretion on the ground, and if the aircraft is not moving under its own power, PED T-PED may be used by passengers upon announcement from the crew. Sufficient time must be available for cabin crew to advise the passengers before the flight proceeds.

kontext:
8.3.10.3 Controlled Rest - Flight Crew Members

During all phases of flight each flight crew member shall remain alert. If a lack of alertness is encountered or fatigue is experienced the controlled rest procedure can be organized by the Commander (CMD) if workload permits. Controlled rest taken in this way has always to be considered as duty time.
To cover unexpected fatigue the controlled rest procedure can be used.
Controlled rest means a period of Time «off task», which may include actual sleep. Its use may be decided by the commander as follows: controlled rest should be taken during low workload phases

only one crew member at a time shall take rest

the harness should be used and the seat positioned to minimize unintentional interference with the controls

the crew member on duty should be briefed before taking over full controls

the aircraft must be flown with both, auto throttle and autopilot fully operational

the flying crew member shall wear the headset

system intervention, which would normally require a cross check should be avoided until the resting crew member resumes his duties

the rest period should not be longer than 45 minutes, followed by a recovery period of 20 minutes an appropriate alarm system in close contact with the cabin crew shall be

established. Procedure detailed in 8.3.10.3.1 - Controlled Rest

Alarm/Communication Procedure between Flight Crew and Cabin

Crew

controlled rest periods should terminate at least 30 minutes before top of

descent

at least a 20-minute period should be allowed between rest periods

If necessary, a flight crew member may take more than one rest period according

to the restrictions above.
Controlled rest according to the procedure above shall not be considered to be

part of a rest period for purposes of calculating flight time limitations nor used to justify any duty period.

Supernumerary flight crew members may be requested by the Commander (CMD) to occupy an assigned station on the flight deck, whenever he deems such course of action necessary in the interest of safety.

8.3.10.3.1 Controlled Rest Alarm/Communication Procedure between Flight Crew and Cabin Crew

To establish an appropriate alarm system, the following procedure shall be followed: before the start of the controlled rest period, the flight crew informs the SEN briefs the SEN on this procedure

the active flight crew member calls the SEN every 20 minutes and reports

8.3.11.2 Cabin Crew Members

During take-off and landing, and whenever deemed necessary by the Commander (CMD) in the interest of safety, each cabin crew member shall be properly secured by all safety belts and harnesses provided.
In case of an unscheduled request to the cabin crew members to take their seats and to secure their seat belts (i.e. except for take-off and landing) the Commander (CMD) will announce through the Public Announcement (PA) system. kontext: 1.4.2.2 Duties and Responsibilities of Senior Cabin Attendants (SEN)
The Senior Cabin Attendant (SEN) is directly responsible to the Commander (CMD) of the flight for the cabin safety.

The authorities of a Senior Cabin Attendant (SEN) are: to issue legal and mandatory instructions towards the Cabin Attendants (CAB)

to request access to the Aircraft Cabin Log (ACL)

to reject an aircraft regarding unsatisfactory technical cabin issues

to request a debriefing within the whole crew or with an individual crew member of the operational crew

to request a staff appraisal

The responsibilities are: to direct, coordinate and organize the functions and tasks of the cabin crew and, at the prescribed times, report “cabin and galley secure” or “cabin and galley not secure”

to be responsible to the Commander (CMD) for the conduct and

coordination of cabin safety procedures and for their observance by the cabin crew and by all passengers information of the flight crew about all irregularities and malfunctions observed by cabin crew members or passengers

to contact the flight crew for instructions when deemed necessary

to ensure that he applies all operational procedures and checklists in accordance with the Operations Manual (OM) and the Cabin Safety

Procedures Manual (CSPM)

completion of all cabin related documents

to function as the communication link between flight and cabin crew and,

when necessary, the passengers

checking of the catering and the relevant equipment

to direct – when necessary – cabin emergency procedures and an

emergency evacuation

OM-A Responsibilities

discontinue non-safety related duties during turbulence in absence of any instruction from the flight crew, advise the flight crew of the level of turbulence and the need for the fasten seat belt signs to be switched on.
This should be followed by the cabin crew securing the passenger cabin and other applicable areas

check the distribution tool at least once a week or before flight duty after a longer period away; read and acknowledge the relevant contents

not to operate as crew member on an airplane unless he is qualified for duty in accordance with 5.3 - Cabin Crew.

check e-mail at least once a week and before flight or training duties, whichever results in more current information

to conduct familiarisation flights for Senior Cabin Attendants (SEN) and Cabin Attendants (CAB), if training according to OM-D 2.5.2 is completed

in case of suspension or revocation of the personal cabin crew attestation by the competent authority, that the cabin crew attestation must be returned to the respective superior and the HCC has to be informed without delay

He is responsible to adapt the operationally applicable elements of the SSCC defined in OMM 1.1 to the given situation and implement them in a mission- focussed manner.

Notwithstanding the overriding authority of the Commander (CMD) it is of utmost importance that the Senior Cabin Attendant (SEN), at any time, draws the attention of the Commander (CMD) to facts, circumstances or unfavourable variables which may impair cabin safety and which may not yet have been

noticed by the Commander (CMD).

2 App. 1.5 Selection Process for Direct Entry Copilots and Commanders Announcement of vacancies for copilot positions shall be published via helvetic career center or other job advertising platforms.
Application shall be done through the helvetic career center.
After a first triage, the candidate will be invited to an information event.
Thereafter, the following steps need to be passed successfully.
The candidate may repeat one of the first three selection steps once. However, this is subject to Nominated Person Flight Operations (FOP) decision.

2 App. 1.5.1 Selection Steps

2 App. 1.5.1.1 Aptitude Testing

The HUPEX (Human Potential Explorer) test is a powerful, culture-independent PC tool for measuring situational awareness under stress.
Candidates having participated in an information event need to pass this test with more than 220 points.
Other aptitude testing tools in accordance with CAT.GEN.MPA 175 and IATA aptitude testing guidance are acceptable.

2 App. 1.5.1.2 Test of General Knowledge

Candidates having successfully passed the HUPEX or equivalent test are invited to perform the following knowledge test: test tailored to the position applied for. Written or question database.
Copilots: basic ATPL questions Commanders: EASA Air Ops and OM-C 1 Route Manual general part questions

2 App. 1.4.1.2 Flying Skills Evaluation

Refer to 2 App. 1.6.2 - Flying Skills Evaluation

2 App. 1.4.1.3 Psychological Review

Refer to 2 App. 1.6.3 - Psychological Assessment

2 App. 1.4.2 Decision Board

The operational decision board consists of:
Accountable Manager (ACM)

Nominated Person Flight Operations (FOP)

Nominated Person Training (TNG)

Crew Manager (CMR)

The Corporate Management (GL) decision board consists of: at least one corporate management member and one person appointed by one of the other corporate management members

The following 3 different variants of decisions exist: positive

negative at present time: new process may be initiated earliest after 12 months and once again only

negative: no new process within helvetic

2 App. 1.5 Selection Process for Direct Entry Copilots and Commanders Announcement of vacancies for copilot positions shall be published via helvetic career center or other job advertising platforms.
Application shall be done through the helvetic career center.
After a first triage, the candidate will be invited to an information event.
Thereafter, the following steps need to be passed successfully.
The candidate may repeat one of the first three selection steps once. However, this is subject to Nominated Person Flight Operations (FOP) decision.

2 App. 1.5.1 Selection Steps

2 App. 1.5.1.1 Aptitude Testing

The HUPEX (Human Potential Explorer) test is a powerful, culture-independent PC tool for measuring situational awareness under stress.
Candidates having participated in an information event need to pass this test with more than 220 points.
Other aptitude testing tools in accordance with CAT.GEN.MPA 175 and IATA aptitude testing guidance are acceptable.

2 App. 1.5.1.2 Test of General Knowledge

correspondence to candidates shall be mailed within 36 hours after the event

2 App. 1.6 Selection Steps Details 2 App. 1.6.1 Information Event

During this event, helvetic and general employment terms shall be introduced to the applicants. Further additional facts and benefits shall be provided to applicants or potential applicants. Also, time for questions shall be accounted for.
Under normal circumstances, only invited candidates shall be allowed to participate. Typically, invitations to the information event are furnished to people having applied for employment at helvetic and passing the preliminary application file review by the department head. Alternatively, this presentation can be downloaded from the helvetic homepage.
In some cases (e.g. applicants or potential applicants who live abroad) this information event can be replaced by a slide show published on the internet. If questions arise, they shall be answered either by phone or by email.

2 App. 1.6.2 Flying Skills Evaluation

The decision board of the process selection for employment shall be provided with reliable information about the competency-based skills of candidates.
Candidates shall be employed only after having demonstrated adequate skills to successfully complete a conversion or upgrading course within the allotted budget of time and resources.

Irrespective of their previous experience, rank or origin (e.g. ab-initio, direct entry

COP or CMD, internal APCP or upgrade candidates), all candidates perform their flying skills evaluation tailored to their role.

Note: APCP candidates will be closely monitored and supported during their training program. For APCP candidates, after the completion of the MCC

course module, the flying skill's evaluation shall be scheduled earliest

approximately three months before commencing a TR course.

2 App. 1.6.2.1 Bridge Course

The purpose of the bridge course is to prepare candidates for their skill evaluation in any type of simulator and consists of: announcement of relevant topics to be prepared and presented by candidates towards their peers

discussion of such relevant topics during a classroom event lead by Flying Skills Assessment Personnel

presentation and conduct of the simulator assessment serving the purpose of a joint simulator briefing, meaning that no additional briefing will be required or planned before the simulator event

Candidates shall present the listed topics to peers starting on an empty white board (no powerpoint presentation or similarly prepared documents desired), time allowed will be 5 to a maximum of 7 minutes depending on inter-action between peers.

2 App. 1.6.2.1.1 Bridge Course – Contents for APCP ab and initio Candidates

principle Aviate – Navigate – Communicate meaning conclusion for daily operations associated parameters to be categorised under which header

basic scanning technique (glass cockpit) automatic vs. manual flying monitoring of static parameters vs. dynamic parameters

SAW Orientation in space Navigation determination of position (RMI/RMI, RMI/DIST) interception of (any) Line of Position (LOP), terminology, inbound outbound, consideration of amount of angular displacement

wind corrections, principle track time corrections, inbound outbound use of flight path vector

2 App. 1.3 helvetic Airline Pilot Cadet Program (APCP) 2 App. 1.3.1 Aim

helvetic has introduced the Airline Pilot Cadet Program (APCP) as the main selection program for co-pilots. helvetic will accompany the students throughout the main part of the basic training and will evaluate helvetic specific requirements during this phase. This program allows to supervise the behaviour and the progress of the student over a long period in order to assure that the student fulfills all requirements to be employed as a helvetic co-pilot.
After the successful completion of the program, the candidate will be positively hired as co-pilot (COP) and helvetic will issue an employment contract within 12 months.
A negative decision during any step of the program (except psychological assessment and decision boards) means only that the APCP is cancelled. The candidate can apply again after the training for a copilot position (according to demand). He must then undergo the normal selection process of helvetic.

2 App. 1.3.2 Program Overview

kontext:
8.0.1.6 Decision Finding Process (FORD-Model)

A decision shall be made after a proper evaluation of several options.
In order to be able to make a decision, a structured way is of great importance.
Therefore following model should be used as a guideline:
FORD-Model

A structured decision-making process consists of four phases:
F acts

O ptions

R isk Benefit

D ecision

collect Facts: how is the actual situation?

what problem are we facing at?

search look for Options: what kind of solutions for the problem do we have?

what kind of options are possible? “time” or “no time” to delay a landing?

evaluate Risk versus Benefit

what is the risk and benefit of every single option?

make a Decision which of the above mentioned options is used for the actual situation or

problem?

As a situation may change depending on the actions taken and the nature of the

problem, the FORD model should also be used for a reassessment of the situation.

Nur noch durch den PM im Debriefing nach dem Flug
Nur wenn OCC einen neuen Entscheid verlangt

fragen.zitat: As a situation may change depending on the actions taken and the nature of the problem, the FORD model should also be used for a reassessment of the situation.
fragen.frage_en: How should the FORD model be used after a decision has been taken?
antworten_en: For reassessment, as the situation may change due to the actions taken
Not at all; the decision is binding until landing
Only by the PM in the debriefing after the flight
Only if OCC requests a new decision

fragen.frage: Was kennzeichnet Level 3 (Opposition) des STOP-Modells?
antworten: Die Übernahme der Controls mit dem Callout «MY CONTROLS»
Eine zweite/dritte klare Aussage mit Ansprache beim Vornamen und erneuter Betonung der Bedenken
Das Klären der Situation mit Fragen wie «confirm, you intend to …»
Eine PAN-PAN-Meldung an ATC mit Bitte um Unterstützung
fragen.erklaerung: Auf Level 3 wird eine zweite/dritte klare Aussage gemacht, der andere wird beim Vornamen angesprochen und Bedenken und Vorsichtsmassnahmen werden nochmals betont.
fragen.zitat: a second/ third clear statement (addressing the other one by his first name) shall be given by emphasizing again concerns and required precautions
fragen.frage_en: What characterises level 3 (Opposition) of the STOP model?
antworten_en: Taking over the controls with the callout 'MY CONTROLS'
A second/third clear statement, addressing the other by first name and emphasizing the concerns again
Clarifying the situation with questions like 'confirm, you intend to …'
A PAN-PAN call to ATC requesting assistance
fragen.erklaerung_en: At level 3, a second/third clear statement is given, addressing the other crew member by his first name and emphasizing concerns and required precautions again.
kontext:
8.0.1.3 CRM Intervention Method

Philosophies, policies and procedures define the framework for safe and normal operations. Abnormal and emergency procedures describe ways how to stay within or return to the desired envelope.
However real life might create conditions or combinations thereof no defined procedure for recovery exists.
Situations which require intervention by a crew member to avoid hazardous outcomes may arise either during normal or abnormal operations.
Many callouts for both normal and abnormal conditions are clearly defined.
The following intervention-model has been established as a guideline if any situation is encountered in which a feedback to the other crew member cannot be performed by a defined callout.
The STOP-Model A structured intervention consists of four phases:
S ituation clarification what happens

T ell your concern(s) state your concerns precautions

O pposition emphasize precautions again

P AN-PAN take action

Situation Clarification – Level 1 A crew member is in doubt about the outcome of an arising situation and not sure about all factors which might be affected. He has to find out if circumstances are as they seem to be. Clarifying the situation with the involved crew member(s)

is required. At the end, all crew members should have the same level of

information and an agreement of the proceedings shall have been reached.

Samples of adequate wordings to initiate communication:

confirm, you intend to

would you explain why

I do not understand

Tell your concern(s) – Level 2 Should a crew member remain concerned after clarification of the situation he shall clearly state his concerns and advise the necessary precautions.
Samples of adequate wordings to initiate communication:
I am concerned about as

it makes me feel uncomfortable think about

I do not like and I suggest to

Opposition – Level 3 Should the other crew member not change his behavior or action and continue to endanger operations,
a second/ third clear statement (addressing the other one by his first name) shall be given by emphasizing again concerns and required precautions

Samples of adequate wordings to initiate communication:
Max – this will turn out very bad stop it now

John – immediately revert now to procedure

Peter – I am very scared about stop this as

PAN-PAN – Level 4 Should still no agreement have been achieved between the two parties and a threat will become imminent, the intervening crew member shall take action and return to safe operations.

Samples of adequate wordings to initiate communication:

my controls

I decide now to and we will proceed as follows

now we immediately do

Subsequent Should level 3 or 4 have been initiated, the following procedure shall be

applied after the flight: debriefing between parties involved

file a report (confidential if deemed necessary)

Operational communication is usually held at level 1 or eventually level 2.
Whenever a level other than 1 is applied, the addressed crew member shall be made aware of the corresponding level in an unmistakable way

fragen.frage: Was tut das intervenierende Crew Member auf Level 4 (PAN-PAN) des STOP-Modells?
antworten: Es setzt eine PAN-PAN-Dringlichkeitsmeldung an ATC ab
Es informiert OCC und wartet auf deren Anweisungen
Es ergreift selbst Massnahmen und führt in einen sicheren Betrieb zurück
Es dokumentiert den Vorfall sofort im Tech Log
fragen.erklaerung: Ist keine Einigung erzielt und droht eine unmittelbare Gefahr, ergreift das intervenierende Crew Member Massnahmen und kehrt zu sicherem Betrieb zurück (z.B. «my controls»).
fragen.zitat: Should still no agreement have been achieved between the two parties and a threat will become imminent, the intervening crew member shall take action and return to safe operations.
fragen.frage_en: What does the intervening crew member do at level 4 (PAN-PAN) of the STOP model?
antworten_en: He transmits a PAN-PAN urgency call to ATC
He informs OCC and waits for their instructions
He takes action and returns to safe operations
He immediately documents the event in the tech log
fragen.erklaerung_en: If no agreement has been achieved and a threat becomes imminent, the intervening crew member takes action and returns to safe operations (e.g. 'my controls').

The Threat and Error Management (TEM) Model should be used as a tool kit in order to build up defenses. if a threat occurs it can prevent an error (threat management)

if an error occurs, it can be used to trap the error (error management)

if the aircraft is in an undesired state it can be used to mitigate the state (undesired state management)

The effectiveness of the defenses increases with knowledge, experience and discipline.

O perational (e.g. aircraft technical status, aerodrome specials) P ilot condition (e.g. fatigue, stress, operational pressure, distractions)

kontext:
8.0.1.7.1 The Model

There are three basic components in the TEM model, from the perspective of flight crews: threats, errors and undesired aircraft states.
The model proposes that threats and errors are part of everyday aviation operations that must be managed by flight crews, since both threats and errors carry the potential to generate undesired aircraft states.

8.0.1.7.1.1 Threats

A Threat is defined as an event (in relation to the environment or the aircraft) or an error (from another aircraft, air traffic control or maintenance) occurring outside the influence of the flight crew

(not caused by the flight crew).
It increases the operational complexity of a flight and requires crew attention and management if safety margins are to be maintained. adverse weather, airport conditions, terrain, environmental other traffic, ATC requirements and or errors operational pressure, aircraft malfunctions, operational maintenance error, ground handling error, cabin events, crew scheduling errors systematic or organisational deficiencies, hardware design, latent training deficiencies, ATC systematic deficiencies other stress, fatigue, distractions

Threats can both be expected (anticipated) or unexpected (unanticipated).
This is dependent on knowledge and experience.

8.0.1.7.1.2 Errors

Errors are defined “actions or inactions by the flight crew that lead to deviations from organizational or flight crew intentions or expectations”. Unmanaged and/or mismanaged errors frequently lead to undesired aircraft states. Errors in the operational context thus tend to reduce the margins of safety and increase the probability of adverse events. intentional non- Intentional and conscious violations of SOPs or compliance errors regulations, including shortcuts or omission of (violations) required briefings or checklists.
Errors including slips, lapses or mistakes in the procedural execution of regulations or procedures. errors The intention is correct but the execution is flawed.
Occurs when information is incorrectly transmitted or communication interpreted within the flight crew or between the errors flight crew and external sources such as air traffic control. proficiency errors Indicate a lack of knowledge or stick and rudder skill. (skills errors) Discretionary decisions not covered by regulation and procedure that unnecessarily increases risk. operational decision errors Examples include extreme manoeuvres on approach, choosing to fly into adverse weather, or over- reliance on automation.

Errors can be spontaneous (i.e., without direct linkage to specific, obvious threats), linked to threats, or part of an error chain. Examples of errors would

include the inability to maintain stabilised approach parameters,

executing a wrong automation mode, failing to give a required callout,

or misinterpreting an ATC clearance.

8.0.1.7.1.3 Undesired Aircraft States

Undesired aircraft states are defined as “flight crew-induced aircraft position or speed deviations, misapplication of flight controls, or incorrect systems configuration, associated with a reduction in margins of safety”.
Undesired aircraft states that result from ineffective threat and/or error management may lead to compromising situations and reduce margins of safety in flight operations. Often considered on the cusp of becoming an incident or accident, undesired aircraft states must be managed by flight crews.

aircraft control (attitude)

vertical, lateral or speed deviations

unnecessary weather penetration

aircraft unauthorized airspace penetration handling operation outside aircraft limitations

unstable approach

continued landing after unstable approach

long, floated, firm or off-centreline landing

ground proceeding towards wrong taxiway/runway navigation

wrong taxiway, ramp, gate or hold spot

incorrect systems configuration

incorrect flight controls configuration incorrect

aircraft incorrect automation configuration

configurations incorrect engine configuration

incorrect weight and balance configuration.

kontext:
8.0.1.7.2 Threat and Error Countermeasures

8.0.1.7.2.1 Threat Management

Threat management is a building block to error management and undesired aircraft state management. Although the threat-error linkage is not necessarily straightforward or it might not be always possible to establish a linear relationship between errors and undesired states, archival data demonstrates that mismanaged threats are normally linked to flight crew errors. Those, in turn, are then oftentimes linked to undesired aircraft states. Threat management provides the most proactive option to maintain margins of safety in flight operations, by voiding safety-compromising situations at their roots. As threat managers, flight crews are the last line of defense to keep threats from impacting flight operations.

8.0.1.7.2.2 Error Management

Regardless of the type of error, an error’s effect on safety depends on whether the flight crew detects and responds to the error before it leads to an undesired aircraft state and to a potential unsafe outcome.
This is why one of the objectives of Threat and Error Management (TEM) is to understand error management (i.e. detection and response), rather than solely focusing on error causality (i.e. causation and commission).
From the safety perspective, operational errors that are timely detected and promptly responded to (i.e. properly managed) are errors that do not lead to undesired aircraft states and do not reduce margins of safety in flight operations,

and thus become operationally inconsequential.
In addition to its safety value, proper error management represents an example of successful human performance, presenting both learning and training value.
There are three types of error responses:

trap:

the error is detected and managed before it becomes consequential

deteriorate:

the error is detected but the crew’s action or inaction leads to a negative

outcome

fail to respond:

the crew fails to react to the error either because it is undetected or ignored

From the three error responses there are three possible error outcomes:
Inconsequential: the error has no effect on the safe completion of the flight, or was made irrelevant by successful flight crew error management. This is the most common outcome, a fact that is illustrative of the robust nature of the aviation system

Undesired Aircraft State: defined as a position, condition or attitude of an aircraft that clearly reduces safety margins and is a result of actions by the flight crew.
The error results in the aircraft being unnecessarily placed in a condition that increases risk. This includes incorrect vertical or lateral navigation, unstable approaches, low fuel state, lining up for wrong runway and reduced separation.

Additional Error: an error by the flight crew that now needs to be managed

8.0.1.7.2.3 Undesired Aircraft State Handling

The undesirable aircraft states can be: mitigated

deteriorated

fail to respond: flight crew failure to respond to the situation There are three possible outcomes of the undesired aircraft state:

Recovery:

is an outcome that indicates the risk has been managed

Additional Error:

the actions initiate a new cycle of error and management

Crew-Based Occurrence

(e.g. incident or accident)

8.3.0.8 Fleet Configuration

Modern airplanes used in airline operations usually carry standardised equipment and vary amongst each other only rarely within the same fleet.
Should a specific airplane within the fleet carry different equipment which could result in operational issues, training according to OM-D 2.1.2 Differences and Familiarisation Training shall be performed by each crew member before operating this specific tail number.

8.3.0.9 8.3.0.9 MCC Principles

This chapter intends to create a mental link between higher level policies and lower level SOPs, aiming to distinguish between CRM- and MCC-principles. „Playground“ we are aware that Knowledge, Skills and Attitudes (KSA) are to be seen as fundamentals

helvetic management creates a working environment enabling flight crews intrinsically motivating themselves

we are willing to accept that striving for self-discipline and a high level of performance is fundamental

we accept that safety is paramount and not negotiable, remaining aware at the same time that safety must be embedded in a commercially effective and efficient environment

we are willing to accept that operational daily life often offers „grey zones“ requiring all parties involved to apply a holistic problem-solving process potentially leading to various suitable solutions

we take full responsibility for decisions taken when faced with situations where no procedures or guidance exists

we do not “hide” behind regulations or superiors

„Operational conclusions“ we are aware that defined requirements and SOPs shall contribute to

reduce tiring discussions about minor, non-safety relevant items

we are aware of a general increase in complexity and counteract associated

risks by remaining vigilant about the „big picture“ while reducing workload and distraction by refraining from non safety-relevant micro-management

we refrain from exaggerated individual interpretations and implementation at

purely theoretical levels without enhancing safety at a practical level

when rating risks we aim to base our judgement at a realistic level based on

the current environment meaning that we refrain from drawing conclusions based on exaggerated assumptions

we are aware of the difference between „experience” and „expertise“, remaining mentally open for technological and procedural developments

based on „what“ rather than „who“ is right

we refrain from inventing or applying derived SOPs based on oral transmission by whoever, we challenge peers distributing rumours to apply SOPs as published while aiming to capture the “spirit behind”

„Operational behaviour“ we respect the roles and associated duties as PF and PM

we actively adhere to our own and accept the peer’s role as PF and PM

we are aware that the PF‘s workload is normally higher than the PM‘s purely based on his role, meaning the PM should refrain from inputs a split second before the PF is expected to act

to minimise misunderstandings, both PF and PM refrain from performing duties of the other role unless asked to do so by their peer
the PM accepts decisions and proceedings taken by the PF as long as he remains within the defined framework

both flight crew members shall refrain from forcing peers to adjust non safety-relevant minor items to their individual preferences going beyond SOPs

we welcome sharing of experience by contributing individual thoughts as long as they are clearly declared as such and not communicated as „best industry practice“ in any form of operational recommendations or orders

we communicate in a positive-minded, straightforward and direct manner by using clear and unhidden statements, irrespective of each role or function

8.6.3 Acceptance by the Crew

The Commander (CMD) has to be aware of all operational and technical consequences of the failure concerned (deferred item).
In case of doubt the crew shall request advice from: the Nominated Person Continuing Airworthiness (PCA), or the Nominated Person Flight Operations (FOP) via the OCC.

The Commander (CMD) may require a repair although dispatch is permitted by Minimum Equipment List (MEL) and even though departure will be delayed. The reason for such a decision must be reported with an Occurrence Report (OR).

The Commander (CMD) is required to consult the Aircraft Technical Log (ATL) for other deferred items in order to asses their interrelationship.
The Commander (CMD) confirms his acceptance or non-acceptance in writing in the Aircraft Technical Log (ATL).

kontext:
8.6.3 Acceptance by the Crew

The Commander (CMD) has to be aware of all operational and technical consequences of the failure concerned (deferred item).
In case of doubt the crew shall request advice from: the Nominated Person Continuing Airworthiness (PCA), or the Nominated Person Flight Operations (FOP) via the OCC.
The Commander (CMD) may require a repair although dispatch is permitted by Minimum Equipment List (MEL) and even though departure will be delayed. The reason for such a decision must be reported with an Occurrence Report (OR).
The Commander (CMD) is required to consult the Aircraft Technical Log (ATL) for other deferred items in order to asses their interrelationship.
The Commander (CMD) confirms his acceptance or non-acceptance in writing in the Aircraft Technical Log (ATL).

kontext:
8.6.2 Minimum Equipment List (MEL) Application

At any helvetic Maintenance Base (e.g. ZRH, BRN, GVA, the maintenance organization will make every effort to have the aircraft fully serviceable prior to scheduled departure

if it becomes evident that inoperative equipment cannot be made serviceable before scheduled departure and that the MEL has to be applied, the Commander (CMD) shall be informed as soon as possible

approved maintenance personnel will make appropriate ATL entries or the flight crew will make appropriate entries in the ATL (action side): “deferred according to MEL”

At Outstations: the flight crew will enter the defective system or component in the ATL (complaint side)

the flight crew will determine if the Minimum Equipment List (MEL) can be applied.

the flight crew will make appropriate entries in the ATL (action side): “deferred according to MEL”

latest upon arrival at the home base in Zurich the flight crew will inform the maintenance organization about the deferred item
The Minimum Equipment List (MEL) is applicable until the aircraft moves under own power with the intention to fly.

kontext:
8.1.8.2 Methods, Procedures and Responsibility for the Preparation and

Acceptance of the Mass and Balance (Load) Sheet

A mass and balance document must be prepared in duplicate for each helvetic flight. This document will be called loadsheet. One copy of it is to be carried on the aircraft and
the other, after acceptance by the Commander (CMD), must remain available at the departure station for at least three days.

Both pilots shall verify the correctness of the loadsheet by signature, if not an EFB created loadsheet.
At specific aerodromes the flight crew receives a computerized loadsheet which is calculated by the ground handling partners. For description of such a loadsheet refer to 8.1.8.7 - Computerized Loadsheet in Departure Control System (DCS) Format. These subcontractors have been checked prior to approval and are responsible for the correctness of the calculations. Information about airport ground handling stations providing computerized loadsheets are to be found on the Flight Assignment. Any loadsheet must contain details of the mass and disposition of all loaded items, including fuel, and must indicate whether standard or actual mass values have been used.
The loadsheet must contain the name (i.e. three-letter-code) of the person who prepared it. The loading supervisor, or in his absence the Commander (CMD), must confirm by signature that the load and its distribution are as stated.
The loadsheet must be acceptable to and countersigned by the aircraft Commander (CMD). He must be informed of any late changes and the details entered in the Last Minute Changes (LMC) sections of both the original and duplicate documents.

The loadsheet does not contain information about the aircraft type, however operational manuals and AHM560 contain a clear link between aircraft registration and aircraft type.

The person who is approved to calculate the loadsheet (handling agent, copilot) is responsible for its correctness. The Commander (CMD) must verify some major items only and focus his attention on a feasibility check to prevent gross errors.
The Commander (CMD) shall therefore check correctness of the following items by signing the loadsheet and not accept wrong or exceeded data: registration and flight number

crew composition

date and edition number

fuel figures (take-off and trip fuel) and distribution

exceedance of limitations (ZFM, regulated TOM or LM, CG)

feasibility check (rough check if DOM number of PAX 100 kg fuel, corresponds to the actual TOM on the load sheet within reasonable limits)

loading and load distribution

pantry code

type of passenger weights (1)

NOTOC if regulations require Note 1: The pantry code itself does not indicate the type of passenger

weights to be used. The flight crew briefing will indicate which weights

to be used (i.e. scheduled or charter).

In case of special charter flights (e.g. hockey team, orchestra)

adjustments to the standard weights may apply. In this case, a manual paper load-sheet shall be created by the crew or a detailed

verification of the DCS-loadsheet values shall be performed.
For adjustments to the standard weights refer to 8.1.8.3.3 - Non-

standard Passenger Mass Values.

OM-A 8 Operating Procedures

kontext:
8.1.8.5 Last Minute Changes Procedure

As explained in the definition, Last Minute Changes (LMC) to the load sheet are only permitted if the changes of the load – either plus or minus – are within the limits permitted in the Operations Manual OM-B 6.
The changes have to be entered into the Last Minute Change (LMC) sections of the load sheet. If there is no defined place for last minute changes on the loadsheet (e.g. on ACARS loadsheet), it shall be noted somewhere in open space.
As least the following content shall be stated: type of LMC (e.g. Pax., Load, Crew)

changed weight 88kg)
CMD signature and 3LC (The signature confirms the correct application of the LMC according to the limitations in OM-B 6.)

In exceptional cases – if time limitations request to do so – changes may be

relayed to the flight crew via radio, cellular telephone or the ground service interphone. The flight crew and ground staff will then amend their copies

accordingly.

The load message sent to the destination must contain the corrected figures for the actual load of passengers, cargo, baggage and mail.

OM-A 8 Operating Procedures

Als automatisch ungültig; er kann ignoriert werden
Als gültig bis zu einer allfälligen Annullierung
Als ungültig; er ist dem Swiss FOCA zu melden
fragen.erklaerung: NOTAMs sind auf eine Gültigkeit von bis zu 90 Tagen limitiert; ein älterer NOTAM gilt als verdächtig, und bei operationeller Relevanz ist seine Gültigkeit zu verifizieren.
fragen.zitat: Should this limit be exceeded, the NOTAM must be judged as being suspect and its validity should be verified in case of any operational relevance

As automatically invalid; it can be ignored

As invalid; it must be reported to the Swiss FOCA
fragen.erklaerung_en: NOTAMs are limited to a validity of up to 90 days; an older NOTAM must be judged as suspect and its validity verified if operationally relevant.
kontext:
8.1.0 General Policy

EASA Air Operations uses the following expressions: planning (pre-flight (i.e. before off-block))

fuel management and in-flight re-planning (always in-flight)

During the planning stage, before commencement of each flight or series of flights, flight crews shall perform flight preparation duties to include: current maps (enroute) and charts (e.g. STAR, IAC, SID, taxi charts)

aerodrome operating hours and NOTAMs: aerodromes of departure, en- route alternates (ERA), fuel enroute alternate (Fuel-ERA), destination, destination alternate, additional ones up to the flight crew

during check-in, enroute area NOTAMs can usually not be consulted in a realistic manner as clear references to defined waypoints are usually missing. However, in case of flights into areas which dictate to do so (e.g. unfamiliar areas outside Central Europe, politically critical countries) enroute NOTAMs shall be checked. Based on ICAO regulations, NOTAMs are limited to a period of validity up to 90 days.
Should this limit be exceeded, the NOTAM must be judged as being suspect and its validity should be verified in case of any operational relevance

meteorological conditions at departure, en-route alternates (ERA), destination and destination alternate: general weather, wind, visibility and ceiling (if required) RNP APCH operations: before selecting a destination, where the approach

depends exclusively on RNAV capability respectively on GPS-reception and

functionality, related NOTAMs shall be considered

RAIM shall be verified and granted at ETA 15 minutes: for RAIM-prediction and Fault Detection and Exclusion (FDE) refer

to 8.3.2.8.3 - RNAV and RNP Specification and Accuracy Matrix (only applicable for RNP APCH)

operational Flight Plan (OFP)

airplane performance: take-off and landing calculations, mass and balance

airplane airworthiness and status with special attention regarding the planned operation (RVSM, MNPS; etc): Aircraft Technical Log (ATL),

Minimum Equipment List (MEL) and Configuration List (CDL)

The flight will be accepted and initiated by the Commander by signing the OFP.

More than 2000 kg

kontext:
8.1.10 Operational Flight Plan (OFP)

An Operational Flight Plan (OFP) shall be used for all flights and will be prepared by Operations Control (OCC).
An Operational Flight Plan (OFP) must show the name of the originator. It must be signed by the Commander (CMD) before the commencement of the flight.
By signing the Operational Flight Plan (OFP) the Commander (CMD): certifies that the flight has been planned according to the regulations stipulated in OM-A, OM-B and OM-C

confirms that he has carried out a briefing or self-briefing when operating into or out of an aerodrome category B or C or special route

flight preparation according to 8.1.0 - General Policy performed

The Commander (CMD) is responsible for the correct recording of all data required according to 8.1.10.1 - OFP – Format and Content By default the flight planning system PPS is calculating all flight plans with one destination alternate and no take-off alternate. All other destination alternates (called standard alternates) are displayed at the end of the route section of the OFP. (Refer to 8.1.10.2.4 - Destination Alternates, Notes and ATC Flightplan).
If changes to the OFP are required, the following options are available:
Task Action

change destination alternate remove destination alternate via Flight Briefing Documentation Tool or (ADDNAR calculation)

contact OCC add a second destination alternate

Additionally the The Operational Flight Plan (OFP) shall be recalculated by OCC in case of:

aircraft registration changed

or on request of the Commander (CMD)

or actual ZFM differs by more than 2000kg

In exceptional cases, if the OFP needs to be adapted and cannot be delivered to

the flight crew within reasonable time, OCC shall recalculate the OFP and communicate the changes to the flight crew. In any case, the required minimum

fuel must be reconfirmed between OCC and the flight crew. The OFP shall be

available on the EFB before block-off.

kontext:
8.1.7.3.1 Taxi Fuel

Taxi fuel contains the total amount of fuel expected to be used prior to take-off, including allowances for local conditions as:
NOTAMs

meteorological conditions (e.g. winter operations, remote de-icing)

ATS procedures (e.g. LVP, collaborative decision-making (CDM))

APU operation

any anticipated delays (e.g. long taxi times)

The OFP includes a common type specific amount of taxi fuel. Any anticipated additional required amount of fuel shall be added by the flight crew.
Additional required taxi fuel may be planned in section discretionary fuel considering the fuel check before take-off

according to 8.3.7.2 - Fuel Monitoring and Fuel Checks.

Dass er an alle Standard Alternates übermittelt wurde

kontext: 8.1.9.3 Commander’s Responsibility
During the crew briefing the Commander (CMD) must verify that a ATC flight plan has been filed with sufficient time of notice prior to departure.

Under normal circumstances the ATS unit for the departure and arrival stations transmits Actual Time of Departure (ATD) and Actual Time of Arrival (ATA) to respective ATS units. The ATC flight plan will therefore be automatically activated and deactivated.
On the rare occasion of: an IFR flight departing under VFR from an airport without ATS service

an IFR flight ending as a VFR flight at an airport without ATS service

the Commander (CMD) must ensure that an Actual Time of Departure (ATD) respectively an Actual Time of Arrival (ATA) is relayed by: phone by a qualified ground representative, or radio by the flight crew

to the appropriate ATS unit immediately after departure respectively after landing.

fragen.frage_en: A passenger has to be removed from a helvetic aircraft. Whom does the flight crew inform?
antworten_en: The local police directly, who collect the passenger
The OCC duty officer, who orders the offloading
The handling agent, who initiates the appropriate action
The Senior Cabin Attendant, who escorts the passenger
fragen.erklaerung_en: The flight crew informs the handling agent, who initiates the appropriate action and may call upon law enforcement officers if necessary.
kontext:
8.2.3 Procedures for the Refusal of Embarkation

A passenger shall be refused carriage and he shall be removed from the aircraft when, in the exercise of reasonable discretion, the handling staff or the Commander (CMD) decides that: it is necessary in the interest of the safety of the aircraft or its occupants, or it is necessary to prevent violation of laws, regulations or decrees of any country to be flown from, into or over, or the conduct, behavior or appearance of the passenger make him objectionable to other passengers, or the age, mental or physical condition of the passenger requires special assistance, which cannot be provided

Any person who appears to be under the influence of alcohol or drugs to the extent that the safety of the aircraft or its occupants is likely to be endangered, shall be refused embarkation.
Whenever it becomes necessary to remove a passenger from a helvetic aircraft, the flight crew shall inform the handling agent, who will initiate the appropriate action.

If it seems necessary, he may call upon the service of law enforcement officers.
If a passenger was refused from transportation the crew must issue an occurrence report (Occurrence Report – OR).

fragen.frage: Welcher der folgenden Gründe ist in OM-A 8.2.3 als Grund für eine Refusal of Embarkation aufgeführt?
antworten: Der Passagier benötigt spezielle Hilfe, die nicht geleistet werden kann
Der Passagier hat keine Sitzplatzreservierung auf der PIL
Der Passagier reist mit mehr als einem Carry-on Baggage
Der Passagier hat beim Boarding keinen Boarding Pass vorgezeigt
fragen.erklaerung: Ein Grund ist, wenn Alter, mentaler oder physischer Zustand des Passagiers spezielle Hilfe erfordert, die nicht geleistet werden kann.
fragen.zitat: the age, mental or physical condition of the passenger requires special assistance, which cannot be provided
fragen.frage_en: Which of the following is listed in OM-A 8.2.3 as a reason for refusal of embarkation?
antworten_en: The passenger requires special assistance which cannot be provided
The passenger has no seat reservation on the PIL
The passenger travels with more than one carry-on bag
The passenger did not show a boarding pass at boarding
fragen.erklaerung_en: One reason is that the age, mental or physical condition of the passenger requires special assistance which cannot be provided.

fragen.frage: Wo müssen Passagiere der Kategorien WCHR, WCHS und WCHC innerhalb der zugeteilten Sitzreihe sitzen?
antworten: Am Gang, damit die Cabin Crew sie rasch erreicht
Direkt an den Overwing Exits, nahe beim Ausgang
In der letzten Reihe vor der hinteren Galley
Am Fenster, damit sie andere bei einer Evakuierung nicht behindern
fragen.erklaerung: Sie sind am Fenster zu platzieren, damit sie bei einer Evakuierung ohne andere zu behindern ans Ende der Schlange bei den Emergency Exits geführt werden können.
fragen.zitat: They shall be seated next to the window. In this way, when the aircraft is being evacuated, they can – without impeding others – be assisted to reach the end of the line forming at the emergency exits and to leave the aircraft.
fragen.frage_en: Where within the allocated seat row shall WCHR, WCHS and WCHC passengers be seated?
antworten_en: On the aisle, so the cabin crew can reach them quickly
Directly at the overwing exits, close to the exit
In the last row in front of the aft galley
Next to the window, so they do not impede others in an evacuation
fragen.erklaerung_en: They shall be seated next to the window so that, in an evacuation, they can be assisted to the end of the line at the emergency exits without impeding others.
kontext:
8.2.2.3.2 Handling and Boarding

Before accepting sick, disabled and handicapped passengers for transportation, helvetic shall have ascertained the availability, from departure to arrival, of staff trained and qualified to meet their needs and of the appropriate medical equipment.
The number of PRM`s shall not exceed the number of able bodied persons.
They shall be briefed separately by the crew. Consider that in an emergency, the cabin crew can only assist them, once the cabin has been evacuated.
Passengers with disabilities as circumscribed under WCHR, WCHS and WCHC above, shall be allocated seat rows between passenger cabin doors and over- wing but not at the over wing exits. (for airplane specific limitations refer to CSPM 2)

They shall be seated next to the window. In this way, when the aircraft is being evacuated, they can – without impeding others – be assisted to reach the end of the line forming at the emergency exits and to leave the aircraft.

Sick and disabled passengers and PRM should be boarded separately (normally prior to all other passengers) as well as disembarked separately (normally after all other passengers have left the cabin).
Note: It is the care company’s duty to escort the PRM to and from their seat (not only to and from the aircraft door) and to assist with cabin baggage storage.

The Commander (CMD) shall be notified by the Senior Cabin Attendant (SEN) if Persons with Reduced Mobility (PRM) are listed on the Passenger Information

List (PIL).
For the carriage of gas cylinders, drugs, medicines, other medical material, wet cell or lithium battery powered wheel chairs refer to the 9.4.4 - Carriage of Wheelchairs and Other Mobility Aids and 10 - Security.

No transportation, under any circumstances, shall be provided to a person who:

has a contagious or infectious disease (e.g. open tuberculosis, infectious

hepatitis; scarlet fever, diphtheria, chickenpox)

has suffered a heart attack or stroke within the last eight weeks

requires medical treatment by pneumatically or electrically operated

apparatus, which, for specific reasons, is not allowed to be operated on board (for limitations refer to the Operations Manual OM-A 10)

fragen.frage: Was ist beim Briefing von PRM bezüglich der Hilfe durch die Cabin Crew in einem Notfall zu berücksichtigen?
antworten: Die Cabin Crew evakuiert PRM immer als Erste
Die Cabin Crew kann ihnen erst helfen, wenn die Kabine evakuiert ist
Die Hilfe erfolgt ausschliesslich durch die Flight Crew
PRM werden während der Evakuierung von ABP getragen
fragen.erklaerung: PRM sind separat zu briefen; in einem Notfall kann die Cabin Crew ihnen erst helfen, wenn die Kabine evakuiert wurde.
fragen.zitat: They shall be briefed separately by the crew. Consider that in an emergency, the cabin crew can only assist them, once the cabin has been evacuated.
fragen.frage_en: When briefing PRMs, what must be considered regarding cabin crew assistance in an emergency?
antworten_en: The cabin crew always evacuates PRMs first
The cabin crew can only assist them once the cabin has been evacuated
Assistance is provided exclusively by the flight crew
PRMs are carried by ABPs during the evacuation
fragen.erklaerung_en: PRMs shall be briefed separately; in an emergency the cabin crew can only assist them once the cabin has been evacuated.

fragen.frage: Fremde Crew Members reisen in Uniform als Passagiere mit. Was gilt bezüglich Able Bodied Persons (ABP)?
antworten: Sie dürfen nur mit Zustimmung ihres Operators als ABP dienen
Sie werden nur bei einer geplanten Evakuierung als ABP gebrieft
Sie sind als ABP einzusetzen
Sie dürfen nicht als ABP eingesetzt werden
fragen.erklaerung: Sind fremde Crew Members in Uniform an Bord, sind sie als ABP einzusetzen; bei freien Overwing-Exit-Sitzen sollen sie dorthin umgesetzt und gebrieft werden.
fragen.zitat: Whenever foreign crew members are on board in uniform they shall be used as ABP.
fragen.frage_en: Foreign crew members in uniform are travelling as passengers. What applies regarding Able Bodied Persons (ABP)?
antworten_en: They may act as ABP only with their operator's consent
They are briefed as ABP only for a prepared evacuation
They shall be used as ABP
They must not be used as ABP
fragen.erklaerung_en: Whenever foreign crew members are on board in uniform they shall be used as ABP; if overwing exit seats are free they should be reseated there and briefed.
kontext:
8.2.2.3.4 Able Bodied Person (ABP)

Suitable, Able Bodied Persons (ABP) are: crew on dead heading or pleasure travel.
Whenever foreign crew members are on board in uniform they shall be used as ABP.

If seats at the over-wing exits are empty ABPs should be reseated and be placed at the over-wing exits or close by. They shall be briefed about the exits and asked if they would help in case of an emergency.

policemen

firemen

military persons in uniform

medical personnel (doctors, nurses)

others who seem physically and mentally fit to perform the task

Choose, command, reseat, brief suitable passengers for the following duties: to open emergency exits upon your order, if required

to assist children and passengers with reduced mobility, or injured passengers

to assist crew in taking care of an UMNR in case of an emergency (e.g. evacuation) to assist in removing and operating ditching, survival and emergency

equipment

to guard unsafe door and exits or damaged escape slides

to assist passengers sliding down the slides

to assist passengers on the ground

to assist crew in handling of a security threat

(e.g. unruly passengers, hijack situations)

Note: An Able Bodied Person (ABP) should not take his own decision.
He is to follow the specific orders given by the cabin crew members.

A clear and precise briefing is of utmost importance.

Note: Cabin Crew shall be aware that a child under the age of 12 years,

separated from the accompanying adult, who is traveling in another cabin class, shall be considered as an UMNR therefore a ABP is required in case of emergency.

8.2.2.4 Transportation of Inadmissible Passengers, Deportees and Persons in Custody

Refer to: Ground Operations Manual (GOM) 4.1.5 - Special Category Passengers

kontext:
8.2.2.4.1 DEPA Flights – Special Procedures

General For DEPA charter flights the following special procedures shall be applied:

Any Flight-Phase any crew member not feeling physically and/or mentally able to conduct a DEPA flight shall contact CCO as soon as possible to arrange a replacement

the deportees may be bonded and may wear helmets
the crew is not allowed to communicate with the deportees. The communication shall be done via the police officers

deportees may act highly emotional especially during boarding, trying to prevent the transportation by all means (e.g. crying, aggressive behaviour, threatening)

additional information can be found in the special briefing. Procedures in the special briefing supersede any content of this paragraph

Pre-Flight special police briefing (CMD and SEN) will normally be organised by Fedpol

check-in time may be extended as per special briefing

Aircraft Security Search (ASS) shall be performed and completed before boarding starts

during boarding of deportees, the flight crew members shall be inside the cockpit and the cockpit door shall be closed

no crew member present in the front galley area during boarding

before commencing the flight, all passengers must be briefed about the type specific matters (i.e. location of emergency exits) and verify that there are no open questions concerning the safety procedures

conduct the safety briefing after boarding of all passengers as follows:

the cabin crew shall omit all public announcements as per CCM except for chapter 4 Safety the safety briefing shall be held as per CCM 4.3 in English language only In-Flight crew members shall not wear nametags

cabin crew members shall not wear ties or foulards to minimize the distraction of the police officers on board, no public announcements from the cockpit and in the cabin shall be done, except

in case of emergency

the responsibility for all passenger relevant issues on board (i.e.

medical, pax disturbance) lies with the responsible police officers as long as the flight safety is not directly affected

Post-Flight during de-boarding, the cockpit crew shall be inside the cockpit and the

cockpit door shall be closed

the SEN shall be present in the forward galley and both CABs shall wait

in the rear galley

Aircraft Security Search (ASS) shall be performed after de-boarding

fragen.frage: Was gilt auf einem DEPA-Flug im Flug für Public Announcements aus dem Cockpit und in der Kabine?

Keine, ausser im Notfall
Normale Announcements gemäss CCM in Englisch
Nur Announcements in der Landessprache der Destination
fragen.erklaerung: Um die Polizeibeamten nicht abzulenken, werden im Flug keine Public Announcements aus Cockpit und Kabine gemacht, ausser im Notfall.
fragen.zitat: to minimize the distraction of the police officers on board, no public announcements from the cockpit and in the cabin shall be done, except in case of emergency

Normal announcements according to CCM in English
Only announcements in the language of the destination country
fragen.erklaerung_en: To minimise distraction of the police officers, no public announcements from the cockpit and in the cabin shall be made in flight, except in case of emergency.

fragen.frage: Auf der PIL sind Sitze aus Trim- und Balance-Gründen blockiert. Unter welcher Bedingung dürfen Passagiere dorthin umgesetzt werden?
antworten: Wenn der SEN die Umsetzung im Cabin Log einträgt
Wenn höchstens zwei Passagiere umgesetzt werden
Nur mit Zustimmung des Commanders
Sobald das Boarding abgeschlossen ist
fragen.erklaerung: In aus Trim- und Balance-Gründen blockierte Sitze darf ohne Zustimmung des Commanders niemand umgesetzt werden; Passagiere, die sich selbst umsetzen, werden zurückgeschickt.
fragen.zitat: If there are blocked seats on the Passenger Information List (PIL) because of trim and balance, it is not allowed to reseat passengers into those seats without the Commander’s approval.
fragen.frage_en: Seats are blocked on the PIL for trim and balance reasons. Under which condition may passengers be reseated into them?
