Only with the Commander's approval
As soon as boarding is completed
fragen.erklaerung_en: It is not allowed to reseat passengers into seats blocked for trim and balance without the Commander's approval; passengers who reseat themselves are moved back.
kontext:
8.2.2.2 Allocation of Seats

The allocation of seats to passengers by ground staff depends upon the aircraft type, its seating version, aspects of mass and center of gravity and the class of transportation (if any) held by the individual passenger.
Aircraft type-specific instructions for crew concerning seating restrictions for passengers are listed in the Cabin Safety and Procedures Manual CSPM 2.1.2.5 Seating Restrictions Passengers who should be seated where they will not obstruct access to safety equipment or exits or otherwise impede the crew in carrying out their duties are: persons, who are physically or mentally handicapped to the extent that they would have difficulty in moving quickly if asked to do so

persons, whose sight or hearing is impaired to the extent that they might not readily become aware of instructions given to begin evacuating the aircraft

children and infants, whether or not they are accompanied by an adult

persons in custody and those who are being deported

persons whose physical size would prevent them from being able to move quickly

persons with guide dogs or pet animals

Reseating groups of passengers without Commander (CMD) approval is not permitted.
However, the cabin crew members are authorised to reseat able-bodied

passengers and persons with reduced mobility (PRM).

Refer to 8.2.2.3.3 - Able Bodied Person (ABP)

CSPM 2.1.2.7.3 Able Bodied Person (ABP)

If there are blocked seats on the Passenger Information List (PIL) because of

trim and balance, it is not allowed to reseat passengers into those seats without the Commander’s approval.
If passengers reseat themselves without crew approval, cabin crew shall move them back to their original seats.

It is noted with the time on the OFP
It is only received by the Commander
It is acknowledged by the assigned flight crew member (read back)

kontext:
8.3.15.5 Prior to Take -off

The Senior Cabin Attendant (SEN), having received the appropriate cabin report from each cabin attendant, shall report this to the flight crew, confirming: passengers are seated with seat belts fastened, backrests are upright and tables or trays are in the stowed position and armrests are in down position

all infants are correctly restraint

all window shutters are open

equipment and baggage is properly secured, galleys and lavatories are checked, locked, secured, stowage spaces and bins are closed

all exits and escape paths are unobstructed, curtains and doors are secured in the open position

all doors are automatic

passenger briefing is completed (refer to OM-0 4 CCM)

the use of 8.3.28 - Portable Electronic Devices (PED) are strictly adhered to (CSPM 2 Portable Electronic Devices)

check all electronic devices disconnected from in-seat USB power supply

cabin lights shall be adapted to the light conditions outside of the aircraft: during day the lights should be dimmed

during night the lights shall be switched off in order to improve the night

vision of cabin crew and passengers,

(refer to CSPM 5)

electronic galley equipment (oven, coffee maker) are switched off

cabin attendants occupy their assigned positions stations and have their

safety belts and, if installed, their harnesses fastened

lavatory check performed according to the lavatory check procedure (door

must be locked)

For callouts refer to 8.3 Appendix 1, Prior to Take-off CSPM 2 Appendix 1

Communication Wording
The cabin secure report must be acknowledged by the assigned flight crew member (read back).

When lining up at the departure runway the assigned flight crew member shall alert the cabin crew through an announcement.

kontext:
8.3.28.5 Commanders Authority

The final authority to allow use of PED T-PED within the limits shown, rests with the Commander (CMD). If necessary in the interest of safety, he may restrict the use of PED T-PED.
This applies especially to situations like air turbulence (stowage of loose devices) or low visibility conditions (avoid any potential interference with the avionics systems).
At the commander’s discretion on the ground, and if the aircraft is not moving under its own power, PED T-PED may be used by passengers upon announcement from the crew.

Sufficient time must be available for cabin crew to advise the passengers before the flight proceeds.
Recharging of electronic equipment using the aircraft's electrical system is authorized only at defined ports.

OM-A 8 Operating Procedures

Always, immediately after the doors are closed

kontext:
8.3.15.4 Prior to Taxiing

Whilst embarking of passengers the cabin crew must be present in the cabin.
The minimum crew during embarkation is defined in 8.2.2.1.2 - Minimum Number of Cabin Crew required during Ground Operations with Passengers CSPM 2.1.2.1.1 - Minimum Number of Cabin Crew required during Ground Operations with Passengers. all cabin crew members must be stationed according to the defined boarding position (refer to CSPM 5), until the boarding is completed

Cabin Attendants (CAB) must distribute the infant belts and if necessary the infant life vest and explain how to use them. Passengers must be informed to return the respective equipment to the cabin crew while leaving the aircraft.
After passenger boarding the Senior Cabin Attendant (SEN) shall report the total passenger (headcount) on board to the Commander (CMD). He will then verify the total according to the load sheet and orders the doors to be closed.
For callouts refer to 8.3 Appendix 1, After Boarding CSPM 2 Appendix 1 Communication Wording After closing of all doors and after the appropriate announcement of the flight crew for arming the doors, each Cabin Attendant (CAB) shall ensure that each assisting means for emergency evacuation, that deploys automatically, is armed at the doors and emergency exits for which he has been designated responsible (i.e. arming lever armed).
For callouts refer to 8.3 Appendix 1, Cabin Crew Arm the Slide CSPM 2

Appendix 1 Communication Wording.
Cabin crew member must check if the seating of handicapped passengers, children, infants and persons in custody complies with the provisions of 8.2.2.2 -

Allocation of Seats. If not, they must arrange for their reseating.

The cabin crew shall ensure that: all passengers are seated

no food, beverage or tableware is located at any passenger seat

food and beverage trays (folding tables), as well as passengers backrests are in the upright position

procedures regarding 8.3.28 - Portable Electronic Devices (PED) are strictly adhered to

In addition, the cabin crew shall be ascertained that all passenger and crew baggage, catering equipment and other cabin load is properly secured and stowed where it cannot impede evacuation or cause injury by falling, or other movement. Overhead bins shall be closed.
The cabin crew must strictly enforce the no smoking instruction.
All exits and escape paths shall be unobstructed. If it is necessary to pass through a doorway or curtain to reach any required emergency exit from any passenger seat, the door or curtain shall be secured in the open position.
All relevant emergency equipment shall remain easily accessible for immediate use.
When the cabin is ready for taxi, the SEN shall report this to the flight deck only if required according to the aircraft specific procedures.
For callouts refer to 8.3 Appendix 1, Cabin Crew Arm the Slide CSPM 2 Appendix 1 Communication Wording

kontext:
8.3.21.2 RAAR PPAA FORD NITS

Whenever for technical or operational reasons during a flight abnormal or emergency procedures must be applied all company policies remain intact.
Abnormal and emergency procedures consist of four major phases:
R ecognition

A nalysis

A ction

R eassessment

During the application of abnormal and emergency procedures the Crew Resource Management (CRM) becomes, compared with normal operations, an even more crucial component. Therefore, the Commander (CMD) must concentrate with the highest priority on the assessment and distribution of its human and technical resources and to constantly reevaluate and optimize his decisions. The crew must prevent itself from any form of actionist behavior and uncoordinated or unfocused dealing with the problem at hand.
Whenever confronted with an emergency or abnormal situation, the first priority lies in the proper flying and monitoring of the aircraft.

Crew duties must be distributed clearly, basically the following sequence applies:
P ower the PF takes the initiative. Check thrust and order appropriate

setting for the engine(s) operating normally P erformance check configuration and minimum maximum speed

A nalysis both pilots shall assess the situation, where the lead of the

analyze lies with the Pilot Monitoring (PM)

A ction action shall be taken according to emergency abnormal

checklist, OM-B abnormal operation, flight procedures and knowledge

Use company channels and co-operate as soon as possible with the cabin crew.
Create favorable conditions for approach and landing by e.g:

requesting ATC assistance (Priority, Emergency)

careful selection of landing airport with suitable weather conditions, approach aids, runway as applicable

For the abnormal operation helvetic uses abnormal and emergency checklists.
All checklists are named.
When the situation changes to the worse the aim for the safety of the aircraft, its passengers, crew and cargo become the only operational goal.
If this goal can no longer be achieved by the use of the helvetic Standard Operating Procedures (SOP), diversion from these published procedures will be accepted. Any diversion from published procedures for the safety of the aircraft, its passengers, crew and cargo must be exercised only after due consideration by the crew (i.e. no matter how inconvenient such a decision might be for either or both helvetic and passengers).
If the helvetic Standard Operating Procedures (SOP) seem no longer adequate to deal with the situation at hand, an emergency must be declared.
As a general guideline, a declaration of an emergency or urgency can be evaluated and communicated to ATC as follows:
EICAS WARNING land at the nearest suitable airport:

fragen.frage: Welche der folgenden Situationen erfordert gemäss OM-A in jedem Fall die Erklärung eines Notfalls?
antworten: Ausfall eines Packs im Cruise
Ausfall eines Generators mit verfügbarem Backup
Eine Diversion wegen Wetter an der Destination
Severe Icing, das die sichere Flugdurchführung beeinträchtigt
fragen.erklaerung: Severe Icing, das die sichere Durchführung des Flugs beeinträchtigt, ist eine der Bedingungen, bei denen immer ein Notfall zu erklären ist.
fragen.zitat: severe icing conditions affecting the safe conduct of the flight
fragen.frage_en: Which of the following situations always requires an emergency to be declared according to OM-A?
antworten_en: Failure of one pack in cruise
Failure of one generator with backup available
A diversion due to weather at destination
Severe icing affecting the safe conduct of the flight
fragen.erklaerung_en: Severe icing conditions affecting the safe conduct of the flight are one of the conditions for which an emergency must always be declared.
kontext:
“PAN PAN, PAN PAN, PAN PAN”

However, an emergency must always be declared, if one of the following conditions exists: fire or smoke on board or

structural damage or low fuel (i.e. when it becomes obvious that the fuel on board will drop to the final reserve before landing)

or
severe icing conditions affecting the safe conduct of the flight

or security threat on board

or

pilot incapacitation

By declaring an emergency the crew:

legalizes all measure taken for the safety of the aircraft, its passengers, crew and cargo, even when it diverts from published legal rules or

helvetic Standard Operating Procedures (SOP) and even when they are contrary to legal requirements, as long as the safe return of the flight

remains to be the visible goal of that measure

ensures all possible help and support by other involved parties (e.g. ATC)

ensures priority over all other aircraft

A crew which decides to declare an emergency based on the situational assessment will always receive the full support of the operational management.
An emergency must be declared as follows: setting the transponder to code 7700

for ATC communication refer to 12.3.7.2 - Declaration of an Emergency

fragen.frage_en: Analysis phase of an abnormal procedure: what is the Pilot Flying (PF) responsible for?

kontext:
8.3.21.2.2 Analysis Phase

With the analysis phase the work split between the Pilot Flying (PF) and the Pilot Monitoring (PM) begins.

The Pilot Flying (PF) is responsible for: the control of the aircraft in attitude and flight path

the navigation

the ATC communication

The Pilot Monitoring (PM) is responsible for: the evaluation of the situation

the briefing of the Pilot Flying (PF) about the intended course of action

At the end of the analysis phase the flight crew should have a plan how to deal with the abnormality on a short run.

kontext:
8.3.21.2.4 Reassessment Phase

The reassessment phase serves the synchronization of all involved parties and the decision about the following strategy.
Therefore the Pilot Monitoring (PM) briefs the Pilot Flying (PF) about: the status of the flight (technical, operational)

the remaining resources and possible limitations

the remaining options if the trouble shooting has been unsuccessful

The flight crew members then decide upon their intentions and communicate them, as appropriate, to:
A TC

The end of the reassessment phase may lead to: a return to normal operations

kontext:
8.3.21.5.3 Evacuation Required

When the need for an emergency evacuation arises it must be clearly ordered and carried out expeditiously. The objective of an evacuation is to remove the passengers from the aircraft as fast as possible according to the situation.
Generally, the Commander (CMD) will initiate an evacuation.
But any crew member can order an emergency evacuation when: the aircraft is on ground and ceased moving, and there is severe structural damage, or there is explosive fire, or after ditching

An emergency evacuation is ordered by shouting: for callout refer to 8.3 Appendix 1, Evacuation Orders CSPM 2 Appendix 1 Communication Wording

the order must be shouted continuously and it supersedes all previously given orders.
An emergency evacuation cannot be canceled – once initiated it must be carried out by all aircraft occupants.

Note: once initiated, an evacuation must not be stopped!

passengers must leave their carry-on baggage in the aircraft and should be directed to a safe distance away from the aircraft.

fragen.frage: Wie unterscheidet sich eine Rapid Disembarkation von einer Emergency Evacuation?

kontext:
8.3.21.5.2 Rapid Disembarkation

For certain reasons the Commander (CMD) may want to abandon the airplane without taking the risks of an emergency evacuation. In this case he may order a rapid disembarkation:
For callouts refer to 8.3 Appendix 1, Rapid Disembarkation Order CSPM 2 Appendix 1 Communication Wording

Other, than during an emergency evacuation, the passengers and the crew

would leave the airplane expeditiously, but not in a hurry.

This procedure shall only be applied if stairs or jet ways are available.
Typical scenarios for a decision to execute a rapid disembarkation are in e.g.:

bomb threats,

or being parked next to an aircraft which is suffering from an open fire

Before initiating the procedure the flight crew has to ensure that the engines are

shut down, the jetty and or stairs are in place and the escape slides are not armed.

kontext:
8.3.21.9 Duties of the Commander after an Abnormal or Emergency

Situation

Whenever one of the following is true: distress situation

accident

serious incident

unsolved security threat (1)

any event causing emotional stress which impairs fitness to fulfill flight duties

the Commander (CMD) shall perform the following duties as soon as practicable after the flight: inform Operations Control Center (OCC) or the Piquet Officer (PQO)

do not continue operation until released by FOP, ACM or PQO

coordinate with the PQO if a deactivation of the flight recorders is required. If necessary, the deactivation of all flight recorders shall be done in coordination with maintenance

if required, coordinate passenger care

if required, coordinate with local authorities (if support is required, contact FOP via OCC)

write an occurrence report

Note 1: This excludes straightforward situations that the crew can resolve

independently by following established procedures and verifying that the threat has been fully cleared - without requiring a

back-office risk assessment - such as:

unruly passenger level 1-2 events

threat level 1-2 situations

laser beam attacks

offloading of passengers or baggage
clearing of suspicious items

8.3.19.6.2 Company Communication

During normal operation no call to OCC or MCC is required.
Whenever the aircraft is on the ground with engines shut down, the helvetic mobile phone must be switched on and checked for adequate signal reception.

In case of operational irregularities(1), OCC shall be contacted as follows: on ground: via mobile phone

in-flight: via ACARS

backup communication tool in ZRH area: company frequency (callsign: “helvetic Ops”)

Note 1: Examples: offloading of luggage/cargo due to overload, in-flight return diversion, CB’s over the alps eventually influence another helvetic flight or special assistance required such as WCHC) or delay of more than 15 minutes to schedule or a change in technical status of the aircraft which has operational impact (e.g. APU u/s)

In case of technical irregularities, MCC shall be contacted as follows: on ground: via mobile phone

in-flight(2): via ACARS to OCC

backup communication tool in ZRH area(2):

OCC via company frequency (callsign: “helvetic Ops”)

Note 2: Technical irregularities requiring maintenance assistance or action

upon arrival should be reported by stating only the ATA Chapter.
For technical assistance needed during flight, the topic may be

discussed in accordance with general communication discipline, using one's own words.

kontext:
8.3.2.24 Meteorological Information

Enroute Monitoring:
During enroute phases current weather reports (e.g. ATIS, METAR via ACARS, VOLMET) shall be checked and recorded for: adequate, emergency aerodrome or Fuel Enroute Alternate (Fuel-ERA) during the time where an enroute diversion to that aerodrome would be considered in case of a sudden need

destination alternate(s) if either conditions at the destination itself or the destination alternate are likely to be critical due to any reasons (e.g. traffic situation, meteorological conditions, political unrest, strike, increased threat, technical issues)

Refer to 2.4.7.7 - Flight Monitoring for further information regarding flight continuation, diversion or termination.

Destination Monitoring:
The latest available meteorological information must be obtained and evaluated before commencing an approach. Due regard must also be given to the runway surface conditions. The best source of information during this part of a flight provides the ATIS.
Flight crews are allowed to start any approach into an aerodrome until reaching a

certain height which is defined in 8.4.5.7 - Approach Ban.
However, the situation in-flight might change in such a way that according to the latest information a landing cannot be made at both the destination and destination alternate.

Therefore, a diversion to an enroute alternate shall be initiated as soon as the

flight crew becomes aware of such a situation, taking into account the remaining

fuel on board.

kontext:
11.6.1 Emergency Evacuation Procedure

After the complete stop of the airplane, apply the Emergency/Parking Brake, press the Cockpit Door LOCK Button to unlock the door, set SLAT/FLAP Lever to 5, set Thrust Levers to IDLE, set the Engine 1 and 2 START/STOP Selectors to STOP, PULL and ROTATE the Engine 1 and 2 FIRE EXTINGUISHER Handles, PUSH the APU EMER STOP Button IN, PUSH the Fire Extinguisher APU Button, PUSH the DUMP Button IN and notify the ATC.

After fire extinguisher agent discharge, in case of the fire alarm persistence, the fire should be visually confirmed by the crew or confirmed by requesting ground personnel's help. The crewmembers must identify if an engine remains on fire; the associated exit door(s) should not be used.

At this moment, the CMD shall command the emergency evacuation through the P.A. system. In case he is unable to do so, the command is given by the next ranking and capable crewmember.
The cabin crew must check outside condition and only open exits which are not obstructed and not in direct fire-area.

The alert system and the P.A. will be unavailable after setting the BATT 1 and BATT 2 Knobs to OFF.

In case of ditching, after completing the QRH procedures, pilots must dress the

life vests and should go to the passenger cabin to assure the complete evacuation of the airplane

and to supervise the after evacuation tasks. If it is not possible to reach the passenger cabin, both pilots have to evacuate the airplane through the cockpit window.

kontext: 7.2.1 Modification of the Limits on Flight Duty, Duty or Rest Periods
During actual flight operation, which starts after the whole crew has reported for any duty, the Commander (CMD) shall have the possibility to modify the limits

on flight duty, duty and rest periods in the event of conditions described as unforeseen circumstances.
The exercise of commander’s discretion shall be considered exceptional and shall be avoided at home base when standby or reserve crew members are available.
The conditions shall comply with the following: the maximum daily FDP which results after applying 7.1.7 - Maximum Daily Flight Duty Periode (FDP) or 7.1.9 - Split Duty may not be increased by more than 2 hours.

the maximum basic daily FDP that results after applying 7.1.7.1 - Maximum Daily FDP for Acclimatised Crew Members shall be used to calculate the limits of commander’s discretion, if commander’s discretion is applied to an FDP which has been extended under the provisions of 7.1.7.3 - Maximum Daily FDP for Acclimatised Crew Members with the Use of Extensions without In-flight Rest

if on the final sector within a FDP the allowed increase is exceeded because of unforeseen circumstances after take-off, the flight may continue to the planned destination or alternate aerodrome the rest period following the FDP may be reduced but can never be less

than 10 hours

The commander shall consult all crew members on their alertness levels before deciding the modifications.
Additionally, he shall take due consideration of additional factors that might decrease a crew member’s alertness levels, such as:
WOCL encroachment

weather conditions

complexity of the operation and/or airport environment

airplane malfunctions or specifications

flight with training or supervisory duties

increased number of sectors

circadian disruption

individual conditions of affected crew members (time since awake, sleep- related factor, workload, etc.)

7.2.2 Duties in case of Modification of the Limits on Flight Duty, Duty or Rest Periods

helvetic will assess on a regular basis the series of pairings where commander’s

discretion has been exercised in order to be aware of possible inconsistencies in their rostering. The FRMS meeting monitors the amount of FTL modifications and other FTL exceedances via the BI tool according to 2.4.5.1.8 - FRMS Meeting.

The Commander (CMD) shall submit an IT report to helvetic flight operations

management whenever a limit on flight duty, duty or rest period has been

modified by his discretion or whenever a limitation as stated within this chapter has been violated in excess of one hour. This report shall be handled according

to OMM 7 Reporting Scheme.

Whenever the above-mentioned modification or a reported violation is beyond one hour, helvetic shall send a copy of the report to the competent authority not

later than 28 days after the event.

The RPO will monitor FTL exceedances and request reports from the commander, whenever a report is missing.

Planned schedules must allow for flights to be completed within the maximum

kontext:
7.2.4 Delayed Reporting or Short-notice Flight Cancellation

In the event of unforeseen circumstances a delayed reporting procedure may be applied if the time until the scheduled reporting time is more than one hour at home base or more than 30 minutes away from home base and the crew member can remain at his suitable accommodation.
In such a case, if the crew member is informed by phone (or by SMS in case of possible interference with sleeping patterns) about the delayed reporting time, the maximum Flight Duty Period (FDP) is calculated as follows:
One notification of a delay leads to the calculation of the maximum FDP according to when the delay is less than 4 hours, the maximum FDP is calculated based on the original reporting time and the FDP starts counting at the delayed reporting time

when the delay is 4 hours or more, the maximum FDP is calculated based on the more limiting of the original or the delayed reporting time and the FDP starts counting at the delayed reporting time

If the reporting time is further amended, the FDP starts counting 1 hour after the second notification or at the original delayed reporting time if this is earlier As an exception,

when the operator informs the crew member of a delay of 10 hours or more in reporting time and the crew member is not further disturbed by the operator, such delay of 10 hours or more counts as a rest

period.
Any delay which is communicated to the crew member 10 hours or more before the delayed reporting time does not count as delayed reporting and no additional regulations apply.

In the event when the first flight segment(s) has to be removed (but the following ones remain) or changed to another flight segment(s), and this change is done

less than one hour ahead of original reporting time, a ground duty is added in the

duration of 5min starting at the original reporting time.

If due to an unforeseen circumstance flight must be cancelled after the reporting time for duty, ground duty is added which starts at the original reporting time, and

finishes either at the time when decision for cancellation was made (if crew was

not yet at the aircraft) or 30min after the decision was made (if crew performed any flight duty prior to the affected one).

One notification of a delay leads to the calculation of the maximum FDP according to when the delay is less than 4 hours, the maximum FDP is calculated based on the original reporting time and the FDP starts counting at the delayed reporting time

when the delay is 4 hours or more, the maximum FDP is calculated based on the more limiting of the original or the delayed reporting time and the FDP starts counting at the delayed reporting time
If the reporting time is further amended, the FDP starts counting 1 hour after the second notification or at the original delayed reporting time if this is earlier

As an exception, when the operator informs the crew member of a delay of 10 hours or more in reporting time and the crew member is not further disturbed by the operator, such delay of 10 hours or more counts as a rest

period.
Any delay which is communicated to the crew member 10 hours or more before the delayed reporting time does not count as delayed reporting and no additional regulations apply.

In the event when the first flight segment(s) has to be removed (but the following ones remain) or changed to another flight segment(s), and this change is done

less than one hour ahead of original reporting time, a ground duty is added in the

duration of 5min starting at the original reporting time.

If due to an unforeseen circumstance flight must be cancelled after the reporting time for duty, ground duty is added which starts at the original reporting time, and

finishes either at the time when decision for cancellation was made (if crew was

not yet at the aircraft) or 30min after the decision was made (if crew performed any flight duty prior to the affected one).

kontext:
7.1.1 General

All information about flight and duty time limitations and rest requirements, as well as the rules about exceedances of flight duty time limitations and/or reductions of rest periods, are established for all flight and cabin crew members of helvetic and are in compliance with EASA AIR OPS PART ORO - Subpart FTL, relevant Certification Specification (CS.FTL) and the complementary national provisions of Switzerland.
All flights are planned as to be completed within the allowable flight duty period, taking into account the time necessary for all pre-flight duties, all subsequent flights, turn-arounds and all post flight duties. helvetic will publish weekly duty rosters for its crew members four weeks in advance. The duty roster will be published latest every Sunday evening. helvetic may modify these flight and duty time limitations after approval from FOCA Switzerland.
Both, the individual crew member and helvetic, are responsible for strict observance of these regulations.
No crew member shall begin a flight duty period if it is foreseeable, that duty time limitations as stated within this chapter will be violated.
Apart from flying for helvetic, no crew member is allowed to fly privately for financial gain, or commercially for a third party without the approval of helvetic flight operations management.

kontext:
7.0.1 Fatigue Risk Management Policy

As a commitment to the continuous improvement of safety, helvetic has a Fatigue Risk Management System (FRMS) to manage fatigue-related risks.
FRMS applies to all operations as defined in the Operations Manuals, is based on the Safety, Security and Compliance Policy stated in OMM 1.1 Safety and Security Policy, Objectives and Commitment and is an integral part of the Safety Management System (SMS) described in OMM Chapter 4.
The FRMS describes the processes used for identifying fatigue hazards, assessing the associated risks, and developing, implementing, and monitoring controls and mitigations. The chapter 7.3 - Fatigue Risk Management System (FRMS) also describes the safety assurance processes used to ensure that the FRMS meets its safety objectives, and how the FRMS is integrated with our industry-leading SMS programs.
As non-work-related factors are controlled by employees and work-related causes of fatigue are driven by helvetic, both of them are jointly responsible to manage and mitigate fatigue.

kontext:
11.6 Reporting of Occurrence

Any cockpit or cabin crew member shall report to the commander any fault, failure, malfunction or defect which she/he believes may affect the airworthiness or safe operation of the aircraft, including emergency systems, and any incident that endangered or could have endangered the safety of operation. The tables in chapter 11.6.2 - Mandatory Occurrence Reporting list the expected reporter (flight crew, cabin crew, maintenance staff and ground handling) to each mandatory occurrence. However, during flight operation the crew may define one crew member who writes the report. The final responsibility lies with the CMD.
If a crew member other than the CMD writes the report, the safety management will ensure the CMD of the affected flight will be informed as well.
Any occurrences shall be reported as fast as reasonably possible, but no later than 72 hours.

Guideline for checking if operational occurrence or other legal reporting requirement is present:

1. First check with: a. 11.6.2 - Mandatory Occurrence Reporting b. 11.7 - List of Other Legal Reporting Requirements Note: Table of Contents for faster access is presented on next page.

2. Depending on the severity of the occurrence decide between: a. Accident or Serious Incident Reporting (Definition in 11.2 - Definitions)

b. Otherwise Occurence Reporting

c. Check if Occurrence requires immediate ATC Notification as specified

in 11.6.2.4 - ATC Reporting

Note:
As a general rule: Whenever you are in doubt, file an “Occurence Report” via the helvetic SMS Tool.

11.6.1 Accident and Serious Incident Reporting

The Flight Crew shall notify without delay the helvetic OCC and Piquet Officer whenever he or any other crew member learns of the occurrence of an accident or serious incident. This should be done as best suitable via phone, ACARS or company frequency.

kontext:
11.9.3 Official Investigation

An official investigation serves to identify the chain of events and its root causes

with the aim to prevent reoccurrence of similar events. Official investigations are

conducted by national authorities. ICAO Annex 13 (international) and

“Verordnung über die Sicherheitsuntersuchung von Zwischenfällen im

Verkehrswesen (VSZV)” (national) serve as guidelines for an official investigation.

Note: Since official investigations have shown to result in legal action against

aviation employees in certain cases,

helvetic strongly recommended action for employees directly involved in the event is to take private notes about the

occurrence, but not make any official statement before securing legal advice
of a specialist lawyer company.

kontext:
8.1.12.1 Aircraft Document Briefcase

All helvetic aircraft are carrying a briefcase or booklet (“blue FOCA-folder”)

containing aircraft documents.

Original documents must be in this booklet. Other documents are available as

copy on the EFB.

In case of loss or theft of the documents this folder, the operation may continue until the flight reaches its destination or a place where replacement documents

can be provided.

kontext:
8.1.11.2.2 Aircraft Technical Log (ATL) – Utilisation

The following sub-chapters provide instructions for the use of the ATL in normal and abnormal situations. These chapters are sorted by scenario and provide examples to increase user-friendliness.

8.1.11.2.2.1 Pre-Flight – Incomplete Tech-Log

If, prior to a flight, an aircraft has an incomplete tech-log entry, the commander shall perform the following steps: call OCC to contact previous crew for verification of the aircraft status

if OCC is unable to reach the previous crew, contact MCC to verify the aircraft status MCC shall check aircraft history of technical messages

ATL shall be closed by the operating crew verify fuel state via Flight Briefing Documentation Tool

IQSMS report shall be filed for tracking Area of Occurence: Technical Type of Occurrence: Technical Data Event Classification: Technical Documentation (ATL, MEL, Aircraft Status Report)

8.1.11.2.2.2 Pre-Flight – Aircraft Acceptance Prior to any flight, the aircraft's airworthiness and technical condition shall be assessed and confirmed by the commander by reviewing the following:

ATL to familiarise himself with any technical failure, maintenance actions

that may have occurred during previous flights and to ensure that all

recorded defect entries have been appropriately assessed and answered by helvetic maintenance and/or the contracted maintenance organisation

Acceptable Deferred Defects (ADD), briefing cards (BC) and associated MEL references as detailed in the technical information system-generated

aircraft status report

Note: If multiple MEL items are applied, the aircraft must not take off unless it

is confirmed that the interaction between inoperative components or systems will not result in an unacceptable degradation in the level of

safety and or undue increase in crew workload.

The commander confirms the aircraft acceptance by signing the appropriate ATL

field.

8.1.11.2.2.3 Pre-flight – Inspection (PFI)

During the pre-flight inspection (PFI) the availability, accessibility and serviceability of the flight deck systems and emergency equipment must be assured in accordance with:
OM-B E1 2.1.4 External Inspection OM-B E2 2.1.4 External Inspection

After the completion of the pre-flight inspection the commander is responsible that the following fields are completed in the ATL: section A, a/c registration section D, flight number section E, departure airport section F, date section P, cross in box “Crew Entry” section J, cross in box “PFI” section J, time and date of PFI section J, commander or deputy 3LC section J, commander or deputy signature

The PFI may be conducted by either the commander or the copilot and is acknowledged by signing the appropriate field in the ATL.
Prior to departure the commander must remove the orange colored carbon copy (station copy) which must remain at the point of departure.

(Example: Preflight ATL)

8.1.11.2.2.4 Post-Flight – No Items Listed (NIL)
After completion of a flight with no technical occurrence, the commander shall: enter “NIL” in the complaint section of the ATL

fill out fields as per 8.1.11.2.1.1 - Aircraft Technical Log Page Contents Description of COMPLAINT Side

(Example: NIL)

8.1.11.2.2.5 Defect Entry - General

In case of technical occurrences the commander shall defer a defect as detailed in the “Complaint” section of the ATL provided that such defects can be deferred in accordance with the company Minimum Equipment List (MEL) and: no maintenance action (M) is required prior to dispatch unless a Crew Applied MEL Procedure (CAMP) can be applied the defect is considered to have no airworthiness and/or safety consequences

The commander should notify helvetic maintenance of any defect deferred in the aircraft technical log by means of the “Crew Deferral” process prior to the next departure. After arrival from the last flight of the day, MCC shall be informed by the flight crew about any defects recorded in the ATL or technical issues discovered during post-flight inspection.
The commander of the aircraft is responsible to accurately enter details of any observed complaint in the ATL. Whenever a defect is recorded a new log slip must be used. Before opening a new log slip, cross out the complaint section of the actual log slip and sign it in the respective box.
The station copy with the recorded defect must remain on the departure station.
The commander must complete the following fields when entering a defect in to the ATL: section A, a/c registration

kontext:
11.9.4.1 Flight and Cockpit Voice Recorder Systems

Flight recorders on the helvetic Embraer fleet are digital recording units (DVDR) combining three different functionalities. Recording of: audio information from cockpit area microphones and primary crew microphones [cockpit voice recorder (CVR)]. datalink messages [data link recorder (DLR)] all available flight data [flight data recorder (FDR)] CVRs have at least 2 hours of voice recording capacity and must only be de- activated to protect records in due time.
FDRs have a flight time recording capacity which allows read out or de-activation in due time after an occurrence. De-activation during flight or on ground by the flight crew is not allowed.
Note: If a flight is conducted with a deactivated CVR check with MCC for MEL Regulation(s).

The DVDR automatically starts recording audio information as soon as the

aircraft is powered up. Flight data recording begins when the first engine is started. After power down the DVDRcontinue recording audio information for 10 minutes.
In the event the airplane becomes involved in an accident or serious incident, the

Commander must ensure the protection of all related flight records, and if

necessary, the associated DVDR to the extent possible.

This can include the

retention of the DVDR in safe custody until its disposition.

The removal of the flight recorder systems from the aircraft will be determined by

the investigating authority in the state conducting the investigation with due regard to the seriousness of the occurrence.

kontext:
3.10.2 Windshear Prevention Recovery

Windshear escape maneuver due to EGPWS announcement:
Thrust Levers MAX When moving the thrust levers press TO/GA Button.

Flight Director Escape Guidance Cue FOLLOW Maintain airplane configuration. Do not change gear and flap position until terrain clearance is assured and above 1500 ft AGL or after WSHEAR label is removed from PFD.

The windshear escape guidance mode does not automatically revert to any other flight guidance mode. The pilot must manually select another mode or press TO/GA Button in order to exit windshear escape guidance.

Pitch 15°,

kontext:
3.22.1 Emergency Descent

This maneuver is designed to bring the airplane down to a safe altitude in the minimum amount of time.
It follows a rapid depressurization or any other situation requiring immediate and rapid loss of altitude. This procedure should be accomplishing by the crew members from memory.

During an emergency descent, a permanent communication in the cockpit should be maintained to identify a possible pilot incapacitation.
If structural damage is suspected, use flight controls with care, limit speed as appropriate and evaluate the use of landing gear to expedite the descent. When turbulence is encountered, reduce to turbulent air penetration speed.

kontext:
0.5.4 Abnormal and Emergency QAC (Memory Items)

In any abnormal or emergency situation, maintaining control of the aircraft remains the highest priority.
The primary purpose of the Abnormal and Emergency section of the QAC is to assist the flight crew in promptly executing memory items in response to non- routine events.
To ensure rapid access and execution,

memory items shall be performed as expeditiously as possible with the aid of the QAC. In situations requiring immediate corrective action (e.g. jammed control column), memory items must be applied by heart.

Emergency and abnormal checklists take precedence over normal checklists, except in cases where the flight crew determines that deviation from this principle is necessary to maintain the highest level of safety.

DITCHING

For descent, set transponder to 7700, pull the aural warning CBs (C7 and C31) and set no smoking/fasten belts signs and ELT to ON. Set the landing data.
At 10000 ft AGL, press the pressurization dump button. When the differential pressure is 0.2 psid or below, limit maximum airspeed to 160 KIAS and open the direct vision window. If required, extend flap/slat as necessary to maintain the airspeed below 160 KIAS. Set pressurization to manual mode and hold the cabin alt controller down for 50 seconds.
For ditching configuration, press the terrain inhibit button, set landing gear up and set slat/flap to the maximum available deflection. Unlock the cockpit door.
Press the APU emergency stop button.
Just before water contact, announce impact to the cabin.
After ditching, set thrust levers to IDLE, set the start/stop selectors to STOP, pull the fire-extinguishing handles, announce emergency evacuation and set batteries to OFF.

kontext:
3.6.3 Engine Failure above V1

If an engine failure occurs above V1, control airplane direction, aiming to keep airplane on runway centerline by smoothly applying rudder.
As soon as an Engine Failure or FIRE is recognized (not always followed by loss of thrust) and affected engine identified, check maximum thrust on EICAS.

After rotation, set aileron in neutral and use rudder and yaw trim to keep wings level. High aileron input raises the spoilers and increases drag.

As reference, the slip/skid indicator is approximately to off center and

between 0° to 5° of bank after engine failure. It depends on speed, gross weight,

and altitude. Generally the control wheel in the neutral position is a good indication of the lowest drag for single engine.
Crew must keep close attention at first positive rate of climb to retract landing gear, monitoring airplane profile.
The TO mode first guidance is based on takeoff weight and flap setting, limited to a minimum pitch of 7° and maximum of 18°.
Crew must follow the flight director guidance to maintain V2 to V2 10 KIAS up to acceleration altitude, according to the following three different conditions: engine failure below V2: pitch for V2

engine failure between V2 and V2 10 KIAS: pitch for the present speed

engine failure above V2 10 KIAS: pitch for V2 10 KIAS Takeoff thrust is limited to 5 (optionally 10) minutes after takeoff. It is recommended that emergency procedures to be accomplished as soon as safe

altitude has been reached (at least 400 ft AGL or according to local minimums).

When engine failure occurs after takeoff, noise abatement procedures no longer apply.

Following an Engine Failure, ATTCS adjusts operating engine thrust to its

respective RSV mode. If the maximum thrust is not reached for any reason, advance the thrust levers to maximum thrust.

On departure procedures with acceleration altitudes above 1000 ft, emphasize

during takeoff briefing that, in the event of an Engine Failure, Engine Fire (with loss of thrust),

or any other malfunction requiring a memory item, actions can be

commanded at an altitude lower than the acceleration altitude, but not lower than 400 ft.

Airplane must be stabilized and on the profile.

For One Engine Inoperative, limit the bank angle to:

15° at V2

20° at V2 5 KIAS

25° at V2 10 KIAS

kontext:
8.3.8.5 Wind Shear

In order to avoid dangerous wind shear phenomena it is important to know what wind shear is and in which meteorological and geographical environment it can be expected.
The following definition seems to be the most suitable for aviation:

wind shear is any rapid change in wind direction or speed along the flight path of an aircraft

Wind shear, with or without turbulence, alters the lift force acting on an aircraft, resulting in a significant sinking or rising motion.

Therefore, wind shear may be categorized as:

increasing performance shear caused by increasing headwind or decreasing

tailwind component or vertical updrafts

decreasing performance shear caused by decreasing headwind or

increasing tailwind component or vertical downdrafts

Conditions for potentially hazardous wind shears are:

convective conditions (e.g. thunderstorms, rain or snow showers)

frontal systems

jet streams

strong or gusty surface winds

other cases (temperature inversion, mountain waves, sea breeze circulations)

Wind shear events are typically one to two miles in diameter and mostly occur near the ground (typically below 500 ft AGL) during take-off and landing. Both situations would see the aircraft in a low energy condition. Therefore, there is only limited time for wind shear recognition and counteraction, typically 5 to 15 seconds.
Several factors can impede wind shear recognition: marginal weather conditions

high crew work load conditions

illusion of normality; during the initial part of the wind shear encounter, everything may appear normal; even severe wind shear onset may not

provide dramatic early indications to the flight crew

Standard response of the flight crew should be: control of flight path through pitch attitude; resistance to a downward change

in pitch attitude as normal response to low airspeed

immediate increase of thrust, maximum thrust shall be applied

an approach shall be aborted

unusual stick forces may be required to maintain pitch attitude during

airspeed variations away from normal target airspeed

low airspeed must be accepted, flying at airspeeds below normal reference

speeds may be required in order to utilize the full performance capability of the aircraft (speed increments under expected wind shear threat are stated

in Operations Manual OM-B)

The term downburst describes a severe downward rush of air and its outburst of

damaging winds near the ground. It has been classified into macroburst and microburst. They are different in their size with radial outflow at the earth’s surface lasting from 3 to 20 minutes.

Downbursts can occur wherever convective weather conditions exist.
Approximately 5% of all thunderstorms produce microburst.
Downdrafts associated with microburst are typically only a few hundred to thousand meters across. When the downburst hits the ground, it spreads out horizontally and may form one or more horizontal vortex rings around the downdraft up to 2 000 ft AGL.
In downbursts with vortices very powerful updrafts and roll forces in conjunction with wind speed changes up to 45 knots can be expected.
The time period over which wind speeds exceed half the peak value may last from 1 to 8 minutes. Depending on the movement and the height of the base of parent cloud, microburst may occur as: stationary or moving

surface or midair

wet or dry

Microburst has occurred in relatively dry conditions of light rain or precipitation that evaporates before reaching the earth’s surface.
Frontal wind shear is present in both cold and warm fronts, but exists in a different relative location in each type of front. Because the cold front boundary slopes back behind the frontal surface, the wind shear line also slopes back. The frontal boundary of the warm front slopes upward ahead of the surface front and

so does the wind shear. Significant wind shears can be expected if there is a large difference in surface temperature 6°C) across the front and if the front is moving rapidly at more than 30 knots.
Large wind speeds changes near the ground can be found in many

meteorological situations, including the frontal conditions. Terrain irregularities or

buildings, which interrupt the wind flow, can produce significant wind shears close to the ground.

kontext:
8.3.8.5.1 Precautions

Avoidance is the best precaution. In case of unexpected severe wind shear encounter during take-off or approach, special precautionary techniques should be applied by the flight crew to reduce the effect of wind shear. Generally a low energy situation (e.g. low and slow) should be avoided or, if not avoidable, be limited to the shortest possible period of time.
The following precautions should be taken into consideration: thrust setting: maximum take-off thrust should be used for take-off; it shortens the take-off roll and provides the best climb performance,

which leads to increasing altitude available for recovery if required

during approach thrust reductions should be minimized or delayed

runway selection: the longest suitable runway should be used taking into consideration crosswind and tailwind limitations and obstacles in take-off or landing path

flap selection: the flap setting is dependent on the type of aircraft; although for take-off greater flap setting provides better performance for wind shear encounters on the runway and lesser flap setting gives better performance in the air, the performance difference for different flap settings is rather small

airspeed: available field length and runway condition must be taken into consideration when increasing airspeed for take-off or landing (speed

increments according to the Operations Manual OM-B); the take-off airspeed should be increased at rotation to improve the ability to negotiate a wind shear after lift-off; increased airspeed improves the flight path, reduces potential exposure to flight near stick shaker speed, and reduces the workload of the flight crew; during an approach increased airspeed (speed

increment) improves climb performance capability and reduces the potential

for flight at stick shaker speed during recovery from wind shear encounter;

the increased speed should be maintained into the flare; runway limitations,

especially the effect of wet runways, shall be taken into due consideration

use of auto throttle, autopilot and flight director: for take-off only speed- referenced flight directors with wind shear recovery guidance should be

used, if available; during approach flight director, autopilot and auto throttle

should be used to the maximum extent practical; this will relieve the workload of the flight crew and give them more time to monitor instruments

and weather conditions

kontext:
8.3.8.5.1 Precautions

Avoidance is the best precaution. In case of unexpected severe wind shear encounter during take-off or approach, special precautionary techniques should be applied by the flight crew to reduce the effect of wind shear. Generally a low energy situation (e.g. low and slow) should be avoided or, if not avoidable, be limited to the shortest possible period of time.
The following precautions should be taken into consideration: thrust setting: maximum take-off thrust should be used for take-off; it shortens the take-off roll and provides the best climb performance, which leads to increasing altitude available for recovery if required

during approach thrust reductions should be minimized or delayed

runway selection: the longest suitable runway should be used taking into consideration crosswind and tailwind limitations and obstacles in take-off or landing path

flap selection: the flap setting is dependent on the type of aircraft; although for take-off greater flap setting provides better performance for wind shear encounters on the runway and lesser flap setting gives better performance in the air, the performance difference for different flap settings is rather small

airspeed: available field length and runway condition must be taken into consideration when increasing airspeed for take-off or landing (speed

increments according to the Operations Manual OM-B); the take-off airspeed should be increased at rotation to improve the ability to negotiate a wind shear after lift-off; increased airspeed improves the flight path, reduces potential exposure to flight near stick shaker speed, and reduces the workload of the flight crew; during an approach increased airspeed (speed

increment) improves climb performance capability and reduces the potential

for flight at stick shaker speed during recovery from wind shear encounter;

the increased speed should be maintained into the flare; runway limitations,

especially the effect of wet runways, shall be taken into due consideration

use of auto throttle, autopilot and flight director: for take-off only speed- referenced flight directors with wind shear recovery guidance should be

used, if available;

during approach flight director, autopilot and auto throttle

should be used to the maximum extent practical; this will relieve the workload of the flight crew

and give them more time to monitor instruments

and weather conditions

Die Flaps-Stellung hat keinen Einfluss, da Wind Shear nur die Airspeed betrifft
Mehr Flaps sind auf der Runway, weniger Flaps in der Luft günstiger; der Unterschied ist eher gering
fragen.erklaerung: Eine grössere Flaps-Stellung bietet bessere Performance bei Wind Shear auf der Runway, eine kleinere in der Luft; der Performance-Unterschied ist laut OM-A jedoch eher gering. Die Wahl ist typenabhängig.

kontext:
PFD: WSHEAR AHEAD

Voice message: “MONITOR RADAR DISPLAY”

Whenever a windshear is suspected during takeoff the following precautions are taken: consider delaying the takeoff until conditions improve,

use maximum takeoff thrust instead of reduced thrust,

use flap 1 unless limited by obstacle clearance or runway length, increase airspeed (or V2) to get the best performance compromise during windshear,

use the longest runway available with the lowest possibility of a windshear

encounter,

turn ON the weather radar to enable it before initiating the takeoff run,

crew should monitor airspeed trend during takeoff run. The airspeed trend may have abrupt variations or may freeze for a while. If a windshear

encounter happens before V1, evaluate the possibility to reject takeoff. A

high tailwind component may increase the ground speed and so the runway distance required to stop the airplane,

develop an awareness of normal airspeed, attitude, and vertical speed. The crew should closely monitor the vertical flight path instruments, such as, vertical speed and altimeters, and callout any deviations.

kontext:
2.3.3.3.10 Crosswind Takeoff

The airplane has a good control capability during takeoff with crosswind. There is no special related procedure. Maintain directional control using positive rudder and small control wheel inputs.

Runway alignment and smooth symmetrical thrust application are recommended when operating at contaminated runways.

At low speed, use the rudder pedal steering to maintain runway centerline until the rudder becomes effective. Directional deviation is corrected immediately with

smooth and positive control inputs.

During crosswind takeoffs, command control wheel into the wind to maintain wings level throughout the takeoff run.
Care should be taken to avoid using an excessive amount of control wheel to avoid causing unnecessary spoiler deployment.

During rotation, maintain control wheel in the displaced position to keep the wings level during liftoff. Smoothly recover from the sideslip by slowly neutralizing the control wheel and rudder pedals after liftoff.

fragen.frage: (E1) Beim Rollout auf kontaminierter Runway mit Crosswind und Thrust Reverser driftet das Flugzeug zur Lee-Seite. Wie wird es gemäss OM-B zur Centerline zurückgebracht?

Reverser auf MIN REV, Brakes lösen bzw. Autobrake trennen, mit Rudder und Differential Braking korrigieren
Emergency/Parking Brake setzen und mit asymmetrischem Reverse Thrust korrigieren
Autobrake auf HI erhöhen und das Control Wheel voll gegen den Wind halten
fragen.erklaerung: Reverser auf MIN REV reduzieren und Brakes lösen bzw. Autobrake trennen; das minimiert die seitliche Reverser-Kraft und verbessert die Cornering Forces der Reifen. Dann mit Rudder und Differential Braking zur Centerline zurück.
fragen.zitat: To bring the airplane back to the runway centerline, set thrust reverser to MIN REV by simply alleaviating the force applied to the thrust lever, and release the brakes or disengage the autobrake.
fragen.frage_en: (E1) During the rollout on a contaminated runway with crosswind and thrust reverser applied, the airplane drifts to the downwind side. How is it brought back to the centerline according to OM-B?
antworten_en: Increase to MAX REV and correct with nose wheel steering via the handwheel
Reverser to MIN REV, release brakes or disengage autobrake, correct with rudder and differential braking
Set the emergency/parking brake and correct with asymmetric reverse thrust
Increase autobrake to HI and hold the control wheel fully into the wind
fragen.erklaerung_en: Set the thrust reverser to MIN REV and release the brakes or disengage the autobrake; this minimizes the reverser side force and improves the tire cornering forces. Then use rudder and differential braking to realign with the centerline.
kontext:
2.6.1.8 Crosswind Landing

Four methods for crosswind landing can be used:
Sideslip: In the sideslip condition, the airplane longitudinal axis remains parallel to the runway course, but the airplane no longer flies straight along its original track. Downwind rudder combined with

aileron applied into the wind. The upwind wheels touchdown before downwind wheels.

Crab: Proper rudder and upwind aileron. On slippery runways, the

crab may be maintained to touchdown, reducing the drift toward the downwind when touchdown.

De-Crab: On final approach, the crab is accomplished. Just before touchdown while flaring, downwind rudder is applied to align the airplane with the runway centerline simultaneously with aileron control (to keep wings level) into the wind. Both main landing gears touch down simultaneously.

Crab and Sideslip: The crab method is applied until the touchdown.
When the upwind wheels touchdown, a slight increase in downwind rudder simultaneously with aileron aligns the airplane with the runway centerline while keep the wing level. This combined method may be used during strong crosswind.

Especially when landing on contaminated runways, in case the landing rollout is performed with crosswind and thrust reverser applied, a tendency to drift the airplane to the runway downwind side may occur. On that condition the landing gear tire cornering forces available may not be enough to counteract that drift.

To bring the airplane back to the runway centerline, set thrust reverser to MIN

REV by simply alleaviating the force applied to the thrust lever, and release the

brakes or disengage the autobrake.

This minimizes the thrust reverser side force component and improves the landing gear tire cornering forces available to

realign the airplane with the runway centerline.

Apply rudder and differential braking as required to realign the airplane with the centerline. Once the airplane is back on the centerline, reapply braking and

symmetrical thrust reverser as required to decelerate the airplane.

kontext: 8.3.8.13.1 Description
Fog will only form and persist if particular values of temperature, humidity and wind all exist simultaneously.

Small changes of any one of these parameters will result in variations in the extent, density and depth of the fog and it is this sensitivity, which is responsible for its extreme and continuous variability. Even under stable conditions, a large variation in the vertical plane of the concentration and size of water droplets is known to occur, with a tendency for the greater concentration to be at the higher levels. As it is, these factors are responsible for the visual range within the fog to increase closer to the ground.
Assuming the general case of density increasing with height, any slant visual range will be less than the RVR.

Only at very low eye levels (less than 30 ft) will the SVR be nearly the same as the RVR. Nevertheless, in certain conditions, where fog density changes rapidly below 30 ft, poor correlation will be obtained and it is still best to make no

assumptions about visual reference from the reported RVR.

The dense and lifted fogs yield basically similar visual sequences. Where once obtained, the visual segment increases. This sequence is to be expected when

the approach is made through low cloud with or without fog underneath or into a

fog where the pilot has been unable to see the ground beforehand.

kontext:
8.4.8.3 ATC Low Visibility Procedures

The ATC Low Visibility Procedures (LVP) are ground procedures at the airport, designed to prevent the entry of ground vehicles and taxiing aircraft into areas protected for take-off and landing. In addition they protect the sensitive areas of the ILS transmission and regulate the flow of air traffic on the approach.
ATC Low Visibility Procedures (LVP) become effective when the touch down zone (TDZ) Runway Visual Range (RVR) falls to 600 m or below or the ceiling is 200 ft or below. ATC will always report the touch down zone (TDZ) Runway Visual Range (RVR).

Midfield point (MID) RVR values and roll-out RVR values will only be reported if: they are less than the TDZ RVR and below 800 m

when less than 400 m

when requested by the pilot

kontext:
8.4.4 Low Visibility Take-off (LVTO)

A Low Visibility Take-off (LVTO) is a take-off with the reported Runway Visual Range (RVR) of less than 550 m.
However, if at the airport of departure no Low Visibility Procedures (LVP) are established, or if established Low Visibility Procedures are not in force, the lowest authorized RVR for take-off is 400 m. For further details refer to 8.1.3.3 - Take-off Minima.

The maximum Runway Visual Range (RVR) at take-off is rather independent of the aircraft type and aircraft equipment, with the exception of very low Runway Visual Range (RVR) values. The take-off minima are mainly determined by the airport installations (e.g. runway lighting system, RVR measurement system).

A static take-off shall be performed if the visibility RVR is at or close to the take-

off minimum.

For the static take-off procedure refer to type specific OM-B.

If it is necessary to abandon the take-off and visibility is very limited, directional

control with reference to the runway lights will become progressively more difficult as speed is reduced, especially with brake application. As soon as the

first red white centreline lights pass under the nose of the aircraft, there are

900 m of runway left and ground speed should in no case be higher than 100 kts.
Remember that the far end of the runway may have less braking action due to

rubber deposit. If all centreline lights are red, there is less than 300 m runway available and action should be taken accordingly.

Note: The closer centreline and touchdown zone lights cannot be seen as clearly as those further away because of a relatively low light beam

angle.

kontext:
8.2.4.2.2 Clear Ice

Clear ice is a layer of ice, which is transparent (and thus difficult to detect) formed during precipitation of relatively large rain drops. They partly freeze on impact upon a cold surface, releasing latent heat, which enables the remainder of the water to spread evenly. Since no air is trapped the result is a clear or glazed appearance.
Crews must be especially aware of the difficulty to detect clear ice and, in some situation, its presence may only be detected by touch. It can form on aircraft surfaces below a layer of snow and rime ice.
Significant deposits can form on upper wing surfaces in the vicinity of fuel tanks after fuelling with low temperature fuel,
or when sufficient super cooled fuel remained in tanks after a long flight at high altitude. This has occurred with ambient temperatures as high as 14°C.
Conversely, fuelling with relatively warm fuel can cause dry falling snow to melt with the danger of refreezing on the upper surface of the wing.

kontext:
8.2.4.20 Ramp and Taxi Precautions

Icy conditions on the ramp and in the gate area means that the push back vehicle may not be able to develop sufficient traction to push the aircraft with its engines running. Therefore, it is recommended to have the aircraft pushed back, to a position from which it can taxi forward, before starting engines. Standing on an icy patch even idle thrust may be sufficient to move the aircraft forward, although the parking brake is set.
Abnormal engine indications may occur during engine start especially caused by the low oil temperature (and therefore high viscosity), with oil pressure exceeding normal limits until the oil temperature rises. This is acceptable provided the engine is operated at not more than idle thrust until the indications are back to normal.
There is a possibility for engine inlet ice to build-up during taxi and ground holding operation. Ice can form in engine inlets at temperatures above 10°C with high humidity present during extensive ground holds with the engines at idle.

If visible moisture is present with a temperature below that specified in the Operations Manual OM-B, engine nacelle anti-ice systems shall be switched on after completion of the engine start procedure.
Probe and sensor heating systems shall be switched on before taxiing, according

to the checklist procedures.

Taxi shall take place with great care and significantly lower speeds than normal.

Neither aircraft, nor ground vehicles are capable of stopping quickly on icy or

contaminated surfaces. When guide lamp installations are available, use of them shall be made to align the aircraft in the gate area. Snow may cover the normal

taxi markings. Braking and steering capabilities shall be tested frequently.

Maintaining a greater distance than normal from other traffic helps to avoid jet- blast, which could adversely affect anti-ice treatment and prevents from blow of

contaminants into the aircraft.

Engine thrust may need to be higher than normal to overcome the drag caused by slush or snow. Changes should be made slowly and carefully to avoid blowing

equipment or contaminants into other aircraft. At intervals during prolonged taxi and immediately before take-off, engines shall be run up to higher settings as specified in the Operations Manual OM-B.
Flaps should be kept up when taxiing through slush or standing water, with pre-take-off checks held until the flaps can be lowered again.

Holding shall be done well clear of an active runway as a landing aircraft is more likely to deviate from the centreline when braking conditions are marginal.
Slush thrown up by landing aircraft can be ingested by engines, cause airframe damage and degrade the anti-ice treatment.

kontext:
1.4.7.1 Operation in Icing Conditions

Icing conditions may exist whenever the Outside Air Temperature (OAT) on the ground or for takeoff, or Total Air Temperature (TAT) inflight, is 10°C or below and visible moisture in any form is present (such as clouds, fog with visibility of one mile or less, rain, snow, sleet, and ice crystals).
Icing conditions may also exist when the OAT on the ground and for takeoff is 10°C or below when operating on ramps, taxiways, or runways where surface snow, ice, standing water, or slush may be ingested by the engines, or freeze on engines, nacelles, or engine sensor probes.

CAUTION:
On ground, do not rely on visual icing evidence or ice detector actuation to turn on the anti-icing system. use the temperature and visual moisture criteria as specified above.

delaying the use of the

anti- icing system until ice build-up is visible from the cockpit may result in ice ingestion and possible engine damage or flame-out.

kontext:
2.3.1.8 Taxi Under Adverse Weather

Taxi on a wet or contaminated surface requires lower speeds.
Use the nose wheel steering with caution to avoid skidding during turns.
During cold weather, use minimum thrust for breakaway and taxiing, to avoid blowing snow or slush on personnel or airplanes nearby.
Use firm brake pressure on taxi stops whenever pavement conditions permit in order to warm up the brakes and dry moisture buildup within the disk stack.

Antiskid protection is not provided below 10 kt, so apply brakes accordingly.

During taxi, “cold set” (the condition where the tire retains the flat shape it had while parked) may induce vibration in the airplane. Vibration should disappear as the tires recover their elasticity during taxi. Turns should be performed at the largest turning radius, preferably at a speed which does not require braking during the turn. Maintain a greater than normal distance behind other airplanes while taxiing in snow or slush-covered runways, to avoid contamination by snow blown by jet blasts.
During low visibility or unfamiliar airport operation observe the ground markings and consider requesting a FOLLOW ME vehicle to proceed taxiing safely.

kontext:
2.8.3.3.14 Landing

Note: Conduct a positive landing to ensure initial wheel spin-up and to establish firm ground contact upon touchdown, achieving wheel load as quickly as possible. Such technique avoids hydroplaning on wet runways and reduces the strength of any ice bond that might have been eventually

formed on brake and wheel assemblies during flight.

If landing on wet or slippery runways, the following considerations apply:

Anticipate the approach procedures and speeds: well-planned and

executed approach, flare, and touchdown minimize the landing distance.

Immediately after touchdown, check the ground spoiler automatic deployment when thrust levers are reduced to idle.

Lower the nose wheel immediately to the runway to decrease lift and increase main gear loading.

Apply thrust reversers cautiously and observe how the airplane responds before full reverse is used.

Note: During landing,
the engine must be commanded from MAX REV to MIN REV at or above 60 KIAS, and it is recommended to close them when reaching 30 KIAS.

If necessary, thrust reverser may be used to bring the

airplane to a full stop.
Do not use asymmetric thrust reverser on slippery runways.

Apply brakes with moderate-to-firm pressure, smoothly and symmetrically.

If no braking action is felt, hydroplaning may be occurring. In this case, do

not apply Emergency/Parking Brake as it removes antiskid protection.
Maintain runway centerline and keep braking until the airplane is

decelerated.

back to 2.6.1 - Landing.

kontext:
2.8.3.3.2 External Inspection

When operating in cold weather, the flight crew must carefully inspect the

airframe and dedicate special attention to areas where snow, ice, or frost could interfere in normal systems operation.

Wheel Chocks IN PLACE Smart Probes/TAT Sensor/Ice Detector CHECK

Verify free of ice, snow, and residual deicing/anti icing fluid.

Probes must be unblocked. Even small portions of remaining contamination may result in erroneous readings.

Air Conditioning Inlets/Outlets CLEAR OF ICE OR SNOW Protective Covers CHECK REMOVED

If required, leave engine covers installed until engine start.

Engines (including the core aft of fan blades) CLEAR OF ICE OR SNOW Heavy accumulation of ice or snow in the inlet, on the spinner, on the fan

blades or on the booster area must be removed prior to start.

Light ice similar to hoarfrost or light snow may be removed by performing

engine run-up.

A small area of thin ice at the basis of the inlet near the drain in front of the

fan blades is allowable.
Ensure that the fan is free to rotate

Landing Gear CLEAR OF ICE, UNOBSTRUCTED

Fuselage FREE OF FROST, ICE OR SNOW

Light hoarfrost on the fuselage is allowable provided that surface details

such as painting and markings are visible.

A physical inspection may be performed to ensure that there is no frost, ice

or snow accumulation.

OM-B E1 2 Normal Procedures

Wing, Tail and Control Surfaces FREE OF FROST, ICE OR SNOW

The wings upper and lower surfaces, as well as ailerons must be free of ice, snow, and frost.
A thin layer of frost up to 3 mm is acceptable on the wings lower surface.

Visual inspection of the wing upper surface may be performed from a passenger cabin window. A physical inspection may be performed to ensure

that there is no frost, ice or snow accumulation.

Cold fuel may result in frost on the wings upper surface. Expect this kind of frost when fuel remaining in each wing tank exceeds 3420 kg.

Check all control surfaces, including gaps and hinges for signs of contamination.

As the horizontal stabilizer upper surface is not visible from the ground and cockpit, the condition of the wing upper surface may be used as a reference to decide whether deicing/anti-icing is required for the horizontal stabilizer.

kontext:
8.3.8.2 Thunderstorms

Thunderstorms are classified as:

frontal thunderstorms

air mass thunderstorms

Frontal thunderstorms may exist as:

warm front thunderstorms

cold front thunderstorms

occluded front thunderstorms

Air mass thunderstorms are divided into:

convective thunderstorms

orographic thunderstorms

Frontal thunderstorms form in squall lines and generate heavy rain and possibly hail and produce strong gusty winds and possibly tornadoes.
Large horizontal wind changes in speed and direction at different altitudes are characteristic for a frontal thunderstorm. Resulting airflows in the storm accelerate to much higher vertical speeds, which ultimately results in higher horizontal wind speeds at the surface.
Air mass thunderstorms are caused either by thermal convection or by moist air moving uphill on the windward side of a mountain.
Air mass thunderstorms appear to be randomly distributed in unstable air and develop from local heating of the earth’s surface. As the heated air rises it cools and subsequently forms cumulus clouds. As the cumulus stage continues to develop, precipitation forms in the higher portion of the cloud and falls out.
Precipitation signals the beginning of the mature stage and pressure of a downdraft.
In the later stages of development, the heated updraft creating the thunderstorm is cut off by rainfall, and the thunderstorm begins to dissipate. Many thunderstorms produce an associated cold air gust front as a result of the down flow and out rushing rain-cooled air. These gust fronts are usually very turbulent and are a serious threat during take-off and landing.
The vertical extension of thunderstorms is up to 25 000 ft during winter time and up to the troposphere during summer, the horizontal range is 10 to 20 km.
Besides the dangerous situations already mentioned, there may be additional dangers from sudden heavy precipitation with poor visibility below the clouds, possibly hail showers, heavy icing formation, and severe turbulence.

Lightning is not a direct danger for the crew and passengers of an aircraft in flight, as the electrical load will remain at the surface of the aircraft (Faraday Cage). Lightning strikes may, however, disturb or damage the navigation system.

OM-A 8 Operating Procedures

If storm clouds have to be over flown, vertical separation from cloud tops of at least 5 000 ft must always be maintained. It is difficult to estimate this separation, but Air Traffic Control (ATC) or meteorological charts may provide information about the altitude of the cloud.
If the aircraft is not equipped with radar or if the radar is inoperative, any cloud that appears, through visual inspection: tall,

or growing rapidly, or with an anvil top

shall be laterally avoided by at least 10 NM.

The radar equipment shall be intermittently operated on long ranges in order to

avoid the development of situations where no alternative remains but the penetration of hazardous areas.

Flying under a cumulonimbus overhang shall be avoided, too. If it is unavoidable, antenna tilt shall occasionally be selected to full up to determine, if possible, whether precipitation (which may be hail) exists in or is falling from the overhang.
Flight crews are strongly advised to continue monitoring the weather radar in order to select the safest track for penetration under all circumstances.
The local activity of thunderstorms can often be of relatively short nature, (i.e. 20 to 30 minutes). Therefore, if a take-off or landing is planned during times of thunderstorm activity, consideration of the development of the storm shall determine whether avoidance of the worst effects can be accomplished with a delay.
Rule of thumb to estimate buildup of thunderstorms (ts):
Calculate difference in temperature between FL180 (500 hPa) and FL50 (850 hPa).
If difference is: 25° or less: no ts or very unlikely

26° - 27°: ts possible

28° - 31°: ts likely

32° or more: severe ts likely
