kontext:
8.3.8.3.2 Flight Procedures in Icing Conditions

It is important for flight crews to understand, that aircraft equipped with anti- and deice systems, which are approved for flight into known icing conditions, are not necessarily certified for: freezing rain, or freezing drizzle, or for a mixture of super cooled droplets and snow or ice particles

Some airfoils are degraded by even a thin accumulation of ice aft of the wing deicing area. Ice accumulation in that part of the wing is possible when exposed to freezing rain or freezing drizzle.
For this reason, the Operations Manual OM-B must always be consulted for aircraft type specific information regarding flight into known icing conditions.
The following information describes generally applicable flight procedures in icing conditions. Particular attention is drawn to the danger of uncommanded and uncontrolled roll upset as well as tail plane stall.
Anti-ice equipment must be turned on prior to entering areas with the risk of icing. Flights into known severe icing conditions are prohibited.

If, nevertheless, severe icing conditions are encountered, the flight path (laterally or vertically) shall be altered as quickly as possible. Minimum safe speeds associated with icing conditions must be observed strictly. Stalling speeds with contaminated

wings are higher than normal. A stall may therefore be entered without warning.
In winter jet streams and storm centers intensified clear air turbulence is more common. Weather conditions for destinations and alternates must be checked more frequently, as ceilings and visibility can be very low. Particular care must be

taken when there are reports of freezing rain or drizzle. There is the possibility of

longer holding times in adverse conditions when landing weather is at or below minimum.

The approach briefing must include information about the landing conditions, braking, use of reverse thrust, flaps and spoilers, as well as ground handling and

taxiing techniques.

kontext:
8.3.8.3.1 Types of Ice

The usual cloud sized small droplets tend to follow the aerodynamic flow around the wing. They are swept away, while larger, heavier droplets tend to impinge aft of the leading edge. The larger (and hence heavier) the droplet (drizzle or rain sized), the further aft it will impinge. Furthermore, large droplets are relatively warm and as a result they tend to run back and spread out in liquid state before freezing. This effect is known as flow back. Its effect depends directly upon size, temperature and velocity of water droplets and wing surface temperature.
Impingement and flow back result in ice collecting not only on the leading edge, but also on the upper and lower surfaces of a wing, where there may be no ice protection.
Rime Ice Rime ice is associated with stratiform clouds and forms when droplets are small and the temperature is relatively cold (-15°C or below). Not all of the droplets follow the airflow. Some impact upon the wing and tail plane leading edges with little or no flow back, freezing quickly into rime ice. Therefore, leading edge anti-

and deicing equipment is relatively effective against this type of ice.
Clear Ice Clear ice is associated with cumuliform clouds and forms when the temperature

is relatively warm (-10°C or above). Droplet sizes are relatively large (drizzle or

rain sized), and they tend to impinge further aft and flow back before freezing to

form sheet ice on the upper and lower surfaces of the wing. These areas may not be protected by anti- and deicing equipment. Any deposit greater than light can

significantly degrade performance, causing problems in roll and pitch control

with, in the extreme case, uncontrollable pitch up and stall.
Clear ice can form on airfoil surfaces with few visual cues to the flight crew. The

absence of the usual indications, such as ice formation on the windshield posts

and wipers, does not mean that clear ice is not forming. The terms freezing drizzle or freezing rain in a terminal forecast or weather report indicate a strong

probability of conditions for clear ice.
Mixed Ice

Mixed ice is a combination of clear and rime ice with all the hazards of both. It forms when droplets vary in size (e.g. drizzle in stratiform clouds) and the

temperature is in the range of -10°C to -15°C. The proportional makeup varies

with the weather system.

kontext:
8.3.8.3.3 Exposure to Severe Icing

Severe icing is often associated with super cooled large droplets (i.e. freezing drizzle or rain). Icing certification rules do not cover flights into these conditions.
Droplets covered by icing certification envelopes are so small that they are usually below the threshold of radar detectability.
For specific information regarding handling techniques if inadvertently encountering severe icing conditions refer to the Operations Manual OM-B.
The most effective means of identifying severe icing conditions are cues that can be seen, felt or heard. This includes visual inspection of aircraft surfaces.
At temperatures near freezing it may be possible to detect large droplets splashing or splattering upon impact with the windscreen.
When exposed to severe icing in the form of super cooled large droplets, the flight crew must perform the following actions:
autopilot disengagement, manual flying of the aircraft; the autopilot may mask important cues or may self-disconnect and present unusual attitudes or control conditions

advice to Air Traffic Control (ATC) and prompt exit of the conditions, using control inputs that are as smooth and small as possible

change of heading, altitude, or both to find an area that is warmer than freezing, substantially colder than the current ambient temperature, or free of clouds

when severe icing conditions exist, reporting may assist other crews in maintaining vigilance; submission of a PIREP of the observed icing conditions is recommended; it is important not to understate the conditions or effects of the icing observed

kontext:
8.3.8.3.4 Control Anomalies in Icing Conditions

The formation of ice on the aircraft structure could create a situation from which the flight crew might have difficulties recovering and, in some instances, may not be able to recover at all. For this reason, the following information describes two particular types of control upsets likely to be encountered during flight in severe icing conditions.
Roll Upset Roll upset is an un-commanded and un-controlled roll phenomenon, which may occur as a consequence of, or prior to, a wing stall, due to: anomalous forces, that cause the ailerons to deflect, or loss of effectiveness of the ailerons

Deflections of ailerons or loss of aileron effectiveness may be caused by ice accumulation in a sensitive area of the wing aft of the de-icing area. It occurs under unusual circumstances associated with super cooled large droplets and rarely under normal cloud droplets in a very narrow temperature range near freezing level. Roll upset can result from severe icing conditions even without the usual symptoms of ice accumulation or a perceived aerodynamic stall.
Pilots can minimize the chance of a roll upset by being sensitive to cues that identify severe icing conditions and by promptly exiting the severe icing conditions before control or handling characteristics of the aircraft are degraded to a hazardous level.

It is important to review the Operations Manual OM-B for aircraft type specific information. Additionally, pilots should check any available bulletins related to icing by the aircraft manufacturer.

Tail Plane Stall

Tail plane (empennage) stall is another significant hazard of airframe icing. Sharp

edged surfaces are more susceptible to collecting ice than large and blunt ones.

For this reason, the tail plane may begin accumulating ice before the wings and can accumulate it faster. There have been reports of ice on the tail plane without

any visible ice on the wing. This can also occur, if the tail plane has not been or cannot be deiced.

A tail plane stall occurs when, as with the wing, the critical angle of attack is

exceeded. Since the horizontal stabilizer counters the natural nose down tendency caused by the center of lift of the main wing being located aft of the

center of gravity, the aircraft will react by pitching nose down, sometimes uncontrollably, when the tail plane is stalled.

Application of flaps can aggravate or

initiate the stall. Use caution when applying flaps during approach, if there is the possibility of icing on the tail plane.

Perhaps the most important characteristic of a tail plane stall is the relatively high airspeed at the onset and, if it occurs, the suddenness and magnitude of the nose down pitch. A stall is more likely to occur when the flaps are approaching the fully extended position, after nose down pitch and airspeed changes following flap extension, or during flight through wind gusts.
Once a tail plane stall is encountered, the stall condition tends to worsen with increased airspeed and possibly may worsen with increased power settings at the same flap setting. Airspeed, at any flap setting, in excess of the aircraft manufacturer’s recommendations for the flight and environmental conditions, accompanied by un-cleared ice contamination on the tail plane, may result in a tail plane stall and uncommanded pitch down from which a recovery may not be possible. A tail plane stall may occur at speeds less than the flap extension speed.

kontext:
8.3.8.3.3 Exposure to Severe Icing

Severe icing is often associated with super cooled large droplets (i.e. freezing drizzle or rain). Icing certification rules do not cover flights into these conditions.
Droplets covered by icing certification envelopes are so small that they are usually below the threshold of radar detectability.

For specific information regarding handling techniques if inadvertently encountering severe icing conditions refer to the Operations Manual OM-B.
The most effective means of identifying severe icing conditions are cues that can be seen, felt or heard. This includes visual inspection of aircraft surfaces.
At temperatures near freezing it may be possible to detect large droplets splashing or splattering upon impact with the windscreen.
When exposed to severe icing in the form of super cooled large droplets, the flight crew must perform the following actions: autopilot disengagement, manual flying of the aircraft; the autopilot may mask important cues or may self-disconnect and present unusual attitudes or control conditions

advice to Air Traffic Control (ATC) and prompt exit of the conditions, using control inputs that are as smooth and small as possible

change of heading, altitude, or both to find an area that is warmer than freezing, substantially colder than the current ambient temperature, or free of clouds

when severe icing conditions exist, reporting may assist other crews in maintaining vigilance; submission of a PIREP of the observed icing conditions is recommended; it is important not to understate the conditions or effects of the icing observed

kontext:
2.8.3.6 Lightning Strike

Even though the airplane is adequately protected against lightning strike effects, operating procedures should be established in an attempt to avoid such phenomenon.

In-flight lightning avoidance is closely associated with thunderstorm avoidance.
Therefore, avoid penetration of thunderstorms. Maintain visual contact with

thunderstorms during the daytime and lightning at night. Check the radar for precipitation, review all available types of weather information, examine other pilot reports and follow ATC instructions. Even with a good weather report

received and understood, pay close attention to storms that develop rapidly

along the route in a given area which cannot be predicted. While enroute, continuously update weather briefings through the use of radio contact and airborne equipment for actual storm avoidance.
Remember that radar detects only liquid droplets, not the cloud itself. Only rain suspended in the cloud will produce a radar echo, which may lead to occasional encounters with hail and lightning.
If possible, circumnavigate the detected thundercloud or area by 25 miles or more when traffic conditions permit.
Be aware that lightning can strike an airplane miles away from the extreme side of a developed thunderstorm. Reports of airplane receiving strikes in clear air at 25 NM or more from the nearest storm are common.
The following paragraphs summarize the conditions in which strikes are most

common:
Meteorological conditions: incident reports show that an airplane must be within or beneath a cloud to receive a strike, or in or near regions of precipitation.
Incident reports show that in over 80% of the strikes, the airplane was within a

cloud and experiencing some precipitation and turbulence. But other strikes may

occur in a cloud where there is no precipitation nearby, in clear air reasonably

distant from a thundercloud, during snowstorms and in clouds over erupting volcanoes. Flight through or in the vicinity of a cold front, warm front, stationary

front, unstable air or squall lines increases the probability of lightning strikes.

Incident reports also show that lightning strikes occur most commonly under light or heavy turbulence conditions.

flight regime: Takeoff, climb, level flight, descent or approach

altitude: strikes are more common between 5000 ft and 20000 ft, but may

occur at virtually all flight altitudes.

Lightning strike incidents at lower altitudes are far more frequent since at higher altitude airplanes can divert

around thunderclouds with greater ease.

outside air temperature: most strike incidents have occurred when the

airplane is flying in temperatures near or at freezing level. Strikes may also occur at temperatures as high as 25°C, or as low as -45°C.

Metal airplanes produce a phenomenon called Faraday Cage effect, which distributes electrical charges along the airframe in such a manner that occupants and internal components will not receive the high current that causes injury and damage. Internal components and systems have also special protections against side effects of the lightning strike.
Direct effects which result from a lightning strike may be:

pit marks often seen along the fuselage or holes in the trailing edge of wing and tail tips

melting of rivets

puncturing of nonmetallic structures

slight deformation of metal skins and structure

welding or roughening of moveable hinges and bearings

damage to other parts that may conduct lightning current other than the airframe, such as bonding or diverted straps and pitot tubes

Effects caused by the flash-induced electromagnetic field and the increase of the voltage due to the current at the airplane structure are defined as indirect effects and may be: interruption of instruments and navigation equipment

damage to electronic and electrical equipment popping of circuit breakers

loss of electrical power

engine flame-out

Report the lightning strike to maintenance.

kontext:
TILT FUNCTION

The inner knob on the CCD provides tilt control giving the pilot manual control of the antenna tilt angle. The CCD inner knob is a dedicated tilt knob if VAR Gain is not active. Tilt can be varied between 15 degrees up (clockwise rotation) and 15 degrees down (counterclockwise rotation).

Adjusts on tilt minimizes ground clutter when viewing weather targets.
To find the ideal tilt angle after the airplane is airborne, adjust the TILT control so that ground clutter does not interfere with viewing of weather targets.

Usually, this can be done by tilting the antenna downward in 1° increments until ground targets begin to appear at the display periphery. When ground targets are displayed, move the tilt angle upward in 1° increments

until the ground targets begin to disappear.

Ground returns can be distinguished from strong storm cells by watching for closer ground targets with each small downward increment of tilt. The more the downward tilt, the closer the ground targets that are displayed.

Proper tilt adjustment is a pilot judgment, but typically the best tilt angle lies where ground targets are barely visible or just off the radar image.

If either one or both ice detectors are failed, the crew must set the Ice Protection MODE Selector to ON when icing conditions exist or are anticipated at or below 10°C TAT with visible moisture.
Note: When flying in icing conditions, an increased level of awareness is necessary for any mistrim condition that may be masked by the autopilot.
Keep the airplane trimmed at all times.
Consider turning autopilot off if flying in severe icing conditions.

Engine Parameters MONITOR

Operation in icing conditions may result in ice accretion on the fan blades and spinner. During ice shedding procedure, ice is unevenly shed and fan unbalance may occur resulting in higher than normal vibration indication.
When ice shedding is complete, the fan vibration should return to a normal indication level for the associated engine.
Pitch Attitude and Airspeed MONITOR

CAUTION: Even small accumulations of ice on the wing leading edge may change the stall characteristics or the stall protection system

warning margin.
Use the green dot as the minimum airspeed. The green dot accounts for ice accretion (STALL PROT ICE SPEED message displayed on EICAS).

Note: Closely monitor the TAT indication and presence of moisture.

If environmental ice conditions exist, even intermittent, check the

windshield, windshield wiper (if installed) and wing surface for ice

accumulation. To visualize ice formation, if necessary, use a flashlight on the windshield and the wing inspection light on the wing.

If any ice formation is detected or suspected and the Ice Protection System was not automatically activated, select the Ice Protection MODE

Selector to ON. When flying in detected or suspected icing conditions, use ice speeds as reference.

kontext:
AUTO (AUTOMATIC MODE)

The automatic mode is designed to provide hands-off operation, with important information to avoid weather hazard in any phase of flight.
The system uses airplane altitude, intended flight path, and flight phase, to present weather relevant to the current flight conditions.
There is no need to fine-tune the tilt angle to find the weather or to separate the weather from the ground.

The key feature of the automatic weather mode is the discrimination of weather relevant to the intended airplane flight path, called "primary weather". The weather outside this area is called "secondary weather".
The MFD WEATHER window presents the word AUTO when the auto mode is selected.

8.3.2.42.6 Application of Wheel Brakes

The standard procedure is based on a normal touchdown (distance, speed, configuration) and recommended for dry, wet and contaminated runway conditions. The PF must decide whether immediate brake application is required for deceleration, or braking may be delayed compatible with:

available runway length after touchdown touchdown speed

aircraft gross mass

runway surface friction conditions

wind component

availability of reverse thrust

At beginning of brake application, the pilot calls out “braking”. Once initiated, depress the brake pedals until taxi speed is reached.

Continuous light application

of wheel brakes may result in unequal brake efficiency on individual wheels, causing wide temperature spreads across the landing gear assembly.

Do not

modulate braking by pumping pedals.
The increase in stopping distance on a slippery, wet or contaminated surface

should never be underestimated against dry concrete.

kontext:
8.3.8.8 Volcanic Ash Clouds

Flying through an ash cloud should be avoided by all means because of extreme hazard for the engines and the aircraft. Volcanic ash may extend for several hundred miles, and eruptions may send ash plumes up to 40 000 ft.
The weather radar can detect neither ash clouds nor volcanic dust.
If the aircraft enters an ash cloud the flight crew can expect: smoke, dust or acrid odors similar to electric sparks in the cockpit

at night heavy static discharges around the windshield

at night, St. Elmo fire or other static discharges accompanied by a bright orange glow in the engine inlets

engine surge or overheat

engine failure

unreliable airspeed indication

pressurization and electrical systems may be affected

When encountering ash cloud the following procedures are recommended: turn on continuous ignition

declare an emergency do not climb in order to over fly the ash cloud

reduce power to idle to provide additional engine stall margin and lower

turbine temperature

try to escape the ash cloud by descending and flying a 180° turn (if terrain clearance permits)

monitor attitude versus airspeed

keep as many engines running as possible

restart any engine, which was shut down due to EGT exceeding the limits; if an engine fails to restart repeated attempts should be made immediately to

avoid solidification of molten ash on the turbine blades,

turn on all accessory air bleeds including all air conditioning packs, nacelles,

and wing anti-ice; this will provide an additional engine stall margin by

reducing engine pressure

For additional procedures refer to the type specific OM-B.

Following an encounter with an ash cloud a landing at the next suitable airport is mandatory. If the visibility through the windshield is impaired a runway with auto land capability should be considered.

Flight crews are requested to make special air reports: when a volcanic eruption is observed, or when volcanic ash cloud is observed or encountered

Information on volcanic activities, including pre-eruption activity, volcanic eruption and volcanic ash clouds are transmitted to aircraft operating on routes that could be affected.
This information is also published by NOTAM and SIGMET up to a 12 hours validity period and, if necessary, recommendations on re-routings will be included.

kontext:
8.3.8.10.1 Procedures and Operational Considerations

An aerodrome shall not be used for flight planning, if during time of planned operation sandstorm (SS) and/or duststorm (DS) with visibility below 500 m and/or wind above 20 kts is reported in TAF/METAR.
When on the ground, airplanes shall ideally be kept under cover if dust storms are forecast or in progress. Alternatively, all engine blanks, cockpit covers and gloves for the various system and instrument intakes and probes shall be fitted.
These shall be carefully removed before flight to ensure that accumulations of dust are not deposited in the orifices which the covers are designed to protect.
For E-Jet refer to type specific OM-B 3.20 Sandstorm Operation.
Take-off into an active sandstorm is prohibited.
No flight shall intentionally be flown on instruments through an area of known or forecast sandstorm. Flying through an active sandstorm must be avoided by appropriate altitude selection or circumnavigation even if considerable detour or refueling en-route becomes necessary.
Mutual information on development of a sandstorm by pilots and ATC is of great importance for early and adequate avoidance of these severe weather areas. If it becomes evident, that it is impossible to avoid such an area, it is necessary to land at the next suitable airport.
If a landing in a sandstorm (SS) or dust storm (DS) is unavoidable (e.g. emergency), the following risks shall be taken into account: clogging of pitot tubes

electrical static e.g. unreliable NDB stations, difficulty with HF communication)

reduction of engine performance

visual illusions after changing over from instrument- to visual flying

landing lights should be used with care. Reflected light may reduce the

visibility and cause false impressions

reverse thrust may considerably reduce visibility

sand or dust covering the airport may reduce the ability to assess the RWY dimensions

the brake efficiency may be affected

Refueling during a sandstorm is strictly forbidden.

kontext:
2.8.3.9.2 In Flight Operations

Flight operation in volcanic ash are extremely hazardous and must be avoided.
However, volcanic ash/duct clouds may sometimes extend for hundreds of miles, reaching altitudes above 60000 ft and an encounter may be unavoidable.

In case of an inadvertent encounter, proceed as follows:
Volcanic Ash Area EXIT AVOID

Consider performing a 180° turn. Due to the dimensions of the ash clouds, a 180° turn could be the fastest way to exit an ash cloud.

Crew Oxygen Masks (if necessary) DON, 100% If a significant amount of volcanic ash fills the cockpit or if there is a strong smell or sulphur, don an oxygen mask and select 100%.
Ignition 1 and 2 Knobs Autothrottle DISENGAGE
The autothrottle must be kept disconnected to prevent thrust increase due to smart probes contamination.

2.8.3.8.3 Operational Procedures

2.8.3.8.3.1 Pre-Flight Inspection

Verify that no accumulation of sand exists in the engine inlets.
Use a lint-free cloth to remove any accumulated sand.

2.8.3.8.3.2 Power Up

If available, prefer using a GPU for the airplane power up.

Minimize thrust for crossbleed starts.

Apply thrust just high enough for adequate manifold pressure.

Consider location for minimum FOD ingestion prior to crossbleed start.

2.8.3.8.3.3 Taxi

Avoid engine overhanging unpaved surfaces.

If possible, leave engines at idle.

Minimize thrust assist from outboard engine in 180 deg turn, particularly if outboard engine overhangs unpaved surfaces.

Minimize breakaway thrust.
If possible, apply less than 40% N1.

Minimize taxi thrust.

Avoid allowing airplane to come to complete stop.

Avoid taxiing closely behind other airplane where FOD may be blown.

2.8.3.8.3.4 Takeoff

If possible, accomplish rolling takeoffs. Initial 30 KIAS taxi speed before

applying thrust eliminates vortices formed at typical takeoff thrust settings

Whenever possible, takeoff with FLAP 4

in order to reduce the airplane ground run and the engines sand/dust ingestion.

If allowed, extend the flaps shortly before initiating the takeoff procedure.

This will reduce sand/dust accumulation on the flap/ slat mechanisms.

Minimize breakaway thrust.

Use derated thrust settings whenever practical. This will help reduce the engines degradation.

2.8.3.8.3.5 In-Flight

Avoid airborne sand whenever possible.

Consider reducing thrust to maintain ITT as low as possible.

2.8.3.8.3.6 Landing And Taxiing

Avoid using reverser thrust on dry runways.

2.8.3.8.3.7 Engine Shutdown

If ground power is supplied to the airplane after engine shutdown, turn off an electrical equipment which is not required. This practice will reduce the heat generated unnecessarily and will substantially prolong the service life of the equipment.

2.8.3.8.3.8 After Shutdown

Install covers and shields.

Inspect for evidence of fluid leaks that might accumulate sand.

Clean the area appropriately and try to eliminate source of fluid leak.

During the inspection, wipe any detected bird remains from the airplane surfaces with detergent.

2.8.3.9.2 In Flight Operations

Flight operation in volcanic ash are extremely hazardous and must be avoided.
However, volcanic ash/duct clouds may sometimes extend for hundreds of miles, reaching altitudes above 60000 ft and an encounter may be unavoidable.
In case of an inadvertent encounter, proceed as follows:
Volcanic Ash Area EXIT AVOID Consider performing a 180° turn. Due to the dimensions of the ash clouds, a 180° turn could be the fastest way to exit an ash cloud.
Crew Oxygen Masks (if necessary) DON, 100% If a significant amount of volcanic ash fills the cockpit or if there is a strong smell or sulphur, don an oxygen mask and select 100%.
Ignition 1 and 2 Knobs Autothrottle DISENGAGE The autothrottle must be kept disconnected to prevent thrust increase due to smart probes contamination.
Ice Protection MODE Selector
This action will increase bleed air extraction from the engines and further improve the engine stall margin.

kontext: ITT MONITOR

SHUTDOWN the affected engine.

kontext:
2.5.1.2.3 Instrument Approaches

Approximately 50 NM before descent, pilots should perform the approach briefing.
It is recommended to set instruments before the briefing.
For items to be covered by the briefing, refer to OM-A 8.3.2.26 Approach Briefing.
Pilots must keep close attention to the altitude and speed restrictions according

to the charts. Some airports are provided with contingency and special procedures.
Based on the information available, like NOTAMs, weather reports, forecast, ATC reports, PIREPs, the crew should calculate the landing distance for the current conditions. Compare the calculated distance with the runway distance available.

If conditions change during descent and approach, the crew should consider recalculating the required landing distance. At pilot’s discretion, reassess the conditions and evaluate if a maximum performance landing should be considered.

Speeds are set according to the weight and flap selection, considering weather status (CAT II, ice conditions and so on).
On the FPL page, the waypoint altitude constraint during descent must be assigned as DES. The Constraint type is displayed directly above altitude constraints. The FMS automatically assigns constraints in the first half of the flight plan as climb (CLB). Those in the last half are assigned as descent (DES).

If necessary, the pilots can change the constraint type. For climb constraints, C and CLB are accepted pilot entries. For descent constraints, D or DES are accepted pilot entries.
Select the Autobrake according to runway conditions and type of operation. The

use of Thrust Reversers must be briefed to decide which taxiway is supposed to

be used to vacate the runway. Pilots must evaluate special runway conditions,

like slippery and contaminated. In case the crew plans to use additional speed

for the approach due to wind gusts on surface, the landing distance is increased.
It is necessary to discuss the outcome on the landing distance during the

approach briefing.

Airplane status and operational restrictions must be discussed during the briefing. If any failure that affects the required landing distance occurs in the final

approach, consider a missed approach. Evaluate the situation and the runway length available. Failures that affect the landing distance are commonly

associated to brakes, ground spoilers, and thrust reversers.

Perform an instrument crosscheck as soon as cleared by ATC to intercept the final approach course. Crosscheck radios and minimums for that specific approach. For far ILS captures, verify if intercepted course is in accordance with

the MARKERS indications and the PFD MAP display. If any discrepancy is

found, disengage the AP and take the appropriate corrective action.
Adjust the altimeter setting when passing Transition Level, or according to ATC.

the second part provides additional information

kontext:
App. 1   Configuration Deviation List (CDL)   App. 1.0-1
For dispatch with airframe or engine parts missing, refer to the
CONFIGURATION DEVIATION LIST [CDL] in this appendix.
For certain scenarios that result in increased fuel burn, the CDL contained in the
AFM only provides performance corrections through the Drag Index method. As
this method is not compatible with the flight planning system, it cannot be used
directly for dispatch planning purposes.
To address this limitation, the CDL from the DDPM (Dispatch Deviation
Procedures Manual) is published as an appendix to the SAMBA document. For
the aforementioned drag-inducing scenarios,

the DDPM CDL provides a
Simplified Method, which enables the calculation of both the additional fuel burn
and the associated performance penalties

.
The DDPM is linked to the MMEL and contains the detailed operational and
maintenance procedures required for the dispatch of an aircraft with inoperative
or missing items. The DDPM CDL will be incorporated into the MEL with the next
revision.

fragen.frage: Was ist die Ursache für FD VERT MODE OFF kurz vor oder nach dem Touchdown?
antworten: Ein Miscompare zwischen den beiden Glideslope Receivern in Pistennähe
Ein Ausfall des Radio Altimeter 2
Eine zu hohe Sinkrate unter 50 ft
Ein Wechsel der aktiven FMS-Seite beim Flare
fragen.erklaerung: Flugzeuge mit Autoland haben zwei Glideslope-Antennen im Radome. Nahe der Touchdown Zone steigt die Anfälligkeit für einen Miscompare zwischen den beiden Receivern. Wird einer erkannt, erscheint FD VERT MODE OFF.

fragen.frage_en: What causes FD VERT MODE OFF shortly before or after touchdown?
antworten_en: A miscompare between the two glideslope receivers close to the runway
A failure of radio altimeter 2
An excessive sink rate below 50 ft
A change of the active FMS page during the flare
fragen.erklaerung_en: Airplanes with autoland have two glideslope antennas in the radome. Close to the touchdown zone the susceptibility to a miscompare between both receivers increases. If a miscompare is detected, FD VERT MODE OFF is displayed.
kontext:
2.2.2 Additional Information
The airplanes equipped with Autoland system have two glideslope antennas
installed in the radome area, one on each side of the airplane. The received
glideslope signals are continuously monitored for miscompare detection.
When the airplane approaches the runway (close to the touchdown zone), it
increases the susceptibility to a miscompare between both glideslope receivers.
If a miscompare is detected, the message FD VERT MODE OFF is displayed

.
Although this behavior commonly occurs after touchdown, in some cases it is
possible to observe it also during flare just before main gear touchdown.
When this behavior is observed, the message disappears after a few seconds
and no crew or maintenance action is required.
A future PRIMUS Epic software version is under development to address this
issue.

fragen.frage_en: After landing BRK OVERHEAT is displayed. For how many flight cycles can the crew enable dispatch with the SAMBA procedure?
antworten_en: Up to 10 flight cycles
Up to 3 flight cycles
Until the next A-check

kontext:
2.6.1 Procedure
This procedure may be performed when the CAS message BRK OVERHEAT
appears after landing to allow airplane dispatch, providing the flight crew with the
necessary actions to verify the wheels and

authorize dispatch for up to 10 flight
cycles

.
1. Apply the parking brake to secure the airplane in place.
2. Inform ground crew that brakes are hot, instruct to keep clear, and delay
chock installation if not in place yet.
3. Wait until the BRK OVERHEAT message disappears. With the CAS
message no longer displayed, the wheel chock can be safely positioned
against landing gear wheels if not already in place, and parking brake can
be released to allow faster cooling of the brake.
WARNING: CAREFULLY APPROACH THE LANDING GEAR ASSEMBLY AT A
DISTANCE JUST ENOUGH TO SAFELY POSITION THE WHEELS
CHOCKS. ONLY GET NEAR THE FRONT OR THE BACK OF THE
TIRE. IF YOU DO NOT OBEY THIS PRECAUTION, INJURY TO
PERSONS CAN OCCUR.
4. After brake temperature indications are GREEN, examine the wheel/tire
assemblies for flat tire.
5. If no flat tire is found, report to MCC to initiate the required documentation
and monitoring process for the next 10 flight cycles, then proceed with flight
preparations.

fragen.frage: Ab welcher Bremstemperatur am Boden erscheint BRK OVERHEAT, und welches Risiko besteht dabei?
antworten: Ab 650 °C, der Reifen könnte sofort platzen
Ab 450 °C, die Hydraulikleitungen könnten lecken
Ab mindestens 520 °C, die Fuse Plugs der Räder könnten schmelzen
Ab 300 °C, die Bremsscheiben könnten sich verziehen
fragen.erklaerung: BRK OVERHEAT erscheint, wenn ein Brake Temperature Sensor am Boden mindestens 520 °C erreicht. Dann können die Räder heiss genug sein, dass die Fuse Plugs schmelzen.
fragen.zitat: reaches at least 520°C on ground
fragen.frage_en: From which brake temperature on ground is BRK OVERHEAT displayed, and what is the risk?
antworten_en: From 650 °C, the tire may burst immediately
From 450 °C, the hydraulic lines may leak
From at least 520 °C, the wheel fuse plugs may melt
From 300 °C, the brake discs may warp
fragen.erklaerung_en: BRK OVERHEAT is displayed when a brake temperature sensor reaches at least 520 °C on ground. The wheel temperatures may then be high enough to melt the wheel fuse plugs.
kontext:
2.6.2 Additional Information
The BRK OVERHEAT message can be displayed on EICAS if the brake
temperature sensor in any of the four brake assemblies

reaches at least 520°C
on ground

. This temperature means that the wheel temperatures may be high
enough to cause the wheel fuse plugs to melt. The message remains displayed
as long as this temperature scenario persists.
Embraer received field reports about the BRK OVERHEAT message being
shown with no effect to the fuse plugs and tire condition. In such cases the AMM
describes the necessary inspections to authorize a dispatch of 10 flight cycles
(FC) until further inspections are required. This initial assessment to authorize a
dispatch is normally performed by maintenance personnel but may also be
performed by flight crew as described in this document.

fragen.frage: Welche Kombination führt zum Fuel Leak aus dem RH Wing Tank Vent NACA?
antworten: Volle Tanks beim Takeoff und ein Steilkurvenflug
Cruise über FL370 mit Wing Anti-Ice ON
OBIGGS im High Flow Mode im Descent und Turbulenz, die das Wing Float Vent Valve schliesst
Ein defektes Refuel Valve und hohe OAT
fragen.erklaerung: Im Descent arbeitet das OBIGGS im High Flow Mode und erhöht den Druck im Tank. Schliesst Turbulenz das Wing Float Vent Valve, drückt der Überdruck die Dichtung gegen die Rippe, und Fuel wird über den Ventilationskanal und die NACA nach aussen gedrückt.
fragen.zitat: When the airplane is under turbulence, acceleration variations can cause the wing float vent valve to temporarily close
fragen.frage_en: Which combination leads to the fuel leak from the RH wing tank vent NACA?
antworten_en: Full tanks at takeoff and a steep turn
Cruise above FL370 with wing anti-ice ON
OBIGGS in high flow mode during descent and turbulence closing the wing float vent valve
A defective refuel valve and high OAT
fragen.erklaerung_en: During descent the OBIGGS operates in high flow mode and increases the tank pressure. If turbulence closes the wing float vent valve, the pressure pushes the seal against the rib and fuel is pushed through the ventilation duct and out of the NACA.
kontext:
3.1.2 Additional Information
It was reported by an operator the occurrence of fuel leak of approximately 300
kg of fuel from the RH wing tank vent NACA, preceded by a moderate
turbulence. The fuel leak has resulted in fuel imbalance, and the EICAS
message FUEL IMBALANCE was displayed. The flight crew has declared
emergency, has accomplished the associated procedure and landed safely.
The On-Board Inert Gas Generation System (OBIGGS) was operating in high
flow mode, which is its normal condition during descent. The event occurred
during this flight phase, from 23000 ft to 5000 ft and it lasted approximately 7
minutes.
The wing tank ventilation is achieved by a wing float vent valve located in the
interface between the surge tank and wing tank and by a ventilation duct on the
innermost part of the wing tank (see figure 1).
The OBIGGS receives air from bleed system through the Air Preparation System
and flows enriched nitrogen air into the fuel tanks, minimizing the fuel tank
flammability during normal flight and ground operation.
During descent, after the TOD (Top of Descent), the OBIGGS starts to operate in
high flow mode, and significantly increases the amount of inert gas injection into
the fuel tank.
As the ambient pressure increases in this flight phase, the OBIGGS in high flow
mode prevents oxygen air flow from entering in the tank.

When the airplane is under turbulence, acceleration variations can cause the
wing float vent valve to temporarily close

, as illustrated in figure 2.
While the descent has initiated and the OBIGGS is in high flow mode, increasing
the pressure inside the wing tank, if turbulence closes the float vent valve, the
increased pressure inside the tank pushes the valve seal against the rib surface,
preventing it from reopening.
Depending on the fuel quantity in the wing tank, the increased pressure may
push a certain fuel amount through the ventilation duct until the duct is no longer
submerged and pressure is equalized with the surge tank.
In this scenario, the pushed fuel amount flows overboard through the wing tank
vent NACA (figure 3).
When the pressure is equalized the fuel leak stops and the wing float vent valve
reopens (figure 4).
Between 1850 kg and 1100 kg, and the OBIGGS is in high flow mode.
The fuel leak stops when the each wing tank reaches around 1100~1350 kg,
since the ventilation duct would not be submerged and the air passes through
the duct.
After crossing 4000 ft AGL or after landing gear extension, the OBBIGS returns
to normal flow mode and the event will not occur. The pressure inside the wing
tank when the OBIGGS is in normal flow mode is not enough to keep the wing
float vent valve closed in the referred scenario. The event is not likely to occur in
the left wing tank, as the left wing surge tank is connected to the center tank
through a fuel return duct.

fragen.frage: Bei welcher Fuel-Menge im Wing Tank stoppt der Leak von selbst?

Bei etwa 500 kg pro Wing Tank
Bei etwa 1100 bis 1350 kg pro Wing Tank
Erst wenn der Tank leer ist
fragen.erklaerung: Der Leak stoppt bei etwa 1100 bis 1350 kg pro Wing Tank, weil der Ventilationskanal dann nicht mehr unter Fuel liegt und Luft durchströmt.
fragen.zitat: The fuel leak stops when the each wing tank reaches around 1100~1350 kg
fragen.frage_en: At which fuel quantity in the wing tank does the leak stop by itself?

At around 1100 to 1350 kg per wing tank
Only when the tank is empty

From top of descent
As soon as the turbulence stops
From FL250 downwards

3.2.1 Procedure
RA flags or a miscompare of readouts between RA 1 und RA 2 may be observed
at the parking stand.
Usually, the abnormal condition will disappear latest after all ground equipment
has been removed. In some occasions the failure disappears after leaving the
parking position.
If the RA flag persists before take-off, perform standard abnormal procedures.
After power up,

a warmup period of a minimum of five minutes is required to
obtain reliable RA readouts
in any case.

fragen.frage_en: At the stand, an RA shows a flag or a miscompare. What is the typical cause?
antworten_en: Multipath from reflections off buildings, vehicles and objects below the antennas
A software fault in the FMS
Moisture in the pitot lines
An incorrectly set minimums selection
fragen.erklaerung_en: On ground the RA can be disturbed by the multipath effect, i.e. strong signals reflected from buildings and vehicles. A clean area of 5.0 m radius below the antennas is needed.
kontext:
3.2.2 Additional Information
While on ground, the radio altimeters operation might be disturbed by the
“multipath” effect, due to the strong signals reflected from buildings and vehicles.
To guarantee that the radio altimeter system operates properly,

it is necessary to
have a clean area of 5.0 m radius below the radio altimeter antennas

and to
make sure that the aircraft is far from buildings or other structures. Objects such
as tools, tool carts/boxes, stairs, drainage grates, metal covers on the ground,
etc. or structures near the radio altimeter antennas can disturb radio altitude
readouts.

fragen.frage: Die RA Flag besteht nach dem Wegfahren vom Stand immer noch bis vor den Takeoff. Was gilt?
antworten: Trotzdem starten, das Problem löst sich in der Luft
Den RA im MCDU deselektieren und starten
Die Standard Abnormal Procedures anwenden
Einen RA-Reset über die MAU durchführen
fragen.erklaerung: Meist verschwindet die Störung, sobald das Ground Equipment weg ist oder nach dem Wegfahren. Besteht die RA Flag vor dem Takeoff weiter, werden die Standard Abnormal Procedures angewendet.

fragen.frage_en: The RA flag still persists after leaving the stand until before takeoff. What applies?
antworten_en: Take off anyway, the problem resolves in the air
Deselect the RA in the MCDU and take off
Perform the standard abnormal procedures
Reset the RA via the MAU
fragen.erklaerung_en: Usually the condition disappears once ground equipment has been removed or after leaving the parking position. If the RA flag persists before takeoff, the standard abnormal procedures are performed.
kontext:
3.2.1 Procedure
RA flags or a miscompare of readouts between RA 1 und RA 2 may be observed
at the parking stand.
Usually, the abnormal condition will disappear latest after all ground equipment
has been removed. In some occasions the failure disappears after leaving the
parking position.
If the RA flag persists before take-off, perform standard abnormal procedures

.
After power up, a warmup period of a minimum of five minutes is required to
obtain reliable RA readouts in any case.

fragen.frage: Welche Einträge müssen bei Nutzung des Secondary Flight Plan gelöscht werden, um FMS-Resets zu verhindern?

Die Alternate im Active Flight Plan

When using the Secondary Flight Plan function, the following entries shall be

TO/GA, flaps 5, gear UP, 180 kt, VS +1000 ft/min

TO/GA, flaps 4, positive rate gear UP, manual 150 kt, at 150 kt FLCH, HDG
fragen.erklaerung_en: Without FMS speeds the airplane does not accelerate to Vref+20 / Vac after TO/GA. Therefore: TO/GA (initial pitch 8°), flaps 4, positive rate gear UP, manual speed 150 kt, at 150 kt FLCH, HDG. After level-off the climb sequence with manual speed bug.
kontext:
3.3.1.2 Procedure for FMS-Reset during Approach
(Flaps FULL on final approach)
Continuation of Approach
select Manual Speed
engage AT
verify or select “green” FGCS-modes
continue approach normally using manual speeds
Discontinued Approach
follow standard Discontinued Approach Procedure using “green” FGCS-
modes
Go-Around
Follow the standard Go-Around procedure considering the following peculiarities:
Since the FMS speeds are not available, the aircraft will not accelerate to
Vref+20 / Vac after pressing the TO/GA Button. Therefore, the following
sequence should be followed:
push TO/GA button
(in GA mode the aircraft will pitch to 8° initially)

set Flaps 4
positive rate → Gear - UP
set manual speed 150 kt
at 150 kt → select FLCH
select HDG
after level-off → perform climb sequence and set speed bug manually to
accelerate to appropriate speed
Note: For approaches with Flaps 5, use Flaps 2 and speed 160 kt during go-
around.
ATL-Entry
Perform an ATL Entry describing the event.
If a reset was possible, enter N/A on the action side.
Note: This entry helps to track further occurrences.

Das FMS über die MAU zurücksetzen
VAP um 1 oder 2 kt erhöhen

Re-enter the complete Perf Init
Reset the FMS via the MAU
Increase the VAP by 1 or 2 kt

To recover the performance predictions,

change the VAP adding 1 or 2 knots to

Nur vom Landing Weight
Von der Kombination aus VAP, ISA-Abweichung und Missed Approach Altitude
Von der Anzahl Waypoints in der STAR
fragen.erklaerung: Das Verhalten hängt von der Kombination aus eingegebener VAP, ISA-Abweichung und Missed Approach Altitude ab. Deshalb lassen sich keine bestimmten Speeds definieren, und eine erneute Perf-Eingabe hilft nicht immer.
fragen.zitat: This behaviour depends on the combination of the VAP inserted, ISA deviation, and missed approach altitude
fragen.frage_en: What does the loss of FMS predictions after VAP insertion depend on?
antworten_en: The selected cost index
Only the landing weight
The combination of VAP, ISA deviation and missed approach altitude
The number of waypoints in the STAR
fragen.erklaerung_en: The behaviour depends on the combination of the VAP inserted, ISA deviation and missed approach altitude. Specific speeds therefore cannot be defined, and re-inserting the perf data may not help.
kontext:
3.4.2 Additional Information
Embraer has received field reports stating that the vertical flight plan and the
performance data disappeared in different phases of flight.
The investigations show that if certain values for the landing approach speed
(VAP from the landing page) are inserted and landing speeds are activated, the
FMS predictions may be lost (refer to Figure 1 and Figure 2).

This behaviour depends on the combination of the VAP inserted, ISA deviation,
and missed approach altitude

.
Therefore, specific speeds at which this occurs cannot be defined. Moreover, re-
inserting the perf data may not recover the lost information.

VAP insertion   lost
Reference: FOL 190E2-002/23

Reset von FMS 1 über das MCDU
Reset von MAU 2 und MAU 3
Neuladen der Nav Database

pilots should perform the reset of MAU 2 and

. This procedure allows the FMS to clear the display and allows the entry

fragen.frage: Welcher typische Fehler passiert bei der CPDLC Message „CLEARED TO [position] VIA [route clearance]“ (UM79)?
antworten: Die Crew ignoriert die Höhenangabe der Clearance
Die Crew antwortet mit UNABLE statt WILCO
Die Crew lädt die Route doppelt
Die Crew fliegt DIRECT TO zur letzten Position statt die Route mit LOAD zu laden
fragen.erklaerung: In den meisten Fällen wählen Crews manuell DIRECT TO zur letzten freigegebenen Position, statt mit dem LOAD Prompt die ganze neue Route ins FMS zu laden. So wird eine falsche Route geflogen.
fragen.zitat: the crews are manually selecting DIRECT TO the last cleared position, instead of using the LOAD prompt
fragen.frage_en: Which typical mistake happens with the CPDLC message "CLEARED TO [position] VIA [route clearance]" (UM79)?
antworten_en: The crew ignores the altitude in the clearance
The crew responds UNABLE instead of WILCO
The crew loads the route twice
The crew flies DIRECT TO the last position instead of loading the route with LOAD
fragen.erklaerung_en: In most cases crews manually select DIRECT TO the last cleared position instead of using the LOAD prompt that would load the entire new route into the FMS. An incorrect route is then flown.
kontext:
3.6.2 Additional Information
Embraer received reports from the authorities regarding a common
misinterpretation of the CPDLC message “CLEARED TO [position] VIA [route
clearance]” - uplink message UM79 - in which pilots are incorrectly loading the
route messages causing operational impact due to flying the incorrect route.
In most cases,

the crews are manually selecting DIRECT TO the last cleared
position, instead of using the LOAD prompt

that would load the entire new route
into the FMS.
The “CLEARED TO [position] VIA [route clearance]” is an uplink message sent
by ATC and is expected that the pilot follows the new route informed by the ATC
instead of the current route in the flight plan.
Refer to Figure 1 for an example of this message:
Figure 1: ATC Uplink Message
This message aims to inform pilots that the flight must continue to OSN through
a designated route: CLEARED TO OSN VIA ROUTE CLEARANCE (X) and (Y).
Refer to Figure 2.
Figure 2: Modified flight plan
Reference: FOL 190E2-002/24

fragen.frage: Auf ATC UPLINK Seite 1/2 steht --CONTINUED--. Was bedeutet das?
antworten: Die Route wurde bereits automatisch ins FMS geladen
Die Message ist nicht vollständig, mit NEXT und ATC CLNC die revidierte Route ansehen
Die Message ist abgelaufen und muss neu angefordert werden
ATC wird die Route später in einer separaten Message schicken
fragen.erklaerung: --CONTINUED-- zeigt, dass die Message nicht vollständig ist. Mit NEXT und dann ATC CLNC auf Seite 2/2 sieht man die revidierte Route.
fragen.zitat: The --CONTINUED-- prompt on ATC UPLINK page 1/2 indicates that the message is not completed
fragen.frage_en: ATC UPLINK page 1/2 shows --CONTINUED--. What does this mean?
antworten_en: The route has already been loaded into the FMS automatically
The message is not complete, use NEXT and ATC CLNC to view the revised route
The message has expired and must be requested again
ATC will send the route later in a separate message
fragen.erklaerung_en: --CONTINUED-- indicates that the message is not complete. Push NEXT and then ATC CLNC on page 2/2 to view the revised route.
kontext:
3.6.1 Procedure
When the CPDLC message “CLEARED TO [position] VIA ROUTE CLEARANCE”
is received, the pilot should review all pages of the message on the ATC
CLEARENCE pages.

The --CONTINUED-- prompt on ATC UPLINK page 1/2 indicates that the
message is not completed

. Push NEXT and then ATC CLNC on the ATC
UPLINK page 2/2 to view the revised ROUTE as per Figure 3.
Figure 3: ATC Uplink pages
In the example above, the revised routing is the same that is referenced by VIA
ROUTE CLEARANCE on page 1 of the message.
Then, the clearance should be loaded into the FMS and reviewed (in a modified
state) before accepting the clearance. This action is done by pushing the APPLY
(LSK 2R) on the ATC UPLINK 2/2 page to create the modified flight plan. See
Figure 4:
Figure 4: Uplink Message Load on the FMS
After loading and activating the uplinked message on the FMS, the pilot should
return to the ATC UPLINK page 2/2 and push the ACCEPT on LSK 1R to accept
the clearance and include a WILCO in the response to the ATC. See Figure 5.
Figure 5: Wilco Response to the ATC
The flight crew should respond to the clearance with REJECT when:
the FMS indicates its incapacity to load the clearance such as being unable
to load it entirely or only partially, and the flight crew was unable to resolve
the clearance
or
the FMS highlights any inconsistencies or discontinuities with the route
modification that are not addressed by AIP (or appropriate publication) or
cannot be resolved by the flight crew.
Note: The FMS checks the clearance to ensure it is correctly formatted
and compatible with the FMS navigation database.
A discontinuity resulting from the loading of a CPDLC route clearance is not
necessarily a reason to respond to the clearance with REJECT, as these can be
appropriate in some circumstances.
For further details about the functionality, refer to Example 8 of “Honeywell’s
ATN CPDLC for Embraer E-Jets NGFMS” familiarization guide.
